# Decisions

- The terminal's first draw, and every draw after a resize, compares the new frame against blank cells (`Buffer::blank_diff_iter`, `BlankDiff`) instead of against a previous buffer it had just allocated and cleared, so the first frame allocates one screen buffer, not two (2026-11-14, Nanocode 1.0 CLI track: first frame toward 1.3 ms). A stale draw already clears every line, so a cell left blank (a space with default colours and no modifiers) needs no output; `BlankDiff` tests those fields directly rather than calling `Cell::eq`, because a second caller made `Cell::eq` stop being inlined and slowed the steady state by 3.5 to 6% in the first version. `TerminalSession::draw` marks the frame stale when the area differs from the previous frame's, reuses the current buffer when its area matches and allocates it otherwise; the frame encoding moved, unchanged, into `Frame::encode` so both diffs share it. Master to this change: first frame at 240x70 user instructions 2,467,629 to 1,666,934 (-32.4%), page faults 698 to 565; at 80x24 1,111,200 to 1,018,172 (-8.4%), faults 462 to 440; 60 frames at 240x70 95.98M to 95.17M (-0.8%), at 80x24 32.547M to 32.561M (+0.04%). Measured with the TUI crate's output/tuirender harness (dist profile, a pty at the given size, `perf stat -e instructions:u,instructions:k,page-faults`, 5 interleaved rounds, medians, on the hosted Hand); the bytes written for 1 and 60 frames at 80x24 and 240x70 have equal MD5s across master and all three changes. nanocode-ts does not use nanocode-tui. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-tui --no-deps -- -D warnings`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tui --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, rustfmt on the changed lines (crates/tui already has six unformatted spots on master, left as they are). Files: crates/tui/src/terminal.rs, crates/tui/src/ui/buffer.rs.
- fix(code-mode): a nested call a script makes reaches its tool before the cell drops it at the script's end, also while the cell journal is still writing the call's Running entry, so an unawaited call is started and then abandoned as on a host whose journal writes at once (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: unawaited calls). `journaled_call` (code_mode/mod.rs) persists a call's Running entry before it runs the tool, so that recovery reads an unknown outcome instead of running it twice. When the script ended (`RuntimeEvent::Done` or `Error`) while such a write was in flight, `drive_cell` returned and dropped the call before its tool ran, yet the cell reported it to the observer as started (NestedCallStarted with no completion) and to the model as "Nested calls that had not returned when the script ended without awaiting them were abandoned: 1 slow. Whether each took effect is unknown." A sink that answers at once (the cm-conf native-host runner's in-memory CellJournalSink) hid it; nanocode-ts's SQL journal, whose writes cross the host bridge, showed it: `tools.slow({}); text("main")` never invoked slow, and of three unawaited calls only the first could run. `drive_cell` now counts the calls whose journal write is pending and, when the script ends, polls the pending calls and the cell's journal flush (which holds the same lock) until each call has started, then drops them as before; a call that finishes in that moment is abandoned like the others. Cell end already waits on that lock in `mark_finished`, so the journal adds no new wait, and a sink that answers at once never waits. Conformance with output/cm-conf (git-ignored; nanocode-ts cm/ts-unawaited, whose host also starts a tool call cancelled before it began, see its DECISIONS.md): async/unawaited-call-abandoned-notice, output/exit-with-unawaited-call and tools/unawaited-calls-counted-by-name fail on ts-node and ts-workerd for both backends before (0 of 1, 0 of 1 and 0 of 3 tool calls) and pass after; with this change and not the host's, they still fail (the call starts in the poll that drops it, and the host skips it); native-host is unchanged, every case it runs passing before and after (1,192 of 1,192 runs, both backends; with the in-memory sink the new wait never waits). Commands: `cargo build --release --bin run` in output/cm-conf/native and `run --cases 'output/cm-conf/cases/*.jsonl' --backend both` with this commit and its parent; `NANOCODE_TS=… NANOCODE_WASM_PATH=… node output/cm-conf/ts/run.ts --backend both` and `node output/cm-conf/workerd/run.ts --backend both` with the module built from each: ts-node 1,225 to 1,231 passing runs of 1,245 and ts-workerd 1,134 to 1,187 of 1,202, which also count the suite's runner changes (the workerd runner records its model, the scripted model answers a Codex compaction request); the one pass to fail, durability/timer-due-during-downtime on ts-node Claude, calls no tool and printed fired false (its 300 ms timer measured under 300 ms by Date.now on the loaded machine), and passes on rerun with either module. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode --no-deps -- -D warnings` pass natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs.

- fix(agent): nanocode-agent builds for wasm32 on its own: it turns on nanocode-code-mode's `local-cells` for wasm targets (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: ts-replay). `OneLog` is the cell journal sink every turn-log host uses (`OneLogJournals`, `OneLog::journals`, read back in `cells`), so crates/runtime/agent/src/one_log.rs imports `CellJournal`, `CellJournalSink`, `CellJournalUpdate`, `CellJournals`, `JournalEntry` and `JournaledCallState` from `nanocode_tool_host::code_mode`. On wasm32 that module is the remote-only stub unless nanocode-code-mode's `local-cells` is on, and only the `nanocode` crate turned it on, so `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` failed on master with E0432 on one_log.rs:11 (earlier entries worked around it with `-p nanocode-code-mode --features nanocode-code-mode/local-cells`). nanocode-ts, the wasm host of this turn log, built only because its `nanocode` dependency has default features. crates/runtime/agent/Cargo.toml now has `[target.'cfg(target_family = "wasm")'.dependencies] nanocode-code-mode = { workspace = true, features = ["local-cells"] }`; nanocode-code-mode was already in nanocode-agent's graph through nanocode-tool-host, so Cargo.lock adds only that edge and no package. Native builds are unchanged (the full `code_mode` module is always there off wasm). Consequence: any wasm build that links nanocode-agent (every `nanocode` build) carries the cell engine, as every known one (nanocode-ts) already did; gating the journal code on a nanocode-agent feature would have added a Cargo feature, which AGENTS.md rules out. nanocode-ts's own Cargo.lock gains the same edge when it next moves its pin. Checks: `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (before: E0432 on wasm32), `cargo clippy --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent --no-deps -- -D warnings` on both targets, `cargo fmt -p nanocode-agent -- --check`. Files: crates/runtime/agent/Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock.

- feat(claude-client): `ClaudeClient` shares one `admission::Admission` across every clone, so a session and all of its subagents send model requests through one AIMD window that honors `retry-after` (2026-11-14). `ClaudeClient::post` takes a `Permit` before `post_admitted` sends: the window starts open, the first 429 or 529 of an epoch halves it to half the requests in flight, every accepted request at a full window grows it by 1/window, and a `retry-after` closes admission for every clone until it passes. Before this, each agent retried a 429 on its own clock, so 2,000 subagents kept hitting a rate-limited provider with 10 rejected attempts per accepted call, exhausted their throttled retries and lost about half the children. A permit is taken before the request is sent and released at the response headers, so no dispatched request is held or replayed. State is one `nanocode_sync::Atom` with a `Notify` for waiters (lock-free, native and wasm32). Measurement: output/ratelimit-bench (in-process mock Claude transport with a token bucket of 50 requests/s, 50 ms latency, retry-after 1, jsonl store, 2,000 subagents spawned in batches of 100, 4 tokio workers, 300 s limit) on master 22f8297d9, interleaved: before saturation 0.143, wasted attempts per accepted call 10.59, 990 of 2,000 children done in 300 s, peak in flight 223; after saturation 0.965, wasted 0.105, 2,000 of 2,000 done in 83.1 s, peak in flight 100. The same pair on 62a0936e4: before 0.182 / 7.67 / 1,287 done and 0.243 / 5.08 / 1,711 done, after 0.968 / 0.096 / 2,000 done in 82.8 s. Checks: cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -- -D warnings; cargo +1.97.1 check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client --target wasm32-unknown-unknown. Downstream: nanocode-ts picks it up with the sdk-revision bump; with remoteSubagents each child Durable Object has its own client, so the window is per child there.

- fix(codex): a Codex session's Code Mode contract leaves out the Claude-shaped tools a hand advertises (Bash, Read, Edit, Write, TaskOutput, TaskStop), so gpt-6-luna writes its edits with apply_patch and runs commands with exec_command as upstream Codex does; and Claude's Read shows a BMP or PNM image as PNG instead of failing (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 Codex parity: make-mips-interpreter, prove-plus-comm). A hand built by nanocode::hand::tools advertises both families (apply_patch, exec_command, view_image, write_stdin, Read, Edit, Write, Bash, TaskStop) and nanocode-ts opens sessions without hand_tools, so a Codex session's exec description declared Claude's tools beside Codex's. Across the 87 nanox (codex:gpt-6-luna:high, Code Mode) attempts in ~/nc-live/report.json, 1,904 exec calls, 38 cells failed to parse, and the nested tool named in each: Edit 18 of 168 cells (10.7%; 13 of them the same slip, `"old_string","new_string:"..."`, a key with its colon inside the quotes), Bash 10 of 745, exec_command 4 of 413, web__run 3 of 36, Write 1 of 78, Read 0 of 294 and apply_patch 0 of 75, whose one argument is a string. Each such cell costs a model turn (473d0b90 a00001: 7). Upstream Codex has no Edit, Read, Write or Bash: its code mode nests the model's own tools (exec_command, write_stdin, apply_patch, view_image, update_plan). New `CodeModeToolPolicy::hidden_host_tool` (default false); the Codex standard policy answers true for those six names, and `EmbeddedToolRuntime` drops host definitions a session's policy hides from the model contract and from `contains` (so a direct call to one is refused), never the session's own local tools. Only host (hand) definitions are filtered and only in the embedded runtime, where each session's Tools carry its own backend's policy (nanocode-ts selects claude or codex workspace tools per provider); the native registry is left alone because a hand's own Tools carry both policies. The hand still runs a hidden tool if a cell names it (it gets no selected_tools from this); an explicit nanocode-ts hand_tools policy still narrows further. Claude sessions are unchanged. Read: Claude Code 2.1.300's binary-extension list refused `.bmp` and the image path refused any format but PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP; both failed the call, which rejects the cell's Promise.all and abandons its other calls (473d0b90 a00003: `Promise.all([tools.Bash(...), tools.Read({file_path:"/tmp/frame.bmp"})])` failed with "unsupported image format" and the Bash call ended "outcome unknown"). nanocode-image already decodes BMP and PNM, so a new cross-target module, nanocode-backend-claude-tools tools/image.rs (`media_type`, `decode`, with media.rs's decode limits; nanocode-image becomes a dependency on every target), lets `media::image_block` (machine and confined files, which hands use) and the host file tool's `read_image` (wasm hosts, now also for the .bmp extension) decode them and send PNG, the same thing Codex's view_image does with them; `.bmp` leaves BINARY_EXTENSIONS. Checked with output/a27-new and output/a27-base (the same harness on this change and on 8aecea52b): hidden builds the Codex `tool_runtime` over a mock code-only hand that publishes the real hand catalog and lists what the exec description declares: before, Bash, Read, Edit, Write, TaskStop, exec_command, write_stdin, apply_patch, view_image; after, exec_command, write_stdin, apply_patch, view_image, while the same runtime without the Codex policy still declares all nine. bmp runs `Promise.all([tools.Read({file_path: 'frame.bmp'}), tools.Read({file_path: 'note.txt'})])` in LocalCells over the hand's tools with a 320x200 24-bit BMP: before, the script fails with the binary-file error and abandons the other Read; after, it completes with the text and a data:image/png result. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools`, natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, clippy on the same crates, `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 200 8` and the same with `--scenario runtime`. Release note: the contract change is brain-side (nanocode-ts must pin this commit; hands need nothing new), the Read change is hand-side (the nanocode CLI that serves hands must be rebuilt).
- A signal trap nests at most `max_depth` deep (2026-11-14). Since 67d612220 a signal that arrives while its own trap runs runs the trap again, nested; a PIPE trap that writes to the pipe that raised it (`{ trap 'echo t >&2' PIPE; ...; } 2>&1 | head -c 1`) raised PIPE again without end, and psh overflowed its stack (the native binary aborted, the WebAssembly module stopped with `Maximum call stack size exceeded`). bash 5.2 recurses the same way and dies of SIGSEGV. Each nested signal trap now counts as a level of the subshell and function limit (ShellConfig::max_depth, D1050); past it the trap does not run, and `trap: SIGPIPE: maximum nesting level exceeded (N)` is printed. A trap that nests to a bounded depth (signals/2 and 3, 20 deep) runs as before. psh-spec unchanged (brush 3005, oils 2418). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/trap.rs.
- fix(claude): with a Code Mode host, the Claude environment's primary working directory is the working directory of the hand where scripts run, not the brain's placeholder workspace (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 nano against Claude Code: kv-store-grpc 58 s against 29 s, sam-cell-seg, make-mips-interpreter). nanocode-ts builds the runtime with `.workspace("/")`, so every nano attempt's run.started reports `"workspace":"/"` and the system prompt's environment says "Primary working directory: /" while the slot's hand runs in /app (nanoeval's DECISIONS records the model looking for its files in /tmp before running pwd); Claude Code's environment says /app. The model then spends its first model call on `tools.hands()` and ALL_TOOLS to find where it is: kv-store-grpc a00019, make-mips-interpreter a00143, sam-cell-seg a00251 and feal-linear-cryptanalysis a00073 all open that way (2.3 to 4.8 s and one model call each), Claude Code never does. This is the Claude side of 5667dc4c7: `Tools::hand_working_directory(session_id)` asks the Code Mode host (`CodeModeHost::working_directory`, the hand the session's placement resolves to), and the Claude runtime, when its tools have a Code Mode host, gives the agent a workspace resolver that answers it and falls back to the configured workspace when scripts run locally or no hand is attached yet. The resolved directory reaches the environment section (computed at the session's first request), run.started and durable children's workspace. Checked with output/refusal-recovery/cwd.py and cwd-alongside.py (nanocode exec --runner-connect against nanocode hand --listen --cd DIR, debug builds of origin/master and of this change): `--runner-mode replace` names the hand's directory before and after (the CLI already configures it), alongside names the brain's directory before and after (scripts run locally, so the resolver falls back). `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-backend-claude`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, passed. Not run: a nanocode-ts rebuild and nanoeval rerun, which is where the change shows. Files: crates/runtime/tool-host/src/selection.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/runtime.rs.

- fix(claude): a response that Claude's safety classifier stops (stop_reason refusal) is asked again once per turn, as Claude Code 2.1.318 does, instead of ending the turn (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 feal-linear-cryptanalysis: nano 0/2 against Claude Code's 1/1). Both nano attempts (nanoeval 8999a51d a00082, ec71aa6d a00073) read feal.c in their first cell and their second model call ended with stop_reason refusal after 801 output tokens; nanocode failed the turn with "provider refused the request (stop_reason=refusal); turn stopped" 14 s in, while Claude Code on the same row (8999a51d a00083) wrote the attack in its second call and passed. What Claude Code does, measured with the official 2.1.318 linux-x64 binary (`-p --output-format stream-json --dangerously-skip-permissions --model claude-opus-5-5 --effort high`, as nanoeval runs it) against a scripted Messages endpoint that ends chosen responses with refusal (output/refusal-recovery/stub.py): when the refused response has finished blocks it sends the next request with them as the assistant message (text, signed thinking, and finished tool_use blocks, each answered with an is_error result "Interrupted: …", since it runs tools while the response streams) followed by the user text "Your response above was stopped by a safety classifier — this is not a tool or API error. The rest of it was withheld, and tool calls in it that had not finished did not run. Do not produce that content again, even reworded." (with an "Exception: …" sentence only when a tool call was interrupted); unfinished blocks (a text or thinking block without content_block_stop) are dropped, and when nothing finished it sends the same request again. Once per turn: refuse,ok and refuse:empty,ok go on (2 requests); refuse,refuse; refuse:empty,refuse; refuse,refuse:empty and refuse,tool,refuse end the turn with "API Error: Opus 5.5's safeguards flagged this message". nanocode now does the same: `MessageAccumulator::finish` drops the blocks still open when the stop reason is refusal (it failed with "message_stop before content_block_stop: stop_reason=refusal" before), and the Claude agent loop, on a refusal while `Cursor::refusal_recovered` is false (serde default, so a restarted turn keeps the count), keeps the finished thinking and text blocks and appends that note when any text was kept, otherwise resends unchanged, and continues with the next model step; a second refusal in the turn fails as before. tool_use blocks are not kept: nanocode dispatches tools only after the response is validated, so none ran, which the note's sentence already says. Checked with output/refusal-recovery/run.py (nanocode exec, debug build, against the same stub): before, refuse,ok exited 1 after 1 request and refuse:partialtext,ok exited 1 with the protocol error; after, refuse,ok sends a second request with [assistant "some text", user note] and exits 0, refuse:empty,ok, refuse:nosig,ok and refuse:partialtext,ok resend the first request unchanged and exit 0, refuse,refuse,ok exits 1 after 2 requests with the refusal error. Also compared Claude Code 2.1.318's system prompt with the pinned 2.1.304 blocks for a refusal lever: the identity and the security paragraph ("Assist with authorized security testing, defensive security, CTF challenges …") are identical; 2.1.318 adds Session-specific guidance, Memory, a Fast mode line and a paragraph on recreating games and drops "Write code that reads like the surrounding code", and its attribution reminder names the model in Co-Authored-By; none bears on refusals, so the pin is unchanged here. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, passed; bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 200 passed. Not run: a nanocode-ts rebuild and nanoeval rerun. Files: crates/backends/claude/client/src/lib.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/agent/durable.rs.

- psh-wasm and psh-wasm-core take nanocode-bytes, and the psh workspace's Cargo.lock follows (2026-11-14). 8978566a7 moved nanocode-shell to nanocode-bytes without updating crates/patches/psh/Cargo.lock, so a `--locked` build of the psh workspace (how nanocode-ts builds dist/psh.wasm) failed to resolve, and without `--locked` psh-wasm failed to compile: its host still returned the registry `bytes::Bytes` where nanocode-shell's traits now take `nanocode_bytes::Bytes`. Both crates now name the dependency `bytes = { package = "nanocode-bytes", path = ... }`, so their sources are unchanged, and the registry `bytes` leaves the psh lock. Checked on gak-9: `cargo build --locked -p psh-wasm-core` and `-p psh-wasm` for wasm32-unknown-unknown with the wasm profile, and `cargo clippy --locked -p psh-wasm-core -p psh-wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown -- -D warnings`. Upstream delta: psh-wasm Cargo.toml, psh-wasm-core Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock.
- perf(python): the C API's pointer-keyed maps hash with one folded multiply instead of SipHash (2026-11-14, Georgios: the nanocode-python hill climb, faster than Pyodide). Every object that crosses between RustPython and C looks itself up in maps keyed by an address (the proxy of a Rust object, the C type of a class, a function's definition, a module's state, the wasm arity table), and std's default hasher, SipHash-1-3 with a random key, was about a quarter of msgpack's time in a native profile (`hash_one` 13.4% and `DefaultHasher::write` 7.0% of packing). crates/core/python-capi/src/address.rs is a `BuildHasher` for those maps: a `usize` is folded once with the Fibonacci multiplier (the 64-bit golden-ratio constant, as nanocode-sync's `SeededState` folds), with no random key, since the keys are addresses this process allocated and no input chooses them. nanocode-sync's hasher was not reused because that crate would bring serde into python.wasm. The maps are now built in const thread-local initializers. msgpack 1.2.4 (5,000 records of six fields, best of 5, ms, 5 interleaved rounds, before then after): native release pack 30.1/21.2, 31.2/22.2, 29.4/25.8, 29.4/23.4, 35.6/23.0 (medians 30.1 and 23.0, -24%), unpack 40.7/37.2, 44.7/28.4, 46.8/38.8, 40.2/50.1, 42.7/36.6 (medians 42.7 and 37.2); python.wasm pack 40.5/27.0, 29.2/28.0, 29.6/24.8, 30.9/23.5, 33.4/25.5 (medians 30.9 and 25.5, -18%), unpack 36.3/41.9, 35.3/36.5, 30.1/25.9, 27.3/24.5, 37.8/34.7 (medians 35.3 and 34.7). Pyodide 314.0.7's msgpack 1.1.2 on the same work: pack 6.5, unpack 8.8. python.wasm 28,414,663 to 28,404,046 bytes (-10,617). Unchanged: msgpack's tests 154 passed and 7 skipped natively and in python.wasm, regex 101/101, markupsafe's checks. Commands: `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-python-capi -p nanocode-python --no-deps -- -D warnings` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs`. Files: crates/core/python-capi/src/{address.rs,api.rs,bridge.rs,cast.rs,lib.rs,module.rs}.
- psh counts ended children only while a CHLD trap is set (2026-11-14). After 67d612220 every program, utility, subshell and command substitution that ended set the pending CHLD bit, so the next command took the signal path (a boxed future and take_signals). Now Sched and NestedSigs keep a flag that `trap` sets for the top vproc's CHLD trap; setting the trap starts the count afresh, as bash only reports children that end after the trap is set. Tracker::poll_stop reads an atomic flag before it takes the lock. Interleaved medians of 11 runs of the release binary on the hosted Hand (5 cores, load about 2.3) against 0fbbc51, before today's psh changes: before this change 500 programs took 735 ms against 696 (+5.6%) and 300 background jobs 265 against 245 (+8.2%); after it 708 against 716 and 276 against 283, a 200,000-iteration builtin loop 190 against 187, 100,000 function calls 102 against 101, 3,000 utility pipelines 34.3 against 34.7, 5,000 subshells 10.6 against 10.5 and 5,000 command substitutions 14.0 against 14.3 (all within 2%, p95 within the same spread). psh-spec unchanged. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/trap.rs, sched.rs, signals.rs, state.rs; psh-os lifecycle.rs.
- A subshell that reads `BASHPID` runs in a forked process (2026-11-14). Where the host forks (Host::prepare_fork, the standalone shell) and the subshell's descriptors are all files, a `( ... )` whose text names `BASHPID` runs in a forked copy of the shell (the D1900 fork of a background job, without its INT and QUIT ignores), as bash runs a subshell in a process: it has a process id of its own, takes the signals sent to it, runs its own traps for them, keeps the signals its parent ignores, and dies of SIGQUIT, which only the shell itself ignores. `kill` of the copy's own process id delivers the signal before `kill` returns, so a trap runs before the subshell ends. The death of such a subshell by a signal is reported as `DESCRIPTION COMMAND`, as bash does. The text check keeps every other subshell in-process: forking costs about 1 ms. Command substitutions and pipeline stages still run in-process: their output is a psh pipe, not a file, so `$BASHPID` there still fails (signals 34, 38). psh-spec: brush 3001->3005 (signals 28, 29, 33, 42). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, signals.rs.
- Job signal reports and stops of an in-process shell (2026-11-14). The program of a background job that a signal ends no longer sets the foreground report (Core::fg_signal), so `wait` of a killed job was reported a second time as the death of `wait` itself (`Terminated  wait $pid`). A stop signal that an in-process `sh` or `bash` takes without a trap stops that shell until SIGCONT (NestedSigs::stop_until_cont), which its caller sees through ExtProc::poll_stop as a stopped job, and `kill 0` with a stop signal from such a shell no longer reaches psh's own process group, so `sh -c '(kill -STOP 0; ...)'` under `set -m` stops the job instead of psh. psh-spec: brush 3000->3001 (jobs/2), oils 2355->2360 and agent 725->727 also match stderr (builtin-kill 0, 3, 4, 15, 16, wait/10). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, state.rs.
- `$BASH`, an ignored SIGQUIT, signals ignored at start and SIGPIPE traps for builtins (2026-11-14). `$BASH` names the program psh runs in (ShellConfig::own_program), or `/bin/bash` when there is none, and is set again when a shell starts afresh. Running `$BASH` starts a nested shell, or the real psh when the script reads `$$` (D1413). The standalone shell now catches SIGQUIT and the shell ignores it unless it is trapped, as bash does; before, SIGQUIT killed psh. A signal ignored when a non-interactive shell started can't be trapped or reset: `trap -p` shows it as `''` and `trap ACTION SIG` and `trap - SIG` do nothing (new Host::ignored_at_start, the Unix host's inherited ignores; default empty, so embedded hosts are unchanged; nested shells lock what they start with ignored). A builtin whose write meets a closed pipe runs the vproc's PIPE trap after the command and fails with status 1, or only fails when PIPE is ignored; without a trap it still ends the vproc with 141. A shell psh runs in-process that signals psh's own process id now wakes psh's waits, so a SIGTERM it sends ends the wait at once. psh-spec: brush 2995->3000/3171 (kill/9, signals 15, 16, 18, 25, arguments/99); basic/6 now fails: it compared `type -P $0` with `type -P $BASH` and passed only while `$BASH` was empty, since the harness runs psh as `psh`, a name not on PATH. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/mod.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, host.rs, lib.rs, signals.rs, state.rs, util/nested.rs; psh-os unix/mod.rs; psh lib.rs.
- fix(zstd): a zero-bit add after a full 64-bit container no longer shifts by 64 (2026-11-14, e2e pass). Every debug build of the CLI died on its first durable write: `nanocode exec` printed the reply and then "thread 'nanocode-jsonl' panicked at crates/core/zstd/src/encode/bits.rs:25:27: attempt to shift left with overflow" and "durability store failed: JSONL durability worker stopped", rc 1, and the session was not saved. Cause: `BitWriter::add` flushed only when `count + bits > 64`, so an add that filled the container exactly left `count == 64`, and a following add of 0 bits (a zero-width FSE or Huffman state) evaluated `value << 64`. Release builds wrap the shift amount and the mask is 0 for 0 bits, so release output was already right. Change: flush when `count + bits >= 64`. A flush writes whole bytes in order, so the encoded bytes are identical; only the point where the container drains moves. Verified with the debug binary: the same exec against the Messages mock saves the session, rc 0, and resumes. Files: crates/core/zstd/src/encode/bits.rs.
- deps(http): nanocode-http carries its own HTTP types and HTTP/1 head parser, and nanocode-bytes its own byte buffer; http and httparse leave the registry, and bytes leaves every nanocode crate (2026-11-14). What: `nanocode_http::types` holds what the compiler found nanocode calls of http 1.4.2: `header` (`HeaderName` with the standard names, `HeaderValue`, `HeaderMap` with its entries and iterators, kept as a vector of buckets in insertion order whose removal swaps the last bucket in, as http's does), `Method`, `StatusCode`, `Version`, `uri` (`Uri`, `Scheme`, `Authority`, `PathAndQuery`, `Port`, parsed by http's rules, errors included), `Request` and `Response` with their `Parts` and builders, and `Error`; `nanocode_http::parse` is httparse's `Request`/`Response`/`Header`/`Status` parser in the default configuration that wire.rs and nanocode-websocket use; `nanocode_http::{Method, StatusCode, Version, header}` now name these types. nanocode-bytes (crates/core/bytes) gives `Bytes` (static, `Arc<Vec<u8>>` or `from_owner` storage behind a window; `slice`, `split_to`, `split_off`, `truncate`, `try_into_mut`) and `BytesMut` (a `Vec<u8>`) to nanocode-http, nanocode-shell, nanocode-mpp, nanocode-sandbox, nanocode-backend-claude-client and nanocode-sim. tool-runtime's reserved-header check uses `contains` instead of a constant pattern, since `HeaderName` compares by text. Why: DEPENDENCIES.md's goal of nothing outside the async baseline; bytes stays in the graph only as tokio's dependency (its `io-util` feature) and leaves with tokio. Equal (seeded harnesses in output/, each against the crate it replaces): httparse-equality, httparse =1.10.1, 10,000,000 requests and responses built from valid, mutated, truncated and random bytes (bad line ends, versions, status codes, tokens, header names and values, too few header slots), comparing the status, every parsed field and the slots: 0 differing. http-equality, http =1.4.2, 5,000,000 cases over URIs (pieces, random bytes, IPv6, userinfo, ports, long schemes, 65,535-byte paths) with every accessor, Display and Debug, `Authority` and `PathAndQuery` alone, header names (`from_bytes`, `from_lowercase`, 65,535-byte names), header values (`to_str`, Debug, sensitive, ordering), methods, status codes from bytes and all 65,536 `u16` values, random sequences of up to 40 header-map operations compared after each, and request and response builders: 0 differing; it catches a header map that removes in place, a header value that admits DEL and an authority that allows 7 colons. bytes-equality, bytes =1.12.1, 1,000,000 sequences of up to 24 operations (every constructor, clone, slice, split_to and split_off with panics compared, truncate, clear, drop, `Vec::from`, comparisons, Debug and hex), 12.5M operations: 0 differing; `try_into_mut` reuses the buffer in 101,812 cases where bytes reused it in 104,795 (bytes also reuses a buffer that a clone promoted), so the harness compares the content after the caller's copy, as nanocode-shell's append does. Cost (release, one core, load 4 to 5, median of 7 interleaved runs): a 189-byte request with 7 headers parses in 214 ns against httparse's 145 (no SIMD); building a 12-header map and looking up 4 names takes 1.0 µs against 0.72 (a linear scan instead of a hash); a URI parses in 100 ns against 105. Checks: cargo check --workspace --all-targets passes; wasm32-unknown-unknown cargo check --lib of nanocode-http, nanocode-bytes, nanocode-backend-codex, nanocode-backend-codex-client, nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-backend-claude-client, nanocode-shell, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-tool-runtime and nanocode-observability passes; clippy of the changed crates adds no warning; `nanocode-sim --tidy` is clean; nanocode-sim seeds 0..50,000 of `--scenario http_server`, 50,000..55,000 with `--twice`, 0..20,000 of `--scenario websocket` and 20,000..25,000 with `--twice` pass, the five mutations of those scenarios are caught by 187 to 265 seeds of 0..400, and seeds 7790000000000..+1,000 of `runtime --store kv --wire http`, 7791000000000..+1,000 with `--store memory` and 7792000000000..+500 with `--store kv --twice` pass. The release nanocode-sim built from this commit on master 8aecea52b passes seeds 0..20,000 of `--scenario http_server`, 0..10,000 of `websocket`, 0..5,000 of `mpp`, 0..2,000 of `sync` and 7793000000000..+400 of `runtime --store kv --wire http`. Downstream (tempoxyz/pyramid, pyramid-core, pyramid2): `nanocode_http::{Method, StatusCode, Version, header::*}` and nanocode-websocket's `client::{Request, Response}` and `server::{Request, Response, ErrorResponse}` are nanocode's own types rather than http's, so code that hands http crate values to them converts (pyramid2's `accept_hdr_async_with_config` callback keeps the same methods); `ProtocolError::HttparseError` holds `nanocode_http::parse::Error`; `nanocode_http::Response::{extensions, extensions_mut}` are gone (nothing read them); request bodies and nanocode-shell's file and fetch APIs take `nanocode_bytes::Bytes` instead of `bytes::Bytes`. Code search finds no other use in pyramid or pyramid-core.
- The Claude harness's cache_control placement stays as it is for DeepSeek on the Tempo gateway's Vercel route, where it has no effect (2026-11-14, ~/hill/analysis/ds-claude-cost.md). Probed live through a meter proxy (`~/wt/ds-claude-cost/probe.py`, `probe2.py`; 28 calls, $0.058): a ~22k-token prompt, then the same prompt extended (B), cut over halfway through its second half (C) and repeated, with no cache_control, a block breakpoint after the first 11k tokens, one on the last block, and top-level cache_control. Every mode gave the same counts (A 0, B 22,272 cached, C 16,384) and no cache_creation tokens, so the provider caches each prompt by prefix in 256-token pages, and a breakpoint neither creates an entry nor limits a hit. Three sessions sharing a 4k prefix, interleaved, each hit their own full previous prompt (10,496 then 11,264), the same as one session alone, so nothing evicts across sessions. In cmp2 trials the cached count is the previous prompt floored to a page in every arm, misses (22% of calls for stock-claude, 36% for m3-claude and 28% for m3-codex in the m3 window) do not depend on the gap between calls, and they fall back to an older call's prompt or the shared system prefix, which is provider behavior. The parity mock (77765bb, scenarios edit, bg, read, par, bad, maxtok, out) shows no prefix break between consecutive requests. Per call, nanocode-claude matches stock Claude Code 2.1.300 on DeepSeek: median output 363 vs 386 tokens, thinking kept in context in both (growth after a call is 1.01x vs 1.02x its output), first call 3.7k vs 15.7k tokens. The m3 cost gap to stock-claude ($0.0957 vs $0.0937 per pass on 24 tasks) is one trial: without winning-avg-corewars (m3 $0.425 in 102 calls) it is $0.0793 vs $0.0800 per pass. What is left is calls per trial (claude 25-31, codex 21), which is the model's strategy under the upstream prompt.
- feat(codex): a Codex session's `exec` cell that gives no `yield_time_ms` first yields after 30,000 ms, as codex-cli's (`DEFAULT_CODE_MODE_EXEC_YIELD_TIME_MS = 30_000` in core/src/config/mod.rs, applied with `request.yield_time_ms.get_or_insert(default_exec_yield_time_ms)` in core/src/tools/code_mode/mod.rs, openai/codex 7924f95), while `wait` keeps 10,000 ms (`DEFAULT_WAIT_YIELD_TIME_MS`) (2026-11-14). nanocode used `spec::DEFAULT_YIELD` (10 s, plus the 1 s observer grace, so 11 s) for both, so a Codex model's cell yielded and spent a `wait` turn on work codex-cli would have returned in one call. `Tools` gains `with_exec_yield`, a harness default for the first yield only, and `exec_yield()`, which is `cell_yield` when set and that default otherwise; an explicit `cell_yield` (`--cell-yield-ms`, nanocode-ts `cellYieldMs`) still sets both and wins. The Codex harness's `tool_runtime` (builtin_tools/mod.rs) sets 30 s; the Claude harness sets nothing and keeps 10 s. The native runtime (`CodeModeRuntime::set_exec_yield`, the hand-routed pragma) and the embedded runtime the WebAssembly brain uses (its `exec` pragma and spec) read `exec_yield`, and their `wait` reads `cell_yield` only; the `exec` description says "Defaults to 30000 ms", as codex-cli's template renders it, and `wait`'s still says 10000. A cell's journal record took the wait default as its yield and now takes the exec default. Checked with output/exec-yield (tool-host model specs and pragma): default 10000/10000 with no pragma, Codex 30000/10000 with `{"yield_time_ms":30000}`, Codex with `cell_yield(5 s)` 5000/5000 with `{"yield_time_ms":5000}`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-backend-codex`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and `cargo clippy` on them with `-D warnings`. Files: crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{selection.rs,runtime/execution.rs,embedded/runtime.rs}, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs, crates/backends/codex/src/builtin_tools/mod.rs.

- fix(codex): the WebAssembly brain (nanocode-ts, which runs the eval's nanox and nanoxd arms) sends upstream Codex's permissions developer message and environment filesystem element, as the native build and stock codex-cli under `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` do, instead of a wasm-only `<host_execution_context>` (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 install-windows-3.11, nanox 1/4 against cx 3/3). On `target_family = "wasm"` `permissions_instructions` (model/input.rs) returned "Execution permissions are supplied and enforced by the host for each tool and selected environment. The embedded runtime does not grant filesystem, network, or escalation access." and `push_filesystem` (model/context.rs) wrote nothing, so the model never read `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`, "Approval policy is currently never" or the `<filesystem>` element, while luna.md tells it what to do when "you receive an auto-review rejection". The deployed nanocode_wasm.wasm (nanoeval 614bbac's nanocode-ts) holds the host_execution_context string twice and "Approval policy is currently never" zero times. In run 8feaf3f8 attempt a00151 nanox had Windows 3.11 booted to its desktop (its last screendump, 1024x768 Cirrus, decoded from agent/events.jsonl) when it ended the turn with "An automatic safety review blocked starting the Windows VM", with reasoning "an auto-review policy is blocking the final VM action ... The system classifies this action as high risk"; no tool result held any refusal (68 calls, none failed by policy). Scanning the agent messages of all 87 nanox and 79 cx trajectories in report.json for auto-review or safety-review claims finds only that one. The two other nanox failures are the model's own choices, not the harness's: e5581bd1 a00015 started QEMU with `-usb -device usb-kbd`, so monitor `sendkey` went to the USB keyboard and the DOS "No RTL8029 adapter" prompt never took a key, and c876ad68 a00061 waited 4 s after Enter on a black Cirrus frame and gave up while Windows was still loading (a00151 shows the desktop 25 s later). Effort (high), transport retries (0), compactions (0) and image results (full-size PNGs, 720x400 and 1024x768) were the same as cx or did not differ. Change: both functions lose their wasm variants, so every build sends the same bytes. Checked: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, without warnings; `cargo build --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` gives an rlib with "host_execution_context" 0 times and "Approval policy is currently never", "danger-full-access" and "permission_profile type" once each; the native mock capture in output/codex-direct (request-1.json) shows the developer message the wasm brain now sends. Needs a nanocode-ts release and Worker redeploy to reach the eval.

- `nanocode-sim --scenario sync` runs nanocode-sync's Notify, Semaphore, bounded mpsc, watch and broadcast under the simulator's seeded scheduler, with cancellation, and checks each against what tokio::sync promises (2026-11-14). The scripted equality harnesses behind ea495845b and a8c0e66d3 compare single operations with tokio; nothing drove the primitives with several tasks interleaved and futures dropped mid-wait. Each seed runs five worlds at once in one executor: Notify (one to three waiters needing one to four wakes each, some taking the wake through `enable`, some giving up after a seeded timeout and trying again; a notifier that calls `notify_one` or `notify_last` only once every earlier call has woken someone, then a second Notify whose waiters `enable` before one `notify_waiters`), Semaphore (one to three permits, two to four holders taking one up to all of them with `acquire_many` or `try_acquire_many`, some abandoning the wait, and an adder calling `add_permits` up to three times), bounded mpsc (capacity one to four, one to three senders using `send`, `reserve` then `Permit::send`, or `try_send`, some cancelled, and a receiver that sometimes calls `close` and drains), watch (one to ten values sent with `send`, `send_replace` or `send_modify` to one to three receivers whose `changed` may be cancelled) and broadcast (capacity one to four, one to ten values, one to three receivers). Every task pauses between steps (none, a yield or a seeded sleep). Checks: no lost wakeup (each `notify_one` wakes a waiter or leaves the one stored permit, a cancelled waiter that was picked passes the wake on, and every waiter enabled before `notify_waiters` wakes); semaphore permits are never held beyond the total, all return when the holders leave, and a waiter or `try_acquire` never gets permits while an earlier waiter that no release has woken is still queued (wakes are seen through a wrapping waker, since a woken waiter already owns its permits); mpsc delivers each message whose send returned `Ok` exactly once, in each sender's order, never has more in flight than its capacity, and after `close` still delivers what was sent; a watch receiver sees strictly increasing values and ends on the last one; a broadcast receiver sees values in order, and a `Lagged(n)` skips exactly to the oldest value its ring (the capacity rounded up to a power of two, as tokio does) keeps. Mutations, one per invariant: `skip_notify` (one notify fewer), `leak_permit` (a holder forgets a permit), `reverse_queue` (the model queues waiters in reverse), `resend` (a sender sends a message twice), `shrink_capacity` (the model's capacity is one smaller), `watch_rewind` (the model expects one more value), `broadcast_extra` (an unrecorded extra value) and `ring_off_by_one` (the model's ring is one larger); caught by 400, 390, 90, 379, 295, 400, 400 and 207 of seeds 0..400. bin/nanocode-sim/cfo.sh rows: `sync` (8), `sync_twice` (2) and a canary per mutation. Seeds 0..300,000 pass and 300,000..330,000 pass with `--twice`, so no bug was found: the primitives keep tokio's promises under every interleaving one thread can produce. Not covered: races between threads (the simulator runs one), which is where a lock-free primitive can still go wrong; for example two clones of a watch `Sender` publishing at once can store their versions out of order (`publish` takes the version and sets the value in two steps), which needs a multi-threaded checker to show.
- `nanocode-sim --scenario mpp` runs nanocode-mpp's payment flow (`flow::send_with_exchange`) against a scripted payee and a scripted payment provider, and checks that every payment it makes is settled once, the way the payee's answer requires (2026-11-14). The flow had no simulation: it decides, for each 402 challenge, whether to pay, and after a paid request whether to commit, roll back or abandon the payment, which is where money is lost or double-spent. The payee (an `Exchange`) answers the first request with 200 or with 402 and one to three `Payment` challenges (`tempo` or a method the provider does not support, sometimes expired, and sometimes a zero-amount challenge from another realm, which the flow must refuse as a cross-realm proof); each paid request gets a seeded fate: 200 or 201, another 402 with fresh challenges (one in ten reusing an earlier challenge id), 400, 403 or 409, 500 or 503 (each with or without a `payment-receipt`), or a connection reset after the request was sent. The provider supports `tempo`/`charge`, makes a credential per payment (one payment in twenty fails for insufficient balance) and records every pay, commit, rollback, invalidate and abandon. The flow retries one to four times; requests are GET or POST with a body. Checks: no more payments than retries; no challenge paid twice; only supported, unexpired, non-proof challenges paid; each paid credential presented exactly once, on the request after its payment; each payment settled exactly once and as the answer to its request requires (a 2xx or any answer with a receipt commits, a 4xx or 402 without one rolls back, a 5xx without one or a reset abandons, since the payee may have taken the money); nothing settled that was not paid; every request carries the caller's body; the status returned is the last answer's. Mutations: `drop_abandon` (the provider loses abandon calls) caught by 107 seeds of 0..400, and `receipt_on_refusal` (the payee adds a receipt to a refusal that the model treats as receiptless) by 69. bin/nanocode-sim/cfo.sh rows: `mpp` (8), `mpp_twice` (2) and a canary per mutation. Seeds 0..202,000 pass, and 202,000..222,000 with `--twice`; over the last 220,000 of them the flow made 180,776 payments, 90,367 commits, 36,502 rollbacks and 53,907 abandons, all as the model requires, so the flow keeps its accounting. Not covered: prepaid session credentials (`prepaid_credential`), `intent="session"` receipts and 410 invalidation, and `pay_with_management`. Noted, not changed: `protocol::now_seconds` reads `std::time::SystemTime` directly, not nanocode-platform's clock, so challenge expiry ignores a platform host's time; the scenario uses expiry dates far in the past. On a3f421924 the scenario passes seeds 0..20,000 and 20,000..22,000 with `--twice`, both mutations are caught as above, `--tidy` is clean and clippy on nanocode-sim is clean.
- docs(sla): SLA.md holds live time to first token on two open models through the metered Tempo Gateway route: `vercel/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017` at low effort and `boundless/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` at high effort, nanocode 77765bb against Claude Code 2.1.325 on Messages and Codex CLI 0.166.0 on Responses, 12 sessions of 3 turns per client from the hosted Hand (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 latency track). nanocode wins 8 of 12 p50 cells: every DeepSeek Messages turn (1,685, 1,641 and 1,233 ms against 1,814, 1,667 and 1,700), DeepSeek Responses turns 1 and 3 (1,116 against 3,102 ms on turn 1), GLM Messages turn 2 and GLM Responses turns 2 and 3. It loses DeepSeek Responses turn 2 (+480 ms), GLM Messages turns 1 and 3 (+1,622 and +317 ms) and GLM Responses turn 1 (+404 ms), and the p99 of DeepSeek Messages (5.4 to 10.9 s, all session 0) and GLM Responses (15 to 24 s). Those samples are provider time: the proxy shows each request lasting the whole sample for 6 to 105 output tokens, and nanocode's request reaches the proxy 3 to 6 ms p50 after Enter against 75 to 136 ms for Claude Code and 57 to 101 ms for Codex CLI. `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` answered Workers AI's "3021: rate limiting: inference request per min rate reached" inside 200 streams and gateway payment 500s while the cmp GLM eval ran on the same account, so GLM runs on its Boundless listing. The first token is the reply's: nanocode-ts `bench/sla/run.ts --live` matches the mark anywhere on screen, and every client draws reasoning before the reply (nanocode `∴`, Claude Code `● Thinking…` with its text, Codex its status header), which matched 0.1 to 6 s early. The measurement used a local copy of run.ts whose live lanes wait for the mark after the reply bullet (`●` not followed by `Thinking` for nanocode and Claude Code, `•` directly before it for Codex), record each turn's Enter wall time, and write each turn's timestamped screen chunks (`SLA_STREAM`); replaying the 288 recorded turns found no missed reply and two nanocode turns matched 55 and 108 ms early, in reasoning streamed under a redrawn earlier reply. Requiring the mark within 60 characters of the bullet moves both to the reply and changes no p50 or p99. Commands, from nanocode-ts 177b460 with `NC_BIN_NOW` a wrapper adding `--harness claude|codex --thinking low|high --no-tempo-tools`, `CLAUDE_BIN` adding `--effort`, and `HOME`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `CODEX_HOME` per model: `node bench/sla/run-ttft.ts --live --lanes=live-nc-claude@now,live-claude --claude-model=<id> --samples=12 --turns=3 --settle=3000 --timeout=60000 --label=ttft-<model>-claude` and the same with `--lanes=live-nc-codex@now,live-codex --codex-model=<id>`. Codex used a `model_catalog_json` entry from its unknown-model fallback, as the cmp evals do. Ready on Responses is 253 to 272 ms against 51 to 53 ms on Messages, because the CLI lists `/v1/models` synchronously before the composer opens. Gateway cost for the whole session, pilots and discarded runs included: $0.29 (DeepSeek $0.16, GLM $0.13).
- `nanocode-sim --scenario egress` drives the sandbox's egress proxy end to end over simulated sockets, and the proxy runs under a platform host: its tunnels, intercepted connections and upgraded replies were spawned with `nanocode_platform::spawn_task`, which always calls `tokio::spawn`, and now go through `nanocode_platform::spawn`, which hands them to an installed host (2026-11-14). The proxy dialed upstream with `tokio::net::lookup_host` and `TcpStream::connect` inline in `Proxy::dial`; a `Dial` trait (`resolve(host, port)`, `connect(address)` returning a boxed `Duplex`, crates/integrations/sandbox/src/egress/proxy.rs) now holds those two calls, `Network` implements it with the same tokio calls (nodelay included), `Proxy::new` uses it and `Proxy::dialing` replaces it, so the reach rules (allowlist, private and denied addresses, refusal texts) still run inside the proxy on whatever addresses the dialer resolves. The SOCKS path to the tailnet keeps its own TCP connection. Under the simulator's host every `spawn_task` call in the proxy panicked with "there is no reactor running" (231 of the scenario's first 300 seeds, every seed with a CONNECT to an allowed host), and an embedder with a host of its own (workerd) would fail the same way; `spawn` is what the rest of the platform-seam change uses for fire-and-forget tasks, and nothing in the proxy kept their join handles. The scenario: up to 5 concurrent client connections to one `Proxy` (Identity::Fixed, Reach::Listed, no secrets, so nothing is intercepted), each with a CONNECT tunnel (payload up to 6,000 bytes, echoed by the upstream) or a plain-HTTP GET or POST with an absolute URL (body up to 6,000 bytes, answered 200, 201, 404 or 500 with up to 6,000 bytes), to one of seven hosts: two public, a private one on `private_hosts`, a private one not on it, one off the allowlist, one that does not resolve and one whose address refuses connections; socket reads and writes arrive in seeded pieces as small as one byte, and the upstream answers after a seeded delay. Checks: each client sees what the policy says (403 with the allowlist or private-address text, 502 "does not resolve" or "can't be reached", or the upstream's status and exact bytes); the proxy opens exactly one upstream connection per allowed request and none for refused ones; each tunnel's upstream receives the client's bytes exactly; each origin receives the request in origin form with its host header, without the hop-by-hop `proxy-connection` header, and with the client's body; no hang, and the same trace on a second run. Mutations: `widen_allowlist` (the proxy's allowlist also names the denied host) and `corrupt_tunnel_byte` (the upstream flips a bit in its first echo); caught by 129 and 191 of seeds 0..400. bin/nanocode-sim/cfo.sh rows: `egress` (8), `egress_twice` (2) and a canary per mutation. The first sweep also failed 2 seeds of 100,000 (41392 and 105199) because two plain requests to one host could share a path and the origin answered both with the first one's script; paths now start with the request's index. With that, seeds 0..112,000 and 200,000..400,000 pass, 400,000..420,000 pass with `--twice`, and `--tidy` is clean. Not covered: TLS interception (secrets bound to a host), the SOCKS tailnet path and the `accept` loop's per-source limits. On a3f421924 the scenario passes seeds 0..5,000, both mutations are caught as above, `--tidy` is clean and clippy on nanocode-sandbox and nanocode-sim is clean.
- fix(code-mode): a `wait` that would yield with nothing to report keeps waiting for the cell's next report up to the empty-poll minimum, 5 s, the floor Codex and nanocode-process already give an empty `write_stdin` (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 Codex parity: fix-ocaml-gc and dna-insert). In tb21-full run 8feaf3f8 attempt a00123 (nanox, codex:gpt-6-luna:high, Code Mode) the model followed the Codex backend's `<code_mode_orchestration>` prompt: each build ran in one cell that looped `write_stdin` with `yield_time_ms: 30000`, and after the cell yielded at 11 s the model called `wait` with `yield_time_ms: 1000` 159 times, 138 of which answered "The script printed nothing since the last yield. Nested calls still running: 1 write_stdin." It took 195 model calls, 21.4 M input tokens and $0.266 against Codex CLI 0.166's 43 calls, 3.2 M tokens and $0.062 on the same task (attempt a00124), which polled `write_stdin` itself every 31 s; both passed. Upstream Codex's code-mode `wait` has no floor (codex-rs code-mode-runtime `resolve_yield_timeout`), but its `write_stdin` with no input waits at least `MIN_EMPTY_YIELD_TIME_MS` (5,000 ms), and a `wait` is that poll for a cell. Now `wait_inner` passes `ObservationMode::YieldAfter` a second time, the larger of the yield and `MIN_POLL_YIELD_MS` (new in nanocode-process-contracts beside `DEFAULT_POLL_YIELD_MS`; nanocode-process's empty-poll clamp now names it instead of the literal). When the yield passes with nothing buffered (no output, no returned nested call, no notification, nothing queued), `observe_updates` moves its deadline to that time and returns as soon as the cell prints, a nested call returns or a notification arrives, or the cell ends. A yield of 5 s or more, exec's first yield, a revived cell's observation and terminate are unchanged, and a `wait` that has something to report still answers at its own yield. The hold stays under any brain's remote deadline (its operation timeout plus the yield it named). Measured with the harness in `output/wait-hold` (LocalCells, a cell whose nested tool sleeps 12 s three times and prints after each, exec yield 2 s, then `wait` until it completes), interleaved against `output/wait-hold-base` built from 10ae02b71: with `yield_time_ms: 1000` 34 waits (31 empty) before and 9 and 8 waits (6 and 5 empty) after, 36.0 s either way, and an early answer 2.0 s into a wait when a chunk printed; with `yield_time_ms: 30000` 2 waits before and after. Checks: `cargo check --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-process`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-process-contracts --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, clippy on both crates without new warnings, `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 400 8 --scenario runtime --twice` (400 passed). Not changed: the exec yields at 11 s in every sampled nano and nanox attempt of these runs, although nanoeval's `CELL_YIELD_MS` is 120,000, which a host-side check should explain.
- fix(codex): a Responses WebSocket that sends no frame for 300 s fails the attempt with a retryable `ResponsesError::ReceiveTimeout`, natively and in the wasm host transport, so a stalled stream reconnects and retries instead of hanging the turn (2026-11-14, nanoeval make-mips-interpreter: nanox 0/6 vs codex-cli 1/3). Upstream codex-cli bounds every websocket read with `stream_idle_timeout` (codex-rs/codex-api responses_websocket.rs, `tokio::time::timeout(idle_timeout, ws_stream.next())`, default `DEFAULT_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS = 300_000` in model-provider-info) and retries the stream; nanocode bounded only the HTTPS SSE path, and only natively (`IdleTimer::within` was a no-op on wasm), while `ResponsesSocket::next_text` awaited the next frame forever on both targets. Evidence: nanoeval run 473d0b90 attempt a00002 (nanox, codex:gpt-6-luna:high, Cloudflare brain over responses_websocket_v2) logged its last event 41 s in, after model call 6, then nothing for 1,275 s until the Worker was redeployed at 05:32:55Z and the revived turn (event seq generation 2, a fresh `model.connection.started`) redid model call 7 in 58 s; the attempt ended at 1,570 s with no frame saved. The timeout is upstream's 300 s; the native socket wraps each wait in `nanocode_platform::timeout` (the pump batches frames and `try_next_text` drains them first, so a timer is armed only when the reader actually waits, and an `IdleTimer` field would make the socket `!Sync`), the wasm socket keeps one lazily reset `IdleTimer` per socket, now real on wasm and cleared when it fires. Checked with output/ws-stall (a mock Responses WebSocket that accepts the request and then sends nothing, or only `response.created`, on its first connection and answers normally on later ones), master 10ae02b71 and this change run side by side: on master both cases still waited after 420 s on the first connection (HUNG, 1 connection, 1 request); with this change both completed after 301.1 s on a second connection (2 connections, 2 requests, text "ok"). The wasm host path is checked by build only. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex-client`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, passed; clippy -D warnings reports only the existing `reconnect_delay` const-fn lint in retry.rs.
- feat(codex): Codex models can call their tools directly instead of through Code Mode, for an A/B of whether Code Mode costs gpt-6-luna on reasoning-heavy Terminal-Bench tasks (2026-11-14; nanoeval had nanocode `codex:gpt-6-luna:high` at 0 of 6 against codex-cli's 3 of 5 on feal-differential-cryptanalysis, with fewer experiments run). The switch is the one the harness already had: `CodexHarness::direct_tools_for` builds the tools `DirectOnly`, and the developer message then leaves out `<code_mode_orchestration>` because it keys on the exposure. It was ignored whenever a hand placed the session (`direct && !remote`), which is every nanocode-ts session with `hands`; now it holds there too. A `DirectOnly` `EmbeddedToolRuntime` treats its Code Mode host as direct: the model gets the hand's own tool definitions (`exec_command`, `write_stdin`, `update_plan`, `apply_patch`, `view_image`) and no exec or wait, and each call goes to `CodeModeHost::call` (a function call's arguments as JSON, a freeform call's text as a string, as a cell's nested call sends them). `CodeModeExecutors` implements `call` by sending it to the session's placed hand through `call_on`, with its authorizer, and the native runtime does the same for a direct workspace tool on a hand instead of refusing it. Hands need nothing new: `RemoteOperation::Call` runs `execute_nested_tool` on the hand, also in the pinned `nanocode-cli-3f97ab0`. The CLI takes `--codex-orchestration direct` or `NANOCODE_CODEX_ORCHESTRATION=direct`; code-mode stays the default, and the run telemetry's `orchestration` stays `local_code_mode` (`ModelConfig::orchestration()` is public and constant), so a direct run shows by its tool names. Checked with output/codex-direct against a mock Responses server, `nanocode exec -m gpt-6-luna`: by default the request carries `exec` and `wait` and the Code Mode block; with the variable it carries the six direct tools and no block, and the model's `exec_command` answers `direct-ok-42` in Codex's text, run locally and, with `--runner-connect` to a `nanocode hand --listen` in replace mode, in the hand's directory. output/codex-direct/embedded drives a `DirectOnly` embedded runtime over a code-only mock hand: specs `apply_patch` and `exec_command`, both calls reach `call` with `{"cmd":"echo hi"}` and `"*** Begin Patch"`; without `DirectOnly` it offers exec and wait and refuses both, as before.

- CHLD traps, nested signal traps and stopped jobs (2026-11-14). The shell counts each child that ends (a program, a utility, a subshell, a command substitution, a background job of its own) and runs the CHLD trap once for each at its next safepoint. Outside POSIX mode `wait` runs the trap and goes on waiting, in POSIX mode a trapped CHLD ends `wait` with 145, as bash does. A signal that arrives while its trap runs runs the trap again, nested, also after the trap's last command, so `trap 'kill -USR1 $$' USR1` nests as deep as bash. A CHLD that ends inside a trap waits for the trap to end. Job control: the Unix host waits with WSTOPPED and reports a stop through a new ExtProc::poll_stop (default Pending, so other hosts are unchanged). Under `set -m` a foreground program that stops becomes a stopped job with status 128+n, `wait` returns 128+n for a stopped job (with bash's warning when it was stopped already), `wait` without operands leaves stopped jobs out, `fg` and `bg` (new, `no job control` without `set -m`) send SIGCONT, `jobs -s`/`-r` select by state, and `kill` follows SIGTERM or SIGHUP to a stopped job with SIGCONT. Each program under `set -m` leads a process group of its own (new SpawnSpec::group, POSIX_SPAWN_SETPGROUP or setpgid), so `kill -STOP 0` in a job stops only the job. A real program that a nested `sh` runs for a script that reads `$$` (D1413) takes the signals sent to that shell and passes its stop up, and a forked job copy stops itself when its program stops, so the job shows stopped in both cases. Left out: job notifications, `kill 0` from a shell psh runs in-process (it still reaches psh's own group, jobs/2), and the job text of a foreground program is its argv, not the source text (command/43). psh-spec: brush 2975->2995/3171 (signals 2, 3, 44 to 48, jobs 1, 3 to 6, 9 to 11, 14, kill 16 to 18), oils 2418, agent 727, utils 999 unchanged, no regressions. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, builtins/mod.rs, builtins/trap.rs, builtins/core_tests.rs, exec.rs, host.rs, jobs.rs, lib.rs, sched.rs, state.rs, util.rs, util/nested.rs; psh-os lifecycle.rs, unix/spawn.rs.
- PATH lookup follows bash for relative and empty entries (2026-11-14). An empty entry searches the working directory. A program found past an entry that names the working directory is remembered with that fact, and runs as `./name` while the working directory has a program of that name, as bash's hash table does. With PATH unset, a program in the working directory runs by its name and is not hashed. `command -V` shows the absolute path of a program found through a relative entry (`command -v` keeps it relative), `hash -t` shows a relative entry that names a program as `./path`, and a relative `hash -p` path is kept even when nothing is there. Programs still start by their absolute path: SpawnSpec::program stays absolute for hosts without a working directory of their own, so `$0` and `$_` of a program run through a relative entry keep their known difference. psh-spec: brush 2967->2975/3171 (path_search 0, 1, 2, 6, 8, 10, 13 and command/33), oils 2418, agent 727, utils 999 unchanged. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/hash.rs, builtins/command.rs, util.rs.
- fix(claude): a Claude session with the default tools journals its Code Mode cells through the host's cell journal sink, as a Codex session does, so `nanocode exec --continue` after a crash revives a yielded cell and loads the session's `store()` values (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: CLI restart). The Claude harness (`ClaudeHarness::build`, runtime.rs) called `HostServices::prepare_tools` only on an explicit `settings.tools`; with none, as in `nanocode exec` and the TUI, `install_default_tools_with_providers` built Claude's default tool selection and never prepared it, so agent-host never attached `DurableCellJournals` (it does that in `prepare_tools`) and the session's cells and stored values lived in that process's memory only. The Codex harness always prepares (it starts from `Tools::default()` when none is given), so on the same CLI a Codex session revived its cells after a restart while a Claude session answered `exec cell 1 not found` to a `wait` on the yielded cell and `load` read `undefined`. `install_default_tools_with_providers` now takes the harness's `prepare` and applies it to the selection it uses, explicit or default, so both harnesses prepare every selection the same way; the public `install_default_tools*` functions pass `Ok`, which keeps them as they were, and the wasm path prepares an explicit selection exactly as before. On the default selection `prepare_tools` also records the session as having no Code Mode host (the value already assumed for an unknown session) and sets the runner pool and process route store that the function sets from the same services anyway. Conformance, native-cli (output/cm-conf cli/run.ts against the scripted model; release `nanocode` built from origin/master and from this change in the same target directory), 3 runs each: Claude fail 3 of 3 to pass 3 of 3 on durability/store-before-crash-survives (`load: undefined`), durability/store-persists-after-resumed-cell (`undefined,undefined`), durability/store-persists-across-restart (`after restart: undefined`), durability/terminate-revived-cell, durability/yielded-cell-wait-after-restart and runner/crash-mid-timer (`exec cell 1 not found`), and on async/crash-mid-timer-resumes-remaining-time and async/crash-mid-timer-cleared-stays-cleared (`Script failed` with no output), which the suite had kept off native-cli on the belief that the CLI keeps cells in memory only and now runs there; Codex passes all eight before and after. Full native-cli suite, 1,436 runs: Claude 494 of 502 to 502 of 502, Codex 474 of 475 both times (durability/notify-not-resent-on-replay, where the CLI runner cannot see the journal and crashes after the cell finished), 0 runs from pass to fail. The suite's CLI runner also waits for the killed process to exit before it relaunches: since `nanocode exec --continue` refuses a session whose owner process is alive, an unreaped child made yielded-cell-wait-after-restart fail with `is running a turn in nanocode process N`. native-host drives `LocalCells` without the harness and is unaffected. Commands: `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` and `cargo clippy --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude --no-deps -- -D warnings`, natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent-host`, nanocode-ts `cargo check --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` against this checkout, rustfmt --check finds no new difference in the changed files. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/{runtime.rs,defaults.rs}.

- fix(djs): a builtin, host, bound or callable-Proxy function's `Function.prototype.toString` is `function name() { [native code] }` on one line, as V8 prints it, instead of QuickJS's three lines (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: JS parity). Both are NativeFunction text and spec-valid, but models compare such strings against what Node printed (`String(Math.max) === "function max() { [native code] }"`, feature checks for native methods), and the differential fuzz lane classed the difference as implementation-defined whitespace. Adopted only because nothing else moved: with output/gate.sh on dev-georgios the test262 subset passes 8,631 of 9,288 before and after with identical pass sets (77 of its 80 Function/prototype/toString tests in both), and the 25 edge cells are byte-identical; repros/fn-tostring.js now prints Node's seven lines exactly. djs's own vm test expectation for `map`'s text follows. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/builtins/function.rs, builtins/function.ts, builtins/gen/*, crates/djs-core/src/vm/tests.rs.

- fix(djs): `Array.prototype.join`, `toString` and `toLocaleString`, and `%TypedArray%.prototype.join` and `toLocaleString` give `""` for a receiver that a join is already joining, as V8, JavaScriptCore and SpiderMonkey do, instead of recursing to `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: JS parity). The spec has no cycle check, so `const a = [1]; a.push(a); String(a)` overflows the stack per the letter, but every engine models write for returns `"1,"`, and the differential fuzz lane counted it as djs's `join-cycle` divergence from Node. The order is V8's (`CycleProtectedArrayJoin`, array-join.tq): ToObject, length and ToString(separator) run first, then the receiver is pushed on the realm's join stack or, already there, answered with `""`, and popped in a `finally` so a throwing element leaves the stack as it found it. The stack is a new realm slot, `Intrinsic::JoinStack`: an internal ValueArray, undefined until the first join, grown by `value_array_reserve` as `KeptObjects` is, traced and compacted with the heap, and reset whenever a run's bottom frame finishes (`bottom_done`), so a run cut short by a fault cannot leave entries for the next. `%ArrayJoinEnter(o)` and `%ArrayJoinLeave()` are pure leaves (the hot loop runs them in place; `ArrayJoinEnter` allocates before it changes anything, so it is also on the out-of-memory retry list), and `join`'s `@fast` entry declines when the receiver is on the stack, so an array an element's `toString` made all-primitive still answers `""` as in V8. Checked on dev-georgios against Node 24.22 with output/cm-fuzz/one.sh: repros/join-cycle.js RangeError before, `"1,"` after and in Node; a 13-case join edge script (work/join-edge.js without its last case, which is Function.prototype.toString: nested cycles, an element that rewrites the array then joins it, a separator whose toString joins the receiver, an array-like with a self-joining element, a throwing element followed by more joins, toLocaleString cycles and toLocaleString calling join, a Uint8Array whose Number toLocaleString joins it, 1,000-deep non-cyclic nesting, `[a, a]` self-cycles) 10 cases differ from Node before and 0 after. Gate (output/gate.sh, the fuzz lane's): test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 passing before and after with identical pass sets, the 25 edge cells byte-identical. Cost in instructions (cachegrind on the djsfuzz runner, whole run): 200k `[1, 2, i].join()` 1,017.1M to 1,024.6M (+0.7%, the `@fast` entry's stack check); 50k `[o, i, o].join("-")` with a `toString` object 1,516.3M to 1,576.1M (+3.9%: about 1,200 per slow-path join, of which the `finally` is about 330, measured by building without it, and dispatching the two intrinsics through `call_intrinsic` instead of the hot loop cost 360 more); 50k `String([1, [2, i], [3, [4]]])` 3,563.3M to 3,686.9M (+3.5%). Files: crates/patches/djs/builtins/array.ts, typedarray.ts, intrinsics.d.ts, builtins/gen/*, crates/djs-core/src/builtins/array.rs, builtins/fast.rs, bytecode/intrinsics.rs, interp/realm.rs, interp/run.rs, interp/run/hot.rs, interp/run/intrinsics.rs.

- fix(djs): `**` and `Math.pow` give Node's bits on Linux: `Number::exponentiate` (interp/conv.rs) takes V8's two shortcuts and djs-libm's `pow` is the C library's that V8 then calls, musl's current one (Arm's optimized-routines pow, which glibc 2.28+ ships), with the multiply-adds that glibc's FMA build fuses written as `fma` calls (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: JS parity). V8's `math::pow` (src/numbers/ieee754.cc, with `use_std_math_pow`, the default) answers `x ** 2` with `x * x` and `x ** 0.5` with `sqrt(x + 0)` (+Infinity for an infinite x) and everything else with `std::pow`; the fdlibm `pow` from libm 0.2.16 is within 1 ulp but not glibc's, so models writing Node-flavored JS saw `2 ** 1.5`, `2 ** -2.5` and friends differ in the last digit (the differential fuzz lane's `pow-ulp` class). glibc picks its FMA variant of `pow` at load time on x86-64 CPUs with FMA, and GCC contracts `a * b + c` there by default; compiled from musl's source, the non-FMA C path disagreed with glibc on 4,538 of 10M inputs and the FMA path with `-ffp-contract=off` on 4,512, so the port follows the contracted build's fused operations as its disassembly shows them (21 `vfmadd`/`vfmsub`), and libm's exact `fma` (hardware through runtime detection on x86-64, software on wasm32) makes the result the same bits on every target. The tables are pow_data.c's and exp_data.c's, through `hf64!`. Checked on dev-georgios against glibc 2.39 `pow` with output/powcheck (native) and output/powwasm (wasm32 in Node): 10M random inputs over five shapes (|x| in 2^±20 with |y| < 60, x in [0.5, 2] with |y| < 1e4, any finite positive x with |y| < 4, wide exponents for both, negative x with integer y and small x with |y| < 300; xorshift seed 0x9e3779b97f4a7c15) mismatch 0 native and 0 wasm after, 671,141 before (all 1 ulp); a second 10M at seed 0x1234567887654321 0 and 0 (669,647 before); 6,050,176 special and boundary pairs (signed zeros, infinities, NaN, subnormals, integers, odd and even y, 2^±1074 results, overflow and underflow edges) 0 and 0 (4,002 before); 6M with y fixed at 12 common exponents 0 (358,327 before). Node 24.22 agrees with glibc on all of the first 10M; on the fixed-exponent 6M it differs in 868, exactly at y = 2 (427 of 500k, each `x * x`) and y = 0.5 (441, each `sqrt(x)`), which is what the shortcuts cover. At the JS level, 300k `x ** y` (work/powjs.js: those exponents, random y, negative x with integer y) hash the same as Node after and differently before, also with the libm port alone. Cost in instructions (cachegrind on the djsfuzz runner, whole run): 200k `Math.pow(1.0001, i % 1000) + (i * 0.37) ** 1.7` 511.9M to 513.5M (+0.3%), 200k `i ** 0.5 + Math.pow(1.0001, i % 1000)` 442.5M to 438.1M (-1.0%); per call in output/powcheck 258.7 to 257.4 (1M inputs, two reps minus one), 63 to 47 ns (7 interleaved runs of 30M, medians); wasm32 in Node 68.3 to 287.7 ns per call (6 interleaved runs, medians), the software `fma`. Gate (output/gate.sh): test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical pass sets, 25 edge cells byte-identical. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-libm/src/math/pow.rs, math/mod.rs (the fdlibm helper only `pow` used), src/lib.rs, Cargo.toml; crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/interp/conv.rs.

- feat(code-mode): a native host can give cells the CPU budget wasm hosts have, and none is set by default (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: limits policy). `set_interrupt_checks` (a cell stops with `Script stopped: one synchronous run exceeded this host's CPU budget for a cell` after that many slices of 200,000 fuel without an input) existed only on wasm. Natively a synchronous run yields its tokio worker every slice, so `exec` returns `Script running` at `yield_time_ms` and the loop holds one worker until `wait` terminates it; the 2026-11-11 terminate entry left a watchdog as a policy decision. The decision: on a machine its user owns that stays the default, since the model sees the running cell and ends it, a long synchronous computation the user asked for is legitimate there, and the rest of the process keeps running on the other workers; a host that runs unattended opts in. `set_interrupt_checks` and the slice count now exist on both targets (one `AtomicU64` instead of the wasm thread-local; wasm still starts at `DEFAULT_INTERRUPT_CHECKS`, 10,000, native at none), nanocode re-exports it under `nanocode::code_mode`, and the nanocode binary reads `NANOCODE_CELL_INTERRUPT_CHECKS`. Natively each slice adds a relaxed load and a compare before its `yield_now`. Conformance: limits/configured-interrupt-checks, limits/cpu-exhausted-next-cell-runs and the new limits/configured-budget-stops-sync-loop (cell_interrupt_checks 500, `while (true) {}`) now run on native-host and native-cli as well as the ts hosts and pass; before, native-host noted "cell_interrupt_checks has no native setting" and the loop was still running at its yield; the default-native cases (sync-loop-native-yields, sync-loop-native-terminate, microtask-loop-native-yields, regex-backtracking-native-yields) are unchanged. Commands: as for the store() writes entry below, plus `cargo clippy --offline --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-cli -- -D warnings`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/{host.rs,lib.rs}, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs, crates/nanocode/src/tools.rs, bin/nanocode/src/cells.rs.

- fix(code-mode): native hosts cap a cell's heap at half the memory available to the process when the first cell starts, and the nanocode binary and SDK can set the cap (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 Code Mode conformance track: limits policy). Natively `CELL_MEMORY` was `usize::MAX`, so a cell was bounded only by djs's u32 arena (about 4 GiB), and a runaway cell in a process with less memory than that (a container, a CI runner, a systemd unit with a memory limit, a small VM) made the kernel kill the whole process with every session and subagent in it. On Linux the default is now measured once, at the first cell (crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/memory.rs): the smaller of `/proc/meminfo` MemAvailable and, for each cgroup v2 level from the process's own up to the root, `memory.max` less `memory.current` plus `inactive_file`; then halved, because a native arena that grows is moved into a new block by the allocator and for that moment holds both copies (djs-core heap/arena.rs `reserve`: "A native allocator moves a block that grows, a copy of the whole arena"). Other targets keep no default cap (macOS and Windows have no reading here; nanocode-ts sets its own through `cell_memory_bytes`). `set_cell_memory` still overrides it and the new `cell_memory()` reads it; nanocode re-exports both under `nanocode::code_mode`, and the nanocode binary reads `NANOCODE_CELL_MEMORY` (bytes; a value that is not a whole number stops it at startup).
