- deps(tls): tokio-rustls leaves for nanocode-tls's own async TLS stream, `nanocode_tls::{connect, accept, TlsStream, ClientStream, ServerStream}` (`crates/core/tls/src/stream.rs`, 462 lines over rustls's public `ConnectionCommon` API and tokio's `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite`; 2026-11-14, TLS plan step 3). It keeps tokio-rustls 0.26.4's algorithm move for move (the handshake loop, the flush after it, `poll_fill_buf` over `Reader::into_first_chunk`, partial and vectored writes with `is_write_vectored` true, shutdown with close_notify, `NotConnected` on shutdown counted as done), without early data, `LazyConfigAcceptor` and the `AsRawFd` impls nothing used; the read and write shutdown state is one four-state enum. A rustls error stays wrapped as `io::Error(InvalidData, rustls::Error)`, so `peer_discarded_record` and the Claude BadRecordMac retry still see it, and a handshake cut short is still `UnexpectedEof` "tls handshake eof". nanocode-tls re-exports rustls, so websocket, MPP and tool-runtime name `nanocode_tls::rustls` instead of `tokio_rustls::rustls`. Callers: nanocode-http `connect::tls` (returns `ClientStream`), nanocode-websocket `MaybeTlsStream::Rustls`, tool-runtime's remote dial, the sandbox egress proxy (accept and upstream connect), store-sql's Postgres stream and the MPP proxy. The stream sits on tokio's two IO traits only, so moving it to nanocode's own runtime is swapping those traits. Checked: output/tls-stream-equal runs 10,000 seeded scripts, each once over tokio-rustls =0.26.4 and once over the new stream, on tokio duplex pipes (4 to 74 KiB) behind a wrapper that injects Pending on 0 to 59% of reads, writes and flushes and cuts reads and writes to 1 to 17,000 bytes: handshakes, up to 300 KB each way in plain or 1 to 16-buffer vectored writes, then close_notify, a drop without close_notify, double shutdown, a write after shutdown, half close with the server's close_notify, or a connection cut mid-record (the 9 outcome classes, from clean close to `UnexpectedEof` and `BrokenPipe` mid-handshake); every returned length, byte, error kind and message and rustls error downcast is identical, 0 differences of 10,000 (getrandom seeded and a fixed `TimeProvider` so both runs draw the same keys). Live through the Hand's HTTPS proxy: output/tls-live unchanged (api.anthropic.com 401, github.com, www.google.com and tls-v1-2.badssl.com:1012 200, expired, wrong.host, self-signed and untrusted-root refused); the sandbox egress `Tls` server through `nanocode_tls::accept` serves a 1 MiB body to curl over TLS 1.2 and 1.3 (6 of 6) and to OpenSSL 3.0.13 s_client for the 3 TLS 1.2 ECDSA suites and 3 TLS 1.3 suites x X25519, P-256, P-384 (12 of 12; X25519MLKEM768 is not in OpenSSL 3.0). nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --wire http and --scenario websocket, seeds 1..30, pass. `cargo metadata` resolves 157 to 156 packages (37 to 36 third-party).
- fix(claude): a reply that ends the turn with no visible text gets one nudge, as Claude Code 2.1.300 does, instead of ending the run (2026-11-14). In 2.1.300's query loop, when a response stops with `end_turn` (or `stop_sequence`), is not an API error, and none of its text blocks has non-whitespace text (empty or thinking-only), stock drops that response and continues once per turn (guard `thinkingOnlyNudged`), with messages `[...U, fe]`. `fe` is a meta user message `[Your previous response had no visible output. Please continue and produce a user-visible response.]`, which lands as a text block after the last tool results and before the `<total_tokens>` system message. A second such reply ends the run (`nudge_exhausted`). Its stream layer throws `Stream completed with message_start but no content blocks completed` only when there is no content block and no stop_reason (`yp.length===0&&!Af`), so a stock reply with `end_turn` and no blocks reaches the nudge, not a retry. nanocode accepted that reply as the final answer. That lost ds and glm winning-avg-corewars (nc-claude a1-t2: the last call was a 200 with no tokens, then nc exit 0 and reward 0). Probe lb14 empty-nc-claude: 2 requests and the run over, against 3 requests and DONE-AFTER-EMPTY for stock. Change: in crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs, after the max-tokens and context recoveries, an `end_turn` response with no tool call, no server-tool effect and no non-blank text is dropped from `pending`, once per turn (`Cursor::thinking_only_nudged`, `serde(default)`, so cursors from before this change resume). The nudge text is appended to the last non-system message when that message is a user message, and pushed as a new user message otherwise, so the request matches stock's. `stop_sequence` is not nudged, because nanocode still rejects that stop reason, and server-tool results are not dropped. In crates/backends/claude/client/src/lib.rs, `finish()` returns the retryable `IncompleteStream` instead of the fatal `Protocol("missing final stop_reason")` when a stream stops with no stop_reason and no content block, which is stock's throw. Measured with ~/wt/se-probe (lb14's mock, extended with thinking-only steps and an EMPTIES count of empty replies before text), against stock 2.1.300 and a debug nanocode built from this tree: for s_empty.json (Bash, a reply with message_start, message_delta end_turn and message_stop but no blocks, then text) and s_think.json (the same with a thinking-only reply), stock sends 3 requests and ends with DONE-AFTER-EMPTY, and so does this tree; af6c014 sent 2 and ended with no answer (thinking-only: it printed the thinking and exited 0). In both, the third request's last user message is the tool result followed by the nudge text block, then the `<total_tokens>` system message, and the nudge block is byte-identical to stock's. The rest of that message differs only as before this change (nanocode writes `type` first and leaves out `is_error: false`). With three empty replies in a row (EMPTIES=3), stock and this tree each send 3 requests and end with an empty result. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps` of the same crates with `-D warnings` passed. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/{agent.rs,agent/durable.rs}, crates/backends/claude/client/src/lib.rs.
- fix(claude): direct sessions run a foreground command that starts with a long `sleep`, as Claude Code 2.1.300 does in print mode; only a Bash call from a Code Mode cell is refused (2026-11-14). In the 2.1.300 binary the refusal in Bash `validateInput` (`jrs`: the first part of the command is exactly `sleep N` with N at least 25) runs only when `l6()&&!Ec()&&pse()&&s.remoteCall?.constraints.background!=="forbidden"&&!n.run_in_background&&s.shellWallCapMs===void 0`. `l6()` is the GrowthBook flag `tengu_amber_sentinel`, default false, and the message it pairs with sends the model to the Monitor tool. The leaderboard's `-p` runs on DeepSeek and GLM never see that flag, so stock runs the command. nanocode has refused it unconditionally since a81ec4e87 (entry of 2026-11-13, from Claude Code 2.1.316 on Opus), and its Bash description says nothing about it. Evidence: probe ~/hill/analysis/lb14 bg-nc-claude against bg-stock-claude: for `sleep 150; echo fgdone` nanocode answered `Blocked: sleep 150 followed by: echo fgdone ...`, while stock ran it. Hosted ds stock-claude made 17 foreground Bash calls with a leading `sleep` of 25 s or more across 51 trials (the old nanocode build, which had no block, made 16). In cmp2-ds-m3-claude-extract-moves-from-video-a1-t0 the refusal pushed the model into foreground wait loops (gaps of 98 to 701 s and 708 to 1318 s between calls), and the trial timed out at 1800 s. Change: crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/bash.rs refuses only when the call id carries `/code-`. That is the same test that already picks the nested timeout, and it matches the place where nanocode offers a Monitor-like wait: native Claude models reach Bash only from cells (CodeModeOnly exposure), and a cell can wait with timers. Direct sessions expose Bash as DirectOnly, so their calls never carry `/code-` and now run the command. Not changed: a foreground command that passes its timeout is still moved to the background (entry of 2026-11-13), where stock 2.1.300 kills a sleep-led one with `Exit code 143` / `Command timed out after 2m 0s`. Measured with ~/wt/se-probe (a copy of lb14's mock14.py/run14.py, script s_sleep.json: `sleep 30 && echo hi`, then `sleep 150; echo fgdone`, then DONE), against stock 2.1.300 and a debug nanocode built from this tree, model deepseek-v4.1-flash via the custom endpoint: stock runs `sleep 30 && echo hi` and returns `hi` after 30.4 s, then kills `sleep 150; echo fgdone` at 150.5 s (`Exit code 143` / `Command timed out after 2m 0s`). nanocode af6c014 refuses both at once (3 requests in 0.1 s, both `Blocked: ...`). This tree returns `hi` after 30.1 s and moves the second command to the background at 150.1 s, 3 requests like stock. A Code Mode cell under claude-opus-5-5 (s_cell.json, `await tools.Bash({command: 'sleep 30 && echo hi'})`) is still refused with the same message. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps` of the same crates with `-D warnings` passed. Files: crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/bash.rs.
- fix(codex): a custom model's `prompt_cache_key` is the session ID, as Codex 0.162.1 sends, instead of one of 4 prefix-hash buckets (2026-11-14). The earlier entry that made `nanocode-prefix-` Codex's default key gave custom models `nanocode-prefix-<sha256(model, tools, instructions)>-<sha256(session ID)[0] % 4>`, so every concurrent session with the same tools and prompt shared one of 4 keys; it said itself that models before GPT-5.6 route by key and overflow above about 15 requests a minute per key, and 5 or more concurrent Terminal-Bench trials on one route put several sessions on each key. On the Vercel DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash route, in the same 30-minute windows, nc-codex lost 7.9% of the previous call's input from cache (3,123 tokens a call, full misses on 6.7% of calls) against 3.2% for nc-claude, which sends no key, and 3.4% for stock Codex, which sends its session UUID, the same value as its `session-id` header, on every request (~/hill/analysis/cost-backlog.md finding 1; stock's ~/hill/parity/runs/stock-codex/req.jsonl). `ModelPromptCache::key` now returns the session ID (the lineage ID it was seeded with, so a spawned thread gets its own, as each Codex thread sends its own ID) for a custom model, and `CUSTOM_MODEL_KEY_BUCKETS` goes. The built-in OpenAI models keep `nanocode-prefix-<hex>`, byte for byte: OpenAI routes GPT-5.6 and later by prefix and the key only separates cache accounting, which is why a shared key let a new gpt-6-luna session read its 11k-token prefix from cache. A restored session keeps the key its checkpoint holds, and an explicit or durable key still wins. Workers AI's `x-session-affinity`, which copies the key, now pins each session to a replica as stock Codex's key does. Checked with the parity mock (`NC=<debug build> ~/hill/parity/run.py nc-codex-cachekey-a nc-codex-cachekey-b`, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, 4 requests each): each run sends one key on all 4 requests, its own session UUID (`01a1d849-8876-…`, `01a1d849-a114-…`), equal to its `session-id` header, as stock does; the master build sent `nanocode-prefix-c88c7882f72ed04e1505892fa5a718bb-1`; the first request bodies differ otherwise only in message IDs and the run's working directory. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex`, native and wasm32-unknown-unknown, passes without warnings. crates/backends/codex/src/prompt_cache.rs.
- perf(durability): natively, `MemoryStore`'s driver runs on the durability store's own thread (`nanocode-durability-store`, shared_store.rs `spawn_driver`, now `pub(crate)`) instead of on the Tokio runtime that created the store (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 CLI performance track: one-shot reply). `SharedStore` already drives every store on that thread's current-thread runtime (D-entry (11) of the five-roots swarm work, 30ac1a33f), but an in-memory store (`nc exec --ephemeral`, the terminal's `--ephemeral`, the SDK's default) kept its own driver task on the host runtime, so each store operation crossed threads four times: the session's worker woke the store thread, which sent the command back to the memory driver on the worker, which woke the store thread with the result, which woke the worker. With both drivers on the store thread the middle two hops are a local wake inside that runtime. A one-shot crossed threads about 29 times between the worker and the store thread; `bpftrace` on `sched:sched_wakeup` over 10 one-shots counted 173 worker-to-store and 117 store-to-worker wakeups before, 95 and 49 after. A platform host (nanocode-sim) still gets the driver, as before, and WebAssembly still drives it with `spawn_local`, so nanocode-ts runs none of this change. `MemoryStore::new` no longer needs a Tokio runtime natively, as `SharedStore::new` already did not. Measured on dev-georgios (load 60 to 110) with release builds of 62a0936e4 with the observability change above, with and without this one, `perf stat` around the bench/cli fixture's one-shot (`nanocode exec --gateway vercel --gateway-base-url <fixture>/v1 -m luna --ephemeral "Reply BENCH[run=…]"` under tools/netguard.sh), 3 interleaved batches of 6 runs (18 each), medians: context switches 56 to 42, kernel instructions 20,168,114 to 19,971,174 (-1.0%), user instructions 12,522,092 to 12,500,335, task-clock 12.81 to 12.56 ms; bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=oneshot --only=nc --rounds=4` alternating release builds of 62a0936e4 and of both changes over 3 batches (12 samples each, load 77, so times are relative): request end to exit 22.05 to 17.75 ms, wall 76.66 to 71.29 ms, CPU 17.77 to 16.87 ms, spawn to request 50.91 and 51.68 ms. `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-durability --no-deps -- -D warnings`, and again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, pass. Files: crates/runtime/durability/src/memory.rs, crates/runtime/durability/src/shared_store.rs.

- perf(observability): `ObservabilityGuard::shutdown` starts its scoped thread only when there is both a tracer and a meter provider to shut down at once; with one or none it shuts them down on the calling thread (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 CLI performance track: one-shot reply). Every `nc exec` and terminal session dropped the guard on exit, and `shutdown` always spawned and joined a thread for the tracer, even with telemetry off (`NANOCODE_TELEMETRY=off`, as the benchmark runs) where both providers are `None`: the thread did nothing but cost a `clone3`, a stack, mimalloc's thread init and teardown, and a join on the exit path. In a `perf record -F 20000 --call-graph dwarf` of six one-shots of the dist build at 62a0936e4 against bench/cli's fixture under tools/netguard.sh, the guard's drop was 10 of the 165 main-thread samples (1.3% of all of nanocode's 785). With both providers the tracer still shuts down on its own thread while the meter shuts down on the caller, as before, and a panicking tracer shutdown is still ignored. Measured on dev-georgios (load 60 to 110, so counters rather than times) with release builds of 62a0936e4 with and without the change, `perf stat -e instructions:u,instructions:k,page-faults,task-clock,context-switches` around `nanocode exec --gateway vercel --gateway-base-url <fixture>/v1 -m luna --ephemeral "Reply BENCH[run=…]"` under netguard, 3 interleaved batches of 6 runs (18 each), medians: user instructions 12,598,224 to 12,521,930 (-76K, -0.6%), kernel instructions 20,509,704 to 20,183,298 (-326K, -1.6%), task-clock 13.13 to 12.14 ms, page faults 2,008 to 2,006; `strace -f -e clone3` counts 11 threads started per one-shot before and 10 after. nanocode-ts does not run this code (the guard is native-only). `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-observability --no-deps -- -D warnings` passes. Files: crates/integrations/observability/src/lib.rs.

- deps(tls): rustls-graviola leaves for nanocode-tls's own rustls provider, `nanocode_tls::provider()` (`crates/core/tls/src/provider/`, 1,213 lines over graviola; 2026-11-14, TLS plan step 6). It offers what rustls-graviola 0.4.0's `default_provider()` did, in the same order: the 3 TLS 1.3 and 6 TLS 1.2 ECDHE suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), the groups X25519MLKEM768, X25519, secp256r1 and secp384r1, and the same `WebPkiSupportedAlgorithms` table (ECDSA P-256 and P-384 with SHA-256/384/512, Ed25519, RSA-PSS and PKCS#1 with SHA-256/384/512). Two things differ: the key provider loads only ECDSA P-256 server keys (PKCS#8 or SEC1), which is every key nanocode serves with (the sandbox's egress leaves from `KeyPair::generate` and the MPP proxy's key), and refuses RSA, P-384 and Ed25519 with a typed `rustls::Error::General`; CA keys of those types still sign certificates through graviola directly. rustls-graviola's `Ticketer` is gone, since no server config sets one. The hash and HMAC providers are one generic over graviola's `Hash`, and the verification algorithms one struct of function pointers. `install_default_rustls_crypto_provider()` and the sandbox's egress `provider()` use it; the MPP proxy keeps taking the installed default. nanocode-tls turns on rustls's tls12 feature itself (sandbox and mpp already did). Checked: output/tls-equal patches getrandom with a seeded generator and gives every config a fixed `TimeProvider`, then runs 150 cases (3 TLS 1.3 suites x 4 groups, 6 TLS 1.2 suites x 3 groups, with and without ALPN, server keys P-256, P-384, RSA-2048 and Ed25519 from openssl), each as two connections (the second resumes) carrying 0, 1, 16383, 16384, 16385 and 1 MiB both ways, a TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate and close_notify from both sides: every transcript with nanocode's provider on the client, the server or both is byte-identical to rustls-graviola on both (468 compared pairs, about 4.4 MB each, 0 differences); suite, group and `supported_schemes()` lists are equal; nanocode's server refuses the 108 non-P-256 cases at `with_single_cert`, as intended. output/tls-live through the Hand's HTTPS proxy unchanged. nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --wire http and --scenario websocket, seeds 1..30: all pass (the simulated wire carries no TLS). `cargo metadata` resolves 158 to 157 packages (38 to 37 third-party).
- deps(tls): webpki-root-certs leaves for a Mozilla root table nanocode generates itself (2026-11-14, TLS plan step 2, the generated-table alternative). `scripts/generate-mozilla-roots.py` reads CCADB's IncludedCACertificateReportPEMCSV (the report webpki-root-certs is generated from), keeps the roots with the Websites trust bit, checks each certificate against its SHA-256 fingerprint and writes them, sorted by fingerprint as webpki-root-certs orders them, as concatenated DER to `crates/core/platform/src/trust/mozilla_roots.der` (118,538 bytes); `nanocode_platform::trust::mozilla_roots()` splits it by each certificate's DER length. The patched rustls-platform-verifier's Linux fallback (a host without a CA bundle) trusts that table instead of webpki-root-certs, and its wasm32 branch no longer adds bundled roots: nothing builds the verifier on wasm32, and an empty store there is webpki's `NoRootAnchors`. Updating the table is rerunning the script; Mozilla changes the list several times a year. Checked: today's report gives 112 roots, each byte-equal to its entry in webpki-root-certs 1.0.10; 1.0.10's other 8 are roots Mozilla has removed since. output/roots-check: `mozilla_roots()` adds 112 of 112 to a `RootCertStore`; `system_roots()` gives the 122 roots of the Hand's bundle, and with `SSL_CERT_FILE` missing and `SSL_CERT_DIR` empty the 112 generated ones. `cargo metadata` resolves 159 to 158 packages (39 to 38 third-party). output/tls-live through the Hand's HTTPS proxy unchanged (anthropic 401, github, google and badssl TLS 1.2 200, four bad certificates refused).
- deps(webpki): the vendored rustls-webpki carries untrusted 0.9.0 itself as `src/untrusted.rs` (`Input`, `Reader`, `EndOfInput`, `read_all_optional`, 150 lines, crate-private, without the `no_panic::Slice` wrapper, docs or tests), and its 259 `untrusted::` paths became `crate::untrusted::` (2026-11-14, TLS plan step 1). untrusted had no other user, so it leaves the graph (`cargo metadata` resolves 160 to 159 packages, 40 to 39 third-party). Checked: output/untrusted-equal runs 1,000,000 seeded scripts (read_byte, read_bytes, skip, peek, at_end, read_partial with failing closures, read_bytes_to_end, skip_to_end, read_all and read_all_optional with incomplete reads) over random inputs through crates.io untrusted =0.9.0 and the copy: 0 differences. output/tls-live through the Hand's HTTPS proxy: api.anthropic.com 401, github.com, www.google.com and tls-v1-2.badssl.com:1012 200, expired, wrong.host, self-signed and untrusted-root badssl refused, the same as before.
- perf(turnlog): a commit serializes its records by reference straight into one byte buffer; estimating the snapshot check's compressed state from a measured density was tried and not kept (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `Lease::commit` built its row with `crate::encode(&floor.iter().chain(&writer.buffer).cloned().collect::<Vec<_>>())`: a deep clone of every buffered record, one String per record from `serde_json::to_string`, appended to another String. `record::encode_all` now writes each record with `serde_json::to_writer` into one `Vec<u8>` over the floor and buffer by reference, and the writer hands those bytes to the stream, the boundary row and the history without a UTF-8 round trip (`encode` keeps its signature). Rows are byte-identical. nanocode-ts output/prof.ts (200 turns of each kind, wasm after wasm-opt, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, three interleaved rounds, dev-georgios, load 70-110): 32.13, 33.25, 32.26M instructions per turn before, 32.00, 32.32, 31.98M after (-0.6% to -2.8%). output/turnlog-replay (2,318,664 bytes of a stored nanocode-ts session replayed with FAIL_EVERY=7 REOPEN_EVERY=5) stores the same bytes and reopens to the same fold digests. Tried and not kept: the writer kept the packed and plain sizes of the last state it compressed and, while the state stayed within `ratio` times that plain size, scaled the state's length by that density instead of deflating the whole state at each snapshot check (still compressing for real, and re-deciding, when the estimate said a snapshot was due). It took another 1.5% (31.68, 31.39, 31.73M in the same rounds), but a larger state compresses better than a smaller one, so the estimate runs high and a snapshot came later than the ratio allows: at 100 turns (DUMP=1) 2,349,546 bytes stored and a 469,229-byte snapshot against 2,264,880 and 406,485, +3.7% stored and a cold read past `ratio` times the compressed state. The first version, which wrote a snapshot on the estimate alone, wrote two snapshots where one was due (2,727,908 bytes against 2,276,751). Checks: `nanocode-sim --scenario turns --policy turnlog` seeds 0..2000 `--twice` with faults and 0..500 `--calm --snapshot-ratio 1` (all pass); `cargo clippy --no-deps -D warnings` of nanocode-turnlog native and wasm32; rustfmt of the changed files. Files: crates/core/turnlog/src/{record.rs,writer.rs}.
- scripts/build-cli.sh lays out the Linux CLI's hot code with what runs to the first frame first: the training runs the terminal interface once more on its own, to its first frame and a second after it (`train-cli.py <binary> startup`), and BOLT places the functions that run there first, then the rest, each group in the order `-reorder-functions=cdsort` gives (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 CLI performance: startup RSS <= 12 MB). Before, cdsort spread the code the first frame runs over the whole 4 MB hot `.text`, plus code only the first frame runs, which the training's profile did not cover, in `.text.cold`. Linux maps file pages 64 KB around each fault, so every 64 KB block touched stays resident. With fault-around set to 4 KB for one run of each build (`perf record -e page-faults -d`, `/sys/kernel/debug/fault_around_bytes`), the first frame and the second after it touched 762 `.text` pages in 65 blocks and 34 `.text.cold` pages in 23 blocks; now they touch 627 pages in 49 blocks, all in the first 2.5 MB, and 11 cold pages in 10 blocks. How it is built: `train-cli.py <binary> startup` runs only the terminal session: it waits for the screen to settle, waits `MEMORY_AFTER_FIRST_FRAME` (1 s, when bench/cli reads memory) and quits. Its profiles go in `startup/` and are merged with the training's. A first BOLT pass with cdsort writes `-generate-function-order`, `scripts/order-cli.py` puts that list's functions that appear in a startup profile (a nonzero edge from or to them) first, and the final pass uses `-reorder-functions=user -function-order` with otherwise unchanged flags. The extra pass costs about a minute and peaks at 8.5 GB, as the others do, and they run one after another. Measured on dev-georgios with the same pre-BOLT dist binary and training for every build (BOLT 19), bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe --only=nc --rounds=3`, alternating builds in 3 batches (9 samples each, load average 55 to 137 from other jobs). Final script against the shipped layout: RSS 1 s after the first frame 13.47 to 12.34 MB; under `perf stat`, page faults 857 to 834, kernel instructions 12.37M to 12.24M, user instructions 9.13M both, task clock 8.07 to 7.83 ms. An earlier round against the same baseline: 13.32 to 12.24 MB, 846 to 820 faults, kernel 12.98M to 11.88M. The startup run's profile with plain cdsort (13.36 MB, 859 faults) left this unchanged, so the order is what helps. One-shot (`--parts=oneshot`, 6 batches, 18 samples each): user 9.68M and 9.69M, kernel 12.02M and 12.23M, page faults 886 and 889, task clock 7.98 and 7.74 ms, within noise. Measured and not adopted, on the new layout through an LD_PRELOAD constructor: `madvise(MADV_POPULATE_READ)` of `__hot_start..__hot_end` at startup cut 32 faults but cost 30.0M kernel instructions against 17.8M and 14.06 MB against 12.15 MB (3 samples). Over only the 2.5 MB the startup code spans it cut 32 faults (868 against 900), and its kernel instructions were 13.9M against 13.5M with RSS 13.19 against 12.15 MB (9 and 12 samples): mapping every page costs more than the faults it saves and keeps untouched pages resident. `MADV_WILLNEED` only reads into the page cache and maps nothing. `.rodata` stays as the linker lays it out: the first frame touches 264 of its pages, spread over 6.5 MB, so 3 MB is resident. But its 8,098 symbols cover 0.87 MB, and half the touched addresses lie more than 10 KB past the nearest symbol (anonymous constants and merged strings), so an lld `--symbol-ordering-file` cannot name them, and BOLT's `-reorder-data` needs a memory-access profile, which instrumentation does not record. nanocode-ts does not go through this script: its wasm is unchanged. Commands: llvm-bolt-19 on `target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/dist/nanocode` with each layout, the build's steps run by hand in the order build-cli.sh runs them, and `sh -n scripts/build-cli.sh`. Files: scripts/build-cli.sh, scripts/train-cli.py, scripts/order-cli.py.
- bin/nanocode-sim `--scenario turns --policy turnlog` also runs Code Mode cells through the real `OneLog`, `OneLogStore` and `OneLogJournals` (bin/nanocode-sim/src/cells.rs), with a host crash at every persist point (2026-11-14, Georgios: make the simulator see the cell journal bug of cfd8999c7). Each seed runs 1 to 3 turns in one session, each with one cell: synchronous, waiting on a timer, calling `charge` (External) or `Read` (None), and the header saved alone or with the cell's first entries. A turn is the sequence the runtime writes: submit, start, the model step checkpoint (`StateStore::commit`, `Settle::Durable`), the cell's saves, the next step, `forget` and finish. A host (`CellHost`, a `LogHost` over a `BTreeMap`) refuses the next append or dies after an op, at a uniformly drawn op, 0 to `RESTART_CAP - 1` times per turn. A reopened incarnation reads the turn, the checkpoint and the journal (`sink().load`, `Fold::cells`), and then resumes the cell, reruns a cell that never reached disk, or asks the model again. Invariants: `cell_model_once` (no recovered turn asks the model again for the step of a cell that waited on a timer or a running External call when the host died), `cell_lost` (the journal of such a cell survives), `cell_external_once` (a charge runs at most once, and a completed turn charged once or reported the outcome unknown) and `cell_rows` (a turn without a crash commits 2 rows with a synchronous or `Read` cell and 3 with a timer or `charge` cell). `OneLog::sink` returns the `CellJournalSink` that `journals` already built, as `gate` returns the `EffectGate`. The simulator found that `OneLog`'s `close` (finish, cancel, withdraw) returned "finished turn ... is missing" after it committed the finish when `Policy.retain_finished` is `Some(0)`, since the commit retires the turn before the record is read: all 2,000 seeds of `--retain 0` panicked on it. `close` now builds the returned record from the turn it finishes. Mutations of `OneLogJournals::save`, each built separately and run over seeds 0..2000 with `--twice` (the same counts with `--retain 0`): buffer-only (`if external.is_empty() {`, the rule before cfd8999c7) fails 678 seeds (cell_model_once 338, cell_rows 293, cell_lost 47; timer cells commit 2.00 rows); without the timed branch (`!(fresh || pending)`, a row at every cell start as in cfd8999c7) fails 687 (cell_rows: synchronous 3.00, Read 3.00, charge 3.52 rows); without `pending` (`!(timed && fresh)`) fails 366 (cell_model_once 178, cell_rows 164, cell_lost 24: a timer armed after a header saved alone); External calls buffered (`if !(timed && (fresh || pending)) {`) fails 728 (cell_model_once 372, cell_rows 281, cell_lost 75). No mutation makes `cell_external_once` the first failure, since a lost External row first makes recovery ask the model again. Unmutated: `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 10000 5 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` passed 10,000 of 10,000 (31 s on the 5-core hosted Hand), and the same with `--retain 0` passed 10,000 of 10,000 (36 s). Over seeds 0..2000: 3,968 cell turns, 3,956 crashes, 1,338 recovered turns that asked the model again for a cell that never waited, 544 charges reported unknown, 993 charges, and rows per crash-free turn synchronous 2.00 (319 turns), timer 3.00 (341), charge 3.00 (329), Read 2.00 (293). The simulator drives the sink with the updates Code Mode writes, not QuickJS cells, so the save order follows replay.rs (`persist`, `mark_finished`) as read, not as run.
- `nanocode-turnlog` bounds the rows a cold open reads: `TurnLog::snapshot_rows(Some(n))` and `Policy.snapshot_rows` write a snapshot once n rows follow the last one, the load query finds the last snapshot by a reverse key scan, and `OneLog` turn pages start at the turn's first event (2026-11-14, Georgios: make a cold open read a bounded number of rows independent of session length). Why it was not bounded: (1) the load query's `SELECT MAX(seq) ... WHERE substr(body, 1, 1) = 's'` cannot use the key, so SQLite visited every row of the scope before the outer range read; (2) the byte rule (snapshot plus tail above ratio x the compressed state) never fires when the log is the state: a durable-cloudflare session of 203 turns had 418 `r` rows (260,314 B) and no `s` row, so a cold open read every row twice (812-828 rows from that one statement). Cold reads in rows grow with length under the byte rule even when it fires, because the tail it allows grows with the state. Now `Writer::tail_rows` counts the stored rows after the last snapshot's first row (its parts included, recounted at open) and `Lease::commit` writes the snapshot in place of the row when `tail_rows >= n`, besides the byte rule. A cold open then reads at most 2 x (n + one commit's parts) + 1 log rows: the subquery is `SELECT seq ... ORDER BY seq DESC LIMIT 1`, which walks the key backwards and stops at the snapshot. A log written before this change loads as before once, and its next commit becomes a snapshot. The limit is caller policy because it trades snapshot bytes (old snapshots stay, deleting a row bills as a write) against cold rows. Readers: older events stay in segments that `TurnLog::history` scans lazily, but `OneLog::turn_page` from cursor 0 scanned every segment to filter one turn's events, so snapshots moved the cold read into paging (first build: 24 scans reading 814 rows at 203 turns). `paged` now starts at `max(after, turn.first - 1)` for a turn the fold knows, because a turn's events follow its admission event. Measured with durable-cloudflare output/turns.mjs (local workerd, `TURNS=1 LONG=5|43|200`, one run each, 3 cold opens per run, each cold open = restart, one turn, one warm turn; rows of the cold turn and the warm turn after it; ms of the cold turn on the shared 5-core Hand), build-0624213 against nanocode-ts 0624213 with `snapshot_rows: Some(n)` and this SDK (wasm built with `cargo build --profile wasm` and `wasm-opt -O3` as scripts/build.mjs does, dropped into the release dry-run bundle): 8 turns 100/108/116 rows before, 100/108/116 with n = 32 (below n, unchanged); 46 turns 252/260/268 (log statement 184/192/200) before, 122/130/72 (54/62/4) with n = 32, 124/132/140 (56/64/72) with n = 64; 203 turns 880/888/896 (812/820/828) before, 90/98/106 (22/30/38) with n = 32, 102/110/118 (34/42/50) with n = 64. Cold turn ms: before 288/211/284, 302/289/207, 358/542/300; n = 32 206/244/264, 187/194/165, 188/201/196; n = 64 (with other agents' load) 259/323/249, 263/291/234. Warm turns are unchanged: reply 2 rows written, cell 2, timer 3, charge 3, 0 read. Cost, stored bytes at 203 turns: 260,314 B before, 281,806 B of rows plus 12 snapshots of 1,734,602 B (largest 260,619) with n = 32, 275,515 B plus 6 snapshots of 912,163 B with n = 64; at 46 turns n = 32 wrote 3 snapshots (170,689 B), n = 64 one (54,823 B). The snapshot is near the whole log because the state is the conversation, so stored bytes grow about as length squared over n. nanocode-sim takes `--snapshot-rows N` and asserts after each commit that a cold load would read at most N + the commit's extra parts + 1 rows. The `snapshot_rows_ignored` mutation is caught on 274 of 300 seeds (`sweep.sh 0 300 5 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --snapshot-rows 4 --mutation snapshot_rows_ignored`). Checks: `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 2000 5 --scenario turns --policy turnlog` with `--twice`, `--twice --retain 0`, `--twice --snapshot-rows 4`, `--twice --retain 0 --snapshot-rows 0` `--twice --snapshot-rows 3 --row-limit 1024` and `--twice --calm --snapshot-rows 2`: 2,000 of 2,000 pass each, 0 panics. durable-cloudflare `npm run drill` with the n = 64 bundle: 3 of 3 scenarios complete with no failures. `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog -p nanocode-agent` natively, `-p nanocode-turnlog` with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `-p nanocode-agent -p nanocode-code-mode --features nanocode-code-mode/local-cells` with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (nanocode-agent alone does not build for wasm32 on master, as noted above). `cargo clippy --no-deps -- -D warnings` for nanocode-turnlog on both targets, and for nanocode-agent and nanocode-sim natively with `-A clippy::useless_conversion`. rustfmt on the changed files. Files: crates/core/turnlog/src/{host,writer}.rs, crates/runtime/agent/src/one_log.rs, bin/nanocode-sim/src/{main,turnlog,turns}.rs.
- fix(code-mode, codex): image tool results that exceed the hand's `max_frame_bytes` are shrunk to fit instead of dropped, and a compact nested call sends an image's data URL once (2026-11-13, Terminal-Bench extract-moves-from-video trace review of nanocode 999400a8: 5 per-call drops and a cell that lost 3 images in one Codex attempt, 3 of 4 view_image results and a whole cell output in a Claude attempt). Causes: Codex's view_image put the file's bytes unresized into both `output` (`input_image`) and `structured_result.image_url`, and Claude's Read result carries its image block in both `output` and `structured_result.content`, so one 1280x720 frame or a ~440 KB JPEG crossed the 1 MiB hand->brain frame and `reply_text` replaced the result with `remote frame of N bytes exceeds ... the result was not sent`; a cell whose `image()` items summed past 1 MiB lost its whole output. Three changes. (1) A brain that understands it sends `shared_images: true` on its requests (the client always does now; an older brain doesn't, and gets what it got before); the hand then encodes a compact nested call or a `Call` reply whose structured result repeats a data URL of its `output` images with that string set to null and `output_images: {JSON pointer: output index}`, and `ReceivedCalls`/`output_from_wire` put the string back, so JS still sees `result.image_url` and `result.content[0]`, byte for byte. (2) `Outgoing::encode` on the hand, when a reply, update or detached update is over the connection's limit, shrinks the frame's distinct `data:image/...;base64,` strings in proportion to their size so that they and the rest of the frame fit the limit: each image over its share goes through `nanocode_image::fit_data_url`, which composites alpha over white (as Claude Read's JPEG step does), encodes a JPEG at the prompt path's quality 85 (Codex's) at full size, and while it is still too big scales both sides by sqrt(share / size) and tries again; only when that fails does the old cut or drop path run. This matches what the CLIs do with images too large for their limits (Codex CLI resizes to fit, Claude Code downsizes and re-encodes as JPEG at falling quality) applied to our one extra limit, the frame. (3) Codex view_image goes through `nanocode_image::load_for_prompt_data_url` (now built for wasm too) as Codex CLI's view_image does: resized to the high (2048 px, 2,500 patches) or original limits, PNG, JPEG and WebP kept, other formats as PNG, and an undecodable file is the tool error `unable to process image at ...` instead of an `application/octet-stream` data URL the brain later swapped for a placeholder; a 1280x720 frame is within the high limits and is unchanged by this step. Measured with output/image-frame-budget (a HandCore with a stub HandHost whose session runs the real Codex `WorkspaceToolRuntime` view_image and `ClaudeWorkspaceFiles` Read, wrapped as claude_files.rs does, driven over the wire at max_frame_bytes 1,048,576; gak-9): 1280x720 PNGs of 1.71 MB and 1280x720 JPEGs of 443 KB. On origin/master e4779d26f: view_image call reply 4,559,807 bytes, dropped; Read call 1,181,388, dropped; a cell of 4 view_images 9,120,231 and of 4 Reads 2,365,635, both `the script's output was not sent`. With this change: view_image call 160,669 bytes (the PNG as a 1280x720 JPEG), Read call 590,862 (the JPEG unchanged, sent once), the view_image cell's 4 update frames about 160,700 each and its reply 642,259, the Read cell's updates about 591,000 each (unchanged) and its reply 628,139 (4 images at 1280x720, about 157,000 bytes each); every image decodes and comes out of the brain's `prepare_output_images` as an image at 1280x720, and the structured results' copies equal the output's. With noisier frames (PNG 2.68 MB, JPEG 1.43 MB) a 4-image view_image cell comes out at 766x431 per image in a 641,455-byte reply. Not done: shrinking runs on the hand's sending task, not a blocking worker (one 1280x720 decode and encode); the VM path's `VIEW_IMAGE_WIRE_COPIES` estimate in view_image/native.rs is untouched (every caller passes no wire limit); a non-compact brain still gets both copies. Commands: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-image -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-backend-claude` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --lib` on code-mode, image and backend-codex natively and for wasm32 (no warnings). Files: crates/core/image/src/lib.rs, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/remote/{client.rs,compact.rs,frame.rs,hand.rs,mod.rs}, crates/backends/codex/src/builtin_tools/view_image/{host.rs,native.rs}.
- The interactive CLI starts the paying proxy and the connection warm-up after its first frame instead of before it (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 CLI performance track: toward the 1.3 ms first frame). tempo::apply bound the proxy's listener and spawned nanocode-paying-proxy on the main thread before the async runtime existed; that thread generated the proxy's CA key, wrote the certificate bundle, built a runtime and spawned mpp-forward-proxy, and `clients.warming()` (DNS and connections to the model hosts) was spawned on the runtime: all of it ran while the main thread was still drawing. Now `pay_tools` only binds (the listener queues connections until the proxy accepts them, and the tool environment with its address, token and bundle path is the same) and returns the thread's spawn as `tempo::Start`, which `Closing` hands to run_with; run_with spawns one task that waits for `app::FIRST_FRAME` (a `tokio::sync::Notify` the event loop signals after its first successful draw; notify_one keeps the permit if the task is not waiting yet) for the TUI and resumed sessions, then starts the proxy and the warm-up; `nc exec` and the other commands run them at once, as before. A shell command needs a model turn first, so the proxy is up long before one runs. Measured on dev-georgios (load 65-80) with both builds from scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, BOLT 19): bpftrace from exec to the first frame's write (20 kHz samples, 20 runs each, interleaved): threads created before the first frame 174 to 130 (8.7 to 6.5 per run), samples on threads other than main 714 to 514 (-28%), main thread 775 and 784 (unchanged: the main thread is the first frame's critical path, so on an idle machine its latency moves little); whole-process counters to exit, which include the deferred work (suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc, 4 interleaved batches under perf stat, 16 samples each): user instructions 9.17M and 9.22M, kernel 12.64M and 12.56M, page faults 884 and 882, resident memory 1 s after the first frame 24.6 and 24.4 MB (with the bench's telemetry). Checked: 2 s into the TUI and 0.6 s into `nc exec`, the process has its mpp-forward-proxy thread and /tmp/mpp-forward-proxy-PID.pem. nanocode-ts does not run this code (bin/nanocode only). Commands: `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-cli --no-deps -- -D warnings`, rustfmt. Files: bin/nanocode/src/{app,lib,tempo}.rs.
- fix(codex): with a Code Mode host and no configured working directory, the environment context's `cwd` is the working directory of the hand where Code Mode scripts run, not the brain's placeholder workspace `/` (2026-11-14, Terminal-Bench 2.1 make-mips-interpreter: nanox 0/2 against Codex CLI 0.166.0's 1/1). The Worker (nanocode-ts build-f1b2093, `workspace: false`, `hands: 'always'`) builds the runtime with `.workspace("/")`, so `EmbeddedToolRuntime::working_directory` was `/`, and Codex's `<environment_context>` told the model `<cwd>/</cwd>` even though nanoeval starts the slot's hand with `-C /app` and that hand advertises `workspace: "/app"` (the `hands` tool in the same eval answered `{"hands":["slot"],"here":"slot","about":{"slot":{"workspace":"/app",...}}}`). gpt-6-luna believed it: in nanoeval run ec71aa6d attempt a00145 its first command was `pwd` with `workdir:"/"` (answer `/`), every `exec_command` passed `workdir:"/"`, it wrote `/vm.js` instead of `/app/vm.js`, and the verifier's `node /app/vm.js` failed with `Cannot find module '/app/vm.js'` after the interpreter had booted Doom and saved a correct frame. Codex CLI in the same task got `/app` as its cwd and wrote `/app/vm.js` (a00146, passed). run.started also reported `"workspace":"/"` on c876ad68 a00027, the other nanox attempt, which happened to use absolute `/app` paths and failed for an unrelated reason (its interpreter never saved `/tmp/frame.bmp` within the verifier's 30 s). `CodeModeHost` gets `working_directory(session_id)`, by default the `workspace` of `describe()`; `CodeModeExecutors` answers the one from the hand its placement for the session resolves to (no answer when scripts run locally or the hand is not attached); `ToolRuntime::context_directory` uses it for the embedded runtime and falls back to the runtime's working directory, and the three places the Codex backend captures the context use it. A configured execution-environment working directory still wins, as before, and a hand that attaches or changes later moves the `cwd` through the existing environment diff. The Claude backend is unchanged: without a configured directory it prints no working directory line. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, passed. Not run: a nanocode-ts rebuild and nanoeval rerun. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/{embedded/mod.rs,remote/executors.rs}, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{embedded/runtime.rs,runtime/execution.rs}, crates/backends/codex/src/model/run/{mod.rs,turn.rs}.
- perf(djs): restoring the image swaps the compile buffers and the identifier atom cache into the fresh heap instead of taking them, and an empty `CodeBuf` builds no label vector (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: cell overhead). `Heap::restore_image` moved `compile_scratch` and `ident_atoms` over with `mem::take`, which builds a default `resolve::Scratch` (and its `CodeBuf`, `ParserSpare`, peephole and stack scratches) in the old heap only to drop it with that heap; `mem::swap` hands the fresh heap's defaults back instead, so each cell builds and drops one `Scratch` rather than two. `CodeBuf::default` went through `make(0)`, whose `vec![UNPLACED; 0]` runs the fill path for nothing; it is now the struct of empty vectors, which matters because the compiler `take`s `scratch.out` once per function and `Scratch::default` builds one. output/cellbench, instructions per cell (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, N 1200 minus N 200, over 1000, interleaved twice, dev-georgios): empty cell 86.4k -> 85.9k with the swap alone, 85.6k with both (-0.9%); 16 sequential tool calls 1,133.8k -> 1,133.0k; the agent cell 949.1k -> 948.7k (the swap is in both); compiling the 8 corpus cells 34.67M -> 34.63M per round (-0.1%). test262 subset 8,631 passing, identical pass set; edge cells print the same; disassembly of 442 files identical; nanocode-ts Node overhead bench completes every cell. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/mod.rs, bytecode/code.rs.

- Rejected: keeping a session's wire order between requests so `wire_messages` handles only new history messages (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `wire_messages` clones every history message into the request's list, separates tool-result companions and moves each tool-change system message after the user messages that follow it, for every model request; in a Node CPU profile of output/prof.ts (one session of 1,200 turns) its collect was 2.0% self after 24812571d. The variant kept the ordered list, the held tool-change messages and the wire ids seen in a `Slot` on the session and, while the new history extended the ids seen, ran only the new messages through the same order as a stream (users go out at once, tool changes wait for the next message that is neither, which equals the backward bubbling: 200,000 random role sequences, cut anywhere, identical), then copied the list. The profile frame left (claude group 17.5% to 15.9% of samples), but output/prof.ts `perf stat -e instructions:u`, eight interleaved pairs, measured 33.98, 33.48, 33.58, 33.59, 33.65, 33.49, 34.00, 33.65M instructions per turn on master and 34.04, 33.31, 33.16, 33.13, 33.85, 33.72, 33.14, 33.77M with it (mean -0.5%, inside the spread), for a second list of every message per session, so it stays out.
- perf(djs): `ErrorConstruct`, the body every Error and NativeError constructor runs, captures the stack itself instead of calling `RecordStack`, so `new Error` runs one prelude call fewer (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: the new Error gap to QuickJS). `RecordStack` is not inlined by djs-bgen (its `if` falls through, 0230), so each error paid a JS frame push and return for it; ErrorConstruct now holds `if (CaptureStack(o)) { FinishErrorStack(o); }`, and djs-bgen inlines FinishErrorStack there as it did into RecordStack. The trace is unchanged: CaptureStack skips the prelude frames at the top either way. The other RecordStack callers (disposable, web, the AggregateError path) keep it. Instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, best of 3, interleaved, dev-georgios, djsrun): 200,000 `new Error` 1,926.6M -> 1,818.2M (-5.6%, 9.6k -> 9.1k per error; QuickJS 7.8k); the same from three nested calls 2,315.5M -> 2,207.1M (-4.7%; QuickJS 2,845.3M); generators, compute and promises unchanged. cellbench per cell (N 1200 minus N 200, over 1000, interleaved twice): empty 89.0k -> 89.1k (+0.1%), agent 993.9k both. test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 passing, the same set; the 25 edge cells print the same output and events as the build before this change. Files: crates/patches/djs/builtins/error.ts and its generated builtins/gen/{prelude,prelude-slim,prelude-noembed}.js, resume-points.txt (`cargo run -p djs-bgen` in crates/patches/djs).
- SLA.md records the 2026-11-14 latency round: live Codex against Codex CLI 0.166.0 on gpt-6-luna and gpt-6.1-sol, mock throughput, and the deployed Worker split by `server-timing` (2026-11-14). nanocode leads Codex CLI on every gpt-6-luna turn (1,022 against 1,500 ms p50 on turn 1) and on the first gpt-6.1-sol turn, and trails it by 70 to 320 ms p50 on later gpt-6.1-sol turns. A new Worker session spends 836 to 905 ms p50 in Durable Object start before its `fetch` runs, against 59 to 65 ms of session work to response headers, so object start, not admission, is the cold first turn's pre-header cost. The Worker client draws at the provider's rate (0.99 of its window on Claude). Commands: nanocode-ts `bench/sla/run.ts` lanes `live-nc-codex@now,live-codex` and `nc@now,nc-claude@now,claude,codex` from dev-georgios, and gak-9's `p99.mjs` with 12 rounds of 3 turns per provider against durable-cloudflare fbc9a2b.

- POSIX mode: `set -o posix`, `shopt -so posix`, `bash -o posix` and `--posix` turn it on, where psh used to stop the script as unsupported (2026-11-13). This reverses upstream's D002, which left POSIX mode out of scope. In POSIX mode a special builtin comes before a function of the same name; a function can't be defined with a special builtin's name (status 2, ends the shell); assignments in front of a special builtin stay set and exported; and a special builtin's errors end the shell: status 2 (usage errors such as `set -o bogus`, `shift abc`, `export --help`, `return` outside a function) unless its status is tested, assignment errors (`readonly r=2` on a readonly variable, `export 1x=2`, `unset` of a readonly or invalid name) and a `.` file that can't be read even when tested, and a failed redirection on it (`exec 3<missing`, `: >/missing/f`). Errors that come back through `command` or `builtin` don't end the shell. An assignment error with no command, or in front of a special builtin, ends the shell. In front of another command, a readonly variable abandons the line in POSIX mode; outside it, the error is printed and the command runs (bash). `command declare a=$v` expands as a declaration; `alias x` and bare `alias` print without the `alias ` prefix (`-p` keeps it); `echo` with xpg_echo takes no options; `shift` past the end says the count is out of range; `break` and `continue` outside a loop are silent; `exit` with too many arguments is status 1; a trapped signal ends `read` with 128+n. The fast path in now.rs is skipped in POSIX mode. Two fixes outside POSIX mode: `type` without -a reports only the first kind it finds, where it listed both a function and the builtin it shadows, and `export r=2`/`readonly r=2` on a readonly variable say `r: readonly variable` without the builtin's name, as bash does. psh-spec (upstream psh's suites, bash 5.3 goldens): oils 2413->2418/2511, brush 2941->2967/3171, agent 727/727, utils unchanged; of the 35 POSIX-mode cases, only the CHLD trap interrupting `wait` still fails (psh runs no CHLD traps yet). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/alias.rs, builtins/command.rs, builtins/declare.rs, builtins/eval.rs, builtins/mod.rs, builtins/read.rs, builtins/set.rs, builtins/shopt.rs, exec.rs, invocation.rs, lib.rs, now.rs, state.rs.
- perf(djs): the identifier atom cache keeps the image's atoms from cell to cell, and `atom_str` and JSON.parse's object keys look atoms up in it (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: cell overhead). `Heap::ident_atoms` (the parser's identifier text -> atom table, D-entry of the compiler buffer reuse) started empty again in every cell, because `restore_image` built a fresh heap without it, so each cell's first compile hashed every bootstrap and prelude name into the global atom index again; `atom_str` (host glue, builtins, the code-mode engine) and `JSON.parse` keys (each tool result) went to the keyed atom index every time. `IdentAtoms` is now two `AtomTexts` tables: `stable` for atoms that are in the image (integer atoms and string atoms below the image's atom count, which a restore cannot renumber) and `fresh` for atoms the cell created; `restore_image` carries the cache over and `restart` empties `fresh` (and `stable` only when the image's atom count changed); `forget_string_atoms`, which renumbers atoms, drops the whole cache. `atom_str` goes through `atom_utf8_cached`, as identifiers do; a JSON key without escapes whose bytes are ASCII is looked up in it after the per-parse key cache misses and inserted after `atom_utf16`. With an intern log (compile cache recording) all of it is bypassed, as before. Tried and not kept: `atom_str` straight to the keyed index while the parser and JSON use the cache: empty cell 87.7k, seq16 1,159k (against 86.5k and 1,134k); the cache functions without `#[inline]`: compile +0.65% (35.20M per corpus round against 34.97M). output/cellbench, instructions per cell (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, N 1200 minus N 200, over 1000, interleaved, dev-georgios): empty cell 88.8k -> 86.5k (-2.6%), one tool call 233.1k -> 227.1k (-2.6%), 16 sequential tool calls 1,194.4k -> 1,133.5k (-5.1%), the agent cell 995.5k -> 952.7k (-4.3%), compiling the 8 corpus cells 34.97M -> 34.88M per round (-0.3%). test262 subset 8,631 passing, identical pass set; the 42 edge cells (41 before plus one of JSON keys with escapes, non-ASCII, `__proto__` and integer keys) and three repetitions of the corpus cell print the same; disassembly of 442 files identical. nanocode-ts: Node overhead bench completes every cell; workerd A/B within noise (tool 6.5 -> 5.5 ms CPU per turn over 4 rounds). Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/compiler/parser.rs, heap/atom.rs, heap/mod.rs, json/parse.rs.

- perf(djs): adding a property remembers the last shape transition (from shape, key, flags, to child) and returns it without searching the transition list when the next add is the same (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: the new Error gap to QuickJS). `Heap::shape_child` binary-searched the parent's transitions on every add of a property that leaves an object in shape mode; `Heap::last_transition` holds the last answer, found or created, and is cleared wherever the shape caches are (`gc`, `compact`) and in `release_top`, which truncates the arena. Instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, best of 3, interleaved, dev-georgios, djsrun): 200,000 `new Error` 1,963.2M -> 1,926.6M (-1.9%, 9.8k -> 9.6k per error); objects, promises, compute and generators unchanged (within 0.01%). test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 passing, the same set; the 25 edge cells print the same output and events. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/{compact,gc,mod,shape}.rs.
- perf(djs): `new Error` finds `Error` and `Error.stackTraceLimit` through slot indexes remembered from the last lookup, skips `prepareStackTrace` with one lookup when it is absent, and walks the frames into a buffer the heap keeps (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: the new Error gap to QuickJS). Each capture looked up `Error` on the constructors object, `stackTraceLimit` and `prepareStackTrace` on it by name (~770 instructions), and `raw_frames` allocated a fresh Vec and read each frame's previous bp, previous hp, return pc and flags one value at a time. `realm::error_constructor_cached` and `stack_trace_limit_cached` try `data_at` with the slot index (`Heap::error_ctor_slot`, `stack_limit_slot`) and fall back to the lookup, refreshing the index; a stale index, an accessor or a deleted property fails `data_at` and takes the old path. `prepare_stack_trace` returns early when `own_entry_index` finds no `prepareStackTrace`. `raw_frames` fills a caller's Vec, the raw capture reuses `Heap::frame_scratch`, the four header values come from one `read_values`, and `in_prelude` reads only the template's script (`template::debug_script`) instead of the whole `debug_info`. Instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, best of 3, interleaved, dev-georgios, djsrun): 200,000 `new Error("x"+(i&7))` reading `message` 2,126.5M -> 1,963.2M (-7.7%, 10.6k -> 9.8k per error; QuickJS 1,564.1M, 7.8k); generators, compute, objects and promises unchanged (within 0.02%). test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 passing, the same set; the 25 edge cells print the same output and events, stack traces included. - perf(djs): a generator stepped by `for-of` or spread resumes and suspends through one read of its state slots: `resume_hit` checks the class, kind, state and `next` itself and enters the saved frame without `generator_resume`'s mode handling, and `yield_hit` stores state, frame, pc and frame offset in one write (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: the generator gap to QuickJS). Before, each step went through `plain_generator`/`as_generator` (class check, then `state_of` and the kind slot read one by one), `generator_resume` (state, frame, pc and frame offset read slot by slot, each with its bounds check, then the mode match) and `suspend_frame` (four `set_object_slot` calls, four bounds checks and four write barriers). `Arena::read_values`/`write_values` and `Heap::object_slots`/`set_object_slots` read or write N consecutive values with one bounds check and one barrier; `generator_resume` uses the read too, and its frame entry is `enter_saved`, shared with `resume_hit`. `iter_plan` returns `Slow` before anything else when the iterator is not an ArrayIterator, which every generator step reached first; `installed_intrinsic` is `#[inline]`. Instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, best of 3, interleaved, dev-georgios, djsrun): `function* g(n){for(let i=0;i<n;i++)yield i}` iterated by `for-of` 20 x 100,000 times 3,737.3M -> 3,309.3M (-11.5%, 1,869 -> 1,655 per yield; QuickJS 2,231.7M, 1,116 per yield); compute, objects, promises, forEach and new Error unchanged (within 0.01%). test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 passing, the same set; the 25 edge cells print the same output and events. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/{arena,object}.rs, interp/realm.rs, interp/run/{iter,suspend}.rs.
- perf(claude): a request's cache layout and conversation digests cost O(new messages): each history message carries a wire id that changes only when the message does, and `WireCache` keeps the cache layout and the digests of the messages it has seen by that id (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). Every model request walked the whole conversation three times before encoding a byte: `validate_cache_layout` visited every block's `cache_slot` (twice more for `cache_floors_with` and `cache_prefix_with`, once in `prepare_cached_wire`), the tool-change scan visited every block again, and `api_body` asked every message for its two digests (a `OnceLock` read per message, a BLAKE3 hash for any message rebuilt since) before `Hashed::shared` compared them. `CacheLayout` is now a fixed summary (breakpoint count, whether a 5m or 1h TTL was seen, whether a 1h one followed a 5m one, the last eligible block's TTL, the first invalid block's error) that composes left to right (`then`), so `MessageLayout` (that summary plus the tool-change flag) of a prefix extends by one message; `WireCache::layout` keeps one prefix layout per message keyed by `WireMessage::wire_id` and recomputes only past the first id that differs. `HistoryMessage` gets its id from a process-wide counter when it is made and a fresh one from `make_mut`; clones share it, since they share the bytes. `Hashed` keeps the ids beside the digests, so `api_body` asks only the messages past the shared ids for digests. Messages without an id (`Message`, `Cow`) behave as before. Validation answers the same errors in the same order: a block's error is kept and reported before the breakpoint count and the TTL order. Same bytes: output/claude-wire (400 rounds of growing, truncated and re-marked conversations with ids keyed by content, every seventh round without ids, each request built through the cache and again uncached) `CHECK=1` bad 0, with explicit markers and with automatic `cache_control` (`AUTO=1`); `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime` seeds 0..400 and `--wire http` 0..200 pass. nanocode-ts output/prof.ts (one session of 1,200 turns, wasm after wasm-opt, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, interleaved): 38.70, 39.45, 38.76M instructions per turn on master, 33.46, 33.56, 33.49M here (-13.5%); in its Node CPU profile `HistoryMessage::digests` (4.3% self), `ContentBlock::cache_slot` (1.7%) and `validate_cache_layout` (0.9%) leave. nanocode-ts bench/overhead.ts on Node and the workerd harness complete every cell. Files: crates/backends/claude/client/src/{lib.rs,wire_cache.rs,subscription_wire.rs}, crates/backends/claude/src/{agent.rs,agent/history.rs}.
- A durable root no longer stalls on a subagent completion operation that nothing will resume, in either of two ways nanocode-sim's runtime scenario found (2026-11-14, from the "did not settle" failures cfo.sh logged on dev-georgios at 0a9ed13f2, 7fb9c473e, f223811c7 and 1ec87b2d0). Both end with the root's session holding a `subagent-completion:…=Pending` operation, an empty `pending_completions` and every turn Completed, so `Nanocode::settle` never answers true. (1) A completion's route was claimed only after the parent answered it. `Registry::route_completions` and `dispatch_parent` (crates/runtime/subagents/src/runtime.rs) checked `completion_routes` early and inserted the route once `route_prompt_request` returned. In that window the parent's own `wait` output could show the same child's result: `observe_completions` found no route, claimed it, read the result when the tool output reached the model and acknowledged the completion, and then the route came back Started, a completion turn whose durable operation the parent had just admitted for a completion that was already acknowledged. A crash before that turn finished left the operation Pending with nothing to route it again. Seen on `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 3931660894656356396` (with debug prints, since removed): the batch of agents 6 and 8 steered into turn 1 and came back Undelivered, agent 8's completion was routed alone as `subagent-completion:01a1cd0e-672d-7002-…:1`, the wait output's notice acknowledged it while that route was in flight, the parent admitted and started the turn (`execute`, `started`) at 48.12 s and the crash at 48.77 s cut it. Now `claim_route` takes the route in one `try_update` just before the route is asked (refused only when the same revision is already routed, as the early check refuses), `route_completions` drops the members it cannot claim, and a failed route gives its claims back (`release_route`); an observation that comes while the route is in flight finds it held, as one that comes after it always did. (2) A completion turn interrupted by a crash was resumed only by the parent's next admission. `Agent::admit` resumes the interrupted turns a reopened session lists, in order, before it admits a new request, and nothing else resumes them, which is right for a host's own turns, since the host submits them again. A completion turn has no such host: when its completions reached the parent another way (here steered into the resumed turn 1 and acknowledged) and the root's client had no turn left to submit, the operation stayed Pending. On `--store kv --seed 2946428715947094085` the batch of agents 1 and 2 was admitted before the second crash, resumed after it (`resume`, deferred behind turn 1), began after turn 1 and was cut by the third crash at 113.5 s, after both completions had been acknowledged. Now, once the registry has restored a root and marked it Ready, it asks the root's agent for its interrupted requests (`Agent::interrupted_requests`) and, when one is a completion's, resumes them (`Agent::resume_interrupted_turns`, the same `resume_interrupted(None)` the next admission would run, so the order and the replay of finished operations are unchanged; a host that called `leave_interrupted_turns_to_host` lists none). A resumed completion turn repeats a notice the parent has read, which the parent answers as it answers any completion; it is not new work replayed, since the operation was admitted before the crash. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): the 1,061 distinct seeds cfo.sh recorded as "did not settle" (all commits, all runtime rows) fail 4 times on master's binary (8fb3da51c: 3931660894656356396, 2946428715947094085 and 3861423173092502222 with `--store kv`, 2587510668217995464 with `--store kv --calm`), once with (1) alone (2946428715947094085) and 0 times with both; on 2946428715947094085 the run with both is the same as without until the third crash, after which the batch resumes and both roots settle. The gate on this tree: `nanocode-sim --tidy` clean; `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets` passes; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-subagents -p nanocode-agent-core` and `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for both report nothing in them; seeds 7720000000000..+3,000 of `--store kv`, `--store memory` and `--store kv --twice` pass, 9,000 of 9,000.
- feat(python): CPython 3.13's C API starts, as crates/core/python-capi (nanocode-python-capi), and `markupsafe._speedups` is compiled into python3: `import markupsafe` runs its C escape instead of the pure-Python one (2026-11-14, Georgios: run the top compiled Python packages in plain wasm32 with a C API layer written in Rust, CPython's object layout and package C compiled with clang and linked statically, no Pyodide). How it is built: each directory of crates/core/python-capi/ext is one extension module named by its dotted name and holds its C sources as released (ext/markupsafe._speedups/_speedups.c and LICENSE.txt from the markupsafe 3.0.4 sdist); build.rs compiles them with `-O2 -DNDEBUG -fvisibility=hidden` against CPython 3.13.9's public headers (include/cpython, Include/ of the release without internal/, with its LICENSE) and an include/pyconfig.h that takes every size from the compiler (`__SIZEOF_POINTER__`, `__SIZEOF_LONG__` and so on), so one file serves wasm32 and 64-bit hosts; it renames each `PyInit_<last>` to `PyInit_<dotted name with _>` so two packages' `_speedups` cannot collide, writes the objects into a static archive itself (the ar format, no ar tool) and generates the table of init functions. On wasm32 it compiles freestanding with `-nostdlibinc` and include/libc, the declarations Python.h needs (assert, ctype, errno, inttypes, math, pthread_key_t, stdio, stdlib, string, sys/stat, sys/types, unistd, wchar): no wasi-libc; memcpy and friends come from Rust's compiler_builtins. Native builds use the system headers. The compiler is NANOCODE_CC, else CC_<target>, else clang for wasm or a cross target and cc otherwise, so native nanocode-python now needs a C compiler. The Rust side: #[repr(C)] PyObject, PyTypeObject (all 3.13 slots, tp_flags as c_ulong), PyASCIIObject, PyCompactUnicodeObject, PyModuleDef, PyMethodDef and PyModuleDef_Slot, checked against offsetof and sizeof from the headers for wasm32 (a WASI build of a probe) and x86_64: PyTypeObject 208 and 416 bytes, tp_flags at 84 and 168, PyASCIIObject 20 and 40, PyCompactUnicodeObject 28 and 56, PyModuleDef 52 and 104, the state bits kind 2-4, compact 5, ascii 6, and the immortal refcount 0x3fffffff and 0xffffffff. Exported with #[unsafe(no_mangle)]: PyUnicode_New (compact objects of kind 1, 2 or 4 by maxchar, NUL-terminated, hash -1), PyModuleDef_Init (types the definition and numbers it with an atomic counter, as CPython does), _Py_Dealloc, and the type objects PyType_Type, PyUnicode_Type (UNICODE_SUBCLASS, its dealloc frees the compact layout) and PyModuleDef_Type. A safe API on top (Extension::methods, Method::call, Owned with a refcount that follows 3.13's Py_DECREF, Units to read a str) is what nanocode-python uses: crates/core/python/src/capi.rs registers every compiled extension as a native module of the interpreter, so the BuiltinImporter finds `markupsafe._speedups` by its dotted name, and builds one builtin function per PyMethodDef through a new `PyMethodDef::new_dyn` in the vendored rustpython-vm (a method definition over a leaked closure, once per method per interpreter). Calls convert at the boundary: a str becomes a compact CPython str (ASCII by copy), the result is read back by kind, and a result that is the argument returns the argument itself, so `_escape_inner(s) is s` holds for text with nothing to escape as in CPython. Not yet: METH_VARARGS, METH_FASTCALL and keywords (SystemError naming the convention), arguments other than str (TypeError: the C API has no CPython object for 'int' yet), the error indicator (a NULL return raises CPython's SystemError text), module state, Py_mod_create and Py_mod_exec and single-phase init (ImportError with the reason), and module self (NULL is passed). The second crate with unsafe code after nanocode-sys: calling C and laying out its objects is unsafe by nature, and keeping it here keeps the C build out of nanocode-sys, which every crate uses. Checked on dev-georgios through nanocode-ts's build (wasm32-unknown-unknown, wasm-opt -Oz, baked): markupsafe 3.0.4's Python files with the module, `markupsafe._escape_inner is markupsafe._speedups._escape_inner`, the C escape equals `_native._escape_inner` on '', ASCII, quotes and ampersands, Latin-1, CJK, an astral emoji, 1,000 characters and a lone surrogate; 50 escapes of a 70,000-character string take 57 ms in C against 166 ms in pure Python (Pyodide 314.0.7, which calls the same C on CPython: 26 ms, its pure Python 68 ms). bench/python/score.ts (nanocode-ts): compiled modules 0/274 to 1/274, packages 0/18 to 1/18, C API symbols exported 0/538 to 5/538, limits 4/4. python.wasm 27,347,029 to 27,363,835 bytes (+16,806); interleaved, 4 rounds each of compile, instantiate, `print(1)` and a json, re and Counter script in ms: before 72.6/23.1/66.3/303.5, 48.3/25.8/73.4/318.6, 44.6/10.9/58.2/304.1, 36.0/13.0/46.8/269.1, after 39.5/9.7/48.2/315.8, 31.5/19.2/52.8/241.1, 39.2/10.0/48.8/295.6, 36.3/11.4/53.3/370.0 (load ~89 on the EPYC; within noise). Commands: `cargo check --offline -p nanocode-python` and `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-python-capi -p nanocode-python` (native, no warnings in the new code), `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs` (78 crates). Not run: the native nanocode binary end to end. Files: crates/core/python-capi/{Cargo.toml,build.rs,src/lib.rs,include/**,ext/markupsafe._speedups/*}, crates/core/python/{Cargo.toml,src/lib.rs,src/capi.rs}, crates/patches/rustpython-vm/src/function/method.rs, Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock.

- fix(claude): direct-tool sessions carry Claude Code's conversation context: the attribution reminder, the environment as a system message and the tokens left after each tool round (2026-11-14). Claude Code 2.1.300, as the leaderboard runs it on DeepSeek and GLM, puts a `<system-reminder>` on git and pull request attribution before the first prompt, sends the environment as a `system`-role message right after it (" - "-bulleted working directory, git, platform, shell ("unknown" without SHELL), OS version, the untrusted-downloads rule, "You are powered by the model <model>.", `<total_tokens>15000000 tokens left</total_tokens>` and "Today's date is <date>.") instead of a system block, and after each tool result appends a `system` message `<total_tokens>N tokens left</total_tokens>`, N being 15,000,000 less the last response's input, cache and output tokens (real stock requests: 14,983,608 then 14,983,213 as the context grew). nanocode sent none of these and kept the environment in the system prompt. In direct sessions that are not remote (the ones that get WebSearch and WebFetch: models other than Claude), `upstream_context()` now does the same; the other sessions are unchanged.
