- perf(code-mode): a Code Mode tool call no longer chains a `catch` on its promise when it is made; the promise of a call made through `tools` gets that `catch` just before it is rejected (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: cell overhead). `code-tools.mjs` wrapped every call in `helpers.observe`, `promise.catch(ignore)`, so a failing call the cell never awaits is not an unhandled rejection: one derived promise, its reaction records and one more job per call, whether or not it fails. `callTool` (bootstrap.js) now keeps the promise in the call's settlers when it came through `tools` (`invokeTool`'s `observed`), and `pump` calls `catch(ignore)` on it only on the failure paths (a failed result, or a result whose JSON does not parse), right before `reject`: the promise has a handler when it rejects, as before, and a successful call creates nothing more than its own promise. Calls made by a host prelude (`invokeTool(name, input, true)`) were not observed and still are not; a call that throws before reaching the host (`dispatch`'s catch, such as a circular input) still returns an observed rejected promise; the missing-tool proxy's `unavailable` path is unchanged. The order of the cell's own reactions is unchanged; the no-op job of the derived promise, which ran before them, is gone. Tried and not kept: `Promise.withResolvers()` in `callTool` instead of the executor closure, +4.6k instructions per call (seq16 1,268k against 1,194k with the executor). output/cellbench, instructions per cell (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, N 1200 minus N 200, over 1000, interleaved twice, dev-georgios): 16 sequential tool calls 1,320.7k -> 1,194.4k (-9.6%, 7.9k per call), 16 parallel 1,439.1k -> 1,312.8k (-8.8%), one call 243.3k -> 233.1k (-4.2%), the agent cell 1,020.5k -> 995.5k (-2.4%), the empty cell 88.9k -> 88.7k. The 41 edge cells (the 25 of ~/djs2/edge, the 8 corpus cells and 6 new ones: an unawaited failing call, a failing call awaited later, a circular input, reaction order between a call and a microtask, a cell that only starts a failing call, `allSettled` over a failure, a success and a missing tool) print the same events and output under PRINT=1 EVENTS=1, except the bootstrap line numbers in two stack traces (825 -> 838), which move with the added lines. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/bootstrap.js, crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/code-tools.mjs.
- fix(codex): a generation keeps trying after its attempts are spent, as Codex 0.162.1 reconnects its stream (2026-11-14). Codex retries a request on a 5xx or a transport failure up to 4 times, and when a request fails anyway, or a 401, 402, 403, 404, 408, 409, 413 or 422 comes back, or the stream fails or drops, it reconnects up to 5 times with a fresh request budget (200 ms doubling); only a 400, a 429 that is not a rate_limit_error and terminal provider errors end the turn. nanocode stopped after 5 attempts and treated 402 as final, which ended 7 nc-codex trials in cmp2 where stock Codex survived 9 server errors in a row and then a 402 (the gateway's voucher race). A generation now gets 5 reconnects on top of its attempt budget, each with a full replay and a fresh budget, for any failure except a 400, a 429 and terminal provider errors. Measured against ~/hill/retrymock (scripted 402, 4xx, 5xx, in-stream failures and drops), with stock Codex 0.162.1 and nanocode on the same plans: a 402 or 404 then success, 2 posts and success for both (before: 1 post, failed); 29 500s then success, 30 posts and success for both (before: 5 posts, failed); nine 502s then a 402, 11 posts and success for both (before: failed at the 402); a 400, 1 post and failed for both. Six in-stream failures or drops then success: stock fails after 6 posts, nanocode succeeds on the 7th, because its attempt budget also covers in-stream failures. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex-client`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, passed. Files: crates/backends/codex/client/src/tower/{attempt.rs,middleware/retry.rs}.
- nanocode's `python3` and `python` run nanocode-python, a program of its own (bin/nanocode-python, package nanocode-python-cli: nanocode-python's new `serve`), which nanocode downloads the first time a command runs it, instead of RustPython inside every nanocode: the shipped x86_64 Linux nanocode 61,952,936 to 46,191,160 bytes (-15.8 MB, -25%), its xz download 18.6 to 13.0 MB and gzip 27.2 to 19.4 MB (2026-11-14, Georgios via the Nanocode 1.0 coordinator: "fetch Python on first use (with integrity check and an offline-clear error)"). The bundled `python3` is `Mode::SandboxOnly`: on a machine it runs only when `PSH_UTILS_FORCE` names it, and otherwise the name is the machine's own python3 or not found, so most installs never download it. scripts/build-cli.sh builds nanocode-python first for nanocode-cli (same profile and flags, stripped, beside nanocode in the output directory) and builds nanocode with `NANOCODE_PYTHON_SHA256`, its SHA-256; release-cli.sh publishes it as nanocode-python-SHA256.xz, so every nanocode names the one program it was built with and a later release never replaces it. The utility (bin/nanocode/src/python.rs) runs ~/.nanocode/bin/nanocode-python-SHA256 when it is there; otherwise it downloads the .xz from the release (`NANOCODE_RELEASE` overrides the address, as for install), decompresses it with nanocode-compression's xz, refuses it unless its SHA-256 is the recorded one, and writes it under a temporary name, made executable and renamed into place. A failed download prints, with status 1, "python3: Python is downloaded the first time a command runs it, and getting URL failed: REASON; connect to the network and run the command again"; a wrong digest names both digests the same way. A build without the digest (cargo build) runs the nanocode-python built beside its executable, or says how to build one. The program gets the arguments with python3 or python as argv[0], the shell's environment, working directory and stdin, writes its own output, and is killed when the command is cancelled (status 128 + SIGTERM); its exit status is the command's, and it applies the same limits and messages as the in-process utility (`ending` and `limits` are now shared). The interpreter is no longer kept between commands of one shell: each python3 starts one, about 20 ms more per command after the first (three `python3 -c 'print(1)'` in one psh-shell 0.04 to 0.10 s; a dict, json and re script 0.27 to 0.31 s user). nanocode-python's `serve` forgets the interpreter instead of finalizing it at exit, which would run during the thread-local destructors and panic (as the utility's kept interpreter never finalizes either). WebAssembly hosts and nanocode-shell keep the in-process utility unchanged. First frame and one-shot (bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc`, 3 interleaved batches under `perf stat`, 12 samples each, against c2c17d578's build): user instructions median 10.0M to 9.37M, kernel 12.3M to 12.1M, page faults 892 to 866, task clock 7.7 and 7.9 ms (load ~60). Checked on dev-georgios with a local release: the download, a run from the kept program with the release unreachable (status 3 from `SystemExit(3)`), stdin, a file argument, writing a file, a missing module (127 and the message), cancelling an endless loop (no process left), an unreachable release and a corrupted .xz (both messages, nothing installed). nanocode-python is 15,963,800 bytes, 6,050,164 as xz. Commands: `cargo clippy --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-python-cli -p nanocode-python --no-deps -- -D warnings`, nanocode-python for wasm32-unknown-unknown, rustfmt on the changed files. Files: Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, bin/nanocode/{Cargo.toml,src/lib.rs,src/python.rs}, bin/nanocode-python, crates/core/python/src/{lib,psh}.rs, scripts/build-cli.sh, scripts/release-cli.sh.
- Releases also publish each nanocode binary compressed with xz (`xz -9e`, nanocode-TARGET.xz beside nanocode-TARGET.gz, both in SHA256SUMS), and install downloads the .xz when the machine has an `xz` command and the release lists one, the .gz otherwise (2026-11-14, Georgios via the Nanocode 1.0 coordinator: "ship xz compression"). For the x86_64 Linux build of c2c17d578 (61,952,936 bytes) the download is 27,186,668 bytes as gzip -9 and 18,556,136 as xz -9 (-32%); macOS has no `xz` by default, so a Mac without Homebrew's keeps the .gz, as does a minimal Linux image; the .gz stays for them and for installs of older install scripts. The checksum file and the installed binary's recorded digest are the downloaded file's, so an install that switches format downloads once more. Checked: install against a local release with both files picks the .xz with `xz` on PATH and the .gz with a PATH without it, each verifying the digest and installing a binary byte-identical to the one packed. release-cli.sh now needs `xz` on the machine that runs it. Files: install, scripts/release-cli.sh.
- nanocode-sim's websocket model checks the server's echo of the client's close frame against the client's frame limit, as it checks every frame the server's script sends (2026-11-14, from cfo.sh on dev-georgios: three failed websocket jobs at f99925e9a and 395967ffd). In a script that ends with the client closing (`ending=ClientClose`), the scripted server answers the client's close frame with the same payload, and `model::expect` stepped that echo through `Model::step` without `Model::header_failure`, so it expected the echo to arrive as `Close(...)` whatever its length. nanocode-websocket's client refuses any frame whose declared length passes `frame_bytes_max` before it reads the payload (protocol.rs, `parse_buffered`), control frames included, as tungstenite's `max_frame_size` does, and the model applies the same rule to every other server frame. When the seeded close reason made the echo longer than a small seeded frame limit, the client failed with `MessageTooLong` and the model disagreed: `--scenario websocket --seed 3637587009283885203` (`frame_max=18`, a 69-byte close payload with code 1012), 285820483474327115 (`frame_max=35`) and 899746385473657248 (`frame_max=9`) failed so. The client is right and the model was not, so only the model changes: the echo goes through `header_failure` first and fails as any oversized frame does. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): the three seeds fail on 395967ffd's binary and pass with this change; seeds 7700000000000..+200,000 of `--scenario websocket` pass (121 s at 8 jobs).
- `scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs` refuses nanocode-tui the SDK's crates by name instead of every crate in core/, and passes again (2026-11-14, release hygiene; it replaces the `allowedDependencies` table that fe013a99c's entry of the same day, below, describes). fe013a99c let nanocode-tui reach four named core crates. The next commits to master included a0f27d28a, which made the TUI write `nanocode_trace::` where it wrote `tracing::`, and the script threw `crates/tui crate depends on crates/core: nanocode-tui → nanocode-trace`: the third time in three days that replacing an external crate with one of ours tripped this rule (nanocode-sync and nanocode-sys on 2026-11-12, nanocode-trace on 2026-11-14), and none of the three is a layering mistake. core/ is no longer only the SDK's contracts: of its 49 crates 10 carry SDK values, tool contracts or durability contracts, and most of the others are plumbing or replacements for external crates, eight of them under the external crate's own name (cfg-if, getrandom, indexmap, itoa, once_cell, serde_derive, shlex, unicode-normalization). A list of the core crates the TUI may use therefore changes with every such commit, and nothing runs the script to say so. The rule keeps what it was written for on 2026-10-14 (e832fa71a), a terminal UI that knows nothing of the SDK, stated the other way round: `crates/tui` stays refused runtime/, backends/, integrations/ and the facade by directory, and `forbiddenDependencies` refuses nanocode-tui, at any depth, nanocode-types-core, nanocode-durability-core and nanocode-tool-contracts (the seven other crates that carry SDK values or contracts depend on one of them: nanocode-types, nanocode-agent-types, nanocode-agent-core, nanocode-tools, nanocode-tool-provider, nanocode-image, nanocode-turnlog) and the SDK crates of crates/README.md's core table that reach none of the three: nanocode-tools-macros, nanocode-process-contracts, nanocode-http, nanocode-mcp, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-schema, nanocode-home and nanocode-audio. What this gives up: a new crate in core/ that the TUI must not use has to be added to that set, where before it was refused without being named; a new plumbing or replacement crate needs nothing. `allowedDependencies` and its condition leave the script. Checked on dev-georgios at 2367c144e: the script prints `Layering verified for 77 core, runtime, integration and tui crates.`; a copy that collects violations instead of throwing lists none, lists `nanocode-tui → nanocode-sync → nanocode-platform` once nanocode-platform is added to the TUI's set (the set is applied at depth), and with fe013a99c's table lists the nanocode-trace path. No Rust file changes.
- Release builds no longer carry the builder's paths: `scripts/build-cli.sh` passes `--remap-path-prefix` for the checkout, `$CARGO_HOME` and the toolchain's library sources, and a hand pinned by commit is built by the same script (2026-11-14, release hygiene). Before, counted with `strings -a -n 6 <binary> | grep -c`: nanocode-cli-3f97ab0's x86_64 binary has 243 strings with `/home/<user>/.cargo/registry/src/` (the builder's home and user name); the rolling release's aarch64-apple-darwin binary has 979 with `/Users/<user>/` (835 registry, 95 cargo git checkouts, 49 the rustup toolchain's `lib/rustlib/src/rust`, which rustc names instead of `/rustc/<hash>` where rust-src is installed), its nanocode-cua-driver 619, and its Linux binaries the container's `/usr/local/cargo/registry` (735 on x86_64) and `/src/target/` (4); BOLT writes its command line, with the checkout and target paths, into `.note.bolt_info`. They are the file names of panic locations in dependencies; workspace crates are compiled with relative paths (`crates/...`) and carry none. Where the flags live: cargo 1.97.0 refuses `trim-paths` and profile `rustflags` in a manifest (`feature ... is not stabilized`), and a `.cargo/config.toml` cannot name the builder's home, so they are in the one script every release goes through: `--remap-path-prefix=<checkout>=/src`, `<CARGO_HOME or ~/.cargo>=/cargo` and `<sysroot>/lib/rustlib/src/rust=/rustc/<commit-hash>`. A dependency's panic still names crate, version, file and line (`/cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/tokio-1.52.3/src/...`), std's stay `/rustc/<hash>/library/...` as a toolchain without rust-src prints them (a small program with slab 0.4.12: a panic inside core prints `/rustc/<hash>/library/core/src/iter/adapters/step_by.rs:35:9` from a toolchain without rust-src and from one with rust-src and the remap, and the builder's toolchain path from one with rust-src and no remap; the binaries of the first two are the same size), and the paths no longer depend on who builds. RUSTFLAGS reaches target artifacts only, since the script always passes `--target`, so build scripts and proc macros are not rebuilt for it. The script changes in four places: a new lane for a glibc-suffixed target (`*-linux-gnu.*`) runs `cargo zigbuild` with the remap and no BOLT, which is the command pinned hands were built with by hand; the Linux lane adds the remap to its flags and strips `.note.bolt_info`; the lane for the other targets (macOS) sets RUSTFLAGS; and `release-cli.sh` builds nanocode-cua-driver through build-cli.sh instead of a bare `cargo build`. How a release is built now: the rolling `nanocode-cli` release with `scripts/release-cli.sh [--publish]`, as before; a pinned hand (`nanocode-cli-<commit>`) at the detached commit, with zig 0.13.0 and cargo-zigbuild on PATH, with `scripts/build-cli.sh nanocode-cli nanocode x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31`, which prints the binary's path, `target/cli/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31/nanocode` (`CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true` on a builder without network), then `gzip -9` and SHA256SUMS as before; `strings -a -n 6 <binary> | grep -c -e /home/ -e /Users/` prints 0 for a binary fit to upload. No release was cut for this change: the next pinned hand and the next rolling release pick it up. Measured on dev-georgios (Rust 1.97.0, zig 0.13.0), pinned-hand lane at 6bec51c06, before with `cargo zigbuild --locked --offline --profile dist --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.2.31 -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`, after with the script: strings with `/home/` 213 -> 0, with the user name 213 -> 0, with the checkout path 0 -> 0, with `/cargo/registry/src/` 0 -> 213, with `/rustc/<hash>/` 111 -> 111, workspace paths (`crates/...rs`) 1,061 -> 1,061; 66,007,888 -> 66,016,272 bytes (gzip -9: 28,696,589 -> 28,703,317). Both print `nanocode 0.7.0`; output/d1-background (Bash, exec_command, exec_command_tty) gives the same lines for both but for pids and milliseconds; output/psh-differential (117 cases, with and without `--own-processes`) differs from bash in the same two known cases for both, and in `missing-python` in 3 of 8 runs of the before binary and 4 of 8 of the after one; nanoeval aa573cb's directory-slot lane (extract-todos, uppercase-message, write-greeting, three slots) passes with NANOEVAL_NANOCODE naming either binary, and all six attempts error when it names a shell script, so the lane runs the file it is given. Linux lane at fe013a99c with BOLT 19 (the container has 21), after only: 66,286,520 bytes, 0 strings with `/home/`, the user name or the checkout, 209 with `/cargo/registry/src/`, no `.note.bolt_info`, `nanocode 0.7.0`, and the same nanoeval lane passes; at de77f76e8, before this lane had `-use-old-text`, 235 -> 0 and the checkout path once (BOLT's note) -> 0, 73,305,944 -> 73,302,648 bytes. What the remap does to code, read from that lane's cargo output at de77f76e8, which has symbols and is built with the wrappers off as release-cli.sh's container sets them: the same 45,265 functions by name, 45,263 of the same size (two static-type initialisers of rustpython-vm are 77 and 35 bytes smaller), and 42,138 of the 42,190 that objdump lists have the same instructions once addresses are masked; the 52 that differ (27 `OnceCell<PyRef<PyType>>::try_init` of rustpython-vm, 25 others) have the same number of instructions in 49 cases, and the one read differs in two pairs of constants loaded in the other order. The cause is not established: beside the remap the two trees differ in the git name, hash and commit time that rustpython-vm's build.rs embeds, because the after tree is two script-only commits ahead; .rodata is 4,096 bytes smaller. The pinned-hand lane cannot show as much, because it is not reproducible as built here, with the wrappers of .cargo/config.toml (buildcache and `-Zthreads=0`): a third build of the before tree with a remap that matches no path differs from the first by 192 bytes and in 89 of 124,128 runs of code between padding (35,821 of 10.2 million instructions), and before and after differ in 1,064 runs (387,881 instructions), so its 8,384 bytes are not attributed to the remap. Not run: both macOS lanes (a stub `cargo` on PATH shows the command lines and RUSTFLAGS the script issues for nanocode and nanocode-cua-driver) and the container lane with BOLT 21; the instrumenting llvm-bolt needs more than 10 GB for this binary (11.0 GB peak here).

- deps(tls): nanocode's own once_cell gives rustls the `race::OnceBox` it names, over std's `OnceLock`; once_cell 1.21.4 leaves (2026-11-13, Georgios: remove itoa, shlex, cfg-if, getrandom and once_cell from nanocode-cli's tree). With tracing-core gone, rustls 0.23.45 is its only user: rustls always depends on once_cell with the `alloc` and `race` features, adds `std` with its own `std` feature, and only uses `once_cell::race::OnceBox` for its process-default `CryptoProvider` when built without `std`; nanocode-tls builds rustls with `std` on every target that has it, where rustls keeps the provider in `std::sync::OnceLock` and never reaches once_cell. crates/core/once_cell takes the crates.io name and version 1.21.4 (a workspace member in `[patch.crates-io]`, satisfying rustls's `^1.16`) and has `race::OnceBox` (`new`, `const`; `get`; `set`, which returns the box back when the cell is already set; `get_or_init`; `Default`; `Debug` as `OnceBox(<address>)`, `0x0` while empty, as once_cell prints it) as a wrapper of `OnceLock<Box<T>>`, so no unsafe code. It declares the `alloc`, `race` and `std` features as empty lists only because rustls names them and Cargo refuses a patch without a feature a dependent asks for; they gate nothing. Not equal: once_cell's `OnceBox::get_or_init` may run the initializer on several racing threads and keep the first box stored, where `OnceLock` runs it once and makes the others wait (nothing here calls it); `with_value`, `get_or_try_init`, `OnceRef`, `OnceNonZeroUsize`, `OnceBool`, `unsync`, `sync` and `Lazy` are not written (unused). - deps(trace): nanocode-trace carries nanocode's spans, events and their dispatch to nanocode-observability; tracing 0.1.44 and tracing-core 0.1.36 leave (2026-11-13, Georgios: own every dependency outside the accepted runtime and TLS set). Nothing outside the workspace used tracing (its users were nanocode's crates and the rustls-platform-verifier, rustpython-vm and rustpython-codegen patches), so nanocode-trace (crates/core/trace) is a workspace crate under its own name and the 132 Rust files that wrote `tracing::` or `tracing_core::` now write `nanocode_trace::`, with no other change at those sites. It has the parts nanocode uses: the `span!`, `event!`, `enabled!`, `trace!` to `error!` and `*_span!` macros as macro_rules with tracing's syntax (`target:`, `parent:`, `name:`, dotted and string-literal field names, `%` and `?`, braced fields, `field::Empty`, format arguments), `Span` (`enter`, `entered`, `in_scope`, `record`, `record_all`, `follows_from`, `current`, `or_current`, `with_subscriber`), `Instrument`, `Metadata`, `Level`, `LevelFilter`, `FieldSet`, `ValueSet`, `Visit`, `Value` (integers to 128 bits, floats, bool, str, `Display`, `Debug`, errors), `Event`, `Attributes`, `Record`, `Current`, `Id`, `Subscriber`, `Interest`, `Dispatch` and `set_global_default`. Dispatch is one global `OnceLock<Dispatch>`; each callsite caches its `Interest` in one `AtomicU32` beside the generation it was computed in, and `rebuild_interest_cache` bumps the generation, so a callsite asks the subscriber again on its next hit (tracing-core keeps a registry of callsites and dispatchers behind locks and checks a thread-local scoped dispatcher on every event: 40 `Mutex`, `RwLock` and `thread_local` sites); the global maximum level is an `AtomicU8`. Not equal: there are no scoped dispatchers (`with_default`, `set_default`, `DefaultGuard`), since nanocode installs one global subscriber, no `WeakDispatch`, no `log` bridge, `#[instrument]` or `valuable`; a rebuilt interest cache is refilled callsite by callsite on use rather than at once. Equal, output/trace-equality: one driver (driver.rs, built twice: against tracing with master's nanocode-observability, and against nanocode-trace with this commit's) runs 20,000 seeded steps of events and spans (numbers to 128 bits, NaN and infinities, text with quotes, escapes, control characters and non-ASCII, `Debug` and `Display` values, error chains, nested and entered spans, `record` into `Empty` fields, follows-from, `Instrument`ed futures, metrics events) through nanocode-observability's log writer and OTLP file export, over 3 seeds, the compact, pretty and json formats and 8 pairs of log and OTLP filters (default, trace, off, per-target levels, `target=off`, span-name and span-field filters such as `nanocode[op.name{session.id=3}]=trace` and `[{status}]=debug`): the log bytes (timestamps and busy/idle durations masked), the exported spans, logs and metrics (ids renumbered, times masked) and stdout are identical in 72 of 72 runs. Speed (output/trace-equality/instructions.sh, `perf stat -e instructions:u` per operation, tracing then nanocode-trace): an event below the level filter 7 and 7, an event of a disabled target 392 and 366, a disabled span 29 and 18, an enabled event written to the log 6,456 and 6,437, a span created, entered, recorded and closed 22,861 and 22,750, `Span::current` 318 and 319; bench.sh wall medians of 7 under load 80 to 140 move both ways within noise (event 1,507 to 1,328 ns, span 6,042 to 5,976 ns, current 36 to 48 ns). Compile, output/trace-compile (`cargo build -j 1` of an empty crate depending on each, from empty target directories, five rounds): release 1.14 to 1.35 s of user time for tracing, tracing-core, pin-project-lite and once_cell, 0.53 to 0.63 s for nanocode-trace and pin-project-lite; debug 0.79 and 0.63 s. Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` 159 to 158 (third-party 45 to 43); nanocode-cli third-party 41 to 39 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and on aarch64-apple-darwin. - fix(websocket): the client accepts a 101 whose Connection header lists `Upgrade` among other tokens, such as `Connection: keep-alive, Upgrade` (2026-11-13, found by `nanocode-sim --scenario websocket`). RFC 6455 4.1 asks the client to fail only when Connection lacks a token that is a case-insensitive match for `Upgrade`, and the server side here already splits the request's Connection into tokens, but `VerifyData::verify` (crates/core/websocket/src/handshake.rs) compared the whole value with `Upgrade`, so such a server's handshake failed with `MissingConnectionUpgradeHeader`. It now splits on commas and trims each token; Upgrade is still one value matched without case, as 4.1 says. Not equal to before: a response whose Connection is a token list holding Upgrade now connects; one without the token still fails the same way. Replay: `nanocode-sim --scenario websocket --seed 96` (a valid head with `keep-alive, Upgrade` and no frames; first failing seed 61). Sweeps (release): before, `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 20000 8 --scenario websocket` passed=15875 failed=4125, all this failure; after, `sweep.sh 0 100000 8 --scenario websocket` passed=100000 failed=0 panics=0 and `sweep.sh 100000 120000 8 --scenario websocket --twice` passed=20000 failed=0. The scenario's observation check is the invariant that catches it, with `--mutation corrupt_payload` caught as in the previous entry. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-websocket` (native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-websocket -p nanocode-sim` (no new warnings). Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` 158 to 158. Files: crates/core/websocket/src/handshake.rs.
- sim(websocket): bin/nanocode-sim drives nanocode-websocket's client over a simulated in-memory socket against a scripted server, `--scenario websocket` (2026-11-13, Georgios: find bugs with the deterministic simulator). nanocode-websocket needs no Tokio runtime, only tokio's `AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` traits and io-util extension futures, so `client_async_with_config` runs under the simulator's executor and virtual clock with randomness from the simulated host. The socket (websocket/socket.rs) is two byte queues with wakers: the server writes the seeded script (websocket/script.rs) in seeded pieces with `nanocode_platform::sleep` gaps, the head in at most 8 pieces so the handshake's flood check stays out of the way, and can end with EOF or a reset at any byte; the client-to-server queue has a seeded capacity (1 byte to 300 KB or unbounded) and seeded vectored writes, so backpressure reaches the client's write path and its large-payload path. The script covers 101 heads with right, wrong and missing Sec-WebSocket-Accept, missing Upgrade or Connection, header name and value case, `Connection: keep-alive, Upgrade`, non-101 statuses, HTTP/1.0, an unrequested subprotocol, 125 headers, a 69 KB head, malformed status lines, heads up to 32 KB, frames in the same write as the head; text (multi-byte UTF-8 cut across fragments) and binary messages of 0, 1, 125-127, 65535-65537, 131071-131073 bytes and up to 1.2 MB, split into up to 6 fragments with pings and pongs between them, 16- and 64-bit lengths for small payloads; server pings, closes with no payload, allowed codes and reasons, and forbidden codes; client sends, pings and closes with and without a frame; seeded frame and message limits and read buffers; and one violation at a time (reserved bits, unknown opcodes, a masked server frame, control frames over 125 bytes or fragmented, invalid or truncated UTF-8, a one-byte close, a close reason that is not UTF-8, a length with the high bit set, a continuation with nothing to continue, a new message inside a fragmented one, a frame after a close). websocket/model.rs is the oracle: it walks the script as RFC 6455 says and names what the client must yield (every complete message before a fault exactly once, in order, byte-identical, then the typed error or the end), the pongs and close frames it owes. The judge checks the client's observations against it (for a reset, a prefix followed by the reset), that every client frame the scripted server parses is masked, minimal and well-formed, that what the client sent arrives intact and nothing data-like follows its close, that no task hangs (the executor's Stuck) and the run ends before 30 virtual minutes, and with `--twice` that a seed replays to the same trace digest. Mutations the simulator catches: `corrupt_payload` (one payload byte flipped on the wire: 293 of seeds 0..500), `drop_client_byte` (the server loses a client byte: 341 of 500), `hold_eof` (the server's EOF never arrives: 240 of 500, as hangs). The tidy check now covers crates/core/websocket/src. Sweep `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 20000 8 --scenario websocket` (release): passed=15875 failed=4125, every failure the client refusing a 101 whose Connection header is `keep-alive, Upgrade` (fixed in the next commit; smallest replay `nanocode-sim --scenario websocket --seed 96`, a valid head and no frames); with that fix 0..3000 passed=3000 failed=0 and `--seeds 0..1000 --twice` passed=1000. Not equal to before: the sim now depends on nanocode-websocket, nanocode-digest and nanocode-sys (all already in its tree through nanocode). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sim` (no new warnings), `nanocode-sim --scenario websocket --seeds 0..500 --mutation <each>`. Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` 158 to 158. - nanocode-http fails a response head longer than `HEAD_BYTES_MAX` (417,792 bytes) with `HeadTooLarge` even when one read delivers it whole (2026-11-13, Georgios: find bugs with nanocode-sim and mocked responses). `Connection::head` checked the bound only while the head was incomplete; a complete head in the buffer was parsed and accepted whatever its length, so a server's oversized head passed when it arrived in one piece, the connection went back to the pool, and the next request rode a connection whose response had broken the client's own limit. Now the parsed head's length is checked before it is consumed. Found by `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --wire http` (the entry below), whose server sometimes sends a head over the bound and whose invariant says such a connection must not carry another request. Reproduce on the parent commit: `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --wire http --seed 109` fails with `connection 3 carried a new request after a malformed response`; `sweep.sh 0 2000 8 --scenario runtime --wire http` failed 11 seeds before (109, 403, 534, 616, 641, 734, 1633, 1697, 1703, 1858, 1969, all that message) and 0 after, and `2000 6000` passed every seed after. Heads under the bound are parsed as before. Commands: `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-http -p nanocode-sim` (only nanocode-sys's three existing warnings), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-http --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. - `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --wire http` runs the whole runtime with the real Claude client over nanocode-http's HTTP/1.1 client on simulated sockets, against an in-simulator HTTP/1.1 server in front of the scripted model, and judges three new invariants, each with a mutation the simulator catches (2026-11-13, Georgios: find bugs with nanocode-sim and mocked responses over our own HTTP client). Until now the runtime scenario replaced the client's transport (`ClaudeClient::with_transport`), so nanocode-http, its pool, framing and content decoding never ran under the simulator. bin/nanocode-sim/src/socket.rs is a simulated socket pair (two byte queues with wakers on the simulator's executor; the client side reads and writes in seeded pieces, 1 to 7 bytes on a fifth of connections, and sees EOF, a reset or a broken pipe as TCP would). bin/nanocode-sim/src/httpd.rs is the server: a `Connect` that refuses, hangs past the connect timeout or spawns a connection task, which parses each request with nanocode-http's own parser, checks method, path, Host, x-api-key, anthropic-version and that the body is not content-encoded, and answers per a seeded fate: close without processing, process and reset before answering (an uncertain outcome), 429/500/502/503/529 with Retry-After or retry-after-ms, 307/308 redirects up to 3 hops to the same or another host, or the model's SSE answer encoded as identity, gzip, deflate, br (stored meta-blocks) or zstd (raw blocks), framed by content-length, chunked (with chunk extensions and a trailer) or connection close, preceded at times by 100 and 103 responses, written in up to 8 pieces with gaps, with faults: duplicate processing, a slow head up to 180 s, a malformed status line, content-length, conflicting lengths, chunk size or chunk end, a stray content-encoding, 101 headers, a head over HEAD_BYTES_MAX, a reset, an EOF or a stall of 121 to 600 s mid-body, stray bytes after a complete response, `connection: close`, and idle keep-alive connections closed after 0 to 5 s. Fault rates are drawn per seed (30% of seeds calm), from a separate RNG so `--wire transport` seeds replay as before. New invariants: (1) the model server sees every tool_use's result exactly once, in the next message, and none it did not call (server.rs, both wires; mutation `tool-result-twice` duplicates one tool_result in the request, caught by 291 of 300 seeds on each wire); (2) a connection carries a new request only after a complete, reusable response: never after a close-delimited body, `connection: close`, a malformed head or framing, stray bytes, or a stalled body (mutation `http-reuse-dirty` hands the client such a connection again, caught by 156 of 300); (3) a client still connected when a slow head or stalled body has waited past its read timeout (120 s, plus 1 s) is a hang (mutation `http-no-read-timeout` builds the client without its read timeout, caught by 45 of 300). The existing ones (each effect once, no invented assistant message, acknowledged turns kept, everything settles within 1,800 s, `--twice` replays the trace digest) apply too. Results (release, 8 jobs on dev-georgios at load 60 to 90): `sweep.sh 0 6000 8 --scenario runtime --wire http` and `0 4000` passed every seed, `0 1000 --wire http --twice` passed 1000, and `0 3000 --scenario runtime` (transport, with the new tool-result check) passed 3000; 500 seeds made 18,622 model requests over 10,386 connections with 9,666 reuses and 2,455 faults, 4 of 1,440 turns failing as the fault budget allows. The first 2,000-seed sweep failed 19 seeds: 11 were stray bytes the server wrote in a later piece than the body's end, which no client can tell from a next response, so stray bytes now go out in the same write as the body's last byte; 8 were nanocode-http accepting a head over its bound, fixed in the next entry. - nanocode-http reads its clock through nanocode-platform (`now`, `timeout`) instead of `tokio::time`, and `ClientBuilder::connector` takes a `Connect` that opens each connection in place of DNS, TCP, proxies and TLS (2026-11-13, Georgios: find bugs with nanocode-sim by running the Claude and Codex clients over nanocode-http on simulated sockets). The client's whole-request deadline, its per-read timeout, the head read and the pool's idle clock were `tokio::time::{Instant, timeout, timeout_at}`, which need a Tokio runtime with timers and cannot run in the simulator's virtual time; they are now `nanocode_platform::{now, timeout}`, and `timeout_at(deadline)` is `timeout(deadline.saturating_duration_since(now()))`, which elapses at once for a passed deadline as `tokio::time::timeout_at` does. Without an installed platform host, which is every binary but nanocode-sim, `nanocode_platform::timeout` is `tokio::time::timeout` and `now` is `std::time::Instant::now` (the same clock as `tokio::time::Instant` outside a paused test runtime), so production timing is the same calls as before; with the simulator's host they run on its virtual clock. A connector replaces only `connect::stream`: the connect timeout, pool, request writing, framing, redirects and decoding are unchanged, and a client without one connects as before. - deps(json): nanocode's own indexmap keeps the insertion order of serde_json's `preserve_order` maps and RustPython's dicts, sets and compiler tables; indexmap 2.14.0, hashbrown 0.17.1 and equivalent 1.0.2 leave (2026-11-13, Georgios: own every dependency outside the accepted runtime and TLS set). crates/core/indexmap takes the crates.io name and version 2.14.0 (a workspace member in `[patch.crates-io]`; serde_json 1.0.150 asks `^2.2.3`, rustpython-vm, -stdlib and -codegen ask 2.14.0 and no longer name the `std` feature, the only one they asked for, so the crate declares none). Entries live in a `Vec` of key and value buckets. A map of at most 8 entries (`LINEAR_ENTRIES_MAX`) has no index and finds a key by comparing the keys in order, without hashing; a larger one keeps an open-addressing table of `u64` slots at most 3/4 full (`LOAD_NUMERATOR`/`LOAD_DENOMINATOR`, picked by output/indexmap-equal/load-sweep.sh over 1/2, 5/8, 3/4 and 7/8), each slot holding the entry's index plus one in its low bits and the hash's high bits as a tag, with linear probing and backward-shift deletion, and the entries' hashes beside the slots so growing and removing never rehash a key; `shift_remove`, `shift_insert` and `move_index` renumber the moved entries by probing each when they are few (`SHIFT_PROBE_SLOTS_PER_ENTRY`) and by one pass over the slots otherwise. Every invariant the table relies on (a free slot exists, an entry's slot is found, indexes fit beside the tag) is an assert. The default hasher stays std's `RandomState` (SipHash with random keys per map), as indexmap's was, so keys in parsed JSON cannot be picked to collide. API: what serde_json and the RustPython crates call, `IndexMap` (constructors with capacity and hasher, `insert`, `insert_full`, `shift_insert`, `entry` with `Entry`, `OccupiedEntry` and `VacantEntry`, the `get` family, `swap_` and `shift_remove` by key, index and entry, `pop`, `retain`, `drain`, `move_index`, `sort_unstable_keys`, `reserve`, `first`, `last`, `get_index(_mut)`, the iterators, `Index`, `Extend`, `FromIterator`, `PartialEq`, `Debug`, `Clone`, `Default`) and `IndexSet` (the same plus `swap_take`, `shift_take`, `is_subset`). Not equal: lookups take `Q: Hash + Eq` with `K: Borrow<Q>` instead of indexmap's `Equivalent` trait (every caller here passes a borrowed key); there is no rayon, serde, borsh, arbitrary or quickcheck support, no `Slice` types, `splice`, `extract_if`, `get_disjoint_mut` or the rest of the API nothing here calls; a map of up to 8 entries never calls the hasher, so a `Hash` impl with side effects sees fewer calls. Equal, output/indexmap-equal (indexmap =2.14.0 beside the new crate by path, and serde_json =1.0.150 with `preserve_order` built once over each): `ops` runs 2,000 seeded sequences of 20,000 operations on both maps and sets with string and integer keys (every call above, each `Entry` path, iteration forward and back, `nth`, `count`, `size_hint`, clones, equality after reordering, `Debug`), comparing every result and both whole maps after each step: 1,732,962,727 checks, 0 differences; `json` parses, edits and writes (compact and pretty) 4,911 JSON files on dev-georgios (the cargo registry and Python packages, 109 MB) and 100,000 seeded documents (1.26 GB): 5,282,365 compared outputs, 0 differences. Mutations of table.rs that break swap_remove's renumbering, shift_remove's last index, the growth point or the backward-shift condition each fail within the first seed. Speed (output/indexmap-equal/bench, `perf stat -e instructions:u` per round, three runs, upstream then ours): serde_json parse of 491 of those files 312.7M to 261.7M (-16%), serialize 67.6M to 67.5M, a stream of event objects 598.2M to 447.5M (-25%); 8 string keys insert 43.9M to 19.2M, get 32.4M to 14.5M, remove 44.4M to 15.5M; 12 to 65,536 string keys insert +0.4% to +17% (12: 36.6M to 42.9M; 1,024: 26.6M to 27.3M) and get +2% to +6%; u64 keys insert -5% to -63% and get -4% to +4%, but 8 u64 keys get 11.5M to 1.9M; remove from 64 entries +8.5%, from 1,024 and 16,384 entries -4% and -10%. Cycles are noisier under load (80 to 140): insert of 1,024 keys 10.0M to 12.1M (+20%), get of 1,024 equal, parse 157.8M to 129.5M; wall time, median of 21 interleaved rounds: parse 66.7 to 52.2 ms, serialize 176.2 to 189.0 ms (+7%, equal instructions), events 161.2 to 112.6 ms, 8 keys insert 31.8 to 11.0 ms and get 24.3 to 13.0 ms, 12 keys insert 11.7 to 12.5 ms, 1,024 keys insert 12.7 to 15.2 ms and get 16.1 to 15.7 ms. Compile, output/indexmap-compile (`cargo build -j 1` of a crate depending on each, from empty target directories, five rounds): release 1.14 to 1.38 s of user time with indexmap, hashbrown and equivalent, 0.37 to 0.40 s with ours; debug 1.01 and 0.35 s. - deps(json): nanocode's own itoa formats integers for serde_json, http and RustPython, and itoa 1.0.18 leaves (2026-11-13, Georgios: remove itoa, shlex, cfg-if, getrandom and once_cell from nanocode-cli's tree). crates/core/itoa takes the crates.io name and version 1.0.18 (a workspace member in `[patch.crates-io]`, as unicode-normalization does), satisfying http's and RustPython's `^1` and serde_json's `^1.0`, with the API they call: `Buffer` (`new`, now `const`, `Default`, `Clone`, `Copy`, `format`) and the sealed `Integer` with `MAX_STR_LEN` for u8 to u128, i8 to i128, usize and isize. It writes from the end of a 40-byte buffer four digits per step from a two-digit table, a u128 of 10^16 or more split by 10^16 through a 128-bit multiply by the reciprocal (Granlund and Montgomery; the constant derived with shift 51 and checked in Python over 200,000 random values and the edges), each 16-digit chunk as two 8-digit halves at fixed offsets. The buffer is nanocode-sys's new `DecimalText<N>` (crates/core/sys/src/decimal.rs): its only writers put a table pair, a quad, a digit below ten or a minus sign, so every byte stays ASCII and `text` returns the written tail through `from_utf8_unchecked`; with a safe `str::from_utf8` instead, every call paid 4 to 7 ns (37% to 120% slower than itoa: u64 0..999 4.5 to 9.0 ns, u64 of 1 to 20 digits 19.2 to 26.3 ns). So itoa now depends on nanocode-sys and serde_json waits for nanocode-sys to compile: `cargo build --release --locked -p nanocode-types-core --timings` from empty target directories without scripts/buildcache, master then this, twice (load 70 to 110): serde_json ends at 9.2 and 7.1 s, then 9.7 and 11.6 s, beside serde (derive), which nanocode crates wait for anyway, ending at 10.6 and 8.2 s, then 8.7 and 11.4 s, so at most ~0.1 s reaches the critical path here. Not equal: `Buffer::new` fills its 40 bytes with '0' where itoa leaves them uninitialized; `Integer` has no hidden `Buffer` type. Equal, output/itoa/equal (itoa =1.0.18 beside the new crate by path): every u8, i8, u16 and i16 (263,168 values, also against `Display`), 13,284 edges (each power of ten and of two with neighbors, in every width and sign, MIN and MAX), and 563,125,000 values seeded 20261113 over u32, i32, u64, i64, u128, i128, usize and isize (uniform bits, uniform digit counts, shifted, negated, also against `Display` for one in 64): 563,401,452 comparisons, 0 differences, and `MAX_STR_LEN` equal for all twelve types. Speed, `perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u` per call (output/itoa/perf.sh: 1,000,000 seeded values, 11 rounds minus 1), itoa then nanocode: u64 of 1 to 20 digits 79.0 to 68.7 cycles, u64 0..999 19.9 to 13.3, u64 of uniform bits 55.4 to 53.5, i64 91.5 to 77.9, u32 62.6 to 51.6, i32 57.6 to 44.0, u8 22.2 to 21.9, u16 24.4 to 18.4, i16 45.3 to 39.7, u128 of 1 to 39 digits 114.9 to 119.8 (+4%), i128 130.1 to 138.4 (+6%): a u128 below 10^16 takes the inlined u64 path (one digit 25.8 to 9.9 cycles) and one of 17 to 39 digits takes 5 to 15% more cycles (17 digits 52.7 to 62.6); nothing here formats a u128 on a hot path. serde_json 1.0.150 `to_writer` per integer (output/itoa/json-old and json-new, one program built without and with the patch, three alternating runs): Vec<u64> of 1 to 20 digits 91.6, 89.1, 92.0 to 88.6, 88.0, 92.7 cycles, Vec<i64> 103.2, 101.6, 107.7 to 102.4, 100.6, 101.0, Vec<u32> 0..999 31.1, 31.6, 29.2 to 30.4, 28.4, 29.6, `Value::to_string` of a number 214.0, 211.7, 221.9 to 213.3, 217.7, 215.5; instructions rise (u64 108 to 129) since the whole formatter inlines into serde_json, cycles are equal within noise. - perf(turnlog): a snapshot check that finds the snapshot not yet worth writing schedules the next check where the measured growth says it will be, instead of right at the size the state has now (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `Lease::commit` writes a snapshot when the log since the last one (`writer.snapshot + writer.tail`) exceeds `ratio` times the compressed state, and to know the compressed size it serializes the fold and deflates all of it (`codec::pack(SNAPSHOT, …)`). When that check failed it set the next check at `ratio * packed - snapshot`, the point where the snapshot would have been due had the state stopped growing; in a session that keeps its turns, the state grows with the log, so the next check failed the same way after a little more log, and each one deflated the whole state again (hundreds of KB at level 6). A Node CPU profile of 200 Workers-style turns had `codec::pack` under `Lease::commit` at 12.5% of the process with one snapshot written in the whole run. `Writer::tried` keeps the tail and compressed size of the last failed check; the next failed check projects the linear trend between the two, `ratio` times compressed growth per byte of tail, and sets the check at the tail where the snapshot becomes due under it (`(gap * due - grown * tail) / (gap - grown)`), or at `ratio` times the current tail when the state grows at least as fast as the log (the snapshot never pays off at that rate, so the trend is measured again after the log grows by the same factor). The check is never earlier than before (`max(due, projected)`); while the trend holds the snapshot is written at the same commit as before, and `tried` resets with every snapshot and on reopen. Rows unchanged: output/turnlog-replay prints the same stored bytes and fold hashes (and the same with `FAIL_EVERY=7 REOPEN_EVERY=5`), instructions 5.35G -> 3.86G (-28%); nanocode-ts prof.ts DUMP=1 at 100 turns writes 3,134 record rows and 1 snapshot row both before and after (bytes within noise), reopens and runs a turn. Instructions per turn (prof.ts, 200 turns of each kind, wasm after wasm-opt, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, interleaved): 53.0, 50.0, 51.2, 47.6M -> 37.4, 39.0, 39.3M (-24%). bench/overhead.ts --n=20 completes every cell. Rejected first: estimating the compressed size from the last measured ratio and deflating only when the estimate said due (identical replay output, -17.5% replay instructions, but prof.ts 46.2, 50.1, 47.8M -> 47.7, 50.2, 48.2M: every check sits right at the boundary, so the estimate said due as often as not). Commands: `cargo clippy --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog --no-deps -- -D warnings` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, rustfmt. Files: crates/core/turnlog/src/writer.rs.
- perf(djs): in WebAssembly the arena grows in place where the allocator can extend it, instead of moving after a Rust temporary (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: memory). wasm32's dlmalloc grows a block in place only when the chunk after it is free or is the top chunk with room for the growth; otherwise `realloc` copies the arena to a new block and frees the old one, and since linear memory never shrinks, memory ends at the old size plus the new. The arena is usually the last block, but a Rust buffer that lives while it grows (JSON.parse's value stack, join's part list, split's ranges, the mark stack) is carved from the top chunk right after it, and dlmalloc's `try_realloc_chunk` does not grow memory for an in-place extension even when the top chunk is the next chunk, so every growth past the top chunk's slack moved: a 100,000-row JSON round trip held a 41 MB arena in 107 MB of memory. `Arena::reserve` on wasm32 now first allocates blocks of the growth's size (`hold_until_past`) and holds them until one lands at or after the arena's end, then frees them all before `try_reserve_exact`: a block from a free chunk below the arena only fills that hole for the moment, and the one from the top chunk extends memory by the growth right after the arena (dlmalloc's `sys_alloc`), which the free merges back into the top chunk, so the realloc extends in place; if a live buffer sits after the arena the probe lands past it and the realloc moves as before into that memory, with no more growth than before. Native builds are unchanged. output/wasmrun (djs-embed to wasm32, run in Node 24; wasm memory at exit, base -> new): limit 2 GiB: 100,000-row JSON round trip 107.3 -> 69.6 MB, 20,000-object map/filter x40 21.2 -> 18.4, 2M short objects 3.6 -> 2.8, Map of arrays x30 22.1 -> 10.8, 20x20,000 objects 14.8 -> 9.3, 50,000 lines join/split/map 21.0 -> 21.6, 200,000 kept objects x20 maps 214.3 -> 214.3 (its heap is 3x live data, the GC's growth rule); with nanocode-ts's Workers cell limit of 32 MiB (half of the gateway's 64 MiB `RUNTIME_MEMORY_BUDGET_BYTES`): 50,000 rows 60.3 -> 41.5, 70,000 rows 69.8 -> 55.9, 80,000 kept objects 64.5 -> 34.4. - scripts/build-cli.sh runs BOLT with `-use-old-text`, so the optimized code goes into the original `.text`'s place instead of a new segment after a kept copy of the original: the shipped Linux nanocode 73,188,176 to 64,791,600 bytes (-8.4 MB, -11.5%) (2026-11-14, Georgios: "the install size of nc being 70mb hurts a bit, on the default CLI especially"). The BOLT output kept the linker's 44.1 MB `.text` as `.bolt.org.text` and added its own 3.3 MB `.text` and 5.4 MB `.text.cold`; now `.text` (3.3 MB, hot) and `.text.cold` (40.3 MB) sit at the original address, and the stripped pre-BOLT binary is 60,588,760 bytes, so BOLT now adds 4.2 MB (its new `.eh_frame` beside the original `.bolt.org.eh_frame`, which stays in the first segment) where it added 12.6 MB. Where the new code does not fit, BOLT falls back to a new segment as before. Both binaries came from the same dist build and profile (BOLT 19, dev-georgios); bench/cli `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc` alternating them in 3 batches under `perf stat` (12 samples each, load average ~80 from other jobs): user instructions median 10.16M and 10.15M, kernel 12.26M and 12.22M, page faults 892 and 893, task clock 7.7 and 7.9 ms. - perf(djs): comparing two flat strings for equality reads each one's kind once and compares their bytes (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: Array callbacks). `Heap::str_eq` (heap/string.rs) resolved both strings, read their lengths, read their widths through `str_is_two_byte` (a `cell_kind` each), read both cached hashes and then built the two views through `str_view`, reading the kinds again: about 160 instructions for two short distinct strings, which every `===` between strings that are not the same cell pays, as in `items.filter(t => t.status === "open")` over parsed JSON. Two `Str8` or two `Str16` cells now go through `flat_fast` (one kind read each) and a slice comparison, which checks the lengths first; a `Str8` against a `Str16` is unequal, as the width check already concluded (a two-byte cell always holds a unit above 0xFF); ropes, slices and append ropes keep the previous path. The cached-hash shortcut no longer applies to flat strings: two distinct flat strings of the same length now compare bytes up to their first difference. Instructions per callback (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, ~/djs2/cb/k, 100,000 objects from `JSON.parse`, 30 minus 10 rounds): findIndex(t => t.id === 'id99999') 947 -> 833 (-12%, qjs 608), filter(t => t.status === 'open') 1,008 -> 979 (-2.9%, qjs 871); numeric field compare, find, sort, generators, new Error, compute, loops and promises unchanged; output/cellbench empty cell 90,040 -> 90,024, agent cell 1,024,711 -> 1,024,170, ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 35.21M -> 35.22M per round. Test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines (16-way), the 25 edge cells print the same; checks, clippy (native and wasm32) and rustfmt as in the entries below.
- perf(claude): the conversation digest chain survives between turns and resumes from the last message whose bytes did not change, instead of rehashing every message's digests for each request whose history differs from the last one anywhere (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `api_body` keeps a rolling BLAKE3 over each message's `sent` and `read` digests (the `conversation` digest that `durable_input` records); the chain lived in `Assembled` with the body, which `WireCache` keeps only while a `keep_body` guard is held, and was thrown away whenever the new request did not extend the old one exactly, which happens every turn because the cache breakpoint moves off the previous last message. So every request rehashed the whole history, one BLAKE3 block per message, and a Node CPU profile of 300 Workers-style turns had BLAKE3 under `api_body` at 3.6% and rising with the session. `wire_cache::Hashed` now lives in its own `Slot` (kept between turns: 64 bytes per message) with `marks`, a copy of the two hashers taken before each message that carries a cache marker (`MessageDigests::marked`, read differing from sent), at most one per breakpoint of the current request; the next request resumes from the end when the whole previous history is shared, else from the last mark at or before the shared prefix, and hashes only from there. The body is still reused only while kept, now up to the shared prefix capped by its own `ends`. Same bytes and digests: output/claude-wire (400 rounds of a growing two-breakpoint conversation, the body kept two rounds in three, a truncation every 50 rounds, one or two requests per round) compares the cached request's body and `durable_input` with an uncached `prepare_wire`: 0 differences before and after. nanocode-ts output/prof.ts (wasm after wasm-opt, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, interleaved): 200 turns of each kind 56.9, 59.0, 59.7M -> 51.3, 52.4, 51.3M instructions per turn (-12%); 100 turns 45.3, 46.6, 47.5M -> 46.2, 45.8, 43.2M (-3%, within noise of a shorter history). bench/overhead.ts --n=20 completes every cell; prof.ts DUMP=1 reopens the database, reads the last turn and runs one more. Commands: `cargo clippy --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client -p nanocode-backend-claude --no-deps -- -D warnings` and the client for wasm32-unknown-unknown, rustfmt on the changed files. Files: crates/backends/claude/client/src/{lib,wire_cache}.rs.
- perf(djs): the parser's stand-in for the finished top level allocates nothing (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `finish_unit_with` (and `free_names`) moved the top level out of `Parser::f` by replacing it with `FuncState::new`, which built a full function state: a scope vector with the body scope and 32 reserved phase-1 instructions, two allocations per compile that were freed unused. `FuncState::vacant` builds the stand-in with no scope and no reserve (`FuncState::build` with `open` false; `reusing` passes true); `FuncState::new` goes, and lazy.rs calls `reusing` with a default spare. output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 35.09M -> 34.97M per round (-0.3%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 25.78k -> 25.10k (-2.7%); the empty cell 89.42k -> 88.86k (-0.6%); the agent cell 1,023.0k -> 1,021.1k. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical to the previous commit's, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- `OneLogJournals::save` commits a Code Mode cell's first save only when the cell arms a timer before another row commits (2026-11-14, Georgios: get Code Mode turns back to fewer rows without losing recovery). cfd8999c7 committed a row at every cell start, so a synchronous cell cost one row more than before. The crash it covered is a host that dies while the cell waits. A cell waits on a timer (a `JournalEntry::Timeout`), a nested call or the model. A nested External call already commits its own row with the buffered header, and a nested call without effects returns before a host can die with any useful probability. `OneLog::unsaved` now holds each cell whose header is only buffered, keyed by session and cell with the fold's committed `seq` at that save. A save commits when it carries an External call, or when it carries a `Timeout` and the header is new or no row committed since it was buffered. A finished cell or `forget` removes the key. Rows per turn in durable-cloudflare `output/turns.mjs` (local workerd, mean of 5 turns, objects' own SQL), build-2672c04 then this change: reply 2 and 2, `text("ok")` cell 3 and 2, timer cell 3 and 3, `tools.charge` cell 4 and 3. nanocode-ts `Journal.committed` in durable-vercel `output/journal.ts` gives the same transactions per turn (2, 3, 3, 4 on build-90e28af, 2, 2, 3, 3 with this change). durable-vercel `npm run drill` passes all 8 runs, the 4 `waiting` runs included, and durable-cloudflare `npm run drill` passes its 3 scenarios (with the `MCP_LISTINGS_KV` namespace added to its scripts/local-runtime.mjs), both with a local nanocode-ts pack at this change. `bin/nanocode-sim/sweep.sh 0 2000 5 --scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` passed 2000 of 2000, and the same with `--retain 0` passed 1000 of 1000 (the simulator does not drive cell journals). `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent` passes natively and for wasm32 with `nanocode-code-mode/local-cells`, and `cargo +1.97.1 clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-agent -- -D warnings` passes with `-A clippy::useless_conversion` for the existing nanocode-sys warnings.
- perf(djs): a function's scopes keep their binding lists for the next function, and a template's local names go into the heap without a copy (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `FuncState::recycle` cleared `scopes`, freeing each scope's `vars`, `funcs` and `copies` vectors, so every scope that declared a binding allocated again in the next compile (`add_var`: a quarter of a compile's remaining allocator calls); `alloc_info` collected the local names' atom ids into a `Vec<u32>` before writing them into the `U32Array`. Recycled scopes now go, emptied, into `func::Spare::scope_pool`, which `FuncState::reusing` and `new_scope` draw from (`pooled_scope`), and `alloc_u32_array` writes the ids straight from the atoms. Allocator calls per round of the corpus 6,010 -> 5,076 (-16%). output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 35.24M -> 35.09M per round (-0.4%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 26.31k -> 25.80k (-1.9%); the empty cell 90.0k -> 89.36k (-0.7%); the agent cell 1,025.4k -> 1,023.0k. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- perf(djs): a negative number literal compiles to one push of the negative number instead of a push and `neg` (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: Array callbacks). `-5` was `push_i8 5; neg`, and `neg` is not in the hot loop's own arms (`decline_fast` runs it), so a callback like `x => x === -5` or `i !== -1` left `run_hot` once per call. The parser (compiler/expr.rs `parse_unary_inner`) now replaces a `-` whose operand is a number token and compiled to exactly one `push_i8`, `push_i32` or `push_const` with `emit_number` of the negated value (`-0` stays a constant, a dropped trailing constant is popped). `Array.prototype.sort`'s comparator recognizer (builtins/array.rs `comparator_of`) matches `push_i8 -1; return` where it matched `push1; neg; return`. Instructions per callback as in the entry below: findIndex(o=>o===-5) 758 -> 569 (-25%, qjs 350); the object sort comparator `p.k<q.k?-1:p.k>q.k?1:0` 89.53M -> 89.57M per round (+0.04%, still recognized); ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 38.90M -> 38.86M per round; everything else as before. Values printed for `1/-0`, `-1.5`, `-1e300`, `-0x10`, `-(1).toString()`, `-1n`, `-2147483648`, `-2147483649`, `-128`, `-129`, `Object.is(-0, 0)`, `-NaN`, `- 1 + 2`, `-1 * -1` match qjs. Test262, edge cells and commands as in the entry below.
- perf(djs): a dense `forEach`, `map`, `filter`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex` or `reduce` callback that returns is entered again for the next element without the general `each_return` step (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: Array callbacks). `Exec::each_again` (interp/run/each.rs), called first by `each_return`, takes the case every element of a plain dense loop hits: the frame is still the callback's, mode and k are ints, the result needs no conversion (a boolean for the predicate modes, anything for map and reduce), the next element is below `len` and present in the elements store, and the store into `a` (map at k, filter at its length, reduce's box) succeeds through `create_element_fast`. It then writes k, kValue, the arguments, the padding and the locals straight into the arena slots with the hot loop's `ld`/`st`/`fill` (made `pub(super)` in hot.rs) and returns the new stack top; anything else (a truthy find, a hole, a non-boolean predicate result, an async callback, the end) falls through to the previous path unchanged. `NEW_TARGET` is not rewritten: only a construct frame writes it and the callback frame is never one (writing it cost 9 instructions per callback). Instructions per callback (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, ~/djs2/cb/k: arrays of 100,000 ints, 30 minus 10 rounds over 2,000,000 callbacks; qjs 2024-01-13 from Debian alongside): find(x=>x===99999) 577 -> 539 (qjs 350), findIndex 569 -> 539, empty forEach 371 -> 349 (qjs 434), some 532 -> 502 (498), every 531 -> 498 (498), map(x=>x*2) 800 -> 726 (812), filter 819 -> 783 (702), reduce((p,x)=>p+x,0) 731 -> 604 (573), forEach writing a closure variable 724 -> 702 (788). Unchanged (+-0.01%): sort and object sort comparators, generators, new Error, compute, loops, promises; output/cellbench empty cell 91,915 -> 91,918, agent cell 1,061,785 -> 1,061,361, one tool call 250,180 -> 250,182. Tried and not kept: doing the same from the hot loop's `return` arm (no exit from `run_hot`, the arm takes `each_again` through `heap_call!` and goes on at pc 0), which took find to 481 and the empty forEach to 274 but moved register allocation in `run_hot` for every other opcode: an empty counted loop +2.4%, `loop0` +0.1 to +2.9%, generators +0.5%, the object sort +0.5% across three arrangements of the arm (with the backedge budget, without it, sharing the return's safepoint tail). Test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines (16-way), the 25 edge cells print the same (PRINT=1 EVENTS=1). Commands: `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p djs-core -p djs-embed -p nanocode-code-mode-engine -p nanocode-code-mode` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --no-deps -- -D warnings` on the same, rustfmt.
- The paying proxy writes its certificate bundle straight to the file: the CA's PEM, then the system bundle file streamed with `io::copy` (`copy_file_range` on Linux), instead of building the whole bundle in a `Vec` from a `fs::read` of the system file (2026-11-13, Georgios: "i dont wanna leave any performance on the table", toward the 1.3 ms first frame). Classifying the TUI's page faults to its first frame (`perf record -e page-faults -d`, 3 runs) found 766 of 965 in anonymous memory, and the proxy's thread took about 12% of them for two 182 KB buffers. When the roots do not come from one file the bundle is still each decoded root's PEM, now written one at a time; a missing-roots error is returned before the file is created. Checked: the bundle written before and after is 182,352 bytes with 122 certificates and everything after the CA is byte-identical to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Measured on dev-georgios with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19), bench/cli's `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe --only=nc` alternating the builds in 5 batches of 3 rounds under `perf stat` (15 samples each): page faults to the first frame 947 to 862, kernel instructions 12.81M to 12.28M (user 9.73M and 9.85M); without it, 6 batches of 3 with `--parts=firstframe,oneshot` (18 samples each, load average 54 to 99 from other jobs, so times are relative): resident memory 1 s after the first frame 14.44 to 13.99 MB (anonymous 2.82 to 2.57 MB), CPU to the first frame 10.26 to 9.78 ms, one-shot peak RSS 14.25 to 13.75 MB. `cargo clippy -p nanocode-cli` passes.
- perf(djs): the bracket scanners keep their stack inline and the pattern scan's buffers outlive a compile (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). Every lookahead scan (`is_arrow_head` for each `(`, `skip_group`, `for_head_is_c_style`, `PatternScan::scan` for object and array literals) allocated its bracket stack, and `PatternScan::scan` also its parallel `opens` vector, and every compile started `PatternScan` with an empty `entries` vector: about a fifth of a compile's allocator calls. `scan::Brackets` holds the first `INLINE_DEPTH` (32) brackets in an array and only deeper ones in a vector; `PatternScan` keeps `opens`, and its `entries` and `opens` move into `ParserSpare` between compiles (`PatternScan::reusing`, `take_buffers`). Allocator calls per round of the corpus 7,955 -> 6,010 (-24%). output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 35.51M -> 35.24M per round (-0.8%); the agent cell 1,031.3k -> 1,025.4k (-0.6%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 26.19k -> 26.32k and the empty cell 89.73k -> 90.0k (+0.3%), from the larger spare moved in and out of each parser. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- graviola, through rustls-graviola, is the only crypto provider on every target, and ring leaves every Cargo.toml and the lock with getrandom 0.2.17, windows-sys 0.52.0, windows-targets 0.52.6 and its eight windows_* target crates, 12 packages (2026-11-13, Georgios: remove ring so graviola is the only provider). Before, rustls used graviola only on aarch64-apple-darwin and ring on every other target (nanocode-tls's `install_default_rustls_crypto_provider`), the egress proxy always built its rustls configs on ring's provider (nanocode-sandbox's `provider()`, with tokio-rustls's `ring` feature), and ring generated, read and signed the egress certificates' keys (crates/integrations/sandbox/src/egress/certificate.rs) and the paying proxy's (bin/nanocode/src/tempo/x509.rs). Now nanocode-tls installs `rustls_graviola::default_provider()` on every native target, nanocode-sandbox's `provider()` is the same provider, and no crate asks rustls or tokio-rustls for ring. The keys use graviola's own types: a new key is a P-256 `StaticPrivateKey::new_random` written as PKCS#8 by `SigningKey::<P256>::to_pkcs8_der` (138 bytes, `P256_PKCS8_BYTES`: PKCS#8 v1 around an RFC 5915 ECPrivateKey that carries the public key and no parameters, the same layout ring wrote); a CA key is read from PKCS#8 as Ed25519, ECDSA P-256, ECDSA P-384 or RSA in the order and with the algorithms it had (`Ed25519SigningKey::from_pkcs8_der`, `SigningKey::<P256/P384>::from_pkcs8_der`, `rsa::SigningKey::from_pkcs8_der` signing PKCS#1 v1.5 with SHA-256); hashes are graviola's SHA-256. graviola signs ECDSA as fixed r and s, so `ecdsa_signature` writes the DER SEQUENCE of two INTEGERs with nanocode-x509's `sequence` and `unsigned_integer` (the CLI with its own DER helpers), which is the form ring returned; graviola keeps no borrowed public key, so `KeyPair` stores the encoded public key it read (the uncompressed point, the 32-byte Ed25519 key, the PKCS#1 RSAPublicKey, encoded into a buffer the size of the PKCS#8 document that contains it). `KeyPair::generate` builds the key pair from the key it made instead of parsing its own PKCS#8 again, which would derive the public point twice more. The public API of nanocode_sandbox::egress (`KeyPair`, `Issuer`, `Tls`, `DnType`, `ExtendedKeyUsagePurpose`) is unchanged. Why rustls-webpki is vendored: rustls-webpki 0.103's `alloc` feature is `["ring?/alloc", "pki-types/alloc"]`, and Cargo puts an optional dependency named by a weak feature into the lock whenever the feature is on (rustls always turns `alloc` on), so with every `ring` feature off ring still resolved in Cargo.lock and `cargo metadata` with its 11 packages, though nothing built it (`cargo tree -i ring --target all` was empty). crates/patches/rustls-webpki is rustls-webpki 0.103.16 with its ring and aws-lc-rs backends removed, as upstream did for 0.104 (0.104.0-alpha.4 dropped `ring?/alloc`): Cargo.toml without the two optional dependencies and their features (and without dev-dependencies), lib.rs without `mod ring_algs`, `mod aws_lc_rs_algs`, the `webpki::ring` and `webpki::aws_lc_rs` re-exports and their feature rows, `ALL_VERIFICATION_ALGS` empty (it held only those backends' algorithms; rustls takes its verification algorithms from the provider), verify_cert.rs without its tests module (it needed a backend), and src/ring_algs.rs, aws_lc_rs_algs.rs, alg_tests.rs and the three data/alg-*.der files they read deleted; every other file is byte for byte the published crate (8,188 of 10,197 lines). It is patched in the root [patch.crates-io] beside rustls-platform-verifier and goes when rustls 0.24 brings rustls-webpki 0.104. Targets: nanocode ships aarch64 and x86_64 macOS and Linux (install, scripts/release-cli.sh), all of which graviola supports; wasm32 has no TLS before or after (nanocode-tls is empty there, nanocode-sandbox is unix-only); x86_64-pc-windows-gnu now uses graviola too. graviola has code only for x86_64 and aarch64 and refuses to compile elsewhere, so nanocode-tls, nanocode-sandbox and nanocode-cli no longer build for other architectures (riscv64, which the sandbox's seccomp filter knows, 32-bit ARM and x86, s390x and the rest), where ring built; no nanocode build targets them, and keeping ring behind a `cfg(not(any(target_arch = "x86_64", target_arch = "aarch64")))` gate would have kept it and its 11 packages in the lock. graviola also asserts CPU features the first time it runs: on x86_64 AES-NI, PCLMULQDQ, BMI1, ADX, AVX and AVX2 (Intel from Broadwell, 2014; AMD from Zen, 2017), on aarch64 AES, SHA2, PMULL and NEON; on an older CPU every TLS connection and every egress certificate now panics, where ring ran anywhere. The provider's handshake differs on Linux and Intel macOS in one way: graviola offers X25519MLKEM768 first (then X25519, P-256, P-384), as it already did on Apple Silicon, where ring offered X25519, P-256, P-384; output/ring-equal's client against badssl.com saw connections reset by the server in 6 of 8 runs (13 resets in 64 connections) with graviola's groups, 0 of 8 with ring and 0 of 8 with graviola without X25519MLKEM768, and none against api.anthropic.com, github.com, www.google.com and the other hosts below; kept as graviola's default, as on Apple Silicon. Equal, output/ring-equal (its own workspace: master's certificate.rs and x509.rs with ring =0.17.14 beside this change's with graviola =0.4.1, the generated keys passed in so both sides sign the same key): for 19 OpenSSL-made keys (3 Ed25519, 5 P-256, 5 P-384, 2 each of RSA 2048, 3072 and 4096) and 400 generated P-256 keys (200 by graviola's `generate`, 200 by ring's `generate_pkcs8`), the subject public key info, public key, serial, key identifier, signature algorithm and PKCS#8 are equal; 8 messages of up to 2,000 bytes per key are signed by both, Ed25519 and RSA signatures are byte-identical, and every ECDSA signature verifies with both ring and graviola (a message with one more byte is refused); for every OpenSSL-made key, leaves for example.com, api.anthropic.com, 127.0.0.1, ::1 and a-b.c.example.test, with no extended key usage and with server and client auth, unbounded and with a fixed 30-day validity, issued under the OpenSSL-made CA certificate (`Issuer::from_certificate`) and under a self-signed CA from the same key, have byte-identical to-be-signed certificates and signature algorithms, and `openssl verify -x509_strict -purpose sslserver` accepts every unbounded leaf of both builds; self-signed CAs have equal to-be-signed bytes (the whole PEM for Ed25519 and RSA) and `openssl verify -x509_strict` accepts them; a CA certificate given another key is refused; graviola re-encodes each of ring's 200 PKCS#8 documents byte for byte, ring loads all of graviola's, OpenSSL parses them (`openssl pkey`, 10); the paying proxy's self-signed CA and leaves for the five hosts from 50 key pairs are byte-identical to-be-signed and pass OpenSSL; 22,711 checks, 0 failures, 848 OpenSSL runs. Through the proxy (`Egress::tcp` with a secret on each host so it intercepts, a self-signed CA and `Tls::from_ca` with OpenSSL-made P-256, P-384, Ed25519, RSA-2048 and RSA-4096 CAs, the same binary built from master and from this change), curl and `openssl s_client -x509_strict -verify_return_error` with TLS 1.2 and with TLS 1.3 verify the minted chain (result 0) for example.com, www.google.com, api.github.com and 1.1.1.1 under both builds: 144 of 144. nanocode-http with graviola: api.anthropic.com/v1/models with an invalid key 401, github.com, www.google.com, the TLS 1.2-only tls-v1-2.badssl.com:1012, ecc256, ecc384 and rsa4096.badssl.com 200 (apart from the resets above), and expired, wrong.host, self-signed, untrusted-root and sha384.badssl.com (expired since 2022) refused, as by master's build; no local Postgres on dev-georgios, so store-sql's TLS was not run. Speed (output/ring-equal's bench, two P-256 keys, a self-signed CA and one leaf, medians of 9 interleaved rounds of 300, three runs on CPUs 0-7 of dev-georgios at load 46): the egress certificates 76.8, 79.0, 79.1 µs with ring and 71.6, 73.5, 73.6 µs with graviola; the paying proxy's 83.0, 86.4, 86.4 and 77.7, 80.2, 80.2 µs. Size: the release nanocode (stripped, `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli` on x86_64 Linux) grows from 94,568,120 to 95,755,128 bytes and its .text from 58,784,976 to 59,896,080: graviola, with ML-KEM and its generic paths, is larger than the ring it replaces on Linux. Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` 175 to 163 (third-party 68 to 55: the 12, and rustls-webpki now a path crate); nanocode-cli on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 144 to 145 (third-party 48 to 48: ring and getrandom 0.2.17 leave, graviola, rustls-graviola and getrandom 0.3.4 join, rustls-webpki is vendored) and on aarch64-apple-darwin 148 to 146 (51 to 48); cc stays for mimalloc.
