- perf(djs): string literals are cooked, pooled and copied into the heap without a temporary allocation (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). A string literal cost up to three `malloc`s: `cooked_string` built a fresh `Vec<u16>`, `alloc_units` collected a Latin-1 copy into another `Vec<u8>` before `Heap::alloc_latin1`, and `str_pool_get` kept its own `units.to_vec()` per distinct string; string property keys (`atom_of_units`) did the first two. Literals and keys now cook into the parser's `units` buffer (`cooked_string_const`, `cooked_string_atom`), `alloc_units` narrows into its `latin1` buffer, and the pool keeps every string's units in one `str_units` vector with `(start, len, Str)` entries; all three are `ParserSpare` buffers kept between compiles. Allocator calls (uprobes on `__rdl_alloc` and `__rdl_realloc`) per round of the corpus 11,970 -> 7,955 (-34%). output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 36.28M -> 35.51M per round (-2.1%); the trivial cell (`text('ok')`) 106.07k -> 105.72k; the agent cell 1,036.7k -> 1,031.3k; `new AsyncFunction("")` 26.0k -> 26.1-26.2k and the empty cell 89.5k -> 89.7k (+0.2%), from the larger spare moved in and out of the parser. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- perf(durability): sealing a receipt keeps a copy of the operation and stages its payloads with the store's known keys at the next `stage_records_unless`, instead of staging its whole payload tree at once with nothing known (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `JournalState::seal_receipts` (RECEIPT_LEAF is 1, so every settled operation) called `OperationState::stage_unless` with `|_| false`: every payload in the operation's checkpoint and output, with its whole closure, became a `StoreRecord` with a fresh copy of its text (`format!("={content}")`, chunk and node texts), and `stage_records_unless` then threw away almost all of them as already committed (`Fenced::save`'s `committed.contains`). A Node CPU profile of 300 Workers-style turns (nanocode-ts output/prof.ts, names-kept wasm) put `seal_receipts` at 10.4% of the process and the filter at 3.8%, growing with the session. The copy goes into `JournalState::sealing`, the operation is released as before (staged with every key known, which stages nothing), and `stage_records_unless` stages the copies with its `known`, which stops at a committed payload and skips committed chunks before copying them, the same pruning it already applies to unsealed operations (a committed payload's closure was committed with it). An inline payload's record is built with one exact-size allocation instead of `format!`. Same records reach the store: output/prof.ts with DUMP=1 (row counts and bytes of the log table, then a second runtime reopens the same SQLite database, reads the last turn and runs one more): 760 rows both, bytes within run-to-run noise (424,923 and 425,115 before, 426,085 and 424,635 after), reopened turn completed, turn after reopen completed. Instructions per turn (prof.ts, 100 turns of five cell kinds, the wasm build after wasm-opt, `perf stat -e instructions:u`, interleaved 3 times): 49.8, 51.5, 50.7M -> 47.7, 47.8, 48.0M (-5.6%). Commands: `cargo clippy --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core -p nanocode-durability --no-deps -- -D warnings` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, rustfmt. Files: crates/core/durability/src/{state,payload}.rs.
- perf(djs): name resolution keeps its per-function tables between compiles (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `resolve::finish` allocated, every compile, a vector of resolved references per function, a storage vector and a local-name vector per function (`assign_storage`), the template list, the classification path and the source's `LineTable`, and freed them all at its end. They now live in `resolve::Scratch` (`resolved`, `storages`, `templates`, `path`, `line_table`): the per-function vectors are cleared and reused by function index, `assign_storage` fills the pair it is given, and `LineTable::rebuild` refills a table's line starts in place (`LineTable::new` calls it). Memory: those vectors at the largest compile's size. output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 37.43M -> 36.28M per round (-3.1%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 27.8k -> 26.0k (-6.4%); the empty cell 91.43k -> 89.49k (-2.1%); the agent cell 1,048.3k -> 1,036.7k (-1.1%). djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- perf(djs): the parser's own buffers outlive a compile (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `Parser::new` started every compile with empty vectors for its suspended functions (`stack`), finished functions (`done`, whose 680-byte `FuncState`s were copied on every doubling), break targets, identifier bytes, pattern bindings, open iterators and the string constant pool, and `finish_unit_with` collected `done` into a new `Vec<FuncState>` that `resolve::finish` freed. They now come from `ParserSpare` in `Heap::compile_scratch` (`resolve::Scratch::parser`), which `Parser`'s `Drop` refills with the emptied vectors on every path, and `finish_unit_with` moves the functions into `Scratch::funcs`, which `resolve::finish` drains into the spare function states and keeps. Memory: the vectors at the largest size a compile needed, as with the existing scratch buffers. output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 37.98M -> 37.43M per round (-1.4%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 28.6k -> 27.8k (-2.8%); the empty cell 91.67k -> 91.41k; the agent cell 1,049.7k -> 1,048.3k. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- perf(djs): the stack checker's first pass reads each instruction's size from its effect table, and reference classification reuses one path vector (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `stack::walk` (bytecode/stack.rs) decoded every instruction of a finished function twice: its first pass, which marks instruction starts and inline caches, went through `Op::from_u8` and `OpInfo` for the size and the phase-1 flag; `EFFECT`, the table its second pass already reads, now also carries the phase-1 bit (`PHASE1_OP`), so the first pass is one table load per byte; the second pass stops at a no-fallthrough instruction before computing the next pc and records the fall-through depth inline instead of through `reach`. `resolve::classify` built a fresh `Vec` for the scope path of every free-name reference; `free_names` and `finish` now pass one that it clears. output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit (dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 38.86M -> 37.98M per round (-2.2%); the empty cell 91.9k -> 91.7k; the agent cell 1,061.8k -> 1,049.7k (-1.1%). djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; checks as in the entries below.
- perf(turnlog): records rows are compressed by one deflate stream that lives with the writer, instead of a new compressor primed with the 32 KB history for every row (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 nanocode-ts per-turn CPU). `codec::pack` built a `Deflate` per commit and `set_dictionary` re-inserted the whole window into its hash chains before compressing a row of usually a few hundred bytes; a Node CPU profile of 600 Workers-style turns put `Deflate::deflate` under `Lease::commit` at 18.7% of the process. `codec::Stream` keeps the `Deflate` (level 7, `STREAM_LEVEL`) in `Writer::stream`: each row is compressed with a sync flush and closed with an empty final fixed block (`FINAL_EMPTY_BLOCK`), so the row stays a complete raw deflate stream whose dictionary is the history the reader already rebuilds (the compressor's window is that history plus the rows since, and deflate never reaches back past 32 KB). The stream is dropped, and the next commit builds one from `history` as before, after a snapshot, a boundary row, a failed append or a reopen. The format is unchanged: old rows load through the same `unpack`, and older readers read new rows. Checked with output/turnlog-replay (the 19,081 records of a stored nanocode-ts session replayed into a `MemoryLog`, snapshot ratio 2): the reopened fold equals the written one and hashes the same as before (ae389c70…, 6c2ed4c3…), also with `FAIL_EVERY=7 REOPEN_EVERY=5` (every 7th append fails, the log reopens every 5 rows: 294 and 607 failures, reopened equals written); stored bytes 760,748 -> 759,315 and 1,568,230 -> 1,548,229; instructions 8.19G -> 5.35G (-35%). nanocode-ts output/prof.ts (the wasm build after wasm-opt, 100 turns of five cell kinds, `perf stat -e instructions:u` on the process, interleaved 3 times): 55.2, 56.3, 56.9M -> 50.7, 51.3, 51.2M instructions per turn (-9%). bench/overhead.ts --n=20 completes every cell. Commands: `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --no-deps -- -D warnings` on it for both, rustfmt. Files: crates/core/turnlog/src/{codec,writer}.rs.
- perf(djs): a compile's function states keep their buffers for the next compile, and `new Function` builds its source in one allocation (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). A compile made a `FuncState` per function with 15 fresh vectors (code, scopes, vars, refs, lines, consts, labels and the rest) that grew from empty and were freed in `resolve::finish`: with the source strings, 107 `malloc` and 43 `realloc` calls per compile of the corpus, 8% of its instructions in glibc's allocator. `FuncState::recycle` now empties them into a `func::Spare` (the phase-1 instructions come back through `CodeBuf::take_finished` and `reclaim`), `resolve::Scratch` keeps the last compile's spares (`spares`, replaced by each compile's own, so what it holds follows the last unit's size) and `Parser::new` and `begin_function` build each function on one (`FuncState::reusing`, which `FuncState::new` calls with an empty one). `compile_function` (builtins/eval.rs) writes the prefix, parameters, body and suffix into one `String` of their summed length through `Heap::push_str_to` instead of growing a `Vec` from two intermediate `String`s. malloc and realloc calls (uprobes) over 3 rounds of the corpus 49,870 -> 21,984. output/cellbench, instructions, interleaved against the previous commit: ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js 41.08M -> 38.86M per round (-5.4%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 30.8k -> 28.8k; the empty cell 94.1k -> 91.7k (-2.6%); the agent cell 1,091.5k -> 1,060.8k (-2.8%). Against the commit before both: compile -11.3%, empty cell -2.1%, agent cell -2.4%. djsdis output of the 442 files byte-identical, test262 subset 8,631 of 9,288 with identical result lines, edge and corpus cells print the same; commands as in the entry below.
- perf(djs): the parser's identifier atoms outlive a compile (2026-11-14, nanocode 1.0 djs track: compile cost). `IdentAtoms` (compiler/parser.rs), the table from an unescaped identifier's bytes to its atom, moves from the parser to the heap (`Heap::ident_atoms`) and keeps its own copy of the text, so a name the VM has compiled before (`const`, `tools`, `map`, `length`) is no longer hashed with the heap's keyed hash and probed through the atom table (and then the base's) again in every compile: that first lookup per compile was most of `ident_atom`'s 9% of compile instructions. Atom ids are stable and atoms are never freed (heap/atom.rs), so collections, compaction and `release_top` leave the table valid; a heap restored from an image (`restore_image`, `reset_to`) is a new `Heap` with an empty one; a compile recorded for the compile cache (`intern_log`) interns every identifier through the heap as before, so its blob logs them. Memory: a 16-byte slot (the table at most half full) and the text per distinct identifier, which grows as the atom table does. output/cellbench, instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u`, interleaved runs, dev-georgios): ~/djs2/corpus/compile.js (160 `new AsyncFunction` compiles of eight real Code Mode cells, 80.6 KB of source, per round = N 11 minus N 1, over 10) 43.83M -> 41.08M (-6.3%); `new AsyncFunction("")` 31.9k -> 30.8k; the empty cell 93.6k -> 94.1k and the agent cell 1,086k -> 1,092k (+0.5%): their compiles are cheaper and the rest moves with code layout in interpreter functions this does not touch (`Exec::call`, `decline_fast`, `installed_intrinsic` in a perf diff). Bytecode: output/djsdis on 442 files (the corpus cells, bootstrap.js, the agent cell, test262's harness and 400 sampled tests) is byte-identical; the test262 subset passes 8,631 of 9,288 before and after with identical result lines (16-way); the 25 edge cells and the 8 corpus cells give the same events (PRINT=1 EVENTS=1). Commands: `cargo check --offline --locked --lib -p djs-core -p djs-embed -p nanocode-code-mode-engine -p nanocode-code-mode` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --no-deps -- -D warnings` on the same (and djs-core with its default features from crates/patches/djs), rustfmt.

- nanocode-url parses, joins and serializes URLs itself, and url, idna, idna_adapter, form_urlencoded and percent-encoding leave every Cargo.toml and the lock (2026-11-13, Georgios: remove url and its transitive packages). crates/core/url (about 2,200 lines, no dependencies, builds for wasm32) is the WHATWG URL Standard's basic parser as a state machine over a record, serialized once into the string and offsets url 2.5.8 kept, so `Url` has url's API where callers use it: `parse`, `join`, `as_str`, `scheme`, `username`, `password`, `host` (`Host::Domain`, `Ipv4`, `Ipv6`), `host_str`, `domain`, `port`, `port_or_known_default`, `path`, `path_segments`, `query`, `fragment`, `authority`, `has_host`, `has_authority`, `cannot_be_a_base`, `origin` with `ascii_serialization`, `query_pairs`, `query_pairs_mut` (`append_pair`, `extend_pairs`, `clear`, `finish`), `set_fragment`, `set_query`, `set_path`, `set_username`, `set_password`, `ParseError` with url's variants and messages, `Display`, `Debug` in url's shape, `FromStr`, ordering and hashing by the serialization; `nanocode_url::form` replaces form_urlencoded (`byte_serialize` returns a `String`, `parse`, `Serializer`) and `nanocode_url::punycode` is RFC 3492. Hosts: ASCII domains lowercased, IPv4 in every WHATWG number form, IPv6 with brackets and zero compression, opaque hosts of other schemes percent-encoded. IDNA without Unicode tables: a non-ASCII label is lowercased with `char::to_lowercase` and punycode-encoded, after three cheap UTS 46 mappings (fullwidth ASCII U+FF01 to U+FF5E to ASCII, the ideographic full stops U+3002, U+FF0E and U+FF61 to `.`, and the ignored U+00AD, U+034F, U+200B, U+2060, U+FEFF and variation selectors dropped); a label with a control, whitespace, U+FFFD or a noncharacter is refused with `IdnaError`, and an `xn--` label must decode to valid non-ASCII text. There is no NFKC, NFC, bidi or joiner check, so `http://loC𝐀𝐋𝐇𝐨𝐬𝐭` becomes a punycode host where url maps it to localhost. nanocode-schema's `idn-hostname` and `idn-email` formats, idna's other user, now map with nanocode's own unicode-normalization (NFKC, then lowercase, then NFC) and check what UTS 46 checked with idna's tables in format_compat.rs: hyphens in decoded labels, NFC of decoded labels, the RFC 5893 bidi rule over ranges of right-to-left, Arabic-number and European-number code points, and the RFC 5892 rule for U+200C (after a virama, or between Arabic letters). The icu_* stack, zerovec, yoke, tinystr, litemap, writeable, potential_utf, utf8_iter, utf16_iter, write16, displaydoc, synstructure and stable_deref_trait stay: rustpython-unicode uses icu_normalizer and icu_properties for Python's unicodedata, and idna_adapter without features never pulled them in. Equality, harness /home/ubuntu/dev/scratch/url-equal (its own workspace with url =2.5.8, idna =1.1.0 and this crate by path): every accessor, `Debug`, `Display`, `origin`, `query_pairs` and, where the serializations agree, the setters and `query_pairs_mut` with nine values, compared over 497,647 inputs, 10,751,103 comparisons. The 97 URL literals in the tree (format placeholders filled) and their 23,808 joins with the tree's 256 relative literals agree in every comparison, as do 50,000 seeded `byte_serialize`, `parse` and `Serializer` runs and punycode encodes, decodes and junk decodes. Of 904 WHATWG urltestdata.json entries url 2.5.8 produces the expected href for 839 and nanocode-url for 877; the one where url is right and nanocode-url wrong is the NFKC host above. Of 200,000 seeded URLs and 272,838 seeded joins, 21,684 differ, and the harness sorts every difference into a case where url departs from the URL Standard and nanocode-url follows it: `..` removing a drive-letter-like segment (`c|`, `C:`) outside `file:` (url keeps it, 11,508), `file:` paths with leading empty segments or `w|` (url collapses or keeps them, 5,298), `\` in a relative reference against a non-special base (url takes it for `/`, 2,719), `///host` against a special base (url fails with EmptyHost, 1,813, WPT `///test` against `http://example.org/` among them), a non-special port followed by `\` (url accepts it, 346); and 189 `set_path` calls on a URL whose serialization carries `/.` (`git:/.//a`), where url keeps the `/.`. No caller's URL has any of these shapes. Schema formats, harness /home/ubuntu/dev/scratch/url-schema-old and url-schema-new (the same program against master's nanocode-schema and this one): the JSON-Schema-Test-Suite's format-idn-hostname, format-idn-email and format-hostname (177 strings) give 173 expected answers both before and after (the same four miss), and 200,000 seeded hostnames from Latin, Greek, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, CJK, joiner, virama, fullwidth and `xn--` pieces (25,596 valid) give one different answer, `XN--9bＡ`, which idna refused and the mapping now accepts. Live: no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY on dev-georgios (its ~/.nanocode/auth.json holds a ChatGPT login only), so no Claude request ran. output/url-smoke runs nanocode-http and nanocode-mcp-http against a Python server: a GET of /start/redirect-relative?x=1 follows `Location: sub/../../target/x?q=a%20b&e=1#frag` to /target/x?q=a%20b&e=1, an absolute redirect to localhost is followed, and `discover_server` on http://127.0.0.1:18931/mcp reads the 401 challenge's resource_metadata, the protected resource metadata and the authorization server metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/auth and returns the issuer, endpoints, resource and scopes; a Location with raw non-ASCII bytes is not followed, as before (`HeaderValue::to_str` refuses it). Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` 204 to 200 (third-party 98 to 93); nanocode-cli on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 173 to 169 (third-party 78 to 73) and on aarch64-apple-darwin 177 to 173 (81 to 76). API: `nanocode_http::Url` is now `nanocode_url::Url`, not `url::Url`; a host that passes a `url::Url` to nanocode (tempoxyz/pyramid's MCP OAuth discovery and its `check_url` closure) parses it as `nanocode_http::Url` instead. Commands: `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`; `cargo clippy --locked --all-targets` of nanocode-url, nanocode-http, nanocode-mcp, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-schema, nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-backend-claude-client, nanocode-backend-codex-client, nanocode-chatgpt-extension, nanocode-tool-runtime and nanocode-cli (only nanocode-sys's three and rustpython-ruff_python_ast's seven existing warnings, as on master); `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` of the same ten libraries; rustfmt on the changed files; `nanocode-sim --tidy` (a dev build) reports nothing in the changed files, only master's four findings in router.rs, claude_bash.rs, host_tools.rs and sync/lib.rs. `scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs` stops on master's nanocode-backend-codex-client → nanocode-image before and after. Files: crates/core/url/src/{lib,parser,host,encode,form,punycode}.rs, crates/core/schema/src/format_compat.rs, and the `url::` imports in nanocode-http, nanocode-mcp, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-schema, the Claude and Codex clients and driver, nanocode-chatgpt-extension and nanocode-tool-runtime.
- `nc exec` ends its Tokio runtime with `shutdown_background` instead of `shutdown_timeout(1 s)`, so a one-shot exits once its own work is done instead of waiting for blocking tasks it no longer needs (2026-11-13, Georgios approved: "make one-shot nc exit without waiting for background work, after confirming identity-file and session writes are durable before exit"). With real network a one-shot lingered 2 to 107 ms after the reply: `shutdown_timeout` waits for running `spawn_blocking` threads, and at that point they were still resolving the Tempo tool hosts (`getaddrinfo`) and loading about 240 files of /etc/ssl/certs for a connection the startup warm-up opened. What a one-shot writes is finished before the runtime ends: `exec` awaits `agent.flush()`, the host runtime's shutdown and the session archive before it returns, and `tempo::close` (removing the proxy's bundle file and closing payment sessions) still runs before shutdown; identity passes are written to a temporary file, fsynced and renamed (`tempo/identity.rs` `save`), so an abandoned save leaves at most an orphan `.tmp`, never a torn pass, and the payment-channel store is SQLite, whose transactions are atomic. The terminal interface and other commands keep `shutdown_timeout`. Measured on dev-georgios at 427b7d811 with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19), bench/cli's `suite.mjs --parts=oneshot --only=nc` alternating the builds over 6 batches of 3 rounds (18 samples each, load average 30, so times are relative): with real network, reply end to exit p50 6.84 to 5.55 ms, p90 60.20 to 8.82 ms, max 106.95 to 9.18 ms, wall p90 81.26 to 32.41 ms; under tools/netguard.sh (the published benchmark's sandbox) p50 4.53 and 4.60 ms, max 20.74 to 7.98 ms; CPU unchanged (9.77 and 9.89 ms with network). `--parts=store --sessions=60 --storerounds=3`: 60 sessions saved with 0 failures and 66 store files in both, `sessions` prints the same 6,115 bytes, and `--continue` sends the same 62,921-byte request. `cargo clippy -p nanocode-cli` passes.
- A remote child's settle is durable when its journal write returns, and only a resumed child asks the host for its pending turn (2026-11-13, Georgios: route child execution to separate Durable Objects with full parity). Subagent journal writes reach `OneLogStore::replace`, not `commit`, so 427b7d811's `settle_durably` never committed them: `replace` now commits too when it is set. `Registry::pending_turn` consults the `PendingTurnResolver` only for a session with `resume_attempts > 0`, so a new turn of a restored child never adopts the child's last finished request. Measured with nanocode-ts `remoteSubagents` on local workerd and the mock Claude (hosted Hand): 40 children killed 8 s after all finished make no model call after the restart (before: every child the journal still showed running got a resume turn), and in 300 children killed at 150 every extra child call after the restart is a recovery of a turn in flight at the kill (a repeated model call or a nested call whose outcome is unknown), as with in-object children.
- `RuntimeBuilder::child_host` runs each subagent behind the parent's own registry on a host-provided `ChildHost` (2026-11-13, Georgios: route child execution to separate Durable Objects with full parity). `RemoteChildren` (crates/runtime/agent/src/remote.rs) gives each child an `AgentHandle` whose backend sends turns, steers, cancel and close to the host, so spawn, `send_agent_message` (urgent and deferred), `interrupt_agent`, `close_agent`, budgets, lineage, usage and completion notices stay the registry's, and the child's delegation tools run in the parent through `call_tool`. A child checkpoint is the marker `{"remote_child":true}`, and `restore` reopens it on the host. Recovery: a restored remote child's first turn asks `ChildHost::pending` through the registry's new `PendingTurnResolver`, so an unfinished or undelivered child turn resumes under its own request ID instead of a new resume turn, and `OneLog::settle_durably` commits a `Settle::Durable` journal write at once, since a remote child's settle has no later child log commit to ride on (without it a parent restart re-ran every child it had finished: 192 of 192 after an 8 s wait). The completed turn report also carries `ok.usage`. Measured with nanocode-ts `remoteSubagents` on local workerd and the mock Claude of durable-cloudflare scripts/measure-swarm.mjs (hosted Hand, one run each): per-actor transcripts of scripts/parity-subagents.mjs match in-object subagents except that `wait_agent` shows `status.output` the in-object run had already delivered; 200 children finish in 17.4 s against 6.1 s with parent WebAssembly memory 17.8 MB against 37.6 MB and 1.34 against 2.24 parent SQL rows per agent (one workerd hosts all 201 objects, so child first calls p50 7.5 s against 2.0 s); 300 children killed at 150 restart in 0.51 s, list in 3.6 s and run 300 first child calls against 305 in-object.

- SLA.md records the deployed Worker on nanocode-ts build-4ed9bef: an unwarmed new session's first model request waits for its MCP servers' handshakes (427 to 1,814 ms after admission), and a session warmed by `POST /warm` 2 s before its first turn starts it 45 to 103 ms after admission, with provider time equal to later turns' (2026-11-13, gak-9; nanocode-ts DECISIONS.md has the trace).
- A brain names the yield of every cell it sends to a hand, so a hand yields when the brain's deadline expects it (2026-11-13, Georgios: make a longer default cell yield work end to end). `ToolsBuilder::cell_yield` reached only the cells a brain ran itself. For a cell on a hand the brain's exec and wait descriptions and its deadline assumed the protocol's 10 s while the hand's own `--cell-yield-ms` decided, and `RemoteClient` gives up on an operation after `operation_timeout` plus the `yield_time_ms` the operation names (the `// @exec:` pragma of an Execute's source, the input of a Wait) or zero. An eval host that started its hands with `--cell-yield-ms 120000` behind a brain with a 30 s operation timeout therefore lost every cell without a pragma that ran past 30 s: "remote operation deadline elapsed; outcome unknown; cancellation requested; no retry", and the cell's command was cancelled. The yield is now the brain's, written where each number is known. (1) A tool runtime built with `cell_yield` writes it into every Execute and Wait that names none before it routes them: the native runtime for a hand placement (its own cells already had it through `set_default_yield`), the embedded runtime (`code_mode_host`, the only runtime on WebAssembly) for any host that supports cells. `source_yielding` adds `yield_time_ms` to the source's pragma or prepends one, the form `source_with_options` gives a `yield_time_ms` argument, so a hand released before this change follows it; a source the hand refuses (empty, a JSON wrapper, an invalid pragma) is passed as it is and keeps its error. `wait_yielding` adds it to wait's arguments unless they terminate the cell. (2) A `RemoteClient` with an operation timeout writes the protocol's `DEFAULT_YIELD` into an Execute or Wait that still names none, so its deadline always covers a yield it asked for and a hand's own default never applies to it. `Tools::cell_yield` and the builder method now exist on WebAssembly, the embedded runtime's exec and wait descriptions state the number as the native runtime's did, and Claude's exec schema states it instead of a fixed 10000. `nanocode hand --cell-yield-ms` stays for a brain that names no yield: one with neither a cell yield nor an operation timeout (the CLI without `--runner-call-timeout-ms`), or one built before this change. Its help says so and a hand started with it prints one line saying that a brain which names no yield and gives up sooner takes the cell for lost. That last case, an older brain with an operation timeout shorter than the flag, still fails with the deadline message above, which is the older brain's: set the yield on the brain. Unchanged: a `yield_time_ms` the model names wins, and a brain with neither policy nor timeout sends what it sent. Changed for a brain with a timeout and no cell yield: its deadline for an exec or wait without a yield is 10 s later, the yield the hand always took. Not changed and now longer: a command that never ends, such as a server started in the foreground by mistake, holds its exec until the yield (61.0 s at 60 s, 11.0 s before). Measured with a scripted Responses endpoint, brains built from this tree and two hands, the binary released as nanocode-cli-3f97ab0 (sha256 1b88a8b2e0e9d443a9f199b3ca6e1a45e9c81b34ad02850e151466b45884f65b) and one built from this tree, with the same times on both; the cell is `await tools.Bash({ command: "echo started; /bin/sleep N; echo finished" })`. Brain with a 60 s cell yield and a 30 s operation timeout, through both runtimes (`code_mode_host` over a `SocketTransport` with `request_timeout`, and a `Runner` in replace mode with `call_timeout`): N=45 completes in one exec after 45.0 s; N=90 answers "Script running" after 61.0 s and one wait without a yield completes it 29.0 s later; exec's description, wait's description and wait's schema say "Defaults to 60000 ms". The same brain without a cell yield: N=25 yields after 11.0 s, a wait yields after 11.0 s and the next completes after 3.0 s, as before. With the cell yield, a pragma naming 5000 yields after 5.0 s, waits naming 3000 and 60000 return after 3.0 s and 12.0 s, a pragma naming 50000 completes N=45 in one exec, and a pragma with only `max_output_tokens` takes the yield (N=15 completes in one exec). Hand started with `--cell-yield-ms 120000` and N=45: the CLI of this tree with `--runner-call-timeout-ms 30000` yields after 11.0 s and four waits complete the cell at 45.0 s; without the timeout it completes in one exec after 45.0 s; a brain with a 60 s cell yield follows its 60 s; the CLI released as nanocode-cli-3f97ab0 with `--runner-call-timeout-ms 30000` fails after 30.0 s with the deadline message, against either hand. The harness is output/cell-yield (harness.mjs, the cells, and yield_brain.rs, which is examples/brain.rs with `--cell-yield-ms`, `--pool` and a base URL for the endpoint). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-python -p nanocode-psh -p nanocode-psh-embedded -p nanocode-shell -p psh -p psh-os -p psh-engine -p psh-utils -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -- -D warnings`, the same with `--lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-code-mode and nanocode-tool-host, and `cargo check --locked --lib` of those crates and nanocode for the host and `wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass. Without `--no-deps` clippy stops in nanocode-sys, which this change does not touch (`useless_conversion` in crates/core/sys/src/unix/mod.rs, `missing_const_for_fn` in webp.rs on wasm32). Not run: the Claude exec schema through a Messages endpoint, and a cell yield with local cells on WebAssembly. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/{spec,mod}.rs, lib.rs and remote/client.rs, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{selection.rs,runtime/execution.rs,embedded/runtime.rs}, crates/backends/claude/src/claude_tools.rs, bin/nanocode/src/{cli,lib}.rs.
- SLA.md's live Claude 5.5 table is the release build of 6638af866 against 5f299dbce and Claude Code 2.1.318 with unique prompts per session (2026-11-13, hosted Hand, 6 sessions of 3 turns per model, interleaved): nanocode now leads on every turn of every model, first turn by 1.1 to 1.3 s and later turns by 0.2 to 0.8 s, and its later turns no longer spread (Haiku 5.5 turn 2 564 to 984 ms against 525 to 3,557 at 5f299dbce; Sonnet 861 to 1,106 against 850 to 2,651; Opus 696 to 1,320 against 1,001 to 3,589).
- The Claude Messages stream reads its response to the end after `message_stop`, so the connection goes back to the pool and the next turn reuses it (2026-11-13, Georgios: explain and fix why nanocode loses turn 2 on Opus, Sonnet and Haiku). The stream returned `message_stop` and dropped the response; nanocode-http's `Response` drop returns a connection only when the chunked terminator is already buffered, and through a network it usually arrives in a later record, so the connection was closed and the next turn opened a new one (DNS, TCP and TLS, 0.5 to 1 s through the hosted Hand's egress proxy). A logging CONNECT proxy in front of nc-final (bench/sla, live claude-haiku-5-5, 4 sessions of 3 turns) showed it: in 3 of 4 sessions the connection closed right after turn 1's response and turn 2 opened a new one and took 1,186 to 1,747 ms, against 681 to 846 ms for turn 1. The local mock writes the terminator with `message_stop`, which is why mock runs never showed it. The stream now hands the rest of the response to a spawned task that reads it to its end (only after `message_stop`, the protocol's end, so a cancelled stream still closes its connection and stops the generation). Interleaved A/B, debug builds of 4c6ba92 without and with the change, live claude-haiku-5-5 through the same proxy, 3 rounds of 3 sessions each, Enter to the first token drawn, all samples: turn 2 without 629 to 1,369 ms (p50 845), with 542 to 814 (p50 667); turn 3 without 607 to 1,439 (p50 1,022), with 520 to 1,287 (p50 690); turn 1 unchanged (531 to 2,234 and 628 to 1,011). Request bodies, cache use and model behavior did not differ: a logging reverse proxy showed every nanocode request reading the prompt cache, and with the connection kept a plain undici client sent 14 requests 3.5 s apart on one connection in 531 to 672 ms. The live bench also gave every session the same prompts, so nanocode's byte-identical turns read cache entries other sessions wrote; bench/sla's live prompt now carries the run's id. A Tools catalog revision covers an embedded Code Mode host too: it adds a hash of the host's tool definitions for the embedded session, so attaching or detaching a hand between preconnect and the first turn moves it, and on WebAssembly, which has no dynamic providers or runner pool, it is that hash alone (empty without a host) instead of None, so a Worker session's first turn reuses the runtime and request factory its preconnect built. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-host` and `-p nanocode-backend-claude-client`, each again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and clippy on both pass (only nanocode-sys's existing warnings).
- Under `set_manual_resume(true)` a restored subagent journal starts nothing until the host decides (2026-11-13, Georgios: fix subagents failing at turn start). The restore task redelivered the journal's pending messages and launched its unstarted agents as soon as it restored, whatever `manual_resume` said, so only interrupted agents waited for `resume_restored` or `discard_restored`. tempoxyz/pyramid opens each turn's root session with manual resume and closes what an earlier turn left (`discard_restored`) unless a handoff moved it, yet 15 agents a handoff had journaled hours before each started a turn at the next turn's start and failed with `could not start agent N: durability execution policy failed: invalid durability state: ...`. The restore task now keeps those messages and unstarted agents as the root's `RestoredWork` when manual resume is on: `resume_restored` delivers and launches them after resuming the interrupted ones, and `discard_restored` closes every interrupted, unstarted and messaged agent and fails each kept message (`message N was discarded with restored agent M`). Without manual resume nothing changes. Checked: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents` native and wasm32, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents`; output/manual-resume (epoch 1 leaves an unstarted child in a MemoryStore journal, epoch 2 reopens it with capacity 4, manual resume and an unreachable model): before, the child made 2 model requests right after restore and stayed Failed after `discard_restored`; after, 0 requests and Closed.
- A paid attempt refused for identity starts over unpaid with the new pass (2026-11-13): when a paid attempt is answered 401 or 403 with `Identity-Attestation-Required` and no `Payment-Receipt`, bin/nanocode/src/tempo/identity.rs gets the pass as it does for an unpaid one, then sends the request again with the pass and without the payment credential; the server's 402 goes back to the payment flow, which rolls back the refused credential (no receipt) and pays the new challenge, and that paid attempt carries the pass. The paid attempt itself is still never sent again, and an answer with a receipt (a payment that may have settled) is left alone. A service can only learn the payer from the paid attempt, so a gate that admits a listed wallet or a verified email (Boundless's `deepseek-v4.1-flash-abliterated`) can only ask for the pass there; before this, the prover never answered it.
- scripts/build-cli.sh passes BOLT `-icf=all` only when the llvm-bolt it runs lists `--icf=<value>` in `--help-hidden` (LLVM 20 and later, where ICF has levels), and `-icf=1` otherwise (2026-11-13, Georgios: build the CLI benchmarks on Ubuntu boxes). BOLT 19, Ubuntu 24.04's `bolt-19` package, has `--icf` as a boolean and refuses `-icf=all`, so every build there needed the script patched by hand (the measurements of 95aee2808, 4be51211a, 18e5355b3, 223cb39ba and f223811c7 were made that way). The linker's `--icf=all` is unchanged. Checked: `/usr/lib/llvm-19/bin/llvm-bolt --help-hidden` shows a bare `--icf` and the script picks `1`; the release container's bolt-21 was not run here. `sh -n scripts/build-cli.sh` passes.
- The paying proxy's CA and leaf keys are ring's `EcdsaKeyPair` (P-256, ECDSA with SHA-256, the signature ring returns already in the DER form the certificate carries), not nanocode-tempo's `SigningKey` (2026-11-13, Georgios: "keep going" on startup CPU toward a 1.3 ms first frame). ring is already in the CLI through rustls and rustls-webpki and its P-256 is assembly, where nanocode-tempo's is generic field arithmetic: after the bundle change `Modulus::mul`, `Curve::add` and `Modulus::pow` were 8.5% of the TUI's samples to its first frame, for two key generations and the CA's self-signature on the proxy's thread. ring writes the PKCS#8 document (with the public key, as before), so the hand-written ECPrivateKey and PKCS#8 encoding and its constants go. Checked: a rustls client trusting only the CA completes a TLS 1.3 handshake with the proxy's `server_config` for a host (a scratch test, not committed), and `openssl verify -purpose sslserver` accepts a leaf it signs (prime256v1, ecdsa-with-SHA256, DNS name). Measured on dev-georgios with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19 with `-icf=1`) on bench/cli's `suite.mjs --only=nc`, alternating the builds in batches of 3 rounds, medians (load average 27 to 29 from other jobs, so times are relative): under `perf stat` (15 samples each) a one-shot 16.66M to 10.32M user instructions (kernel 12.21M and 12.36M), the TUI to its first frame 16.08M to 9.67M (kernel 12.46M and 12.54M); without it (18 samples each) CPU to the first frame 7.72 to 7.26 ms, one-shot CPU 7.24 to 6.56 ms, resident memory 1 s after the first frame 14.11 and 14.07 MB; binary 73,225,544 to 73,213,264 bytes. `cargo clippy -p nanocode-cli` passes.
- The paying proxy's certificate bundle is its CA followed by the bytes of the system's bundle file when the native roots come from one file, and it decodes and re-encodes the native trust store only otherwise (2026-11-13, Georgios: "keep going" on startup CPU toward a 1.3 ms first frame). `nanocode_platform::trust::native_bundle_file()` names that file: `SSL_CERT_FILE` when set and a file, else on unix outside macOS the first candidate file of the probe list, and none when `SSL_CERT_DIR` has a non-empty entry or on macOS and Windows, which read the system store. A profile of the TUI to its first frame (perf record, 8 runs) had the paying proxy's thread at 37% of the process's samples, most of it `load_pem`, `load_paths` and their `statx`: 121 roots decoded from the bundle and again from 121 files in /etc/ssl/certs, sorted, deduplicated and base64-encoded back into the same PEM. What changes for programs the shell runs: on a Linux system whose roots are in a candidate file and also in /etc/ssl/certs or /etc/pki/tls/certs, a root that is only in such a directory is no longer in the bundle; update-ca-certificates and update-ca-trust write every root into the file, and OpenSSL clients still read their default directory beside `SSL_CERT_FILE`. Checked on dev-georgios (Ubuntu 24.04): the bundle written before and after is 182,352 bytes with 122 certificates, Python's `ssl.create_default_context(cafile=…)` loads 122 roots from each, and after the change everything past the CA is byte-identical to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt. Measured with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19 with `-icf=1`) on bench/cli's `suite.mjs --only=nc`, alternating the builds in batches of 3 rounds, medians (load average 27 to 30 from other jobs, so times are relative): under `perf stat` (15 samples each) a one-shot 32.06M to 16.66M user and 19.41M to 12.05M kernel instructions, the TUI to its first frame 31.43M to 16.05M and 19.62M to 12.28M; without it (18 samples each) CPU to the first frame 9.89 to 7.43 ms, resident memory 1 s after it 14.71 to 14.12 MB (anonymous 3.48 to 2.86 MB), one-shot CPU 9.12 to 6.95 ms, one-shot peak RSS 14.25 MB both. `cargo clippy -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-cli` passes, and `cargo clippy -p nanocode-platform` for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu.
- The native trust store tells repeated roots apart by the device and inode of the `fs::metadata` it already reads for each directory entry, not by `fs::canonicalize` (2026-11-13, Georgios: fix the one-word reply that got 0.3 ms slower). Canonicalizing walks every path component with `readlink`, about 8 calls per certificate, so an nc one-shot on Ubuntu made 800 `readlink` calls (724 failing with EINVAL) where 7837aae16 made 6, and this was the 4.83 to 5.12 ms one-word reply regression between the 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13 cli-bench runs. Other platforms keep `canonicalize`, since they have no inode in `Metadata` and load these paths only from `SSL_CERT_FILE` or `SSL_CERT_DIR`. Measured on dev-georgios with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19 with `-icf=1`), bench/cli's `suite.mjs --parts=oneshot --only=nc` alternating the builds over 6 batches of 3 rounds under `perf stat` (18 samples each, medians): kernel instructions 27.0M to 19.7M (7837aae16: 24.2M), user instructions 34.5M to 32.1M, readlink calls 800 to 6, the same certificate files opened; over 8 more alternating batches of 3 (load average 32, so times are relative) one-shot CPU 11.09 to 9.96 ms (7837aae16: 11.46). `cargo clippy -p nanocode-platform` passes for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and x86_64-pc-windows-gnu.
- SLA.md holds the live claude-haiku-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5 first-token numbers against Claude Code 2.1.318 (hosted Hand, 6 sessions of 3 turns), the first-turn gain from the tool-catalog revision (Responses 2.59 to 2.04 ms p50, 3954a7a46), and the deployed Worker's TTFT (durable-cloudflare 7c43bb3 on nanocode-ts build-1a597dd, version b1bdc8aa, measured from gak-9): warm first delta 738 to 1,574 ms on Claude with the provider's own start 566 to 774 ms, cold 2.8 to 4.2 s, where the first provider request from a new Durable Object costs 1 s or more above a warm one. Open: nanocode's turn-2 spread on live Claude, the remaining 0.6 to 0.9 ms first-turn Responses gap, and the cold Worker's first provider connection. (2026-11-13)

- A tool catalog has a revision, so the Codex backend keeps the tool runtime and request factory it builds when the session preconnects and its first turn uses them while the catalog is unchanged (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: add the SDK tool-catalog revision so the first turn reuses the prebuilt tool runtime). `DynamicToolProvider::catalog_revision` (crates/core/tool-provider/src/lib.rs) answers `None` by default, which means the provider cannot vouch for its catalog; nanocode-mcp-tools' `Mcp` answers its catalog's `revision`, which `begin_server`, `complete` and a search that activates tools each increment (crates/integrations/mcp-tools/src/catalog.rs), and the tool-runtime `Mcp` wrapper and tool-host's `Gated` pass it on. A runner pool vouches through `WorkspaceRouter::catalog_revision` (default `None`): the attachment router answers the pool's committed `revision` only while it has no runners and no executors, since a connected runner's routes and tools change without a commit. `Tools::catalog_revision` collects the pool's and every provider's, `None` if any is. `ModelRun::preconnect` (crates/backends/codex/src/model/run/mod.rs) builds `tool_runtime` and `attempt_factory` into a `PreparedSession` (workspace, config, model, request ID and the catalog revision it was built at, state.rs) when the revision is known and unchanged across the build, refreshing it when a later preconnect (the first keystroke) finds the revision moved; the first turn takes it through `session_tools` only when all five still match and builds its own otherwise. This replaces the warm-and-drop of ef2a8f5e3, whose earlier attempt to keep the factory sent a first request without the 129 MCP tools registered after it was built: now an MCP server that registers in between moves the revision and the turn builds afresh. Checked: a debug build recorded the first turn taking the prepared session on bench/sla; request bodies of the first two turns are byte-identical to 5df4a7bac's after IDs when the same MCP servers had registered (in another pair the new build's first request carried more MCP tools than the old one's, which had not finished registering; neither ever sends a stale catalog, since the turn compares the revision it reads then). Measured with bench/sla (dev-georgios, load 30, 16 sessions of 3 turns, 5df4a7bac and this tree interleaved), Enter to request headers at the mock, p50 / p99: Codex turn 1 2.59 / 4.83 to 2.04 / 7.68 ms, turns 2 and 3 1.14 to 1.44 ms in both. Open: the rest of the first turn's gap (about 0.6 to 0.9 ms) is outside the tool runtime and factory: the first context capture, user input preparation and first history serialization. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-mcp-tools -p nanocode-tool-runtime -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-tool-provider` in a fresh target directory (warnings only in nanocode-sys, as on master).
- Code Mode's local toolset shares one copy of its nested tool metadata between every session that has the same tools, instead of building a fresh one for each cell (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 durability, Georgios: hold 100K subagents in one nanocode-ts Durable Object under 128 MB). `CodeModeToolset::shared_nested_tool_metadata` defaults to `nested_tool_metadata().into()`, a new `Vec<Value>` of every tool's schema on each execution, and `LocalTools`, the toolset nanocode-ts runs, used that default. The copy is kept by the cell's `CellRecord.tools`, which `CellJournals` holds in `finished` until the same session executes again, and by the session's `CodeModeRuntime` in `LocalCells.sessions`; a finished subagent's session never executes again, so each child kept its own copy for the life of the Durable Object. A counting global allocator with sampled allocation sites in the wasm build (temporary, not committed) put 66% of sampled live bytes at `LocalTools::shared_nested_tool_metadata` in a 1,500-child swarm (`scripts/measure-swarm.mjs` in durable-cloudflare: a root cell spawns the children in batches of 50, each calls submit_result against a mock Claude, 64 running at once). `LocalTools` now overrides it: a process-wide `Atom<Vec<Weak<[Value]>>>` (the pattern of tool-host's registry) returns a live `Arc<[Value]>` equal to the metadata just built, or stores a new one and drops dead entries. Measured in workerd (miniflare, durable-cloudflare, 3,000 children, before and after interleaved twice, the release wasm of nanocode-ts): linear memory at the end 530 and 482 MB before, 234 and 234 MB after; peak workerd RSS 1,686 and 1,611 MB before, 1,278 and 1,279 MB after; settled in 49.9 and 51.2 s before, 51.0 and 49.8 s after; SQL bytes per child 10,108 and 9,187 before, 9,228 and 9,270 after. With the instrumented build, live heap at about 1,000 finished children went from 245 MB to 57 MB, about 40 KB per child. Natively it changes nothing measurable, as expected, since the CLI's tools come from tool-host's registry, which already shares them: output/durability-ledger `swarm`, 20,000 agents at 1,000 concurrent, interleaved twice, max RSS 1,740 and 1,716 MB before and 1,694 and 1,740 after in memory, 1,249 and 1,218 before and 1,256 and 1,249 after on JSONL, settle times within 1 s. What is left per child in the Durable Object, from a fold report of the same build: the OneLog `Fold` keeps the whole materialized state in memory, about 19 KB of content-addressed `b3:` values per child (24 per child: the child's prompt with the subagent instructions, its registry leaf and journal deltas, the Claude state head, the session checkpoint, the root's completion messages), 9 KB of hot events and 2.4 KB of cell updates, all reachable (garbage 0); so 100K children in 128 MB needs those values out of memory or the children out of the parent's Durable Object, which this does not do. `cargo clippy --locked --offline --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -- -D warnings` and `cargo check --locked --offline --lib -p nanocode-code-mode --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` report nothing. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/local.rs.
- A Python run that stopped in the middle of an import no longer leaves that module half-made for the next run (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 RustPython-in-WASM, Georgios). Over a filesystem that answers misses later (nanocode-ts' layered cache in a Durable Object), a run stops at the first file it lacks, the host fetches it and runs the program again in the same interpreter. A run that stopped inside `import statistics` left `statistics` in `sys.modules` with `__spec__._initializing` still true, so the rerun's import returned the partial module and failed with `AttributeError: partially initialized module 'statistics' has no attribute 'mean'` (on the Cloudflare demo, 2026-11-13). boot.py keeps `_unfinished`: `_start` sets it and `_finish` clears it unless the run was stopped, and a `_start` that finds it set drops every module whose spec is still initializing before the program runs, so the rerun imports them whole. Modules a finished run imported are kept as before. Checked with nanocode-ts' Bash over a MemoryFileSystem with `sync` hidden (the layered cache): `python3 -c "import statistics; print(statistics.mean([1,2,3]))"` failed with that error before and prints 2 now, also beside a `subprocess` call; over the synchronous filesystem output is unchanged. Files: crates/core/python/src/boot.py.
- SLA.md adds the Workers and Durable Objects bounds as measured in local workerd, the first turn against later ones, and live Claude against Claude Code (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios). The Workers column comes from durable-cloudflare `scripts/measure-sla.mjs` (its DECISIONS.md has the runs), live Claude from nanocode-ts bench/sla's `--key` lanes on the hosted Hand with its API key; the numbers and their hosts are in SLA.md. The tool call and Code Mode cell bounds on Workers stay estimates, marked so.
- The Codex backend builds a throwaway tool runtime and request factory, and the Claude backend its system text and tool wire encoding, when the session preconnects (at its start and when someone starts typing), so a session's first request does not pay the one-time initialization later requests skip (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: make the first turn's request build as fast as later ones). perf on a frame-pointer build of nanocode (cpu-clock every 20 µs, 10 sessions per backend, samples between Enter and the request reaching the bench/sla mock) put the Codex first turn at 3.4 ms of CPU against 1.3 ms on the second: `attempt_factory` 1.8 ms (`model_contract` 0.86, `tool_runtime` 0.68, `request_profile` 0.38), with one-time `Once` and `OnceLock` initialization 1.1 ms and page faults 0.8 ms inside it; and the Claude first turn at 0.5 ms more than the second (`resolve_context`, `current_system`, tool spec serialization and the `WireCache` entries). `ModelRun::preconnect` (crates/backends/codex/src/model/run/mod.rs) now builds `tool_runtime` and `attempt_factory` for the default workspace and drops them while no session exists, and the Claude driver's `LifecycleBackend::preconnect` calls `State::prewarm` (crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs), which, for a session with no kept context, initializes `current_system` and encodes the system and `available_tools` into the wire cache. Keeping the Codex runtime and factory for the first turn instead was tried and dropped: MCP servers register their tools after the session starts, and the kept factory sent a first request without their 129 tools; the turn still builds its own. Measured with bench/sla (dev-georgios, load 30, 12 sessions of 3 turns, interleaved with 5f299dbce's build), Enter to request headers at the mock, p50: Codex turn 1 3.34 to 2.33 ms (turn 2 1.11 and 1.22), Claude turn 1 1.82 to 1.70 ms (turn 2 1.08 and 1.19). The Claude request bodies of both builds are byte-identical after IDs; the Codex ones too apart from which MCP tools had registered by turn 1, which differs between runs of either build. Open: the rest of the Codex gap is the first turn's own `tool_runtime` and `attempt_factory`, which a factory kept from preconnect would remove once the tool catalog can say it has not changed. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-agent` (a fresh target directory, no warnings).
- A session's event pump delivers the first delta after any other event at once and stops holding deltas when a non-delta event follows, instead of holding the first token of every reply for the whole coalescing window (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: measure and optimize nanocode-ts on Workers and Durable Objects). `run` in crates/runtime/agent/src/session_events.rs waited, before delivering a batch that ends in a delta, until `window` had passed since the last delivery of any batch. A reply's first delta follows `run.started` and the model call's start by a few milliseconds, so it waited almost the whole window: on durable-cloudflare, whose `EVENT_COALESCE_MS` is 100, the first token reached a `?live=1` client about 100 ms after the provider sent it on every turn. Now `flushed` is set only when the delivered batch held a delta, so the window spaces deltas from deltas and the first one goes out with nothing to wait for, and while a batch waits, the pump keeps reading its sources and ends the wait when a non-delta event (the message, a tool call, the run's end) arrives, since that batch is delivered then anyway. Deltas within a stream are still delivered at most once per window. Measured with durable-cloudflare `scripts/measure-sla.mjs` (Miniflare's workerd, durable-cloudflare's bundle on nanocode-ts build-81eada9 with only `nanocode_wasm.wasm` replaced through `NANOCODE_WASM_PATH`, a provider in the Node process streaming one token per event, `EVENT_COALESCE_MS` 100; hosted Hand, 5 cores; 6 fresh workerd processes of 3 turns per build and provider, interleaved), p50: 2,000 tokens at 1,000 tok/s, provider's first token to the client's first delta on warm turns 96 to 101 ms before, 1.2 to 2.6 ms after (Claude and Responses alike), POST to first delta 111 to 118 ms before and 10 to 20 ms after, cold turns 202 to 298 ms before and 98 to 121 after; the provider's last token to the client's last delta on Responses turns 6.3 to 8.2 ms before and 1.9 to 3.2 ms after (34 to 45 ms and 3.1 to 3.6 ms on cold turns), and on Claude turns 5.8 to 7.0 ms both ways, where the last delta is followed by no event of its own until the message; 200 tokens unpaced, first token 5.8 to 6.7 ms before and 2.2 to 3.6 ms after on warm turns. The client sees about 1,000 tok/s either way (1,048 before, since the held tokens arrived in one burst). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-agent` natively and with the nanocode-ts wasm build (`node scripts/build.mjs`) of this tree.
- scripts/train-cli.py trains BOLT with nanocode's Tempo tools on, as a user's nc starts (2026-11-13, Georgios: "continue startup code/data layout and BOLT toward 15 MB"). Training set `NANOCODE_NO_TEMPO_TOOLS=true`, so the startup work every default session does (the MCP clients that connect to mercator.sh and the Tempo gateway, their TLS handshakes, the gateway offers and the paying proxy's setup) never reached the profile, and BOLT left it in the original text section: of the 2.8 MB of nc's code executed by the first frame, 1.3 MB sat outside the hot section, spread over 42.7 MB, and the kernel's 64 KB fault-around mapped cold neighbors with each page. The training run now reaches those hosts like a user's (and fails to connect when offline, as nc does there). Same input binary (nanocode master 3f97ab009, dist, non-PIE), BOLT 19 (`-icf=1`), on dev-georgios (EPYC 4585PX, load 30 to 36 from other jobs): the hot section grows from 2.87 to 3.10 MB. Resident memory 1 s after the first frame, with network (output ncmem.py, 10 rounds alternating builds, medians): 19.94 to 16.41 MB, nc's code 8.49 to 5.03 MB, read-only data 3.34 MB in both, anonymous 5.6 and 5.5 MB. Under bench/cli's netguard (loopback only, `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc`, 4 batches of 4 rounds alternating, 16 samples each): first-frame RSS 15.23 to 13.44 MB, `exec` max RSS 15.75 to 14.00 MB; times on this loaded host are not comparable and are measured on a quiet box in the benchmark rerun.
- 2026-11-13: **A custom model on the Codex harness gets Codex's own unknown-model base instructions (`prompts/codex-unknown-model.md`, codex-rs `models-manager/prompt.md` at rust-v0.162.1, the same bytes at ac9db7d8, pinned in upstream.json) instead of nanocode's GLM prompt. Glm53, Kimi and Mimo keep `glm.md`.** `model_info_from_slug` gives an unknown model `BASE_INSTRUCTIONS`, which is this file, and stock Codex 0.162.1 sent it to DeepSeek in cmp2. Stock sent it without the "## Planning" and "## `update_plan`" sections (17,119 bytes, ~/hill/analysis/losses/stock-codex-instructions.txt) because its exec run had no update_plan tool. nanocode's Codex harness offers update_plan, so the file goes in whole. The loss analysis (~/hill/analysis/LOSSES.md, section 3) swapped the 17,119-byte text into nc-codex requests through a proxy on DeepSeek, 4 pairs: all 8 passed, agent time 1,143 to 782 s (-32%), calls 102 to 70 (-31%), cost +14%. The apply_patch detours the GLM prompt's wording led to went away. n is 1-2 per task, so this is kept off master until a paired eval (costfix third arm) measures it.
- 2026-11-13: **nc takes a prompt that begins with a hyphen as the prompt. The prompt positional takes hyphen values (`Argument::allow_hyphen_values`, new in nanocode-arguments): at such a positional an unknown short or long flag is the value, as it already was at a trailing positional such as `BrowserHost.args`, and known flags still parse as flags.** TB2.1's pytorch-model-recovery instruction begins "- You are given…". clap read it as an unknown flag ("error: unexpected argument '- ' found"), as nanocode-arguments, which replaced clap, does too (an unknown short flag `- `), so `nc exec` exited 2 in 0.04 s without a model call. That cost 0 of 6 nanocode trials against 4 of 4 stock on DeepSeek in cmp2, and the same on GLM (~/hill/analysis/LOSSES.md). Passed after `--`, both harnesses passed it 2 of 2 there. Scripted mock, 2026-11-13, `nc exec … "- You are given a file. Reply DONE."`: 4c2c2ca exits 2 with no request in either harness. This commit sends the text in the first request in both harnesses and exits 0. A prompt beginning with "-- " is also passed through unchanged. Flags before the prompt parse as before.
- 2026-11-13: **No Code Mode wording without Code Mode. The Codex empty-response nudge asks for "a tool" call instead of "exec" when the session's tools are not in Code Mode. spawn_agent's description in a direct session says "Start independent subtasks in parallel, wait for and reduce their results, then dispatch dependent stages." instead of "When Code Mode is available, build multi-agent pipelines in it: …".** In DirectOnly sessions there is no `exec` tool. Telling the model to "call exec" after an empty response pointed it at a tool that does not exist, and the spawn_agent text described a mode the session lacks. `empty_response` takes the session's `Tools` and picks the text by `exposure().is_available_in_code_mode()`, as `code_mode_instructions` already does. `DelegationTools::direct_tools` is a new trait method that defaults to `tools`. The runtime's `Delegation` implements it with `nanocode_subagents::install_direct_tools` / `install_direct_claude_tools`, which build spawn_agent with `code_mode: false`. Its cached definition is keyed by policy and that flag. Both harnesses call it when the session is direct and not remote, so that covers children and `nc --subagents` after the previous change. Native sessions keep the exact text. Scripted mocks, 2026-11-13: one reasoning-only response, then the next request: 4c2c2ca "…no exec call… call exec…", this commit "…no tool call… call a tool…". `--subagents` on a custom model in both harnesses: spawn_agent offered without "Code Mode" in its description.
- 2026-11-13: **The GLM-family base prompt (`prompts/glm.md`, which Glm53, Kimi, Mimo and every custom model get) leaves out its "# Using skills" section unless the host's instructions carry a skill catalog ("### Available skills").** The section is about 4.8 KB, about 1,000 tokens. It explains how to read skills listed under "## Skills" / "### Available skills", including through orchestrator `skills.list` / `skills.read` tools. nanocode itself lists no skills to the model (nanocode-home's skill set only feeds the terminal picker), so a catalog can only come in `additional_instructions`, and `nc exec` never has one. In cmp2 every nc-codex call paid for it. codex-rs ac9db7d8 likewise sets `include_skills_usage_instructions: false` for an unknown model. `ModelConfig::base_system_prompt` now drops the section, from its heading to the next H1 or the end, for those models when `system_prompt` is unset and the instructions lack the catalog heading. A caller's own `system_prompt` is never edited, and the other prompts are unchanged. First Codex request on vercel/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 through the meter proxy, 2026-11-13: 5,494 to 4,486 input tokens (26,346 to 21,555 bytes). The developer prompt now ends with the "# Destructive Actions" section.
- 2026-11-13: **Codex `exec_command` and `write_stdin` apply the documented 10,000-token default when `max_output_tokens` is omitted. A custom model's direct tool calls get upstream's unknown-model truncation, 10,000 bytes, as their output budget.** The tool definition says "Defaults to 10000 tokens". But `effective_token_limit(None)` was `usize::MAX`, so an omitted budget meant everything up to the 1 MiB capture. Only the history's `TOOL_OUTPUT_TOKEN_LIMIT` (12,000 tokens, about 48 KB) then bounded it. In cmp2 the model passed `max_output_tokens` on about 9% of calls. One regex-chess output of 103,721 tokens went into history as 48,023 bytes and was resent on about 74 later calls. codex-rs ac9db7d8 resolves an omitted budget to `DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` (10,000, unified_exec). It then truncates exec output with the smaller of that and the model's `truncation_policy` (`ExecCommandToolOutput::model_output_policy`), and for an unknown model the policy is `TruncationPolicyConfig::bytes(10_000)`. Here `nanocode_process_contracts::DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` is 10,000. The Codex shell handlers pass `min(requested or 10,000, context.output_token_budget())`. The Codex run gives a direct tool call `Model::tool_output_token_budget()`, which is 2,500 tokens (10,000 bytes at the 4 bytes per token the process crate truncates by) for `Model::Custom` and unlimited (`DEFAULT_TOOL_OUTPUT_TOKENS`) for other models, as before. Code Mode cells keep their own budget. Truncation stays the process crate's head and tail with the "Warning: truncated output (original token count: N)" header, the same format as upstream's `formatted_truncate_text`, with "tokens truncated" where upstream's byte policy says "chars truncated". Scripted mock (one `exec_command` of `seq 1 100000` with no budget, then the next request's `function_call_output` read), 2026-11-13: 4c2c2ca records 48,025 bytes, this commit 10,217 bytes. Stock Codex never exceeded 10,222 in cmp2. `seq 1 2000` (8,893 bytes of output) passes unchanged.
- 2026-11-13: **For a custom model the Codex harness now sends what upstream sends for an unknown model: `parallel_tool_calls: true`, no `reasoning.context` and no `text.verbosity` (and no `text` at all without a strict output schema).** `Model::uses_responses_lite` and `Model::supports_verbosity` are false only for `Model::Custom`. codex-rs ac9db7d8 sends `parallel_tool_calls: prompt.parallel_tool_calls && !model_info.use_responses_lite`, where the prompt is always true (`build_prompt`). It sets `reasoning.context = all_turns` only under Responses Lite and sends verbosity only when `support_verbosity`. The unknown-model fallback (`model_info_from_slug`) has use_responses_lite false and support_verbosity false. Stock Codex 0.162.1's DeepSeek requests in cmp2 match this (`"parallel_tool_calls": true, "reasoning": {"effort": "low", "summary": "auto"}`, no `text`). nanocode hard-coded false, `all_turns` and `low` for every model. In cmp2 that meant 1.14 tool calls per model turn against stock's 1.23, about one extra model call per trial. Every Codex tool already reports `supports_parallel_tool_calls`. Native and gateway models (Astra, Sol, Terra, Luna, DaybreakBlue, Glm53, Kimi, Mimo) send what they sent before. First request on vercel/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 through the meter proxy, 2026-11-13: `{"parallel_tool_calls": true, "reasoning": {"effort": "low", "summary": "auto"}}`, 5,494 input tokens (5,492 before; 26,346 bytes).
- 2026-11-13: **The Codex harness leaves out web search (`web.run`) and image generation (`image_gen.imagegen`) in sessions whose model gets the harness tools directly (non-native models, custom endpoints), as upstream does for an unknown model.** codex-rs ac9db7d8's `model_info_from_slug` fallback gives an unknown model no image tool, `image_generation_available` also needs the provider's capability, and stock Codex 0.162.1 on the board runs with web search off. nanocode enabled both by default (`Tools::default`) and registered them for any endpoint. Only a named gateway got the "unsupported" wrapper, so a custom endpoint advertised both namespaces, about 13.5 KB. Their handlers call `{api_base_url}/alpha/search` and the image endpoint, which a custom endpoint does not serve. In cmp2 all 8 `web.run` calls found in nc-codex request bodies came back "unsupported call: run". The DirectOnly branch of the Codex runtime's tools factory now also sets `web_search(false).image_generation(false)`. The agent's `validate_tool_selection` then drops their builtin names, and `tool_runtime` registers no handler. A known OpenAI model keeps both. First Codex request of `nc exec "Reply with the single word DONE."` on vercel/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017 through the meter proxy, 2026-11-13: 8,934 to 5,492 input tokens (40,301 to 26,401 bytes). Tools are now exec_command, write_stdin, update_plan, apply_patch and view_image.
- 2026-11-13: **Subagent tools are off by default for models that get the harness tools directly (non-native, DirectOnly sessions); `nc --subagents` turns them back on, `--no-subagents` still turns them off everywhere.** A cmp2 forensics pass (TB2.1 on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash through the Vercel route) found every nc request carrying submit_result, spawn_agent, send_agent_message, list_agents, wait_agent, interrupt_agent and close_agent: 10-13 KB of schema on every call in a one-shot run that never delegates. Stock Codex runs with multi_agent off there. `CodexHarness::direct_subagents` and `ClaudeHarness::direct_subagents` (default false) decide whether a direct session that is not remote gets them. A child session keeps them because it needs submit_result to return its result. nc maps `--no-subagents` / default / `--subagents` to `host::Subagents::{Off, NativeModels, AllModels}`. spawn_agent's `output_contract` is recursive (`$ref: #/$defs/node`) and is left that way. Making it non-recursive would need either a depth cap, which AGENTS.md rules out, or a contract passed as a string, which changes the tool's shape. Measured through the meter proxy on vercel/deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash-1017, each value the same in two sends, 2026-11-13: nc 4c2c2ca's first Codex request body as captured gives 16,389 input tokens with max_output_tokens absent, 1000 or 65536. The same body without spawn_agent gives 10,428. With spawn_agent's output_contract replaced by a plain string property (no $defs) it gives 10,895. With none of the 7 tools it gives 8,932. So the route expands the recursive schema by about 5,500 tokens beyond spawn_agent's own ~830. With max_output_tokens 1 the same bodies count 11,260 and 10,426: requests that small land on a backend that does not expand it, which is why a max_tokens=1 probe alone hides the cost. First request of `nc exec "Reply with the single word DONE."` through the proxy, 4c2c2ca against this commit: Codex harness 16,389 to 8,934 input tokens (51,502 to 40,301 request bytes), Claude harness 12,359 to 4,064 (28,685 to 15,925 bytes). Neither tool list has any subagent tool any more.
- `nc` takes the model's window and longest reply as flags, `--context-window` and `--max-output-tokens`, with `NANOCODE_CONTEXT_WINDOW` and `NANOCODE_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS` as their environment fallbacks as other flags have, instead of reading the two variables on its own; and the Codex harness no longer caps a custom model's window at 872,000 (`MAX_CONTEXT_WINDOW_TOKENS`) without saying so (2026-11-12). `Model::context_window_limit` is `None` for a custom model, whose window nanocode cannot know, so the caller's value stands, and the known model's maximum otherwise; the Codex builders (`OpenAiBuilder` and `CodexBuilder`, `model` and `context_window_tokens`), spawn and resume clamp only to it. `nc` refuses a window over a known Codex model's maximum (`--context-window 2000000 is over gpt-6.1-sol's window of 872000 tokens`, exit 1) where it ran at 872,000; `--max-output-tokens` sets the Claude harness's `max_tokens`, and Codex requests carry no reply limit, as upstream Codex sends none. Before, `NANOCODE_CONTEXT_WINDOW=1048576` gave `@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash` 1,048,576 in the Claude harness and 872,000 in the Codex harness. Measured with output/limit-check (`OpenAi::builder(..).model(m).context_window_tokens(n).build()?.config()`, the order `CodexHarness` uses: model first, then `configure`): at 9c01116 a custom model given 1,048,576 or 2,000,000 got 872,000; here it keeps them, and gpt-6.1-sol still gets 872,000. A window set before the model is still clamped to the maximum of the model selected at that moment (the default GPT model: a custom model given 1,048,576 that way gets 872,000), which nc never does. In `nc exec` a custom model's Codex window reaches no request (only GPT models get an auto-compaction limit; the window bounds the tool-output trim of a manual compaction), so against a local mock the first requests are byte for byte the same in both builds with the variables or the flags: Claude 27,951 bytes with `max_tokens` 65536 (32768 with neither, as before), Codex 50,406 bytes.
- Models that are not native to the harness (custom endpoint models that follow `--harness`) get the harness's own tools directly instead of only Code Mode's `exec` and `wait` (2026-11-12). `CodexHarness::direct_tools_for` and `ClaudeHarness::direct_tools_for` take a per-request predicate; when it holds and no remote Code Mode host is attached, the Codex harness builds its tools with `ToolExposure::DirectOnly` (`exec_command`, `write_stdin`, `apply_patch` and the rest as upstream Codex offers them, without the Code Mode instructions) and the Claude harness installs its tools with `DirectOnly` and runs without `code_only` (`Read`, `Edit`, `Write`, `Bash`, `TaskOutput`, `TaskStop` with the upstream system blocks, no Code Mode block). `nc` sets it for every model that is neither a known Claude model nor in `Model::ALL`, so native models keep Code Mode. Measured first over 116 Terminal-Bench 2.1 transcripts of GLM-5.3-Flash in both harnesses (2,767 Code Mode cells): 45 cells failed with `SyntaxError` and 15 with `ReferenceError`, mostly C, Python or heredoc text quoted inside JS strings and `apply_patch` template literals, and 498 cells (18%) called a tool without `text()` and returned no output, so the model ran the command again. Checked with `nc exec` against the Gateway (`@cf/zai-org/glm-5.3-flash`): the request carries the direct tools above, and a task that writes C containing a quote, backticks and double quotes, compiles it and appends to a file passes in both harnesses with plain `apply_patch`/`exec_command` and `Write`/`Bash` calls.
- On Linux the vendored verifier trusts the bundled Mozilla roots (`webpki-root-certs`, as on wasm32) when the system offers none, instead of failing to build (2026-11-12). An HTTPS client cannot be built without its verifier (reqwest 0.13's `Client::new` panicked on the build this was found in, before nanocode-http replaced reqwest), and `verification::others::Verifier::new_inner` returned `No CA certificates were loaded from the system` on images without `/etc/ssl/certs`, so `nc exec` exited 101 at startup even for a plain http model endpoint (Terminal-Bench 2.1's merge-diff-arc-agi-task and financial-document-processor images, Ubuntu 24.04 without ca-certificates). `system::roots` now adds `webpki_root_certs::TLS_SERVER_ROOT_CERTS` when the native load gives an empty store and logs a warning with the count, so verification stays on and the sandbox egress (`system_roots`) gets the same store. Checked in both images with `--network none`: the previous build panics (exit 101), this one reaches the endpoint and reports `failed to list models` (exit 1).
