Before, `follows_harness` (bin/nanocode/src/host.rs) moved a custom model to the chosen harness only on the Tempo route, so a natively routed custom id always ran on Codex, and the Claude harness sent `Tempo::OUTPUT_TOKENS` as `max_tokens` with no window for compaction. The two limits are read once when the host is built and an unparsable value is refused with its name. The commit first added its own `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_MESSAGES_URL` (the full Messages URL, with `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` sent as a Bearer token); upstream's `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` (5f299dbce, `<base>/messages`, the key as `x-api-key`) covers the endpoint, so that variable is gone. What remains is the Bearer token, for gateways that take `Authorization` rather than `x-api-key`: the credential is the first set of `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (`x-api-key`), `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` (`Authorization: Bearer`, as Claude Code sends `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`), `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, so a nanocode variable wins over a generic one left in the environment, and without any of them nanocode refuses to start as before. Checked against a local Messages mock, 2026-11-13: with `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` set and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` also in the environment the request carries `authorization: Bearer <token>` and no `x-api-key`; with `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` it carries `x-api-key`; `--harness claude -m mock/custom-model` runs on the Claude harness.
- Bash runs `sleep N &`, and a command that begins with `sleep` is moved to the background at its timeout like any other (2026-11-13). Two rules about a leading `sleep` did more than they meant to. The refusal of a81ec4e87 takes the first part of the command up to an operator and counts a single `&` as one, so `sleep 30 &` and `sleep 30 & echo started` were refused as `standalone sleep 30` and `sleep 30 followed by: echo started` although neither waits; output/d1-background has had Bash at 20 of 21 since then for that case. A `sleep` that is put in the background (`&` not followed by `&`) is now exempt; `sleep 30 && x`, `sleep 30; x` and `sleep 30 | x` are refused as before. And a foreground command whose first word is `sleep` was stopped at its timeout with `Bash command timed out after 120s` where every other command is moved (Claude Code 2.1.304's auto-backgrounding leaves it out): in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 runs of the Claude harness on a hand (Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-13) 7 calls such as `sleep 240; tail log` lost 840 s that way and the rest of each command never ran. Since a81ec4e87 a leading sleep of 25 s or more does not start at all, so what still reached that rule was a short or unparsed sleep in front of real work (`sleep 5; make`, `sleep 5m; tail log`), where stopping throws the work away. The exception is gone: at its timeout such a command is moved and its end is reported like any other. Checked with output/cells (release build, Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`): `sleep 30 &` and `sleep 30 & echo started` were refused and now return at once with exit code 0 and `started`; `sleep 30 && echo done` is refused as before; `sleep 3; echo the rest ran` with `timeout: 1000` failed with `command executor: Bash command timed out after 1s` and is now moved, and its end notice shows `the rest ran`. output/d1-background, with and without `--own-processes`: Bash leaves a job alive at the end of the turn in 21 of 21 ways and exec_command in 22 of 22; output/psh-differential: 115 of 117 through Bash in both modes and through psh directly, 108 through exec_command, as before. The clippy and check commands of the entry three below report nothing. Not verified: a model. Files: crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/bash.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/claude_bash.rs.
- A Bash `timeout` above the maximum still runs with the maximum, and the result says so (2026-11-13). Since 2026-11-12 a larger value is reduced without a word, as Claude Code does; before that the call was refused with `timeout must be 1 to 600000 milliseconds`. In a Terminal-Bench 2.1 trajectory of the earlier build that refusal is what made the model plan around ten minutes (`weighing whether a 10-minute Bash timeout is enough for the compile and sampling`), and on the newer builds a call with `timeout: 1200000` learned of the limit only when it was moved at 600 s. Refusing again was weighed and not chosen: in a cell a refusal rejects the call's promise, which fails the script and abandons the calls beside it, and it costs a model call before any work has started, while a reduced timeout loses nothing, because at the maximum the command is moved to the background and keeps running. So the call runs and is told: the message of a command moved at the maximum ends with `The call asked for a timeout of 1200000 ms, more than the maximum of 600000 ms, so the command had the maximum.`, a `run_in_background` command over 7,200,000 ms gets the same sentence in its start message, and a command that finishes in time has it in `message`, which stays null otherwise (the output schema's `message` says both). The model's own call still receives the JSON of a finished result whose `message` is set; only a background result is shown as its message. Checked with output/cells (release build, Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`): `echo ok` with `timeout: 1200000` returned `message: null` before and the sentence now; `echo started; /bin/sleep 615; echo late` with `timeout: 1200000` is moved at 600.0 s, as before, and its message now ends with the sentence; `timeout: 0` is rejected as before. The clippy and check commands of the entry two below report nothing. Not verified: a model; a `run_in_background` command over two hours (the same branch, not run). - A Bash call from a Code Mode cell waits for its command up to the maximum, 600,000 ms, when it has no `timeout` (2026-11-13). The default was Claude Code's 120,000 ms for every call. A cell is not a model's turn: the model awaits the call in the cell and then waits on the cell, and it almost never passes a `timeout` there (3 of 1,688 Bash calls in the Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness on a hand, Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-13; 30 of 383 on the builds of a week earlier, 18 of them 600000). In that run and its partial rerun, 31 calls in 14 attempts were moved to the background at 120 s underneath a model that was waiting on their cell, mostly with `wait` and `yield_time_ms: 600000`: it meant to wait in the foreground. From each move to the command's end notice, or to the attempt's end where none came, 7,533 s passed in all (an upper bound of the cost, since it holds the time the commands still needed); after 13 of the 31 the model started the same work again and two copies competed; three were stopped by the 10 minutes a moved command gets. One task that passed on the earlier builds with `timeout: 600000` on its long command, whose death came back as that call's own result, failed in five of five attempts. Now a nested call (its ID holds `/code-`) without `timeout` gets `MAX_TIMEOUT_MS` from an executor that moves a command to the background at its timeout (`BashExecutor::nested_timeout_ms`, which the native executor answers with the maximum). The model's own calls keep 120,000, and so do the host adapters, whose shell stops a command at its timeout instead of moving it. The reason the longer default is safe is that the cell, not the call, is what gives control back: `exec` yields on its own clock. What it was checked against, with output/cells on a release build (Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`): a 130 s command awaited without a `timeout` gave `Script running` at 11.0 s (the 10 s default and `OBSERVER_YIELD_GRACE`), and the `wait` with `yield_time_ms: 600000` returned at 130.0 s with the command's output, where the hand released at 2c64cbe6a returned at 120.0 s with the notice of the move and reported the end with the next cell at 140 s; three 4 s commands in a row under a 3 s yield give the same yields at 3.0 and 8.0 s and the result at 12.0 s as before; a server started in the foreground by mistake yields at 11 s, `wait` with `terminate: true` ends the cell, and the server is gone 0.1 s later, because a cancelled call kills its command's process group (2026-11-12), so the mistake costs one `wait`; left alone it now holds its call for 600 s instead of 120 s before it is moved; a 615 s command is moved at 600.0 s and its end is reported with its output. Memory does not grow with the wait: a foreground command keeps at most `NESTED_STREAM_BYTES` of each stream and the rest goes to its file under the 5 GiB cap. Deadlines between a brain and a hand, read in the code: `RemoteClient`'s `operation_timeout` (30 s where an eval harness's Worker hosts the brain, which uses the same value for its connection, the hand's catalog and a parked hand's return) bounds each operation's reply beyond the `yield_time_ms` the operation carries, and an `exec` or `wait` replies at its yield whatever its nested calls are doing, so 11 s is inside 30 s and a `wait` of 600,000 ms has 630 s for a yield at 601 s; a hand's callback deadline bounds calls from the hand to its brain, which Bash does not make. A Bash call that a brain sends to a hand as one operation outside a cell has the operation timeout alone; that path keeps the 120,000 ms default and is not touched here. The declaration: the Bash description a native session and a hand give has one sentence after the pinned `timeout` line (kept apart as `NESTED_TIMEOUT`, and the definition panics if the pinned line is gone): "A call from an exec cell without `timeout` waits the maximum instead, because the cell yields on its own clock; a command that reaches its `timeout` moves to the background and keeps running, and a `timeout` above the maximum counts as the maximum." prompts/code_mode.md gains one sentence that tells the model to await a long command in its cell instead of starting it in the background and polling, with the ten minutes and how a moved command's end is reported (+426 bytes of system prompt). A hand delivers the default, the results and the description by itself; the sentence in the instructions needs a brain built from this commit. The clippy and check commands of the entry below report nothing. Not verified: a model, so whether it now waits in the foreground and stops restarting work is not measured; a brain on a Worker against this hand (the deadlines are read, not run there); macOS. - The end of a background Bash command on a hand or a runner says how the command ended, shows its last output and reaches the model when it happens (2026-11-13). In Terminal-Bench 2.1 runs of the Claude harness on a hand (Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-13) one task failed in five of five attempts on the builds since 2026-11-12 and passed on the earlier ones. Its program is killed by the kernel when it reaches the machine's memory limit. Earlier that came back as the foreground call's own result, with `Killed` and `EXIT 137` in the same second. Now, in three attempts, the command had been moved to the background at its timeout, and its end notice read `completed (exit code 0)`, carried no output, and arrived with the result of the cell that was running, 84 to 250 s after the kill. The model took the program to be finishing and waited 550 to 780 s on a dead job, whose orphaned workers kept `pgrep` answering; two attempts read the job's output file and one found `Killed` and `EXIT=137` there. Reproduced with output/cells against the hand released at 2c64cbe6a (with `--own-processes`; a `timeout` of 1 s stands for the 120 s, the same code path; a program that sends itself SIGKILL stands for the kernel): the status in the notice is the shell's, and it is true. `program; echo EXIT=$?`, the same under `bash -c`, and `program | tail -5` end with 0 because their last command succeeded; the program alone, and a shell that is killed itself, were reported as `failed with exit code 137`. psh passes a child's SIGKILL on as 137 and prints bash's `Killed` line, and the job table keeps what the shell returned, so nothing was misreported: the notice left out what would have told the model. Four changes. First, the notice ends with the command's last output: the final 1,024 bytes of its output file from the first whole line (`STALL_TAIL_BYTES`, the bound Claude Code's notice of a command that waits for input already has), under `Output:` when that is all of it, under `Last output (the end of N bytes, all in the output file):` when it is not, or `The command printed nothing.`; the notices of a command stopped at its background time limit or at the output cap end the same way. Second, a status of 128 + N is named for the signals whose numbers Linux and macOS share (HUP, INT, QUIT, ILL, ABRT, FPE, KILL, SEGV, PIPE, ALRM, TERM): `failed with exit code 137, a shell's status for a command that SIGKILL ended`. Third, on Linux every command reads `oom_kill` in `memory.events` of the hand's own cgroup (the `0::` line of `/proc/self/cgroup` under `/sys/fs/cgroup`) when it starts and when it ends, and when the counter moved the notice says `The kernel killed N process(es) in this machine's memory group for lack of memory while the command ran: oom_kill in memory.events went from A to B.`, whatever the exit status; a foreground result has the same sentence in brackets as the last line of `stderr`, where a cut stream's notice already goes. The counter belongs to the group, so the sentence does not name the command that lost the process. Where the counter cannot be read and the status is 137, the notice says that the kernel also sends SIGKILL when memory runs out and that whether it did is a guess; where it can be read and did not move, nothing is said. Fourth, delivery: `CodeModeToolset` and `CodeModeToolPolicy` gain `session_notice(session_id)`, a future that resolves when the session has a notice to deliver, and an `exec` or `wait` that is observing a cell yields when it resolves, the way it yields for a steering message: it first takes the updates already queued, so a cell that has just finished returns its result, and otherwise it returns `Script running with cell ID N` with the notice. A `wait` yields at once for a notice that was already there; an `exec` does not, because its own result or first yield carries it as before, and a short cell after a job's end should not become a yield. The start message of a background command now says `Its end is reported with its exit status and last output: an exec or wait call that is waiting when it finishes returns then, and otherwise the next one reports it.` A session bound to an agent, whose notices go to the agent at once, gets the same text. Checked with output/cells (release build, Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`; with the brain of the same build and with the one released at 2c64cbe6a the output is identical, so a hand delivers all of this alone): the five kill cases now show `Killed` and `EXIT=137` under `Output:` (the pipeline shows only what `tail` printed, as bash would); with the hand in a cgroup limited to 3 GiB (`systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=3G -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p OOMPolicy=continue`) and a program that allocates 4 GiB, the wrapper and the pipeline are still `completed (exit code 0)` and the notice adds that the kernel killed 1 process, `oom_kill` from 0 to 1 and from 1 to 2, and the same command in the foreground returns `EXIT=137`, psh's `Killed` line and the bracketed sentence; a command that dies 19 s into a 40 s polling loop reached the model at 41.1 s before, with the loop's result, and reaches it at 19.0 s, inside a `wait` with `yield_time_ms: 600000`; one that died between the yield and the `wait` reached it at 82.2 s before and 0.0 s into the `wait` now; one that died after its cell ended arrives with the next cell's first yield, as before. 300 `true` commands in one cell take a median of 398 ms on master and 418 ms with the two reads, 0.07 ms a command (12 interleaved runs each at load 25 to 30). `cargo clippy --locked --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -- -D warnings` and `cargo check --locked --offline --lib` of the last four, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, report nothing. Not verified: a model with the new notice; a kill inside a pipeline that is not the kernel's stays invisible (status 0 and no `Killed` line, as in bash); cgroup v1 and macOS have no counter here, so a 137 there gets the sentence that marks a guess; a job that a finished command left behind with `nohup` or `setsid` reports nothing, as before. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/claude_bash.rs, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/{toolset.rs,code_mode/mod.rs}, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{policy.rs,runtime/registry.rs}.
- SLA.md states what nanocode adds between Enter and the first token, the rendered throughput, the first tool call, a Code Mode cell, startup and resume after a crash, the bound each holds per surface (native CLI, nanocode-ts on Node, on Workers and Durable Objects), and the measurements behind them, with Claude Code 2.1.318 and Codex CLI 0.166.0 against the same mock and live (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: publish measured latency targets and beat Claude Code and Codex CLI). The harness is nanocode-ts `bench/sla` (`run.ts`, `fixture.ts`, `ts.ts`): a terminal per lane under `script`, a mock of the Anthropic Messages and OpenAI Responses APIs that records when each request's headers arrive, on which connection and how old it is, and marks each turn's first and last token with letters no other turn uses, so a diffing renderer cannot hide them; live lanes use the real providers and endpoints that refuse a bogus key. Headline, p50 on the mock: nanocode's overhead 3.0 to 4.2 ms on a warm turn against Claude Code's 83 to 85 and Codex CLI's 53 to 55, the first tool call 11 to 15 ms against 95 to 98, ready 15 ms against 451 and 819. Bounds not measured yet (Workers and Durable Objects, live Claude, DeepSeek and GLM) are marked so in SLA.md, not guessed.
- `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points the Claude backend at any Anthropic Messages endpoint, with `NANOCODE_ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as its key, as `NANOCODE_OPENAI_BASE_URL` does for the Responses backend (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: measure every provider against a local mock and live). bin/nanocode/src/custom_endpoint.rs builds `ClaudeClient::new(nanocode_http::client(), "<base>/messages", key)` when the variable is set and no Claude client is supplied yet (`ModelClients::supplies_claude`, host.rs), and refuses to start without a key. It lets the latency harness run the Claude backend against its mock, and Anthropic-compatible providers (DeepSeek, GLM) without a Claude login. - A session opens its model connection when it starts, and again when someone starts typing into an empty composer, so the first request of a turn finds a pooled connection instead of opening one on its path (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios). nanocode-http gains `Client::preconnect(url)`, which opens a connection to the URL's destination and checks it into the pool, through the `destination` that `send` already used (crates/core/http/src/client/mod.rs). The Codex client's `ResponsesHttp::preconnect` does it for the Responses endpoint (not for a host, the ChatGPT gateway or a layer that sends elsewhere; a no-op on wasm32, where fetch pools), its tower service's `Connect` request now preconnects HTTPS as it did WebSocket, and `run/mod.rs` no longer limits the session-start preconnect to WebSocket. The Claude client gains `transport::preconnect` and `ClaudeClient::preconnect`; the Claude agent spawns it at creation and answers `LifecycleBackend::preconnect` with it. bin/nanocode's `App::prepare_turn` runs on the first character typed or pasted into an empty composer: it prewarms syntax highlighting (`nanocode_tui::highlight::prewarm`) and spawns `agent.preconnect()`, so a connection the provider closed while the session sat idle is reopened while the person types. Measured with nanocode-ts `bench/sla` (mock): turn 1's request arrives on a connection opened about 1.7 s earlier, at session start, for the Responses and the Claude paths, where it was opened on the request path before (0.26 ms old on arrival, as Claude Code's and Codex CLI's are, about 0.2 ms). nanocode's overhead (Enter to request at the provider, plus token sent to token drawn), p50 / p99 of 10 sessions: Responses turn 1 7.30 / 10.27 ms, turn 2 3.02 / 7.38, turn 3 3.61 / 9.09; Claude 3.78 / 10.78, 3.55 / 5.29, 4.22 / 7.31; against the same mock Claude Code 2.1.318 190.2 / 232.4, 84.7 / 130.9, 83.2 / 134.0 and Codex CLI 0.166.0 73.1 / 246.5, 55.4 / 67.9, 52.8 / 81.2. Checks: those of the connection-reuse entry below.
- nanocode-http's `Response` hands its connection back to the pool when it is dropped after its message ended, so a session's model requests reuse one connection instead of opening one each (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 latency SLA, Georgios: drive nanocode's latency overhead to zero and beat Claude Code and Codex CLI). The Claude and Responses stream readers stop at `message_stop` and `response.completed` and drop the `Response` there, before the chunked body's terminator is read, so `Incoming` never reached `finish` and the connection closed with it: on the mock every one of 36 turns (12 sessions of 3) arrived on a new connection, so on a live provider every turn paid a TCP and TLS handshake. `impl Drop for Response` (crates/core/http/src/client/response.rs) calls `Incoming::release`, which settles the bytes already buffered, reads once more without waiting (`now_or_never`) to take a terminator already in the socket's buffer, and checks the connection in when the message ended and nothing failed; otherwise it is dropped as before. A body that has not ended is never waited for. `error_for_status` clones the URL since `Response` now has a destructor. - A completion steered into a parent that still lists a turn reads its steer receipt as soon as the parent's admitted requests settle and no turn is left, instead of waiting only for the next run event (2026-11-13, from the same cfo.sh failures, Georgios: fix the rare "did not settle" failures in the whole-runtime simulation). `NoticeOutcome::of_route` (crates/runtime/subagents/src/runtime.rs) took the receipt itself only when the parent had no turn controls at the moment the route returned Steered, and otherwise waited for `of_steers`, which answers a watched steer on the parent's next `RunCompleted` or `RunFailed`. A turn's request claim leaves `turn_controls` only after its result resolves, in the task `tracked` spawns, which is after the backend published the turn's terminal event. A route that returns Steered in that window, as one does at once when `identified_steer_accepted` finds the steer accepted before a crash, sees a turn that has already published its last event; when no other run follows, the watcher never answers and the completion stays in `pending_completions`. Seen once, with logging added to 1ff234038 and the entry below: after the second crash of `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 49693259242473932`, agent 1's revision-3 completion, steered before the crash, routed as Steered and its notice never settled while the other three completions did, leaving `pending_completions: [(AgentId(1), 3)]`, the state cfo.sh logged for this seed at 999400a81. That run depended on the process's hash and thread-RNG keys: the seed has passed every run since (120 runs each of 999400a81's binary, of 1ff234038 with the entry below, and of 1ff234038 with both entries, and its cfo.sh job of 741 seeds in one process on each), so no seed shows the difference. `Agent::requests_settled` returns a future that waits for the `settled` signal of every request admitted when it is called, in key order. `of_route` now loops: without a parent it waits for the watcher; without turn controls it reads the receipt; otherwise it waits, biased, for the watcher or for those requests to settle, and looks again. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): with the entry below, the four seeds of that entry pass, and seeds 1794556500000000000..+4,000 of `--store kv` and the next 2,000 of `--store kv --twice` all pass.
- A subagent completion whose request ID already names an unfinished durable operation of its parent runs as its own turn, alone, instead of being steered into a running turn or batched with other completions, so the operation finishes and the parent's later turns are not blocked behind it (2026-11-13, from the runtime scenario's "did not settle" failures that cfo.sh logged on dev-georgios at 999400a81 and 2fd631f41, Georgios: fix the rare "did not settle" failures in the whole-runtime simulation). Root cause: a completion that reaches a parent with no accepting turn is submitted as a turn, and the parent's durability policy admits an operation under the completion's request ID (`subagent-completion:<session>:<revision>[:<attempt>]`) before the turn runs. When a crash fell between that admission and the turn's start, the restored registry routed the completion again under the same ID, and if the parent was running a resumed turn by then, the Claude driver's `route` steered the completion into it: the turn read it and finished, the steer receipt said Accepted and the notice was acked, but the operation stayed Pending in the parent's session, so every later turn failed with "durable operation `turn-1` is blocked by unfinished operation `subagent-completion:…:1`" and the root never settled. On `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 1794551987480396597` (crashes at 9.5 s and 42.5 s) root 1's stored turns end as `turn-0=Completed` and `subagent-completion:…:1=Pending`, and its turn-1 and turn-2 fail on that block; seed 2254413763390168085 ends the same way. A batch would leave the operation Pending too, since it routes under its own `…:batch-<key>` ID. The fix: `LifecycleBackend::unfinished_request` (false by default) asks whether an operation of that ID exists and is not terminal, through `Agent::unfinished_request`, `Owned`, `ClaudeExecutionPolicy` and the Codex `ExecutionPolicy` (durable and lazy alike) to `DurableOwner::unfinished_operation`, a new session-driver command that reads the operation's status after the caller's authorization. When it answers true, the Claude driver's `route` and the Codex driver's `RoutePrompt` skip the steer and start the turn (the Codex driver through `accept_idle_route`), which takes up the operation, and `Registry::dispatch_parent_batch` routes the completion alone under its own ID, as it also does when the check fails. `completion_request_id` builds the ID for the three places that built it. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): 1794551987480396597 and 2254413763390168085 (`--store kv`) fail on master's binary (2fd631f41) and pass with this change; the tree with the two entries above, built without this change, fails both again. 1265550401772960989 (`--store kv --calm`) and 1843697481294244027 (`--store memory`), cfo.sh's other two failures at 999400a81 with a Pending `subagent-completion:…:1`, fail there on every run and pass on master since 2fd631f41's ordering fixes moved their schedules; on 1ff234038 (999400a81's parent, which differs only in nanocode-turnlog) this change alone makes both pass. With this change alone on master: the four seeds pass, and seeds 1794556500000000000..+4,000 of `--store kv` and the next 2,000 of `--store kv --twice` all pass. The crate checks are in the `join_in_order` entry two above, run on the tree with all three. Open: a batch is orphaned the same way. When a crash falls between a batch's admission and its turn, the restored registry can form a different batch because another completion became ready meanwhile, and the first batch's operation stays Pending: `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 1794555092696313594` fails so with this change (`subagent-completion:…:1:batch-b3:332d…=Pending`, a batch of agents 6 and 7 admitted before the second crash and routed after it as a batch of 5, 6 and 7 under a new ID) and passes on master's binary, whose timing differs; cfo.sh logged the same Pending batch in 41 failed jobs at ccf5a4802, 95aee2808, d83e8c450 and d4dfa9d67. A fix needs the registry to learn a parent's unfinished completion operations after a restart, which nothing exposes yet.
- Tokio tasks spawn through three non-generic boxes in nanocode-platform, so a crate that spawns no longer instantiates Tokio's task harness once per future type (2026-11-13, Georgios: lower compilation time). crates/core/platform/src/native.rs gains `spawn_task` (pins the future as `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send>>` and hands it to `tokio::spawn`), `spawn_on` (the same on a `runtime::Handle`) and `spawn_blocking` (boxes the `FnOnce`), all `#[track_caller]` so Tokio still records the caller, and `spawn` boxes before choosing between a platform Host and Tokio; every `tokio::spawn`, `Handle::spawn` and `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` in bin/nanocode, the Claude and Codex backends and clients, agent-core, mcp-http, mcp-tools, chatgpt-extension, process, sandbox, tool-runtime, code-mode, durability and nanocode-sync's `Actor`, `hand_off` and `detached` calls them instead. Tokio's `RawTask` vtable, `Harness::poll`, `poll_future`, `set_stage`, `take_output` and `catch_unwind` were instantiated per spawned future type: `cargo rustc -p nanocode-cli --lib -- --emit=llvm-ir` counted 2,583,515 LLVM IR lines in 55,323 functions before and 1,841,355 in 33,628 after (on 6744c3b9c, 43 commits earlier, with the same change) (llvm-lines-style count, Tokio's harness 314 copies before, the per-output-type handful after). Behavior is unchanged: the same JoinHandle, abort, panic propagation and Host routing; each spawn makes one more allocation and polls through one vtable call. Measured on gak-9 (M1 Max, CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=6, load 18 to 47 from other agents, so CPU time is the steadier figure) with interleaved fresh target dirs (output/cold2.py, rustc wrapper off): release cold 1,080.0 to 1,060.1 CPU-s (median of 2; wall 207.1 to 208.5 s, inside the load noise), release rebuild after touching bin/nanocode/src/lib.rs 49.7 to 39.5 s wall and 133.2 to 109.7 CPU-s (nanocode-cli 47.2 to 37.4 s), dev cold 400.7 to 401.7 CPU-s and a dev rebuild after touching crates/core/types-core/src/lib.rs 22.7 to 22.0 CPU-s (both unchanged: unoptimized codegen of the copies was cheap). Release nanocode is 89,487,488 to 87,083,360 bytes on aarch64-apple-darwin. Spawn microbenchmark (output/spawn-bench: 200,000 spawn-and-await, 200,000 fan-out through oneshot channels, 20,000 spawn_blocking, 9 interleaved rounds, mimalloc): M1 Max sequential 301.9 to 309.3 ns per task with 4 workers and 170.5 to 174.1 with 1, fan-out 500.1 to 596.1 ns with 4 workers (the extra allocation freed on another worker) and 208.7 to 210.6 with 1, spawn_blocking unchanged (8,798.6 to 8,797.2 ns); x86_64 hosted Hand (load 11) sequential 386.4 to 373.5, fan-out 378.3 to 477.9 with 4 workers and 452.5 to 441.4 with 1. - A Code Mode cell keeps its pending tool calls in an array indexed by call id instead of a Map (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 djs track: per-cell overhead). `callTool` and the pump (crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/bootstrap.js) did a `Map.prototype.set`, `get` and `delete` per tool call, about 1.9k instructions each in djs, whose Map methods are self-hosted builtins; ids are the host's `next_tool_id`, which starts at 1 for each cell and only grows, so `pendingTools[id]` is a dense array, and a settled call's slot becomes `undefined` so its resolvers are not kept. output/cellbench (as in the entries below): one tool call 259,982 → 253,388 instructions per cell, 16 sequential calls 1,412,875 → 1,339,308 (−5.2%, 4.6k per call), 16 parallel calls 1,537,664 → 1,458,089. Measured against it and not kept: `Promise.withResolvers()` in place of `new Promise` with an executor (16 sequential calls 1,397,723, more than the executor), and dropping `observe`'s `catch` (8k per call less, but an unobserved failing call would then end the cell as an unhandled rejection). 25 edge cells (the 19 of the settle change, and failing tools through a new `Fail*` stub: caught with its `message`, `tool` and payload fields, unobserved, in `Promise.allSettled`, uncaught, and awaited after a timer) give the same events before and after. Commands: the checks and clippy of the entries below.
- `OneLogJournals::save` commits a row when a Code Mode cell starts (2026-11-13). Since 999400a81 and before, the first save of a cell (its header) was only buffered, and a row came with the cell's first External call. A host that dies while the cell waits, before that call, lost the cell and the session checkpoint of the model step that started it, so recovery asked the model for the step again. nanocodexyz/durable-vercel's `npm run drill` failed all four `waiting` runs on nanocode-ts build-f1b2093 ("the recovered drive asked the model for the cell again") and passes all of them with this change. The cost is one row per cell: durable-cloudflare `output/sqlturn` text and tool turns write 3 statements and 3 rows instead of 2 (1.2 and 1.3 KB of parameters), and reply turns stay at 2. In durable-cloudflare's crash matrix, the runs that lose the commit in flight (s = c - 1) show no double charge and report the last one as unknown. Double charges appear only in runs that restore an older snapshot and so lose commits that were already acknowledged. `cargo check` passes native and wasm, and `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes for nanocode-agent.
- A Claude Bash stream that was cut says so in its last line, and a file keeps everything the command printed (2026-11-13). A call from a Code Mode cell gets 128 KiB of stdout and of stderr (`NESTED_STREAM_BYTES`, measured on 2026-11-05), and a longer stream came back cut with `truncated: true` and nothing else; a cell that takes `.stdout` never reads that flag. In a Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness on a hand (Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-13) 5 of 69 finished attempts had a Bash result cut this way and two lost their task to it: `(await tools.Bash({ command: "cat FILE" })).stdout.split("\n")` on a file of 1,661,422 bytes parsed its first 8% as the whole, and `base64 -w0` of JPEGs of 110 to 886 KB showed the model the top 43% of each page, which it took for noise in the scan. The exec description already said that a shell's base64 is cut off. The other ways output reaches a cell or a model say when they cut: exec_command and a cell's own output begin with "Warning: truncated output (original token count: N)" and mark the gap, and Read refuses a file over 256 KiB with a message that names both sizes. Now, first, the file every native command already streams its output to (`<temp>/nanocode/<session>/tasks/<task id>.output`: stdout and stderr as they came, secrets redacted) is kept instead of deleted when the result was cut, and the result names it in `output_file` and `output_bytes`, which are null otherwise (`BashExecution::Cut`). It stays as a background command's file does, until the temporary directory is cleared, under the same 5 GiB cap. Second, a stream that was cut ends with one line, `[stdout cut after its first 131072 bytes: the command printed 1661422 bytes in all, stdout and stderr together, and FILE holds them]`, or, where no file was kept (a host's shell, a file that could not be created), `… the rest was not kept, so send the command's output to a file and read it in parts]`. So `text(r.stdout)` and the last element of a `split` show it, `JSON.parse` throws and a data URL no longer decodes. The line goes to the stream that reached the limit, and to stdout when the result cannot tell which (`bounded_output`); the model's own calls, cut at 30,000 bytes, and the host adapters' TaskOutput get it too. Third, the output schema's `stdout` has one sentence, which the exec description renders above the field in the declaration: "At most 131072 bytes of what the command printed: when it printed more, or is still running in the background, the last line says so in brackets and names `output_file`, which holds all of it." (a host's ends at "in brackets"), and the sentence about Bash results in prompts/code_mode.md says the same and to read that file in parts with another command. The limit itself stays where it was measured. A hand sends each nested result to its brain in one frame under the connection's `max_frame_bytes` (1 MiB where an eval harness's Worker hosts the brain; a frame over it is logged as not sent), and no limit under that bound would have held the 1.66 MB file: what makes a cut safe is that it cannot be missed and that the rest can be read. Checked with output/cells (release build, Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`): the `cat` cell above reported 131,072 bytes and 3,277 lines before; after, 131,305 bytes whose last line is the notice, with `truncated: true` and `output_bytes: 1661422`; a cell that then reads `output_file` with `tail -c +N FILE | head -c 100000` in a loop collected 1,661,422 bytes and 41,536 lines; the base64 of a 500,000-byte file ends with the notice naming 666,668 bytes; a command that fills only stderr has the line only there, one that fills both has it in both; exactly 131,072 bytes are not cut, and a command that was not cut leaves no file. The declaration of a hand's Bash takes the exec description of its five Claude tools from 11,423 to 12,092 bytes, and the system prompt grows by 373 bytes with the sentence. output/d1-background and output/psh-differential give what the two entries below report. `cargo clippy --locked --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -- -D warnings` and `cargo check --locked --offline --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, report nothing. Not run: a model with the new result, declaration and sentence; a call of the model's own that is cut at 30,000 bytes; the host adapters' Bash and TaskOutput at run time (they compile for wasm32 and share the code of the line); macOS and Windows. Files: crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/bash.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/{claude_bash,claude_output,host_tools}.rs, crates/backends/claude/prompts/code_mode.md.
- A Claude Bash result has the same fields whether the command finished or is still running, and a command in the background says so in `stdout` (2026-11-13). A command that passed its `timeout`, or was started with `run_in_background`, resolved to `{ task_id, status, background, output_file, message }` and a finished one to `{ stdout, stderr, exit_code, interrupted, truncated }`: two shapes without a field in common. The Code Mode instructions name `result.stdout` and `result.exit_code` since 2026-11-12, and cells follow them: in a Terminal-Bench 2.1 run of the Claude harness on a hand (Haiku 5.5, 2026-11-13) 458 of 636 cells printed a Bash result as `text(r.stdout + r.stderr)`. For a command moved to the background that is `undefined + undefined`: the cell printed `NaN` in 6 of 69 attempts, the notice with the task ID and the output file never reached the model, and one model started a two-minute command again because it seemed to have printed nothing, and ran out of time. Now both results have `stdout`, `stderr`, `exit_code`, `interrupted`, `truncated`, `background`, `status`, `task_id`, `output_file` and `message`. For a background command `stdout` is the message and a newline, so `text(r.stdout)` and `text(r.stdout + r.stderr)` both show that it is still running, its ID and where its output goes; `stderr` is empty, `exit_code` is null, and `message` stays as it was. A finished command has `background: false`, `status: "completed"` and null `task_id`, `output_file` and `message`. The output schema is one object instead of a `oneOf` of two, since a cell written for one variant read `undefined` from the other, and its `stdout`, `exit_code` and `background` have descriptions, which the exec description renders as comments in the declaration. The host adapters' TaskOutput had the same trap (`{ task_id, status }` while running, `{ task_id, status, error }` for a task that ended without a result) and now always has `stdout`, `stderr`, `exit_code`, `truncated` and `error`: a running task says so in `stdout`, and one that ended without a result has its error in `stderr` too. prompts/code_mode.md says in one sentence that `stdout` and `stderr` are strings in every Bash result. Looked at and left as they are: `text()` prints `NaN` for NaN, which a cell may compute and a Bash result can no longer produce; exec_command and write_stdin keep Codex's result, whose `output` is always a string and whose `exit_code` and `session_id` are optional by its schema; Read is a string or content blocks, Edit and Write are strings, TaskStop is one object, and a call that fails rejects in every tool. Checked with output/cells (`harness.mjs`: a scripted Responses endpoint sends each cell of a JSON file to `nanocode exec --runner-connect` against `nanocode hand --listen` and prints what the model would receive), release build on Linux x86_64, hand with `--own-processes`: `const r = await tools.Bash({ command: "echo started; /bin/sleep 6; echo finished", timeout: 1500 }); text(r.stdout + r.stderr)` printed `NaN` before, also on the hand released at 1f10a22ea, and the whole notice after; the same with `run_in_background`; `Object.keys(r)` is the same ten names for both; the end of the job is still reported with the next result. output/d1-background, with and without `--own-processes`: exec_command leaves a job alive at the end of the turn in 22 of 22 ways and Bash in 20 of 21, as master before this change. The Bash case that fails is `sleep N &` with N of 25 or more, which the leading-sleep rule of a81ec4e87 refuses although it does not wait; the harness gained `true; sleep N &`, the same job, which stays alive. `cargo clippy --locked --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -- -D warnings` and `cargo check --locked --offline --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-code-mode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, report nothing. Not run: a model with the new result; the host adapters' Bash and TaskOutput at run time (they compile for wasm32). Files: crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/bash.rs, crates/backends/claude/src/{claude_output,host_tools}.rs, crates/backends/claude/prompts/code_mode.md.
- psh's `time` reports what its pipeline took, as bash does (2026-11-13). The parser kept `time` and `time -p` in the tree and the engine ran the pipeline and reported nothing: `time sleep 0.2` printed no line where bash prints three on stderr. In a Terminal-Bench 2.1 trajectory a model timed a script that way to judge its speed and got no figure. `run_pipeline` now reads the host's clocks before a timed pipeline and writes the report to the shell's stderr after it (psh-engine/src/timing.rs): bash's lines (`\nreal\t%3lR\nuser\t%3lU\nsys\t%3lS`) by default, `TIMEFORMAT` when it is set (`%[p][l]R`, `U` and `S`, `%P`, `%%`; nothing when it is empty; bash's "invalid format character" for anything else), and `real %2R`, `user %2U`, `sys %2S` for `time -p` and for `time --`, which bash's grammar takes for `-p` too. A time is rounded to milliseconds and then cut to its precision, as bash formats it. As in bash 5.2 the report follows an `exit` inside the pipeline and not a `return`, the pipeline's own redirections do not take it (`time cmd 2>/dev/null` still reports, `{ time cmd; } 2>/dev/null` does not), and a timed job (`time cmd &`) reports when it ends, for which a job of one command no longer skips its pipeline when that pipeline is timed. `Host::cpu_times` (zero by default) is the user and system time of the shell's process and of the children it has waited for; psh-os answers with `getrusage` for both, so `user` and `sys` include the programs the pipeline ran, and the `times` builtin prints the same clocks instead of four zeroes. A host without processes of its own (wasm, the test host) reports real time from `Host::now` and no CPU time, and so does Windows for now. Where the shell runs inside its embedder's process (a hand without `--own-processes`) the shell's own share is that whole process's. Checked on Linux x86_64 with a release build, each command under `psh-shell -c` beside bash 5.2: `time python3 -c 'sum(range(3*10**7))'` gave real 0.526 s and user 0.475 s against bash's 0.473 and 0.462; a 200,000-step `while` loop of builtins user 0.334 s of 0.338 s real; `time -p cmd | cat`, a bare `time` and `time -p`, `( time true ) 2>&1 | cat -A` and `type time` print what bash prints. output/psh-differential gains eight cases (the default and the POSIX lines with their figures masked, `--`, the real time of `sleep 1` as `%0R` and `%0lR`, the user time of a program alone and in a pipeline, `TIMEFORMAT` with every directive, empty and invalid, statuses and redirections, `exit`, `return`, `break` and a job, the keyword and `times`): through a hand's Bash tool with `--own-processes` 115 of 117 cases agree with bash, where 107 of 109 did; the two that differ are the known ones (a here-document larger than a pipe, `find -exec` of a missing program). psh directly: 115. Through a hand that runs commands in its own process: 114 or 115, because `echo x | missing-program` leaves `PIPESTATUS` 0 or 141 from run to run there, as it does on the hand built before this change. Through exec_command: 107, the others differing in the wording on stderr as before. `cargo test --locked --offline` in crates/patches/psh: 718 tests pass, among them `time_reports_what_its_pipeline_took` on the test host and `formats_as_bash_does`; the three that fail are the ones that need corpora this repository does not hold (awk `vendored_suites`, jq `upstream_suites`, search `agrees_with_the_gnu_corpus`). `cargo clippy --locked --offline --all-targets -p psh -p psh-os -p psh-engine -p psh-utils -p psh-syntax` and `cargo check --locked --offline --lib -p psh-engine -p psh-utils --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` report nothing. Not like bash: `%P` of a pipeline shorter than a millisecond (bash 5.2 printed 100.00 for `time true`, psh divides what its clocks gave); `set -o posix`, which psh refuses, so bash's POSIX-mode default never applies. Not run: macOS (the same `getrusage` code) and Windows. Files: crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/{timing,exec,host,lib,tests}.rs and builtins/command.rs, psh-os/src/unix/mod.rs, psh-syntax/src/parser.rs.

The code-mode journal types they use are in nanocode-code-mode on both targets; the gates and the import split are reverted, nothing else changes. - A Code Mode cell settles through one promise, and a cell that stored nothing returns a terminal encoded once at setup (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 djs track: per-cell overhead). `runCell`'s `finish` (crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/bootstrap.js) raced the script's promise against a `stopped` promise inside an async function (an async call, two `new Promise`, three `then` and four closures), then awaited a third promise for the host's settle; now the script's `then` and `stopCell` call `nativeSettled` once (`end`), the settle event resolves the one promise `finish` returns, and a throw other than `exit()` resolves it at once as before (no settle, so an unhandled rejection does not replace the thrown error). `terminal()` returns the `{"type":"done","stored":{}}` text made in `prepareCell` when no store was written. Splitting an empty cell first (variants of runCell built in output/cellbench): the host's fixed cost was 26.6k instructions, compiling the empty async function 40k, starting the pump 8k, `finish` 48k and the terminal 15.5k. output/cellbench as above: an empty cell 123,615 → 97,099 instructions (−21%), `text('ok')` 142,170 → 115,116, one tool call 288,400 → 261,512, 16 sequential tool calls 1,440,191 → 1,410,367. 19 edge cells (`exit()` before, after and inside a timer and after a tool, thrown errors, strings and `undefined`, a throw beside an unhandled rejection, background rejections, timers that fire and that are dropped, `store` with and without a throw, a background tool call, `yield_control`, a missing tool, a cell that never settles) produce the same events, texts and stores before and after; the only difference is the bootstrap's own line in stack frames (`runCell (nanocode:bootstrap:821:28)` → `825`). Commands: the checks and clippy above.
- An `await` whose resumption would be the very next job goes on in place (2026-11-13, nanocode 1.0 djs track: async/await cost). `await_value` (crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/interp/run/suspend.rs) suspended the frame, queued a reaction job and returned to the job loop even when the frame was the bottom frame of a job, the job queue was empty and the value fulfilled without user code (a fulfilled plain promise, or a value with no callable `then`): then the loop's next step is ClearKeptObjects and that very job, and nothing else can run in between, so the frame now runs ClearKeptObjects, pushes the value and continues (`settled_in_place`). A frame entered by a caller (the first `await` of a call), an async generator, a pending or rejected promise, a thenable and a non-empty queue take the old path, so the order of every other job is unchanged. Measured with output/cellbench (a release build driving `EmbeddedHost` cells with three stub tools; `perf stat -e instructions:u` of 200 and 1,200 cells, the difference per cell, two rounds, the same both times): `let s = 0; for (let i = 0; i < 1000; i++) s += await i` 2,047,974 → 1,065,209 instructions (−48%), the same loop awaiting one fulfilled `Promise.resolve(1)` 2,713,660 → 1,594,921 (−41%), `s = await f(s)` over an async `f` 4,161,524 → 3,040,780 (−27%); an empty cell 123,593 → 123,679, 16 sequential tool calls 1,438,013 → 1,440,113 and an 861-byte agent cell (a listing, a Map and two parallel tool calls) 1,134,007 → 1,132,752. A script of 30 interleavings (await of values, fulfilled and rejected promises, a thenable, a getter on `then`, a Promise subclass, `.then` chains, `queueMicrotask`, timers, nested async calls) prints the same order as Node 18.19.1 on both builds. test262 at 2e58f87 (output/t262: indirect eval of the harness and the test in a fresh djs-embed instance, sloppy and strict; 9,300 files of async functions and arrows, await, for-await-of, async generators, Promise, AsyncFunction, AsyncFromSyncIteratorPrototype, classes, new.target, this, eval and Function): 8,631 pass before and after, the same files, 4,360 of them async or Promise tests. - rustpython-host_env's `enum_certificates` (`ssl.enum_certificates`) reads the Windows system stores through nanocode-sys's certificate_store, and schannel 0.1.29 leaves the lock, the last of the seven packages outside the accepted set on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (2026-11-13). crates/core/sys/src/certificate_store.rs already opened the current user's ROOT store for nanocode-platform's trust roots with the same calls schannel makes (CertOpenStore with CERT_STORE_PROV_SYSTEM_W, CertEnumCertificatesInStore, and CertGetEnhancedKeyUsage read the way schannel's `valid_uses` reads it, CRYPT_E_NOT_FOUND with no identifiers meaning every use); it now takes the store by `Location` (CurrentUser or LocalMachine, CERT_SYSTEM_STORE_CURRENT_USER_ID or CERT_SYSTEM_STORE_LOCAL_MACHINE_ID) and name in `system_certificates`, `current_user_roots` is `system_certificates(CurrentUser, "ROOT")`, and each `Certificate` also carries its dwCertEncodingType. crates/patches/rustpython-host_env/src/cert_store.rs opens the named store for the current user and then the local machine as before, skips a location that fails to open, maps `Usages::All` and `Identifiers` to `CertificateUses::All` and `Oids`, wraps a usage error in `io::Error::other` as it did schannel's, and classifies the encoding with its own `encoding_type`; its raw CERT_CONTEXT read is gone, and enum_crls is unchanged. Differences from schannel: the store name is encoded with `str::encode_utf16`, the same units as schannel's `OsStr::encode_wide` for a `&str`; each certificate also gets a CertVerifyTimeValidity call (nanocode-platform uses it, enum_certificates ignores it); the CTL_USAGE buffer is u64-aligned where schannel's was a byte vector cast to CTL_USAGE. No new unsafe: the calls were already in nanocode-sys. No harness: this is the same Windows API calls in the same order, with no pure logic beyond the usage mapping, which certificate_store.rs carries over from schannel's `valid_uses` line for line, and no Windows machine can run it here. - rustpython-host_env's `create_junction` (`_winapi.CreateJunction`) makes the junction through nanocode-sys's own `junction::create`, and junction 2.0.0 and scopeguard 1.2.0 leave the lock (2026-11-13). crates/core/sys/src/junction.rs (Windows only) does what junction 2.0.0's `create` did, the only junction function RustPython called: it resolves the target with GetFullPathNameW, strips a `\\?\` prefix, builds the mount point REPARSE_DATA_BUFFER (`mount_point_buffer`: tag IO_REPARSE_TAG_MOUNT_POINT, data length, the substitute name `\??\` plus the target and the print name the target, each NUL-terminated, offsets and lengths in bytes, little-endian), creates the directory, opens it with GENERIC_READ and GENERIC_WRITE, no sharing and FILE_FLAG_OPEN_REPARSE_POINT with FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS, retries the open once after enabling SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege (OpenProcessToken, LookupPrivilegeValueW, AdjustTokenPrivileges, ERROR_NOT_ALL_ASSIGNED as an error) when the first open is refused, and sends the buffer with DeviceIoControl(FSCTL_SET_REPARSE_POINT). The token handle closes in Drop, where junction used scopeguard. FSCTL_SET_REPARSE_POINT is a named constant (0x000900A4, winioctl.h) so nanocode-sys needs no windows-sys Win32_System_Ioctl feature; the features it adds (Win32_Security, Win32_Storage_FileSystem, Win32_System_IO, Win32_System_SystemServices, Win32_System_Threading) are all already on in nanocode-cli's and nanocode-python's Windows graphs (22 windows-sys features before and after), so they compile nothing new. Differences from junction, all on inputs it handled worse: a target longer than the reparse buffer holds (more than 4,089 UTF-16 units after the prefix) is refused before the directory is created, where junction created and opened the directory first and left it behind, with the same InvalidInput error and "`target` is too long" message; a target with an interior NUL is refused with InvalidInput, where junction resolved only the part before the NUL; GetFullPathNameW is called once for the size and once for the path, and if the second call still needs more room (the current directory changed in between) that is an error, where junction looped until it fitted. New unsafe in nanocode-sys, each block one call: GetFullPathNameW (twice), DeviceIoControl, OpenProcessToken with GetCurrentProcess, LookupPrivilegeValueW, AdjustTokenPrivileges, GetLastError and CloseHandle. Equality harness output/windows-equality: junction 2.0.0's buffer-building code ported verbatim (its REPARSE_DATA_BUFFER and MountPointReparseBuffer structs, BytesAsReparseDataBuffer, the saturating length checks and raw writes) against a verbatim copy of `mount_point_buffer`, comparing the in_buffer_size bytes junction hands DeviceIoControl, or the error kind and message: for seeds 11, 12345 and 987654321, 62,500 random targets each (random UTF-16 units including NULs and surrogates, lengths up to 9,000 with a quarter clustered at 4,080 to 4,099, a third with the verbatim prefix), every length from 0 to 4,200 with and without the prefix, and the real inputs above (119,898 with this file in the tree) as targets: 190,800 cases per seed, 174,263 to 174,335 built and 16,465 to 16,537 too long, all identical, the accept/refuse boundary at 4,089 units included. Run as in the entry before (`windows-equality <seed> 1000000`), all identical. - rustpython-host_env's last parking_lot uses on Windows are std's, and parking_lot 0.12.5, parking_lot_core 0.9.12, lock_api 0.4.14, redox_syscall 0.5.18 and bitflags 2.13.1 leave the lock (2026-11-13). The 2026-11-12 entry that moved RustPython onto its own lock_api layer kept parking_lot as a Windows-only dependency of rustpython-host_env for two places, both changed here. crates/patches/rustpython-host_env/src/windows.rs's `init_winsock` runs WSAStartup once through `std::sync::Once` instead of `parking_lot::Once`: the same call_once semantics, where a thread that arrives while another runs the closure waits for it, which this needs because no socket call may run before WSAStartup returns, so it adds no blocking that was not there. crates/patches/rustpython-host_env/src/ctypes.rs's library cache and per-library handle use `std::sync::RwLock` and `Mutex`, taking the guard through a poisoned lock with `PoisonError::into_inner` as fs/append_log.rs already does, where parking_lot's locks do not poison; they were blocking locks before and are now. ctypes.rs is compiled only with the `ctypes` feature, which needs libffi and libloading, neither of which is in the lock, so no configuration builds it before or after; its edit is the same mechanical one, and its other host_env neighbours under the unbuildable `ssl` feature (ssl/config.rs, keylog.rs, session.rs, verify.rs) and rustpython-vm's `threading` code still name parking_lot, as they did on every target before. - RustPython's Windows code builds its NUL-terminated UTF-16 strings with rustpython-host_env's own `wide_string` module, and widestring leaves the lock (2026-11-13). crates/patches/rustpython-host_env/src/wide_string.rs (Windows only) has what the three crates used of widestring 1.2.1, under the same names so each call site only changes its path: `WideCStr` (a `#[repr(transparent)]` slice that ends in its one NUL, built only after the check, with the two unsafe reference casts asserting the terminator), `WideCString` (a boxed slice with its NUL), and the errors `ContainsNul` (with `nul_position`), `MissingNulTerminator` and `NulError`, with widestring's Display strings. The constructors keep widestring's rules: `from_vec`, `from_str` and `from_os_str` (OsStr::encode_wide) reject a NUL anywhere but the last unit and append one when missing; `from_vec_truncate` cuts at the first NUL; `WideCStr::from_slice` and `from_slice_mut` need a final NUL and no other; `from_slice_truncate` cuts after the first NUL; `from_ptr_str` scans to the NUL. Accessors are `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `len`, `is_empty`, `as_slice`, `as_slice_with_nul`, `to_os_string`, `to_string_lossy`, `into_vec_with_nul`, Deref, AsRef, Borrow, ToOwned and widestring's Debug format. Where a container needed no invariant it is plain std: winreg's `SetValue` builds a `Vec<u16>` instead of a `WideString` and host winreg takes `&[u16]` instead of `&WideStr`; time.rs decodes time zone names with `char::decode_utf16` and the replacement character instead of `decode_utf16_lossy`; windows.rs reads the service pack with `String::from_utf16` instead of `U16CStr::to_string`; tkinter (not built) decodes UTF-32 with `char::from_u32`; nt.rs's `execve` builds each environment string with the checked `from_str` and an `expect` (its NULs are rejected just above) instead of `from_str_unchecked` in an unsafe block. The vm's `ToPyException` impls name the new error types. Differences from widestring: the error types are not generic over the unit type and `ContainsNul` no longer carries the rejected vector (nothing read it). Equality harness output/windows-equality (widestring =1.2.1 against a verbatim copy of wide_string.rs without its two OsStr wrappers, which are `from_vec(encode_wide)` and `OsString::from_wide` in both): for seeds 11, 12345 and 987654321, 1,000,000 seeded random UTF-16 sequences each (NULs, unpaired high and low surrogates, BMP and ASCII, some up to 2,000 units, a quarter NUL-terminated) and as many random strings (NUL, astral, two-byte and ASCII characters), plus 119,845 real inputs (Windows paths, registry keys, environment strings, store names and the first 50 lines of every .rs, .md and .py file under crates/), with and without a terminating NUL: from_vec, from_vec_truncate, from_str, from_slice, from_slice_mut, from_slice_truncate and from_ptr_str give the same accept or reject decision, error kind, nul_position, Display string, units with and without the NUL, len, to_string_lossy and Debug output, about 1.24 million cases per function per seed; decode_utf16_lossy, String::from_utf16 against U16Str::to_string, and char::from_u32 against U32String::to_string_lossy agree on every input. Run with `cargo build --offline --release` in output/windows-equality, then `windows-equality <seed> 1000000`: all three seeds report identical.
