- psh-utils's WHATWG UTF-8 decoder (rg `-E utf-8`) finds its valid prefix with nanocode-sys's own SIMD UTF-8 validator, `nanocode_sys::utf8::valid_up_to` (crates/core/sys/src/utf8.rs), instead of `std::str::from_utf8`, restoring most of what simdutf8 gave encoding_rs (2026-11-13). The validator is Keiser and Lemire's lookup algorithm as simdjson and simdutf8 use it: 64-byte blocks, an all-ASCII block only checking that the previous block did not end inside a character, otherwise three 16-entry nibble tables (first byte's high and low nibble, second byte's high nibble) whose AND flags too-short, too-long, overlong, surrogate, too-large and stray-continuation pairs, XORed with the third- and fourth-byte continuation requirements from saturating subtractions of the bytes two and three back, and the incomplete-tail check of the last 3 bytes; AVX2 (two 32-byte vectors, `alignr` over a cross-lane permute for the previous bytes, `pshufb` lookups) on x86_64 when `std::is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")`, NEON (four 16-byte vectors, `vextq_u8`, `vqtbl1q_u8`) on aarch64, nothing elsewhere (wasm32 builds only the scalar path). It stops at the first block with an error, steps back to the start of the last character that began before that block (at most 4 bytes) and lets `std::str::from_utf8` answer from there, so the result is `from_utf8`'s `valid_up_to` (or the length) by construction: everything before that character was checked complete and valid by the blocks, and the tail under 64 bytes always goes through std. psh-utils gains a path dependency on nanocode-sys (psh's own Cargo.lock adds it; the root graph already had it). Unsafe blocks and invariants: `valid_blocks_avx2` call (blocks * 64 <= length asserted, AVX2 detected) and its two 32-byte loads per block inside that bound; the two 32-byte table loads from local arrays; `valid_blocks_neon` call (same bound) with its `vld1q_u8_x4` per block and `vld1q_u8` of the 16-byte tables. Equal: output/utf8-equal compares `valid_up_to` and a copy whose `simd()` returns false against `std::str::from_utf8(..).map_or_else(|e| e.valid_up_to(), ..)`: every 1-byte and every 2-byte sequence from a C0-FF lead, 14 three- and four-byte lead families crossed with continuation, ASCII, lead and invalid bytes, each placed at 21 offsets around the 64-byte block boundaries (0-3, 60-67, 124-129, 190-192) after ASCII or NUL filler or a multibyte run, then followed by ASCII and by 70 bytes of generated text; plus 300,000 seeded texts (ASCII, Latin, CJK, emoji, random scalars, up to 256 KiB) with byte overwrites, truncations, inserted 80/C0/E0/ED/F0/F4/F5/FF bytes and deletions, their halves at a random cut, and random byte strings: 4,347,736 checks on x86_64 (hosted Hand, AVX2) and 4,347,736 on aarch64 (gak-9), 0 differences. output/enc-bench runs psh-utils's decoders from origin/master and from this tree in lockstep over 20,000 seeded streams in 14 encodings (random bytes, ASCII with high bytes, encoded text, long ASCII runs, UTF-8 BOM starts; 178 MB) with random input chunks (1-64 KiB or 1-16 B) and output sizes (4 B-8 KiB): every call's result, bytes read and bytes written and the output equal, 15,191,627 calls on each architecture, 0 differences. Measured (validator alone over 4 MiB in 8 KiB calls, median of 11 interleaved rounds, MB/s std -> nanocode-sys): aarch64 (gak-9, load 17) ASCII 29,950 -> 70,567, Latin text 923 -> 11,716, CJK 4,502 -> 29,533, emoji 2,008 -> 10,181, random scalars 3,980 -> 37,197; x86_64 (hosted Hand, load 27, so read ratios) ASCII 47,775 -> 85,449, Latin 250 -> 10,190, CJK 1,565 -> 25,958, emoji 727 -> 18,690, random 1,555 -> 68,243. The decoder as rg drives it (8 MiB, 8 KiB chunks into a 64 KiB output, median of 9 interleaved rounds, MB/s before -> after): aarch64 (load 9) UTF-8 ASCII 6,868 -> 7,973, UTF-8 with 1 in 6 characters non-ASCII 506 -> 4,442, CJK 1,336 -> 4,262; x86_64 (load 39) mixed 61 -> 4,788, CJK 144 -> 517. Tried and not kept: checking the other decoders' ASCII runs 32 bytes at a time before the u64 words: on aarch64 pure ASCII windows-1252, Shift_JIS and EUC-KR went 5,652 -> 6,249, 5,630 -> 6,259 and 5,813 -> 6,286 MB/s (the run is a copy already), but windows-1252 text with an accented letter every 20 bytes went 738 -> 669, so the u64 word loop stays. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys` for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown (no warnings), in crates/patches/psh `cargo clippy --locked -p psh-utils` (the three older `chunks_exact` warnings in codec.rs and dump.rs only), `cargo check --locked --lib -p psh-utils --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p psh-utils -p psh`, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` at the root.
- nanocode-sys's own base64 (crates/core/sys/src/base64.rs: `nanocode_sys::base64::{Engine, Alphabet, DecodePadding, STANDARD, STANDARD_NO_PAD, URL_SAFE, URL_SAFE_NO_PAD, DecodeError, encoded_length}`) encodes and decodes for every nanocode crate, with AVX2 on x86_64 and NEON on aarch64 as base64-simd did, and the base64 crate leaves the workspace's own dependencies (2026-11-13). Callers moved from `base64::engine::general_purpose::{STANDARD, URL_SAFE_NO_PAD}` and `base64::encoded_len`: nanocode-backend-claude (host tools, prompt data URLs), -claude-client (subscription PKCE), -claude-tools (media), nanocode-backend-codex (image generation, view_image, served tools), -codex-client (ChatGPT and subscription auth, compaction, connector), nanocode-audio, nanocode-durability-core (blob and row), nanocode-turnlog (row codec, STANDARD_NO_PAD), nanocode-store-sql (Postgres SCRAM), nanocode-image, nanocode-mcp (OAuth), nanocode-schema (`contentEncoding: base64`), nanocode-websocket (handshake), nanocode-computer, nanocode-computer-repl, nanocode-sandbox (egress proxy and redaction), nanocode-tool-runtime and nanocode-code-mode-engine, whose forgiving `fromBase64` engine is `Engine::new(Alphabet::Standard, true, DecodePadding::Indifferent, true)`; the workspace's `base64 = "0.22.1"` line goes. nanocode-http's proxy authorization (crates/core/http/src/connect.rs, added on master after this change was first written) encodes with `STANDARD` as well, and since reqwest and hyper-util have left master, base64 0.22.1 leaves Cargo.lock entirely (`grep -c 'name = "base64"' Cargo.lock` 1 to 0, rebased on d3ec97b99). nanocode-tempo's constant-time URL-safe codec, psh's `base64` utility and RustPython's binascii keep their own semantics and are untouched. Behavior is base64 0.22.1's `GeneralPurpose` engine: encode as `Engine::encode`/`encode_string` (panicking on a length overflow as base64 does), decode as `Engine::decode` with its order of checks (a lone last byte that is neither a symbol nor `=`, then the body quads in order, each invalid byte or `=` reported as `InvalidByte(offset, byte)`, then the last one to four bytes with its padding, `InvalidLength`, padding-mode (`Canonical` = RequireCanonical, `Indifferent`, `Forbidden` = RequireNone) and trailing-bits `InvalidLastSymbol` rules), and the same `Display` texts. Not equal, on purpose: `decode_vec` truncates its buffer back to its old length on an error where base64 left it grown with zeros (no caller uses `decode_vec`). The SIMD kernels only take whole blocks of valid symbols (AVX2: 24 bytes to 32 symbols with Muła's shuffle and multiply split, symbols from range compares; 32 symbols to 24 bytes with range compares, `maddubs`/`madd` packing and a cross-lane permute; NEON: `vld3q`/`vld4q` deinterleaved 48/64-byte blocks, symbols through a 64-byte `vqtbl4q` table, decode through two `vqtbl4q`/`vqtbx4q` lookups of the decode table), stop at the first block holding any other byte, and the scalar loop (8 symbols into one u64 as base64's `decode_chunk_8`, 4 u64 reads per 24 bytes on encode) decodes from there, so errors are found and reported by the scalar code alone. Detection: `std::is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2")` in the one `simd()` function; NEON is part of every aarch64 target; wasm32 and other targets compile only the scalar code. Unsafe blocks and their invariants: `encode_string`'s `String::as_mut_vec` (only ASCII is written into the vector: the zero fill, alphabet symbols and `=`, so it stays UTF-8 even if a panic unwinds; `is_ascii` is checked before returning, and the vector is truncated back before the panic otherwise); the `encode_avx2` call ((blocks - 1) * 24 + 28 <= input length and blocks * 32 <= output length asserted, AVX2 detected) and its two 16-byte loads and one 32-byte store per block inside those bounds; the `decode_avx2` call (blocks * 32 <= input and blocks * 24 <= output asserted) and its 32-byte load and 16 + 8-byte stores per block; the `encode_neon` call (blocks * 48 <= input, blocks * 64 <= output) with its `vld1q_u8_x4` of the 64-byte symbol table, `vld3q_u8` and `vst4q_u8`; the `decode_neon` call (blocks * 64 <= input, blocks * 48 <= output) with two `vld1q_u8_x4` of the first 128 bytes of the 256-byte decode table, `vld4q_u8` and `vst3q_u8`; that every decode table entry is a sextet or 0xff is a compile-time assertion. Equal: output/base64-equal links base64 =0.22.1 beside nanocode-sys and a copy of base64.rs whose `simd()` returns false (forced scalar): all 24 engines (two alphabets, encode padding on and off, the three padding modes, trailing bits allowed or not), sizes 0 to 1,099 and 4,095 to 2,000,003 bytes plus seeded random ones over random bytes, `encode`, `encode_string` onto a non-empty string, then `decode` of the encoding and of up to five rounds of mutations (symbols replaced by `=`, `+`, `/`, `-`, `_`, whitespace, NUL, 0x80, 0xff and random bytes, truncation, inserted, appended and moved padding, removed bytes) under two random engines each, comparing the bytes or the error variant, offset, byte and text: 2,676,480 checks with 1,073,574 errors compared on x86_64 (hosted Hand, AVX2) and 10,705,824 with 4,292,932 errors on aarch64 (gak-9, M1 Max), 0 differences. Measured with the same harness (release, STANDARD, median of 11 interleaved rounds, GB/s base64 0.22.1 -> nanocode-sys; the forced-scalar copy in brackets): aarch64 (gak-9, load 11) encode 100 B 1.58 -> 2.29 [1.40], 4 KiB 2.50 -> 7.15 [2.42], 64 KiB 2.35 -> 7.07 [2.35], 1 MiB 2.51 -> 8.42 [2.50], 8 MiB 2.51 -> 8.22 [2.48]; decode 100 B 1.78 -> 2.32 [1.40], 4 KiB 2.65 -> 7.68 [2.30], 64 KiB 2.55 -> 7.85 [2.27], 1 MiB 2.73 -> 8.72 [2.39], 8 MiB 2.78 -> 8.63 [2.37]. x86_64 (hosted Hand, load 11 to 18 on 5 cores, so read ratios) encode 100 B 0.27 -> 0.53 [0.31], 4 KiB 0.54 -> 2.39 [0.66], 64 KiB 0.53 -> 1.41 [0.60], 1 MiB 0.38 -> 1.60 [0.41], 8 MiB 0.40 -> 1.64 [0.52]; decode 100 B 0.30 -> 0.46 [0.27], 4 KiB 0.59 -> 2.17 [0.44], 64 KiB 0.46 -> 2.35 [0.42], 1 MiB 0.39 -> 1.68 [0.36], 8 MiB 0.44 -> 1.73 [0.41]. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on nanocode-sys and the 18 crates above (no warnings), the same for nanocode-sys with `--target aarch64-apple-darwin`, `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on nanocode-sys, nanocode-audio, nanocode-durability-core, nanocode-image, nanocode-mcp, nanocode-schema, nanocode-websocket, nanocode-code-mode-engine, nanocode-backend-claude, -claude-client, -claude-tools, nanocode-backend-codex, -codex-client, nanocode-tool-runtime, nanocode-computer-repl and nanocode-turnlog, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- The native trust-store reader reads each root once (2026-11-13, Georgios: "verify root-certificate loading"). On Debian and Ubuntu `load_native_certificates` read `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt`, then every entry of `/etc/ssl/certs`: the same bundle again, 121 `.pem` links and 121 OpenSSL hash links to the same files, so each root was decoded four times before the sort and dedup that already made the result correct. `load_directory` now resolves each entry with `fs::canonicalize` and skips a target already read (the bundle's own path included), so each root is decoded twice (bundle and its single file). Measured on dev-georgios (Ubuntu 24.04, 243 entries in /etc/ssl/certs) with output/trust-bench calling `nanocode_platform::trust::load_native_certificates`, release build: 121 roots before and after; one load in a fresh process 29.8M to 17.9M user instructions and 11.8M to 15.2M kernel instructions (`perf stat -e instructions:u,instructions:k`, the realpath readlinks); six interleaved runs of 40 loads, median 3.40 to 3.48 ms before against 3.12 to 3.20 ms after. The load runs on the thread that starts the paying proxy, not before the first frame. What remains is rustls-pki-types' constant-time base64 decode (19% of samples) and PEM framing (9%). `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-platform` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-platform --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- nanocode-websocket writes a frame whose payload is at least the 128 KiB write threshold from the payload's own buffer with vectored writes instead of copying it into the write buffer (2026-11-13, Georgios: higher performance). crates/core/websocket/src/protocol.rs: `buffer_frame` hands such a frame, when the stream reports `is_write_vectored`, to `buffer_large`, which appends only the header to the write buffer and keeps the payload (masked in place for a client) in `LargePayload`; `write_out` then sends buffer and payload together with `write_vectored` until the payload is out, and frames queued meanwhile (a pong or close reply from the reader, or a close) go to `LargePayload::behind` and follow it, so the order on the wire is unchanged; both large-path functions are `#[cold]`. frame.rs adds `Frame::format_header_into`; stream.rs's `Io` forwards `write_vectored` and `WebSocketStream` reads `is_write_vectored` once from the stream; connect.rs's `MaybeTlsStream` forwards `poll_write_vectored` and `is_write_vectored` (tokio's TcpStream and tokio-rustls report true; the Codex `InflateStream` already forwarded them). Streams that are not vectored keep the copy. When the writes happen is unchanged: such a frame alone exceeds the threshold, so the old code wrote it out at the same call. The payload no longer passes through the write buffer, which also stops that buffer keeping the capacity of the largest frame ever sent. What differs: the number and split of write calls for large frames (two slices per vectored call); the bytes, their order and the flush points are the same. Equality: output/ws-compare `equal` over seeded sessions of random sends (text, binary and fragmented messages to 300 KB, pings, pongs, feeds and flushes, close) compares the bytes on the wire with masking undone over the in-memory stream (random partial writes, random `Pending`, vectored on and off by seed) and over TCP, and the decoded messages and errors for random frame streams fed in random chunks (interleaved pings and pongs inside fragmented messages, close frames with allowed, reserved and invalid codes and reasons, data after close, and one invalid frame per broken session: reserved opcodes and bits, fragmented and oversized control frames, stray continuations, a data frame inside a fragmented message, invalid and incomplete UTF-8 split across fragments, wrong masking, 1-byte closes, frames over 16 MiB and with 64-bit lengths, non-minimal lengths, truncation), plus the same streams under random small `message_bytes_max`, `frame_bytes_max` and read buffer sizes: on this tree 0 differences in 49,600 checks on the hosted Hand (seeds 41 and 42, 2,000 sessions each, 2.7 GB sent) and 0 differences in 148,800 checks (seeds 51 to 54, 3,000 sessions each, 7.95 GB sent) on an Apple M1 Max, against both tungstenite 0.30 and the crate as on master. Measured on the hosted Hand (fat LTO, one codegen unit, user instructions per run, perf stat): client 1 MiB x 400 138,176,686 against 157,719,092 (-12 %; the copy is a `rep movsb` that counts as few instructions), server 1 MiB x 400 20,171,551 against 39,714,810 (-49 %), and on the Apple M1 Max (instructions retired, /usr/bin/time -l) client 1 MiB 148,179,491 against 226,001,748 (-34 %), server 1 MiB 81,875,213 against 160,211,882 (-49 %), client 200 KiB fed 155,425,965 against 227,231,973 (-32 %); wall time over the in-memory stream (11 interleaved rounds, medians): client 1 MiB 0.0129 against 0.0211 s (0.61), server 1 MiB 0.0085 against 0.0163 s (0.52), client 200 KiB fed 0.0086 against 0.0131 s (0.65), and over loopback TCP client 1 MiB 0.062 against 0.078 s (0.80, tungstenite 0.063). Not equal, on purpose: small frames cost more instructions in this harness, 1 KiB fed 196,375,759 against 188,895,637 (+4 %), flushed each 238,041,747 against 230,206,118 (+3 %), 64 B fed +7 %, 64 B flushed each +5 %, about 35 to 40 instructions a frame; it is not the large-path test (a build with that test constant false costs the same) but the code around it under LTO, and it is about 10 ns against the sendto of every flushed message (wall time over the in-memory stream 1 KiB fed 0.0117 against 0.0117 s). Commands: on an Apple M1 Max `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-websocket` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-websocket` (clean).
- nanocode-websocket draws client masking keys from a 4 KiB pool, one getrandom call per 1,024 frames instead of one per 64 (2026-11-13, Georgios: higher performance). crates/core/websocket/src/frame.rs: `MASK_POOL_BYTES` goes from 64 to 1,024 four-byte keys, and the pool is a `Box<[u8; MASK_POOL_BYTES]>` made on a client's first frame (`Option`, so a server's `Protocol` carries none; it was a 256-byte array inline in every `Protocol`). Why 4 KiB: on the hosted Hand (Linux 6.18, x86_64) getrandom costs about 180 ns per call plus about 3.5 ns per byte (`os.getrandom` timed over 20,000 calls: 256 B 924 ns = 14.4 ns per key, 1 KiB 10.5, 4 KiB 6.9, 16 KiB 7.1 ns per key), so 4 KiB is where the per-call cost stops counting; on macOS getentropy takes at most 256 bytes per call, so the number of calls there is unchanged. Keys are still kernel randomness, one fresh 4-byte key per frame in pool order; what goes on the wire differs only in those random keys. Investigation behind this round: the 22 % gap the 2026-11-12 entry measured for 1 KiB sends end to end does not reproduce on master d4dfa9d67. output/ws-compare (tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite =0.30.0, the crate as on origin/master as a path crate, and this tree; it now also runs over an in-memory stream that counts writes and over TCP to a peer that discards, and builds with fat LTO and one codegen unit like the dist profile so instruction counts are deterministic) gives, in user instructions per run of 200,000 messages (perf stat instructions:u, difference of 1 and 3 runs): 1 KiB text fed 188,656,943 for master against 235,670,131 for tungstenite, flushed each 220,406,302 against 270,925,345, 64 B fed 266,487,538 against 395,288,669; strace -f -c of 200,000 1 KiB sends over loopback shows the same 200,002 sendto calls flushing each and 1,568 against 1,569 feeding, and getrandom 3,128 times against tungstenite's 52 (rand's user-space generator); loopback wall times sit within the Hand's noise on either side (1 KiB flushed each 0.384 against 0.392 s, fed 0.036 against 0.043 s, 9 interleaved rounds, medians). So the one gap on the send path was the key source: after this commit 199 getrandom calls per 200,000 client frames (strace), and user instructions are unchanged (1 KiB fed 188,493,197 against 188,656,943, flushed each 220,242,159 against 220,406,302, 64 B fed 266,077,893 against 266,487,538). Equality: output/ws-compare `equal` at the end of this round's commits (see the next entry) compares the bytes each library writes with masking undone, so only the keys may differ. Commands: on an Apple M1 Max `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-websocket` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-websocket` (clean).
- `nanocode-schema`'s regex classes match through bitmaps and case-insensitive classes build from sorted fold tables (2026-11-13). crates/core/schema/src/regex/set.rs: a bracket compiles to a `Class` holding a 128-bit ASCII bitmap, a 1,920-bit bitmap for U+0080 to U+07FF (Latin supplements and extensions, Greek, Cyrillic, Armenian, Hebrew, Arabic and more, filled a 64-bit word at a time) and the intervals above U+07FF for a binary search, so `\p{L}` and other property classes answer two-byte characters with one load instead of a search over hundreds of intervals; `add_set` merges by index. crates/core/schema/src/regex/unicode.rs: the 1,512 case-fold pairs are decoded once into two `LazyLock` tables sorted by source and by target; `fold` searches the first, `unfold` takes the sources folding into a target from the second, and `add_case_variants` takes the targets and sources of each interval by binary search and adds them as one sorted set, instead of scanning all 1,512 pairs twice per class and inserting code points one by one; the earlier draft's generated unicode-unfolds.bin is not needed. Nothing differs. Equality: output/regex-equal `classes 5 300` anchors 345 classes (45 fixed: property classes, script and script-extension classes, negated and combined brackets, ranges across U+007F/U+0080 and U+07FF/U+0800, `(?i:)` property classes; and 300 random brackets of up to four ranges near U+007F, U+0080, U+07FF, U+0800, U+FFFF, U+10000 and U+10FFFF, 40% negated, some with `\p{L}`, `\p{N}`, `\s`, `\w` or a script, 20% under `(?i:)`) and matches every scalar value U+0000 to U+10FFFF with the old and new engines (regress for every value below U+3000 and every seventh above): 383,662,080 matches, 0 differences; `fold` (every code point as `(?i:\u{X})`, `(?i:[\u{X}])` and `(?i:[^\u{X}])`, and 200,000 random ranges with and without `\p{Lu}k`): 1,837,566 patterns, 12,588,752 matches, 0 differences; the random (240,000 patterns), shape (47,982) and real (1,289 patterns, 33,948,393 matches) runs again show 0 differences. Measurements (ns, median of 3 runs of 21 interleaved rounds; M1 Max gak-9, shared): `^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{N} ]*$` on `Ελληνικά Κείμενο 123` 224 → 126 (origin/master 280, regress 244), on Japanese text 161 → 160 (search above U+07FF unchanged), on ASCII 55 → 57; on the hosted x86_64 Hand against origin/master: Greek 193 → 66 (regress 238), Japanese 143 → 131, ASCII 76 → 45. Compiling `(?i:needle)` 4.6 → 1.6 µs (origin/master 4.4 µs, regress 2.8 µs); a bracket now builds its bitmaps, so `^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{N} ]*$` compiles in 8.2 → 10.3 µs (origin/master 6.8 µs, regress 12.9 µs) and the 1,293 real patterns in 11.9 → 12.6 ms. Commands: in output/regex-equal, `regex-equal classes 5 300`, `fold`, `drive 20 random <seed> 30000`, `drive 20 shape <seed> 12000`, `drive 30 real`, `bench pL`, `compile`.
- `nanocode-schema`'s ECMAScript regex engine finds candidate starts before entering the backtracking machine and skips starts that cannot match (2026-11-13). crates/core/schema/src/regex/program.rs and machine.rs: the start prefilter uses memchr (a literal prefix through `memchr` or a `memmem::Finder`, two or three possible first bytes through `memchr2`/`memchr3`, a larger first-byte set through a 16-byte chunked table scan), and zero-width nodes (`\b`, `\B`, `^` and `$` under `m`, empty groups) no longer hide the prefix behind them; a required literal (the longest run of literal characters every match contains, outside alternations, optional loops, backreferences and lookbehinds, kept only when the prefix does not already contain it) is searched once, searched again only when the start passes it, and ends the search when absent; up to the first fixed characters' ASCII masks (the lead) reject a start without entering the machine; a pattern that begins, after capture groups, with an unbounded one-character loop and has no backreference skips past the whole run after a failed attempt, since every later start inside the run reaches a subset of the same continuation positions (this turns quadratic searches such as `\w+[\\](\w+\.)*\w+\.\w+`, `.+:.+(#.+)?` and `[a-z]+@[a-z]+\.com` linear); `Alt` and `EnterLoop` carry a first-byte guard from the same prefix analysis, applied only when matching forward, so an alternative or greedy iteration that cannot start at the next byte is skipped without a backtrack entry; one-character loops give back (greedy) or take (lazy) characters only at positions where the continuation's single-character instruction matches; runs of two or more literal characters become one `Literal` instruction compared with `starts_with`/`ends_with` (the backward half serves lookbehinds); the machine reads ASCII bytes directly and decodes UTF-8 only for wider characters; lookarounds share the backtrack stack above a base index instead of swapping in a new vector, with their saved groups on one reused stack; loop and group state is allocated when the first attempt starts. memchr (accepted) becomes a dependency of nanocode-schema; Cargo.lock gains that one edge. Nothing differs: `is_match` and compile errors are identical. Equality: output/regex-equal links origin/master's regex module copied as a path module (before), the new one (after) and regress 0.12.0 with the unicode flag (the engine before both), and compares compile error texts and `is_match`: grammar-random patterns (seeds 1 to 4, 30,000 patterns each plus their `^(?:…)$` forms, 12 short texts each and three 500 to 6,500-byte texts for every fourth: 240,000 patterns, 1,456,419 matches, 0 differences), prefilter-shaped patterns (literal words and escapes with `\b`, `(?m:^)`, lookaheads, lookbehinds, alternations, quantified groups, `\p` classes and backreferences, with long texts carrying the pattern's words and near-misses; seeds 1 to 3, 12,000 each: 47,982 patterns, 419,104 matches, 0 differences, 12 patterns stopped by the 20 s watchdog because they backtrack exponentially), real inputs (1,289 patterns from JSON schemas against 26,297 real strings and 40 3,000-byte concatenations of them: 33,948,393 matches, 0 differences; 4 exponential patterns such as `^((?:.?[0-9]+){3,}(?:[-a-z]+)?)$` stopped by the 30 s watchdog) and every case fold (each code point as `(?i:\u{X})` and bracketed, plus 200,000 random ranges: 1,837,566 patterns, 12,588,752 matches, 0 differences). Measurements (ns per `is_match`, median of 3 runs of 21 interleaved rounds; Linux x86_64 hosted Hand / M1 Max gak-9, both shared; before → after, regress for reference): `needle` over 10.8 KB without it 1,934 → 193 (regress 209) / 3,125 → 357 (375); `(?:foo|bar|baz)\d+` miss 4,252 → 583 (981) / 6,627 → 1,061 (1,579); `\bneedle\b` miss 111,285 → 186 (62,802) / 137,992 → 350 (75,695); `.*needle` miss 6,240,873 → 174 (2,270,597) / 8,051,708 → 354 (2,930,229); `[a-z]+@[a-z]+\.com` miss 337,836 → 197 (187,598) / 571,990 → 346 (213,672); `(?=needle)\w+` miss 206,676 → 190 / 351,607 → 347; `\d+px` miss 2,983 → 139 (4,390) / 3,615 → 346 (3,244); `(?i:needle)` miss 7,839 → 2,233 (3,093) / 15,120 → 4,369 (5,299); `ναι` over Greek-tinged text 3,018 → 189 (210) / 5,889 → 382 (401); anchored `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$` 98 → 43 (87) / 143 → 61 (94); semver 323 → 272 (280) / 586 → 457 (473); uuid 129 → 65 (57) / 186 → 76 (86). All 1,289 real patterns over the 26,297 real strings: 8.54 s → 1.11 s (regress 4.89 s) / 16.54 s → 1.78 s (8.54 s); over the 40 long texts: 2.13 s → 31 ms (regress 762 ms) / 4.08 s → 41 ms (1.42 s). Compiling costs more: the 1,293 real patterns compile in 10.6 → 11.9 ms on the M1 (regress 16.7 ms), about 0.9 µs more per pattern for the finders, guards and lead. Commands: in output/regex-equal, `regex-equal drive 20 random <seed> 30000`, `drive 20 shape <seed> 12000`, `drive 30 real`, `fold`, `bench`, `realbench 7`, `compile`.
- rg and grep check a candidate line with psh-pattern's `is_match`, which stops at the first match state, instead of `shortest_match`, which psh-pattern's grep matcher answers with the leftmost-first match end (the value grep-regex gives) and so keeps scanning greedy repetitions to their end (2026-11-13). crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/search/matcher.rs: the psh-pattern adapter implements `Matcher::is_match` with `RegexMatcher::is_match` (`Engine::search_half` with `earliest`); searcher/core.rs: the slow line loop asks `matches_within_limit` (match limit, then `is_match`) where it asked `shortest_match(..).is_some()`, and `Matcher::shortest_match`, now unused, leaves the crate's trait. Every caller only tested whether a match exists, so outputs do not change, and psh-pattern's `shortest_match` keeps grep-regex's value (output/rx `equal`: psh-pattern's matcher `shortest_match` equals grep-regex 0.1.14's in all cases of seeds 1-8, while an earliest answer differed in about 400 per seed, which is why the matcher's API stays). Equality: output/pdiff (seeded random patterns of Rust keywords, word alternations, classes, anchors and case-insensitive groups, each run through rg -c, rg -c -i, rg -n -w, rg -c -v, grep -c -E, rg -o, rg -c --crlf and rg -l over a 4 MB slice of the corpus, psh of origin/master against this tree) seeds 1-9, 28,000 commands (half with matches): 0 differences in stdout, stderr or status; output/bench.py's 56 commands byte-identical. Measurements (gak-9, psh -c, CPU ms, medians of 7, regex-crate psh / before / after): rg -c '\w+_\w+' big.rs 189 / 171 / 138, rg -c '[a-z]+_[a-z]+' 150 / 161 / 144, rg -o '\bpub fn \w+' 46 / 43 / 39, grep -c -E 'fn|let|impl' 58 / 65 / 59, grep -c -i error 38 / 41 / 38; the others within noise. Not measured on x86: the change is not architecture-specific. Commands: in crates/patches/psh cargo clippy --locked -p psh-utils (only the three existing chunks_exact warnings in codec.rs and dump.rs) and -p psh-pattern, cargo check --locked -p psh-utils (native and wasm32), cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, output/pdiff, output/bench.py.
- psh-pattern searches a regex whose every match starts at a line start ((?m)^, `Look::StartLf` in `look_set_prefix`) with a line-start prefilter when it has no literal one, so the lazy DFA jumps to the next line terminator whenever it falls back to its start state (2026-11-13). crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-pattern/src/literal.rs: `Prefilter::LineStart(terminator)` answers `at` when `at` is 0 or follows the terminator and otherwise one past the next terminator (memchr), `line_start_prefilter` builds it; engine.rs tries it after the prefix literals and the non-ASCII prefilter. Because a prefilter exists, the DFA tags its unanchored start states (a3eb6c746), so in `^\s*fn `, `^\s*$` or `^[a-z]+` the first byte that ends the anchored part sends the search to the next line instead of through the rest of the line; rg's candidate-line checks of `^\s*fn ` stop at the line's first non-blank byte. The matcher's strategy choice (`accelerated`) does not look at this prefilter, and results do not change: a match must start where StartLf holds, which is exactly where the prefilter stops. Equality: output/rx `equal` (whose patterns include ^, $, (?m:^), \A and the multi-line flag) seeds 1-8 x 3,000 on gak-9 and 1-4 on the Hand against origin/master's psh-pattern: 0 differences in results; only the previous commit's `m candidate` choices. Measurements (psh -c, CPU ms, medians of 5 to 7, regex-crate psh / before / after, byte-identical outputs): gak-9 rg -c '^\s*$' big.rs 133 / 222 / 108, rg -c -v '^\s*$' 175 / 266 / 152, rg -c '^[a-z]+' 87 / 212 / 74, rg -c '^\s*\}' 57 / 64 / 51, rg -c '^\s*fn ' 27 / 33 / 28; Hand x86 library level (output/rx bench grep with multi_line as rg builds it, thread CPU ms, medians of 7, origin/master / this tree / grep-regex) '^\s*$' 175.9 / 74.7 / 87.8, '^[a-z]+' 161.0 / 47.7 / 49.8, '^\s*\}' 37.5 / 28.4 / 31.6, '^\s*fn ' 17.0 / 10.6 / 9.2, '^\s*//' (which has a prefix literal) 15.2 / 15.6 / 31.5. Commands: in crates/patches/psh cargo clippy --locked -p psh-pattern, cargo check --locked --lib -p psh-pattern (native and wasm32), cargo check --locked -p psh-utils --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, output/rx equal and bench, output/bench.py.
- psh-pattern's prefix literal extraction shortens literal sets that pass its 64-literal limit instead of giving them up, as regex-syntax's extractor does (2026-11-13). crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-pattern/src/literal.rs: `union` cuts the literals of an alternation that grows past 64 to their first four bytes (`TRIMMED_PREFIX_BYTES`, marked inexact) and gives up only if that is still too many; `cross` cuts the right-hand side to 4, 3, 2 and then 1 byte (`TRIMMED_SUFFIX_BYTES`) before it gives up extending the left side. Case-insensitive words expand to one literal per case variant (`error` is 32, `async` 48 with U+017F for s), so `rg -i 'error|warning|panic'` and `rg -i 'async fn|await'` (whose shared `a` the parser factors out, leaving [aA] times 40 suffixes) had no prefix literals and ran the DFA over every byte; now they get 4-byte case groups that Teddy or the packed tests find. Results do not change: the literals only choose where the DFA starts and which lines are candidates. What differs on purpose: for some patterns the grep matcher's `find_candidate_line` now answers Candidate where it answered Confirmed (or the reverse), because a finite literal set changes `accelerated` and `required_literals`; the lines found are the same. Equality: output/rx `equal` seeds 1-8 x 3,000 cases on gak-9 and 1-4 on the Hand against origin/master's psh-pattern: 0 differences in every result (is_match, find_iter, captures, find_at, shortest, str APIs, the matcher's line loop, find_iter, shortest and captures) and 46 to 64 `m candidate` differences per seed, all Candidate/Confirmed choices with identical lines. Measurements (psh -c, CPU ms, medians, regex-crate psh / before / after, byte-identical outputs): gak-9 (5 runs) rg -c -i 'error|warning|panic' big.rs 35 / 215 / 37, rg -c -i 'async fn|await' 31 / 168 / 30, other commands within noise; Hand x86 library level (output/rx bench grep, the searcher's line loop over big.rs, thread CPU ms, medians of 7, origin/master / this tree with the commit before and after / grep-regex) -i 'error|warning|panic' 168.4 / 12.1 / 17.5, -i 'async fn|await' 99.2 / 6.4 / 12.8. Commands: in crates/patches/psh cargo clippy --locked -p psh-pattern, cargo check --locked --lib -p psh-pattern (native and wasm32), cargo check --locked -p psh-utils --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, output/rx equal and bench, output/bench.py.
- psh-pattern searches for alternations of literals that have no rare byte with Teddy, a SIMD multi-literal kernel in nanocode-sys (`nanocode_sys::teddy`), instead of its portable packed byte tests (2026-11-13, Georgios: psh's regexes ran 20-35% slower than the regex crate they replaced). crates/core/sys/src/teddy.rs: `Teddy::new(prefixes, prefix_len)` builds per-offset low and high nibble masks for up to eight buckets of one- to three-byte prefixes and returns None when neither `is_x86_feature_detected!` (AVX2, else SSSE3) nor `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("neon")` finds a kernel, always on wasm32; `find` looks up 32 (AVX2) or 16 (SSSE3, NEON) haystack bytes per step with `pshufb`/`tbl`, ANDs the bucket bits of each prefix offset and finishes the last bytes with the scalar mask walk. crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-pattern/src/literal.rs: `TeddySet` groups the literals by their ASCII-lowercased form (a group that holds every case variant verifies with `eq_ignore_ascii_case`, others by member), spreads the groups over the buckets in prefix order and verifies each candidate; `Prefilter::from_literals` takes Teddy when the best rare-byte memchr candidate's worst byte ranks above 210 of 255, before the packed tests; `LiteralSet::find` (alternations the engine runs without an automaton) returns a Teddy match directly when exactly one group verified and asks `matches_at` for the preferred literal otherwise. The matcher's choice between the DFA and candidate lines (`accelerates`) and `required_literals` decide as before (`from_literals_with(.., false)`), so only the search itself changes. Without SIMD (wasm32 and other CPUs) the packed tests run as before and stay the reference path; psh-pattern depends on nanocode-sys, already in psh's workspace through psh-utils. Results do not change. - The ruff parser parses on the calling thread when that thread's remaining stack covers the nesting bound it can afford, and goes to the parser thread only when it cannot, so compile(), exec() and eval() no longer pay a thread handoff per call (2026-11-13). crates/core/sys/src/stack.rs adds `current_thread_stack_remaining_bytes`: the thread's stack bounds, read once per thread and cached in a thread local (`pthread_getattr_np` and `pthread_attr_getstack` on Linux and Android, `pthread_get_stackaddr_np` and `pthread_get_stacksize_np` on Apple targets, none elsewhere), and the distance from the address of a local to the low end, or none when the local lies outside them. Unsafe blocks added: those four pthread calls on the calling thread's own handle, the attributes destroyed after `pthread_getattr_np` filled them. crates/patches/rustpython-ruff_python_parser/src/parser/mod.rs: `parse` computes `caller_recursion_depth_max` = (remaining bytes - `PARSE_STACK_BYTES_OUTSIDE_RECURSION_MAX` 64 KiB) / `STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX` 12 KiB - `RECURSION_LEVELS_AFTER_NESTING_STOP_MAX` 4, at most `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` 20,000; with a positive bound it parses in place with `with_recursion` stopping at that depth, and when the nesting stop fired below 20,000 it drops that result and parses the source again on the parser thread with the full bound, as before; without stack bounds (other targets) or room for one level it goes to the parser thread directly. wasm32 parses in place as before. Results do not change: a parse that stays under the lowered bound is the same parse, and every parse that reaches it is redone exactly as the old code did it, so the RecursionError bound stays at depth 20,000 on every thread. Stack bound, output/parsereq `stack` (each construct and the real corpus parsed under forced bounds D of 1 to 8, 10, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 48, 64, 100 and 20,000 on a thread whose stack is painted with a pattern, release): x86_64 on this Hand 124,614 runs, ARM on gak-9 129,582 runs; the most stack used outside recursion 5,027 / 5,263 bytes (budget 64 KiB), the most per level at depth 200 and over 2,802 bytes (generator expressions) / 4,074 bytes (f-strings) (budget 12 KiB), and the high-water mark stayed under D x 12 KiB for every forced D (closest 2,445 / 1,161 bytes under), so the 64 KiB and the four levels after the stop are pure margin. Equality: output/parsereq `digest` links the parser at the previous commit as a path crate and compares the debug-printed AST and every error of 22 generated expression kinds, 9 statement kinds, random and broken nestings at depths up to 50,000 and the real corpus (2,004 files under /usr/lib/python3 on x86, 2,145 files of Homebrew's Python 3.14 on gak-9), each parsed on threads with 8 MiB, 2 MiB, 256 KiB and 64 KiB stacks and with the in-place bound forced low (3,639 / 3,653 parses retried on the parser thread): 48,660 checks on x86 and 50,040 on ARM, 0 differences. output/vmbench `codes` (rustpython-vm at origin/master and with this change) compiles each corpus file and 100 nestings (10 constructs at depths 10 to 50,000) in exec and eval mode at Python call depths 0, 300 and 900 on an 8 MiB VM thread and 0 and 100 on 2 MiB and 4 MiB threads, recording the SHA-256 of the marshalled code object or the exception text with its position: 13,452 + 8,968 + 8,968 results byte-identical on gak-9, 180 and 120 of them RecursionErrors. Measured with output/vmbench `bench` on gak-9 (old and new binaries alternating, 11 rounds, medians, under the machine's load of about 30): compile() of a three-line module 84.15 to 11.45 us, exec() of it 77.41 to 16.00 us, eval() of `a + b * 2` 73.04 to 9.02 us, compile() at Python call depth 600 66.35 to 23.36 us, compile() of rustpython-pylib's inspect.py (127 KB) 37.94 to 35.82 ms. - The subagent runtime ends a parent's watched steers, unparks completions and releases scopes in a fixed order, and cfo.sh no longer labels `runtime_kv_twice` nondeterminism as known (2026-11-13, from the runtime scenario's `--twice` failures on dev-georgios, Georgios: fix the remaining nondeterminism in the whole-runtime simulation). `NoticeOutcome::of_steers` (crates/runtime/subagents/src/runtime.rs) kept the steers it watches in a `HashMap` by request id and, when the parent's run ended, walked it to send each outcome and to spawn the receipt read of each completed one, so with two watched steers the two tasks were spawned in hash order: under bin/nanocode-sim a spawn's order is the task's place in the executor's ready list, so the schedule, and in production the order of the outcomes, followed std's per-process `RandomState` keys. It is a `BTreeMap` now. Found on `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 1794551659224538400`, the one failure in 6,000 fresh seeds after the two entries above: under an LD_PRELOAD that answers getrandom from a counter, starts 1 to 10 gave two digests, and the poll logs agree until a task spawns two tasks at runtime.rs:836 whose first polls wake different tasks; with the map ordered, starts 1 to 10 all pass `--twice`. The same audit of hash-map walks in the crates the scenario runs found two more that act in walk order: `ChildSessions::parked_ids`, whose order `unpark_completions` uses to schedule each parent continuation (each a spawned task), and `release_all`, which releases every root scope through one `join_all` (polled in order); both sort now (`AgentId` and the root session id), as the other walks of `sessions` already did. Walks that collect into a sorted list, a set or a count were left alone. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): the 108 seeds cfo.sh logged pass `--twice`; seeds 1794551987480374721..+24,000 of `--scenario runtime --store kv --twice` with the steer map alone: 23,999 passed, no two digests, and one failed to settle (seed 1794551987480396597: `subagent-completion:...:1` stays Pending; it fails the same way on master and in every run, so it is a liveness bug, not nondeterminism, and is left open). With all three entries, from 1794552503627171137: 12,000 seeds `--store kv --twice`, then 3,000 `--store memory --twice`, 3,000 `--store kv`, and 2,000 each of `--scenario agents --twice` and `--scenario turns --twice`: all passed. Master passes those 3,000 `--store memory --twice` seeds too: without crashes nothing is restored, so no two calls wake together. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-subagents`: no warnings; `nanocode-sim --tidy` clean.
- Code Mode cells and the Claude backend's tool batches take finished calls in the order the calls started when several are ready, through nanocode-sync's new `InOrder`, so the same wake-ups finish the same calls on every run (2026-11-13, from the runtime scenario's `--twice` failures that cfo.sh labelled known on dev-georgios, Georgios: fix the remaining nondeterminism in the whole-runtime simulation). Root cause: tokio's watch channel (1.52.3, sync/watch.rs `BigNotify`) parks each waiting receiver on one of eight `Notify`s picked by `thread_rng_n(8)`, a thread-local generator seeded from std's `RandomState` (that is, from the OS), and `send` wakes the eight in turn, so two receivers polled by one task wake in a random order; `FuturesUnordered` polls its futures in the order their wakers ran. In a Code Mode cell restored after a crash with two `wait_agent` calls pending, the subagent runtime's restoration task (`adopt_journal`) sends `RestorationState::Ready` and both calls wake; whichever was polled first took the subagent's completion, so which call finished, the cell's journal and the next model request changed from process to process. Found on `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 95431492894293191`: under an LD_PRELOAD that answers getrandom from a counter, each counter start gave one digest and starts 1 to 30 gave two (`073b2109e3eb09be` 19 times, `247b830acdbdb043` 11 times), so the source was the OS's randomness and not timing; `NANOCODE_SIM_POLLS` logs, with each wake's task and waker added on a scratch build, then agree until the poll of the restored cell's actor, where one run completed call 4 and the other polled call 3 first and yielded. `InOrder<F>` (crates/core/sync/src/in_order.rs) keeps its futures in a Vec in push order, each behind its own waker that sets a flag and wakes the set's `AtomicWaker`; `poll_ready` (and `Stream::poll_next`) polls the flagged futures front to back, each at most once, and returns the first that finishes, so what it yields depends on which futures were woken and never on the order of the wakes. It replaces `FuturesUnordered` for `drive_cell`'s pending nested calls (crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs) and in both tool-batch loops of crates/backends/claude/src/agent.rs, where it also fixes the order of `journal.complete`; no seed went through the Claude batches, since the scripted model sends one tool call per step. Cost (output/det-bench on dev-georgios, release, n futures on oneshot receivers completed one at a time in a shuffled order, medians of 7 interleaved rounds), per completion, FuturesUnordered against InOrder: 0.178 against 0.140 us at 4, 0.159 against 0.134 at 16, 0.158 against 0.147 at 64, 0.158 against 0.186 at 256, 0.163 against 0.357 at 1,024 and 0.168 against 1.057 at 4,096. It is the same up to a few hundred calls and linear in the pending calls beyond that (`Limits::nested` is `usize::MAX` by default, and each nested call is a tool run that costs far more than a microsecond). The lint: `nanocode-sim --tidy` also scans crates/backends/claude/src, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode, crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src and crates/runtime/tool-host/src, which the runtime scenario runs; it refuses `FuturesUnordered` there, and a `select!` whose next line is not `biased;`, whose first branch comes from the same thread RNG (the class an earlier entry fixed by hand in the Claude backend). claude_bash.rs and host_tools.rs (real processes the simulator never registers) and claude_tools.rs's tool runtime guard keep counted allowances. Putting `FuturesUnordered` back in agent.rs, or deleting `biased;` from `run_cell_actor`'s select, makes it print that line. Checks (release, CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): the 108 seeds cfo.sh logged as `runtime_kv_twice` nondeterminism, replayed with `--twice`, failed 68, 70 and 72 times on master and 47 every time with this change alone; with the entry below too, 0 in 5 rounds. Seeds 1794550701654872419..+6000 of `--scenario runtime --store kv --twice`: master 5,970 passed and 30 failed with two digests, this change and the entry below 6,000 passed; from the same start, 3,000 seeds each of `--store memory --twice` and `--store kv`, and 2,000 each of `--scenario agents --twice` and `--scenario turns --twice` passed. A second range, 1794551659224535314..+6000 `--store kv --twice`, failed once (seed 1794551659224538400), fixed by the next entry. `cargo check --locked --lib` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-sync, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-code-mode-engine and nanocode-backend-claude, and `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sim`: no warnings; `nanocode-sim --tidy` clean. Open: `join_all` and `try_join_all` over more than 30 futures (futures-util switches to `FuturesOrdered`) still poll in wake order; durability's kv.rs and sql.rs commits call `try_join_all` over a state's records, and no seed has shown a divergence through them.
- A Code Mode cell's Math.random seed is eight bytes that `nanocode_platform::fill_random` gives when the cell starts, so a seed of bin/nanocode-sim draws the same host randomness every time it runs in one process (2026-11-13, from the runtime scenario's `--twice` failures that cfo.sh labelled known on dev-georgios, Georgios: fix the remaining nondeterminism in the whole-runtime simulation). fe8966681 read the system once per process into a `static ENTROPY: OnceLock<u64>` and gave each cell the next SplitMix64 output over it, numbered by a process-wide `CELLS` counter. Under a platform host that one read is the host's: the first cell of a process drew one value from the simulator's seeded stream and every later cell drew none, so the second run of a seed in the same process (`--twice`) read the host's stream one value behind the first. Every UUIDv7 after its first cell then differed (their random bits come from the same stream), state ids `state/<uuid v7>` listed in another order in the simulated store, and the digests parted: for `--scenario runtime --store kv --seed 2756763035351909241` the two runs' poll logs agree until the first `kv get state/01a1cd0d-f8a4-7000-...`, `a156-9867f7f29a57` in the first run and `8131-0f159e5162f6` in the second. The seed also carried from one seed to the next through `CELLS`. `random_seed` (crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/host.rs) now draws `size_of::<u64>()` bytes per cell. Without a host that is the per-thread 256-byte kernel buffer of the ids entry (one system call per 32 cells), so the per-cell system call fe8966681 removed stays removed; a WebAssembly host is asked once per cell. Cost (output/det-bench on dev-georgios, release, medians of 7 interleaved rounds of 1,000,000 seeds on CPUs 0-7 beside the fuzz loop): 28.9 ns per seed against 5.7 ns for the process SplitMix. Checks: the 108 seeds cfo.sh logged as `runtime_kv_twice` nondeterminism, replayed with `--twice`, failed 68, 70 and 72 times on master in three rounds and 33, 35 and 36 times with this change alone (47, 47 and 47 with only the entry above, 0 with both). With the entry above and an LD_PRELOAD that answers getrandom from a counter (so std's `RandomState` keys and tokio's thread RNG are fixed), seeds 2756763035351909241, 3997882149476984548 and 1243065452199219612 gave one digest in 12 of 12 single runs and two digests in each `--twice`: state that outlived a run, which this was. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode-engine` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode-engine`: no warnings.
- nanocode-http speaks HTTP/1.1 itself, client and server, over tokio and rustls, and every HTTP call in the workspace goes through it: reqwest, hyper, hyper-util, hyper-rustls, tower, tower-http, tokio-util and 23 more packages leave (2026-11-13, Georgios: replace reqwest and hyper with our own client, toward ~0 dependencies outside the async baseline). `nanocode_http::Client` (crates/core/http/src/client) keeps the reqwest surface the workspace called, so callers changed imports and types only: `ClientBuilder` (`timeout`, `connect_timeout`, `read_timeout`, `redirect`, `default_headers`, `user_agent`, `no_proxy`, `https_only`, `resolve`, the pool settings), `RequestBuilder` (`header`, `headers`, `bearer_auth`, `json`, `body`, `timeout`, `send`), `Response` (`status`, `headers`, `bytes`, `text`, `json`, `chunk`, `bytes_stream`, `error_for_status`), `redirect::Policy` and `blocking::Client`, which runs requests on one owning thread with a current-thread runtime, as reqwest's blocking client does. wire.rs frames both directions (content-length, chunked with trailers, close-delimited, keep-alive) within hyper's bounds, 100 headers and a head of 8,192 + 4,096 × 100 bytes. pool.rs keeps idle connections in an `Atom<BTreeMap<Key, Vec<Idle>>>` keyed by scheme, host, port and proxy, for 90 s as hyper-util does. redirect.rs follows reqwest's rules: 10 hops; 301, 302 and 303 turn a POST into a GET without its body headers; 307 and 308 resend a replayable body; Authorization, Cookie and Proxy-Authorization are dropped across hosts; Referer is set. connect.rs reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY as reqwest and the codex WebSocket connector did, tunnels with HTTP CONNECT (basic credentials from the proxy URL) or SOCKS5/5h, and starts each next address 250 ms after the last (happy eyeballs, as hyper-util). A request on a pooled connection that the peer closed before answering is sent once more (`ATTEMPTS_MAX`), as hyper-util retries a connection closed while idle. server.rs serves HTTP/1.1 with upgrades and replaces hyper's server in nanocode-sandbox's egress proxy and nanocode-cli's Tempo payment proxy; a request body streams to the handler while it runs and ends with its last byte, and an answer that arrives before a request body is fully written (such as a 413 for an upload too large) is relayed rather than turned into a write error, as hyper does, by the server's `send` and by the client alike. The codex WebSocket connector drops its own proxy parsing, CONNECT, SOCKS5 and happy eyeballs (470 lines) for connect.rs. `Client::execute` and `RequestBuilder::send` return `Pending`, one boxed future made inside nanocode-http, as reqwest's `Pending` boxes its request: written as an `async fn`, its state machine was compiled again in every crate that awaited it (38 copies of `Client::send`'s, 14.9 KB each, and 28 of the connect future's), and nanocode-http took 1.35 MB of the release binary's text where reqwest, hyper and hyper-util took 385 KB; boxed, it takes 298 KB (`nm -S` of `cargo rustc --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode -- -C strip=none`). Equal: HTTP/1.1 only, as reqwest was built here (default features off, so no http2); gzip and deflate decoding stays in nanocode-http's content-coding layer; TLS is rustls through nanocode-tls with the same platform verifier. Different on purpose: public signatures that named reqwest now name nanocode-http (`nanocode_backend_claude_client::HttpClient`, `ClaudeClient::messages_api`'s error, nanocode-tool-host's `ToolsBuilder::remote_http_client` and `Tools::remote_http_client`), so tempoxyz/pyramid-core's `ClaudeClient::new(self.connection(..))` swaps its `reqwest_nanocode` client for `nanocode_http::Client`, with the same builder calls, when it next bumps nanocode. nanocode-agent builds `OneLogJournals`, `OneLog::journals` and their cell reads natively only, like the tool-host cell journals they use, so nanocode-agent builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown again (at 999400a81 it fails to resolve `nanocode_tool_host::code_mode::CellJournal` there). The blocking client's job queue is unbounded, as reqwest's is: each caller waits for its own answer, so it holds at most one job per calling thread. Checked: output/http-wire, one local server that captures the bytes of reqwest 0.13.4 and nanocode-http for 28 cases (GET with a query, POST JSON with repeated headers, header replacement, empty bodies on POST, DELETE and HEAD, a chunked request body, the user agent, the 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 rules with and without bodies and across hosts, `Policy::none`, too many redirects, three requests on one pooled connection, chunked and close-delimited responses, `error_for_status`, JSON, gzip, an HTTP proxy with credentials, HTTPS through CONNECT, `no_proxy`, a read timeout, an IPv6 literal with a port): byte-identical requests and the same outcomes, 0 differences. Live on the hosted Hand, whose only way out is its HTTPS_PROXY (a CONNECT proxy; without it the same run cannot connect): output/claude-smoke on claude-haiku-4-5 with an API key streamed an answer (12 SSE events, 7 text deltas, the first at 1.2 s), streamed a forced tool call (`{"city": "Athens"}`) and answered its tool result (`end_turn`); output/ws-smoke through the codex `connect_async` got 101 and its echo from wss://echo.websocket.org, and a 401 handshake refusal from wss://api.openai.com/v1/responses. No live OpenAI turn ran: OpenAI rejects the environment's OPENAI_API_KEY (curl gets the same 401), and `nanocode exec` with NANOCODE_OPENAI_BASE_URL reached /v1/models through the proxy and reported that 401. The egress proxy on dev-georgios (direct internet), with output/egress-check (an allowlist with interception and an injected `x-nanocode-probe` secret) built at 999400a81 and with this change, interleaved twice, through curl: an intercepted GET (200, the secret injected and redacted in the echo), streamed lines (200, 3), a redirect (302), a form POST (200), a 533 KB POST with content-length and chunked (200), 1.4 MB ones that httpbin refuses early (413), a plain-HTTP POST (200), a passthrough CONNECT tunnel (200), a refused host (refused at CONNECT), a gzip answer to a request carrying a secret (502, refused by design) and a WebSocket upgrade (200, as at 999400a81): every result the same for both. Packages: `cargo metadata` resolves 247 to 217 (at 999400a81); built alone on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (`cargo tree --locked -p <crate> -e normal,build`, all packages) nanocode-cli 195 to 175 (aarch64-apple-darwin 196 to 177), nanocode-backend-claude-client 105 to 86, nanocode-backend-codex-client 112 to 92, nanocode-mcp-http 100 to 80, nanocode-observability 100 to 81, nanocode-http 89 to 78; nanocode-sandbox alone 62 to 84, since it now takes nanocode-http with url, its IDNA tables and rustls, which nanocode-cli builds anyway. The release nanocode (`strip`ped) is 97.19 to 96.16 MB, `.text` 93.35 to 92.35 MB; one cold `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli` each on the 5-core Hand, not interleaved and before the `Pending` change, took 308 s and 253 s. `cargo check --locked --workspace --all-targets`, `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps --all-targets` on the 13 changed crates (no warnings), `cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` for nanocode-http, nanocode-platform, nanocode-backend-claude-client, nanocode-backend-codex-client, nanocode-backend-codex, nanocode-mcp-http, nanocode-mcp-tools, nanocode-observability, nanocode-tool-runtime, nanocode-tool-host, nanocode-agent and nanocode-sandbox, and `cargo build --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- `nanocode-turnlog` retires finished turns past a caller retention window (2026-11-13). `TurnLog::retain_finished(Some(n))` and `Policy.retain_finished` keep the n finished turns with the newest final event, and every unfinished turn. Retirement runs after a commit appends its row, so each `Finished` status reaches disk once before its turn can leave the fold and later snapshots. Loading stays a superset of the live fold: rows written before a snapshot still carry retired turns, and an `Admitted` record for a finished turn of the same id replaces it, because only a retired id can be admitted again. A retired request ID is unknown to `turn`, `submit` admits it as a new turn, and its events stay in history. `None` keeps every finished turn. The window is caller policy because it trades request-ID dedupe and status reads against cold reads. bin/nanocode-sim takes `--retain N`, asserts after each commit that the fold holds at most N finished turns, and catches the `retire_skipped` mutation (252 of 300 seeds with `--retain 1`). Calm `--long` runs over seeds 0..20, ratio 2, largest cold read of a scope without retention and with `--retain 8`: 10 turns 2,639 and 2,616 B, 30 turns 6,800 and 3,076 B, 100 turns 19,364 and 5,494 B, 300 turns 59,742 and 12,916 B; total final bytes at 300 turns 3.54 and 2.80 MB; rows per turn 3.15 and 3.22. Retiring before the commit failed `--retain 0` on 919 of 1,000 seeds: a finishing commit that became a snapshot never wrote its `Finished` status. Checks: turnlog sweeps of seeds 0..2000 pass with `--twice`, `--retain 0` and `--retain 2` (both `--twice`), calm `--retain 0`, `--retain 1 --row-limit 1024`, `--retain 0 --snapshot-ratio 1`, and seeds 5000..6000 with `--retain 0`. Every turn mutation is caught in its established configuration with `--retain 1`. `cargo check` passes native and wasm, and `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes for nanocode-turnlog, nanocode-agent and nanocode-sim.
- cfo.sh fuzzes the `seal_skipped` mutation again, as a canary with 4,000 seeds a job over `--live-seqs floor`, and no longer labels "runtime did not settle" and "runtime missing payload record" as known (2026-11-13). The reference policy (`OneLog`) now honours the mutation: with `seal_skipped` it never writes a seal, so the mutation reaches the policy it names; seeds 100..4100 catch it 46 times. A runtime stall is a failure again, since the entry above fixes its causes; the KV twice-mode nondeterminism stays labelled until it is fixed.
- A finished subagent's completion reaches its root parent's turn after crashes and restarts, so a durable task tree settles (2026-11-13, from the runtime scenario of nanocode-sim that cfo.sh fuzzes on dev-georgios, Georgios: "Fix the stuck subagent result"). Before, `runtime_kv` failed 236 of 263 jobs and `runtime_memory` 24 of 265 with "did not settle": the completion was saved as Completed but stayed in `pending_completions`. Four paths left it there. A completion routed as a steer waited for the parent turn's steer event, which never came when the parent had no running turn left to read it; `NoticeOutcome::of_route` now takes the steer receipt itself when the parent has no turn controls. After a restart, a completion whose request ID names an interrupted turn being resumed was routed and could steer into another turn; `Agent::admit` reports that the request resumes an interrupted turn and the prompt is submitted as its own turn. A root session settled again at the revision whose completion was already delivered armed a second completion, whose request ID the parent refused as `InvalidRequest` on every retry; `Registry` no longer arms it, and an `InvalidRequest` moves the completion to its next attempt (`next_completion_attempt`) before it retries. In nanocode-durability's session driver, writes applied within the current revision (deferred) were persisted only by a later write, so an operation that ended on one was lost by a crash after its receipt; the driver now commits deferred writes when the operation finishes (`persist_deferred`, asserting none remain). Checked on dev-georgios with nanocode-sim built from this tree: 120 distinct failing seeds from cfo's failure log (KV, memory, calm and twice) fail 89 times on master's binary (ccf5a4802) and 0 times on this one; fresh seeds, 3,000 each of `--store kv`, `--store memory` and `--store kv --calm`, pass 9,000 of 9,000, and `--store kv --twice` passes 2,995 of 3,000, the 5 failures being the known trace nondeterminism, not a stall. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability -p nanocode-subagents -p nanocode-agent-core` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo clippy --locked` on those and nanocode-sim (no warnings), `nanocode-sim --tidy` (determinism clean).
- `nanocode-sandbox` compiles its seccomp filter itself and installs it through nanocode-sys, and seccompiler 0.5.0 leaves the workspace (2026-11-13). crates/integrations/sandbox/src/seccomp.rs is seccompiler's backend reproduced for what the sandbox uses (32-bit `Ne` and `MaskedEq` conditions, `Allow` and `Errno` actions, x86_64, aarch64 and riscv64): the architecture check (`ld [4]`, `jeq AUDIT_ARCH, 1, 0`, `ret KILL_PROCESS`), `ld [0]`, one block per system call in ascending number (`jeq nr, 0, 1`, then each rule's conditions in reverse order behind its two jumps and a `ret` of the match action, or the three-instruction block of a call without rules, then `ret` of the mismatch action), the helper jumps when a rule's offset would pass 255, the 4,096-instruction limit, and seccompiler's error texts (`Invalid target arch: arm.`, empty rule, identical actions, argument index above 5, too many instructions). `tool_filter(arch, syscalls)` builds the same rules `confine` built (socket only for AF_INET and AF_INET6 with protocol 0 or TCP and a stream type, no `MSG_FASTOPEN` on sendto, sendmsg and sendmmsg, no io_uring, listen, accept, accept4, setsid or setpgid) and adds the same x32 prefix on x86_64; its system call numbers are a parameter (`NATIVE` from libc) so the harness can build the aarch64 program on this Hand. crates/core/sys/src/unix/confine.rs gains `SocketFilter` (`#[repr(C)]` `sock_filter`) and `install_seccomp_filter`, which does what `seccompiler::apply_filter` did (an empty program refused, `prctl(PR_SET_NO_NEW_PRIVS, 1, 0, 0, 0)`, `seccomp(SECCOMP_SET_MODE_FILTER, 0, &sock_fprog)`, a positive answer reported as a thread that failed to synchronize) with seccompiler's error texts (`Error calling `prctl`: ...`, `Error calling `seccomp`: ...`). Unsafe block added: the `seccomp` system call, given a pointer to a local `#[repr(C)]` `sock_fprog` whose filter pointer and length are those of the caller's live slice, the length checked to fit the kernel's 16-bit field first. Not equal, on purpose: seccompiler cast the length to u16 silently, ours returns an error for a program above 65,535 instructions (unreachable, the compiler stops at 4,096). Equality: output/sandbox-confine `seccomp` compares the sandbox's program from the old code (seccompiler, copied from origin/master with the call numbers as a parameter) and the new one instruction by instruction: x86_64 (178 instructions, 1,424 bytes), aarch64 (175 instructions, 1,400 bytes, with aarch64's numbers from libc 0.2.191: socket 198, sendto 206, sendmsg 211, sendmmsg 269, io_uring 425 to 427, listen 201, accept 202, accept4 242, setsid 157, setpgid 154) and riscv64 equal, and `arm` fails alike with `Invalid target arch: arm.`; 60,000 random filters (seeds 1 to 3: up to 900 system calls, up to 3 rules each, rules of up to 59 conditions so the helper jumps occur, random values and masks, random arguments including invalid indices, all three architectures, random errno and action pairs) give equal programs for 12,084 (661,718 instructions) and equal errors for the other 47,916, 0 differences. Installed in a child process on this Hand (Linux 6.18.56), the old and new filters give the same result for 1,912 calls (socket over 7 domains, 18 types, 3 flag sets and 5 protocols; sendto, sendmsg and sendmmsg with and without `MSG_FASTOPEN`; io_uring_setup, io_uring_enter, io_uring_register, listen, accept, accept4, setpgid, setsid; getpid natively and through the x32 bit), 1,880 of them EPERM.
