- nanocode-webp's VP8 loop filter filters sixteen pixels of an edge at once, and nanocode-sys transposes the vertical edges with SSE2 and NEON (2026-11-13, Georgios: restore the speed the replaced codecs lost without changing an output byte). The filter ran per pixel through bounds-checked `pixels[point - k * stride]` reads and short-circuit threshold branches, 49% of lossy decode cycles on cwebp q75 photos (perf, x86_64). crates/core/webp/src/loop_filter.rs now loads the eight taps p3..q3 of an edge as eight `[u8; 16]` lanes (rows of a horizontal edge are copied, a luma vertical edge is sixteen rows of eight bytes transposed, chroma puts blue in lanes 0-7 and red in 8-15 since both planes share the macroblock's thresholds) and runs the simple, inner-edge and macroblock-edge filters branch-free on every lane in safe code that LLVM vectorizes: the thresholds are saturating u8 sums (exact because every edge limit is at most 193, asserted below 255), the clamps of the i32 arithmetic are saturating i8 adds, `clamp(outer + 3 * (q0 - p0))` is three saturating adds of `q0 - p0` (equal for every outer and difference: the sum moves in one direction, and a difference saturated at 127 or -128 already drives the sum to the bound), and the 27/18/9 taps use i16; a lane that fails the thresholds keeps its pixels through a select. Edge order (left, inner verticals, top, inner horizontals, per macroblock in raster order) is unchanged and the pixels of one edge are independent, so the result is the same. The transposes of the vertical edges were then 40% of the filter (byte moves through the stack), so crates/core/sys/src/webp.rs gives `gather_columns(top, bottom, stride) -> Option<Columns>` and `scatter_columns(top, bottom, stride, &Columns) -> bool` (16 rows of 8 bytes to 8 lanes of 16 and back) with SSE2 unpacks on x86_64 and NEON `vtrn` 8x8 transposes on aarch64, loading and storing through `u64` and safe slices; `None`/`false` (wasm32, or a build without the feature) makes loop_filter.rs run its own scalar transpose. Detection is one function, `accelerated()` (`cfg!(target_feature = "sse2")`/`"neon"`, baseline on both). Unsafe blocks (2, both in webp.rs): `unsafe { kernel::gather(top, bottom) }` and `unsafe { kernel::scatter(columns) }`, calls of `#[target_feature(enable = "sse2")]`/`"neon"` functions that take and return only values; invariant: `accelerated()` returned true, so the build enables that feature. nanocode-webp gains nanocode-sys as its one dependency. Equality: output/webp-check (`check`, a copy of nanocode-webp at origin/master renamed reference-webp against this one, comparing header, ICC, EXIF and decode results or errors) over the 154 corpus WebP files (76 VP8, 52 VP8L, 26 VP8X), 44 cwebp files from the corpus's largest JPEGs and PNGs (q30/q75/q95, `-nostrong` simple filter, `-lossless`, q80), 400 synthetic encodes and 5,790 seeded mutants of those files (bit flips, truncations, random runs, random tails: 2,242 decode, 3,548 fail) plus 580 encoder round trips: 0 differences on x86_64 (Hand) and aarch64 (gak-9); output/webp-scalar (the same check against copies of nanocode-webp and nanocode-sys with `accelerated()` false) 598 files and 1,930 mutants, 0 differences on both. Measured (output/webp-check `bench`, thread CPU time, 9 interleaved rounds, medians of whole-corpus decode): x86_64 Hand (load 27 on 5 cores) lossy 93 files 1,778.7 -> 1,348.0 ms (1.32x), lossy+alpha 23 files 44.2 -> 37.3 ms (1.18x), lossless unchanged (687 -> 694 ms); aarch64 gak-9 (load 14 to 19) lossy 1,306.6 -> 983.2 ms (1.33x), lossy+alpha 35.5 -> 29.9 ms (1.19x), lossless 662 -> 660 ms; perf cycles:u on three photos (3072x2048 q75, 2268x1512 q30, 1744x2464 q95, 3 runs) 2.08G -> 1.38G. A safe rewrite of the YUV->RGB upsampling into 16-bit lanes was measured too and was no faster (1.38-1.42G vs 1.42-1.44G cycles), so yuv.rs is unchanged. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-webp -p nanocode-sys` (x86_64 and aarch64), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-webp -p nanocode-sys` native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- nanocode-png expands palette, low-depth gray and tRNS-keyed pixels through fixed-size pixel arrays, with the same pixels (2026-11-13): sampling the decoder on gak-9 (`sample`, 40 passes over the 297-file corpus) put 10% of decode time in `memmove`/`memcpy` called from `Expand::row`: `unpack` handed each pixel out as a slice whose length (3 or 4 for palette entries, 1 or 2 for gray) was only known at run time, so every palette pixel was a library `memcpy` call, and the keyed RGB/gray path compared and copied each pixel the same way. crates/core/png/src/decode.rs: `unpack` is generic over the channel count and passes `&mut [u8; CHANNELS]` (palette RGBA entries are assigned whole, RGB ones as their first three bytes), and for 1, 2 and 4-bit samples it finds the byte and shift with shifts and masks (the samples per byte are a power of two; asserted) instead of a division and remainder per pixel; `Expand::Transparent` dispatches to `keyed::<PIXEL, OUTPUT>` for its four layouts (8 and 16-bit gray and RGB), which compares the pixel with the key as arrays (a key whose length differs from the pixel's never matches, as the slice comparison never did). Safe code only. Equal: output/png-equal (decode of seeded synthetic PNGs, which include palettes of 1 to 256 entries with and without tRNS, 1/2/4/8-bit gray with and without a key, 8 and 16-bit RGB and gray keys, and every corpus PNG whole and mutated, against origin/master's copy): x86_64 12,000 synthetic (9,517 decoded) + 2,856 file checks (766 decoded), aarch64 18,000 synthetic (14,255 decoded) + 3,267 file checks (478 decoded), 0 differences. Measured (output/png-perf, release, thread CPU time, interleaved medians, origin/master against this commit, so with the Paeth commit included): decoding the corpus 568 -> 497 ms on gak-9 (275 files, 11 rounds, load 9 to 11; the Paeth commit alone was 568 -> 559), and 4,244 -> 3,940 ms on the Hand (692 files, 7 rounds, load 23 to 25; the Paeth commit alone was 1.06x). Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-png` (x86_64 and aarch64), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-png --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-png's adaptive filter choice sums each candidate filter's absolute values without writing it, and filters the row once with the winner, with the same bytes (2026-11-13): `adaptive` (crates/core/png/src/filter.rs) wrote every candidate (Sub, Up, Average, Paeth) into the output row, read it back to sum its signed magnitudes, and wrote the winner a fifth time when it was not Paeth. `magnitudes` now runs one pass per candidate that predicts 32 bytes into a stack array and sums that array (`magnitude`, generic over the predictor, with the first pixel's bytes summed through the same predictors as before), and `apply` writes only the winning filter. The sums are the same integers and the tie rule is unchanged (a later candidate wins a tie, in the order Sub, Up, Average, Paeth), so the chosen filters and the IDAT bytes are identical. A version that summed all four candidates in one loop with four accumulators measured 0.63x (it did not vectorize), and one that summed inside the prediction loop 0.69x, so the predict-then-sum form stays. Safe code only. Equal: output/png-equal encodes with this crate and with origin/master's copy and compares the PNG bytes: x86_64 2,000 seeded synthetic images (all eight color types, 1 to 1,500 pixels wide, noise, gradients, flat runs, extreme values) + 692 decoded corpus images, aarch64 2,000 synthetic + 275 corpus images, 0 differences. Measured (output/png-perf, release, thread CPU time, interleaved medians): the filter choice alone (output/png-perf parts, every row of the corpus) 1,054 -> 701 ms on the Hand (1.50x, load 30) and 159 -> 90 ms on gak-9 (1.76x, load 14); `encode` of the decoded 8-bit corpus images 3,496 -> 3,035 ms on the Hand (7 rounds, load 23 to 30) and 425 -> 359 ms on gak-9 (11 rounds, load 8). Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-png` (x86_64 and aarch64), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-png --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-png decodes consecutive Paeth rows two at a time and Paeth rows of 2, 4 and 8 bytes per pixel in 16-bit lanes, with the same pixels (2026-11-13): Paeth is the costliest filter to undo (each pixel waits on the one to its left), and it is most of the image data (306 MB of the 847 MB of filtered rows in the 666 non-interlaced corpus PNGs on the Hand are RGB Paeth rows, 79 MB RGBA Paeth). crates/core/png/src/filter.rs: `unfilter_paeth_pair` undoes a row and the row under it in one pass, pixel i of the lower row right after pixel i of the upper one, so the two dependency chains overlap (`paeth_pair` on bytes for 1, 3, 4 and 6 bytes per pixel; on aarch64 the 3-byte case runs `paeth_pair_wide` in i16 lanes, which the M1 runs 1.15x faster than the byte form, while x86_64 runs the byte form 1.35x faster); `paeth_wide` undoes single Paeth rows of 2, 4 and 8 bytes per pixel in i16 lanes (the byte form compiled to slower code there: 4 bytes per pixel 517 -> 939 MB/s on the M1, 359 -> 679 MB/s on x86_64); 1, 3 and 6 bytes per pixel keep the byte form, which was fastest single-row, and 2 and 8 bytes per pixel do not pair (the pair was slower than `paeth_wide` there). crates/core/png/src/decode.rs: `Rows::next` takes whether another row of the same pass follows and, when this row and the next are both Paeth and the next is already whole in the row buffer, undoes both and hands out the second on the next call without unfiltering it again; it never pairs across Adam7 passes, never reads a filter byte early that the original would not have read (the second row's byte is only looked at, and only a 4 pairs), and the buffer cannot be compacted while a row waits, so every row, error and error order is unchanged. Safe code only; SSE2/SSE4.1 one-row and two-row intrinsics kernels were measured first and were slower than the scalar code (Paeth on RGB rows 404 to 481 MB/s against 633 MB/s on the Hand), so nothing goes to nanocode-sys. Equal: output/png-equal compares this crate with origin/master's copy (output/png-perf/reference-png with its reference-compression) on header, dimensions, color, ICC bytes, decode result and pixel hash: 12,000 seeded synthetic PNGs per machine (every color type and depth, widths 1 to 2,000, Adam7, runs of one filter or mixed filters, an invalid filter byte in 10%, truncated or padded image data, bit flips, levels 0 to 10, IDAT split at random) and every corpus PNG whole and mutated (bit flips, truncation, byte overwrites): x86_64 12,000 synthetic (9,545 decoded) + 2,856 file checks (784 decoded), aarch64 12,000 synthetic (9,545 decoded) + 3,267 file checks (480 decoded), 0 differences. Measured with output/png-perf (release, thread CPU time, interleaved medians): decoding the corpus (`Png::new` + `decode`) 4,478 -> 4,210 ms on the Hand (692 files, 911 MB of pixels, 9 rounds, load 25 to 39) and 568 -> 559 ms on gak-9 (275 files, 145 MB, 11 rounds, load 9 to 17); unfiltering alone (output/png-perf parts, the decoder's pairing rule) 1.18x to 1.29x on the Hand and 1.10x on the M1. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-png` (x86_64 and aarch64), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-png --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-digest's BLAKE3 hashes whole runs of chunks and parent nodes in SIMD lanes through nanocode-sys, reaching 0.8 to 0.95 of the upstream blake3 crate's speed instead of one portable chunk at a time (2026-11-13, Georgios: higher performance with ~0 dependencies; this round restores the SIMD that replacing blake3 lost). crates/core/sys/src/blake3.rs is `nanocode_sys::blake3::Blake3Instructions`: `detect()` returns a token per instruction set (SSE4.1, AVX2 or AVX-512F on x86_64, checked with `is_x86_feature_detected!`; NEON on little-endian aarch64 with `is_aarch64_feature_detected!`; `None` on wasm32 and everywhere else, where the stub methods match on the uninhabited kind), `hash_chunks(chunks: &[[u8; 1024]], key, counter, flags, &mut [[u8; 32]])` hashes N full chunks with counters `counter..counter + N`, and `hash_parents(&[[u8; 64]], key, flags, &mut [[u8; 32]])` hashes N parent blocks (two child chaining values each, `PARENT` added). nanocode-digest now depends on nanocode-sys (a workspace crate; no new package). The kernels port upstream blake3 1.8.7's (CC0/Apache-2.0) `rust_sse41.rs`/`rust_avx2.rs` hash4/hash8, its `blake3_avx512.c` hash16 (16x16 word transposes, `vprord` rotates) and `blake3_neon.c` hash4 to Rust intrinsics in `#[target_feature]` fns: 16 lanes, then 8, then 4, and a last group of 1 to 3 inputs runs the 4-lane kernel with the last input repeated into the spare lanes and their outputs dropped; the rounds are one shared macro over each width's add/xor/rotate fns, generic over `BLOCKS` (16 for chunks, 1 for parents). No closure or `array::map` calls a target-feature fn: those were not inlined and cost 16 calls per 16-lane block (seen in `objdump`), so loads and splats are plain loops. Unsafe blocks, each with its invariant: (1-4) `hash_many`'s calls into `x86::hash_many_sse41`, `x86::hash_many_avx2`, `x86::hash_many_avx512` and `neon::hash_many`: the `Kind` variant is private and built only by `detect()` after the runtime check of `sse4.1`, `sse4.1`+`avx2`, `sse4.1`+`avx2`+`avx512f`, or `neon`, the features those fns enable; (5, 6) SSE4.1 `load`/`store`: `_mm_loadu_si128`/`_mm_storeu_si128` on a `&[u8; 16]`/`&mut [u8; 16]`, valid for an unaligned 16-byte read/write; (7, 8) AVX2 `load`/`store`: `_mm256_loadu_si256`/`_mm256_storeu_si256` on a `&[u8; 32]`/`&mut [u8; 32]` (the AVX-512 kernel stores its outputs' low halves through this one too); (9) AVX-512 `load`: `_mm512_loadu_si512` on a `&[u8; 64]`; (10, 11) NEON `load`/`store`: `vld1q_u8`/`vst1q_u8` on a `&[u8; 16]`/`&mut [u8; 16]` (byte loads, so no alignment is assumed). In crates/core/digest/src/blake3.rs, `Blake3::update` now follows upstream's `Hasher::update`: it first fills a partly filled chunk (finalizing it only when more input follows), then, while more than one chunk of input remains, takes the largest power-of-two subtree that both fits and is aligned to the chunk counter, capped at `SUBTREE_CHUNKS_MAX` = 256 chunks, hashes its chunks with one `hash_chunks` call, reduces the chaining values level by level with `hash_parents` (at most `PARENTS_PER_PASS` = 16, the widest kernel, per call, in place) down to its two children, and pushes both. The stack merges lazily as upstream's does (`merge_stack` keeps `total_chunks.count_ones()` entries before each push and after input lands in the chunk), so it holds `STACK_DEPTH_MAX + 1` chaining values, and `finalize` roots the top two when the input ended exactly on a subtree. The last chunk is still never finalized before more input is known: a subtree of two or more chunks never holds the root, its two children stay unmerged until more input or `finalize`, and the chunk state keeps a remainder of up to 1024 bytes. `blake3()` keeps its single-chunk path and otherwise uses `Blake3::update`. Without a token (wasm32, CPUs without SSE4.1) the same tree code hashes each chunk and parent with the existing portable `compress`. The cap of 256 is measured: at 1 MiB on the Hand 16, 64 and 256 chunks gave 5.2 to 5.7, 5.7 to 6.7 and 7.0 to 7.5 GB/s (upstream 8.0 to 8.4) over three interleaved rounds each; scratch is 16 x 32 bytes for subtrees of up to 16 chunks and 256 x 32 bytes above that, so small inputs do not zero 8 KiB. Not kept: an SSE4.1 single-block compress (upstream's `compress_pre` ported to intrinsics, used for chunk-state blocks, roots and merges) measured 0.78 to 0.91 of the portable `compress` at 1 KiB and no faster at 64 B in the same binary, so single blocks stay portable on every architecture, as upstream does on NEON. Upstream's default build differs per architecture: on x86_64 Linux its build script compiles its assembly (cfgs `blake3_sse2_ffi`, `blake3_sse41_ffi`, `blake3_avx2_ffi`, `blake3_avx512_ffi`), so the x86 comparison is against hand-written assembly; on aarch64 it compiles `blake3_neon.c` (`blake3_neon`) with the portable single-block compress. Checked with output/blake3 (`cargo run --release --bin equal`): `blake3()` and `Blake3::update` against `blake3::hash`/`blake3::Hasher` 1.8.7 and the pre-change crate (output/blake3/before, copied from origin/master) at 48 boundary lengths (0, 1, 63..65, 127..129, 1023..1025, 2047..2049, 3071..3073, 4095..4097, 5120, 7168, 8191..8193, 15360, 15361, 16383..16385, 31744, 31745, 32767..32769, 65535..65537, 131071..131073, 1048575..1048577, 2 MiB + 1024, 4 MiB - 1, 4 MiB, 8 MiB + 1) at offsets 0, 1, 3, 17 and 63, every length 0..=9216 at a random offset, 600 random lengths below 1 MiB, 200 streams below 1 MiB and 20 below 8 MiB in random update sizes (up to 1, 64, 1024, 3000, 20000, 300000 or 2 MiB bytes, `finalize` compared mid-stream after a quarter of the updates, empty updates mixed in), and every file of the worktree (3,055 files on the Hand, 3,068 on gak-9, about 72 MB, each and concatenated, also streamed); a copy whose `detect()` result is replaced by `None` (output/blake3/scalar) checked the forced-portable path the same way: 7,062,540 checks equal on the Hand (AVX-512 token; its 8- and 4-lane kernels cover the 8-, 4- and 2-parent levels and small subtrees) and 7,062,554 on gak-9 (NEON). Measured with output/blake3 (`cargo run --release --bin bench`), thread CPU time (`CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`), before (origin/master's crate) / after / upstream interleaved per round, medians of 11 to 15 rounds, ns per hash. Hand (x86_64 AVX-512, 4-CPU quota at load 25 to 28): 64 B 132 / 129 / 78; 1 KiB 1,671 / 1,809 / 1,506 (same code path; another run 1,521 / 1,697 / 1,527); 16 KiB 31,681 / 2,357 / 2,056 (13.4x, 0.87 of upstream; another run 0.89); 1 MiB 1,790,001 / 139,751 / 124,855 (12.8x, 7.5 GB/s against 8.4, 0.89; another run 0.79); 1 MiB + 1 byte 0.75 to 0.82 of upstream; 1 MiB in 64-byte updates 2,233,865 / 2,165,249 / 1,679,287. gak-9 (M1 Max NEON, load 11 to 14): 64 B 93 / 90 / 83; 1 KiB 1,351 / 1,329 / 1,263; 16 KiB 22,755 / 10,170 / 9,492 (2.24x, 0.93); 1 MiB 1,465,708 / 635,672 / 602,857 (2.31x, 1.65 GB/s against 1.74, 0.95); 1 MiB in 64-byte updates 1,556,456 / 1,639,302 / 1,376,771 (0.94 to 0.95 of before over four runs; `#[inline]` on the chunk state's update did not change it). Small inputs and 64-byte streaming stay on the portable compress, where upstream's single-block assembly leads on x86 (64 B at 0.6 of upstream). `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-digest` for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown (and natively on gak-9), `cargo check --locked --lib` for both crates native and wasm32, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` pass.
- rustpython-common's hashlib SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/hashlib/sha1.rs, sha256.rs, sha512.rs, behind Python's `hashlib`) compress each block with nanocode-sys's SHA instructions when `detect()` finds them and run their unchanged rounds, now `compress_portable`, otherwise, always on WASM (2026-11-13, Georgios: wire the restored SIMD into every user). rustpython-common gains a path dependency on nanocode-sys, which nanocode-platform already brought into its build. Blocks still arrive one at a time from `BlockBuffer::absorb`, so each pays one `detect()` (a cached atomic load), which the measurements below include. Equality: output/sha-users compiles sum_hash.rs and rustpython-common's hashlib block.rs, sha1.rs, sha256.rs and sha512.rs into one binary next to nanocode-sys and checks them against sha1 0.11.0 and sha2 0.11.0 on lengths 0 to 600, 4,095 to 4,097, 1 MiB and 200 seeded random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets 0 to 63, psh's also streamed in random chunks of 0 to 300 bytes: 15,295 comparisons, all equal, on the hosted Hand (x86_64, SHA-NI) and on gak-9 (M1 Max); the portable rounds these files fall back to are unchanged, and the same kernels' forced-portable path is covered by output/sha-check. Throughput in MB/s, median of 9 interleaved rounds of thread CPU time, origin/master's hashlib / this one: hosted Hand (load average 21 to 24) SHA-1 64 B 197 / 535, 1 KiB 397 / 1,461, 1 MiB 452 / 1,706, SHA-256 64 B 104 / 453, 1 KiB 210 / 1,250, 1 MiB 221 / 1,521, SHA-512 1 MiB 357 / 392 (portable on x86 both times); gak-9 (load average 18 to 23) SHA-1 64 B 137 / 567, 1 KiB 262 / 1,611, 1 MiB 293 / 1,965, SHA-256 64 B 88 / 527, 1 KiB 173 / 1,467, 1 MiB 187 / 1,691, SHA-512 64 B 132 / 416, 1 KiB 254 / 1,107, 1 MiB 291 / 1,312. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p rustpython-common` for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown and natively on gak-9, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- psh-utils's SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 (crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/sum_hash.rs, behind sha1sum, sha256sum, shasum and the git object ids) compress with nanocode-sys's SHA instructions when `Sha1Instructions`, `Sha256Instructions` or `Sha512Instructions::detect()` finds them, and keep their own portable rounds otherwise, always on WASM (2026-11-13, Georgios: wire the restored SIMD into every user). psh-utils depends on nanocode-sys by path (`nanocode-sys = { path = "../../core/sys" }` in psh's workspace dependencies) rather than on nanocode-digest: nanocode-digest has no SHA-512/224 or SHA-512/256 and a different streaming shape, so taking only the kernels keeps psh's `Digest` and its output exactly as they were; psh's own MSRV note says 1.96 and nanocode-sys inherits nanocode's 1.97, which only the standalone psh workspace sees. No unsafe code: psh-utils keeps `forbid(unsafe_code)`. Equality: output/sha-users compiles sum_hash.rs and rustpython-common's hashlib block.rs, sha1.rs, sha256.rs and sha512.rs into one binary next to nanocode-sys and checks them against sha1 0.11.0 and sha2 0.11.0 on lengths 0 to 600, 4,095 to 4,097, 1 MiB and 200 seeded random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets 0 to 63, psh's also streamed in random chunks of 0 to 300 bytes: 15,295 comparisons, all equal, on the hosted Hand (x86_64, SHA-NI) and on gak-9 (M1 Max); the portable rounds these files fall back to are unchanged, and the same kernels' forced-portable path is covered by output/sha-check. Throughput in MB/s, median of 9 interleaved rounds of thread CPU time, origin/master's sum_hash.rs / this one: hosted Hand (load average 21 to 24) SHA-1 64 B 126 / 555, 1 KiB 263 / 1,462, 1 MiB 303 / 1,595, SHA-256 64 B 110 / 489, 1 KiB 226 / 1,346, 1 MiB 243 / 1,523, SHA-512 1 MiB 380 / 372 (portable on x86 both times); gak-9 (load average 18 to 23) SHA-1 64 B 96 / 662, 1 KiB 197 / 1,473, 1 MiB 199 / 1,924, SHA-256 64 B 85 / 613, 1 KiB 170 / 1,557, 1 MiB 189 / 1,740, SHA-512 64 B 135 / 462, 1 KiB 255 / 1,041, 1 MiB 290 / 1,194. Equality: xz's pre-change slice-by-8 is one of the paths check_crc compares with crc32fast 1.5.5 (all of the CRC-32 entry's inputs, both machines), so the new and old xz values are equal. Measurements (thread CPU time, interleaved medians of 31 rounds, before / after): Hand (load 27 to 31) 16 B 5.9/8.4 ns, 64 B 27.9/13.3 ns, 1 KiB 499/29.1 ns, 16 KiB 8,153/314 ns, 1 MiB 521/22.7 us; gak-9 (load 16 to 21) 16 B 4.8/1.7 ns, 64 B 21.6/3.3 ns, 1 KiB 548/19.0 ns, 16 KiB 9,114/234 ns, 1 MiB 591/15.0 us. The 16-byte case on x86 (stream flags and footers, 2 to 12 bytes, once per stream) is 2.5 ns slower. xz's CRC-64 (its default check) stays slicing-by-8: folding it with PCLMULQDQ and PMULL needs its own 64-bit keys and Barrett constants and is left for a later change. Commands: cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression, again with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression, cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli.
- psh's `codec::crc32` and `codec::adler32` (gzip, zip and zlib in the archive utilities) call nanocode-sys's `Crc32Instructions` and `Adler32Instructions` when the CPU has them, keeping their slicing-by-8 and chunked loops as the fallback (2026-11-13). psh-utils depends on nanocode-sys through psh's `[workspace.dependencies]` (`nanocode-sys = { path = "../../core/sys" }`), so the psh workspace still builds on its own; nanocode-sys adds no package to psh's Cargo.lock beyond itself (libc and windows-sys were there). Output stays identical: `adler32` keeps returning an empty input's start unreduced, as before, by taking the kernel only for non-empty data. No new unsafe code. Equality (output/crc-harness, check_psh, on the Hand and gak-9): the pre-change and new functions agree, and crc32 equals crc32fast, over every length 0..=6000 at 3 offsets with fixed starts including non-canonical ones, 6,000 random lengths up to 1 MiB with random starts, and empty inputs with four starts (72,021 comparisons on each machine). Measurements (thread CPU time, interleaved medians of 31 rounds, before / after): Hand (load 27 to 31) crc32 64 B 28.2/13.1 ns, 1 KiB 505/29.3 ns, 16 KiB 8,165/318 ns, 1 MiB 521/24.5 us; adler32 64 B 20.6/13.7 ns, 1 KiB 310/24.1 ns, 16 KiB 4,858/199 ns, 1 MiB 308/15.9 us. gak-9 (load 16 to 21) crc32 64 B 21.5/4.0 ns, 1 KiB 544/19.0 ns, 16 KiB 8,978/234 ns, 1 MiB 596/15.1 us; adler32 64 B 16.2/8.1 ns, 1 KiB 365/25.9 ns, 16 KiB 5,973/322 ns, 1 MiB 396/20.6 us. clippy's three `chunks_exact` warnings in codec.rs and dump.rs predate this change. Commands: cd crates/patches/psh && cargo check --locked -p psh-utils, again with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked -p psh-utils; cargo metadata in both workspaces to update the lock files; cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli.
- Adler-32 (`nanocode_compression::checksum::adler32`, zlib and PNG) runs on AVX2 or AVX-512BW on x86_64 and NEON on aarch64 through nanocode-sys (2026-11-13). The 32-lane safe formulation does not reach SIMD speed: measured first against simd-adler32 0.3.10, it ran 6.7 to 7.9 GB/s against 47 GB/s on the Hand (x86_64 builds target SSE2 only) and 3.0 against 32.7 GB/s on M1, so it stays as the fallback (wasm32, x86 without AVX2) and crates/core/sys/src/adler32.rs adds `Adler32Instructions` (`detect()`, `update(start, data)`). Each kernel walks blocks of at most 5,552 bytes (zlib's NMAX, the most bytes before a 32-bit sum can overflow) keeping per-lane totals, the running prefix of totals and position-weighted sums, then folds them in u64 as high += n * low + chunk * prefixes + weighted and reduces mod 65,521 once per block: AVX2 takes 32-byte chunks (`vpsadbw` for totals, `vpmaddubsw` with weights 32..1 and `vpmaddwd` for weighted sums), AVX-512BW the same on 64-byte chunks (weights 64..1, the largest pair 255 * 64 + 255 * 63 = 32,385 stays under i16's 32,767), finishing a 32- to 63-byte rest with AVX2; NEON takes 64-byte chunks with pairwise widening adds for totals and eight u16 column sums (at most 86 * 255 = 21,930 each per block) weighted by `vmlal_u16` at the end of each block. The last bytes short of a chunk run the scalar loop. Any start value, canonical or not, gives the same result as the scalar code, which also reduces at the end. Unsafe blocks and their invariants: (1) the three calls in `Adler32Instructions::update`: a `Kind` is only built by `Kind::detect` after detection confirmed avx2 (Avx2), avx2, avx512f and avx512bw (Avx512) or neon (Neon), every feature the callee enables; (2) x86_64 `load_avx2` and `load_avx512` (`_mm256_loadu_si256`, `_mm512_loadu_si512`) read exactly the 32 or 64 bytes of their `&[u8; N]`, unaligned; (3) aarch64 `load` (`vld1q_u8_x4`) reads the 64 bytes of its `&[u8; 64]`. Equality (output/crc-harness, check_adler): every length 0..=12000 at 5 offsets with seven fixed starts including non-canonical ones (0xFFFFFFFF, 0xFFF1FFF1) and random canonical starts, all-0xFF inputs (the overflow worst case), 30,000 random lengths up to 1 MiB, 400 streamed runs in random chunk sizes, and the same files as the CRC-32 check: the new path, the forced-scalar copy, the pre-change checksum.rs and each kernel all equal simd-adler32 0.3.10, in 530,690 comparisons on the Hand and 431,564 on gak-9. Measurements (thread CPU time, interleaved medians of 41 rounds, before / after / simd-adler32 0.3.10, which uses AVX2 on stable): Hand (load 27 to 31) 64 B 34.0/12.8/12.0 ns, 1 KiB 152/23.8/29.3 ns, 16 KiB 2,176/198/353 ns, 1 MiB 136/14.4/22.9 us; AVX2 alone 1 KiB 29.0 ns, 16 KiB 342 ns, level with simd-adler32. gak-9 (load 16 to 21) 64 B 62.0/8.0/8.3 ns, 1 KiB 368/25.9/31.0 ns, 16 KiB 5,501/323/498 ns, 1 MiB 349/20.5/32.2 us. Small inputs: 1 B 3.9/5.6 ns on the Hand and 1.6/3.6 ns on gak-9 (the scalar code has a one-byte path), 15 B 8.0/9.8 and 7.9/5.3 ns. Commands: cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-compression, again with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-compression (native, wasm32, aarch64-apple-darwin on gak-9), cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli.
- CRC-32 (`nanocode_compression::checksum::crc32`, and through it gzip, zlib, PNG chunks and HTTP gzip) runs on the CPU's carry-less multiply and CRC instructions through nanocode-sys (2026-11-13, restoring the SIMD speed the crc32fast replacement lost). crates/core/sys/src/crc32.rs adds `Crc32Instructions` (`detect()`, `update(start, data)` with crc32fast's start and finish semantics); nanocode-compression keeps its slice-by-16 table as the fallback when `detect()` answers None (wasm32, x86 without PCLMULQDQ, SSE4.1 and SSSE3, aarch64 without CRC), and gains the workspace's nanocode-sys as its one dependency (libc and windows-sys are already in the graph). x86_64: PCLMULQDQ folds four 128-bit lanes by 512 bits from 128 bytes (crc32fast's crossover) and one lane from 16 bytes, shifts the last 1 to 15 bytes in with pshufb, takes 4 to 15 bytes as one shifted block and 1 to 3 bytes with one Barrett step, then reduces with Barrett; with AVX2 and VPCLMULQDQ, four 256-bit lanes fold by 1,024 bits from 256 bytes; with AVX-512F as well, four 512-bit lanes fold by 2,048 bits from 256 bytes (`WIDE_BYTES_MIN` is one 256-byte group: on the Hand the zmm path beats the ymm path at every size from 256 B, 512 B 12.8 against 19.6 ns and 1 KiB 25.6 against 39.9 ns, where crc32fast waits until 2 KiB). aarch64: `__crc32d/w/h/b` below 64 bytes (`FOLD_BYTES_MIN`, measured on M1: 4-stream PMULL folding is level at 64 B and ahead from 80 B), then PMULL folding with 4, 8 or 16 streams (from 256 B and 4 KiB, crc32fast 1.5.5's crossovers, which measured equal or better on M1), finished with two `__crc32d` over the folded 16 bytes and at most one each of `crc32x/w/h/b` for the tail (returning early on an empty tail took 64 B from 4.6 to 3.6 ns); CPUs with CRC but no PMULL run one `__crc32d` chain. Every fold key, the x^64 reduce key, P' and mu' are computed by const fns from the IEEE polynomial 0x04C11DB7 and equal crc32fast's literals (checked in the harness). Unsafe blocks and their invariants: (1) the five calls in `Crc32Instructions::update` into `#[target_feature]` kernels: a `Kind` is only built by `Kind::detect` after `is_x86_feature_detected!` or `is_aarch64_feature_detected!` confirmed every feature the callee enables (pclmulqdq, sse4.1, ssse3; plus avx2 and vpclmulqdq; plus avx512f; crc; crc and aes); (2) x86_64 `load`, `load_medium` and `load_wide` (`_mm_loadu_si128`, `_mm256_loadu_si256`, `_mm512_loadu_si512`) read exactly the 16, 32 or 64 bytes of the `&[u8; N]` they take, as unaligned loads; (3) aarch64 `load` (`vld1q_u8`) reads the 16 bytes of its `&[u8; 16]`. Detection is not cached: crc and aes are static target features on aarch64-apple-darwin, so detection folds to a constant, and an AtomicU8 cache measured slower there (64 B 4.9 against 3.3 ns) and no faster on x86. Equality (output/crc-harness, check_crc): every length 0..=4400 at 16 offsets, 30,000 random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets and starts, 200 constant-byte inputs, 400 streamed runs in random chunk sizes (crc32(crc32(s, a), b) = crc32(s, a ++ b)), and every file under crates/ plus /usr/share/doc on the Hand (4,157 files, 82 MB) and /usr/share/man on gak-9 (5,910 files, 105 MB): the new path, a copy of checksum.rs whose detect() answers None (the table fallback), the pre-change checksum.rs, xz's slice-by-8 and each kernel (pclmulqdq, avx2, avx512 on the Hand; crc, crc+pmull on gak-9) all equal crc32fast 1.5.5, in 736,218 comparisons on the Hand and 641,562 on gak-9. Measurements (thread CPU time, interleaved medians of 41 rounds, before = pre-change slice-by-16 / after / crc32fast 1.5.5): Hand (AMD EPYC 9255, load 27 to 31 on 5 cores) 64 B 23.0/12.8/12.4 ns, 1 KiB 419/29.4/50.4 ns, 16 KiB 6,641/316/324 ns, 1 MiB 431/22.8/19.1 us in that rotation and 17.6 to 20.4 against 17.7 to 20.4 us over three runs without the slow scalar sample in the rotation; 1 B 3.8/7.2/5.5 ns, 15 B 23.0/8.7/9.9 ns, 256 B 98.8/15.6/22.8 ns. gak-9 (M1 Max, load 16 to 21) 64 B 17.0/3.3/3.5 ns, 1 KiB 330/19.0/19.1 ns, 16 KiB 5,425/234/234 ns, 1 MiB 376/15.0/14.9 us; 1 B 1.6/3.0/3.0 ns, 15 B 13.2/2.6/13.1 ns, 256 B 75.7/6.9/7.0 ns. Inputs of 1 to 3 bytes are slower than the table on both machines (one Barrett step on x86, the folding kernel's prologue on M1, where crc32fast costs the same). Commands: cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-compression, again with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-compression (native, wasm32, and aarch64-apple-darwin on gak-9), cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys --target aarch64-apple-ios on gak-9, cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli.
- Five more crates declare exactly the tokio features their own code calls, after fcbb336bb (2026-11-13, toward lighter builds of each crate on its own): nanocode-mcp-http drops `sync`, nanocode-tls `sync`, nanocode-backend-claude-client `rt-multi-thread` natively and `macros` and `sync` on every target, nanocode-backend-codex-client `fs`, `process` and `rt-multi-thread`; and nanocode-computer-repl takes `sync` back, since its `use tokio::{.., sync::{mpsc, oneshot}}` group calls it and it compiled without the feature only because nanocode-mcp-tools turns it on. A feature left only when both checks agreed: no `tokio::<module>` path, `tokio::{..}` use-tree entry or tokio macro in the crate's sources names it (a use-tree-aware scan, output/deps-list/tokio.py plus the scan in this entry's commands), and `cargo check --locked --lib -p <crate>` of that crate alone, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, still compiles (gak-9's output/deps-out/trim.py dropped one feature at a time). nanocode-cli turns every one of these on itself and builds the same tokio. Built alone on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (`cargo tree --locked -p <crate> -e normal,build`, all packages): nanocode-backend-claude-client 106 to 105 (wasm32-unknown-unknown 63 to 62: tokio-macros no longer built) and no multi-threaded runtime, nanocode-backend-codex-client 114 to 112 (tokio's process and signal-hook-registry and the multi-threaded runtime no longer built); nanocode-mcp-http and nanocode-tls change no package, their dependencies still turning `sync` on. `cargo check --locked --lib -p <crate>` for each of the five alone natively (Linux on the Hand, macOS on gak-9) and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, and `cargo clippy --locked --no-deps` on the five.
- The vendored rustpython-host_env reads C's `altzone` only on Solaris and illumos, whose `time.h` declares it, and loses its build script, which compiled a C probe for `altzone` with cc on every fresh build (2026-11-13, toward ~0 dependencies and no C build scripts in our crates, as TIGER_STYLE asks). Equal: the probe found no `altzone` on the targets nanocode ships, so `time.altzone` already took CPython's `timezone - 3600` path there: the build-script outputs of five existing target directories (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu on the hosted Hand, glibc; aarch64-apple-darwin on gak-9, debug and release) carry no `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_altzone`, and neither /usr/include/time.h on the Hand nor the macOS SDK's time.h names `altzone`; a cross build without a target C compiler already skipped the probe. cc stays in the graph for ring and mimalloc, so no package leaves, but rustpython-host_env no longer waits on a build script ahead of rustpython-vm: on gak-9 (load 9 to 11) `cargo clean -p rustpython-host_env` then `cargo check --timings --lib -p rustpython-host_env` five times gave the build script 0.13 s to compile and 0.14 to 0.16 s to run (medians 0.13 and 0.15), now gone. `cargo check --locked --lib -p rustpython-host_env` natively, for wasm32-unknown-unknown and x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- Two dependencies nothing used leave their crates: tracing from nanocode-turnlog (no `tracing::` path or macro anywhere in its source since the one-table rewrite) and bitflags from the vendored rustpython-host_env (its source names no `bitflags`; the other rustpython crates keep theirs) (2026-11-13, cleaning up after the dependency removals). Found with output/deps-list/unused.py, which lists each path package's non-dev dependencies whose library name appears nowhere in its Rust sources (cargo-shear would not install on either machine in time: the Hand's build ran under load 25 to 37 and gak-9's cargo-binstall could not parse its manifest); its other hits are kept on purpose: nanocode-cli's nanocode-agent-host turns on `cua`, rustpython-host_env's rustls-webpki is imported as `webpki`, and psh-wasm-core's four dependencies are used by psh-wasm's sources, which it builds. No package leaves the lock (tracing and bitflags stay for the other crates); two Cargo.lock lines go. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, and `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-turnlog`.
- The workspace's tokio-util no longer turns on `codec`: its one direct user, nanocode-tool-runtime, takes only `sync::CancellationToken` and `DropGuard`, which every tokio-util build has, and reqwest asks for `io` alone, so tokio-util in nanocode-cli builds without its codec module (2026-11-13, toward fewer and lighter dependencies). No package leaves (tokio-util stays for reqwest's `stream`); `cargo tree --locked -p nanocode-cli -e features -i tokio-util` lists `io` and `default` only. Measured on gak-9 (M1 Max, load 9 to 10 on 10 cores) with output/deps-out/feat-timing, two one-crate workspaces pinning tokio-util 0.7.18 with `io` against `io` plus `codec`, `cargo clean -p tokio-util` then `cargo check` interleaved 7 times: 237 ms against 299 ms (medians). `cargo metadata --locked`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tool-runtime` and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-cli awaits Tempo's listing and catalog loads with `futures_util::future::join` instead of the `futures_util::join!` macro, so it no longer turns on futures-util's `async-await-macro` feature and futures-macro (a proc-macro over syn) leaves nanocode-cli's build (2026-11-13, toward Georgios's ~0 dependencies). Same behavior: `join!` expands to polling each future in argument order and `future::join` is the same `Join` of two `MaybeDone`s, polled first then second. Packages nanocode-cli reaches (`cargo tree --locked -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build --prefix none`, third-party): 101 to 100 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, 102 to 101 on aarch64-apple-darwin; futures-macro stays in Cargo.lock only through wasm-streams, reqwest's wasm32 backend, which no wasm crate here builds. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli --no-deps` on the hosted Hand.
- psh-pattern's lazy DFA marks its unanchored start states only when the regex has a prefilter to run from them, as regex-automata's hybrid DFA does (`specialize_start_states` only with a prefilter), so a regex without one stays in the four-transitions-at-a-time loop when it passes back through its start state (2026-11-13). `crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-pattern/src/dfa.rs`: `Dfa::new` takes `specialize_start` and `tag` sets `TAG_START` only then; `engine.rs` builds the prefilter first and passes `prefilter.is_some()` to the forward DFA and `false` to the reverse one, which never looks at the tag. Before, every start state was tagged, so `\w+_\w+`, `[a-z]+_[a-z]+` and `\w+` left the unrolled loop at every byte between words and took the slow path (perf on `rg -c '\w+_\w+'`: 65% of CPU in `Dfa::search_forward`, its hot block the tagged-state branch). Results do not change: the tag only chooses between two loops that compute the same transitions, and with no prefilter the tagged branch did nothing else. Harness output/rx (its own workspace; `old` is psh-pattern at 6744c3b9c as a path crate, `new` the tree, plus regex 1.12 and grep-regex 0.1.14 from crates.io): `equal` (seeded random patterns from literals, classes, looks, groups, repetitions and alternations with random case-insensitive, multi-line, dot-all and Unicode flags; haystacks from slices of the repository's Rust sources, random tokens and random bytes up to 4,000 bytes; bytes and str `is_match`, `is_match_at`, `find_at`, `find_iter`, `captures`, `captures_iter`, `shortest_match`(_at) old against new exactly and against regex except `shortest_match` values, and the grep matcher's `find_candidate_line`, line loop, `find_iter`, `shortest_match` and `captures_at` with \n, \r and \0 terminators and `-w`, old against new and its line loop against grep-regex's for \n) seeds 1, 2 and 3, 11,000 cases, 758,631 checks: 0 differences between old and new; 6 line-loop differences against grep-regex, the same 6 for old (the known `(?m)` judgements in the entry below). `bench grep` (the searcher's line loop over a 115 MB file of the repository's and ~/.cargo/registry's Rust sources, thread CPU ms, interleaved medians of 7, old / new / grep-regex, x86 Hand at load 23 on 5 cores): `\w+_\w+` 149 / 103 / 138, `[a-z]+_[a-z]+` 173 / 117 / 122, `\w+` 248 / 192 / 186; patterns with a prefilter unchanged within noise (`fn|let|impl` 67 / 69, `[A-Z][a-z]+Error` 15 / 13, `^\s*fn ` 13 / 14). psh -c on the same file (output/bench.py, CPU ms of the process, medians of 7, the regex-crate psh before 30db5d32b / before / after, load 25): rg -c `\w+_\w+` 204 / 231 / 194, `[a-z]+_[a-z]+` 188 / 256 / 206, `\w+` 254 / 296 / 278, `^\s*fn ` 43 / 58 / 47, `[0-9]{4,}` 114 / 133 / 112, every output byte-identical across the three. Commands: cargo clippy --locked -p psh-pattern and cargo check --locked -p psh-utils --target wasm32-unknown-unknown in crates/patches/psh, cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, output/rx equal and bench, output/bench.py.
- nanocode-sync's ordered B-tree finds a slot in a node of plain items (no drop, at most 16 bytes, such as `OrdMap<u64, u64>`) with a fixed five-step branchless search, and a lookup that reaches a leaf picks its answer without a branch (2026-11-13). crates/core/sync/src/tree.rs: `count_below` counts the entries ordered before the key by binary lifting over steps 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 (`SEARCH_STEPS`, the bit length of `NODE_ITEM_SLOTS` = 17), each step a `select_unpredictable`, so the loop runs the same five steps whatever a node holds and never mispredicts its exit; `search` turns that count into `Ok`/`Err` exactly as `binary_search_by` did for a total order, and `Locate::pick` (used by `Tree::find`, so `OrdMap::get`, `get_key_value`, `contains_key`, `OrdSet::get` and `contains`) selects the leaf entry or `None` with `select_unpredictable` instead of branching on found. Items that need drop or exceed 16 bytes (`String` keys) keep the early-exit search. Why: `perf stat` of a lookup loop showed std's `binary_search_by` leaving a data-dependent branch on hit or miss at the leaf: 2.10 million branch misses in 12.5 million lookups of a 16-entry `OrdMap<u64, u64>` with 25% hits (imbl 7.0.2: 5,600), which made a missed `get` 2x imbl's on both machines and the 100,000-entry gaps the persistent-collections entry measured (1.25x get). Measured (output/sync-bench getmicro, `perf stat -e cycles:u` on the Hand, AMD EPYC 9255 at load 12 to 15, before -> after, imbl in brackets): 16 entries all hits 350M -> 324M cycles (379M), 25% hits 402M -> 325M (395M) with 2.10M -> 6,260 branch misses; 1,000 entries 678M -> 536M (732M) and 712M -> 516M (716M); 100,000 entries 2,291M -> 1,634M (1,604M) and 2,466M -> 1,585M (1,355M); instructions 1.04G -> 0.93G at 16. On gak-9 (M1 Max, output/sync-bench ordmap2, medians of 5 rounds, two interleaved passes, load 12 to 33), ns per `get`, before -> after (imbl): 16 entries hits 3.6 -> 4.6 (3.9), 25% hits 8.5 to 9.3 -> 5.2 (4.2); 1,000 entries 24.8 -> 21.5 (22.1 to 22.9) and 33.1 to 33.9 -> 26.5 to 29.3 (23.1 to 25.8); 100,000 entries 68 to 76 -> 57 to 69 (55 to 63) and 87 to 108 -> 64 to 67 (56 to 73); clone+insert, clone+remove, range and iteration within noise of before, `String` rows unchanged. The one loss is about 1 ns on an all-hit 16-entry map on M1, where std's four-step loop beat five fixed steps; a non-short-circuit `&` in the step measured 1.6 to 1.9x slower on M1 and was dropped, as were `partition_point` (still a branch on found) and a linear count of the leaf (its trip count follows the leaf's length, so 100,000-entry maps doubled their branch misses). Equal: output/sync-bench getequal, 400 seeds of interleaved inserts and removes over maps of 0 to 20,000 entries (`OrdMap` with u64, u8, i32 and `String` keys, `OrdSet<u64>`), every probe's `get`, `get_key_value`, `contains_key`, `contains` and `OrdSet::get` against imbl =7.0.2 and std's `BTreeMap`, plus a full sweep of the key space and whole-map iteration and length per seed: 28,806,320 checks, 0 differences on the Hand (x86_64) and 28,804,720 on gak-9 (aarch64, before the iteration checks were added). Also measured and left as they are: `Swap::store` is 62 ns against arc-swap 1.9.2's 200 on the Hand and 47 against 86 on gak-9 (326 against 2,122 ns with 16 other threads holding debt nodes), and `Enclosed`/`Atom` new+drop is 20 to 34 ns against arc-swap's 84 to 144, so the store and new+drop rows of the arc-swap entry read arc-swap first and nanocode-sys second. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync` native and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` (no new warnings).
- nanocode-digest's SHA-512 and SHA-384 compress with the ARMv8.2 SHA512 instructions on aarch64 through nanocode-sys (2026-11-13, Georgios: restore the SIMD speed lost when sha2 left). crates/core/sys/src/sha512.rs holds `Sha512Instructions`, made only by `detect()` after `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("sha3")` (Rust's name for FEAT_SHA512 with FEAT_SHA3): `vsha512hq_u64`, `vsha512h2q_u64`, `vsha512su0q_u64`, `vsha512su1q_u64`, two rounds per call with the four state pairs rotating roles, as sha2 0.11's aarch64 backend; the 40 round pairs are unrolled by a local macro, because the loop form left the message words in memory and ran at 1,046 MB/s against sha2's 1,359. x86 keeps the portable rounds: sha2 0.11.0's x86 SHA-512 measured 501 against our 481 MB/s at 1 MiB and 506 against 511 at 16 KiB on the hosted Hand, within the noise of a loaded machine, so an AVX2 message schedule is not worth its unsafe code, and the hosted Hand has no SHA512 instructions (`vsha512rnds2`) to prove a kernel on. `detect()` answers None on x86 and WASM, and nanocode-digest runs its unchanged `compress_portable` there; the round constants are `nanocode_sys::sha512::ROUND_CONSTANTS`. Unsafe blocks, all in crates/core/sys/src/sha512.rs: `Sha512Instructions::compress` calling `arm::compress` (sound because the token exists only after `detect()` saw sha3); `arm::load_bytes` (`vld1q_u8` of a `&[u8; 16]`) and `arm::load_words` (`vld1q_u64` of a `&[u64; 2]`). Equality: output/sha-check (release) compares the new digest, origin/master's digest, a forced-scalar copy (nanocode-sys with `detect()` returning None) and sha1 0.11.0 / sha2 0.11.0 on lengths 0 to 1,100, 4,095 to 4,097, 65,535 to 65,537, 1 MiB and 300 seeded random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets 0 to 63, streamed updates in random chunk sizes (0 to 70,000 bytes) and real files: all equal on the hosted Hand (x86_64, SHA-NI) and gak-9 (M1 Max), 28,160 and 28,295 comparisons over 379 and 436 MB across SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. Throughput on gak-9 in MB/s, median of 9 interleaved rounds of thread CPU time (load average 12 to 45), before / after / sha2 0.11.0: SHA-512 64 B 239 / 528 / 564, 1 KiB 469 / 1,196 / 1,216, 16 KiB 531 / 1,368 / 1,357, 1 MiB 536 / 1,382 / 1,370; SHA-384 64 B 239 / 533 / 564, 1 KiB 469 / 1,202 / 1,216, 16 KiB 533 / 1,373 / 1,366, 1 MiB 540 / 1,387 / 1,378. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` of nanocode-sys and nanocode-digest for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown on the hosted Hand and natively on gak-9, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-digest's SHA-1 compresses with the CPU's SHA instructions through nanocode-sys (2026-11-13, Georgios: restore the SIMD speed lost when sha1 left). crates/core/sys/src/sha1.rs holds `Sha1Instructions`, made only by `detect()`: on x86 after sse2, sha, ssse3 and sse4.1 (`_mm_sha1rnds4_epu32`, `_mm_sha1nexte_epu32`, `_mm_sha1msg1_epu32`, `_mm_sha1msg2_epu32`, as sha1 0.11's x86 backend), on aarch64 after `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("sha2")`, which covers FEAT_SHA1 (`vsha1cq_u32`, `vsha1pq_u32`, `vsha1mq_u32`, `vsha1h_u32`, `vsha1su0q_u32`, `vsha1su1q_u32`). nanocode-digest's `compress` falls back to its unchanged portable rounds (`compress_portable`) when `detect()` answers None, always on WASM; the four round constants are `nanocode_sys::sha1::ROUND_CONSTANTS`. Unsafe blocks, all in crates/core/sys/src/sha1.rs: `Sha1Instructions::compress` calling `x86::compress` and `arm::compress` (sound because the token exists only after `detect()` saw every feature they enable); `x86::load` (`_mm_loadu_si128` of a `&[u8; 16]`); `arm::load_bytes` (`vld1q_u8` of a `&[u8; 16]`) and `arm::load_words` (`vld1q_u32` of a `&[u32; 4]`). Equality: output/sha-check (release) compares the new digest, origin/master's digest, a forced-scalar copy (nanocode-sys with `detect()` returning None) and sha1 0.11.0 / sha2 0.11.0 on lengths 0 to 1,100, 4,095 to 4,097, 65,535 to 65,537, 1 MiB and 300 seeded random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets 0 to 63, streamed updates in random chunk sizes (0 to 70,000 bytes) and real files: all equal on the hosted Hand (x86_64, SHA-NI) and gak-9 (M1 Max), 28,160 and 28,295 comparisons over 379 and 436 MB across SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. Throughput in MB/s, median of 9 interleaved rounds of thread CPU time, before / after / sha1 0.11.0: hosted Hand (load average 20 to 26) 64 B 294 / 583 / 602, 1 KiB 683 / 1,666 / 1,608, 16 KiB 729 / 1,899 / 1,919, 1 MiB 738 / 1,914 / 1,921; gak-9 (load average 40 to 73) 64 B 344 / 725 / 843, 1 KiB 788 / 1,916 / 1,909, 16 KiB 895 / 2,132 / 2,138, 1 MiB 948 / 2,178 / 2,180. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` of nanocode-sys and nanocode-digest for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown on the hosted Hand and natively on gak-9, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-digest's SHA-256 and SHA-224 compress with the CPU's SHA instructions through nanocode-sys (2026-11-13, Georgios: restore the SIMD speed lost when sha2 left). crates/core/sys/src/sha256.rs holds `Sha256Instructions`, a token only `detect()` makes: on x86 after `is_x86_feature_detected!` finds sse2, sha, ssse3 and sse4.1 (`_mm_sha256rnds2_epu32`, `_mm_sha256msg1_epu32`, `_mm_sha256msg2_epu32`, as sha2 0.11's x86 backend), on aarch64 after `is_aarch64_feature_detected!("sha2")` (`vsha256hq_u32`, `vsha256h2q_u32`, `vsha256su0q_u32`, `vsha256su1q_u32`); its `compress(state, blocks)` takes every whole block of an update in one call. nanocode-digest's `compress` asks `detect()` per call and otherwise runs its unchanged portable rounds, now `compress_portable`; WASM and CPUs without the instructions always take that path. The round constants moved to `nanocode_sys::sha256::ROUND_CONSTANTS`, read by both paths. Unsafe blocks, all in crates/core/sys/src/sha256.rs: `Sha256Instructions::compress` calling `x86::compress` and `arm::compress`, `#[target_feature]` functions that are sound to call because the token exists only after `detect()` saw every feature they enable; `x86::load` (`_mm_loadu_si128` of a `&[u8; 16]`: 16 readable bytes, an unaligned load); `arm::load_bytes` (`vld1q_u8` of a `&[u8; 16]`) and `arm::load_words` (`vld1q_u32` of a `&[u32; 4]`). Every intrinsic without a pointer is a safe call inside those `#[target_feature]` functions. Equality: output/sha-check (release) compares the new digest, origin/master's digest, a forced-scalar copy (nanocode-sys with `detect()` returning None) and sha1 0.11.0 / sha2 0.11.0 on lengths 0 to 1,100, 4,095 to 4,097, 65,535 to 65,537, 1 MiB and 300 seeded random lengths up to 1 MiB at random offsets 0 to 63, streamed updates in random chunk sizes (0 to 70,000 bytes) and real files: all equal on the hosted Hand (x86_64, SHA-NI) and gak-9 (M1 Max), 28,160 and 28,295 comparisons over 379 and 436 MB across SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. Throughput in MB/s, median of 9 interleaved rounds of thread CPU time, before / after / sha2 0.11.0: hosted Hand (load average 20 to 26 on 5 cores) SHA-256 64 B 151 / 533 / 576, 1 KiB 270 / 1,555 / 1,563, 16 KiB 316 / 1,770 / 1,784, 1 MiB 310 / 1,694 / 1,810, SHA-224 1 MiB 318 / 1,685 / 1,813; gak-9 (load average 40 to 73 on 10 cores) SHA-256 64 B 151 / 800 / 896, 1 KiB 292 / 1,881 / 1,916, 16 KiB 308 / 2,053 / 1,939, 1 MiB 310 / 2,087 / 2,079, SHA-224 1 MiB 306 / 2,048 / 1,951. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` of nanocode-sys and nanocode-digest for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown on the hosted Hand and natively on gak-9, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- rustpython-vm's build script no longer reruns on every build, so an incremental build stops recompiling rustpython-vm, rustpython-stdlib, nanocode-python and everything above them (2026-11-13, Georgios: lower compilation time). crates/patches/rustpython-vm/build.rs printed `cargo:rerun-if-changed=../../Lib/importlib/_bootstrap.py`, upstream's `../Lib/importlib/_bootstrap.py` rewritten when the crate was vendored (1bd77d4de); from crates/patches/rustpython-vm it names crates/Lib, which does not exist, and cargo reruns a build script whose watched file is missing on every build. The rerun is not free: the script hands rustc `RUSTPYTHON_GIT_*` and `RUSTPYTHON_BUILD_INFO` through `cargo:rustc-env`, so cargo recompiles the crate after each run, then rustpython-stdlib (built on it), nanocode-python and nanocode-cli. The line goes: what upstream watched through it, its vm/Lib/python_builtins/_frozen_importlib*.py symlinks into Lib/importlib, are copies in crates/patches/rustpython-vm/Lib/python_builtins here, which the script's own `python_files` loop already watches, and `py_freeze!` reads nothing else. Found with `cargo build --timings` after `touch bin/nanocode/src/main.rs`: rustpython-vm's `build-script (run)` and the four units above it were the whole rebuild. Behavior: unchanged for a fresh build; the `sys.version` build info (git hash, `git describe --dirty`, commit date) is now written when the script runs, on the first build of a target directory or when a watched .py file changes, rather than on every build, as upstream does. Measured with output-free interleaved rebuilds (python interleave.py: each tree built once, then `touch FILE && cargo <kind> --locked -p nanocode-cli`, before and after alternating, RUSTC_WRAPPER= so buildcache stays out), gak-9 (M1 Max, aarch64, CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=3, load 9 to 32 from other agents), medians: check after touching bin/nanocode/src/main.rs 15.77 s to 0.61 s (5 runs each), after touching crates/core/types-core/src/lib.rs 11.55 s to 3.80 s (3); dev build 16.77 s to 1.97 s (main.rs, 5) and 16.65 s to 9.74 s (types-core, 3); release build 115.81 s to 1.25 s (main.rs, 3) and 223.95 s to 174.65 s (types-core, 2). Hosted Hand (x86_64, 5 cores, load 16 to 37 from other agents, CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2): before, the same main.rs touch took 205.5 s for `cargo check` (one run in the baseline sequence), all of it rustpython-vm, rustpython-stdlib, nanocode-python and nanocode-cli. Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo build --locked [--release] -p nanocode-cli` on both machines (the harness's builds).
- The terminal interface's Tokio runtime has one worker thread, as `exec` and `sessions` already did (2026-11-13, Georgios: "Optimize it - you can figure it out", after being asked whether the TUI should start one worker per core). `Builder::new_multi_thread()` without `worker_threads` starts one worker per CPU, 32 on dev-georgios (AMD EPYC 4585PX, 32 threads), so the TUI ran 35 threads, and each worker's mimalloc heap and stack stayed resident. Swarm work (store writers, python3, psh) already runs on threads of its own. Measured on dev-georgios at 407831762 with both builds made by scripts/build-cli.sh (dist, non-PIE, BOLT 19 with `-icf=1`), bench/cli's `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --only=nc` alternating the builds over 4 batches of 4 rounds (16 samples each, medians, load average 40 to 44 from other jobs, so times are relative): resident memory 1 s after the first frame 24.14 to 20.26 MB, anonymous memory 10.34 to 6.29 MB, threads 35 to 4, CPU to the first frame 46.7 to 36.9 ms, first frame 39.0 to 28.2 ms; `exec` one-shot unchanged (max RSS 17.0 and 16.75 MB). Checked: `--help` and error output of nc and every subcommand (67 cases) are byte-identical to the last clap build (0838af4d5^), apart from the `--identity-*` flags added since. Still open from the same profile: of the 8.7 MB of nc's code resident after the first frame only 2.8 MB is executed (1.3 MB of it outside BOLT's hot section), and 3.2 MB of read-only data is resident where 1.2 MB is read, so the rest is the kernel's fault-around (64 KB) mapping cold neighbors; with fault_around_bytes at 4096 the same process held 10.8 MB. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli` passes.
- Tokio features are declared where they are used, and the `nanocode` facade's example-only dependencies move to dev-dependencies (2026-11-13, Georgios, through the Nanocode 1.0 workstream: audit tokio features per crate and keep only what is used; DEPENDENCIES.md's note from `cargo shear`). Removed after a grep of each crate's sources for the APIs a feature gates and a native and wasm32 check of each crate: `macros` from nanocode-agent-host and nanocode-mcp-tools (no `select!`, `join!`, `pin!` or attribute), `sync` from nanocode-computer-repl, `net` from nanocode-process, `process` from nanocode-tool-runtime, `process` and `rt-multi-thread` from nanocode-backend-claude, `net`, `process` and `rt-multi-thread` from nanocode-backend-codex, `time` from nc-lite. The facade's tokio (`rt`, `sync`, `time`, `macros`, `net`, `fs`), serde_json, nanocode-home and Linux libc were named by no line of crates/nanocode/src; its examples use them, so they are its dev-dependencies now, with the features the examples call (`fs`, `io-util`, `macros`, `net`, `rt-multi-thread`, `signal`, `sync`, `time`; `io-util` and `signal` they had only through unification). A first pass also dropped `process` from nanocode-computer-repl, whose `use tokio::{..}` group the grep missed; the native check refused it (`unresolved import tokio::process`) and it stays. Measured with `cargo tree --locked -e features -i tokio -p <crate>` and `cargo tree -e normal,build -p <crate>` on each changed crate, nanocode and nanocode-cli, before and after: every resolved graph keeps the same tokio features and the same packages (nanocode 214, nanocode-cli 286, nc-lite 219 on top of c58a5df99), because nanocode-sync alone turns on `io-util`, `net`, `rt`, `sync` and `time` natively and the binaries turn on the rest, so nanocode-cli's build and binary cannot change and no release build was timed. What the declarations buy is that a host taking one of these crates alone, or the facade without its examples, no longer asks tokio for what the crate does not call. The rest of the audit, with why nothing else moved: serde_json's `raw_value` is used by the Claude client and backend (`RawValue` in ten files) and `float_roundtrip` keeps parsed numbers exact; `preserve_order` (indexmap, equivalent and hashbrown 0.17, three packages) is bin/nanocode's, whose JSON output order depends on it, and stays with the CLI thread. tracing (two packages of its own) stays: hyper-util and the telemetry crates' public `GenAi` and `Held` use it, and its `attributes` feature, with tracing-attributes and syn's use there, came only through zbus and left with it in c58a5df99. url and idna (two packages each) stay while reqwest and tower-http need them; nanocode-schema's direct idna is free once they go. syn and quote (nanocode-tools-macros) stay: serde_derive, tokio-macros and the RustPython derive crates need syn 2 anyway, so rewriting the macro without them saves no package. regex is no longer in the graph. windows-sys: no Linux, macOS or wasm32 graph contains any windows package (`cargo tree -e normal,build --target <t> --workspace` lists none for x86_64 and aarch64 Linux, x86_64 and aarch64 macOS and wasm32-unknown-unknown); 0.61 stays in the lock for tokio, mio, socket2, rustix and errno on Windows, and nanocode-sys's use (the Windows root store reader, which `cargo check --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-process` builds on gak-9) is live for Windows library builds; 0.52 with windows-targets and eight windows_* crates (ten packages) comes only through ring's aarch64 Windows dependency. Found meanwhile: `cargo check --lib -p nanocode-agent-host --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` fails on master a8a79f3d3 with or without this change (nanocode-agent imports `CellJournal`, `CellJournalSink`, `CellJournalUpdate`, `CellJournals` and `JournaledCallState` from `nanocode_tool_host::code_mode`, which wasm32 does not export). Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p <crate>` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown for the eight library crates, `cargo check --locked -p nc-lite`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode --examples`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on the eight (no warnings).

- bin/nanocode-sim `--scenario runtime` runs the real Nanocode runtime, the Claude backend with Code Mode cells and the subagent runtime, against a scripted model over a faulty network, with crashes and restarts (2026-11-13). network.rs is a `HttpTransport` (ClaudeClient::with_transport) whose per-request fate is drawn from the seed: connect latency up to 20 ms to 3 s, refused before sending (unsent), the response lost after the server processed the request (a duplicate delivery when the client retries), a 429, 500 or 529 with `retry-after-ms`, slow headers up to 180 s, the SSE body split into up to 6 chunks with gaps, truncated with or without a transport error, and duplicate delivery; 3 seeds in 10 (`CALM_PPM`) and `--calm` have none. server.rs is the model: it reads the agent (`SIMROOT r<i> turn <t>` or a child's `SIMCHILD <label> depth <d>` task) and the number of exec steps from the request, answers `wait` when the last tool result says a cell is running, and otherwise plays the seed's plan for that agent and turn as exec cells: `tools.sim_effect` calls with keys unique to the agent, turn and step, spawn_agent + wait_agent of up to 3 children two levels deep, list_agents + send_agent_message, submit_result, then a final text. whole.rs builds a runtime per epoch (`Nanocode::builder().claude(..).tools(sim_effect).durability(..).build()` on the simulator's executor and host), 1 or 2 roots of 1 to 3 turns submitted with request ids `turn-<t>` (a turn that failed while its record is still Pending is resubmitted under the same id, up to 8 times), optional hibernation with up to 4 resident children, cancel_all or close_all at a random time in 1 seed in 5 each, a store (`--store memory`, a MemoryStore with no crashes, or `kv`, a `KeyValueStore` over the store workload's `SimKv`, clean and acknowledging durably, with 0 to 3 crashes in the first 120 s, after which the process's tasks are dropped and the next epoch reopens every root with `open_session` and `await_restored`), and it calls `forget_templates` at each epoch as a new process would. Invariants: an effect key runs at most once across crashes and retries (dispatched work may be reported uncertain, never replayed); every assistant message in any request is one the model sent to that agent, canonically equal (so a truncated stream is never kept as a message); every acknowledged turn's prompt and final text are in the root's later requests (acknowledged means the turn returned the model's final text and `flush` succeeded); a returned turn's text is the model's final text; every root settles (`Runtime::settle`) within 1,800 s of virtual time and its directory lists no active agent; `--twice` gives the same trace digest. Debugging: `NANOCODE_SIM_LOG=warn` prints the runtime's tracing events, `NANOCODE_SIM_POLLS=1` prints which task the executor polls among which ready ones, each spawned task's spawn site (a backtrace, with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=line-tables-only CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none`) and the simulated store's reads, and a `--twice` failure prints the first trace line where the runs part. That found the entries above (time read outside the host, unbiased selects, HashMap order, the UUIDv7 floor, the template cache, SharedStore's per-state order). Results on dev-georgios (32 cores, shared with other jobs), release: `--scenario runtime --seeds 0..20000` before the stop and hibernation knobs: 19,988 of 20,000 passed; with them, 10,000 seeds `--twice` (20 processes of 500, 2m38s wall): 9,962 passed, 19 failed to settle and 19 printed two digests. Open, not fixed: (a) after a retryable model failure (`Settlement::FailAttempt`) the session owner holds a deferred continuation whose payload records were never persisted, and resubmitting the same request id fails for good with `invalid durability state: missing payload record b3:...` from LoadPayloads (session.rs handle_command, payload.rs load_many_noting), so the root never settles: `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --seed 12186` (MemoryStore, no crash), also 15432 and 17253; (b) a subagent completion that stays pending after restarts although `deliver_completions` reports it routed: `--seed 201`, and 3 of `--store kv --calm --seeds 0..300` on a8a79f3d3; (c) about 1 seed in 500 with crashes over kv gives two digests across processes, still a random order after restore (`--seed 1140`: after the subagent root watch starts, the store driver is or is not woken in the same poll). The store, agents and turns scenarios print the same digests as before. Cargo.lock: nanocode-sim gains `nanocode` (default features off, local-cells on), `http` and `tracing`, all in the workspace; no package is added. Commands: `cargo build --locked --release -p nanocode-sim`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sim`.
