- `SharedStore` over a store with concurrent handles (`KeyValueStore`, the only one) applies the writes of one state in the order they were sent (2026-11-13). `drive_concurrently` ran every request on its own handle and task, but the subagent journal writer (child_journal.rs) pipelines `replace_latest` and `replace_deferred` for one state with consecutive expected revisions, so revision r+1's compare-and-swap could run before revision r landed: the writer then failed with `durability state revision conflict: expected 17, found 15` or `key-value store refused to replace version ... while reporting it as current`, and the root's subagent journal stopped persisting. Found by `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --store kv --calm` (a Claude runtime with subagent trees over `KeyValueStore<SimKv>`; replay `--seed 3` and `--seed 7`, and seed 32 without any crash). The driver now keeps, per state id, the requests that write it (`command_state`, as the grouped driver does) behind the one in flight and starts the next when that completes; other states and reads still run concurrently, and a flush still waits for every earlier operation, queued ones included. With a copy of this stack whose shared_store.rs is the old one, `--scenario runtime --store kv --calm` over about 9,500 seeds failed 3,536 (2,097 refused, 784 revision conflicts, the rest roots that never settled behind them); with it 19 fail, all the open liveness failure recorded in the runtime scenario entry. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability` (and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability`. File: crates/runtime/durability/src/shared_store.rs.
- `nanocode_backend_claude::durability::forget_templates()` empties the process-wide cache of decoded prompt templates (`PREFIXES`) (2026-11-13). `hydrate_snapshot` skips reading a template record from the store when the cache has its key, so a process that restored a session once reads less from the store the next time; bin/nanocode-sim restarts a simulated process in the same OS process, where the cache survived the crash and hid the reads a real restart makes (`nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --seed 24 --twice` gave two digests in one process because the second run issued fewer store reads, and a template record lost by the store would not have been noticed). The simulator calls it at the start of every epoch. Production never calls it; nothing else changes. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude` (and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude`. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/durability/{format.rs,mod.rs}.
- The Claude backend, Code Mode and the tool host read monotonic time, sleep and spawn through nanocode-platform and choose in a fixed order, so a whole Nanocode runtime replays a seed exactly under bin/nanocode-sim's host (2026-11-13). Found by `nanocode-sim --scenario runtime` (next entries), whose `--twice` compares the trace digests of two runs of a seed. (1) Real time leaked into virtual waits: code-mode-engine computed a host's park deadline and setTimeout deadlines from `std::time::Instant::now()` and slept the difference on the host clock, so how long a run took on the CPU changed when cells woke (`--scenario runtime --store memory --calm --seeds 0..100 --twice` failed 69 of 100 with different digests, 0 after). Every `Instant::now()` in code-mode-engine (8), Code Mode's code_mode/mod.rs (yield deadlines, stall watches and spans, 16), the Claude backend (agent.rs and agent/keep.rs, 23) and the tool host (5) is now `nanocode_platform::now()`; Claude's `spawn_task` and Code Mode's `spawn` call `nanocode_platform::spawn` and Claude's retry and keep-alive sleeps `nanocode_platform::sleep` (natively they called `tokio::spawn` and `tokio::time::sleep`, which panic outside a Tokio runtime). Without a host each is what it was plus one acquire load. (2) Six `tokio::select!`s in the Claude backend drew a random branch (tokio's thread RNG, seeded per process): admission vs cancellation and the policy-blocked wait in `defer_turn`, opening a Messages response and reading its next event vs cancellation, the retry backoff vs cancellation, and keep's notification vs its sleep. They are `biased` with the cancellation (or notification) first, so a cancellation that is ready is seen before more work, and a ready stream still cannot be starved because cancellation fires once (`--seed 46`: two digests across processes before, one after). (3) Code Mode kept live cells and a cell's pending call receipts in `HashMap`s and walked them to retire, terminate and join the cells of a turn (`terminate_all` too) and to report calls a dead cell left unknown, so which cell's waiter woke first and the order of "outcome unknown" receipts in the transcript changed per process; both are `BTreeMap`s keyed by id now (`--seed 111` diverged across processes before, not after). Over `--scenario runtime --seeds 0..1000 --twice` (network faults, kv crashes) the failures went 41, then 27 after (1), 18 after (2) and (3), and 1 with the UUIDv7 entry (seed 201, a liveness failure, not a digest). The store, agents and turns scenarios print the same digests before and after (md5 of `--seeds 0..400 --twice --verbose` seed lines: store 97d69558, agents c936fb3a, turns 794d17e4, turns --policy turnlog 8e7d012f, on a81ec4e87 and with this stack). Speed: output/dst-bench (a Tokio multi-thread runtime, a Claude runtime over a mock HttpTransport, 300 roots each spawning 4 children whose cells call a tool and submit_result, MemoryStore or JsonlStore; dev-georgios at load 75-80 from other jobs), base a81ec4e87 against this stack, three interleaved rounds, wall s (CPU s): memory 8.40, 7.90, 8.10 (13.2, 12.6, 12.7) against 7.60, 8.45, 7.38 (12.5, 14.7, 11.5); jsonl 76.8, 75.9, 59.6 (60.8, 61.2, 56.6) against 71.8, 69.2, 60.5 (62.0, 60.1, 58.2): within noise. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib` (and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`) and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-code-mode-engine and nanocode-tool-host. Not changed: claude_bash.rs (tokio Instants of a real process), tool-runtime's attachment and remote hosts, and `Instant::now()` in crates the scenario does not reach. Files: crates/backends/claude/src/{agent.rs,agent/keep.rs}, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs, crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/{bytes.rs,cell.rs,host.rs}, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/runtime/{execution.rs,registry.rs}.
- `nanocode_platform::Host` can own the UUIDv7 sequence: `Host::uuid_stamps` (default `None`) returns the `AtomicU64` that `uuid_v7` keeps its last stamp in, and without it `uuid_v7` uses its process-wide `LAST` exactly as before (2026-11-13). `uuid_v7` raises the stamp to at least the last one issued so ids stay ordered within a millisecond; under bin/nanocode-sim that floor outlived a seed, so a second run of the same seed in one process (`--twice`) started its state ids (`state/<uuid v7>`) about 166 s of virtual time later, their order in the simulated store's key listings changed and the run diverged (`nanocode-sim --scenario runtime --seed 194 --twice`: two digests in one process, one digest across processes). The simulator's host now owns a stamp counter and resets it when a seed starts. Production: no host is installed, so the only change is the `host()` load `system_time()` already does. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-platform` (and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, where `uuid_v7` is unchanged), `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-platform`. Files: crates/core/platform/src/{lib.rs,native.rs}.
- bin/nanocode-sim/cfo.sh drops the `seal_skipped` canary, fuzzes the runtime scenario on both stores, and labels known failures (2026-11-13). `--scenario turns --mutation seal_skipped` is caught by no flags: 0 of 20,000 seeds each with the default live seqs, `--live-seqs floor`, `--policy turnlog`, `--calm` and `--row-limit 1024`, while `gap` and `reuse` fail seq_unique just as often without the mutation (21 and 601 of 2,000). Its row failed every batch (1,288 batches in the loop's first 0.84 hours), which buried every other failure, so it leaves the table until the turns scenario catches it. The runtime scenario's rows are `--store memory` and `--store kv` at 8 each, and `--twice` on each store plus `--store kv --calm` at 2 each. A row whose `--scenario` the binary's usage line does not list is skipped, so these rows start with the first master commit that has the scenario, and older commits never run them as usage errors. Known failures are lines of a scenario-name prefix and a fixed string, in `default_known` or in a `known` file in the loop root. A pass job whose every FAIL line matches one is recorded with `"known":true`, and so is each such failing seed. `summary` counts these jobs in a column of their own, and `failures` tags their groups `[known]`. The defaults are the open runtime bugs dst reported: `runtime ... did not settle` (a pending completion after a restart, and a resubmit after a retryable model failure that finds a payload record missing, such as `--scenario runtime --seed 12186`), `runtime ... missing payload record`, and `runtime_kv_twice ... nondeterminism` after KeyValueStore restarts. Each line goes when its bug is fixed. Checked: `bash -n`, and a stub binary with and without the runtime scenario in its usage line: 28 and 23 rows; a runtime job with a "did not settle" seed was recorded as known in the job and seed lines, in `summary` and in `failures`.
- nanocode-computer's Linux backend speaks D-Bus and the X11 protocol itself, and zbus 5.19.0, atspi-common 0.14.0, atspi-proxies 0.14.0 and x11rb 0.13.2 leave with 45 more packages (2026-11-13): zvariant, zvariant_derive, zvariant_utils, zbus_macros, zbus_names, zbus_xml, zbus-lockstep and its macros, x11rb-protocol, async-io, async-executor, async-process, async-signal, async-broadcast, async-channel, async-lock, async-task, async-recursion, async-trait, blocking, polling, piper, futures-lite, fastrand, event-listener-strategy, concurrent-queue, ordered-stream, endi, zcheapstr, serde_repr, static_assertions, memoffset, syn 3.0.9, proc-macro-crate, toml_edit, toml_parser, toml_datetime, winnow, tempfile, uuid, gethostname, uds_windows, hermit-abi, and rustix 1.1.4 with linux-raw-sys 0.12.1 (zbus's async-io was rustix's last user since 7e369c962, so rustix leaves the graph). The new modules sit in crates/integrations/computer/src/linux, beside the only code that uses them. wire.rs is D-Bus marshalling: one `Value` for every D-Bus type, decoding any signature in either byte order within the specification's limits (signatures of 255 bytes, 32 nested arrays and 32 nested structs, arrays of 64 MiB, messages of 128 MiB, zero padding, booleans 0 or 1, UTF-8 strings ending in their one zero byte), and encoding the basic types, structs and variants the backend sends (it sends no arrays, and encoding one panics). dbus.rs is the connection: `unix:path=` and `unix:abstract=` addresses tried in order (other transports are skipped; nothing the backend reaches uses them), SASL EXTERNAL with an empty authorization identity so the bus reads the socket's credentials (an answer longer than "OK", 32 hex digits and CRLF, the longest one the client accepts, is a refusal), Hello, then one owning task per connection that holds the socket: it numbers the calls, hands each reply to its caller's oneshot by serial (and drops the waits of callers that timed out at the next call), sends AddMatch for a watch and RemoveMatch when the watch is forgotten (`unwatch`, which does not block, or the next signal after its receiver closed), forwards a watched sender's signals that pass the backend's filter, answers Peer.Ping and refuses other incoming calls with UnknownObject. Calls reach it through a channel of 64 commands (the tree read's parallelism) and are checked first, as zbus's proxy builder checked them, for a valid bus name and object path, since dbus-daemon disconnects a client that sends an invalid one. a11y.rs holds the AT-SPI values the code tests: the 130 role names indexed by `ATSPI_ROLE_*`, the 44 state bits (a state set of other than two words or with a bit past them reads as no answer, as atspi-common's did) and the five interfaces it checks. xproto.rs is X11: DISPLAY parsed as x11rb parses it ([protocol/]host:display[.screen]), the abstract socket and then /tmp/.X11-unix/X<n>, TCP 6000+n with a loopback peer taken as local, MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE-1 from XAUTHORITY or ~/.Xauthority matched as x11rb matches it (wild family, or the same family and address, and an empty or equal display number; the local address is nanocode_sys::unix::host_name, as x11rb's gethostname), the setup (screens, depths, visuals, pixmap formats, keycodes, resource ids), the 16 core requests x11.rs makes, QueryExtension and XTEST FakeInput. Replies, errors and PropertyNotify events are read in sequence order; an unchecked request's error is dropped once a later reply arrives (x11rb queued it with every other event the connection got, a MappingNotify for each remapped key among them, for as long as the display lived), and events other than PropertyNotify are not kept. The connection uses `Cell` and `RefCell` and is owned by one thread: the launch guard's watcher owns its own connection and ends when the guard shuts that socket down, where x11rb's locked connection was shared with it and woken by a property change on a window made for that. No unsafe code (the crate keeps `unsafe_code = "deny"`); the session bus fallback path takes nanocode_sys::unix::user_id. Atspi's calls keep their shape (`proxy` now checks the names and returns an `Object` whose `call`, `get` and `set` return futures that own their encoded message), and every timeout, bound and message stays as it was. Fixed on the way, in the old code's dependencies: atspi-common's ObjectRef decoding asserts that a non-null reference names a bus, so an app answering Parent or GetSelectedChild with an empty name and a path panicked the step (now such a reference reads as none), and its InterfaceSet fails on any interface name it does not list, so an app with one newer interface read as having none, without text, values, actions or editing (unknown names are now ignored). Not kept: zbus's tcp, launchd and DBUS_COOKIE_SHA1 paths and X11's BIG-REQUESTS (every request here is a few hundred bytes); X errors read "X11 error <code> for request <major>.<minor> on <value>" instead of x11rb's debug text, in the messages that quote them. Behavior, checked with output/linux-cua (its own workspace with a path dependency on crates/integrations/computer and the tree's Cargo.lock; one binary that runs JSON steps through `Computer::new(Provider::native(..))`), run under xvfb-run (1280x800x24, an MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE-1 Xauthority) and dbus-run-session with GTK_MODULES=gail:atk-bridge, openbox as the window manager and a python3-gi GTK 3.24.41 window (label, button, entry, password entry, check box, combo box, spin button, expander, a scrolled 60-line text view and a drawing area that logs presses, releases and motion), with at-spi2-core 2.52.0: 39 steps in pointer mode and the same 39 in watched mode (list_apps twice, get_app_state with and without screenshots and full trees, clicks by action on a button, check box and expander, a right click with no menu, set_value on an entry, a combo box (and an option it lacks), a spin button, type_text through EditableText and as XTEST keys, including é and € that borrow a spare keycode, select_text, perform_secondary_action present and absent, scroll through a scroll bar's Value and with nothing to scroll, press_key F5, ctrl+shift+k and two keys the engine refuses, a focus by GrabFocus, pointer clicks at points, a double and a middle click on an element's extents, a drag, an unknown element, launching an installed .desktop app with startup notification and the focus guard, and an unknown app). Before (a81ec4e87's code, built from 547423275, whose nanocode-computer is the same) and after, the results (every state text, error, screenshot SHA-256 and the app's own log of what reached it) are identical in both modes once pids and the drag's motion count (11 or 10 between two runs of the old code alike) are masked; two runs of the old code match each other the same way. - bin/nanocode-sim/cfo.sh fuzzes nanocode master continuously, as tempoxyz/zempo's CFO (src/scripts/cfo.zig, scripts/cfo_supervisor.sh) fuzzes zempo (2026-11-13). `cfo.sh supervise` loops `cfo.sh run`, copied from the latest master before each run so the loop updates itself. A run fetches master, builds `nanocode-sim` in release into `bins/<commit>` and, for a time budget (`NANOCODE_CFO_BUDGET_SECS`, 3,600 by default, zempo's 60 minutes), keeps `NANOCODE_CFO_WORKERS` jobs (24) running on `NANOCODE_CFO_FUZZ_CPUS` (8-31), each one batch of seeds from a random 62-bit start. Every `NANOCODE_CFO_REFRESH_SECS` (300, zempo's 5 minutes) it fetches master again, builds a new commit on `NANOCODE_CFO_BUILD_CPUS` (0-5) while fuzzing goes on, and moves the next jobs to it. Each job takes the row of a weighted table with the least runtime for its weight, as zempo's table does: store content and store slots 16 each (4 each with `--twice`), agents 16 (4 twice), turns reference and turnlog 8 each, and turnlog twice, calm and `--row-limit 1024` 2 each. The 13 canaries get 1 each, and each must be caught (`MUTATION ... caught`) in a batch of `NANOCODE_CFO_CANARY_SEEDS` (400: on seeds 0..1000 the weakest, `finish_before_row`, is caught by 142). A scenario that the binary's usage line names and the table lacks is added at weight 8, and 2 with `--twice`, so new runtime scenarios are fuzzed as they land. A pass row's batch size adapts so that a job takes about `NANOCODE_CFO_JOB_SECS` (60), at most doubling per job. A job gets `NANOCODE_CFO_TIMEOUT_SECS` (1,800, zempo's 30 minutes) and is killed past it. Results are JSON lines in `results.jsonl`: one per job (time, commit, scenario, kind, first seed, count, ok, exit code, passed, failed, wall seconds, its replay command and first failure), and one per failing seed with the replay command nanocode-sim printed, pointed at the binary that ran it; a failing job's output is kept in `failures/`. `cfo.sh summary [HOURS]` prints runs, seeds, failed jobs and seeds per hour by scenario; `cfo.sh failures [HOURS]` groups failures by scenario and first failing line with the digits taken out, with one replay command each, as zempo's LOOP.md groups them. `cfo.sh install` writes and starts a `systemd --user` unit with `MemoryMax=32G`, `Restart=always` and `Nice=10`. It runs on dev-georgios (32 cores) under /home/ubuntu/dev/scratch/tiger/cfo. Over its first 0.84 hours (7 master commits, of which 61b949495 to 407831762 among them) it ran 26.5 million seeds, 31.5 million per hour: 18.1 million per hour of pass rows (turns reference 7.6, calm 3.0, store slots 2.0, turnlog 1.7, store content 1.7, agents 0.86, turnlog with a row limit 0.38, the `--twice` rows 0.1 to 0.26 each) and 13.4 million of canaries. No pass seed failed. One canary fails every batch: `--scenario turns --mutation seal_skipped` is never caught, on master too (0 of 20,000 seeds with the default live seqs, which never seal; 0 of 20,000 with `--live-seqs floor`, `--policy turnlog`, `--calm` or `--row-limit 1024`; with `--live-seqs gap` or `reuse` the same seq_unique failures come with and without the mutation, 21 and 601 of 2,000), so the check the turns entry pairs with it does not see a skipped seal; it stays in the table as a failing row until the scenario catches it. Checked: `bash -n`, and a 40-second run with 2 workers on the hosted Hand that ran every row and recorded 99 jobs.
- nanocode-durability's runtime asserts its fences, revisions, counters and pipelines (2026-11-13). shared_store.rs: the grouped driver asserts that it never runs more groups than the store's writers, that no state is in two in-flight groups, that a finished group's states were in flight, that its barrier, operation and group counters never go below zero (release builds would wrap them), and that every grouped commit has exactly one answer waiting; a latest write asserts that it stages each record key once. child_journal.rs: pipelined journal writes are asserted to name consecutive revisions when queued; the next revision is a checked add that fails the save before the write is queued, where `saturating_add` clamped it; and a write the store settles with any revision other than its expected one plus one fails the journal (Backend) instead of becoming the owner's revision. memory.rs: an acquire asserts that its fence passes the previous owner's, and a commit asserts that its events take consecutive sequence numbers from the first. session.rs: an event range the store acknowledges must start at or after the next sequence this owner already holds, or the session is poisoned with the existing "does not match the committed events" error, so a store that hands out an event sequence twice is caught. Hot-path cost, measured with output/durability-ledger's swarm (SWARM flat, 10,000 agents, 1,000 concurrent, mock model) on dev-georgios, base 61b949495 against the same commit with these checks, 7 interleaved rounds alternating which build runs first, pinned to cores 0-7 while the continuous fuzzer below held cores 8-31 (load 34 to 64): median CPU seconds base -> with checks were memory 28.7 -> 28.6, jsonl 30.2 -> 30.6, sqlite 34.4 -> 35.1, rows (RowStore over SQLite) 33.7 -> 33.6, and the minimums 27.9 -> 28.0, 29.1 -> 29.1, 34.2 -> 33.7, 32.8 -> 33.1; median settled seconds 8.10 -> 7.41, 10.09 -> 9.63, 15.88 -> 15.35, 15.33 -> 16.34. The differences are inside the run-to-run spread, so every check is `assert!` and none is `debug_assert!`. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown; nanocode-sim with the change, on dev-georgios: `sweep.sh 0 100000 8 --twice` and `--records slots --twice` pass 100,000 of 100,000 each (204 s and 146 s), `--scenario agents --twice`, `--scenario turns --twice` and `--scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` pass 20,000 of 20,000 each, 0 panics and no assertion fired; the store canaries are still caught.
- nanocode-durability-core asserts its own fences, revisions and encodings, and refuses the inputs that would break them, as TIGER_STYLE.md asks (2026-11-13). kv.rs: every head version `KeyValueStore` writes is asserted to parse back to the fence, revision and owner it was written with (`version`, one assertion per field). The two inputs that broke that are refused before anything is written: an acquire with an empty owner id is NotCommitted (it wrote the version `1.0.`, which `Head::parse` refuses, so every later peek, owner read and acquire of that state failed with "invalid key-value state version": one `OwnerId::from(String::new())` made the state unreadable for good), and a replace with a token of fence 0 or an empty owner id is Fenced (no acquire grants either). staged.rs: `Staged::check`, run after every staged write and acquire, asserts that the revision never falls below the base, that there is one payload per staged revision, that the owner's fence never falls below the base owner's and that the head payload is the last staged payload; a staged acquire asserts that its fence passes the one it replaces; `commit_to`'s replay checks that each revision the store answers is the one it committed over plus one and otherwise returns a Backend error (uncertain, since the head moved); and a base store that answers fewer record reads than asked is an error, where `read.next().flatten()` made the missing answers read as absent records. payload.rs: `Layout::of` asserts that its chunks are non-empty, end on character boundaries, cover the content exactly and get one hash each; `manifest_tree` asserts that it holds whole hashes and expects hex where `unwrap_or_default` would have hashed an empty string; the staged overlay that reachability reads through refuses a short answer as StagedStore does. row.rs: the row index asserts that it never un-counts more keys than it counted when it reloads or evicts a state (release builds have no overflow checks, so an underflow of `keys` would wrap and make eviction drop every state). sql.rs gains nothing: its fences and revisions are checked inside its statements and every answer it reads is already parsed into typed errors. Store answers stay typed errors, never assertions (TIGER_STYLE.md: a store is external input). Hot-path cost, measured with output/durability-ledger's swarm (SWARM flat, 10,000 agents, 1,000 concurrent, mock model) on dev-georgios, base 61b949495 against the same commit with these checks, 7 interleaved rounds alternating which build runs first, pinned to cores 0-7 while the continuous fuzzer below held cores 8-31 (load 34 to 64): median CPU seconds base -> with checks were memory 28.7 -> 28.6, jsonl 30.2 -> 30.6, sqlite 34.4 -> 35.1, rows (RowStore over SQLite) 33.7 -> 33.6, and the minimums 27.9 -> 28.0, 29.1 -> 29.1, 34.2 -> 33.7, 32.8 -> 33.1; median settled seconds 8.10 -> 7.41, 10.09 -> 9.63, 15.88 -> 15.35, 15.33 -> 16.34. The differences are inside the run-to-run spread, so every check is `assert!` and none is `debug_assert!`. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown; nanocode-sim with the change, on dev-georgios: `sweep.sh 0 100000 8 --twice` and `--records slots --twice` pass 100,000 of 100,000 each (204 s and 146 s), `--scenario agents --twice`, `--scenario turns --twice` and `--scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` pass 20,000 of 20,000 each, 0 panics and no assertion fired; the store canaries are still caught.
- `RecordCache` bounds its eviction order: a record forgotten and cached again leaves at most one stale order entry per cached record (2026-11-13). `Records::forget` removed a record from `values` but left its key in `order`, and `insert` pushed the key again, so every blank-then-rewrite of a cached record (a commit that blanks a key and writes it again, as Code Mode's cell journal does when a resumed cell writes its journal again) added an order entry that only an eviction under budget pressure would pop: a cache below its budget grew without bound, and when it did evict, popping the stale entry dropped the newer copy of the record first. Each cached record now carries the insert count it was cached at (`inserted`, a u64 whose `checked_add` is asserted never to wrap), `order` holds (key, count) pairs, eviction drops a record only when the popped count is that record's own, and an insert that leaves more than one stale entry per cached record (`STALE_ORDER_PER_VALUE`, the factor that makes the compaction amortized O(1) per insert) keeps only the live entries. Asserted: no blank record is inserted (the rule of the 2026-11-12 entry that RecordCache never caches a blank record), eviction makes room for any record that fits the budget, every cached record has an order entry, the order stays within its bound, and `forget` never un-counts more bytes than are cached. Measured with output/tiger-cache (a `CachedStore` over `MemoryStore` with a 1 MiB budget, each commit blanking and rewriting one of 16 keys; release; 3 interleaved runs on the 5-core hosted Hand): before, RSS grew 97 to 98 bytes per commit (2.0 to 97.8 MB over 1,000,000 commits) in 2.54 to 3.20 s; after, it did not grow (2.5 to 1.1 MB) in 2.62 to 3.10 s. With 20,000 keys over 200,000 commits, which evicts, RSS went from 2.4 to 30.7 MB before and to 15.8 MB after. Public API unchanged. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown; nanocode-sim with the change, on dev-georgios: `sweep.sh 0 100000 8 --twice` and `--records slots --twice` pass 100,000 of 100,000 each (204 s and 146 s), `--scenario agents --twice`, `--scenario turns --twice` and `--scenario turns --policy turnlog --twice` pass 20,000 of 20,000 each, 0 panics and no assertion fired; the store canaries are still caught.
- A refusal is replaced or cleared outside its `RefCell` borrow, and `set_limiter` drops the earlier refusal after it installs the new budget (2026-11-13). `*vm.stopped.borrow_mut() = Some(stop)` in `halt` and `refuel`, and `set_limiter`'s `borrow_mut().take()`, dropped the earlier refusal while the cell was mutably borrowed. That exception holds the traceback of the run it stopped, and freeing those frames can run Python (a generator's `close`, a `__del__`), which steps, refuels and borrows `vm.stopped`: the interpreter panicked with "already mutably borrowed" at vm/limit.rs. Any run after a stopped run in a kept interpreter could reach it (a cancelled python3 in nanocode-shell, then the next python3), and nanocode-ts's RustPython host reruns a script after it stops it for a file the host fetches. `RefCell::replace` and `take` return the earlier value after the borrow ends. `set_limiter` now installs the new fuel and limiter first, so frees that run code are charged to the new run instead of meeting the old limiter. Measured with nanocode-ts's module over a filesystem without a synchronous view (output/pybench/edge.ts, ASYNC=1, 25 scripts): before, 6 scripts ended with the panic; after, all 25 print what they print over a synchronous filesystem. Checked: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python`, and the module built for wasm32-unknown-unknown from this tree.
- `nanocode-turnlog` bounds what a cold start reads and holds, and agent telemetry is no longer durable (2026-11-13). Telemetry: `OneLog` publishes `api.event`, `model.call.started|completed`, `model.attempt.*`, `model.connection.*` and `model.warmup.*` live only, with seq 0 (the path deltas already take), and stores none of them. A 10-turn harness run stores 104 events instead of 136 and 25,252 bytes instead of 26,869 (-6%; compression had already removed most of their cost). Events: a snapshot no longer carries old events. When a snapshot or a boundary row is written, the events since the previous one become a `Segment { first, last, row }` in the fold and leave memory. `TurnLog::history(after, take)` reads old segments on demand through the new `LogHost::scan(scope, from, to)`, one segment per read, and `OneLog::page` and `turn_page` use it. A boundary row (tag `b`) is a row compressed without a dictionary. The writer writes one when the events held in memory exceed the encoded state, so memory for events stays below the state's size whether or not a snapshot fires. Records: `TurnLog::open` drops the content-addressed `b3:` records that no checkpoint reaches, following `EncodedPayload::references` through inline values, and keeps a state whole when a reachable record is a manifest. The next snapshot omits them. Collection runs only at open, because a live durability session remembers the keys it committed (`committed_records`) and does not send one again when its content comes back. A new session does not know a collected key, so it sends it again. output/turnlog-check `snap` (400 commits whose head moves through a chain that leaves records behind) collects 532 of 800 records at open and keeps the 268 reachable ones. A key that becomes unreachable and is referenced again survives, and all 1,200 events page back in order at 5 reopens. `Policy.snapshot_ratio` (`TurnLog::snapshot_ratio`) replaces the fixed 2: a snapshot is written when snapshot plus tail bytes exceed ratio x the compressed state, so a cold start reads at most about ratio x the state, and snapshots add about 1/(ratio - 1) of the row bytes. Code Mode calls leave the open-call set when their cell is forgotten (30 open calls stayed after 100 turns before), and `Glob`, `Grep`, `LS`, `ToolSearch`, `WebFetch`, `WebSearch` and `web_search` are effect class None. Measured with nanocode-sim `--scenario turns --policy turnlog --long N` (one session of N turns, new) and `--snapshot-ratio K` (new). After each seed it opens every scope cold and records rows and bytes read. Calm, per scope, ratio 2 against ratio 4: the largest cold read was 3.2 KB against 5.2 KB at N = 10, 7.0 against 12.9 KB at 30, 20.2 against 24.3 KB at 100 and 57.8 against 93.2 KB at 300. Total row bytes were 2.94 against 2.42 MB at 10 and 4.28 against 3.26 MB at 300 (+21% to +31% for ratio 2), and rows/turn were 3.11-3.24 in all cases, because a snapshot replaces a row. With faults the numbers are close (rows/turn 4.07-4.44). Cold reads in the simulator still grow with N because the fold keeps every finished turn for request-ID deduplication (`admitted` plus `status`, about 440 bytes per turn uncompressed in the native harness). That is the one term that grows with session length. The native harness at 10, 100 and 300 turns cold-opens 23, 230 and 690 rows (25, 173 and 516 KB stored, 0.1, 1.4 and 4.4 MB uncompressed) in 1.1, 9.3 and 25 ms. It writes no snapshot because its state is the conversation (65 KB, 549 KB and 1.74 MB uncompressed, 90% content-addressed records), so the log is already the state. Conversation compaction bounds that, not the log. Fundamental limits found: one row per round trip that dispatches an effect which is neither None nor safe to repeat. A hand's request-ID deduplication does not remove it, because the request ID derives from the call ID and a replayed model step issues new call IDs, so the row that records the call before it leaves is the only fence. A cold start reads at least the live conversation. Checks: `nanocode-sim --scenario turns --policy turnlog --seeds 0..2000 --twice` with faults, `--calm`, `--row-limit 1024` and `--snapshot-ratio 1`, the six mutations (`seal_skipped` with `--without restart`), `--long` sweeps (all seeds pass), `--tidy`, output/turnlog-check `turnlog-check` (REPEAT 1, 10, 30), `snap` (RATIO 1, 2, 4, 8, row limit none and 700) and `crash`, `cargo check` and `cargo clippy -D warnings` native and wasm for the changed crates. `cargo clippy -p nanocode-agent --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` alone fails on master already: the cell journal types need `nanocode-code-mode/local-cells`, which only `nanocode` turns on.
- The vendored rustls-platform-verifier stops using the JNI stack on Android and security-framework on iOS, and jni, jni-sys, jni-macros, jni-sys-macros, combine, simd_cesu8, simdutf8, rustls-platform-verifier-android, walkdir, same-file, winapi-util, rustc_version, semver, security-framework and security-framework-sys leave the graph (2026-11-13, Georgios: "rustls-platform-verifier: replace it with native root loading plus small macOS Security FFI where the platform verifier matters, or show why it must stay"). Why the crate stays: reqwest 0.13's `rustls-no-provider` feature builds every client's verifier with `rustls_platform_verifier::Verifier`, nanocode-tls uses it on macOS and iOS and nanocode-sandbox's proxy reads `system_roots()` from it on Linux, and tempoxyz/pyramid-core patches its own reqwest to this copy (`[patch.crates-io]` by nanocode rev), so the patch path and its public `Verifier`, `BuilderVerifierExt`, `ConfigVerifierExt` and `system_roots` stay as they were; what leaves is what each platform needed besides. Android verifies like Linux, with rustls-webpki over the native roots, instead of calling Java's X509TrustManager through JNI, which also needed the host app to call `rustls_platform_verifier::android::init_hosted` first and otherwise panicked at the first handshake; that `android` module goes. nanocode_platform::trust reads Android's system store from /apex/com.android.conscrypt/cacerts (Android 14 and later, updated through the Conscrypt module) and /system/etc/security/cacerts. Certificates a user added in Android's settings are not read, as on Linux. iOS, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS keep Apple's trust evaluation through nanocode-sys's own Security and CoreFoundation calls (crates/core/sys/src/security.rs, iOS family only, so macOS still links neither framework): `ServerTrust::evaluate` makes the certificates, an SSL server policy for the host, the trust object, its verify date, the stapled OCSP response and the extra anchors (with `SecTrustSetAnchorCertificatesOnly(false)`), and returns `SecTrustEvaluateWithError`'s code and description, which the verifier maps to the same rustls errors as before (host name mismatch, chain failure, extended key usage, revoked; anything else as its description and code). Each Core Foundation object is owned by a value that releases it once. The unsafe blocks, all in nanocode-sys: each `CF*Create`, `SecCertificateCreateWithData`, `SecPolicyCreateSSL` and `SecTrustCreateWithCertificates` result is checked for null before it is wrapped; slices are passed with their own lengths; `CFArrayCreate` gets `kCFTypeArrayCallBacks`, so the array retains its items; `CFStringGetBytes` writes at most the capacity it is given. No iOS simulator exists on gak-9, so the same file was compiled into output/apple-trust on macOS (gak-9, aarch64) and run through a rustls handshake that hands each server's chain to it: example.com (with a stapled OCSP response), www.google.com, api.anthropic.com, chatgpt.com and github.com verify in 3.7 to 5.7 ms; example.com checked as wrong.example.org and wrong.host.badssl.com give -67602 (name mismatch); expired.badssl.com and example.com at a verify date in 2100 give -67818 (expired); self-signed.badssl.com and untrusted-root.badssl.com give -67843 (not trusted); revoked.badssl.com gives -67820 (revoked); given BadSSL's untrusted root as an extra anchor, untrusted-root.badssl.com moves past trust to -67609 (its leaf's usage); bytes that are not a certificate are refused. Packages: `cargo metadata --locked` resolves 372 to 357; webpki-root-certs stays for WASM. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tls -p nanocode-sandbox -p nanocode-platform`, output/verifier-check (the patched crate and nanocode-platform) for aarch64-linux-android and x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, and on gak-9 `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-tls -p nanocode-platform` and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys` for aarch64-apple-ios, aarch64-apple-ios-sim and aarch64-apple-darwin, with output/verifier-check for aarch64-apple-ios.
- Bash refuses a command that starts with `sleep` of 25 seconds or more and is not run in the background, as Claude Code does (2026-11-13). Claude Code 2.1.316's Bash `validateInput` (read from the installed binary, `$As` with `GWr=25`) takes the first part of the command up to an operator and, when it is exactly `sleep N` with N at least 25 and the call has no `run_in_background`, answers `Blocked: sleep N followed by: <rest>` (or `standalone sleep N`) with advice to wait with `run_in_background` instead. On tb21 query-optimize (nanoeval-parity, Opus 5.5 high, 2026-11-13) that refusal is what turned Claude Code away from waiting minutes for the task's slow original query (`sleep 240; cat <task output>` was refused, and the model checked its rewrite against the original on an indexed copy in 1.5 s), while Nano waited: its attempts took 7.2 to 15.0 minutes of agent time against Claude Code's 3.0 to 7.3 at the same 5/5 pass rate. nanocode's `ClaudeBash` now refuses the same commands with the same words, minus Claude Code's sentence about its Monitor tool, which nanocode does not have. It does not stop a Code Mode cell from waiting with timers, which is how most of Nano's waits on that task were written. Checked with output/sleep-block (`cargo run`, a `SandboxBashExecutor` that echoes): `sleep 240; cat /tmp/out`, `sleep 240 && cat /tmp/out`, `sleep 30` and `sleep 25.5 | tee x` are refused with Claude Code's message; `sleep 24.9; ls`, `ls; sleep 240`, `sleepy 300`, `sleep 5m` (Claude Code's pattern takes only plain seconds) and a background `sleep 240; cat /tmp/out` reach the executor. clippy on nanocode-backend-claude-tools, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode` natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown.
- `Tls::from_ca` takes the issuer name and the authority key identifier of the leaves it mints from the CA certificate it is given, and refuses a key that does not match that certificate (2026-11-13). Before, the leaves' issuer was rebuilt from the `names` the caller passed and their authority key identifier was always the SHA-256 of the CA's public key, as rcgen's `Issuer::new` did. That only chains when the CA was made the same way. A CA made by OpenSSL carries a SHA-1 subject key identifier (RFC 5280's first method), so every leaf named an issuer key that no certificate had: through the proxy, curl and `openssl s_client` stopped with verify error 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate) and Python's `ssl` with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED, while Go's crypto/x509 accepted (the previous entry measured this on the rcgen build too). A `names` list in another order or encoding than the certificate's subject would have broken every client the same way, and a CA certificate paired with a different key minted leaves that nothing could verify. Now nanocode-x509 reads a certificate (`parse_certificate`: the subject and public key info as DER, and the subject key identifier extension if present; a malformed or truncated certificate is a `Malformed` error naming the field), and `Issuer::from_certificate(der, key)` uses the subject as the issuer name, the subject key identifier as the authority key identifier (the SHA-256 identifier when the certificate has none, as before), and compares the certificate's public key info with the key's, byte for byte. This is what rcgen's `Issuer::from_ca_cert_der` does. Public API, coordinated with tempoxyz/pyramid-core: `Tls::from_ca(ca, roots, leaves)` drops its `names` argument; pyramid-core's crates/egress/src/lib.rs, the one caller, drops its `names` array and the `DnType` import when it next moves its nanocode pin. Its CA comes from rcgen with those same names and a SHA-256 identifier, so its leaves are byte-for-byte what they were. output/x509-equal (rcgen =0.14.10): for CAs that rcgen made from Ed25519, P-256, P-384 and RSA keys, our leaves' to-be-signed bytes equal both rcgen's `Issuer::new` and its `Issuer::from_ca_cert_der` leaves; for 5 CAs that `openssl req -x509` made (P-256, subject C=US, O=Pyramid, CN=Pyramid egress CA), they equal `from_ca_cert_der`'s leaves for all 5 hosts; 365 comparisons in all, and a CA certificate given another key is refused ("the egress CA: the key does not match the certificate's public key"). Through the proxy with the OpenSSL-made CA, curl and `openssl s_client -x509_strict` now verify (result 0) and Python's strict `ssl` completes the handshake. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-x509 -p nanocode-sandbox`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-x509 -p nanocode-sandbox --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and on gak-9 the same check for aarch64-apple-darwin.
- nanocode-store-sql speaks Postgres itself (2026-11-13, Georgios, through the Nanocode 1.0 workstream: nanocode writes its own small Postgres wire-protocol client as the store's driver and the sqlx adapter moves into pyramid-core). crates/integrations/store-sql/src/postgres is a Postgres client of about 1,700 lines, and `PgSql` (an `Sql` host over a write pool and a read pool, as `SqlxSql::reading`) and `PgTransaction` (statements inside a caller's own transaction, as `SqlxTransaction`) run the stores over it; `PgConnection`, `PgPool`, `PgOptions`, `PgError` and `Notification` are public. `SqlxSql` and the rest of the sqlx side stay in this commit so tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid can move them into their own trees; a later commit removes them and sqlx. What the client speaks: protocol 3.0; `sslmode` disable, prefer (the default, as sqlx's), require and verify-full, over rustls through tokio-rustls, where prefer and require do not check the certificate (libpq's meaning) and verify-full checks it against nanocode-tls's native roots or an `sslrootcert` file; TCP (with `TCP_NODELAY`) and Unix sockets (`?host=/dir`); trust, cleartext password and SCRAM-SHA-256 (no channel binding, the server's signature checked; HMAC and PBKDF2 over nanocode-digest's Sha256), with md5 and passwords that would need SASLprep (non-ASCII) refused by a typed error rather than guessed; the session settings sqlx sends (DateStyle "ISO, MDY", client_encoding UTF8, TimeZone UTC, extra_float_digits 2), so every text rendering the stores read is the same; the extended protocol, with parameters sent as text of type text (OID 25, what sqlx's `&str` binds declare) and results asked for as text; simple queries (`simple`); LISTEN and NOTIFY (`listen`, `notification`). A store transaction is one write and one round trip: BEGIN (and `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off` for `Settle::Ordered`), each statement's Parse (only the first time on a connection), Bind and Execute, COMMIT and one Sync; when a statement fails the server skips to the Sync, and the client sends ROLLBACK. sqlx waits for each statement, so the same transaction costs it one round trip per statement plus BEGIN and COMMIT. Statements are prepared once per connection as `nanocode_<n>` up to 100 per connection (sqlx's default `statement_cache_capacity`, which the stores ran under), and run unnamed past that; a statement is counted prepared only once its ParseComplete arrives, so a pipeline that fails leaves no name the server lacks. Bounds: a server message is refused past 0x3fffffff bytes (the server's MaxAllocSize); reads go through a buffer that starts at 8,192 bytes (PostgreSQL's PQ_RECV_BUFFER_SIZE) and grows to the message in hand. Cancellation: reads land in the connection's own buffer through `read_buf`, so dropping a `notification()` wait loses no bytes; dropping any other operation mid-write or mid-answer leaves the connection marked, and its next operation answers `PgError::Broken` instead of reading a stranger's reply; `PgPool` replaces such a connection on its next acquire. The pool is N slots of `nanocode_sync::Owned<Option<PgConnection>>` behind a Tokio semaphore of N permits, opened on first use; it keeps its TLS configuration and the SCRAM salted password for the salt and iteration count the server last sent (RFC 5802 section 5.1 allows a client to cache it), so its connections after the first skip PBKDF2's 4,096 rounds. Errors are `PgError` (`Io`, `Tls`, `Protocol`, `Authentication`, `Configuration`, `Database` with SQLSTATE, severity, message, detail and hint, `Broken`); `PgError::unavailable` is the rule store-sql's `unavailable` applies to sqlx (connection exceptions 08, 57P01 to 57P03, 25006, I/O, TLS and protocol failures). Notices and parameter-status messages are read and dropped; the client logs nothing. No package joins the graph (base64, rustls, tokio-rustls, nanocode-tls, nanocode-digest and nanocode-platform were in it): `cargo metadata --locked` still lists 395. Checked on the 5-core Linux Hand against PostgreSQL 16.15 of its own (`initdb --auth-host=scram-sha-256`, TLS on, a CA-signed certificate for localhost) with output/durability-ledger, copied from gak-9 and made to build on Linux (`/proc/self/io` and `/proc/self/statm` stand in for `proc_pid_rusage`; `PG_DRIVER=own|sqlx` picks the host, `PG_PORT` the server). Its new src/bin/pgcheck.rs passes 25 of 25 checks: each sslmode answers `pg_stat_ssl` as expected, verify-full passes with the CA file and refuses the server against the native roots (UnknownIssuer); a wrong password is 28P01 and a missing one an authentication error; a Unix socket connects; text with quotes, a backslash and é and a NULL round-trip; a duplicate key is its 23505 and rolls back the transaction's earlier insert while the connection serves on; Ordered runs with `synchronous_commit` off and Durable on; the session settings and the text of a timestamptz and a float8 match sqlx's; 150 distinct statements run twice leave 100 prepared; LISTEN gets two NOTIFYs in order with the sender's pid, and a wait cut off by a 50 ms timeout loses nothing; a query cut off by a timeout leaves its connection refusing with `Broken` and the pool replaces it; 64 tasks share a 2-connection pool; a statement that does not parse fails alone and a repeated one is parsed once. src/bin/rtt.rs puts a proxy with 20 ms each way in front of the server: a three-statement `Sql::transaction` takes a median 258 to 261 ms over sqlx (six round trips) and 43.2 to 43.8 ms over the new client, in three rounds of nine. src/bin/readbench.rs, 15 rounds each, interleaved, sslmode disable unless said: `Sql::run` reading 1 row 0.05 ms (sqlx) against 0.02 ms (own), 10,000 rows of 200 bytes 5.39 against 2.23 ms, 100 rows of 100,000 bytes 8.18 against 3.54 ms; opening 16 pooled connections at once 24.6 against 16.7 ms (own with TLS 22.2 ms; this harness's sqlx has no TLS feature, so its prefer is plain text); one connection alone, without a pool to reuse the salted password, 3.25 against 3.67 ms, PBKDF2 in nanocode-digest being slower than sha2's. matrix.sh `SWARM flat 1000`, 200 at once, three interleaved rounds per driver at load 3 to 9: every run completes 1,000 of 1,000 agents with the same commits (about 11,400), logical bytes (about 41.2 KB per agent) and stored bytes (41.3 to 42.0 KB per agent on pg, 43.3 to 44.0 on pgrows); settled pg 3.27, 7.77 and 8.05 s on sqlx against 7.15, 7.24 and 5.97 s on own, pgrows 2.76, 2.62 and 3.20 against 1.89, 1.72 and 2.37 s; CPU (user+system) pg 4.2+0.6, 4.6+0.4 and 4.8+0.4 s against 4.1+0.4, 4.0+0.4 and 3.8+0.2 s. killresume.sh kills each run after 500 agents settle and resumes it: 1,000 of 1,000 complete on pg and pgrows on both drivers, over TLS and without. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql` (no warnings), `cargo fmt --check -p nanocode-store-sql`. Files: crates/integrations/store-sql/{Cargo.toml,src/lib.rs,src/postgres/*}, Cargo.lock.
- rcgen leaves the workspace: nanocode-sandbox's egress proxy writes its certificates with nanocode-x509, a DER writer of its own, and signs them with ring, the crypto provider the proxy's rustls already links (2026-11-13, Georgios: "rcgen: replace it with a minimal X.509 builder in the workspace"). crates/core/x509 (nanocode-x509, no dependencies beyond nanocode-platform's `civil_from_days`, so it builds for WASM too) has the DER pieces (lengths, integers, object identifiers, bit and octet strings, UTF8String names, UTCTime before 2050 and GeneralizedTime after, as RFC 5280 asks), the extensions the proxy writes (key usage, basic constraints, subject and authority key identifiers, subject alternative names, extended key usage), `Certificate::to_be_signed`, `signed` and PEM. crates/integrations/sandbox/src/egress/certificate.rs holds the keys and the two certificates the proxy makes, each field as rcgen 0.14.10 wrote it: keys come from ring (a new key is ECDSA P-256 in ring's PKCS#8; a CA key is read from PKCS#8 PEM as Ed25519, ECDSA P-256, ECDSA P-384 or RSA with SHA-256, in rcgen's order); the serial is the first 20 bytes of the SHA-256 of the subject's public key with the top bit cleared; key identifiers are the first 20 bytes of the SHA-256 of the subject public key info; validity is 1975-01-01 to 4096-01-01 unless `Leaves::lifetime` sets it; names are UTF8String; the self-signed CA carries critical key usage (certificate sign, CRL sign, digital signature), its subject key identifier and critical basic constraints with path length 0; a leaf carries the authority key identifier, its one DNS or IP subject alternative name and, when `Leaves::usages` names any, extended key usage, and a host that is neither an IP address nor ASCII is an error, as rcgen's `Ia5String` was. Public API, coordinated with tempoxyz/pyramid-core: nanocode_sandbox::egress exports its own `DnType` (rcgen's variants: CountryName, LocalityName, StateOrProvinceName, OrganizationName, OrganizationalUnitName, CommonName, CustomDnType), `ExtendedKeyUsagePurpose` (Any, ServerAuth, ClientAuth, CodeSigning, EmailProtection, TimeStamping, OcspSigning, Other), `KeyPair` (`generate`, `from_pem`, `from_pkcs8`, `serialize_der`) and `Issuer` (`Issuer::new(names, key)`), which `Tls::from_ca`, `Leaves::usages` and `Tls::signed_by` take in place of rcgen's; pyramid-core's crates/egress/src/lib.rs, the one caller, changes only `use rcgen::DnType` to `use nanocode_sandbox::egress::DnType` when it next moves its nanocode pin. Equality, output/x509-equal (rcgen =0.14.10 with x509-parser beside these crates): for 20 self-signed CAs and 5 hosts each (example.com, api.anthropic.com, 127.0.0.1, ::1, a-b.c.example.test), and for CAs that rcgen made from Ed25519, P-256, P-384 and OpenSSL-made RSA-2048 keys with Pyramid's names and lifetimes, with and without two extended key usages, rcgen signing the same public key with the same parameters gives a to-be-signed certificate byte-identical to ours in all 340 comparisons, and the CA PEM is byte-identical to rcgen's; every leaf was fetched through a rustls handshake that trusts only the CA. `openssl verify -x509_strict` accepts the CA and every leaf. Through the proxy itself (output/x509-equal's proxy binary, `Egress::tcp` with a secret on each host so it intercepts, beside the same binary built from 63916b868 with rcgen), curl, a Go 1.22.2 `net/http` client (crypto/x509, the browser-like verifier), Python 3.12's `ssl` with `VERIFY_X509_STRICT` and `openssl s_client -x509_strict` accept the minted chain for example.com, www.google.com, api.github.com and 1.1.1.1 under both builds alike (verify result 0; some answers were 502s from the Hand's own upstream reach, alike in both). Both builds also refuse alike when `from_ca` is given an OpenSSL-made CA, whose subject key identifier is SHA-1 based: the leaf's authority key identifier names a SHA-256 identifier, so curl, Python and OpenSSL find no issuer (verify 20) while Go accepts; that predates this change and the entry above fixes it. Costs: `cargo metadata --locked` resolves 395 packages to 372 (rcgen, x509-parser, der-parser, asn1-rs with its derive and impl crates, oid-registry, rusticata-macros, nom, minimal-lexical, yasna, time with time-core and time-macros, deranged, powerfmt, num-conv, num-bigint, num-integer, bit-vec, data-encoding, lazy_static, pem and base64 0.23 leave; nanocode-x509 joins); `cargo build --release -p rcgen --timings` on the hosted Hand (2 jobs, load 5) spends 12.0 s in the units that leave against 1.6 s for nanocode-x509; the proxy binary's stripped size goes from 3,813,744 to 3,697,616 bytes and its `.text` from 2,605,704 to 2,513,384 (`size -A`, the same harness built from 63916b868 and from this change). Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-x509 -p nanocode-sandbox`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-x509 -p nanocode-sandbox`, and on gak-9 the same check for aarch64-apple-darwin.
- `ClaudeBuilder::automatic_cache`, `adaptive_thinking` and `keep_thinking` are gone (2026-11-13, from the audit Georgios asked for of host knobs that can silently cost money or cache hits against Claude Code). `automatic_cache(false)` sent every request without a cache breakpoint on the conversation, so each turn paid its whole prompt uncached; `keep_thinking` and `adaptive_thinking` changed what thinking a request keeps and how it asks for it away from the per-model behaviour the driver already matches to Claude Code. Their fields stay, at the defaults every caller had (automatic caching on, thinking kept, automatic thinking mode), because session checkpoints store them and a checkpoint restored from an older build still carries its own values. No caller in this repository, nanocode-ts, tempoxyz/pyramid or tempoxyz/pyramid-core used any of the three (`git grep` here and in nanocode-ts, GitHub code search in the other two, 2026-11-13). Kept, with the reason: `cache_one_hour` (Pyramid and pyramid-core set it as a billing choice, and Claude Code itself uses one-hour caching for subscription users), `max_tokens` (nanocode-ts, Pyramid and pyramid-core set it only for models the driver has no limit for, where the driver would otherwise refuse to build), `context_window_tokens` and `auto_compact_window_tokens` (Pyramid's modes and nanocode-ts set them; nanocode-ts defaults Claude's auto-compact window to 200,000, which compacts a 1,000,000-token model earlier than its own window and is nanocode-ts's to settle), `fast_mode`, `effort` and `thinking` (the model and speed a user picks, as Claude Code's /model, /effort and /fast do), `system_blocks` and `system` (a host's own instructions, which `cache_system_prefix_with` still caches), `tool_input_deltas`, `message_threads` and `message_diagnostics` (what the host is told, not what is sent). `cargo check --locked --workspace --lib` and the wasm32-unknown-unknown check of the entry above.
- The image window belongs to the backend, and no host can set one (2026-11-13, Georgios: "make this not configurable or something so that it can't be broken by dumb configuration"). `ImageHistory` carries only the blob store (`ImageHistory::default()`, `with_blob_store`); `ImageHistory::new`, `or_inline_images` and `DEFAULT_INLINE_IMAGES` are gone, and the window is `nanocode_image::ImageWindow`, a value with a private field and three constants: `CLAUDE` (100) and `CLAUDE_LONG_CONTEXT` (600), which the Claude driver picks per request from its context window (the Messages API's per-request image limits, Anthropic's vision documentation), and `CODEX` (8), which the Codex Responses requests use as before. 547423275 fixed the case where a host's `ImageHistory::default().with_blob_store(..)` replaced Claude's 100 with 8 (Nano re-viewed invoice images 41 to 128 times and paid $2.07 to $5.14 an attempt against Claude Code's $0.46 to $0.61), but a host could still pass `ImageHistory::new(8)` and get the same bill without an error; now there is nothing to pass. No caller in this repository, nanocode-ts (which passes only `ImageHistory::default().with_blob_store`), tempoxyz/pyramid or tempoxyz/pyramid-core set a window (GitHub code search for `ImageHistory` and `.images(` in both, 2026-11-13). Checked with output/image-window (`cargo run`): evicted images for 8, 9, 13, 61, 100, 101, 600 and 601 images are 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 50, 500, 550 for `CLAUDE`, 0 up to 600 and 300 at 601 for `CLAUDE_LONG_CONTEXT`, and 0, 4, 8, 56, 92, 96, 592, 596 for `CODEX`, the numbers the two backends produced before. `cargo check --locked --workspace --lib`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, clippy on nanocode-image and both backends.
- nanocode-python keeps the environment of every run in a kept interpreter, and imports implicit namespace packages (2026-11-13). `os.environ._data` is the same dict as `posix.environ` (CPython's `os._createenviron` uses it directly on POSIX), so `_start` in boot.py emptied the environment that `posix._reset` had just loaded: in a kept interpreter (the psh utility's thread, nanocode-shell's `Command`, a WebAssembly host's instance) every run after the first that imported `os` saw an empty `os.environ`. `_start` now copies `posix.environ` before it refills `os.environ`. `_Finder` found only `pkg/__init__.py` and `pkg.py`, so `import pkg.mod` for a directory without `__init__.py` ended as a missing package (127); a directory on the search path is now a namespace portion, used when no regular package or module matches on the whole path (as CPython's PathFinder does), with a loader of its own because this interpreter installs no `_bootstrap_external` and its `NamespaceLoader`. Measured with nanocode-ts's RustPython module (output/pyrs/t7.mjs: three runs in one instance with different environments; output/pybench/dbg.ts): before, run 2 and 3 printed `{}` for `dict(os.environ)` and `import pkg.mod` reported "No module named 'pkg'"; after, each run prints its own environment and `import pkg.mod, pkg.sub.m` prints `42 41 ['./pkg']`. Checked: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python`; the module built for wasm32-unknown-unknown from this tree.
- `nanocode-turnlog` keeps one table and compresses every row (2026-11-13). The table is `nanocode_log (scope, seq, body, PRIMARY KEY (scope, seq)) WITHOUT ROWID`, and `nanocode_snap` is gone. The single writer assigns each seq, so an append is a plain `INSERT` with no `RETURNING` and reads no rows. A second writer on the same scope fails on the key, so the key is a fence. A row body is a tag and base64 raw DEFLATE (`nanocode-compression`, already in the workspace): `r` compresses the records with the last 32 KiB (the DEFLATE window) of the scope's plaintext since the last snapshot as its preset dictionary, `s` is a snapshot with no dictionary, and `+` continues the previous row, so `Policy.max_row_bytes` splits any body at byte boundaries, all parts commit in one transaction and no record is too large. A snapshot replaces the row that triggers it (same seq, no extra row), under the same rule as before: snapshot bytes plus tail bytes above 2 x the compressed state. Old rows are not deleted. On Durable Objects a deleted row bills as a row written, which costs about 1,000 times a row read and more than about six months of storing the row. A cold start therefore runs one `SELECT` from the last `s` row, found in SQLite by `substr(body, 1, 1) = 's'`. `LogHost` is now `load(scope)` and `append(scope, rows)`, and `rows()` decodes stored rows for hosts and harnesses. Measured with output/turnlog-check (10 turns of a Claude Code Mode agent against a mock, MemoryLog and SqlLog over SQLite): 23 rows and 153,489 bytes before, 23 rows and 26,896 bytes now (-82%). A steady turn writes 0.7-4.0 KB against 7.3-21.7 KB. The first turn writes 10.4 KB against 22.2 KB, mostly the system prompt stored once. The reopen folds the same 10 turns and 136 events, and `ROW_LIMIT=1024` reopens 30 turns from parts. output/turnlog-check `snap` makes 400 commits whose state is superseded: 44 snapshots replace rows, reopens at 4 points match, and a cold start reads 4 rows (317 bytes). With a log of events that are never superseded (100 turns, 188 KB), no snapshot is written, because the log is the state. The `crash` binary is unchanged: no second charge, "outcome unknown", and A, R, R, R, F Failed. nanocode-sim `--policy turnlog` (SimHost now holds per-scope keyed rows with conflict checks, and the observer decodes rows with `rows()`) passes seeds 0..3000 `--twice`, with faults, `--calm` and `--row-limit 1024`. All six mutations are caught, and `seal_skipped` with `--without restart`. Over seeds 0..5000 it writes 26.5 MB against 94 MB with faults and 24.5 MB against 68 MB calm, rows/turn are 4.95 against 5.38 with faults and 3.11 calm, and the reference policy writes 16.8 MB and 17.9 MB. On durable-cloudflare's workerd harness (nanocode-ts `onelog` built on this SDK, `node output/sqlturn/run.mjs text|tool|reply 10`), a turn writes 2.0 rows in 3.0 statements and reads 0.0 rows (2.0 before), with 0.9/1.0/0.6 KB of bound parameters against 12.3/14.5/9.0 KB. `npm run drill` passes, and `output/crash/run.mjs` gives the same charges, statuses and unknown reports at every point as the uncompressed layout. The nanocode-ts WebAssembly module grows from 12,989,050 to 13,058,321 bytes (+0.53%), because `nanocode-compression` enters it. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-turnlog -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-mcp-tools -p nanocode-agent -p nanocode`, the same with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` on both targets for the changed crates. The codex-client `default_constructed_unit_structs` lint on wasm and the `nanocode-tui → nanocode-sys` boundary violation are on master already.
- nanocode_platform::fill_random reads the kernel through nanocode-sys's own call, and every crate that called `getrandom::fill` calls `nanocode_platform::fill_random` (2026-11-13, Georgios: "getrandom: route everything through nanocode_platform::fill_random (the OS call directly)"). crates/core/sys/src/random.rs holds the one system call per platform, as getrandom 0.4.3 picks it: `getrandom(2)` on Linux and Android, looped until the buffer is full and retried on `EINTR`; `getentropy(3)` in chunks of 256 bytes (`GETENTROPY_BYTES_MAX`, its documented limit) on macOS and the other Unix systems; `CCRandomGenerateBytes` on iOS, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS; `ProcessPrng` from bcryptprimitives.dll (raw-dylib) on Windows. WASM keeps its host's `fill_random`. Not equal, on purpose: getrandom falls back to reading /dev/urandom when `getrandom(2)` answers ENOSYS (Linux before 3.17) or EPERM (a seccomp filter); ours returns that error, so a confined process sees why it has no randomness. The callers moved: nanocode-backend-codex-client's PKCE verifier, nanocode-mcp-http's OAuth state, nanocode-websocket's handshake key and frame masks, nanocode-chatgpt-extension's bridge token, nanocode-process's jitter seed (its result still dropped, as before), nanocode-tool-runtime's attachment bearer, nanocode-cli's tab token, MPP proxy token, channel salt and P-256 certificate key, and the vendored rustpython-common (`os_random`), rustpython-host_env (`urandom`) and rustpython-stdlib (Mersenne Twister seeding, the WASM `RAND_bytes`); rustpython-common's `wasm_js` feature stays, empty, because rustpython-vm's `wasmbind` names it. Every one of these now also takes the per-thread 256-byte buffer `fill_random` keeps for small reads. output/random-check (release, hosted Hand, Linux 6.x x86_64): reads of 0, 1, 32, 255, 256, 257, 4,096 and 1,048,576 bytes all succeed and differ between two calls; a 16-byte `fill_random` takes 50 ns and a 16-byte `getrandom(2)` 286 ns. Packages: getrandom 0.4.3 has no workspace caller left, but `cargo metadata --locked` still resolves 395 packages, because sqlx-postgres (gakonst/sqlx) depends on rand 0.10.2, which depends on getrandom 0.4.3 and r-efi 6.0.0; those leave with sqlx. getrandom 0.2.17 (ring) and 0.3.4 (graviola, tempfile) are untouched. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-websocket -p nanocode-backend-codex-client -p nanocode-mcp-http -p nanocode-chatgpt-extension -p nanocode-process -p nanocode-tool-runtime`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, the same `cargo clippy --locked --lib`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, and on gak-9 `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform` for aarch64-apple-darwin, aarch64-apple-ios and x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.
