A host that wants a window still sets it with `ImageHistory::new(n)`. Checked with output/image-window (`cargo run`), which prints the images evicted for 8, 9, 13, 61, 100 and 101 images: a host default alone keeps the old 0, 4, 8, 56, 92, 96; a host default filled by the Claude driver's 100 evicts 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 50; `new(8)` keeps 8 whatever the driver offers. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-image -p nanocode-backend-claude` natively, the same with `-p nanocode-backend-codex -p nanocode` for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and clippy on the first two. Live on nanoeval-parity after the fix (nanocode-ts build-9f37888, Worker version 4c3e518e, 2026-11-13, four runs of `--only financial-document-processor --attempts 1` with both agents): Nano passed 4 of 4 at $0.297, $0.333, $0.384 and $0.593 (11 to 16 model calls, 4 to 17 image reads, 82 to 89% of input read from cache, no request after the first that paid more than 15,000 tokens uncached), Claude Code 2.1.318 4 of 4 at $0.362, $0.539, $0.600 and $0.637 (12 to 14 calls). A fifth run hit a gateway payment refusal for both agents and is left out.
- Emiliano Bonassi's email identity client (nanocodexyz/nanocode#1171) lands on master with the fixes tempoxyz/mpp-rs#723 made to the same client in mpp-rs (2026-11-13, Georgios: "merge this too now see if u need to redo anything"): a paid attempt is never sent again after a 401 or 403, since its payment may already have settled; an issuer a service names with a trailing slash matches the trusted issuer it spells; a refused pass stays in memory until a new one replaces it, so another request's paid attempt in flight still carries it; and when getting a new pass is declined or fails, a pass the request did not send that expires more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` from now is sent instead, so a refresh inside the refresh margin that does not happen still answers. Its `--identity-issuer`, `--identity-email` and `--identity-attestation` flags move onto nanocode-arguments (repeatable, comma-separated values split in `GatewayArgs::from_matches`), and its unit tests leave, as AGENTS.md has no tests outside nanocode-sim. Issuer requests still have no timeout of their own: no measured bound exists yet.
- nanocode-sync's `OrdMap`, `OrdSet` and `Vector` copy less on every clone-then-mutate, closing the gaps to imbl 7.0.2 that the persistent-collections entry below measured (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps"). crates/core/sync/src/tree.rs keeps its counted B-tree but types its nodes: a `Leaf` holds only entries and a `Branch` holds entries plus children (each child's count and a `Link` to a leaf or a branch). Each node is one allocation of fixed capacity: 16 entries (`NODE_ITEMS_MAX`, imbl's `ORD_CHUNK_SIZE`; 24 and 32 measured up to 1.9x slower on `String` clone+insert at 1,000 entries and faster nowhere) plus one slot for the entry that overflows before a split. The storage is `nanocode_sys::InlineVec<T, N>` (crates/core/sys/src/inline.rs): `[MaybeUninit<T>; N]` and a length, derefs to a slice, with `push`, `pop`, `insert`, `remove`, `split_off`, `append`, `extend_cloned` and an owning `OwnedItems` iterator. A safe `[Option<T>; N]` version was measured first and left u64 `get` at 100,000 entries at 205 ns against imbl's 98 (the `Option` tag widens `(u64, u64)` to 24 bytes, and leaves carried an unused children array), so the unsafe code lives in nanocode-sys behind that API. A copy is filled in place: `nanocode_sys::new_arc_with(make, fill)` writes an empty node into a fresh `Arc` and clones the entries into its heap slot. `Arc::make_mut` built the 736-byte branch on the stack and copied it (`memcpy` of 736 bytes in `parts_mut` in `--emit asm`), so u64 clone+insert at 1,000 went from 448 to 323 ns (imbl 405). A node is unique when `Arc::strong_count` is 1, because these trees never make a `Weak`, so a mutation pays one `Arc::get_mut` per level. Removal merges two siblings whenever both fit in one node and otherwise borrows half the difference, as imbl does, with a minimum of 5 entries (imbl's `THIRD`). `remove`, `remove_with_key`, `get_mut` and `entry` record the descent once (`Path`, one byte per level) instead of a `contains_key` followed by a second comparing descent. The search stops at the first equal entry for items that need drop or exceed 16 bytes (imbl's rule; std's search always runs full depth); plain items keep std's branchless search, so `String` `get` at 16 entries is 17 ns against 35 before. Iterators walk the current leaf as a slice and keep only branches on their stack; `range` seeks its start by key in one descent; `get_min` and `get_max` follow an edge. `Vector` no longer sits on the counted tree. crates/core/sync/src/spine.rs and vector.rs hold a head part, a middle spine and a tail part: the spine is a persistent radix trie of full 16-item leaves with 32-way branches and a start offset, so an index is shifts and masks, never a scan of counts. `push_back` fills the tail and moves a full tail into the spine; `pop_front` and `pop_back` consume the head or the tail and take a whole leaf from the spine every 16 items. `skip` and `take` drop whole leaves; a pop works out from positions whether a branch emptied instead of scanning its children; a shared leaf copies only its live slots. Leaves are `[Option<A>; 16]` (safe), and a popped slot becomes `None`, so popped items drop as they did with imbl. Widths were measured interleaved: 64-, 32- and 16-item leaves give `Vector<Arc<str>>` clone+push_back at 1,000 items of 437, 251 and 205 ns and clone+pop_front+push_back at 100,000 of 830, 478 and 429; 32-way branches beat 64-way (clone+push_back 100,000: 209 against 259); 16-item leaves with a scan for emptied branches made unshared `pop_front` 1.17x imbl, which the position arithmetic removed. The unsafe blocks added, all in nanocode-sys, and why each holds. In inline.rs: `as_slice` and `as_mut_slice` (`slice::from_raw_parts` over the first `len` slots, which are always initialized; the mutable one borrows `self` exclusively). `pop` (`assume_init_read` of slot `len - 1` after `len` drops, so the item is read exactly once and no longer counted). `Drop` (`drop_in_place` of the initialized prefix). `OwnedItems::next` and `next_back` (`assume_init_read` of slots in `front..back`, each read once as the bounds move past it; the array is moved out of the vector with its length zeroed, so the vector drops nothing; the iterator's own drop reads out the rest). `new_arc_with` (a write through `Arc::as_ptr` of a just-made `Arc<MaybeUninit<T>>` with one strong and no weak owner, so nothing else can reach it, followed by `assume_init` after that full write; a panic in `make` or `fill` drops the slot as uninitialized and leaks rather than double-drops). `insert`, `remove`, `split_off` and `append` are safe on top of these (`MaybeUninit::write`, slice rotation and `swap_with_slice`). Behaviour is unchanged: output/imbl-equal (imbl =7.0.2 beside crates/core/sync; the arc-swap patch line dropped now that the patch is gone) ran 2 seeds of 60,000 operations per configuration on the final code, 9,099,024 checks with 0 differences (and an earlier pass at 64-item leaves gave 0 differences in 4.3 million checks). imbl's `retain` again disagreed with `VecDeque` in 4,773 of 21,361 calls and was replaced as before. Benchmarks: output/imbl-equal/src/bench.rs gained a third column, the deps2-sys code copied into output/imbl-equal/before, plus a clone+remove row that drops each old version. Release build, 11 rounds rotating which of imbl, before and after runs first, median ns per operation, written imbl -> before -> after, on the shared Hand at load 3 to 6 while the equality pass ran. Clone-then-mutate rows: `OrdMap<u64, _>` clone+insert 77 -> 83 -> 56 (16 entries), 433 -> 421 -> 359 (1,000) and 929 -> 887 -> 740 (100,000); `OrdMap<String, _>` clone+insert 431 -> 432 -> 358, 1,122 -> 1,058 -> 979 and 2,686 -> 2,442 -> 1,789. Clone+remove with old versions dropped: u64 73 -> 84 -> 77, 413 -> 423 -> 347 and 1,044 -> 1,087 -> 848; `String` 237 -> 294 -> 225, 992 -> 1,118 -> 883 and 2,771 -> 3,413 -> 2,509. Clone+remove with every version kept: u64 63 -> 69 -> 70, 308 -> 353 -> 276 and 880 -> 1,101 -> 1,036; `String` 198 -> 218 -> 171, 882 -> 1,047 -> 919 and 3,464 -> 4,398 -> 3,626. Lookups and walks at 100,000: `String` `get` 391 -> 627 -> 369, u64 `get` 74 -> 94 -> 93, u64 iteration 4.1 -> 5.7 -> 4.1 and `String` 9.4 -> 14.8 -> 6.7; range of 16: u64 195 -> 357 -> 253 and `String` 469 -> 716 -> 497. `Vector<Arc<str>>` at 100,000: `push_back` 20.5 -> 51.5 -> 16.9, `pop_front` 18.6 -> 73.7 -> 18.0 and index 20.7 -> 76.3 -> 13.6. Its clone+push_back is 363 -> 245 -> 161 (16 items), 550 -> 635 -> 186 (1,000) and 538 -> 946 -> 213 (100,000); clone+pop_front+push_back is 1,034 -> 1,240 -> 350 (1,000) and 1,026 -> 2,329 -> 377 (100,000). Not equal, gaps that remain: a range of 16 is 1.30x imbl for u64 at 100,000 and 1.15x for `String` at 1,000, because our B-tree also keeps entries in branches, so a walk crosses branch entries, and `range` sums child counts to rank its start. Branches are larger than imbl's (736 bytes for `(u64, u64)` against about 330: full entries, a count and a tagged link per child), so u64 clone+remove that keeps every version at 100,000 entries is 1.18x imbl by median, though 0.92x by minimum. u64 `get` at 100,000 is 1.25x by median and 1.08x by minimum. Inserting into an unshared 16-entry u64 map is 26 against 24 ns, and unshared u64 remove at 100,000 is 200 against 174 ns. Against the previous tree, u64 `get` and `insert` at 1,000 are 3 to 13% slower by median and within 6% by minimum. Public API: nanocode-sys gains `InlineVec`, `OwnedItems` and `new_arc_with`, and its description names inline vectors; nanocode-sync's types and their methods are unchanged. `Vector::iter` returns a new unnameable `Iter` in place of the tree's `Items`, with the same traits (`DoubleEndedIterator`, `ExactSizeIterator`, `FusedIterator`, `Clone`). Commands: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-turnlog`, natively and for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-turnlog` on both targets, and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked` lists 418 packages.
- nanocode-sync's own persistent `OrdMap`, `OrdSet` and `Vector` carry the workspace's ordered copy-on-write state, and imbl leaves with imbl-sized-chunks, archery, rand_xoshiro, wide 0.7.33 and safe_arch 0.7.4 (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps"). crates/core/sync/src/tree.rs is a persistent B-tree: each node sits behind an `Arc`, holds 8 to 17 items inline (`NODE_ITEMS_MIN` 8, measured against 16 below) and keeps each child's item count beside it, so a clone is one `Arc` clone and an update copies only the nodes on its path with `Arc::make_mut`. The counts let one tree serve keys and positions: ordered.rs puts `OrdMap` over `(K, V)` entries and `OrdSet` over items, with lookups by `Borrow` like std, and vector.rs indexes by position. Pushes at the right edge split unevenly so that appends fill their nodes, both ends pop without searching, and a removal that leaves a node short takes half of a sibling's surplus rather than one item, so a queue's `pop_front` stops copying the sibling on every pop. Iteration runs two cursor stacks, one per end, bounded by the tree's height; `range` turns its bounds into ranks; owned iteration moves items out of nodes nobody else holds. Only the calls the workspace makes are provided: `new`, `len`, `is_empty`, `get`, `get_key_value`, `get_mut`, `contains_key`/`contains`, `insert`, `remove`, `remove_with_key`, `entry(..).or_default/or_insert/or_insert_with`, `range`, `iter`, `keys`, `values`, `get_min`, `get_max`, `split`, `remove_min`/`remove_max`; and for `Vector`: `push_back`, `pop_front`, `pop_back`, `front`, `back`, `last`, `get`, `get_mut`, `retain`, `skip`, `take`, `clear`, `Index` and `IndexMut`. All three also have `Extend`, `FromIterator`, `IntoIterator` by value and by reference, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Hash`, `Debug`, `Clone`, `Default`, `Serialize` and `Deserialize`. Semantics follow imbl 7.0.2: `insert` replaces the key and the value and returns the old value (`OrdSet::insert` returns the replaced item); an inverted range is empty; `split` leaves out the key; `skip` past the end is empty and `take` past the end panics; hashing and `Debug` walk the entries in order. On the wire `OrdMap` is a serde map, and `OrdSet` and `Vector` are sequences in iteration order. Deserializing inserts in order, so a later duplicate wins, and keeps imbl's `expecting` text ("a sequence") so that error messages match too. Call sites change only `imbl::` to `nanocode_sync::` (`crate::` inside sync), plus `const` on five small accessors (state.rs `seals_steers`, replay.rs `new`, history.rs `is_empty` and `len`, durable.rs `sealed_messages`), which clippy's missing_const_for_fn asks for now that `new`, `len` and `is_empty` are const. Public API: nanocode-durability-core's `OperationState::steer_receipts` and `steers` change type from `imbl::OrdMap` and `imbl::Vector` to `nanocode_sync::OrdMap` and `nanocode_sync::Vector`, with the same serialized bytes. GitHub code search of tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid (default branches) finds no use of these fields or of nanocode's imbl types; pyramid-core depends on imbl itself for its own `HashMap`, `HashSet` and `Vector`, which this change does not touch. Not equal, on purpose: imbl 7.0.2's `Vector::retain` breaks once a vector outgrows one 64-item chunk. output/imbl-equal/src/retain.rs gets a wrong result from 684 of 1,800 retains over vectors of 0 to 300 items; the first comes at 65 items, where keeping the odd numbers of 0..65 returned [42, 11, 23, 3, ...]. On `String` items the harness died with glibc's "double free or corruption". Ours keeps exactly what `VecDeque::retain` keeps, in order, calling the predicate once per item in order as imbl does. nanocode calls `retain` on the slow-wait holders (waits.rs, `Vector<Weak<Holder>>`), so before this change more than 64 registered holders could have corrupted memory. Mutation needs `Clone` items, as imbl's did. Equality: output/imbl-equal (imbl =7.0.2 with serde beside crates/core/sync, the repository's Cargo.lock and arc-swap patch) runs seeded operation sequences on both implementations side by side. It covers `OrdMap<u64, u64>`, `OrdMap<String, u64>`, `OrdSet<u64>`, `OrdSet<String>`, `Vector<u64>` and `Vector<String>` over key spaces of 16, 1,000 and 1,000,000, with bulk rebuilds up to 50,000 entries and 100,000 items. Up to 8 clones are taken mid-sequence and mutated independently. Every result is compared: return values, `get`, `get_mut`, `Index`, ranges with every bound kind walked from both ends interleaved, `split`, `partition`, `entry`, `skip`, `take`, `retain` (call count, and the result against `VecDeque`), equality between clones, owned iteration both ways, and every clone fully compared every 16,384 steps (len, iteration both ways, min and max, `Debug`, `Hash`, serde_json bytes, and decoding each side's bytes into the other). Malformed JSON gives the same error strings. imbl's `retain` result was replaced by `VecDeque`'s before comparing on, and was not called at all on `String` items. 2,160,000 operations (2 seeds, 60,000 per configuration) gave 9,099,024 checks with 0 differences, after earlier runs of 1,507,862 and 377,763 checks with 0 differences; imbl's `retain` disagreed with `VecDeque` in 4,773 of 21,361 calls. Benchmarks (output/imbl-equal/src/bench.rs, release, 5 rounds alternating which side runs first, median ns per operation, imbl -> ours, on the shared 5-core Hand under load from other agents, where single readings vary up to 3x). The `Atom` path, which clones and then mutates, is `OrdMap<u64, _>` clone+insert at 294 -> 237 (16 entries), 1,193 -> 1,064 (1,000) and 3,310 -> 2,353 (100,000), and `OrdMap<String, _>` clone+insert at 1,332 -> 1,302, 3,494 -> 2,796 and 8,895 -> 9,954. Clone+remove of a still-shared map is slower: u64 110 -> 195, 762 -> 1,316 and 3,246 -> 3,919; String 544 -> 903, 2,307 -> 3,240 and 11,660 -> 17,369. For `Vector<Arc<str>>`, clone+push_back is 1,110 -> 678 (16 items), 1,496 -> 2,166 (1,000) and 2,096 -> 3,017 (100,000), and clone+pop_front+push_back is 1,426 -> 1,429, 2,779 -> 3,388 and 2,760 -> 8,584. On 1,000 entries, u64 `get` is 58.5 -> 38.6 and String `get` 274 -> 319. The regressions grow with size: at 100,000 entries String `get` is 1,759 -> 3,340, `range` of 16 is u64 1,084 -> 2,285 and String 1,730 -> 4,345, and u64 iteration is 8.1 -> 30.1. Unshared `Vector` `push_back`, `pop_front` and `index` at 100,000 items are 39.6 -> 163, 33 -> 270 and 43 -> 444. These come from a node being an `Arc` plus one or two `Vec` buffers where imbl's is one allocation with inline 64-slot chunks, and from a deeper tree than imbl's 64-wide nodes and RRB head and tail buffers; inline fixed arrays would close them but were not done here. `NODE_ITEMS_MIN` 16 against 8: String clone+insert at 100,000 was 2.30x imbl's at 16 and 0.84 to 1.12x at 8, u64 stayed within 0.7 to 1.2x at both, and 16 was faster only on lookups. An earlier layout with an `Arc` per item made large `Vector` and lookup paths 4 to 16x slower and was dropped. `cargo metadata --locked` 425 to 418 packages on origin/master efe7f3f12 plus this branch (imbl, imbl-sized-chunks, archery, rand_xoshiro, wide, safe_arch, and rand_core 0.9.5 now that the obs scope removed rand). nanocode-turnlog, added on master meanwhile, keeps its in-memory rows and snapshots in the new `Vector` and `OrdMap` too (its `truncate` calls `retain`, which imbl got wrong past 64 rows), and nanocode-telemetry no longer used imbl after the obs scope rewrote it. version_check (generic-array), equivalent (hashbrown, indexmap) and bytemuck (image) stay for their other users; bitmaps was no longer in the lockfile. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked` for nanocode-sync, nanocode-durability-core, nanocode-durability, nanocode-subagents, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-backend-claude and nanocode-telemetry; `cargo check --locked --lib` for each, native and `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- rustls-native-certs and openssl-probe leave the workspace, and on macOS security-framework and security-framework-sys: nanocode's own trust-store reader, `nanocode_platform::trust::load_native_certificates()`, loads the native roots for nanocode-tls (outside macOS), nanocode-sandbox's egress proxy (outside Linux), the CLI's paying proxy bundle (bin/nanocode/src/tempo/proxy.rs) and the patched rustls-platform-verifier's Linux `system_roots()` (2026-11-12). It lives in nanocode-platform (crates/core/platform/src/trust.rs) because every user reaches it without a cycle and crates that use nanocode-tls from outside this workspace get it from git, where the patched verifier's own API is not there. It is rustls-native-certs 0.8.4 and openssl-probe 0.2.1 reproduced: `SSL_CERT_FILE` set (even empty) or `SSL_CERT_DIR` with a non-empty colon-separated entry loads only those paths; otherwise on unix outside macOS the probe takes `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR` when they exist, else the first existing file of openssl-probe's per-OS candidate list, plus every existing candidate directory in its order (the 18 file and 9 directory paths per cfg are copied verbatim; output/probe-lists.py compares them with openssl-probe's source: equal); files are parsed with rustls-pki-types' PEM iterator (non-certificate sections skipped, errors per section, fused on I/O errors), a directory's entries are followed through symlinks, dangling ones skipped, non-files ignored, not recursed, and the result is sorted by DER bytes and deduplicated; errors keep rustls-native-certs' contexts ("failed to read PEM from file", "opening directory", "reading directory entries", "failed to open file", "failed to load user/admin/system trust settings", "certificate not trusted", "failed to open current user certificate store"), its Display (`context: inner at 'path'`) and its Debug shape (`Error { context, kind: Io { inner, path } | Os(..) | Pem(..) }`), so nanocode-tls logs the same counts and messages and the proxy's `{:?}` error is unchanged. The struct is `NativeCertificates { certificates, errors }` (was `CertificateResult { certs, errors }`); no public nanocode type exposed rustls-native-certs, so pyramid-core and pyramid are unaffected. On macOS nanocode-sys gains trust_settings.rs: `certificates(Domain)` returns each certificate of a trust-settings domain as DER with its TLS trust result, mirroring security-framework 3.7.0 (SecTrustSettingsCopyCertificates, errSecNoTrustSettings as empty; SecTrustSettingsCopyTrustSettings per certificate, settings whose kSecTrustSettingsPolicyName is not CFEqual to "sslServer" skipped, a missing or unconvertible kSecTrustSettingsResult meaning TrustRoot, Unspecified and unknown results skipped; errors as OSStatus with SecCopyErrorMessageString's text, Display and Debug as security-framework's `Error { code, message }`), and the platform loader walks user, admin, system, keeps the first domain's result per DER and keeps TrustRoot and TrustAsRoot (no settings meaning TrustRoot), as rustls-native-certs does. Security and CoreFoundation are reached by dlopen and dlsym at first use, not linked, so nanocode-sys (under nanocode-sync in every binary) does not add `-framework Security` to every macOS link; with security-framework gone `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli --target aarch64-apple-darwin` has neither security-framework nor core-foundation-sys, so the CLI again links neither framework (as the macOS launch entry intended; proxy.rs had brought them back). On Windows nanocode-sys gains certificate_store.rs (windows-sys 0.61.2, already in Cargo.lock): the current user's ROOT system store, each certificate's DER, enhanced key usages (all, or OIDs; the server-authentication OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.7.3.1 makes it usable) and time validity, as schannel 0.1.29 and rustls-native-certs read them. Unsafe blocks added, all in nanocode-sys behind safe functions, each sound because: trust_settings.rs `dlerror` (no preconditions) and `CStr::from_ptr` on its non-null result (a NUL-terminated string valid until the next dl call on this thread; copied at once); `dlopen` (static NUL-terminated framework path); `dlsym` (a handle from dlopen that is never closed, static NUL-terminated names); one block transmuting the 18 non-null dlsym addresses to function pointer types that match Apple's Security and CoreFoundation header declarations; SecCopyErrorMessageString (reserved argument null), SecTrustSettingsCopyCertificates and SecTrustSettingsCopyTrustSettings (out pointers to locals; the certificate a reference borrowed from a live array), CFArrayGetCount and CFArrayGetValueAtIndex (live array, 0 <= index < count, count asserted non-negative), SecCertificateCopyData, CFDataGetLength, CFDataGetBytePtr and `slice::from_raw_parts` (non-null pointer and length of a CFData owned until after the copy), CFStringCreateWithBytes (null allocator, a static str's pointer and length), CFStringGetLength and both CFStringGetBytes calls (size query with a null buffer, then a buffer of exactly the queried length; written and used lengths asserted), CFDictionaryGetValueIfPresent, CFEqual, CFGetTypeID and the two GetTypeID functions (live references; the borrowed handle types carry the owner's lifetime), CFNumberGetValue (kCFNumberSInt64Type into an i64 local, after asserting the value is a CFNumber), and CFRelease in `Owned`'s drop (each Copy or Create result owned exactly once); certificate_store.rs CertOpenStore (system provider, NUL-terminated UTF-16 "ROOT"), CertCloseStore in drop (a store opened once), CertEnumCertificatesInStore (the previous context it frees, or null), `as_ref` on its non-null context (valid until the next enumeration call, used before it), `slice::from_raw_parts` on the context's encoded bytes, CertVerifyTimeValidity (null meaning now, the context's info), both CertGetEnhancedKeyUsage calls (size, then a u64-aligned buffer of at least that size), the reference to the filled CTL_USAGE, `slice::from_raw_parts` over its identifiers only when the count is non-zero, and `CStr::from_ptr` on each NUL-terminated identifier inside that buffer. Not equal: on macOS rustls-native-certs returns the certificates in HashMap order (random per process) and ours in DER order (the same set, now deterministic); a Security or CoreFoundation symbol that cannot be loaded is an error under each domain's context, where the linked crate could not start without it; a trust setting that is not a CFDictionary or a result that is not a CFNumber is an assert, where security-framework passed it to CoreFoundation, which aborts; on Windows a certificate whose usages cannot be read is the error "failed to read certificate usages" and is skipped, where rustls-native-certs panicked on `unwrap`; openssl-probe checked each candidate directory for existence twice and we check once. Not exercised: "reading directory entries" (a directory failing mid-listing), "certificate not trusted" and the user domain on macOS (adding user trust settings needs interactive authorization), and Windows at run time (nanocode-sys and nanocode-platform check and pass clippy for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu). Speed, interleaved: Linux default environment (121 roots) 10 rounds of 20 loads, median 1.46 ms per load before and 1.24 ms after; macOS full load, 7 runs, 80.6 to 91.6 ms before and 80.9 to 91.6 ms after. `cargo metadata` 427 to 425 packages on origin/master efe7f3f12 (489 to 487 and 490 to 488 on the earlier bases it was written against; rustls-native-certs, openssl-probe; security-framework and security-framework-sys leave aarch64-apple-darwin but stay in Cargo.lock for the patched verifier's iOS path; core-foundation and core-foundation-sys stay for nanocode-computer; schannel stays for rustpython-host_env on Windows, whose unused optional native-certs feature still names rustls-native-certs). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-tls -p nanocode-sandbox -p rustls-platform-verifier`; `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-cli`; `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform --target aarch64-apple-darwin` and `--target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-tls --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; nanocode-tls, nanocode-sandbox and the verifier do not check for aarch64-apple-darwin or Windows on this Hand (ring's C build script needs those toolchains), and were not built on the Mac.
- nanocode-platform forbids unsafe code: its `unix` module's libc calls and the iOS CoreFoundation time-zone lookup move unchanged into nanocode-sys, so nanocode-sys is the one crate with unsafe code that nanocode-cli builds besides the vendored patches and nanocode-computer's macOS accessibility calls (2026-11-12). crates/core/platform/src/unix.rs is now crates/core/sys/src/unix/host.rs (a 100% rename in `git diff -M`; re-exported from `nanocode_sys::unix`) and the `apple` module of zone.rs is crates/core/sys/src/apple.rs (compiled for Apple targets other than macOS, as before); `nanocode_platform::unix` re-exports exactly the items it had (`UserEntry`, `SystemRelease`, `user_id`, `process_group`, `user_entry`, `system_release`, `host_name`, `signal_process`, `probe_process`, `signal_group`, `sync_file`, `barrier_sync_file` on Apple, `available_bytes`, `redirect_output`, `thread_cpu_time`, `forbid_core_dumps` on Linux) and `time_zone_name` calls `nanocode_sys::apple::time_zone_name`, so callers are untouched; nanocode-platform drops its `unsafe_code = "deny"` lint block for the workspace's lints and its direct libc dependency. The unsafe blocks that moved, with the invariants recorded when they were written (the nix entry): `getuid`, `getpgrp`; `getpwuid_r` into a `MaybeUninit<passwd>` and a buffer of its stated capacity, read only when it reports success, with `CStr::from_ptr` on the entry's non-null name, directory and shell; `sysconf`; `uname` into a `MaybeUninit<utsname>` read after success; `gethostname` into a 256-byte buffer forced to end in zero; `kill`/`killpg`; `fsync`; `fcntl(F_BARRIERFSYNC)`; `statvfs` on a `CString` path into a `MaybeUninit` read after success; `dup2` onto stdout and stderr; `clock_gettime(CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID)`; `prctl(PR_SET_DUMPABLE, 0)`; and on iOS the CoreFoundation calls (`CFTimeZoneResetSystem`, `CFTimeZoneCopySystem` released with `CFRelease`, `CFTimeZoneGetName`, `CFStringGetLength`, `CFStringGetBytes` into a buffer of three bytes per UTF-16 unit). No behaviour changes: the code is byte for byte the same. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sys -p nanocode-platform` for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-apple-darwin and wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`; the iOS module was not built (no iOS target on the Hand). `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages.
- futures-channel leaves the workspace's crates: nanocode-mcp's `Outgoing` is a `nanocode_sync::unbounded::Receiver<Message>` and its replies travel on tokio's oneshot (2026-11-12). crates/core/sync/src/unbounded.rs is an unbounded channel over tokio's unbounded mpsc (already in nanocode-sync's tree on native and WASM): `channel()`, a cloneable `Sender` with `send` (the message back as the error when the channel is closed or the receiver is gone, as `unbounded_send`'s `into_inner`), `close` (sender-side, as `close_channel`: later sends fail, the receiver yields what was sent before and then `None`, other senders included) and `is_closed`, and a `Receiver` that implements futures' `Stream` (so `next`, `poll_next_unpin` and `tokio::select!` in nanocode-mcp-http and nanocode-mcp-tools work unchanged). A close is a flag plus an end marker queued behind the messages already sent. `Session`'s request replies use `tokio::sync::oneshot` (nanocode-mcp gains tokio with only `sync`, the feature nanocode-sync already enables). Public API change: `nanocode_mcp::Outgoing` was `futures_channel::mpsc::UnboundedReceiver<Message>`; code that only polls it as a `Stream` is unaffected (tempoxyz/pyramid-core and tempoxyz/pyramid: no hits for `Outgoing` from nanocode_mcp in code search). Not equal: a `send` that races a `close` on another thread can return `Ok` and land behind the end marker, where it is dropped unread; futures-channel decides that race inside one state word and reports the send as failed. nanocode-mcp's callers do not observe it: `Session` checks `is_closed` before sending, and a request that loses the race is answered `Error::Closed` by the close that drains `pending`. Proven with output/sync-unbounded, linking futures-channel 0.3.32 beside nanocode-sync: 2,000 seeds of 2,000 random operations (sends from up to six cloned senders, polls with a no-op waker, closes from any sender, sender drops, receiver drop, `is_closed`) comparing every result: 805,964 checks, 0 differences; 8 threads sending 200,000 messages each, all received in per-sender order. Benchmark (release, interleaved, 5 rounds, send and receive in batches of 64): futures-channel 119 to 237 ns per message against 113 to 172 ns. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-sync -p nanocode-mcp -p nanocode-mcp-http -p nanocode-mcp-tools` natively and the first three for wasm32-unknown-unknown, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-mcp -p nanocode-mcp-http --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 489 packages: futures-channel stays in the lock through hyper, hyper-util, reqwest and opentelemetry_sdk, and futures-executor through opentelemetry_sdk (the obs scope's).
- RustPython's atomic cells are rustpython-common's own, and crossbeam-utils leaves rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/atomic/cell.rs is `rustpython_common::atomic::AtomicCell<T>` for builds without the threading feature (nanocode's: its RustPython is single-threaded and `PyRc` is `Rc`): a `Cell<T>` with crossbeam-utils 0.8.22's `AtomicCell` API (`new`, `into_inner`, `store`, `swap`, `as_ptr`, `take`, `load`, `compare_exchange`, `fetch_update`, `fetch_add`/`fetch_sub`/`fetch_and`/`fetch_nand`/`fetch_or`/`fetch_xor`/`fetch_max`/`fetch_min` on the twelve integer types with wrapping arithmetic, `fetch_and`/`fetch_nand`/`fetch_or`/`fetch_xor` on bool, `Default`, `From`, and `Debug` as `AtomicCell { value: .. }`); with threading, atomic.rs re-exports `crossbeam_utils::atomic::AtomicCell`, and crossbeam-utils is an optional dependency of rustpython-common that only its threading feature enables (rustpython-vm's and rustpython-stdlib's threading features reach it through `rustpython-common/threading`). The 29 `use crossbeam_utils::atomic::AtomicCell` lines in rustpython-vm (23) and rustpython-stdlib (6) import `rustpython_common::atomic::AtomicCell`, and no call site changes except socket.rs's `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT`: a static must be Sync, which a `Cell` is not, so it is rustpython-common's `AtomicF64` with Acquire loads and Release stores, the orderings crossbeam's lock-free `AtomicCell<f64>` used (socket.rs compiles only with host_env, which nanocode does not enable and which already fails to build at the base in rustpython-host_env's ctypes.rs). `compare_exchange` compares with `Eq`, as crossbeam does (its byte comparison is a fast path that retries when the bytes differ but the values are equal), and returns the stored value in `Ok` and `Err`; `fetch_update` is crossbeam's loop, so a closure that changes the cell runs again. What nanocode's build calls (found by marking every method deprecated and checking nanocode-python): 1,140 calls in 107 files, `store` 504, `load` 474, `new` 128, `fetch_add` 22 and `fetch_sub` 6 on usize, `swap` 3 (bool, `Option<IterFunc>`), `compare_exchange` 2 (bool), `fetch_update` 1 (usize), and derived `Default` and `Debug`, on bool, usize, isize, i32, u32, u64, i64/`PyHash`, f64, `Option<u64>`, `Option<u128>`, `Option<bool>`, the `Option<fn ..>` number, sequence, mapping and type slots, and the `AwaitableState`, `FutureState`, `Newlines`, `SeenNewline` and `FileMode` enums and flags. Not equal: without threading the type is neither Sync nor `RefUnwindSafe` (nothing in that build needs either; the one static is the `AtomicF64` above), `into_inner` is not `const` (a `const fn` cannot drop a `Cell` field's container), and `is_lock_free` and the deprecated `compare_and_swap` are left out (unused). Equality: output/atomics-equal (run on gak-9) links crossbeam-utils 0.8.22 beside cell.rs and drives both with the same seeded xorshift sequences (300 sequences of 2,000 steps per type) of `new`/`from`, `load`, `store`, `swap`, reads through `as_ptr`, `compare_exchange` that hits and misses, `fetch_update` with random and re-entrant closures, every integer and bool `fetch_` operation, `take`, `Default`, `into_inner`, and `Debug` after every step, on the twelve integer types, bool, f64 (NaN, both zeros, infinities), `Option<fn>`, `Option<u64>`, `Option<u128>`, `Option<bool>`, copies of the enums above, and `Option<Rc<u32>>` with its strong counts compared after every step: 25,486,211 checks, 0 differences. The e2e corpus (1,065 programs) run on gak-9 by binaries built from the base and from this change: 25,472 output lines, 17 differ, all printing object addresses or `hash(nan)` (identity-based), which differ between any two runs (the same 17 lines differ between the base and e86dae0d8 builds). Speed on gak-9: corpus 331.2 s before and 334.5 s after (run side by side); eight microbenchmarks, best of 5 over three alternating rounds: with the release profile a generator loop is 3.6% and an itertools loop 2.5% slower and the other six are within 1.3%, but built with codegen-units=1 the generator loop is 164.5 ms before and 164.7 ms after and all eight are within 2.6% (the 2.6% is a StringIO loop that touches no cell), 1,606 ms to 1,619 ms in total, so the difference follows how the release build splits rustpython-vm into codegen units rather than the cell itself. nanocode-sync no longer uses crossbeam-utils (ad685d75c), so it leaves nanocode-cli with this change: `cargo metadata` stays at 427 packages (crossbeam-utils remains in Cargo.lock as the optional dependency of rustpython-common's threading feature) and `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` goes from 233 to 232 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 237 to 236 (aarch64-apple-darwin). Building rustpython-vm with threading fails before and after with the same 12 errors (`dyn Limiter` is not Send or Sync, `BlockingMutex` where `Mutex` is expected, no `rustpython_host_env::thread`). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-common -p rustpython-vm -p rustpython-stdlib` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-cli` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- The ruff parser's parser-thread constants (`STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX`, `PARSER_STACK_BYTES`) and its `TextLen` import are compiled only for non-wasm targets, where the parser thread exists (2026-11-12): the nesting-bound commit left them unused on wasm32-unknown-unknown, three new warnings there. No code changes otherwise; `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` applies on both. `cargo check --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` (gak-9) shows only the two rustpython-vm warnings present at e86dae0d8; `cargo check -p nanocode-python` passes natively.
- The vendored RustPython crates write their error impls by hand, and thiserror and thiserror-impl leave rustpython-codegen, rustpython-compiler, rustpython-ruff_python_ast and rustpython-vm (2026-11-12). Each `#[derive(thiserror::Error)]` becomes the impls it expanded to: `CodegenError` and the compiler's `ParseError` keep their hand-written `Display` and get `Error::source` returning their `error` field (their `#[source]`); the compiler's `CompileErrorType` and `CompileError` and the vm's `CompileErrorType`/`CompileError` for builds without the compiler (`#[error(transparent)]` variants) get `From` for each variant and `Display` and `source` that forward to the wrapped error; `PythonVersionDeserializationError` and the jit `ArgsError` get `Display` with the same format strings (`Invalid python version `{0}`: expected `major.minor``, `Invalid major version `{0}`: {1}`, the seven jit messages) and `source` returning the `ParseIntError` where it was `#[source]`; rustpython-codegen's `std` feature no longer enables `thiserror/std` (the impls use `core::error::Error`). Equality: the impls are what thiserror 2.0.18 generates for these attributes (format strings copied verbatim, forwarding for transparent variants, `source` only for `#[source]` fields), and SyntaxError/RecursionError messages, which go through these `Display` impls, are covered by the end-to-end corpus. thiserror stays in Cargo.lock and in nanocode-cli's tree through opentelemetry and opentelemetry_sdk, so the package counts do not change (`cargo metadata` 461, `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 265 on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, 268 on aarch64-apple-darwin); these were its only other users in nanocode-cli. `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` on Linux pass.
- The ruff parser bounds its nesting instead of growing its stack, and parses on a long-lived parser thread with a stack sized for that bound; stacker, psm, ar_archive_writer and object leave (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-ruff_python_parser/src/parser/mod.rs: `with_recursion` (the parser's recursion points for expressions, patterns, statement blocks and format specs) counts depth against `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX` = 20,000; the first time it is exceeded the parser records the current token's range and the number of errors so far and ends the token stream (the lexer jumps to the end of the source with no open brackets, f-strings or pending indentation, so every recursion returns at the end-of-file token), and `finish` drops the errors that recovery produced after that point and reports `ParseErrorType::NestingTooDeep`, which rustpython-compiler (`CompileError::from_nesting_too_deep`, also used by `_ast.parse`) turns into the same `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded during compilation` its AST depth check raised for deep trees. On native targets the parse runs on a per-calling-thread worker (`thread_local!`, started on first use, jobs and replies over std mpsc channels, panics carried back and resumed) whose stack is `RECURSION_DEPTH_MAX * STACK_BYTES_PER_RECURSION_MAX` (12 KiB, from the measured maximum of 9,351 bytes per level: nested f-strings in a debug build on aarch64-apple-darwin; release needs at most 4,173), 240 MiB of reserved, lazily committed address space; a worker that cannot be started is a typed `ParserThreadUnavailable` parse error. On wasm32 the parse runs in place with the same bound, as it did under stacker, which never grows the stack there. rustpython-vm's native stack check reads the stack position from the address of a local instead of `psm::stack_pointer`. Measured on gak-9 with the bound lifted and an 8 MiB parser stack (output/stackmeasure), the deepest parse that fits per construct (debug/release): unary minus 2,786/6,319, `not` 2,785/6,319, conditional expressions 4,365/10,927, lambdas 5,238/7,493, `**` 4,224/11,160, lists 1,489/2,747, calls 916/2,776, nested `if` blocks 1,919/6,100, f-strings 896/2,009; each costs one parser level per source level. Equality: output/e2e's deep corpus (532 programs: 14 constructs at depths 50 to 100,000 in eval and exec mode plus `ast.parse`, and with recursion limits 3,000 and 20,000 at depths 2,000 to 15,000; each program in its own process), old e86dae0d8 against this change on gak-9: 529 byte-identical (including the old crash at depth 15,000 with the limit raised, which still overflows codegen's stack, and every depth-100,000 case), 1 a 166 s run that timed out under the harness's 60 s alarm on one side only (both give the same RecursionError when run alone), and 2 differ: `await` chained 100,000 deep, where old parsed it and reported `SyntaxError: await expression cannot be used here` and the parser now stops at depth 20,000 with the RecursionError. Not equal: a source nested deeper than 20,000 parser levels now raises RecursionError even when it also has a syntax error that old reported (old parsed the whole tree first), and even when `sys.setrecursionlimit` was raised above 20,000 with a thread stack big enough for codegen to walk such a tree (old accepted those); a source nested 1,000 to 20,000 deep behaves as before. Cost: compile() of a 3-line source goes from 19.4 to 33-35 us on gak-9 (two thread handoffs per parse; release, 20,000 compiles, 3 interleaved rounds), and each thread that compiles keeps one parked parser thread; spawning a thread per parse cost 73-88 us and was not kept. TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored parser: the worker uses std channels. `cargo metadata` 465 to 461 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 269 to 265 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 272 to 268 (aarch64-apple-darwin); `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` on Linux and `cargo check -p nanocode-python` on aarch64-apple-darwin pass.
- pyexpat parses with rustpython-stdlib's own XML pull reader, and xml 1.3.0 (xml-rs) leaves nanocode-cli and Cargo.lock (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-stdlib/src/pyexpat/reader.rs is an `EventReader` over any `Read` specialised to the one configuration pyexpat's removed `create_config` built (comments and CDATA as their own events, whitespace reported as characters, character data not coalesced, root-level whitespace dropped, several root elements allowed). It decodes one byte at a time from the source exactly as xml-rs's `CharReader` did (byte order mark sniffing for UTF-8 and UTF-16 LE/BE, the `encoding` declaration matched by common prefix against utf-8/utf8, iso-8859-1/latin1, utf-16/utf16 and ascii/us-ascii with the same conflict rules, UTF-8 errors detected only after four bytes or at the end), so the parser thread pulls the same bytes at the same moments and the `NeedMore` handoff across `Parse()` chunks, `LineTracker`'s byte indices and the synchronous backend's replay are unchanged. A lexer (markup tokens, unread characters, `]]>` and `--` handling, the DOCTYPE lexing context) feeds a state machine that splits character data at markup, expands predefined and numeric references, keeps internal DTD general and parameter entities (first definition wins, external ones empty) and re-lexes them in content and in the internal subset (depth 10, 1,000,000 pending characters), resolves namespaces (first binding per element wins, the default namespace, the xml and xmlns rules, unbound prefixes), rejects duplicate attributes, applies the XML 1.0 or 1.1 character classes and the limits xml-rs had by default (names over 256 KiB, more than 65,536 attributes, 1 GiB of text, DOCTYPE or attribute value), and keeps the 16-slot event position queue that decides `CurrentLineNumber` and `CurrentColumnNumber`. pyexpat.rs builds the reader instead of `xml::ParserConfig` (the config parameter and field are gone) and reads `TextPosition` and `QualifiedName` from it. Not equal, and not observable: pyexpat never surfaced xml-rs's errors (both backends stop dispatching at the first one), so `ReaderError` is a fieldless kind without xml-rs's message text or error position, and events no longer carry what pyexpat ignored (prefixes, the namespace map, `StartDocument` and `Doctype` fields); the point where an error stops the stream (the events before it and the bytes consumed) is equal. Equality: output/xml-equal links xml 1.3.0 beside reader.rs and compares per document every event (names with namespace, attributes in order, text), the position after it, the bytes pulled from the source when it is returned, and the error point, once over a counting slice reader and, for documents up to 200 KB, once through a 64-byte `BufReader` over a source returning random 1 to 97 byte reads. Seeds 11 to 15, 150,000 generated documents each (half leaning well-formed, half noisy: declarations with odd versions, encodings and standalone values, DOCTYPEs with general, parameter and external entities, entity chains up to 14 deep, billion laughs, namespaces, CDATA, comments, PIs, byte order marks, UTF-16 LE/BE and Latin-1, names past 256 KiB, 65,535 to 65,537 attributes), each also mutated (truncations, byte flips, inserted markup and bad UTF-8, deletions) plus every prefix of every tenth short one: 9,249,874 documents, 47,852,738 checks, 0 differences. 60,003 real XML, plist, SVG, XSD, sdef and other files from macOS (/System/Library, /Library, /usr/share, /Applications, /opt/homebrew, /private/etc), each as is, with 4 mutations and a random prefix, twice (seeds 21, 22): 720,036 documents, 87,440,363 checks, 0 differences. On the Linux Hand the same harness passes seed 41 (240,324 documents, 1,245,790 checks) and 3,139 files from /usr/share, /usr/lib/python3 and /etc (18,834 documents, 2,045,059 checks) with 0 differences. End to end: 146 Python programs over 3,643 documents (2,810 generated and mutated, 800 real macOS files, 33 edge cases), each through xml.parsers.expat whole and in 1, 5, 7 and 64 byte `Parse()` chunks with and without a namespace separator and `ordered_attributes`, recording every handler with `CurrentLineNumber`, `CurrentColumnNumber` and `CurrentByteIndex`, then xml.dom.minidom, ElementTree `fromstring`/`tostring` and `XMLPullParser` fed 13-byte chunks, and xml.sax: the old (xml 1.3.0) and new e2e binaries print byte-identical 38,776,186-byte outputs (an old binary first resolved xml 1.4.0, which normalises line ends, and differed; pinned to the workspace's 1.3.0 it matches). Benchmarks on gak-9, interleaved: the reader alone over four macOS documents of 1.6 to 2.8 MB, 7 rounds, twice: xml 1.3.0 33.5 and 34.1 MB/s, new 49.3 and 50.0 MB/s; through Python, best of 5, three interleaved rounds: `ElementTree.fromstring` of 2 MB 153 to 161 ms before, 138 to 144 ms after; expat with handlers 360 to 388 ms before, 359 to 375 ms after; minidom 505 to 518 ms before, 507 to 516 ms after (the VM dominates). `cargo metadata` 466 to 465 packages; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 270 to 269 (x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu) and 273 to 272 (aarch64-apple-darwin). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-stdlib` pass.
- rg's `-E`/`--encoding` and its BOM sniffing decode with psh-utils's own WHATWG Encoding Standard decoders instead of encoding_rs 0.8.44; encoding_rs, core_detect, multiversion_no_op and simdutf8 leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). Where: `crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/searcher/encoding/`: `mod.rs` (label lookup trimming the five ASCII whitespace bytes and lowercasing ASCII, without the replacement encoding's labels as `for_label_no_replacement` did; `for_bom`; the `Decoder` with encoding_rs's BOM-removal life cycle, BOM bytes held back across buffers, and its U+FFFD loop; the `Transcode` cursor and the block-compressed `Index`), `unicode.rs` (UTF-8 over `std::str::from_utf8`, UTF-16LE/BE with a four-units-per-word ASCII path), `legacy.rs` (one two-byte machine for the 28 single-byte encodings, Big5, EUC-KR and Shift_JIS; x-user-defined), `gb18030.rs` (gb18030 and GBK), `japanese.rs` (EUC-JP, ISO-2022-JP) and `data.rs`, generated by output/enc-gen/generate.py (then rustfmt) from indexes.json and encodings.json of whatwg/encoding 1d519bf8e5555cef64cf3a712485f41cd1a6a990, the revision encoding_rs 0.8.44's README names, fetched from GitHub; NOTICE carries the WHATWG BSD-3-Clause notice; `decode.rs` and `searcher/mod.rs` change only their imports. Each decoder keeps encoding_rs's control flow so every call reports the same result, bytes read and bytes written as well as the same text: the output room checked before each step (3 bytes; 4 for UTF-8, UTF-16, Big5 and gb18030, and x-user-defined checks 3 even for ASCII), the ASCII runs, the `< 60` punctuation shortcut of the single-byte and EUC-KR decoders, the bytes gb18030, EUC-JP and ISO-2022-JP carry between calls and re-emit (gb18030's pending ASCII digit, ISO-2022-JP's prepended escape byte), and UTF-16's `(OutputFull, 0, 0)` at the end of input. - jiff leaves RustPython: the time module's code for targets that are neither Unix nor Windows (wasm32) uses its own calendar and a jiff-compatible strftime, and the build script dates the commit with nanocode-platform's zone reader; jiff, jiff-core, jiff-static, jiff-tzdb, jiff-tzdb-platform, portable-atomic-util and defmt (with defmt-macros and defmt-parser) leave the lock (2026-11-12). On Linux and macOS time.localtime, gmtime, mktime, strftime, asctime, ctime, timezone, altzone, daylight and tzname never reached jiff: they go through libc in rustpython-host_env and are unchanged; jiff was compiled into nanocode-cli only because rustpython-vm depended on it unconditionally and its build script used it. crates/patches/rustpython-vm/src/stdlib/time/civil.rs (non-Unix, non-Windows only) is a civil DateTime over nanocode-platform's civil_from_days and days_from_civil (now public, and days_from_civil no longer Unix-only), with jiff 0.2.39's limits (years -9999..=9999, Unix seconds -377705023201..=253402207200, the same OverflowErrors), weekday, day of year and ISO week date, and a strftime that reproduces jiff's lenient Display: flags _ 0 - ^ #, widths up to 255 (integer padding capped at 20, the space-padded negative case uncapped), colons, %C %y %g of negative years, %c %x %X %r as jiff's locale-free "%Y M%m %-d, %a %H:%M:%S" family, %f %N %.Nf, and a directive it cannot format (%Z %z %:z %Q %s on a zone-less time, unknown letters, a dangling flag, width or colon, a width past 255) written back literally from its percent sign. The system zone on those targets is what jiff's TimeZone::system() returned on wasm32-unknown-unknown without its js feature, Etc/Unknown, which behaves as UTC with abbreviation "UTC": tm_zone "UTC", tm_gmtoff 0, mktime as UTC. The current time comes from std's SystemTime (it panics on wasm32-unknown-unknown, as jiff's Timestamp::now did with its own message; nanocode's boot.py routes time.time, localtime(), gmtime(), ctime() and strftime without a tuple through the host clock, so only asctime() without arguments reaches it) or, with the wasmbind feature, from JavaScript's Date.now as jiff's js feature did. build.rs takes nanocode-platform as a build dependency: git's commit time (or the clock) is shifted by utc_offset_seconds in the build host's zone (TZ, then /etc/localtime) and printed as "%b %e %Y" and "%H:%M:%S" by hand. nanocode-platform now parses a POSIX rule in TZ with the extended (TZif v3) syntax, rule times from -167 to 167 hours, as jiff and glibc do; before, such a TZ was refused and /etc/localtime used. What is not equal: (1) on wasm32-wasi, which nanocode does not build, jiff read a zone from TZ in the WASI environment; this code uses UTC there as on wasm32-unknown-unknown; (2) with the wasmbind feature, which nothing in nanocode enables, jiff took the browser's zone from Intl and its bundled tzdb; this code uses UTC; (3) for a TZ of the permanent-DST form DST from Jan 1 0:00 to Dec 31 25:00 (EST5EDT,0/0,J365/25), jiff 0.2.39 shows standard time in the five hours after each new year and nanocode-platform (like glibc) stays in DST, which can change the build host's date string within those hours; (4) an invalid TZ falls back to /etc/localtime's zone in nanocode-platform where jiff used UTC (the same on hosts whose /etc/localtime is UTC); (5) a now() reading outside jiff's range is an OverflowError instead of a panic. Equality: output/time-equal links jiff 0.2.39 beside civil.rs (included by path) and compares DateTime::new over random and out-of-range fields, Unix seconds to civil time over the whole range and past both ends with random nanoseconds, to_unix against jiff's to_zoned(Etc/Unknown) (and Etc/Unknown against UTC), the struct_time fields, strftime of every directive under every flag, 18 widths and 0 to 4 colons on boundary and random times, the dot forms, edge strings and random format strings mixing directives, flags, digits, colons and non-ASCII: seeds 1, 2, 3 at 20,000 cases give 724,131, 724,703 and 723,493 checks, seeds 11, 12, 13 at 200,000 cases 5,996,811, 5,996,356 and 6,000,562, 0 differences; build_date runs the old build.rs (jiff) and the new one side by side with git's timestamp stubbed, once per TZ: all 454 files of /usr/share/zoneinfo, 21 TZ values (POSIX rules with southern-hemisphere, half-hour, 45-minute, negative-DST, +13/+14, extended negative and 25-hour rule times; ":name", an absolute path, empty, invalid, "localtime") and TZ unset, each at every transition jiff lists (first 4,000) +-1 s and 900 random times: 2,124,379 checks, differences only in the two permanent-DST strings (6,002 each, case 3). End to end, output/time-e2e builds nanocode-python for wasm32-unknown-unknown from e86dae0d8 and from this tree into a cdylib run by Node with a fixed host clock: four programs (78,126 lines: gmtime, localtime and ctime of 738 timestamps including infinities, NaN and out-of-range values; mktime, asctime and strftime of 1,772 tuples including invalid fields and DST-gap and fold times; 8,817 format strings, every directive under every flag, width and colon count plus random ones, on 8 tuples including years -9999, -50, 1 and 9999; the module constants, struct_time, strptime and error cases) run as 42 slices: 78,258 lines of output, byte-identical. The same corpus was not run natively old against new: on Linux and macOS this change compiles none of the time module's code it edits (only build.rs, whose equality build_date shows), and the scope asked for no more release builds of RustPython on the shared Hand. Speed (release, interleaved, 7 rounds, best): strftime "%a %b %e %H:%M:%S %Y" 150 ns jiff against 203 ns, "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S" 98 against 156, every directive 1,089 against 2,008; seconds to civil fields 7.0 against 27.5 ns; mktime 5.5 against 9.2 ns: slower, and only wasm32 builds run this code. cargo metadata 480 -> 471 packages; nanocode-cli on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu 280 -> 278 and on aarch64-apple-darwin 282 -> 280 packages (cargo tree -e normal,build), nanocode-python on wasm32-unknown-unknown 115 -> 113 (jiff, jiff-core, jiff-tzdb and jiff-tzdb-platform leave; the build script's nanocode-platform brings tokio and getrandom for the host). - RustPython's lock types are built on rustpython-common's own port of the lock_api layer, and parking_lot, parking_lot_core and lock_api leave nanocode-cli (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/lock/api.rs carries what RustPython used of lock_api 0.4.14: the raw-lock traits (`RawMutex`, `RawRwLock` with its `is_locked_exclusive` default, `RawRwLockDowngrade`, `RawRwLockRecursive`, `RawRwLockUpgrade`, `RawRwLockUpgradeDowngrade`, `GetThreadId`), the `GuardSend`/`GuardNoSend` markers, and `Mutex`/`RwLock` with their guards, mapped guards (`map`, `try_map`), `upgradable_read`/`upgrade`, `downgrade`, `read_recursive`/`try_read_recursive`, `get_mut`, `into_inner`, `raw`, `data_ptr` and the same `Send`/`Sync` bounds and `Debug` output (`Mutex { data: .. }`, `<locked>`). Without the `threading` feature (nanocode's build) every PyMutex/PyRwLock is still the Cell-based raw lock of lock/cell_lock.rs, so locking behaves exactly as before; with `threading`, lock/parking.rs adapts parking_lot's raw locks to the new traits and parking_lot becomes an optional dependency of rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib that only their `threading` feature enables (it is on rustpython-host_env only for Windows). The places that took a parking_lot lock outside `threading` now use std: the csv dialect registry and field limit, the interpreter-admission gate (vm/runtime.rs, gc_state.rs) and the `_interpqueues`/`_interpchannels` registries take a `rustpython_common::lock::BlockingMutex` (a `std::sync::Mutex` whose `lock` ignores poisoning, as parking_lot has none), `_interpchannels`' blocked `send()` waits on a `std::sync::Condvar` (`wait`, and `wait_timeout` to the deadline in place of `wait_until`), host_env's `AppendLog` uses `std::sync::Mutex` the same way, hashlib's per-object state is a `PyMutex`, and `_functools`' lru_cache reentrant lock is, without `threading`, a depth counter (parking_lot's reentrant mutex on one thread only ever counted). TigerStyle departure, bounded to the vendored interpreter: these are blocking std locks and a condition variable rather than nanocode-sync primitives, because RustPython's object model hands out guards from shared references everywhere and porting it to an owner-and-mailbox design is a rewrite of the interpreter; the new lock layer uses the same unsafe as lock_api (cells handed out under a held raw lock), which the vendored crates already rely on. The `threading` feature did not build before this change either (`dyn Limiter` is not `Send + Sync` in vm/runtime.rs, _thread.rs and thread.rs, checked at e86dae0d8 on gak-9) and still does not. - nanocode-compression's inflate runs about twice as fast on PNG image data with the same behavior (2026-11-12): nanocode-png spends most of its decode time inflating IDAT streams, where literals are 60% of the output (159 M literals and 12 M matches over the 40 largest corpus PNGs, the matches mostly 64 or more bytes back and 8 bytes long), and the inflate fast loop cost about 19 cycles a symbol. In crates/core/compression/src/inflate the fast loop now works on local copies of the bit reader and the output (they were reached through references and kept in memory, and refill, peek, copy_match and the other small helpers were out-of-line calls at codegen-units 16; they are `#[inline(always)]`); every dynamic block also builds a 4096-entry literal table (table.rs `build_literals`, from the code lengths already sorted for the Huffman table, by doubling as fdeflate 0.3.7 builds its table, and a static one for fixed blocks) whose entries hold one or two root-table literals with their total bits, so a run of literals costs one lookup per two literals and no branch between one and two; matches copy 16-byte chunks from 16 bytes back, 8-byte chunks from 8 and fill at distance 1; the window hands out slices instead of taking the output. The loop keeps zlib-rs's iteration boundaries (two literals, then one symbol, then the input and output exit test), because an error the fast loop finds reads "repeated call with bad state" while the byte-at-a-time path names it: batches of up to three literal entries and one symbol run only while no exit test could fire inside them (output room of 260 + 264 bytes, input of 15 + 11 bytes), then the original loop finishes from the same phase (root-table literals since the last other symbol, mod 3), so every call stops on the same input byte with the same status, counts, bytes, window and message. The decoder state grows by the 16 KiB literal table. Not equal: nothing observable; bytes past what a call produced may still be written, as before (2-byte literal stores, 16-byte match chunks). CRC-32 is unchanged: slicing-by-16 runs at 2.9 GB/s on an M1 Max, a variant with 64-bit loads was slower (2.7 GB/s) and slicing-by-8 slower still (1.6 GB/s), and crc32fast's lead comes from the CRC and carry-less multiply instructions safe portable code cannot use. - nanocode-compression decodes Brotli (RFC 7932) itself: crates/core/compression/src/brotli/ (bits.rs, prefix.rs, header.rs, blocks.rs, commands.rs, window.rs, dictionary.rs, tables.rs) is a streaming decoder written anew, `Decoder::decompress(input, output) -> Result<Progress, DecodeError>` reporting bytes consumed and written and `Status::{NeedsInput, NeedsOutput, Done}`, resumable after any input byte and any output byte, leaving bytes after the last meta-block unconsumed (2026-11-12). Its acceptance follows brotli-decompressor 5.0.3, quirks included: checks run in the same order (simple-code symbols, code length code space, prefix code space, context map runs, nibbles, padding); a meta-block whose commands overrun MLEN fails only where that decoder writes its ring buffer (input exhausted, ring full at the window, stream end), so a non-last one that overruns between those points is accepted as there; a single literal block type runs out after 2^24 literals; distances beyond the window or before any output become dictionary references, with the same invalid-length and invalid-transform failures. The ring buffer is the stream's window (1 << WBITS, 1 KiB to 16 MiB): allocated at the first data meta-block at its length rounded up to a power of two and doubled up to the window as output grows; prefix tables, context maps and tree groups live in vectors reused across meta-blocks, so nothing allocates per symbol. The static dictionary is dictionary.bin (122,784 bytes, taken from brotli-decompressor-5.0.3/src/dictionary/mod.rs and byte-identical to the hex listing of RFC 7932 Appendix A; the RFC states its CRC-32, 0x5136cb04, which matches, and no SHA-256: it is 20e42eb1b511c21806d4d227d07e5dd06877d8ce7b3a817f378f313653f35c70); the 121 transforms of Appendix B and the Lut0/Lut1/Lut2 context tables are data generated from the RFC text. Binary assets are already committed (crates/core/schema/src/*.bin) and no .gitattributes applies; the wasm32 build passes. Not equal: large-window streams (WBITS 0010001) are rejected with `InvalidWindowBits` as RFC 7932 requires, while brotli-decompressor's `BrotliState::new` turns large window on and accepts them; when brotli-decompressor resumes a read from its 8-byte carry buffer it also writes its ring buffer each time that buffer runs dry, so an invalid stream whose non-last meta-block overruns MLEN can fail there in one chunking and succeed in others; bytes written during the call that fails are not reported (`decompress` returns only the error). Equal: output/brotli-equal compares the two decoders driven alike. 4,871 files (repository sources and text, ~/.cargo/registry, /usr/bin binaries, ~/media-corpus images; 0 B to 19.2 MB) and 10 edge inputs (empty, 1 and 2 bytes, 1 MiB zeros, repeated pairs and words, random, text mixed with random) compressed by the brotli crate 8 at all 180 quality 0..=11 and lgwin 10..=24 pairs: 18,959 streams (336.4 MB of output), 94,137 decodes in up to five chunkings (whole input with 1 MiB and 1-byte output, 4096/4096, random 1..64-byte input with random 1..300-byte output, 1-byte input and output up to 64 KiB): 0 differences in bytes, end status or bytes consumed at the end. 15 br responses saved raw from www.google.com, www.cloudflare.com, www.youtube.com, www.facebook.com, www.bing.com, developer.mozilla.org, discord.com, www.shopify.com, www.npmjs.com, cdnjs.cloudflare.com and cdn.jsdelivr.net (github.com and wikipedia.org answered gzip) in four chunkings: 60 checks, 0 differences. 300,000 seeded mutations of 400 valid streams (bit flips, byte replacements, insertions, deletions, truncations) and random byte strings, each whole and in random 1..16-byte chunks: 600,000 checks, of which 363,310 fail, 171,995 end needing input with all input consumed and 64,203 finish in both; 492 large-window ones rejected; 2 differences, both the carry-buffer case above (confirmed with an instrumented copy of brotli-decompressor); output before a failure equal in all but those 2. Benchmark (CPU time per decode, interleaved, 9 rounds, medians, host load 11 to 15 on 5 cores; brotli-decompressor vs ours): source text 33.6 MB q1 w24 303 vs 274 MB/s, 8.4 MB q5 w22 272 vs 280, q9 w16 274 vs 259, q11 w22 328 vs 272, random words 8 MB q5 w22 242 vs 184, binaries 25.2 MB q5 w22 172 vs 195, 4 MB q9 w18 130 vs 161; the copy-heavy text gap (0.76 to 0.94) is the dispatch per command through the resumable step state. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression (also --target wasm32-unknown-unknown), cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-http, cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression -p nanocode-http. - nanocode-jpeg (crates/core/jpeg: no_std + alloc, forbid(unsafe_code), no dependencies) decodes and encodes JPEG as image 0.25.6 did with zune-jpeg 0.4.21 and its own JpegEncoder, ready for the image stack to switch to (no caller changes yet) (2026-11-12). API: header(bytes) -> Header { width, height, color: Luma | Rgb } parses the markers up to the first SOS as image's JpegDecoder::new did; decode(bytes, pixel_bytes_max) -> Decoded { width, height, color, pixels, icc_profile, exif } refuses more than pixel_bytes_max decoded bytes before allocating; encode(pixels, width, height, color, quality, icc_profile). Decoder: a port of zune-jpeg 0.4.21 as image drives it (strict mode off, no size limits, Luma output for a one-component frame and RGB otherwise, CMYK, YCCK and Adobe transforms converted to RGB, the ICC profile only from a complete set of APP2 chunks, the last Exif APP1 segment, orientation not applied): baseline and progressive Huffman, restart intervals, every sampling layout zune accepts, its integer IDCT, upsamplers and YCbCr conversion, its lenient handling of truncated and corrupt data (the 37-byte overread limit, markers inside scans, unknown markers swallowed, the u16 wrap of (dimension + 7) / 8, wrapping arithmetic as zune's release build computes it) and its error messages. zune's x86_64 AVX2 IDCT and color conversion compute the same integers as its scalar code (the AVX2 DC-only mask test cannot misfire and its saturating packs equal the clamps for in-range samples; the aarch64 NEON paths use the same algorithm), so the scalar port matches what image produced on x86_64 and on aarch64. Encoder: image's baseline encoder (libjpeg quality scaling, the standard tables, jfdctint forward DCT, f32 quantization rounded half away from zero, 4:4:4, JFIF APP0, ICC in 65519-byte APP2 chunks) for Luma and RGB. Not equal: where zune panicked because a layout does not fit its buffers (unusual sampling ratios, a scan for a component without a buffer, a mid-stream SOS naming a missing table) or image's encoder asserted on a wrong buffer length, nanocode-jpeg returns a typed error; where zune looped forever (a progressive image ending in a restart marker after its last scan) it returns RestartAtEnd; quality outside 1..=100 is an error instead of being clamped. Equal: output/jpeg-equal links image 0.25.6 (jpeg) and zune-jpeg 0.4.21. Decode: 3,819 real and generated JPEGs (the image-rs, libjpeg-turbo, zune-image, jpeg-decoder and Pillow test images, large photos, and 3,267 made with Pillow and libjpeg-turbo's cjpeg: qualities 1 to 100, 4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0 and 4:1:1, factors such as 2x2,1x2,1x1, 4x4 and 3x1, progressive, restart intervals, grayscale, CMYK, RGB, arithmetic, ICC up to 150 KB, Exif) plus 22,914 seeded mutants (truncation, bit flips, byte overwrites, inserted markers, cut and duplicated runs): 26,733 checks of header, dimensions, color, ICC, Exif, pixels and error against success, 0 differences; 240 inputs where image panicked and 1 where it hung get an error; all 15,470 error messages equal zune's. 40 progressive images ending in a restart marker: 28 hang in image, all return an error here. Encode: 58,677 checks (20,000 seeded random images of 1 to 160 px with no, small, multi-chunk or empty ICC at qualities 1 to 100, edge sizes from 0x0 to 65535x1 and 65536x1, 3,040 decoded real images at 85 and a random quality and every tenth at all 100 qualities, their gray planes), 0 differences; 900 checks that image's encode_image of an L8, La8 or Rgba8 DynamicImage equals encoding its RGB (gray replicated, alpha dropped) as 3 components. Commands: cargo build --release in output/jpeg-equal, then decode 6 21 ~/media-corpus/jpeg, encode 20000 11 ~/media-corpus/jpeg, bench 9 <photos>. cargo metadata: 426 -> 427 packages. Benchmarks (on-CPU time from /proc/thread-self/schedstat, median of 9 interleaved rounds on the loaded 5-core Hand): encode at quality 85 is 14 to 24% faster (12 MP 4:2:0 292.8 -> 231.2 ms, 15.5 MP 366.0 -> 281.8 ms); decode is slower where zune used AVX2: 12 MP baseline 4:2:0 45.6 -> 85.6 ms, 4:4:4 56.7 -> 112.0 ms, grayscale 19.5 -> 29.1 ms, progressive 138.1 -> 155.4 ms, 15.5 MP 77.1 -> 134.5 ms. The scalar IDCT is faster than zune's own scalar IDCT (23.6 against 31.6 ms per 200,000 blocks); the gap is zune's AVX2 IDCT and color conversion, which safe code on the SSE2 baseline cannot reach (a lane-wise IDCT and per-column zero shortcuts were built and measured slower, since SSE2 has no 32-bit vector multiply).
- nanocode-gif (crates/core/gif, new) decodes a GIF's first frame exactly as image 0.25.6's GifDecoder drove gif 0.13.3 and weezl 0.1.12 (2026-11-12); nothing calls it yet. `Gif::new` is `DecodeOptions::read_info` with RGBA output (magic, screen descriptor, global palette, extensions up to the first non-extension block, the 50 MB extension-data memory limit, the unknown-block and control-extension-length errors), and `first_frame` is `GifDecoder::read_image`: `next_frame_info` with its palette check, then either the rows of a full-width frame decoded straight into the zeroed canvas or a separate frame buffer, refused above the caller's allocation limit as image's `Limits::reserve_usize` did, composited with wrapping offsets and transparent black outside it. The streaming decoder is ported state for state (gif's quirks included: an empty first sub-block length swallows the next byte, a trailer needs one more byte to be read, interlaced row order from its iterator), and the LZW decoder is weezl's `DecodeState` with LSB codes and no yield on a full buffer, burst decoding and all (six codes per refill, the deferred-clear and implicit-reset rules, the `KwKwK` case, `InvalidCode` for a code beyond the table), because whether a stray code after the last needed pixel is read, and so errors, depends on how many bits sit in its 64-bit buffer; gif's 8 KiB BufReader windows over image's Cursor decide how sub-block data reaches it, so the decoder feeds it the same slices. Palette indices without a color leave the pixel untouched, as gif's converter does. Equal: output/gif-equal links image =0.25.6 and gif =0.13.3: 36 real GIFs (image-rs/image and image-gif test images, Wikimedia Commons) with 30 seeded mutations each and 3,000 seeded synthetic GIFs (1 to 3 frames with random sizes, offsets, interlacing, transparency, local and global palettes of 2 to 256 colors, out-of-range indices, empty global tables) with 6 mutations each (truncation, bit flips, bytes set to block and extension labels or code sizes): 22,116 checks of header success, dimensions, pixel success and RGBA pixels, 0 differences (12,658 decoded). Decoding the 36 real files (12.6 MB): 109 ms old against 108 ms new on-CPU, min of 7 interleaved runs. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-gif`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-gif --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages 425 -> 426.
- nanocode-png (crates/core/png, new) decodes and encodes PNG exactly as image 0.25.6 drove png 0.17.16 (2026-11-12); nothing calls it yet, the image stack's switch-over follows. `Png::new(bytes, memory_bytes_max)` is `PngDecoder::with_limits` (read_header_info, read_info, read_until_image_data): signature, IHDR checks, the chunk sequence with png's per-chunk rules (ancillary chunks parsed before their CRC is checked and kept on a CRC mismatch, critical ones refused; zero-length chunks never parsed; pHYs, gAMA, cHRM, sRGB, acTL, fcTL, PLTE, tRNS, sBIT, iCCP checks and errors, text chunks ignored), the byte budget png 0.17's `Limits` spends on its chunk buffer's growth, palettes, tRNS, sBIT and the ICC profile, and fdAT-first APNGs; `decode` is `next_frame` with `Transformations::EXPAND` into image's buffer layout (8-bit, or 16-bit as native `u16`), including Adam7, sub-frames from an fcTL before the first IDAT, palette expansion with png's quirks, low-depth gray scaling and tRNS keys. Image data inflates through nanocode-compression's raw inflate after fdeflate's own zlib header test; the stream must end with four trailer bytes (fdeflate's Done) before the next chunk, Adler-32 is not checked (png's default), and every chunk of the IDAT run is read and CRC-checked. The iCCP profile inflates with the Adler-32 check and errors swallowed, as png did. `encode` is png's Writer with Compression::Fast, FilterType::Sub and AdaptiveFilterType::Adaptive (what nanocode-image's `encode_png` and image's `write_to(Png)` use): IHDR, iCCP compressed by nanocode-compression's miniz at level 6 under the name `_`, eXIf, IDAT from fdeflate's fixed-Huffman compressor written anew (its 286 code lengths, header block and run coding, one call per row) or its stored-only fallback when that is smaller, IEND. Equal: output/png-equal links image =0.25.6 and png =0.17.16 beside the crate. Decoding 692 real PNGs (PngSuite, image-rs/image and image-png test images, Wikimedia Commons files) and 4,000 seeded synthetic ones (every color type and depth, interlaced or not, palettes, tRNS, ICC, all compression levels and filters) with 40 and 5 seeded mutations each (truncation, bit flips, chunk bytes rewritten with a fixed CRC, chunks dropped, duplicated, resized): 53,274 checks of header success, dimensions, color type, ICC bytes, pixel success and pixels, 0 differences (14,547 decoded, 38,625 errors, 102 old panics that are errors here). Encoding 3,000 images (692 decoded real images and 2,308 seeded synthetic ones in all eight color types, 1x1 to 300x200, noise, runs and gradients, with random ICC profiles and eXIf) against png's Writer: 3,000 byte comparisons, 0 differences. Measured on-CPU (getrusage, the Hand at load 11 to 15): decoding 40 large PNGs 365 -> 520 ms, of which inflate is 222 -> 330 ms (fdeflate's PNG-tuned double-literal tables against zlib-rs's port, which the rule to inflate with nanocode-compression keeps), CRC-32 over the file 2 -> 22 ms (crc32fast uses PCLMULQDQ; our slicing-by-16 is scalar) and the row work (unfiltering with png's stb-style Paeth, expansion) about equal; encoding 204 decoded RGB/RGBA images 1.38-1.73 s -> 1.76-2.07 s (the fast compressor alone is equal to fdeflate's on 64 MB, 111-124 ms against 111-145 ms, the adaptive filter's four trial filters and the CRC are the rest). `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-png`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-png --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages 424 -> 425.
- nanocode-compression's `adler32` sums 32 lanes per step, so the compiler vectorizes it (2026-11-12): crates/core/compression/src/checksum.rs keeps the byte loop for inputs under 16 bytes and the tail, and for each run of up to 173 chunks of 32 bytes (5,536 bytes, under zlib's 5,552-byte bound before a sum can overflow 32 bits) keeps per-lane byte sums and per-lane prefix sums in `[u32; 32]`, then folds them into the two halves in 64 bits (high += low * length + 32 * prefixes + (32 - lane) * sums) and reduces modulo 65,521 once. Results are the same integers: output/checksum-bench compares it with simd-adler32 0.3.10 on 200,000 seeded slices (lengths 0..20,000, random offsets and random starting checksums) and on all-0xFF inputs of every length 0..11,999: 212,000 checks, 0 differences. Measured: 100 MB went from about 51-104 ms to 18-21 ms (simd-adler32's AVX2 path: 5-9 ms), which the PNG encoder (one Adler-32 over all filtered rows) and every zlib stream nanocode-compression writes or checks (Python's zlib, gzip and zip members, nanocode-http's gzip) share. `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-compression --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`. `cargo metadata` packages unchanged.

Not equal: a level above 10 is an `InvalidInput` error instead of flate2's silent 10 (11 to 255) or 1 (above 255); callers pass 2 (GZIP_LEVEL). Equal: output/http-equal gzip compares flate2's GzEncoder (write_all + finish) with `nanocode_http::gzip` over 600 seeded random inputs (0 B to 4 MiB, text, JSON, runs, random bytes) at levels 0 to 10 and 862 real files (repository sources, ~/media-corpus images, /usr/bin) at every level: 11,941 checks, 0 differences.
