Equality: output/ruff-equal links aho-corasick 1.1.4 with the old matcher (copied from the vendored source) beside the new function and compares 5,000,000 random strings of 0 to 8 characters over the prefix alphabet, quotes, `x`, space and `é`, plus every table entry with five suffixes: 5,000,700 checks, 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 485 packages before and after; `cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build` 294 to 293 packages on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu and 295 to 294 on aarch64-apple-darwin. `cargo check -p rustpython-ruff_python_ast` passes.
- RustPython's bit sets are plain structs in its own code, and bitflagset, radium, ref-cast and ref-cast-impl leave (2026-11-12). The `bitflag!`/`bitflagset!`/`atomic_bitflagset!` invocations become `#[repr(u8)]` enums and small structs over the same integer with only the operations their callers use, with bitflagset 0.0.4's semantics: rustpython-compiler-core's `MakeFunctionFlags` (u8: `new`, `insert`, `contains`, `bits`, `|`, `From<[MakeFunctionFlag; N]>`) and `CoFastFlags` (u8: `from_element`, `from_slice`, `from_bits_retain`, `contains`, `bits`, `ARG`), rustpython-host_env's `FileMode` (io.rs and io_unsupported.rs), `AccessMode` (`from_bits` is `None` for bits outside X, W and R, as bitflagset's `from_bits` was) and `ChFlags`, rustpython-vm's `EvalBreaker` (an `AtomicU8`: `insert`/`remove` are `fetch_or`/`fetch_and` with AcqRel, `contains`/`is_empty` relaxed loads, as before), the `_stat` permission bits and `PyTypeFlags` (u64 with its bit positions as `u8` constants, `from_bits_truncate` keeping only the named positions, `contains`/`insert`/`remove`/`from_element`/`from_slice` asserting the position is below 64 where bitflagset panicked) with `AtomicPyTypeFlags` (`repr(transparent)` over `AtomicU64`, which `__flags__`'s atomic member read relies on; `insert`/`remove` AcqRel read-modify-writes returning whether the bit changed, `contains` relaxed). Debug, Display, iteration and the other set methods nobody called are not reproduced. num-integer stays in Cargo.lock for num-bigint (image) but bitflagset was its only path into nanocode-cli. Equality: output/bitflag-equal links bitflagset 0.0.4 with the old invocations beside the new definitions (extracted from the edited sources) and compares 2,000,000 rounds of random u64 bit patterns through truncate, retain, contains, insert, remove, superset, disjoint, `&`, `|`, `-`, the atomic set's insert/remove/contains and resulting word, `CoFastFlags` and `AccessMode::from_bits` over random bytes, every element constant, every `MakeFunctionFlags` subset and every `CoFastFlags` byte: 36,002,361 checks, 0 differences, in both debug (with `_CREATED_WITH_FLAGS`) and release. `cargo metadata` 489 to 485 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo clippy --locked -p rustpython-compiler-core -p rustpython-host_env -p rustpython-vm` (no warnings in the changed files) pass.
- `Ledger` (19e65d550, the entry that stood here) is removed again (2026-11-12): on Durable Objects it saved no commits and moved a tool result past the next model call. workerd's `transactionSync` is a savepoint, and workerd commits once per event-loop turn that wrote and holds every outgoing request, response and socket send until that commit is confirmed (`ActorSqlite::startImplicitTxnImpl` and the output gate in actor-sqlite.c++). Counting event-loop commits instead of `transactionSync` calls on the durable-cloudflare harness (`node output/sqlturn/run.mjs text|reply 10`), a one-tool-call turn made 5.0 commits before and 5.0 with the ledger, a plain reply 4.0 and 3.9; what fell from 21 to 11 was savepoints. Which writes matter was measured by crashing a turn that calls a side-effecting `charge` tool before each of its commits (14 with the ledger, 22 without), rolling the object's SQLite back offline to the last commit or to the one before it, and restarting (`output/crash/run.mjs`, 70 runs): losing the admission before its 202 loses the turn; losing the cell journal's call record before the tool runs charges twice; losing the tool result before the next model call tells the model a completed charge's outcome is unknown and costs one model call; losing the model's response costs one model call; losing the start status, the background and reset markers, event batches or the post-finish cleanup changed nothing observable. With the ledger the tool result waited for the next durable write, which came after the second model call, so a crash during that call gave the unknown outcome where the direct path had written it. Both builds also report an unknown outcome for a call that had not started when the crash hit between the journal header and its call record.
- Carrying inline caches across recycled Code Mode cells was measured and not built (2026-11-12). Each cell runs on an instance restored from the prepared snapshot (`Instance::reset_written`), so the bootstrap glue's cache sites start cold every cell. Temporary counters in `step_once` (by whether the template is in the image) over the corpus replay (`output/durability-ledger` corpus binary, last week's nc cells) showed the glue taking 26 slow-path steps per `text('ok')` cell, 51 per one-`Bash` cell and 60 per average real cell, of which cache sites (get_global, get_field, get_method, define_field) were 7, 23 and about 26; the rest are `await`, async start and return, and calls of host functions, which leave the hot loop whatever the caches hold. An upper bound, skipping the restore between cells so every cache stays warm (and the restore's own 1.8% is saved), removed 6 and 21 of those steps but no instructions: `text('ok')` 197.1k -> 197.5k and 197.3k -> 198.5k per cell, one `Bash` call 490k -> 503k (the unrestored heap grows and collects). By the profile the cache-miss path (`lookup_ic`) is 0.8% of a trivial cell and the extra steps about 0.5%, under the 3% a change to the restore path would need to be worth its risk.
- The lexer steps over plain runs of template parts and string literals with a byte table (2026-11-12): `scan_template` and `scan_string` advance through ASCII bytes that can't end or escape the literal (`TEMPLATE_PLAIN`, `STRING_PLAIN`) in a tight loop instead of the full per-byte `match`. Compiling 2,000 real Code Mode cells sampled from last week's nc sessions (5 rounds through `new AsyncFunction`, djsrun): 1,628M -> 1,496M instructions (-8.1%; the template table alone -4.9%, an `iter().position` with a `matches!` instead of the table only -1.3%). In the full corpus replay through `CodeModeRuntime` the gain is -0.25% (97.62G -> 97.40G over 77,743 cells, two interleaved runs each): there the scanners are under 1% of instructions, so the djsrun loop overstates the lexer's share and is not a proxy for cell cost. Outputs identical on 5,981 sampled cells; test262 39,325/39,365.
- A Code Mode tool call encodes its result once (2026-11-12). `ToolOutput::from_json` already serializes the structured result into the output text; Code Mode then serialized `structured_result` again in `send_completed_call` (and again in `journaled_call` for journaled cells) to hand it to the cell. `from_json` now records the address and length of the text it made, and the hidden `ToolOutput::structured_json` returns that text only while `output` still holds that exact string (a replaced, regrown or cloned output falls back to encoding, so callers that rewrite the public `output`, such as codex's served builtin tools, are unaffected); `with_structured_result` clears it. Measured with the corpus replay (`output/durability-ledger` corpus binary, now driving cells from a spawned task as nc does), interleaved: a cell with one `Bash` call 531k -> 490k instructions (-7.7%), `text('ok')` flat; outputs byte-identical on 5,981 sampled real cells, `cells.rs` and the edge-case set. The same harness change showed most futex time in the earlier profile came from driving cells from `block_on` on the main thread (wall -30 to -36%, context switches 3.0 -> 1.8 per trivial cell); the remainder is Tokio waking another worker for the spawned cell actor.
- Code Mode's per-cell glue does less work (2026-11-12). Measured by replaying last week's real nc cells (86,188 unique cells from 543 sessions on gak-9, 77,743 without timers) through `CodeModeRuntime` against stub tools in `output/durability-ledger/src/bin/corpus.rs`: a cell costs about 0.12 ms natively, and the fixed cost per cell, not user code, dominates (a `text('ok')` cell was 219k instructions, one tool call 576k, the average real cell 1.38M). Three changes: `finish` waits on a promise settled by the cell's promise or `stopped` instead of `Promise.race` (whose combinator, species and iterator protocol were most of the glue's built-in calls); the terminal record skips `Object.fromEntries` when nothing was stored; and `tools` keeps the declared tools as its own frozen properties with the Proxy as its prototype, so `tools.Bash` is a plain property read and only other names reach the trap (keys, `in`, `then`, freezing, missing tools and `mcp__` routing unchanged). Instructions per cell, interleaved runs: `text('ok')` 219k -> 183k (-16%), one `Bash` call 576k -> 516k (-10%), the whole timer-free corpus -5.7% (107.2G -> 101.1G). Outputs identical on 5,981 sampled real cells, the 43 cells of `cells.rs` and an edge-case set, except the bootstrap's own line numbers in stack frames. What remains, by the same profile: inline caches start cold in every cell (each cell runs on an instance restored from the prepared snapshot, so the glue's first property reads take the slow path, about 50 per trivial cell), compiling the cell (13%), cross-thread wakeups (13% in futex) and serializing each tool result about three times.
- Run `/re/.test(x)` without creating the RegExp when the literal is only the call's receiver: on the slow path a literal's `call_intrinsic %RegExpCreate` already takes, when the code after it is `get_method key; get_loc | get_arg; call1`, `key` resolves on %RegExp.prototype% to the original `test`, `exec` is the original and `x` is a string, the match runs on the literal's compiled program with lastIndex 0 and pushes the boolean, skipping the four instructions. The fresh RegExp could not be observed: nothing else references it, and the `lastIndex` write a `g` or `y` match makes goes to an object that is about to die. Any other code, a non-string argument, a patched prototype, or a match that runs out of steps falls back to creating the object as before. `RegExp.prototype.test` became an `@intrinsic` so the check can name it. Measured against ff718269e (instructions, 1 round): a 500k loop of `/TODO:/.test(s)` -47% (1,961M -> 1,039M, below the 1,369M of hoisting the literal by hand), agent cell -7.2%, kernel suite flat (strings kernel -2.8%), compute and strings cells flat. Output identical on all workloads and on an edge-case script (overridden `test` and `exec`, a getter on `test`, `g`/`y` flags, non-string and missing arguments, ropes, catastrophic backtracking, a `lastIndex` accessor on the prototype). Rejected: handling the literal (creation alone, or creation plus this check) in the hot loop's `call_intrinsic` arm or in `intrinsic_hit`: creation alone made `/TODO:/.test` -11%, but either placement changed `run_hot`'s code and cost +1.5 to +5% on the kernels that run no regexps (loop +5.4%, fib +4.8%, dispatch +3.9%).
- Size a new property-values block by the shape tree: when the shape an object grows into has a single chain of transitions below it (objects built by the same literal or constructor went on to add those properties), allocate exactly the count at the end of the chain (at least len + 1) instead of twice len (at least 4). A two-property literal now takes 32 bytes of values instead of 48. Measured against ceba3f966 (instructions, 1 round, max RSS): compute cell loop -2.1% instr, RSS 24.0 -> 17.4 MB; 300k six-property literals pushed into an array -6.2% instr, RSS 47.4 -> 37.7 MB; 1M `{i, s}` objects pushed into an array went from OutOfMemory at the 64 MB heap cap to finishing in 0.27 s; strings cell and agent cell flat (+0.0%, +0.2%). Kernels flat except objects (class constructor adding x then y) +0.9%: the chain walk on each first allocation costs more than the smaller block saves when nothing survives. Rejected alternatives: caching the prediction in Shape (no spare field; Shape stays 24 bytes). Output identical on all workloads; test262 39,325/39,365.
- djs's hot loop keeps generator resume and `yield` on its decline path (2026-11-12): running them from `iter_next_loc` and `yield` arms of `run_hot` (one out-of-line call each, then the frame reloaded in the loop) took `for (const v of g(1000))` x2000 from 3,696M to 3,434M instructions (-7%), but added 2-4% to the call, loop, object and dispatch kernels, the register-pressure cost of new arms seen before (D2441); copying the suspended frame value by value instead of with `copy_within` took 4,050M. Not adopted.
- djs keeps its collector without a card table or promotion (2026-11-12): both were built and measured and are not adopted. A card table over the old region (marked by the arena's write barrier, by `Arena::wrote` for the hot loop's Box writes and by inline cache fills for their template; a minor collection walking only marked cards plus the roots, stack and interpreter cells, a card staying marked while it references a young cell) gave the same results but +1.4% instructions on the workerd compute cell's loop: `Marker::mark_old`'s 10% of that run's cycles is the trace of the young cells its old slots reach, not the walk over old cells. Promotion on top of it (what a minor collection leaves becomes old, the card table growing over it clean): with the existing thresholds, compute -7.6% instructions but peak RSS 23.7 MB -> 47.0 MB (promoted garbage counts as live); with minor thresholds that allow a full collection's growth and a full collection once promoted data passes its threshold (the live bytes of the last full collection kept in the roots cell), compute +0.8% at 36.5 MB, 300k objects +18.5%, 1M objects -18%; with that and `LIVE_GROWTH` 1, compute +16.6% at 28.6 MB. What is live at a collection in those runs is mostly temporaries that die soon after, so promoting them only moves garbage into the old region. `LIVE_GROWTH` 1 alone: compute 23.7 -> 17.4 MB at +13% instructions.
- `${!a[@]:2}`, `${!a[@]-x}` and the other operator forms indirect through the value of `a[@]` (an unset array is an invalid indirect expansion, several elements an invalid name), as bash does; only the plain form and the default operators on an empty array list keys (2026-11-12). The subscript of a nameref or `unset 'a[…]'` is expanded as one text, so `a[$(echo 2) + 1]` keeps its spaces. A parse error whose message has several lines (the `[[ ]]` ones) gets the `name: line N:` prefix on each, followed by the source line when the last is `syntax error near`. psh-spec: oils 2409->2413, brush 2941/3171 (12 more cases also match stderr). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/eval.rs, expand.rs, lib.rs.
- A builtin whose first argument is `--help` prints what `help NAME` prints and returns 2, quietly when stdout can't be written, through `builtin` and `command` too (not echo, test, [, true, false, :, let, kill) (2026-11-12). `cd` takes combined option letters (the last of -L and -P wins), rejects unknown ones with its usage (status 2), returns 2 for too many arguments, follows CDPATH (printing the directory it found), and with -P resolves `..` physically; `pwd` reads -L/-P only before its first operand, the last one winning. The psh binary keeps an inherited absolute PWD that names the working directory (a symlinked path) as bash does. psh-spec: oils 2406->2409, brush 2923->2941. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/command.rs, builtins/declare.rs, builtins/help.rs, builtins/mod.rs, exec.rs, now.rs; psh lib.rs.
- `declare -fx`/`+x` exports or unexports functions and `declare -ft` sets the trace attribute (the function then sees the DEBUG and RETURN traps); `declare -F` shows `-fx`/`-ft`, and `-F -x`/`-F -t` filter on them (2026-11-12). `+f`, `+F` and `+g` turn their modes off, so `declare +F f` declares a variable. A subscript in a declaration is expanded once more when declare reads it (`declare 'a[$i]=x'`, `declare m[$key]=v` as bash), a subscript may contain `=` (`'m[a=b]=1'`), text after the closing bracket is an invalid identifier, and a compound value to an array element assigns the whole array. `-a` with `-A` warns and lets `-A` win. `export -f` without names lists the exported functions; `export -n` of a missing name creates nothing and its assignment is not exported under `set -a`; `set` shows a lone `'` as `\'`; associative keys quote `@` and not `=`; FUNCNAME is empty when only `source` frames are on the stack; DIRSTACK starts as an array. The subscript reparse (and declare's compound reparse) took the first command its parse listed, which is the innermost command substitution: it now takes the outer one. psh-spec: oils 2403->2406, brush 2898->2923. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/declare.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, expand.rs, lib.rs, state.rs.
- `shopt -s extdebug` implies functrace and acts on the DEBUG trap's status: 1 skips the command, 2 inside a function returns from it (2026-11-12). The DEBUG trap runs at function entry, once per pipeline stage in the parent (without functrace or extdebug), and before an arithmetic for's init, condition and step; the RETURN trap sees the status of the function's last command; BASH_COMMAND shows a simple command as bash prints it (redirections normalized, here-documents kept); `declare -F name` under extdebug prints the definition's line and file. psh-spec: oils 2397->2403, brush 2871->2898. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/declare.rs, builtins/trap.rs, exec.rs, state.rs.

Under `set -u`, reading an element of an unset or declared-only array is an unbound-variable error, and `let` on an unset name ends the shell. `getopts` clamps OPTIND past the end to n+1 and still parses before failing on an invalid variable name (status 1). psh-spec: oils 2381->2390, brush 2864->2866. - `coproc [NAME] command` runs the command as an in-process background job connected by two engine pipes, with `NAME` (default COPROC) an array of the read and write descriptors (chosen downward from 63) and `NAME_PID`; reaping the job unsets both while `NAME_PID` still names it (2026-11-12). Before, `coproc` stopped the script as unsupported. The coproc's future is built behind a boxed call so `run_command_with`'s frame stays the size it was (the 1000-level recursion test in debug builds overflowed otherwise). psh-spec: brush 2857->2862 and the 51 coproc cases kept for later now pass. Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, exec.rs, jobs.rs.

- A background job whose one command is a nested `bash`/`sh` runs it as the forked process itself, and `kill $$` in a forked copy signals the shell (2026-11-12). Since forked background jobs, such a job ran the nested shell in-process inside the copy, so signals sent to its pid hit the copy's own handling and waiting on it lost the signal it died of; `kill $$` in the copy killed the copy. The job now starts the nested shell with `process` set (its own signal handling as a shell, `died_of` from the core), waiting skips `or_signal` for it, a forked copy's ProcGuard releases its procs on drop, and `$$`'s pid in the copy is the real shell's. psh-spec (upstream psh's oils, brush, agent and utils suites, bash 5.3 goldens, run against the vendored crates): brush 2843->2848/3171, agent 726->727/727 (nested-shells/15, wait/14-17, background_jobs/20 were regressions from forking). Upstream delta: psh-engine builtins/jobs.rs, exec.rs, util/nested.rs.

The walk is shared with the eager path (`raw_frames`, `describe_frame`), so the text is the same; with `Error.prepareStackTrace` set, and for a parse error's `<input>` frame, the stack is made at once as before. `CaptureStack` returns whether the stack is pending, so RecordStack no longer reads it back. - `tr` builds its byte table straight from its sets, without random-keyed hash maps (2026-11-12). Since the table of what becomes of each byte was added, every `tr` run filled 256 entries through `HashMap`/`HashSet` lookups seeded by `RandomState` (SipHash), which made the setup most of a small run: through nanocode-ts's glue `for i in $(seq 1 10000); do x=$(echo $i | tr 1 2); done` took 118 to 124 ms against 81 to 82 ms with the module of nanocode 5e15e341f. The sets and the map are now `BTreeSet`/`BTreeMap`, and without -c the table starts as the identity and takes the map's pairs, the deleted bytes and the squeeze flags directly (later pairs of SET1 win, as with the map's inserts). The same loop now takes 81 to 84 ms (three interleaved rounds against 5e15e341f's module: 82 to 88 ms); large inputs keep the table's gain (`seq 1 1000000 | tr 1-5 a-e`: 18 to 20 ms against 119 to 123 ms). Same output as before on 33 tr scripts compared with GNU coreutils 9.4 (ranges, classes, equivalence classes, repeats `[x*]` `[z*2]`, -c -d -s -t and their mixes, escapes, bytes ≥ 0x80) and on the 727 agent cases and 150 tool scripts run through the glue. Upstream delta: none.
- `xxd -l`, `od -N`, `hexdump -n` read only the range they print, and `fold` writes as it reads (2026-11-12). The dump tools read every input whole before cutting it to the length asked for, and fold read its whole input before folding, so `xxd -l 4 /dev/zero`, `od -N 4 -An -tx1 /dev/zero`, `hexdump -n 4 -C /dev/zero` and `cat /dev/urandom | tr -dc 0-9 | fold -w 4 | head -2` read until the module's memory budget ended the script (126 after 0.3 to 19 s), where GNU, vim's xxd and util-linux print and exit. `slurp` takes the end of the range (skip plus length; none for `xxd -r` or without a length) and stops reading there, and fold keeps its line and column across 64 KiB blocks and writes each block's output before reading the next; a file fold cannot open or read now makes it exit 1 after folding the others, as GNU's does, where it exited 0 when another input had data. Found running nanocode-ts's glue over psh-wasm-core: `od -N 4 /dev/zero` worked with nanocode-ts's TypeScript od. Checked with 27 scripts against GNU coreutils 9.4, vim's xxd 9.1 and util-linux 2.39 hexdump (fold with -s, -b, tabs, backspace and CR, a missing file, a file without a newline, 200,000-byte lines; od -j -N, hexdump -s -n, xxd -s -l -p -r on files, pipes and devices): the same output except `hexdump -s` on a pipe, which util-linux refuses with 'Illegal seek' and psh skips; 727 agent cases and 123 tool scripts unchanged through the glue. Upstream delta: none.
- A host can authorize what an agent asks of a Hand, and a Hand reports its version in its catalog (2026-11-12). `HandAuthorizer` (code-mode's remote module, re-exported by nanocode beside `HandToolSelection`) has two async methods, each given the session id and the Hand's name: `authorize_request` sees a `hands` request for a capability with its reason and answers `HandRequestDecision::Allow`, `Pending(reason)` (the tool answers `permission: prompt` with that reason and the Hand is not asked) or `Deny(reason)` (the tool fails with that reason and nothing is requested); `authorize_call` sees one call routed to a Hand (tool name and input, `hand` already taken out) before dispatch and answers `HandCallDecision::Allow` or `Refuse(message)`, which becomes the call's error output with nothing dispatched. Both default to Allow. `CodeModeExecutors::set_authorizer` installs it for the `hands` tool and for `call_on`, so for scripts on the brain, a remote Hand's callbacks naming another Hand and a registry routing through `CodeModeExecutors::calls`; it is asked only for an attached Hand, so naming an unattached one still fails as before. `ToolsBuilder::hand_authorizer` installs it where a registry routes a nested call naming `hand` to the installed `HandCalls`, for a host whose `hand_calls` lead elsewhere (a Hand forwarding to its brain); a host that installs it in both places for one path is asked twice. Selecting an executor (`select`, `set_default`) is the host's own synchronous decision, not the agent's, so it is not authorized. Unset, every path runs as before. The catalog frame, `RemoteCatalog`, `HandDescription` (what `hands` shows in `about`) and `ExecutorOptions` carry `version: Option<String>`, set by an embedder with `Hand::version`; it is written only when set and read with a default, so an old Hand's frame decodes as None and an old brain ignores the field. Checked with output/hand-hooks: `hooks` (a denying authorizer stops `call_on`, a call through `calls()`, the `hands` request and a registry-routed call with the Hand never called or asked; pending answers prompt; allow and unset pass through; catalog frames round trip with and without version, a frame without the field decodes as None, and `HandCore::catalog` writes the version it was given and omits an unset one) passes 20 of 20 and does not build at 21eec9a9b (the API is missing); `compat` at 21eec9a9b decodes a frame carrying `version` but describes the Hand without it (1 of 4 fails), and passes 4 of 4 after. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-tool-host -p nanocode-tool-runtime -p nanocode`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked -p` the same crates `-- -D warnings`. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode/src/remote/{executors,mod,frame,hand}.rs, crates/runtime/tool-host/src/{selection,runtime/registry,runtime/execution}.rs, crates/integrations/tool-runtime/src/remote/{hand,native}.rs, crates/nanocode/src/lib.rs.
- `/pass <email>` switches the address a session's email passes are for (2026-11-13): each pass held in memory remembers the address it was sent to (a pass given with `--identity-attestation` has none), `/pass <email>` drops every pass not for the new address, and a pass is sent or reused only while it is for the current address, so a code verified for the old address after the switch still answers the request that asked for it but nothing after. Stored passes on disk are left alone: they are already read only for their own address.
- Email passes outlive the process, and `nanocode exec` never waits for one it cannot get (2026-11-12): bin/nanocode/src/tempo/identity.rs keeps each verified pass in `mpp-passes/` next to the channel store (`~/.tempo/wallet/`, or `$TEMPO_HOME/wallet/`), one file per (audience, issuer, type) holding the attestation, when it was received and the address it was sent to, written mode 0600 in a 0700 directory through a temporary file and a rename, and never logged. A process loads the passes from issuers it trusts (and, with `--identity-email`, only that address's) at start, deletes an expired one, reads the file again before asking for a code so a pass another process just got is used, and deletes the file when a 401 or 403 refuses the pass it holds; a pass still goes only to the origin it names. `nanocode exec` asks for the code on stdin (an empty line or end of input declines) only when `--identity-email` is set and stdin and stderr are terminals; otherwise a service that asks for a pass gets the stored one or fails at once with what to do instead of waiting for a `/pass` nobody can type.
- nanocode's MPP clients answer MPP's email identity (2026-11-12; every MPP client since 2026-11-13: the Tempo gateway's responses and messages, the Boundless route and the shell's paying proxy, so any MPP service can gate on a verified email): when a route answers 401 or 403 with `Identity-Attestation-Required` (an RFC 8941 list whose inner lists are alternatives, as mppx 0.18.0's `Identity.anyOf` sends them), bin/nanocode/src/tempo/identity.rs gets an email attestation from an issuer in `--identity-issuer` (https://identity.mpp.tempo.xyz unless set; an issuer the server names but the user did not list never sees the address), with `POST /email/otp {email, audience}` and `POST /email/verify {id, code}`, and sends the request again with it in `Identity-Attestation`. The audience is always the request's own origin; nothing goes over plain http but to localhost, every model client that carries a pass is the payments client, which follows no redirects (the shell's paying proxy follows none either), and the attestation is only ever a header, never a notice or a log line. The address comes from `--identity-email` or `/pass <email>`, the code from `/pass <code>` (or a line on stdin under `nanocode exec`), three tries, as mppx's prover asks; `/pass` alone declines. Attestations are kept in memory per (audience, issuer, type) until they expire and one acquisition runs at a time; `--identity-attestation` seeds one obtained elsewhere. The wire, the 300-second refresh margin, the 60-second clock tolerance and the 8,192-character limit are mppx 0.18.0's (extensions/identity/attestation). It differs from mppx in one place on purpose: the exchange below the payment flow resends a paid attempt a 401 rejected for identity with the same payment credential, since a server checks identity before it accepts the credential, and the payment flow above it commits or rolls back on the answer to the resend as before.
- nanocode-cli drops the third-party crates outside the async baseline, scope by scope, each in its own commit with its own entry below (2026-11-12, Georgios: "make this ~0 deps. Get rid of basically everything outside of baseline async stack like Tokio/reqwest"). The scopes and their entries: the TUI (ratatui, crossterm, syntect and onig, pulldown-cmark, unicode-width, unicode-segmentation, wide), the nanocode crates (thiserror, async-trait, nix, tower, unicode-normalization, schemars, tungstenite; regress, fluent-uri, email_address, num-cmp, appendlist, foldhash, tempfile, the digests, uuid, httpdate, subtle, proc-macro-crate), RustPython (vendored, then malachite, num-*, the compression, hash, Unicode and helper crates) and psh (its hashes, JSON, command line, diff, deflate, libm, jq, grep, regex, walker, hasher and byte helpers). Each was proven equal to the crate it replaced by a harness under output/ linking both, with the differences that remain listed in its entry. What stays and why is DEPENDENCIES.md: the async baseline (tokio, reqwest, hyper, rustls, ring, futures, serde, tracing, url and idna, libc, memchr, getrandom), image and png (kept at 0.25.6), clap (kept), opentelemetry's SDK (public types), imbl, RustPython's remaining crates, encoding_rs and rustix, and the crates whose replacement needs unsafe code or a public type change (crossbeam-utils, arc-swap, smallvec, futures-channel). Measured on the 5-core hosted Hand from fresh target directories, 4248aa710 (this request's start) against 4e73b1875 (other threads' commits between them included): `cargo metadata --locked` 710 to 489 packages; on Linux nanocode-cli reaches 299 packages instead of 514 (`cargo tree -p nanocode-cli -e normal,build --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`); `cargo build --release --locked -p nanocode-cli --timings` 5m42s to 4m44s wall, 758 to 453 units, 1,275.2 to 1,031.1 s of summed unit time; the release nanocode 102,406,152 to 99,701,256 bytes; `cargo bloat --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode --crates` (unstripped) 62.6 to 59.4 MiB of .text, file 147.6 to 143.2 MiB. Costs: safe code without SIMD or SHA instructions makes SHA-1 and SHA-256 2 to 10x slower (psh checksums, Python hashlib), BLAKE3 about 12x slower at 1 MiB, crc32 and LZ4 decoding slower in Python, unanchored JSON Schema patterns over long strings slower than regress's memchr start search, and some psh regex patterns 20 to 35% slower; terminal rendering, Markdown, highlighting, the WebSocket receive path, RustPython's parser and small integers got faster.

Two behaviors were found by the harnesses and kept: ignore's Walk keeps the previous root's parent chain alive, so a parent ignore file shared by consecutive roots is compiled and its errors reported once (walk.rs looks parents up in the previous root's chain), and a later root under a directory the visitor skipped stays hidden (search/walk.rs keeps the path filter and, without -L, now also skips reading the directory, which ignore's Walk could not). Not equal: when rg's `-t all`/`-T all` expands to every type and several selections fail (a cleared type, a bad glob), ignore reported whichever failing selection its HashMap yielded first, which changes from run to run; psh reports the first in its own definition order every time. ignore, globset, walkdir, same-file, crossbeam-deque, crossbeam-epoch and crossbeam-utils leave psh, and with them aho-corasick, regex-syntax, log and winapi-util, which after psh-pattern only globset and ignore still used; ignore, globset, crossbeam-deque and crossbeam-epoch leave the root (jni's build still uses walkdir and same-file, the async crates crossbeam-utils). Equal: output/walk-equal compares the new modules with globset 0.4.21 and ignore 0.4.34 on seeded random input: globs 1,000,000 cases (15.3M matches), glob sets 1,000,000 (61M), gitignore 1,000,000 (33.0M), overrides 1,000,000 (32.0M), file types 300,000 (5.7M; 198 builds differ only in the `all` order above), core.excludesFile 1,000,000 (2M), and 288,000 walks over generated trees with nested repos, gitdir files, broken and looping symlinks, unreadable files and directories, custom ignore files, overrides and types (904,008 entries and errors), 0 differences; output/walk-equal/psh_cmp.py runs the release psh of origin/master and the new one on 49,000 seeded random fd, rg, grep -r, find, git (status, ls-files, add -n, check-ignore) and diff -r -x commands over 110 generated trees (.gitignore, .ignore, .fdignore, .rgignore, .git/info/exclude, global excludes, nested repos, negations, `**`, classes, hidden and unicode names, symlink loops, nested roots) and 73 fixed commands on four real trees (a clone of this repository from its root, from crates/patches/psh and from an untracked copy, and ~/.cargo/registry/src with 65,527 files): stdout, stderr and status equal byte for byte, none differing even in order. Benchmark (interleaved, release builds against origin/master's psh, before psh-pattern landed underneath, medians of 21 rounds on the repository clone and 7 on the registry): fd 14.5 to 14.6 ms on the repository and 266 to 231 ms on the registry, fd -H -I 20.0 to 16.6 ms, rg --files 14.2 to 13.1 ms and rg --files -g '!*.md' 286 to 221 ms on the registry, rg -c unwrap 33.1 to 33.8 ms, rg -c -t rust unwrap 394 to 357 ms on the registry, find -name 81.7 to 73.8 ms on the registry, grep -r --include 270 to 271 ms on the registry, git status --porcelain 14.6 to 14.3 ms (81 rounds), the rest within 5%. - psh's regular expressions are its own crate psh-pattern (parser, HIR, Unicode tables generated from regex-syntax 0.8.11's by output/unicode-gen/gen.py, Thompson NFA, PikeVM, lazy DFA, literal prefilters and the grep matcher), used by fd, diff, rg/grep (`search/matcher.rs` implements psh's own matcher interface, `crate::matcher` of the searcher change, over it, and grep's `regex_matcher.rs` adapter from grep-regex is gone), jq, git grep/log, the git excludes-file reader, expr and search/posix's existing tests; regex, grep-regex and grep-matcher leave psh-utils, and regex leaves the root lock too (regex-automata and regex-syntax stay in the psh lock only through globset, ignore and bstr) (2026-11-12). Behaviour copies regex 1.13.1 / grep-regex 0.1.14 where psh can see it: a set parses every pattern before translating any (which error wins), `\x{..}` is a codepoint under `(?-u)`, class union, negation and difference follow regex-syntax's interval sets (including its U+D7FF/U+E000 negation quirk), the matcher's capture_count is explicit groups + 1, and the NFA is built in regex-automata's state order with its literal trie, its bounded UTF-8 caches (10,000 and 1,000 FNV slots) and the reverse NFA's unanchored prefix, so `rg --regex-size-limit` fails exactly where it did (probe: smallest passing limit equal on every pattern tried); a pattern whose optimized prefix literals are exact (regex-automata's Pre strategy) builds no full NFA, has no size limit and is searched as that literal set; a RegexSet's size counts all patterns without capture states. The grep matcher picks line candidates from inner literals exactly when grep-regex did, which depends on whether regex-automata calls the regex accelerated: never for a regex anchored at the haystack start (it builds no prefilter), always for one anchored at the end (its reverse anchored strategy), else when a prefix prefilter exists; the first port ignored the anchors, so with a NUL line terminator `grep -z '^\./src'`, `grep -z '^b'`, `grep -z '[a-z]*o$'` and `rg --null-data '\Ab'` judged records in the whole buffer instead of one by one and differed (`matcher.rs`). Speed, in safe Rust: a packed prefilter (`literal.rs` Packed) tests up to three bytes of up to 8 literal groups (literals equal after ASCII lowercasing share a group and test case pairs with one mask) over 64-byte blocks written so the compiler vectorizes them, used instead of memchr2/memchr3 when the rarest byte set's worst frequency rank exceeds 230 (measured: uppercase sets such as R/O/V stay faster on memchr3, lowercase ones such as e/E, f/l/i on the packed scan; block sizes 16, 32, 64 and 128 measured, 64 kept); a regex whose matches cannot start with an ASCII byte skips ASCII a word at a time (NonAscii prefilter, `\p{Greek}`, `\p{Han}`, `[α-ω]`); the lazy DFA's forward loop runs untagged transitions four at a time (`dfa.rs`). Not equal: `shortest_match` values (the end of some match; regex's depends on which internal engine ran; psh only uses whether one exists and the line holding it); word boundaries next to a custom line terminator that is a word byte (psh never sets one); and with a line terminator other than \n, regexes whose acceleration regex-automata decides by its reverse-suffix, reverse-inner or Teddy choices (which also differ between its native and wasm builds) can still have `(?m)^`/`$` judged per record by one side and in the whole buffer by the other; output/nul (seeded random rg --null-data and grep -z command lines with ^, $, (?m), \A, \z, \b over NUL-, LF- and CRLF-separated files) found none: 7,000 cases, 0 differences (the first port: 2 in 1,000). Harness output/regex-equal (old crates vs psh-pattern, seeded random patterns, haystacks, options, all APIs): earlier seeds 101 and 102, 1,000,000 cases each (270M checks each): 8,102 and 8,882 differing checks, all shortest_match values except 176 and 145 with line_terminator('x'); on this tree seed 101, 200,000 cases (54M checks): 1,574, all shortest_match values except one case with line_terminator('x'); errors 5,429 cases, 0; grep matcher seed 202, 150,000 cases: 12 checks in 9 cases (300,000 cases before the anchor fix: 287), all the harness's own line simulation with a \0 or \r terminator, none of whose reproducers differs through rg --null-data or grep -z; output/probe fuzzpf (regex find_iter/find_at vs psh-pattern on case-insensitive literal sets, alternations and non-ASCII classes over haystacks up to about 1 KB, so the packed blocks run): 90,000 cases, 0. psh -c old (origin/master 1dd3c6ada) vs new, stdout, stderr and exit code: 1,780 commands of output/psh-compare.sh (rg, grep, git grep, fd, jq, sed, diff, expr, bad patterns), find -regex/-iregex/-regextype, rg --regex-size-limit/--dfa-size-limit, git grep -c and 18 counts over the 110 MB file (-i, -S, multi-literal, non-ASCII classes): 0 differences; output/eq/run.py 4,000 random grep/rg cases and encrun.py 5,563 encoding cases: 0 differences apart from 1 case whose output differs between two runs of the old binary (rg -q racing a missing file's error). `cargo metadata` packages: root 495 -> 493, crates/patches/psh 45 -> 43. Interleaved medians of 7 runs (CPU ms, old / first port / now), psh on a 110 MB file of the repository's Rust sources: rg -c fn 26/26/27, -i error 31/93/37, -S impl 28/53/34, -i result 29/73/43, -i 'fn|let' 87/286/78, `Result|Option|Vec` 34/37/39, `fn|let|impl` 69/107/93, `[A-Z][a-z]+Error` 31/30/31, `\w+_\w+` 143/174/181, `[a-z]+_[a-z]+` 129/180/181, `\w+` 207/243/250, -w let 46/51/46, `^\s*fn ` 35/41/36, `[0-9]{4,}` 58/56/61, `\p{Greek}` 202/253/20, `\p{Han}` 201/237/24, `[α-ω]+` 23/254/23, rg -o `\bpub fn \w+` 33/31/27; grep -c, fd, find -regex and the crates/patches/psh tree (rg, grep -r) within noise; still slower: multi-literal sets with common lowercase bytes (regex's SIMD Teddy against a safe scan) and regexes whose lines are confirmed one by one (`\w+_\w+`: about 850,000 candidate lines, each a separate DFA search). - psh's grep and rg search and print with psh's own searcher, printers, matcher interface and ANSI writer; grep-searcher, grep-printer, termcolor and encoding_rs_io leave (2026-11-12). Where: `crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/searcher/` (line buffer, by-line and multi-line strategies, binary detection, and `decode.rs`, the streaming BOM sniffer and transcoder over encoding_rs that encoding_rs_io was, with its quirks kept: a UTF-8 BOM keeps an explicit `-E` decoder, a lone 2-byte FF FE/FE FF file reads as empty), `printer/` (standard, summary and path printers, color specs, hyperlinks, statistics; the statistics clock reads zero on wasm32-unknown-unknown as the patched copy did), `matcher.rs` (the Matcher/Captures interface the searcher, the printers, `rg --json` and grep's own matchers implement) with `regex_matcher.rs` the one adapter from grep-regex's RegexMatcher, and `ansi.rs` (ANSI colors and OSC 8 hyperlinks, written through a stack buffer); `third_party/grep-printer/` and its `[patch.crates-io]` entries in the root and psh workspaces are gone, and NOTICE names the new files. What stays: grep-matcher, only as the trait the adapter calls and as grep-regex's own dependency, until grep-regex leaves; encoding_rs, the WHATWG encoding tables behind `rg -E` and BOM decoding, which psh has no equivalent of; bstr, which rg's flags, fd, awk and globset use. Two changes while porting: line, column and count numbers are formatted into a stack buffer instead of a String per line (as grep-printer's DecimalFormatter did; the first port allocated and printed lines 5 to 10% slower), and the hot searcher and printer functions carry grep-searcher's and grep-printer's inline attributes.
