- perf(djs): ToString of an int32 writes its digits straight into a new one-byte string (length from `ilog10`) instead of a stack buffer that `alloc_latin1` then copied: the copy's wide loads read the digits just stored byte by byte, a store-forwarding conflict on every conversion. Cycles, same binary path, interleaved: compute cell loop (`String(i)` per object) -1.5 to -2.9%, number formatting micro -2.7%, template micro neutral; instructions +0.1% (compute) to +1.2% (template) from the digit count and the arena barrier.
- perf(djs): `Heap::str_view` inlines its flat-string case and leaves ropes, slices and append buffers to an out-of-line `str_view_resolved`; out of line, every call returned its `Option<StrView>` through memory and callers (JSON.stringify's string members among them) reloaded it with one wide load across narrower stores. Store-forwarding conflicts (AMD r0224) -11% to -42% across the scripts; strings cell loop -0.86% instr (2,160M->2,141M), cycles -1.1%; agent script -0.26% instr; strings, json and maps kernels -0.2% to -0.8% instr; native binary +0.6%.
- perf(djs): `plain_species` (the ArraySpeciesCreate check of map, filter and the other Array builtins) reads %Array.prototype%.constructor and %Array%[@@species] through `Heap::data_at` and `Heap::getter_at` instead of `get_own_property`, which returns the property through memory. Agent script -0.77% instr (874.8M->868.1M), cycles within noise; other scripts and kernels unchanged.
- perf(djs): the RegExp pristine check reads %RegExp.prototype%'s methods and flag getters by hinted slot through `Heap::data_at` and a new `Heap::getter_at`, both returning the value in registers; `proto_property` returned a `Property` through memory that the caller reloaded with one wide load across narrower stores, a store-forwarding stall on each of its 13 reads per `replace`/`split`/`match` call (`#[inline(always)]` on `prop_read` instead cost +1% instructions broadly). Strings cell loop -1.8% instr (2,200M->2,160M), cycles -2.8%; agent script -1.5% instr, cycles -5.4%; regex-heavy script -2.2% instr; strings kernel -1.8% instr, others identical.
- perf(djs): iterator result objects `{value, done}` (done results, CreateIterResultObject, Map/Set and RegExp string iterator results, generator returns) reuse the last result's shape (`Heap::new_iter_result`, `iter_result_shape`, cleared at collection and compaction like `rest_shape`) instead of walking the shape tree for each. Nested for-of over 2-element arrays 1,133M->1,053M instr (-7.1%); agent script -0.6%.
- perf(djs): the end of a for-of loop over an Array or String Iterator (the `iter_next_loc` step that finds it done, and the `iter_check_object` after it) runs from the hot loop's out-of-line decline path instead of `step`: the done result is allocated first, then the iterator is marked finished, as `step` does. Inner for-of loops over short arrays paid two `step` round trips per loop. Nested for-of over 2-element arrays 1,183M->1,133M instr (-4.2%); agent script -0.3%; other kernels flat.
- perf(djs): a declined `o[key]` read of an ordinary object with a string key interns the key (as the generic get does, which fills the atom memo) and reads through the megamorphic cache. Keys that are fresh strings (JSON-parsed data, split results) missed the identity memo on every first use and took the generic path. Agent script -1.4% instr (909M->896M), cycles -3.9%; keyed reads of JSON-parsed keys -10.4% instr (2,851M->2,554M); kernels identical.
- perf(djs): `arr.pop()` goes straight to the heap's dense pop from the call site, as `arr.push(x)` does, out of line (inline it cost every @fast call +0.2-0.6% instr). arr_push_pop micro 2,621M->2,544M instr (-3.0%), cycles -10% (407M->367M); other kernels within +0.1% instr.
- perf(djs): `new` reads the constructor's `prototype` through the megamorphic cache (filled on a miss) instead of a full property lookup per construction. class micro 3,801M->3,681M instr (-3.2%), cycles -3.7%; objects kernel -2.5% instr; other kernels identical.
- nanocode-numeric also carries the complex type and the numeric traits RustPython uses, and num-complex, num-traits and num-integer leave every vendored RustPython crate and pymath (2026-11-12); num-complex leaves the build, while num-traits (image, bigdecimal) and num-integer (num-bigint) stay for other crates. traits.rs defines `Zero`, `One`, `Signed`, `Num`, `Pow`, `PrimInt` (`min_value`, `max_value`, `to_be`, `to_le`), `ToPrimitive`, `FromPrimitive`, `Integer` and `ExtendedGcd`, implemented for `BigInt`, `BigUint` and the primitive integers and floats with num-traits 0.2.19's results: integer conversions are `Some` exactly when the value fits, float to integer truncates and is `None` for NaN, infinities and out-of-range values (the same open bounds as num-traits), float `Signed` uses the sign bit (`-0.0` is negative) and `abs_sub` returns 0 when not greater. `BigInt::extended_gcd` is num-integer's default algorithm (truncating division, the Bézout pair it returns is not unique, so it is copied step for step); `Roots`, `Euclid`, `Checked*` and `Const*`, which RustPython does not call, are gone. complex.rs is `Complex<T>`/`Complex64` with num-complex 0.4.6's formulas operation for operation (division by `norm_sqr` without scaling, `inv`, `powi`/`powu` by its square-and-multiply order, `powf` and `powc` through polar form, `exp` with its infinity and NaN cases, `ln`, `norm` as `hypot`, `arg` as `atan2`, real-left `a - z` and `a / z` with `0.0 - x` imaginary parts, `Display` with sign, precision and width as num-complex prints it), so complex arithmetic and the compiler's constant folding of complex powers stay bit-identical. The crate now uses std (the float functions), so it is no longer no_std; it still builds for wasm32. Vendored sources only change `num_traits::`/`num_integer::`/`num_complex::` paths to `nanocode_numeric::`, except four call sites: codegen's `num_traits::pow::pow` is `Pow::pow`, array.rs's `num_traits::cast` and `AsPrimitive` are `wchar_t::try_from` and `as u32`, rustpython-literal's `f64::is_zero` is `== 0.0` and rustpython-host_env's `cvt` bounds on `Copy + PartialOrd + Default` (compares with `I::default()`, which is 0), so those two crates need no numeric dependency. add and sub of limbs now carry through a u128 in one pass. Not equal: NaN sign bits. Rust leaves the sign of a NaN produced from NaN operands unspecified and LLVM may pick either operand per build, so 2,563 of 44,000,000 checks (seed 74) differ only in a NaN's sign bit (from NaN inputs to powi, powf, powc), which no formula change can pin. output/numeric-unit's traits binary compares num-traits 0.2.19 and num-complex 0.4.6 with the new code on seeded floats (raw bit patterns, ±0, ±inf, NaNs, subnormals, integer boundaries ±0.5) and integers: seed 63 3,000,000 rounds (132,000,000 checks) and seed 74 1,000,000 rounds (44,000,000 checks), 0 differences besides those NaN signs; the bigint harness on this tree (seeds 71, 72, 73: 17,486,971 checks) 0 differences. End to end (output/numeric-e2e, against 10815c8b3): the 600-program corpus (seed 7, 11,912 lines) and a second 200-program one (seed 8, 4,014 lines) are byte-identical except 16 and 1 `hash()` of NaN lines, which hash the object's address. Benchmarks (release harness, 5 interleaved rounds of best-of-3, old 10815c8b3 → this tree, ms, min and median, on a quieter Hand than the previous entry): factorial 23.0 → 17.7 (25.4 → 18.9), pidigits 95.2 → 92.5 (112.2 → 108.8), big pow 160.0 → 157.8 (187.4 → 179.9), big str 82.3 → 57.2 (99.2 → 60.4), Fraction sum 28.1 → 29.0 (30.1 → 29.3), Decimal 35.6 → 34.8 (38.8 → 36.9), general 408 → 449 (531 → 517), fib(100,000) 59.3 → 66.6 (65.2 → 76.0, about +15%, the large-number add and sub still 1.2-1.8× malachite's per limb). cargo metadata packages 516 → 515 on deps-python (707 → 706 on the numeric branch); num-traits and num-integer stay in the lock for other workspace crates. Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python, the same with --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-numeric (native and wasm32), cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli, clean.
- nanocode-numeric (crates/core/numeric, new workspace member, no_std + alloc, forbid(unsafe_code), native and wasm32) is RustPython's arbitrary-precision integer, and malachite-bigint, malachite-nz, malachite-base and malachite-q leave every vendored RustPython crate and pymath (2026-11-12). The crate reproduces the malachite-bigint 0.12.0 surface RustPython uses, with its semantics, so the vendored sources only change `malachite_bigint::` to `nanocode_numeric::`: `BigInt` (sign and magnitude), `BigUint` (u64 limbs, one inline limb or a normalized Vec, so small ints never allocate), `Sign`, `ToBigInt`/`ToBigUint`, `ParseBigIntError`, `TryFromBigIntError`, `U32Digits`/`U64Digits`, every operator over values, references and primitives, two's-complement `& | ^ !` and flooring `>>` on negatives, `Pow`, `modpow`/`modinv`, `nth_root`, byte and digit conversions, and the num-traits/num-integer traits malachite-bigint implements (`Zero`, `One`, `Signed`, `Num`, `ToPrimitive`, `FromPrimitive`, `Integer` with num-integer's own `extended_gcd`, `Euclid`, `Roots`, `Checked*`), which keeps num-traits and num-integer as its dependencies until the next change. malachite's observable quirks are kept on purpose: `to_f64`/`to_f32` round to nearest-even, give `Some(±inf)` past the range but `None` for values between MAX and MAX plus half an ulp; zero's `to_bytes_*`/`to_signed_bytes_*` are empty; `BigUint::from_f64` of a negative finite float is `Some(0)`; `from_str_radix` takes one leading `+` and underscores anywhere but first; `Debug` prints like `Display`; formatting goes through `pad_integral`. rustpython-common's `true_div` now takes `nanocode_numeric::rational_to_f64` (Rational→f64 rounded to nearest-even with the same `(value, Ordering)` result, subnormals included, so int/int and its OverflowError stay as they were) and `float_to_ratio` takes `f64_to_ratio`; format.rs's malachite-base `is_negative_zero` is `== 0.0 && is_sign_negative()`; pymath's `malachite-bigint` feature is `bigint` and its unused `num-bigint` alternative is gone. Algorithms: schoolbook multiplication and squaring, Karatsuba from 32 limbs (48 for squares), Toom-3 from 1,200 limbs, Knuth division with a Möller–Granlund reciprocal (also for single-limb division and the decimal base case) and a direct path when the quotient is one limb, Lehmer gcd on 62-bit leading parts, divide-and-conquer int→str from 32 limbs and str→int from 1,024 chunks; the thresholds come from output/numeric-unit's `sweep` binary on this Hand. Nothing Python-visible differs. output/numeric-unit links malachite-bigint 0.12.0 (and malachite-q 0.12.0 for `true_div`/`float_to_ratio`) beside the new crate and compares about 60 operations (arithmetic, floor/ceil/Euclid division, gcd/lcm/extended_gcd, bit operations and shifts on both signs, pow, modpow, modinv, roots, to_str_radix in bases 2..36, Display/Debug/hex/octal/binary formatting with width, fill, sign, `#` and zero padding, bytes both ways and signed, primitive and float conversions both ways, iterators, `from_str_radix`/`parse_bytes` on random valid and invalid text, true division, float ratios) on seeded operands from 0 to 1,500 limbs with 0, ±1, powers of two ±1, all-ones and sparse limbs: seeds 41 (30,000 rounds, ≤1,500 limbs), 42 (300,000 rounds, ≤64 limbs) and 43 (100,000 rounds, ≤300 limbs) made 27,569,615 checks with 0 differences (earlier runs on intermediate versions found and fixed zero's empty bytes and `BigUint::from_f64` of negatives). End to end, output/numeric-e2e links nanocode-python from this tree and from 10815c8b3 (~/w-python-numeric-old) and runs 600 generated programs (gen.py seed 7, 11,912 output lines: + - * / // % divmod, pow with negative and three arguments, bit operations and shifts, comparisons with floats, hash, int() in every base with prefixes, underscores and invalid text, str/repr/format specs and %-formatting, to_bytes/from_bytes, bit_length/bit_count, float(int), as_integer_ratio, round, math gcd/lcm/isqrt/factorial/comb/perm/log, Fraction, Decimal, random.getrandbits/randrange, struct, marshal, pickle, json, the max-str-digits limit and its errors, complex): stdout, stderr and exit are byte-identical except 16 `hash(float('nan'))` lines, which hash the object's address and differ between two runs of the same binary. Release harness, best of 5 interleaved rounds of best-of-3 (old → new, ms; this Hand was shared and loaded, medians in brackets): factorial(5k, 10k, 20k) to str 32.6 → 26.7, pidigits(2,500) 163.9 → 143.6 [189.8 → 181.4], 3**10^6 and 7**400000 mul/div 252.9 → 238.0, str(7**200000) and back 124.7 → 80.4, sum of Fraction(1, k) for k < 1,500 55.6 → 35.7, Decimal sqrt iterations at 300 digits 64.1 → 55.0, a general loop with dicts and small ints 734 → 790 [850 → 883], fib(100,000) 87.2 → 126.2 [115.8 → 131.4]; per operation (`sweep`, new/old time) small-int add, mul and clone are 2-5× faster, one-limb-quotient division 0.6×, mul 1.2-1.4× at 96-256 limbs and 2× at 800, add 1.3× and sub 1.6× at 800 limbs, gcd 1.2× at 8 limbs to 2.7× at 256 and 4× at 800, int→str 1.1-1.5×, str→int 1.2-1.8×, and 4-5× faster than malachite past 2,000 limbs for mul, division and parsing. cargo metadata packages 524 → 516 on deps-python (710 → 707 on the numeric branch). Commands: cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python, the same with --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown, cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-numeric (native and wasm32), clean.
- Python's str and bytes hash() is our own SipHash-2-4, and siphasher leaves rustpython-common (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/siphash.rs is `SipHasher24`, SipHash-2-4 from the SipHash paper keyed by the two 64-bit words `HashSecret` derives from the hash seed, as a `core::hash::Hasher`: bytes are taken eight at a time little-endian with a tail word, the length's low byte goes into the last word, and the integer writes (`write_u8` to `write_u64` and `write_usize`) append the value's native-endian bytes through one short-write path, which is what siphasher 1.0.4 did, so `hash_bytes`, `hash_str`, `hash_value` of any `Hash` type and `hash_iter` (tuples, frozensets) give the same numbers on every target, including wasm32's four-byte `usize` length prefix. hash.rs imports it in place of siphasher's. Nothing is unequal: output/hashes-unit compares, with random keys, 30,000 random sequences per seed of up to 11 mixed writes (bytes of every length, u8, u16, u32, u64, usize, i64, u128) after each write against siphasher 1.0.4, plus `hash_bytes` against siphasher through `[u8]::hash` and the paper's 64 vectors (key 00..0f): seeds 11, 12 and 13 at 3,000 cases give 481,691, 480,821 and 482,073 checks, 0 differences; end to end the corpus in output/e2e prints hash() of 3,000 random ASCII, BMP, astral and numeric strings and their bytes, and set, dict, frozenset and tuple hashes and iteration order, under three fixed hash seeds (which change those lines between seeds): identical. Speed (release, 2,000,000 hashes, best of 8 interleaved): 15.4 vs 13.8 ns for 8 bytes, 25.0 vs 20.3 ns for 32, 115.9 vs 117.9 ns for 256; str caches its hash, so this is paid once per object. `cargo metadata` 525 to 524 packages: with this change nothing in the workspace uses siphasher (699 before and after on the hashes branch, where phf_shared still did). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `hashes-unit 11|12|13 3000`.
- RustPython's scrypt is our own over our SHA-256 HMAC, and scrypt, pbkdf2, salsa20, cipher and inout leave the workspace (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/hashlib/scrypt.rs is RFC 7914: B = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(password, salt, 1, p * 128 * r) through hashlib.rs's own `compute_pbkdf2_hmac`, ROMix over each 128 * r-byte block with BlockMix and Salsa20/8 (four double rounds over 32-bit words, its quarter-round order and rotations 7, 9, 13 and 18), Integerify reading the last 64-byte chunk's first eight bytes, then PBKDF2 over the mixed blocks for the output; it refuses what scrypt 0.12.0's `Params::new` and `scrypt` refused (r or p zero, log2 N not below the word size, 128 * r * N or 128 * r * p overflowing usize, r * p of 2^30 or more, an empty output or one past 2^32 - 1 SHA-256 blocks) and _hashlib's checks and messages, unchanged, still run first, so none of those is reachable from Python. The one difference: scrypt computed r * p in u32, which wraps in a release build for r * p >= 2^32 and could then pass, while ours multiplies in u64; _hashlib's memory limit (at most 2^31 bytes) keeps r * p below 2^24, so no Python call reaches it. `compute_pbkdf2_hmac` now keys one HMAC state and clones it per block and iteration instead of hashing the padded key again each time (same output, two fewer compressions per iteration). Equality: output/hashes-unit compares 300 random scrypt calls per seed (log2 N 1 to 10, r 1 to 8, p 1 to 3, outputs up to 300 bytes) against scrypt 0.12.0, the refusals against `Params::new`, and both RFC 7914 vectors: seeds 11, 12 and 13 at 3,000 cases give 481,691, 480,821 and 482,073 checks, 0 differences; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e) runs 60 random scrypt calls, the RFC vectors and 20 invalid-argument cases through Python: identical. Speed (release, best of 8 interleaved): scrypt with N = 2^14, r = 8, p = 1 takes 108 ms against 61 ms (salsa20 0.11 uses SSE2; ours is portable), and pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', 100,000 iterations) 59 ms against 18 ms for pbkdf2 0.13.0 with sha2's SHA-NI, bounded by SHA-256 itself (the MD5/SHA entry). hmac 0.13.0 stays in the lock (hkdf and the Postgres client use it). `cargo metadata` 530 -> 525 packages (704 -> 699 on the hashes branch). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `hashes-unit 11|12|13 3000`.
- RustPython's BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s are our own, and blake2b_simd and blake2s_simd leave the workspace (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/hashlib/blake2b.rs and blake2s.rs are RFC 7693 (12 and 10 rounds of G over the shared message schedule, 64- and 32-bit words, 128- and 64-bit byte counters, the final block flagged and, for `last_node=True`, the last-node flag set too), and blake2.rs holds the schedule and `Parameters`, which lays out the parameter block from the BLAKE2 specification: digest length, key length, fanout, depth, leaf length, node offset (8 bytes for b, 6 for s), node depth and inner length, zero bytes, then salt and personalization zero-padded to 16 or 8 bytes; a key is the first block, padded with zeros, and the last block is held back until more input or the digest arrives, as the crates did. `state_init_blake2` builds `Parameters` from _hashlib's already validated arguments; `Parameters::block` asserts the same bounds the crates asserted (digest size 1 to 64 or 32, key, salt and person lengths, inner size, node offset below 2^48 for s), and none is reachable from Python since _blake2's checks and messages, unchanged, come first. Nothing is unequal: output/hashes-unit compares each against blake2b_simd 1.0.5 and blake2s_simd 1.0.5 over 15,000 random parameter sets per seed and algorithm (every digest size, keys of every length including none, salts and persons of every length, random fanout, depth, leaf size, node offset, node depth, inner size and last node, inputs up to 8 blocks and 64 KiB in random splits), plus the default constructors, `copy()`, 5 MiB inputs, HMAC over BLAKE2 and the RFC 7693 abc vectors: seeds 11, 12 and 13 at 3,000 cases give 481,691, 480,821 and 482,073 checks, 0 differences; the end-to-end corpus (output/e2e) runs 1,500 random parameter sets per algorithm and all 24 invalid-argument cases per algorithm through Python: identical. Speed (release, best of 8 interleaved rounds of 16 MiB): BLAKE2b 308 vs 614 MiB/s (0.50x), BLAKE2s 158 vs 286 MiB/s (0.55x): the crates pick AVX2 or SSE4.1 at run time, ours is portable Rust without unsafe. constant_time_eq 0.4 stays (blake3 uses it). `cargo metadata` 533 -> 530 packages (706 -> 704 on the hashes branch). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `hashes-unit 11|12|13 3000`.
- RustPython's SHA-3 and SHAKE are our own Keccak sponge, and sha3, shake, keccak and sponge-cursor leave the workspace (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/hashlib/keccak.rs is Keccak-f[1600] from FIPS 202 (24 rounds of theta, rho and pi over the 24-lane cycle, chi, iota) with a byte-position sponge: input is XORed into the 25 lanes little-endian, whole rate-sized blocks a lane at a time, then pad10*1 with the domain suffix (0x06 for SHA3-224/256/384/512 at rates 144, 136, 104 and 72 bytes, 0x1f for SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 at 168 and 136) and squeezing as many rate-sized blocks as the length asks for. `HashState::Sha3` carries the state with its output length and `HashState::Shake` the XOF state; `digest(length)` squeezes from a copy, so `copy()`, repeated digests and shake's `digest(length)`/`hexdigest(length)` behave as before, and the length checks and their errors stay in rustpython-stdlib's _hashlib, unchanged. Nothing is unequal: output/hashes-unit (the previous entry) compares sha3_224 to sha3_512, shake_128 and shake_256 against sha3 0.12.0 and shake 0.1.0 from crates.io, with incremental updates at random split points, mid-stream `copy()`, the one-shot path, 5 MiB inputs, shake output lengths 0 to 600 and up to 20,000, HMAC and PBKDF2 over SHA-3 against hmac 0.13.0 and pbkdf2 0.13.0, and the FIPS 202 vectors: seeds 11, 12 and 13 at 3,000 cases give 481,691, 480,821 and 482,073 checks, 0 differences (the harness first caught a sponge position reset when an update ended inside a partial block, fixed before this commit). End to end the corpus in output/e2e (previous entry) prints the sponge attributes `_capacity_bits`, `_rate_bits` and `_suffix`, shake lengths 0 to 10,000 and every invalid length: identical. Speed (release, best of 8 interleaved rounds of 16 MiB): sha3_224 0.98x, sha3_256 0.85x, sha3_384 0.91x, sha3_512 0.98x, shake_128 0.90x, shake_256 0.97x of the crates (keccak 0.2.2 is portable too). `cargo metadata` 538 -> 533 packages (710 -> 706 on the hashes branch). Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `hashes-unit 11|12|13 3000`.
- RustPython's MD5, SHA-1 and SHA-2 digests are our own, and md-5, sha1 and sha2 leave rustpython-common (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-common/src/hashlib/ holds them, written from RFC 1321 and FIPS 180-4: md5.rs, sha1.rs, sha256.rs (SHA-256 and SHA-224, which differ only in the initial state and the 28-byte truncation) and sha512.rs (SHA-512 and SHA-384), over block.rs, one block buffer with the Merkle-Damgard padding (0x80, zeros, the bit length little-endian for MD5 and big-endian for SHA, 64 bits, or 128 for SHA-512); each state is a plain value, so `copy()` stays a clone and `digest()` finalizes a copy, as before. `HashState` in hashlib.rs holds them in place of the crates' types, `compute_digest` (the one-shot path) now goes through the same `HashState`, and `digest_output_size`/`digest_block_size` read the modules' constants; HMAC and PBKDF2 there were already ours and are unchanged. Python's hashlib exposes no SHA-512/224 or SHA-512/256, so neither is written. Nothing is unequal: output/hashes-unit links rustpython-common beside md-5 0.11.0, sha1 0.11.0 and sha2 0.11.0 from crates.io and compares, for each algorithm, incremental updates at random split points (lengths 0 to 4 blocks plus 3, block-boundary lengths and up to 64 KiB), `copy()` mid-stream continued on both sides, the one-shot path, three 5 MiB inputs fed in random chunks up to 1 MiB, HMAC against hmac 0.13.0's `SimpleHmac` with keys up to 3 blocks, PBKDF2 against pbkdf2 0.13.0, and the FIPS and RFC vectors (MD5 suite, SHA abc, 448-bit and million-a messages, RFC 4231 HMAC, RFC 6070 PBKDF2): seeds 11, 12 and 13 at 3,000 cases give 481,691, 480,821 and 482,073 checks over every hashlib algorithm, 0 differences. End to end, output/e2e runs a 9-file Python corpus (hashlib constructors and attributes, 400 random incremental cases per algorithm and 3 MiB inputs, shake lengths and errors, 3,000 random BLAKE2 parameter sets and each validation error, HMAC over 12 digests, pbkdf2_hmac and scrypt with their errors, hash() of 3,000 str and bytes and set/dict order, compare_digest, file_digest) through nanocode-python at 10815c8b3 and at this series' last commit with three fixed hash seeds: stdout, stderr and exit identical byte for byte once object addresses in reprs are masked (469 lines per seed). Speed (release, output/hashes-unit `bench`, best of 8 interleaved rounds of 16 MiB on this shared 5-core Hand under load, so absolute numbers are low): MD5 117 vs 110 MiB/s (1.06x), but SHA-1 0.14x, SHA-256 0.12x, SHA-224 0.11x, SHA-512 0.38x and SHA-384 0.40x, because sha1 and sha2 pick the CPU's SHA extensions (SHA-NI here) and AVX2 at run time and our code is portable Rust with no unsafe; hashing is not on the interpreter's hot path, and a SHA-NI path would need intrinsics under unsafe. `cargo metadata` 538 packages before and after (710 on the hashes branch): psh-utils still uses md-5, sha1 and sha2 and scrypt still uses sha2, so the lock loses only rustpython-common's three edges. Commands: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo build --release` and `hashes-unit 11|12|13 3000` in output/hashes-unit.
- lzma compresses and decompresses with nanocode-compression's xz, and xz, xz-sys and xz-core leave (2026-11-12). crates/core/compression/src/xz (about 9,200 lines) ports the structure of liblzma 5.8.3, which xz-core 0.1.0-rc.0 transpiled: the `lzma_code` sequencing, raw filter chains with liblzma's validation and initialization order, the .xz stream, block and index encoders and decoders with the index hash, the .lzma (alone) encoder and decoder, the auto decoder, the LZ, LZMA1 and LZMA2 decoders with their fast and slow paths, the LZ encoder with the HC3, HC4, BT2, BT3 and BT4 match finders and the fast and normal parsers with liblzma's price tables, the LZMA2 chunker, the delta filter and the x86, PowerPC, IA-64, ARM, ARM-Thumb, SPARC, ARM64 and RISC-V BCJ filters, and CRC32, CRC64 and SHA-256 for the checks. rustpython-common's compression/lzma.rs keeps its API; only its backend calls and constants changed. Not equal: xz-core's BT2 and BT3 match finders never advance their read position, so `mf=MF_BT2` or `MF_BT3` crashed the whole process with a segmentation fault on almost any input of a few KB, where these now compress, byte-equal to the system's C liblzma 5.4.5 on 2,000 raw-format cases (the rest of the encoder matched that library on 60 HC3, HC4 and BT4 cases as a control); liblzma answers a second call that makes no progress with LZMA_BUF_ERROR, which lzma.rs treated as success and which is now plain success; an LZMA1EXT filter inside an .xz block header, whose options liblzma reads from uninitialized memory, is rejected as "Invalid or unsupported options" (no encoder writes one); memory limits count liblzma's 64-bit structure sizes on every target, so on wasm32 a limit within a few KB of a stream's need could decide differently than the 32-bit C structures did. Proven with output/xz-harness and output/xz-python, against xz 0.4.6-rc.0, xz-sys 0.4.6-rc.0 and xz-core 0.1.0-rc.0: one random call sequence (input splits of 0 and 1 byte and up, output buffers of 0 bytes to 1 MB, run then finish) drives both libraries and compares status or error, totals and bytes after every call, over 18,156 encoder cases (100,406 calls: presets 0 to 9 and extreme, every check, stream encoders with random chains of up to 3 BCJ and delta filters before LZMA1 or LZMA2 and invalid chains, alone and raw encoders, dictionaries from 4,095 bytes to 64 MiB, every lc, lp and pb including invalid ones, both modes, HC3, HC4 and BT4, nice lengths 1 to 274 and depths) and 41,309 decoder cases (335,431 calls through the auto, xz, alone and raw decoders on those outputs, intact and with bit flips, truncation, junk, padding and garbage, under memory limits around each stream's need), 8 MiB inputs of five kinds at presets 0, 6 and 9e, and 68,493 cases (258,977 calls) of lzma.rs's own `Compressor` and `Decompressor` linked old and new, comparing every result, error message, eof, needs_input, unused_data and check, plus 60,000 filter-property and check-support cases; the decoder, encoder and filter parts were also checked alone (25.1 million raw LZMA1 and LZMA2 decode calls with corruptions, 50,000 encoder option-grid cases with 1.0 million calls and 4.4 GB runs past the match finder's 2^32 normalization, 2.4 million checksum cases and 14.9 million BCJ and delta calls), all with 0 differences. End to end, output/e2e's lzma, zipfile (ZIP_LZMA) and tarfile (w:xz) scripts (presets 0 to 9 and extreme, FORMAT_ALONE and FORMAT_RAW, every check, 47 filter chains with delta, every BCJ filter, LZMA1 and custom LZMA2 options, invalid filter specs and properties, incremental LZMACompressor and LZMADecompressor with max_length, 500 bit-flipped streams, memory limits and LZMAFile) give byte-identical stdout, stderr, exit and step counts through nanocode-python at 10815c8b3 and at this commit, as does the whole 11-script corpus (20,412 lines); MF_BT2 and MF_BT3 are left out of it because the old build crashes on them, and a script compressing 200,000 bytes of Lib sources with each now round-trips where the old build died. Release throughput (the Hand ran at load 10 to 55, so per-thread CPU time), old then new: LZMA2 decoding 128 to 140 MB/s on text and 64 to 71 on binary, LZMA1 on random data 20.6 to 31.9; encoding about 10% slower (raw LZMA2 on 2 MiB at preset 6 2.76 to 2.47 MB/s on text and 3.27 to 2.83 on binary, at preset 0 28.6 to 26.1 on text), the normal parser's helper loop kept at liblzma's shape (96 lines) rather than risk equality; CRC64 1.5 to 2.3 GB/s, CRC32 and SHA-256 on par. rustpython-doc's `#[cfg(test)]` module still names `xz::decode_all`; vendored tests are not built. `cargo metadata --locked` 541 to 538 packages (on deps-python; 704 to 701 on the compression branch). Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression` (native and wasm32).
- bz2 compresses and decompresses with nanocode-compression's bzip2, and bzip2 and libbz2-rs-sys leave (2026-11-12). crates/core/compression/src/bzip2 is a port of libbz2-rs-sys 0.2.5 (bzip2 1.0.8) as the bzip2 0.6.1 crate drove it for RustPython: the compressor with work factor 30 (the initial run-length step, mainSort with libbz2's budget accounting and its fallback to fallbackSort, the move-to-front and zero-run coding, Huffman code lengths capped at 17 bits with the weight-halving retry, table counts by symbol count, four refinement passes, selector coding, block and stream CRCs, per-level block sizes and framing), and the fast (not small-memory) decompressor, which pulls input exactly as libbz2 does, seven bytes at a time before the end-of-stream magic and one at a time after it, so `unused_data` and `needs_input` come out the same. rustpython-common's compression/bz2.rs keeps its API and driver loops on `Compressor` and `Decompressor`; its `Bz2Error::Mem` can no longer occur. Not equal: libbz2 panicked through the bzip2 crate on a run with an empty output buffer while output was pending, which now is `Err(Param)` (RustPython never asks for it); after an error the decoder repeats it without consuming input, where libbz2's behavior is unspecified and RustPython refuses further calls; per-call counts differ above 4 GiB in one call, which RustPython's `Chunker` already splits; `Action::Flush`, the small decoder and other work factors are not written, as RustPython uses none of them; level 9 holds about 12 MB where libbz2 aliased its buffers to use about 7.5 MB. Proven with output/bz2-harness, which links bzip2 0.6.1 and libbz2-rs-sys 0.2.5 and compiles the vendored bz2.rs against both: 3,000 one-shot cases (440 MB at levels 1 to 9 over text, binary, random, zeros, periodic, run-length edges, small alphabets and the near-periodic inputs that take the fallback sort) and 200 larger ones (49 MB) compress byte-identically; 16 cases of 3 to 8 MB at levels 1 and 9 agree one-shot, through RustPython's driver, decoding and with trailing data; 17,388 compress calls and 21,510 decompress calls in lockstep (random splits, 0- and 1-byte output buffers, 242 randomised-block streams, 806 streams with trailing junk) agree in outcome, bytes consumed and produced and the bytes themselves after every call; 20,000 corrupted streams (72,703 calls) are accepted or rejected alike with the same error kind and the same output before it; 36,706 calls through the old, new and wired bz2.rs agree in bytes or error, eof, failure, needs_input and unused_data (0 differences everywhere). End to end, output/e2e's bz2, zipfile (ZIP_BZIP2) and tarfile (w:bz2) scripts give byte-identical stdout, stderr, exit and step counts through nanocode-python at 10815c8b3 and at this commit. Release throughput, per-thread CPU time, five interleaved rounds, libbz2-rs-sys then ours: compression 22.8 to 21.9 MB/s (text, level 1), 17.1 to 16.6 (text, level 9), 16.4 to 15.4 (binary, level 1), 12.3 to 11.3 (random, level 9); decompression 60.9 to 60.9 (text, level 1), 20.3 to 17.7 (text, level 9), 15.4 to 15.4 (binary, level 9), 9.1 to 10.2 (random, level 9). `cargo metadata --locked` 543 to 541 packages (on deps-python; 706 to 704 on the compression branch). Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression` (native and wasm32).
- zlib, gzip's deflate streams, zipfile's deflate members, binascii.crc32 and the Unicode database build inflate and deflate with nanocode-compression, and zlib-rs, libz-rs-sys and adler32 leave (2026-11-12). nanocode-compression gains src/inflate (a port of zlib-rs 0.6.8's inflate: zlib, gzip, raw and auto headers, the 32 KiB window, preset dictionaries, the same fast loop and byte-at-a-time state machine, so a call stops on the same input byte, and the same stream messages), src/deflate (a port of zlib-rs 0.6.8's deflate, which is zlib-ng's and not classic zlib's: stored, quick, fast, medium, slow, RLE and Huffman-only strategies with zlib-ng's hashes, match finder, block splitting and trees, every flush mode, dictionaries, zlib and gzip framing) and src/checksum.rs (`crc32` as zlib and crc32fast compute it, slice-by-16 tables built at compile time, and `adler32` as the adler32 1.2.0 crate computes it, including its handling of unreduced start values). rustpython-common's compression/zlib.rs keeps its API and driver loops and holds `Deflate` and `Inflate` where it held zlib-rs `z_stream`s (copies are `Clone`, without the unsafe code it needed); its Z_* constants are written out with zlib's values, `zlib.ZLIB_VERSION` stays "1.3.0-zlib-rs-0.6.8" because that is the library whose output this reproduces, binascii's crc32 and zlib.adler32 call the checksum module, and rustpython-unicode's build.rs inflates Unihan-3.2.0.txt.zlib with `inflate_all`. Not equal: zlib-rs counts totals in a C `unsigned long`, which wraps at 4 GiB on wasm32, while ours are u64 (RustPython only takes differences of them per call, under 4 GiB); `Compress.copy()` and `Decompress.copy()` can no longer fail with "insufficient memory"; bytes of an output buffer past what a call produced may differ (zlib-rs writes them with SIMD chunks), never what Python sees; crc32fast stays in the workspace for flate2 and png. Proven at the unit level against the exact crates, driving zlib-rs through the same low-level z_stream calls RustPython made and ours with the same random sequence of input splits, output sizes (0, 1, small, 16 KiB, large), flushes, clones and dictionaries, comparing status, error, message, bytes consumed, bytes produced and totals after every call: deflate (output/deflate-equality) over 21,559 streaming cases with 2,358,209 calls and 2.5 GB of input, 2,720 cases of RustPython's own compressobj driver, 2,200 cases of 2 to 6 MB through every level from -1 to 9, every strategy, window bits 8 to 15, -9 to -15 and 24 to 31, and memory levels 1 to 9 (9.1 GB), and 2,683 cases with overflow checks on in both libraries, all byte-identical; inflate (output/inflate-equal) over 6,000 cases and 7,381,758 calls, 60% of them on corrupted, truncated or concatenated streams, with 8,200 stream ends, 7,250 data errors, 221,000 dictionary requests and 221,000 mid-stream clones, 0 differences; checksums (output/checksum-equal) over 400,000 lengths and start values, 0 differences. The Unicode tables rustpython-unicode generates are byte-identical. End to end, output/e2e runs the zlib, gzip, zipfile, tarfile, binascii and bz2 scripts (zlib.compress at every level and window, compressobj over every level, strategy, memory level and window with dictionaries, partial feeding, every flush mode and copies, decompressobj with max_length, unconsumed_tail and unused_data, _ZlibDecompressor, 1,000 bit-flipped streams, garbage, gzip members and GzipFile, ZIP_DEFLATED archives, tar.gz) through nanocode-python built at 10815c8b3 and at this commit: stdout, stderr, exit and step counts are byte-identical (18,005 lines). Throughput in release builds, per-thread CPU time in interleaved rounds (the Hand ran at load 15 to 58), zlib-rs then ours: deflate on 4 MiB of Lib sources 293 to 315 MB/s at level 1, 80 to 74 at level 6 and 39.9 to 38.0 at level 9, and 0.81 to 1.23 times zlib-rs over every level and input (level 2 on text is the slowest, at 0.81); inflate 624 to 569 MB/s on text and 492 to 430 on binary (zlib-rs copies with AVX2, which safe code cannot); crc32 1.3 to 4.3 GB/s (crc32fast uses PCLMULQDQ) to 0.5 to 0.6 GB/s, adler32 the same at about 0.6 GB/s. `cargo metadata --locked` 546 to 543 packages (on deps-python; 709 to 706 on the compression branch). Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression` (native and wasm32).
- The frozen standard library's bytecode and RustPython's docstring blob are LZ4 blocks from the new nanocode-compression crate, and lz4_flex and twox-hash leave (2026-11-12). crates/core/compression (package nanocode-compression, `no_std` with alloc, unsafe forbidden, native and wasm32) is where the embedded Python's codecs now live; its src/lz4.rs is the LZ4 block format with a 4-byte little-endian size prefix, the compressor written to make lz4_flex 0.14.0's choices (a 4,096-entry position table, the 4-byte multiplicative hash below 65,535 input bytes and lz4_flex's 64-bit five-byte hash from there, the skip step that grows by one every 32 misses, backward extension, no match search in the last 12 bytes and 5 literal bytes at the end), the decoder a bounds-checked copy into a buffer of the prefixed size with typed `Lz4Error`s. rustpython-compiler-core's frozen.rs (code objects that rustpython-derive-impl compresses at build time and the VM inflates at import) calls it instead of `lz4_flex::{compress_prepend_size, decompress_size_prepended}`; rustpython-doc's build.rs stores its 489,521 bytes of docstring text as an LZ4 block (219,285 bytes) instead of xz -9 (116,468 bytes), which only rustpython-vm's `doc` feature reads at runtime and nanocode-python leaves off, so rustpython-doc and rustpython-vm no longer depend on xz (it stays, for `_lzma`, until its own change). Not equal: lz4_flex hashes large inputs with the 4-byte hash on 32-bit targets, while this always uses the 64-bit one, which is what the proc macro produced on every 64-bit build host, wasm builds included; the decoder's errors are its own (RustPython only ever feeds it its own blocks and panics on failure as before). Proven with output/lz4-equal, which links lz4_flex 0.14.0 beside nanocode-compression: 30,499 inputs (3,000 real files from rustpython-pylib's Lib and rustpython-vm's sources, and 27,499 seeded random inputs of five shapes up to 300 KB, including every size from 65,530 to 65,541 bytes around the table switch) compress byte-identically, each side decompresses the other's blocks to the input, and bit-flipped blocks that both decoders accept give the same output (0 differences); output/doc-blob decodes the old docs.xz and the new docs.lz4 to the same text. End to end, output/e2e runs a corpus of zlib, gzip, zipfile, tarfile and bz2 scripts through nanocode-python built at 10815c8b3 and at this commit: stdout, stderr, exit and step counts are byte-identical (18,006 lines). 8.4 MB of Lib sources, three interleaved release rounds: compression 60 to 101 ms before and 59 to 87 ms after; decompression 18 to 21 ms before and 31 to 43 ms after (lz4_flex copies with wider unchecked writes; a typical frozen module is a few KB, decoded once per import). `cargo metadata --locked` 547 to 546 packages (on deps-python; the compression branch measured 710 to 709 on its base). Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-compression` (native and wasm32).
- rustpython-host_env no longer re-exports system-configuration on macOS; system-configuration and system-configuration-sys leave (2026-11-12). The re-export served only rustpython-stdlib's `_scproxy` module, which is compiled only with the stdlib's host_env feature that nanocode does not enable (crates/core/python registers `stdlib_module_defs` from a stdlib built with `default-features = false`), so no code that nanocode builds used it on any target. Equal by construction: no compiled code changes on Linux or wasm, and on macOS only the unused module goes. `cargo metadata` 549 to 547 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass (macOS was not built here).
- Case mapping and case folding come from rustpython-unicode's own tables built from Unicode 17.0's UnicodeData.txt, CaseFolding.txt and SpecialCasing.txt; icu_casemap, icu_casemap_data, icu_locale and icu_locale_data leave, and writeable leaves rustpython-unicode (2026-11-12). CaseFolding.txt and SpecialCasing.txt 17.0.0 are vendored as published by unicode.org beside the UnicodeData.txt 17.0 already in crates/patches/rustpython-unicode/unicode/latest. build.rs (`generate_case_tables`) writes the simple lowercase, uppercase and titlecase mappings (titlecase defaulting to uppercase as UnicodeData specifies) and the simple fold (CaseFolding C and S), the full fold (F, else C) and the unconditional SpecialCasing titlecase; src/case.rs answers `simple_lowercase`/`uppercase`/`titlecase`/`fold` by binary search (ASCII stays a fast path), `casefold_str`/`casefold_wtf8` by mapping each character through the full fold, and the first-of-word titlecase that `str.title` and `str.capitalize` use by the full titlecase mapping (ICU's `titlecase_segment` with `LeadingAdjustment::None` on a single character, which is what every caller passes; the function asserts it). Lowercasing and sigma handling were already std's and RustPython's own. Equality: output/case-equal links crates.io rustpython-unicode 0.6.0 (on icu_casemap 2.2.0, with the pre-vendoring lock) beside the new crate and compares, for every scalar value, the four simple mappings, `casefold_str`, `title_str`, `capitalize_str` and `swapcase_str` of the character in context, and `character_name`, then 300,000 random strings of the 3,037 characters that case-map plus ß, İ, ı, Σ, ς, U+0345, U+0307, ǅ, ﬁ and ASCII through the str and WTF-8 (with lone surrogates) case functions, and `lookup_name`/`lookup_character` samples: 12,108,596 checks, 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 553 to 549 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- Python float literals and float() strings are parsed by rustpython-literal itself; lexical-parse-float, lexical-parse-integer, lexical-util and hexf-parse leave (2026-11-12). crates/patches/rustpython-literal/src/float.rs: `parse_inner` accepts what lexical's `PYTHON3_LITERAL` format with specials did (an optional sign; case-insensitive inf, infinity or nan; otherwise digits with single underscores only between digits, an optional fraction, at least one mantissa digit and an optional exponent with at least one digit; leading zeros allowed) and hands the digits without underscores to core's correctly rounded `f64` parser, as lexical's result is correctly rounded too; `parse_hex_float` is hexf-parse 0.2.1's `parse_hexf64(_, false)` ported (exact values only: a mantissa that needs more than 64 bits, an exponent that overflows or a value that does not fit an f64 exactly is no value) for `float.fromhex`, with `2.0.powf(exponent)`, which needs std, replaced by building the power of two from its bits (an exponent below -1074 gives 0 and above 1023 infinity, as powf rounds there). Equality: output/float-equal compares 6,000,000 random strings over digits, underscores, signs, dots, exponents, special-value letters and spaces plus formatted random doubles, 22 boundary inputs (overflow, underflow, the smallest subnormal and its halfway points, signed zero and NaN) against lexical-parse-float 1.0.6, and 4,000,000 random hex strings and formatted random hex doubles through `from_hex` against the same function on hexf-parse 0.2.1, comparing bits: 10,000,022 checks, 3,528,484 parsed values, 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 557 to 553 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- Unicode character names come from rustpython-unicode's own tables, built from its vendored UnicodeData.txt; unicode_names2 1.3.0 and 3.1.0, their generators, getopts and phf, phf_codegen, phf_generator and phf_shared 0.11 leave (2026-11-12). rustpython-unicode's build.rs (`generate_names`) splits every UnicodeData 17.0 name into words (17,983 distinct, 161,880 word tokens with a space-or-hyphen bit), keeps the code points sorted for `name` and two permutations sorted by exact name and by UAX44-LM2 loose key, and the CJK ideograph ranges; src/names.rs reads them. `names::name` is unicode_names2 3.1's `name` (explicit names, CJK UNIFIED IDEOGRAPH-hex, Hangul syllables from the jamo tables) for `unicodedata.name`; `names::character` is its `character` (loose matching: case, whitespace, underscores and medial hyphens ignored except in U+1180, the U+116C/U+1180 special case, the jamo parser's quirks, aliases from NameAliases.txt matched by their raw text) for `unicodedata.lookup`; `names::character_unicode_16` is unicode_names2 1.3's `character` for the ruff parser's `\N{...}` escapes: ASCII-uppercased exact names over Unicode 16.0, which is the 17.0 data less the code points and four Bamum aliases 17.0 added (`NAMED_SINCE_UNICODE_17`, `ALIASES_SINCE_UNICODE_17` in build.rs, from comparing the two crates' UnicodeData.txt and NameAliases.txt, including the two CJK range extensions and Extension J). The algorithmic-name table now skips the CJK and Hangul ranges by their UnicodeData range names instead of asking unicode_names2. Not equal by construction: unicode_names2 looks a name up in a perfect hash and then checks only that the candidate's name is a prefix of the input, so an invalid name whose hash lands on a character whose name is its prefix returned that character; ours finds only exact keys. No such input showed up in the harness. Equality: output/names-equal links unicode_names2 3.1.0 and 1.3.0 beside rustpython-unicode: `name` for all 1,112,064 scalar values, and 761,508 lookup inputs through both the loose and the 1.3 functions (every one of the 153,626 names including CJK and Hangul, a quarter of them lowercased, underscored, despaced, dehyphenated, suffixed, padded, random-cased and mutated, every alias three ways, 200,000 random strings over name letters, Hangul and CJK prefixes with valid and invalid tails, the U+1180 cases): 2,635,080 checks, 0 differences. Size: a stripped binary calling `name`, `character` and the 1.3 `character` is 2,080,784 bytes with the two crates and 1,361,368 with ours. Speed (release, 3 rounds): `name` over every code point 6 to 39 ms before, 47 to 106 ms after (a binary search over 40,470 names where unicode_names2 indexes a two-level table); `character` over all 153,626 names 12.6 to 74 ms before, 113 to 551 ms after (each probe decodes a name into a stack buffer); neither is on a hot path. `cargo metadata` 567 to 557 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- RustPython carries its own iterator helpers, hasher, Mersenne Twister and atomics trait; itertools, rapidhash, mt19937, textwrap and phf (with phf_generator, phf_macros and phf_shared) leave, and radium and rand leave these crates (2026-11-12). In crates/patches: rustpython-wtf8/src/iteration.rs has the `Itertools` methods RustPython calls (`collect_vec`, `exactly_one` with an `ExactlyOneError` that iterates the items it read and the rest as itertools' does, `join`, `format`, `map_into`, `peeking_take_while` over `PeekingNext` for `Peekable`, `try_collect`, `zip_eq` panicking with itertools' message, `intersperse`, `collect_array`, `contains`, `process_results`), `Either` and `process_results`, used by wtf8, common, compiler-core, stdlib and vm through their existing paths; frame.rs's `tuples()` of pairs is `pairs()`. rustpython-common/src/random_state.rs is a per-instance randomly seeded hasher (a folded 64x64 multiply over 8-byte words) in place of rapidhash's `quality::RandomState` for the codegen and vm index maps, the intern set, the dict shape hasher and the frozen-module map; both seed randomly per process, so hash order was already not reproducible across runs (codegen's maps are insertion ordered). rustpython-stdlib/src/mersenne_twister.rs is mt19937 3.3.0's MT19937 (init_genrand, init_by_array, genrand_int32 and genrand_res53, get/set state and index, the 5489 default seed) reached under the name `mt19937`, and an unseeded `Random()` takes its 624-word key from getrandom where it went through rand 0.10's thread RNG. rustpython-common/src/atomic.rs's `Radium`, `RadiumBits` and `RadiumNumber` traits give `PyAtomic` (a `Cell` without threading, an atomic with it) radium 1.1.1's load, store, swap, compare_exchange, fetch_update, bit and wrapping add/sub operations. rustpython-derive-impl's `textwrap::dedent` for `py_compile!` sources is ported from textwrap 0.16.4, and its two itertools calls are written out. phf served only the ssl-openssl error tables, which nanocode does not build. Equality: output/mt-equal compares 3,000 seeded keys (1 to 700 words) and the default seed against mt19937 3.3.0 through 2,000 outputs, `gen_res53`, state round trips and 1,500 more outputs after `set_state`/`set_index`: 10,615,000 checks, 0 differences; output/dedent-equal compares 3,000,000 random strings of spaces, tabs, newlines, carriage returns, non-ASCII whitespace and text against textwrap 0.16.4: 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 575 to 567 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- RustPython's vm, stdlib, sre_engine, host_env and pylib build scripts stop using small helper crates; optional, result-like, result-like-derive, pmutil, is-macro, num_enum, num_enum_derive, half, crunchy, glob, constant_time_eq 0.6 and (through rustpython-stdlib's unused uuid dependency) atomic leave, and strum, strum_macros, paste, scopeguard, hex, static_assertions and uuid leave these crates (2026-11-12). In crates/patches: `Optioned<usize>` (sre_engine marks, vm sequence search) is `Option<usize>`; vm/src/like.rs's `option_like!` writes what `#[derive(OptionLike)]` generated for `OptionalArg`, `PySetterValue` and `PyArithmeticValue` (the Option-shaped methods, `From` both ways, `Default`, `IntoIterator`, `Clone`/`Copy`, `copied`/`cloned`/`as_deref`, `transpose`) and protocol/iter.rs has `PyIterReturn`'s `ResultLike` methods written out; their `is_present`/`is_missing`/`present`/`is_assign`/`is_delete`/`assign` are the `is_macro::Is` methods. `TryFrom` for `SreOpcode`, `SreAtCode`, `SreCatCode`, `FormatType` and `PosixSpawnFileActionIdentifier` are generated `match`es over the discriminants with the value as the error (output/c3.py); posix.rs's `PathconfVar`/`SysconfVar` get `iter()` and `FromStr` carrying each variant's `#[cfg]`, `CheckHashPycsMode` a lowercase `Display`/`FromStr` and the codec `StandardError` a lowercase `FromStr`, as strum's derives did. vm/src/half.rs is half 2.7.1's `from_f64_const` (the conversion struct 'e' uses) and `to_f64` ported bit for bit. rustpython-common gains scope.rs (`guard`, `ScopeGuard::into_inner`, `defer!`), hex.rs (lowercase `encode`, `encode_to_slice`) and constant_time.rs (`constant_time_eq`: different lengths are unequal, otherwise an OR of XORs through `black_box`). The unused `named_function!` macro and its `paste` export go, host_env's Windows WSA re-exports are written out, size assertions are `const` asserts, and the vm and pylib build scripts list Lib/ themselves (only to print rerun-if-changed lines and delete .pyc files, so order does not matter). The stdlib code that still names uuid, num_enum or paste (the `uuid` module and the `host_env`, `ssl-openssl` and `sqlite` features) is compiled out in nanocode's feature set; those features of the vendored stdlib no longer build. Equality: output/half-equal compares every f16 bit pattern's `to_f64` and `is_infinite` and 100,327,700 `from_f64` inputs (specials, every f16 value and its neighbours, 50 million random bit patterns and scaled values) against half 2.7.1: 100,458,774 checks, 0 differences. End to end, output/e2e (the numeric agent's e2e runner: `nanocode_python::run` over an in-memory filesystem) runs 446 seeded programs and 12,561 checked expressions (every frozen module's names; 7,500 random regular expressions over search, match, fullmatch, findall, finditer, sub, subn and split with spans, groups and lastindex; struct 'e' packing; bytes.hex with separators; hmac and secrets.compare_digest; codecs with every standard error handler; list and deque index and count; memoryview casts; itertools; int and float formatting; ast.dump and compile of mutated sources; array) through the vendored tree before this change and after: byte-identical output (11,555 lines). `cargo metadata` 589 to 575 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- The rustpython-ruff parser and AST crates lose their helper crates; get-size2, get-size-derive2, attribute-derive, attribute-derive-macro, collection_literals, derive-where, interpolator, manyhow, manyhow-macros, ordermap, proc-macro-utils, quote-use, quote-use-macros, char_str, compact_str, thin-vec, drop_bomb and rustc-hash leave, and static_assertions, itertools and is-macro leave these crates (2026-11-12). In crates/patches: the parser derived `GetSize` on its error types, which turned on every ruff crate's get-size feature, and nothing measures sizes, so the derives and features go. `Name` (rustpython-ruff_python_ast/src/name.rs) is a static `&str` or an `Arc<str>` compared, ordered and hashed by its text as char_str's `CharStr` was; `new_inline`/`new_heap` go and the parser's `NameInterner` shares every name it has seen, where it shared only names over 16 bytes. `DebugText` holds a `Box<str>` (was `CompactString`). AST lists are `Vec` (were `ThinVec`), with rustpython-vm's `Node for ThinVec` impl gone. rustpython-ruff_python_trivia/src/fx_hash.rs is rustc-hash 2.1.3's FxHasher and `FxBuildHasher` ported line for line (multiplier, rotation, the byte hash and its seeds), so every `FxHashSet`/`FxHashMap` of the parser, AST and trivia keeps its order. The scratch buffer's `DebugDropBomb` is a `restored` flag checked by `debug_assert!` on drop with the same message; `assert_eq_size!` lines are `const` asserts on `size_of`; `find_position` is `position`; the `is_macro::Is` derives of the AST and rustpython-literal are written out as the methods somebody calls (output/ismacro_scan.py lists them, output/ismacro_gen.py writes them as is-macro 0.3.8 expands them: `is_*` `const fn` by `match *self`, `as_*`, `expect_*` panicking with `called expect_* on {self:?}`, and the bare variant name taking `self`), and the derive's `#[is(name = ...)]` attributes go. Equality: output/ruff-old (crates.io rustpython-ruff_python_parser 0.16.5 with the pre-vendoring lock) and output/ruff-new (the same program patched to crates/patches) print, for each of the 277 frozen standard-library modules and 20 seeded mutations of each (deleted, inserted, cut and duplicated characters, mostly syntax errors), the Debug text of the module AST, unsupported-syntax errors and tokens, or of the parse error: 5,717 cases, byte-identical output files. Parsing the 277 modules 20 times, 5 interleaved runs each at load 10 to 20: old 4.23 to 7.92 s (median 6.19), new 3.25 to 6.11 s (median 4.67). `cargo metadata` 608 to 589 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass.
- rustpython-host_env drops the host crates nanocode's Python never reaches; rustyline, dns-lookup, mac_address, termios, which, num_cpus, gethostname and socket2 leave its dependencies, and with them clipboard-win, endian-type, error-code, home, nibble_vec, nix 0.29 and radix_trie (2026-11-12). nanocode-python builds rustpython-vm and rustpython-stdlib without their host_env feature, so the modules that used these crates (socket, uuid, termios, readline) are compiled out, and its posix module is crates/core/python/src/posix.py, so host_env's os and posix helpers are never called from Python either. In crates/patches/rustpython-host_env: readline.rs always uses its basic reader (what RustPython uses on wasm: the prompt on stderr, one line from stdin) where rustyline edited the line; socket.rs loses `hostname` (gethostname), `mac_address` (mac_address) and the `dns`/`raw` re-exports (dns-lookup, socket2), which only the compiled-out socket and uuid modules used; termios.rs, used only by the compiled-out termios module, is deleted; os.rs's `cpu_count` is std's `available_parallelism` (1 when unknown) where num_cpus counted; fs.rs's `which`, which rustpython-vm's getpath uses for the executable's path when the interpreter starts, is our own PATH search, ported from which 8.0.5: an absolute name as is, a name with a separator joined to the current directory (leading `.` components dropped), otherwise each PATH entry (a leading `~` component is the home directory; on Windows empty entries skipped and PATHEXT tried) joined with the name, the first that is a file and passes access(X_OK) (on Windows: a file or symlink with an extension, or one GetBinaryTypeW accepts, with the found name's casing). Not equal: builtins.input() when the process's own stdin and stdout are terminals and sys.stdin and sys.stdout are fds 0 and 1 read a plain line instead of a rustyline-edited one; inside nanocode that path would have put the user's terminal in raw mode under the TUI. `cpu_count` can differ from num_cpus where cgroup quotas are fractional, but nanocode's os.cpu_count is posix.py's. Equality: output/which-equal links which 8.0.5 beside a copy of the new `which` and runs 284,000 lookups (71 names: bare, `./`, `../`, nested, absolute, empty, `.`, `/`; over 4,000 random PATHs from 11 entries including `~/bin`, empty, `.`, relative and missing ones, unset and empty PATH; 4 working directories; a tree of executables, plain files, directories, live and dangling symlinks): 0 differences. `cargo metadata` 625 to 608 packages. `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` pass; `cargo check -p rustpython-host_env --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` fails before and after in wmi.rs, which needs the ctypes feature nanocode does not enable, so this configuration never built for Windows.
- The rest of RustPython 0.6.0 is vendored under crates/patches, unchanged, so that taking its third-party dependencies out is a diff (2026-11-12). rustpython-codegen, -common, -compiler, -compiler-core, -derive, -derive-impl, -doc, -host_env, -literal, -stdlib, -unicode and -wtf8 0.6.0, the rustpython-ruff_python_ast, _python_parser, _python_trivia, _source_file and _text_size 0.16.5 crates and pymath 0.2.0 (RustPython's math library, which carries malachite-bigint and num-complex) are copied from crates.io as published, without .cargo-ok, .cargo_vcs_info.json, Cargo.lock, Cargo.toml.orig, their .gitignore files and the test, benchmark and resource directories nothing builds from (rustpython-ruff_python_parser's 11.6 MB of tests and resources, rustpython-unicode's and rustpython-ruff_text_size's tests, pymath's proptest regressions and CI files); `[patch.crates-io]` points each at its directory beside rustpython-vm, rustpython-sre_engine and rustpython-pylib, and the workspace lock loses their 18 source and checksum lines and nothing else. No measurement: the same source builds (`cargo metadata` 625 packages before and after). `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-python` passes.
- perf(djs): JSON.parse inlines its string scanner so the returned token no longer round-trips through memory (a store-forwarding stall that was ~56% of parse self time on short strings). JSON.parse of 20k small objects 1,175M->1,166M instr (-0.8%), cycles -3.5%; parse kernel -1.1% instr, -5% cycles (same-path A/B); JSON round-trip -5% cycles. An earlier attempt measured only long strings (~1%).
- `Object.assign` from a plain source into a target that already has properties reads the source's entries into stack arrays (`plain_entries_into`) instead of collecting its own keys into a `Vec` and looking each one up again: Object.assign micro benchmark (`Object.assign({}, {a:1,b:2}, {c:k})`) 5,435M -> 4,971M instructions (-8.5%); others unchanged.
- Object rest (`const {a, ...rest} = o`) of a plain object with up to 16 properties reads them into stack arrays (`Heap::plain_entries_into`) instead of four `Vec`s, and builds the result with the last rest result's shape (`Heap::rest_shape`, cleared by collections, checked against the keys) instead of a transition search per key: object rest micro benchmark 6,603M -> 5,215M instructions (-21%), destructuring 11,514M -> 10,104M (-12%); kernels unchanged.
- Suspending and resuming a generator or async function copies the frame between the value stack and its saved array with one `copy_within`, instead of a get and a set per value: generator for-of micro benchmark 812M -> 718M instructions (-11.6%), await loop 722M -> 628M (-13%), async function calls 1,443M -> 1,349M (-6.5%); kernels unchanged.
- ToString of an int32 Number writes its digits into a stack buffer and allocates the string once, instead of formatting through the float formatter into a heap `String` first (single digits had a shortcut): template literals with numbers 2,842M -> 2,714M instructions (-4.5%), number formatting micro benchmark -1.5%, json kernel -1.0%, the workerd compute cell's object-building loop (`String(i).padStart(8, '0')`) -1.8%.
- `decline_plain` also finishes a declined unary `+` or `-` of a primitive (`+'42'`) and a template literal's `concat` of up to 16 primitive parts, instead of through `step`: template literal micro benchmark 2,927M -> 2,842M instructions (-2.9%), string-to-number micro benchmark 2,617M -> 2,547M (-2.7%, cycles -13%); kernels unchanged.
- A declined `put_elem` with a string key on an ordinary object stores through the megamorphic cache when its slot for that shape and key is a writable own property (`mega_put`; the get path fills those slots), in `decline_fast` instead of through `step`: an agent-style script that counts by key (`acc[k] = (acc[k] || 0) + 1`) 2,737M -> 2,709M instructions (-1.0%), map-by-key micro benchmark -0.4%; other kernels unchanged.
- A `get_field` or `get_method` whose site cache missed tries the megamorphic cache in `decline_fast` (`decline_field`) before `step`, which tried it only after the way there: a polymorphic read kernel (4 shapes at one site) 3,828M -> 3,477M instructions (-9.2%, cycles -9.4%), dispatch kernel (3 classes' methods at one call site) 5,373M -> 5,109M (-4.9%, cycles -5%); reads of an absent property pay the extra probe (optional chaining micro benchmark +2.5% instructions), other kernels unchanged.
- `decline_fast` finishes the common allocating and checking instructions that the hot loop declines (`object`, `array_from` of up to 16 values, `array_push` into dense storage, `fclosure`, `new_box_init`, `push_atom`, `require_object_coercible`, `to_string` of a primitive) in `decline_plain`, out of line, instead of through `step`; a failed allocation (the heap cap) leaves it to `step` and its retry (D1700). Counting `step_once` entries showed these as the most frequent general-path instructions across the micro suite. Instructions: closures kernel 3,867M -> 3,578M (-7.5%), object literals with Object.assign 5,566M -> 5,432M (cycles -18%), destructuring 12,346M -> 11,498M (cycles -15%), spread 2,659M -> 2,452M (cycles -12%), template literals 3,130M -> 2,927M (cycles -10%), an agent-style script -0.5%; other kernels unchanged.
- `decline_fast` finishes a declined bitwise operator (`&` `|` `^` `<<` `>>`) on two Numbers with ToInt32, and a declined `<` `<=` `>` `>=` on two strings, instead of through `step` (`decline_operator`, out of line): chars kernel (`h = (h * 31 + c) | 0`) 5,721M -> 5,195M instructions (-9.2%, cycles -16%), string comparison micro benchmark 1,479M -> 1,320M instructions (-10.7%, 20.5 -> 15.7 ms, qjs 17.9); other kernels within 0.2% instructions.
- Every intrinsic the hot loop declines runs from `intrinsic_decline` (was `each_dense_decline`, only `%EachDense`) as `step` would run it, except the ones `step` retries after a collection (D1700): counting `step_once` entries showed `%RegExpCreate` (every regex literal), `%HasProperty` and `%GetIterator` among the most frequent general-path instructions. A regex-heavy script 390M -> 371M cycles (-4.9%, instructions -3.7%), an agent-style script instructions -1.1%, closures kernel 3,957M -> 3,867M instructions (-2.3%), strings -2.4%.
- A conditional jump on a value that is not a boolean (`while (a.length)`, `if (obj)`, `x && y`) is finished in `decline_fast` with ToBoolean, out of line in `decline_branch`, instead of through `step`: array push/pop micro benchmark 1,975M -> 1,890M cycles (-4.5%, 90.0 -> 83.8 ms, qjs 81), an agent-style script 1,016M -> 1,002M (-1.4%), a regex-heavy script 401M -> 392M (-2.3%); kernel instruction counts unchanged (objects +6% cycles natively from run_hot's alignment moving 16 bytes, same instructions). Inline in `decline_fast` it cost the agent script +1.4%, rejected.
- A Number `mod` that the hot loop declines (a double or a negative operand) is finished in `decline_fast`, as the string `add` is, instead of through `step`: the loop kernel (`s = (s + i * i) % 1000003`) 117.5 -> 90.7 ms (-23%, instructions -18%), sort 345.8M -> 326.2M instructions; other kernels' instruction counts unchanged. A float arm in `run_hot` itself was faster on the loop (-31%) but moved register allocation there (fib +4.5% instructions), rejected.
- Inline RegExp `proto_property` so the pristine-prototype checks on every exec/test/replace read the 24-byte Property out of registers instead of through a stack copy: an agent-style string-processing script 1,040M -> 1,013M cycles (-2.6%), a regex-heavy replace/split script 390M -> 362M cycles (-7%); kernel suite flat.
- perf(djs): a new RegExp takes the remembered shape of its `lastIndex`. `regexp::create` defined `lastIndex` with `define_own_property`, whose transition search starts from the root shape, the one with the most children (every object literal's first key), on every evaluation of a regex literal; the shape it lands on is now kept in `Heap::regexp_shape` (emptied by collections and compaction, like the other offset caches) and later RegExps adopt it directly (`adopt_shape`, shared with `new_object_from_entries_like`, which also uses the new `plain_props_shape`). `lines.filter(l => /TODO:/.test(l))` over 1,000 lines ×100 23.2→17.6 ms (QuickJS 29), the agent-like script 225→213M cycles (966→936M instructions); `lastIndex` keeps its attributes; strings kernel −1.7% instr, others unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365. (Also corrects the await benchmark's label in the frame-reuse entry below.)
- perf(djs): a generator or async function reuses its saved frame's array. Every `yield` and `await` allocated a new ValueArray for the frame and every resume dropped it; `generator_resume` now leaves the array in the FRAME slot and the next `suspend_frame` fills it again when it is big enough. A minor collection walks the whole old region, so an old array that now holds young values needs no barrier; completion still clears the slot, and the array is only the frame's size. `for (const v of g(1000))` ×100 9.86→9.30 ms (QuickJS 7.1), 100,000 sequential `await`s 8.6→7.85 ms (QuickJS 47), async function calls 17.5→17.1 ms; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): a values Array Iterator over an Array takes a short path in `iter_plan`. The general plan read the iterator's slots through `object_slot` and `object_class` (calls with range checks), its index as an f64, the Array's length through another slot read, and only then the element; `array_values_plan` checks the two classes in place, reads the three slots directly, takes an int32 index and lets `get_element_fast` bound it, and leaves everything else (keys, entries, strings, typed arrays, done, holes) to the general plan. It stays inside the out-of-line `iter_plan`: the same check inlined into the dispatch loop's `iter_next_hit` made for-of 30% faster but cost other code 2–7% in cycles (objects kernel +6.6%), and out of line there 8% in instructions. `for (const v of a)` over 1,000 numbers ×3,000 61.2→48.8 ms (−20% cycles; QuickJS 67), `o.x?.y ?? 0` in a for-of 15.7→14.3 ms; closures kernel −1.7% instr, others unchanged; a mutation/hole/subclass/patched-`next` script prints the same as QuickJS; test262 39,325/39,365.
- `nanocode hand --own-processes` runs every command in a process of its own (2026-11-12). Since psh became the shell, a hand runs a command that is only builtins and psh's utilities inside its own process (nanocode-psh-embedded), which shares the hand's memory and its fate: where memory is limited, `x=$(head -c 400000000 /dev/zero | tr '\0' x); echo ${#x} > hog.txt` ended the hand, not the command. Measured with the hand in a cgroup of 450 MB (`systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=450M -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p OOMPolicy=continue`, output/d1-background/harness.mjs with `--wrap`): by default the kernel killed the hand, and the brain's call ended after 0.19 s with "runner connection failed: … the dispatched operation has an unknown outcome". In the memory-limited microVM slot of an eval harness the same command ended after 30 s with "remote operation deadline elapsed; outcome unknown", where the hand released on 2026-11-06, which ran bash, answered "Process exited with code 137" after 2.5 s. A host that must keep its hand through whatever a command does, such as that harness, now starts it with `--own-processes`: the hand does not register the embedded shell, so every command goes to a psh process (a warm one where one waits), and the same command ends with exit code 137 after 0.19 s with the hand alive and answering. The default is unchanged. With the flag `cat /proc/self/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '` through exec_command names `nanocode psh-shell -lc …`, without it the hand's own command line. Not measured: what the flag costs a short command, a warm psh process instead of a thread of the hand. Commands: `cargo build --locked --offline --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --tool=exec_command --only=custom --cmd=COMMAND --wrap='systemd-run --user --scope -q -p MemoryMax=450M -p MemorySwapMax=0 -p OOMPolicy=continue' [--hand-args=--own-processes]`. Files: bin/nanocode/src/{cli,lib}.rs.
- perf(djs): indexOf and includes of a string over a dense Array compare lengths first. The dense search ran `strict_equals` on every element, which for two strings resolves both and checks width and hashes before the bytes; a string needle now skips non-strings and strings of another length with one read, and calls `str_eq` only for those of its length. `a.indexOf('s' + k)` + `a.includes('zz')` over 1,000 strings ×3,000 26.7→17.3 ms (QuickJS 22.9); results as before for mixed arrays, NaN, ropes and holes; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): for-of resumes a plain generator itself. `iter_next` on a Generator in START or SUSPENDED whose `next` is the original %GeneratorPrototype%.next (`plain_generator`; `GeneratorPrototypeNext` became an intrinsic for the check) resumes the generator's frame directly with a new continuation, `GenStep`, whose return address is the `iter_next` itself: a `yield` (state SUSPENDED) puts the value where the loop body reads it and jumps there, as the Array Iterator fast path does; a return completes the generator and gives `{value, done: true}`; a `yield*`'s raw inner result goes on as the call's result. The `next` and `GeneratorStep` builtin frames and the `{value, done}` object per step are gone. A throw out of the generator completes it on the way out (`gen_step_abort`), as GeneratorStep's catch did, and the caller's handlers and stack line are those of the `iter_next` (`is_retry`). `for (const v of g(1000))` ×100 35.6→10.4 ms (QuickJS 7.3); a 30-case script (yield*, return values, throw, finally, break, destructuring, spread, re-entry) prints the same as QuickJS; kernels unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): JSON.stringify's `Class::Date` holds the Date, not its time value. With an `f64` in it, `Result<Class, StringifyError>` was too big for registers and came back through memory, where the caller re-read the `Obj` and the array flag with a load spanning the callee's narrower stores (a forwarding stall on every value). `Date(Obj)` makes the class 8 bytes; `emit` reads the time value from the Date's slot, which nothing can change between the two. 10 stringifies of 20,000 seven-key records 57.2→50.5 ms (293.7→261.8M cycles for the script, 1,403.6→1,387.2M instructions; QuickJS ≈480 ms); the workerd compute cell's script 122.2→120.6M cycles; Dates serialize as before; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): JSON.parse's `key_colon` is inlined too. It took the key's token by value and returned the token after the colon through memory, the copy the lexer's inlining removed for values; for objects every member paid it. 10 parses of the 1.36 MB array of 20,000 five-key records 51.0→45.4 ms (270→245M cycles for the whole script, 1,297→1,248M instructions); the workerd compute cell's script 127.2→123.7M cycles; native djsrun +14 KB; test262 39,325/39,365.
- nanocode-websocket derives `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` with nanocode-digest's SHA-1, and its private copy goes (2026-11-12). crates/core/websocket/src/sha1.rs was written while nanocode-digest was not yet on master; `derive_accept_key` in handshake.rs now calls `nanocode_digest::Sha1::digest`, so the workspace has one SHA-1. Proven with output/websocket-sha1, which links the removed module beside nanocode-digest: 1,000,000 seeded inputs of 0 to 4,095 bytes, 0 differences (nanocode-digest is itself proven against sha1 0.11.0 in its own entry). `cargo metadata --locked` unchanged at 625 packages. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-websocket`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-websocket --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-tools-macros finds the caller's name for nanocode-tools from its Cargo.toml itself, and proc-macro-crate leaves the workspace's own crates with its use of toml_edit (2026-11-12). `#[tool]` asked proc-macro-crate 3.5.0's `crate_name` which of nanocode-tools, nanocode, nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-tool-runtime and the two backends the crate under compilation depends on and under which name; crates/core/tools-macros/src/manifest.rs does the same lookup (the package itself, or `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR`'s sanitized name in integration tests; then `dependencies` and `dev-dependencies` at the top and under each `target` table, a `package` rename, `workspace = true` resolved through the workspace manifest that `cargo locate-project --workspace` names when `CARGO` is set, the later entry winning, "-" turned to "_"), keeping one answer per process in a `OnceLock` checked against both manifests' modification times where proc-macro-crate kept a `Mutex`ed map; crates/core/tools-macros/src/toml.rs is the TOML reader it needs (tables, dotted and quoted keys, array tables, basic, literal and multi-line strings with escapes, arrays, inline tables, booleans and other scalars, duplicate keys and repeated headers refused), with a 128-level bound on nested values. proc-macro-crate stays in the lock through borsh-derive and zbus's macros. Proven with output/manifest-equal against proc-macro-crate 3.5.0: every Cargo.toml in the registry cache (1,177) and in this repository (82) with `CARGO` unset, 187,198 lookups of every word in each manifest (9,430 found), and the repository's manifests again with `CARGO` set so the workspace manifest comes from `cargo locate-project`, 397 lookups (375 found), with `CARGO_TARGET_TMPDIR` set for every 17th manifest, 0 differences; and output/tool-macro-check, which depends on nanocode-tools renamed to `renamed_tools`, expands `#[renamed_tools::tool]` and prints the tool's definition. `cargo metadata --locked` unchanged at 669 packages. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-tools-macros`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-tools`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-mcp compares a PKCE challenge in constant time itself, and subtle leaves the workspace's own crates (2026-11-12). `Pkce::verifies` used subtle 2.6.1's slice `ct_eq`; `constant_time_equal` in crates/core/mcp/src/oauth.rs does what that did: unequal lengths are unequal at once (subtle's slice comparison does the same, and the challenge's length is public), otherwise every byte pair is XORed into one accumulator through `std::hint::black_box` so the loop cannot stop early, and the result is whether it stayed zero. subtle stays in the lock through rustls and other packages. Proven with output/subtle-equal against subtle 2.6.1: 5,000,000 seeded pairs of up to 64 bytes over a four-byte alphabet (equal, one flipped bit, one extra byte, unrelated), 1,269,483 of them equal, 0 differences. `cargo metadata --locked` unchanged at 669 packages. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-mcp`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-mcp --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
