It is httpdate 1.0.3's `parse_http_date`, read from its source: input that is not all ASCII is rejected, `str::trim` whitespace (vertical tab and form feed included) is removed, then IMF-fixdate (29 bytes), RFC 850 (a full weekday name, `, `, then 22 bytes, two-digit years below 70 in the 2000s and the rest in the 1900s, the byte between year and hour unchecked as httpdate leaves it) and asctime (24 bytes, the day as ` 6` or `06`) are tried in that order, with case-sensitive names and `GMT`; a date is kept only if its seconds, minutes and hours are in range, its year is 1970 to 9999, its day exists in its month (leap years by the Gregorian rule) and its weekday is the one the date falls on, which is what httpdate's round trip through `SystemTime` checks; the result is `UNIX_EPOCH` plus the seconds. `HttpDateError` carries httpdate's message. httpdate's formatter has no caller, so there is none. - nanocode-digest (crates/core/digest) hashes SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, BLAKE3 and XXH64 from scratch, and sha1, sha2, blake3 and xxhash-rust leave every nanocode crate (2026-11-12). The crate has no dependencies and forbids unsafe code: src/sha1.rs, src/sha256.rs (SHA-224 and SHA-256) and src/sha512.rs (SHA-384 and SHA-512) follow FIPS 180-4 with its constant tables, compress whole 64- and 128-byte blocks straight from the input slice (`as_chunks`, no copy) with every round unrolled and the message schedule computed inline (src/unroll.rs), and share src/pending.rs for the partial block and the length padding; src/blake3.rs follows the BLAKE3 spec for the keyless hash: the message schedule is computed at compile time from the spec's permutation, the incremental `Blake3` compresses 64-byte blocks straight from the input and keeps chaining values on a fixed stack of 54 levels (64 bits of input length less the 10 of a 1,024-byte chunk), and a one-shot `blake3` of at most one chunk skips the stack; src/xxh64.rs is the XXH64 spec. The API is what callers used: `Sha1`..`Sha512` with `new`, `update`, `finalize` (taking `&self`, so a hasher held in a struct can be read) and `digest`, each returning a byte array (so `.into()` after `digest` and `finalize` went away), and `OUTPUT_BYTES` where `Sha256::output_size()` was; `blake3`, `Blake3` (`update` chains as blake3's did), `Hash` (Copy, Eq without an early exit as blake3's, Hash, `as_bytes`, `to_hex`, Display and Debug as blake3 prints them) and `Hex` (`as_str`, Display) for blake3's `ArrayString`; `BLAKE3_OUTPUT_BYTES` for `blake3::OUT_LEN`; `xxh64(bytes, seed)`. Switched: store-jsonl, mcp-tools, chatgpt-extension, code-mode, code-mode-engine (WebCrypto's SHA-1/256/384/512 digest), tool-host, agent, backend-codex, codex client, claude client (its kept `Hash`/`Blake3` values and XXH64 seeds), home, image, audio, mcp and durability-core (imports and calls only). What is not equal: a message past FIPS 180-4's 2^64 bits (2^128 for SHA-512) or past BLAKE3's 2^64 chunks panics where the upstream crates wrap; the upstream crates pick SIMD and SHA-NI at run time and ours is portable. Proven with output/digest-equal, which links sha1 0.11.0, sha2 0.11.0, blake3 1.8.7 and xxhash-rust 0.8.19 (the lock's versions) beside nanocode-digest: the FIPS 180-4 examples (`abc`, the 448- and 896-bit messages, a million `a`, the empty message) against their published digests, BLAKE3's 35 test_vectors.json lengths (0 to 102,400, the repeating 0..250 input) one-shot, byte by byte and in 64 random splits each, and 3,000,000 seeded random inputs (lengths up to 20,000, 30% of them within 4 bytes of a multiple of 32, 64, 128 or 1,024, some of one repeated byte, 0 and random seeds for XXH64) hashed one-shot and in up to 200 random `update` pieces, with a mid-stream `finalize` and a clone, and BLAKE3's hex, Display and Debug compared: 57,124,494 checks, 0 differences. Throughput on the hosted Hand (AMD EPYC 9255, CPU time of the thread, three interleaved rounds, upstream against ours, MB/s, 64 B / 1 KiB / 1 MiB): against the soft backends (`--cfg sha2_backend="soft" --cfg sha1_backend="soft"`) SHA-1 ~450/~940/~960 against ~475/~955/~965, SHA-256 ~195/~380/~470 against ~215/~400/~440, SHA-512 ~375/~585/~705 against ~340/~570/~710, so even; against the default build, where sha2 and sha1 take SHA-NI on this CPU, SHA-256 is ~3.7x faster upstream (~845/~1,800/~2,010 against ~230/~405/~510) and SHA-1 ~2x, while sha2's SHA-512 (AVX2) is even with ours; BLAKE3 ~700/~735/~9,500 upstream against ~695/~845/~800 ours, so even up to a chunk and ~12x slower on 1 MiB, where blake3 hashes chunks in parallel with AVX-512 (the largest callers hash request bodies of tens to hundreds of KiB, under a millisecond each); XXH64 even (~8,200/~19,600/~21,700 against ~7,900/~20,100/~20,400). `cargo metadata --locked` 677 to 676 packages: blake3 and xxhash-rust leave and nanocode-digest joins; sha1 (tungstenite) and sha2 0.10.9 and 0.11.0 (sqlx, postgres-protocol, scrypt and the crates/patches psh and RustPython crates, by their own pins) stay in the lock. - A host sets how long a cell runs before it yields when its call names no `yield_time_ms` (2026-11-12). exec waited `INITIAL_YIELD` and wait `DEFAULT_WAIT_YIELD`, the 10 s of the protocol's tool descriptions, and no host could change either: an eval host whose tasks build for minutes got "Script running" and one more model request for every 10 s of every build from a model that named no yield. `CodeModeRuntime::set_default_yield` replaces both for that runtime. A host reaches it through `ToolsBuilder::cell_yield` (`LocalCells::default_yield` for local cells), and `nanocode hand --cell-yield-ms MS` sets it for a hand. - A hand that ends on SIGINT, or because its brain ended it, leaves a reader for what its commands left running, and the reader reaps (2026-11-12). 43e077ff3 made a hand stopped with SIGTERM become `nanocode read-outputs`; a hand ended with Ctrl-C, or one whose run returned (the brain revoked it, another hand took its name), still exited with the read ends of those outputs, so a server left with `&` stayed alive and answered nothing. Decided for each end. SIGTERM keeps the exec in place: the pid stays the stopper's to watch, and sessions still running go on. SIGINT and an end by the brain start `read-outputs` as a process of its own (`leave_reader`: its own process group, the null device as its stdio) and then end as before: whoever started the hand gets the terminal or the exit status back, commands still running end with the hand as they did (their guards stop their groups when the runtime stops), and what finished commands left behind keeps a reader. `read-outputs` also waits for the children it inherited (a thread in `wait` until none is left), so a shell that ends under it does not stay a zombie until the reader exits. Measured with output/d1-background/harness.mjs: after `--signal=SIGINT`, `python3 -m http.server PORT &` left by a Bash call and by an exec_command call answered 200 before and 200 after (before the change 200, then curl's 52), `nohup` and plain `&` sleeps and a `while` loop stayed, and a session still running was stopped as before; after SIGTERM the reader had 1 child and no zombie where it had 2 children, 1 a zombie. Not run: an end by Revoked or Replaced, which takes the same `leave_reader` call as SIGINT, and macOS. `cargo clippy --locked --offline -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-process` reports nothing, for this and for 43e077ff3's handover. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-process`; `cargo build --locked --offline --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --loader=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --tool=Bash --signal=SIGINT --only=server-amp-holds-pipes,…`. - A background job that is not one program runs in a forked copy of the shell and outlives it, as in bash (2026-11-12). psh ran `( … ) &`, `{ …; } &`, `while …; done &`, a function, a builtin and its own utilities (`sleep 300 &`, `tail -f log &`) as a task of the shell's own process: the job ended when the script did, its `$!` was a number no process has, and a later command could not signal it; bash forks for each of these, and agents write exactly these forms. On a host whose shell is its own process (`Host::forks`: the standalone psh on Linux, through `UnixConfig::fork_jobs`; off for embedders, on Windows and wasm, and on macOS until it is run there) `run_background` now forks. A job that is not one simple command forks when its task first runs. A job that is one simple command expands its words first: a program runs as the job's process as before, now also where a utility of psh has its name and `PATH` has the program (`sleep`, `tail`: the process has the program's name and pid, as under bash); a function, a builtin, a shell psh runs itself (`bash script.sh &`) or a utility without a program forks. The parent waits for the copy as for any external, so `$!` is its pid and `wait`, `kill %1`, `jobs`, `disown` and the release at the script's end need nothing new. In the copy the job's vproc is the shell: it takes the process's signals, ignores INT and QUIT as bash's jobs do without job control, has `$BASHPID`, and the process ends with the job's status or by the signal that ended it; the parent's other tasks are forgotten, not dropped (a dropped task would signal the parent's externals). `( … ) &` runs its list in the job's own vproc, as bash forks once for it. A job with a descriptor that is a pipe between two vprocs of the same shell (inside `$( … )` or a pipeline of builtins) stays a task as before, since a copy would not share that pipe. Forking a process that has threads: the host holds what its threads share across the fork (`Host::prepare_fork`: the waiter pool, the escalation count, the readiness registrations and the timers; the engine then holds its wake queue and the embedder's waker) and the copy starts with them empty, with a readiness thread, a signal pipe and a signal watcher of its own. The helper threads of psh-os and the workers of blocking utilities (`Host::thread`) are now threads of the system's own instead of std's: std keeps a table of its threads behind a lock that a starting and an ending thread take, and a copy forked while a waiter thread held it could never start a thread (found by running a script of five jobs again and again: about one copy in 150 hung on that lock). A second hang at about the same rate was the copy's own: a job that ended within the scheduler round in which it forked left the copy parked, since that round still waited for the parent's script; `Shell::step` now leaves the round as soon as the process is a copy. After both, 3,000 runs in a row of a script with six jobs (a subshell with a pipeline of programs, a brace group, a function, `while read …; done < <(seq 20)`, a utility and a program, `wait`, and a job started after it) ended without a hang and with every job's output (debug build, Linux 6.18, glibc 2.39). Measured through a hand started the way an eval slot starts it (the dynamic loader, `nanocode hand --listen`, a scripted Responses endpoint, `nanocode exec --runner-connect`: `output/d1-background/harness.mjs`, and `reference.py` for the same commands under bash 5.2 on pipes and on a terminal), counting what is alive, or has had its effect, at the end of the turn: Bash 12 of 20 ways to leave a job before (130e7f0dc) and 20 of 20 after, bash 20 of 20; exec_command 13 of 21 before, 21 of 21 after, bash 21 of 21; exec_command with `tty: true` 6 of 21 before and after, bash 2 of 21 (on a terminal a job in the shell's group is hung up when the shell exits, under psh as under bash; psh's `nohup`, `setsid` and `disown` jobs get a session at once and stay, where bash's `nohup x &` loses the race with the hangup). The eight that were dead and are alive: `sleep N &`, `tail -f f &`, `(/bin/sleep 1.5; touch f) &`, `(sleep 1.5; touch f) &`, `{ sleep 1.5; touch f; } &`, `f() { sleep 1.5; touch f; }; f &`, `while true; do date > f; sleep 0.2; done &`, `seq 1 40 | while read n; do echo $n > f; sleep 0.2; done &`. No call took longer than its command (Bash at most 323 ms, for a command that sleeps 0.3 s). The standalone psh against bash on 13 scripts (`wait $!` giving a subshell's status 7, `kill %1` giving 143, a later `kill $(cat pid)` stopping a loop, a shell variable read by the job, `bash -c … &`, `true & wait`, `cd /tmp &`): the same files and statuses, psh back in 20 to 40 ms where the script does not wait. The tests of psh, psh-engine and psh-os pass (15, 136, 39), and psh and psh-os check for x86_64-pc-windows-gnu and aarch64-apple-darwin; neither was run there. Not like bash still: on macOS and Windows such a job stays a task and ends with the script; so does a job inside `$( … )` or a pipeline of builtins; the copy has every descriptor the process had open at the fork, also another vproc's private pipe end if one existed at that instant, where bash's copy has the shell's own only; `ps` shows the copy under the shell's command line; rg's own search threads are std's, so a fork in the instant one of them ends could still leave a copy unable to run a parallel rg (not seen). Commands: `cargo build --locked -p psh --bin psh`; `cargo test --locked -p psh-engine -p psh-os -p psh`; `cargo check --locked --lib -p psh-engine --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`; `cargo build --locked --offline --release -p nanocode-cli --bin nanocode`; `node harness.mjs --hand=BIN --loader=/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --tool=Bash|exec_command|exec_command_tty`; `python3 reference.py cases.json pipes|tty DIR`. - Our own RFC 6455 WebSocket, crates/core/websocket (nanocode-websocket, native only like nanocode-tls), does what tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite 0.30 did for the Codex Responses socket and the tool-runtime remote and attachment sockets, and both leave (2026-11-12). It keeps their shape so call sites changed only paths: `WebSocketStream` (futures `Stream`/`Sink`, inherent `close`), `client_async_with_config`, `client_async_tls_with_config`, `connect_async_tls_with_config`, `accept_hdr_async(_with_config)` with the same `server::Callback`/`ErrorResponse` rejections, `MaybeTlsStream`, `Connector`, `Message`, `CloseFrame`, `CloseCode`, `Error` with tungstenite's `Display` texts for every variant that can occur, and http 1's `Request`/`Response`. protocol.rs is tungstenite's state machine (Active, ClosedByUs, ClosedByPeer, CloseAcknowledged, Terminated; the queued pong/close reply and when it is flushed; the server ending after its close reply; reset and send-after-close errors) over a `std::io` adapter that turns `Pending` into `WouldBlock`, with tokio-tungstenite's waker proxy so a split reader and writer both wake; frame.rs parses and writes headers (reserved opcodes rejected once the header is complete, as before), masks client frames with keys drawn 64 at a time from one getrandom call and unmasks in 8-byte words without unsafe; message.rs reassembles fragments with the same incremental UTF-8 check and the same error strings (`incomplete string: Incomplete { buffer: .., buffer_len: .. }`, the lossy invalid sequence); handshake.rs writes the request exactly as tungstenite (Host, Connection, Upgrade, Sec-WebSocket-Version, Sec-WebSocket-Key, then caller headers with `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` and `Origin` recased), parses with httparse (124 headers, 4 KiB reads, the 64 KiB / 512-read attack bounds) and checks the response or request the same way; sha1.rs is a 70-line SHA-1 for Sec-WebSocket-Accept (agent 7 had no SHA-1 crate to share; sha1 stays in the graph through nanocode-audio). Limits are tungstenite's defaults where callers used defaults (64 MiB message, 16 MiB frame, 128 KiB read buffer and write threshold, masked client frames required) and the remote runner's own policy where it set them (`WebSocketConfig::frame_bytes_max`, `message_bytes_max`, `read_buffer_bytes`). Codex keeps its permessage-deflate as it was: the same offer header, `InflateStream` inflating server frames below the socket, and requests sent as one rsv1 text `Frame`. What is not equal: payloads are `Vec<u8>` and `Utf8Bytes` holds a `String` (no unsafe, so no Bytes-backed str); a frame larger than the bytes buffered is read straight into its own buffer instead of through the read buffer (same frames, fewer copies); a getrandom failure is `Error::Io` where rand panicked; a handshake write of 0 bytes is tokio's `WriteZero` error where tungstenite asserted; `Connector` is no longer optional (tool-runtime passes `Connector::Plain` for ws:// where it passed `None`; tungstenite's `None` with wss:// built an empty root store, which no caller reached); unreachable variants are gone (`WriteBufferFull`, unknown control/data opcodes, `accept_unmasked_frames`); `MessageTooLong.size` is u64; `connect_async` in nanocode-backend-codex-client keeps its signature over the new types. output/ws-compare links tokio-tungstenite and tungstenite =0.30.0 beside the new crate and compares them over a scripted stream that splits input at random points and returns random partial writes and `Pending`: sha1 against the sha1 crate on 200,000 inputs and 100,000 client keys (0 differences); 20,000 server handshakes (methods, versions, Connection/Upgrade/version/key variants, bearer callback with 401 and 200 rejections, junk after the request, truncation) comparing response bytes and outcome: 80,000 checks, 0 differences; 20,000 sessions in both roles of random frame streams (fragmented text and binary, UTF-8 split across fragments, invalid and incomplete UTF-8, pings to 140 bytes, fragmented control frames, close codes allowed and not with valid and invalid reasons, 1-byte closes, stray continuations, reserved opcodes and bits, wrong masking, non-minimal lengths, frames to 200 KB, small limits, truncation) interleaved with sends to 2.2 MB, feeds, flushes, pings, pongs, rsv1 frames, closes and sink closes: with non-blocking I/O 60,000 checks and 0 differences (61,929 messages and 87,169 errors observed), with blocking I/O 60,000 checks and 4 differences, all in the server role at 40 % `Pending`, where tungstenite itself decides by whether a write would block (a queued pong or close reply goes out before or after the next frame, and the server reaches Terminated only once its close reply is written, so a later read reports `Remote sent after having closed` or `Sending after closing` instead of the end or `Trying to work with closed connection`); Throughput on the hosted Hand (TCP loopback, interleaved, 7 rounds, medians): receiving 1 KiB text 0.151 s against 0.171 s for 200,000 messages (1,359 against 1,197 MB/s), 1 MiB 0.232 against 0.236 s for 400; sending 1 MiB 0.335 against 0.353 s; sending 1 KiB 0.608 against 0.500 s end to end, while the same client path into a discarding stream encodes 310 to 373 ns per message against 329 to 416, so the gap is not in our framing (the Responses socket sends one request per turn). What differs: the narrower API above; `Recompositions` is not `Clone`, `Display` or `FusedIterator` (unused); the buffers are `Vec`s that allocate on the first decomposed or reordered character rather than past four inline entries; a run of non-starters is held whole as before, bounded by the input. Checks: `cargo check --locked --lib -p unicode-normalization` natively and with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo clippy --locked -p unicode-normalization` (both targets, clean), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude-client` natively and for wasm32, `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-backend-claude-client` (clean), `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql`, `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`, `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs`.
- nix leaves the workspace's crates: their system calls go through safe wrappers in `nanocode_platform::unix` (2026-11-12). crates/core/platform/src/unix.rs is a module of nanocode-platform, whose lints already deny rather than forbid unsafe code for its CoreFoundation call, so the crates that forbid unsafe code (nanocode-home, nanocode-store-jsonl, nanocode-tool-runtime, nanocode-backend-claude-tools, nanocode-cli, the nanocode example runner) keep forbidding it and call `user_id`, `user_entry` (`getpwuid_r` from `_SC_GETPW_R_SIZE_MAX` or 16,384 bytes, doubling on `ERANGE` up to 1,048,576 bytes, nix 0.31.3's bounds; the name decoded lossily, home and shell as raw bytes, as nix did), `system_release` (`uname` sysname and release up to the first zero byte), `host_name` (a 256-byte buffer forced to end in zero, as nix's `gethostname`), `signal_process`, `probe_process` (`kill` with 0), `signal_group`, `process_group`, `sync_file` (`fsync`, not std's `F_FULLFSYNC` on macOS), `barrier_sync_file` (`F_BARRIERFSYNC` on Apple), `available_bytes` (`statvfs` `f_bavail * f_frsize`, saturating; a path with a zero byte is `EINVAL` as nix's `NixPath` made it), `redirect_output` (`dup2` onto stdout and stderr), `thread_cpu_time` (`CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`) and on Linux `forbid_core_dumps` (`PR_SET_DUMPABLE` 0). nanocode-process, which allows unsafe code in its `pre_exec` hook, resets the session signals there with `libc::signal` itself and signals its process groups through the same wrappers; signals and errno values are libc's constants, and errors stay `io::Error`s from the same OS codes nix converted. Not equal: an error message that printed nix's `Errno` (`EINVAL: Invalid argument`) now prints io::Error's (`Invalid argument (os error 22)`), only for `gethostname` in the hand's host name and `prctl` in the example runner, neither of which fails on a working system. Proven with output/nix-equal, linking nix 0.31.3 beside nanocode-platform on the hosted Hand: every uid in /etc/passwd and 20,000 seeded random uids plus 0, 65534, `u32::MAX` and others (39 found, the rest absent), uname, the host name, `statvfs` of 11 paths including /proc, missing, relative, empty and a zero byte, `kill`/`killpg` probes of our pid, pid 1, missing and negative pids (ESRCH and EPERM), `fsync`, and 100,000 thread CPU readings bracketed by nix's: 120,062 checks, 0 differences. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 710 packages: nix 0.31.3 remains through rustpython-host_env and rustyline and nix 0.29.0 through mac_address (python's scope, told), after which nix, memoffset and cfg_aliases leave too. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked` on nanocode-platform, nanocode-process, nanocode-store-jsonl, nanocode-tool-runtime, nanocode-backend-claude-tools, nanocode-home, nanocode-cli and `-p nanocode --examples` (only the existing warnings).
- The workspace's async traits are written out as the boxed futures `async_trait` 0.1.89 expanded them to, and async-trait leaves the workspace's crates (2026-11-12). `output/asynctrait/conv.py` rewrote every `#[async_trait]` trait and impl (31 files: `Tool` impls, `DynamicToolProvider`, `McpOAuthStore`, `BearerSource`, `McpPaymentProvider`, `McpPaymentManagement`, `McpPendingPayment`, `ProcessRouteStore`, `SpawnRouter`, `ComputerExecutor` and their implementations) into the signature the macro generated: the same lifetime parameters (`'life0` for the receiver, one per elided reference or `'_`, then `'async_trait`), the same `where` bounds (`'lifeN: 'async_trait`, `Self: 'async_trait`, plus `Sync` or `Send` on a trait's default methods exactly where the macro added them), the same `Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = R> + Send + 'async_trait>>` (or without `Send` under `?Send`), and a body of `Box::pin(async move { let output: R = { body }; output })`, the macro's own typing of the body. `nanocode_tool_contracts::ToolCallFuture` (`Send` on native, not on WASM, as `Tool` already declares) is the return type of `Tool` impls that build for both, which the `#[tool]` macro in nanocode-tools-macros now emits instead of `#[async_trait]`, and `nanocode_tools::__private` exports it instead of re-exporting `async_trait`; `SpawnRouter` and `BearerSource` use private `BoxFuture`/`LocalBoxFuture` aliases for the same reason, and `McpOAuthStore` and the payment traits name `futures_util::future::BoxFuture` (the same type) to keep clippy's type-complexity lint quiet where the macro had silenced it. Because every trait keeps the macro's exact shape, implementors outside the repository are unaffected: tempoxyz/pyramid-core implements `Tool` with the expanded signature (`fn execute<'life0, 'life1, 'async_trait>(...)`) and still compiles unchanged, and an impl written with `#[async_trait]` still matches every trait here. One difference: the macro moved every by-value argument into the future (`let x = x;`), while `async move` captures only the arguments the body uses, so an unused by-value argument (`_context: ToolContext<'_>`, `_input: ToolInput` in default `recover`) is now dropped when the call returns instead of when the future finishes; all of them are borrowed views or plain data with no `Drop` side effect, so nothing observable changes. Behaviour is otherwise identical by construction (same futures, same boxing, same `Send` bounds), so there is no harness beyond the build. `cargo metadata --locked` stays at 710 packages: async-trait remains in the graph through zbus (Linux accessibility, nanocode-computer), so this removes its proc-macro build from every other crate rather than a package. Checks: `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli` and `cargo clippy --locked` on the 16 crates touched (only the existing otlp.rs, python and `fetch_update` warnings).

- perf(djs): a computed read with a string key goes through the megamorphic cache. `o[k]` has no cache slot of its own, so every read of a string key interned it and looked it up. Now the slow `GetElem`/`GetElem2` path (`lookup_elem`) writes an own or prototype data property it finds into `mega_ic` (`mega_fill`, with `own_words` shared with `ic_own_fill`), and the hot loop's element case, for a string key whose atom `memo_atom` already knows, tries that slot before declining (`keyed_hit`, out of line so the dispatch loop's code is unchanged; slots check their key and shape as named sites' do). `o[ks[j]]` over 50 keys ×20k 58.2→44.7 ms (qjs 41.4), groupBy `reduce` with `acc[x.g] ??= []` 37.2→28.4 ms (qjs 28.8), `ks.forEach(k => n += o[k])` 67.2→57.5 ms, `Object.keys(o).forEach(...)` 90.5→82.5 ms; kernels unchanged (±0.1% instr); a getter/prototype/proxy/typed-array/String/array/delete/freeze script prints the same as QuickJS; test262 39,325/39,365.
- fix(djs): megamorphic cache slots check their key. A get slot of a shape-mode receiver is a shape and a value slot, which only a site's own slot (whose key is fixed) can trust: in the shared `mega_ic`, two keys whose hashes meet in one slot for the same shape and prototype read each other's values (24 keys on 6 shapes through `new Function('o', 'return o.' + k)` sites, ×30: 673 wrong reads; dictionary entries were safe since `data_at` checks the key). The slot's last word, unused by get slots, now holds the key (`MEGA_KEY`), written with the slot and compared before `get_hit`. dispatch kernel 1,783.3→1,787.3M instr (+0.2%), others unchanged; the script reads 0 wrong values; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): the atom memo holds 2,048 strings and is allocated on first intern. 256 slots missed whenever a loop read keys from more distinct string cells than that, as `acc[x.g]` over 1,000 records does; 4,096 (32 KB, all of L1) cost 10% in cycles on `o[k]` loops over 50 keys, and an inline array would put the table in `Heap::over`'s frame, so it is a `Vec` like `mega_ic`, emptied in place. Against the 256 slots: `a.reduce((acc, x) => { (acc[x.g] ??= []).push(x.v); return acc }, {})` over 1,000 records ×300 45.4→37.4 ms (qjs 30.5), `o[ks[j]]` 62.5→57.4 ms, `ks.forEach(k => n += o[k])` 73.4→68.4 ms; kernels unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365.
- perf(djs): interning remembers the atoms of the last strings it saw. `Heap::intern` and `find_string_atom_of` first look in `atom_memo`, 256 slots of string cell → atom indexed by a Fibonacci hash of the offset, filled on every intern and emptied whenever cells move or the arena shrinks (collections, compaction, `release_top`; a restored image starts a fresh heap). A computed key read with strings that are already keys (`o[k]` over `Object.keys(o)`, `for in` bodies, `acc[x.g]`) skipped the array-index parse, flatten check, hash and probe. `o[ks[j]]` over 50 keys ×20k 74.5→62.5 ms (qjs 47.6), `Object.keys(o).forEach(k => n += o[k])` 112.8→102.5 ms, trycatch kernel 1,111.6→1,088.6M instr; other kernels unchanged; test262 39,325/39,365.
- nanocode-tui highlights code with its own syntect port and its own Oniguruma-compatible regex engine, and syntect leaves with onig, onig_sys, bincode, fnv and pkg-config (2026-11-12, DEPENDENCIES.md's syntect row). crates/tui/src/highlight/syntaxes.rs is generated by output/syntect-gen from the same default newlines dump `SyntaxSet::load_defaults_newlines` read (75 syntaxes, 4,460 linked contexts, 8,156 match patterns, 3,639 regex sources, 4,556 scopes over 1,391 atoms; includes resolved by syntect's linker, the two it left unresolved in MATLAB skipped as its `MatchIter` skips them; `first_line_match` and `hidden` are not emitted because nothing in nanocode reads them); grammar.rs holds the data types, the lazily compiled regexes (one `OnceLock` per source, like syntect) and the per-context flattened pattern lists, parser.rs ports `ParseState::parse_line` (earliest match over prototypes, the context and its includes, syntect's tie-breaking, per-line search cache, non-consuming push and pop loop protection, the 100-deep push limit, with_prototype, captures-ordered ops, clear_scopes and restore, backreference substitution escaped as regex-syntax's `escape` did) and highlighter.rs ports `Highlighter`, `HighlightState` and `HighlightIterator` for the eight single-scope theme rules (scores `len * 2^(3 * depth)` as f64, the default style when the style stack underflows, the line cut short where a restore finds nothing cleared). regex.rs and regex/ are an Oniguruma 6.9.10 work-alike for `Syntax::default()` (the Oniguruma syntax, not Ruby's: `(?m)` is dot-all, `(?s)` is an error) with `REGEX_OPTION_CAPTURE_GROUP`: a parser that follows regparse.c token by token (option-only groups take the rest of the alternation, `\1`-`\9` are always backreferences, invalid intervals are literals, `{n,m}` with n>m is possessive, nested quantifier reduction, string splitting before a quantifier, class set operations and nested negation), the regcomp.c tuning that changes results (adjacent string merging, ignore-case unravelling of strings and classes with multi-character case folds, look-behind length checks, division of different-length alternatives and reduction of leading quantifiers, empty checks, quantifier expansion limits, automatic possessification, head-exact and peek-next pushes) and a backtracking machine with onig's stack discipline (marks, cut-to-mark voiding, capture restore, repeat counters, `\b` with onig's Latin-1 word table that counts ² ³ ¹ ¼ ½ ¾ as word characters for `\w` and `\b` but not for `[\w]`); regex/unicode.rs is generated by output/unicode-gen from UCD 16.0.0 (onig 6.9.10's version). Search bounds backtracking with `RETRY_LIMIT_IN_MATCH` (10,000,000 per start position, onig's `DEFAULT_RETRY_LIMIT_IN_MATCH`) and returns `SearchError::RetryLimitInMatch`; the parser treats that error as no match at that position, exactly as syntect's regex wrapper treated onig's retry-limit error, because a line hitting it in real Rust windows-sys code and Makefiles would otherwise lose its highlighting; a substituted backreference regex that fails to compile is `ParseError::Regex` (syntect panicked) and the line falls back to `code_style`. Equality: output/regex-harness compares every regex source against onig 6.5.3 (all 3,639 compile or fail alike) over corpus lines of 75 extensions, seeded random strings with non-ASCII, case-fold and ligature characters, and mutations of matching lines, at three start offsets each: three seeds of 26,336,760, 26,342,412 and 10,936,584 searches, every capture group compared, 0 differences once onig's and our retry-limit errors count as no match (the 35 raw differences are both sides failing on the same line, or our required-byte check returning no match where onig spends its 10,000,000 retries; syntect saw no match in both). output/e2e-harness runs `highlight::line` from master (syntect) and from this commit over real files of the 33 syntaxes that have files on this Hand (repository, ~/.cargo/registry/src, /usr/share, /usr/include, /usr/lib/python3) plus 700-line corpus documents for each of the 75 syntaxes, carrying state across lines and resuming through `state()`/`from_state` with a half line in between as markdown.rs does, plus line-edit, line-shuffle and random-line mutations: two seeds of 762 documents and 381,470 lines with 1 difference and 2,232 documents and 844,524 lines with 0 differences, and syntax_for_token and syntax_for_path over 82,850 names, extensions, paths and random strings with 0 differences. The one difference is not equal on purpose: Makefile's nested-parenthesis look-ahead (the "level 0 ... level 4" pattern, also in Rust) takes about 3 s per search on a corpus line in both engines, onig gives up at its 10,000,000th retry and we finish the search under it with a match, because our retry count is close to but not identical with onig's bytecode (its optimizer merges and skips pushes we do not), so lines that drive a pattern to within a few percent of the limit can highlight differently. Speed, from output/e2e-harness's bench on the shared Hand at load 15 to 23, old and new interleaved: highlighting 156 real files of 33 syntaxes (46,166 lines, 1.4 MB) took five rounds at 9,992 to 21,911 lines/s before and 21,102 to 45,972 after (2.0 to 3.1x); first use (assets, theme, the Rust lookup and one highlighted line in a fresh process, 15 runs each) has a median of 5,429 us before and 3,730 us after; compiling all 3,639 regex sources takes 278 to 298 ms against onig's 372 to 376 ms; searches that run into the retry limit are about 1.5x slower than onig's (regex-harness totals 61.5 s against 42.2 s, dominated by them). `cargo metadata --locked` 645 to 639 packages (710 to 704 on the master it was written against); the port uses the terminal layer's `ui` styles and the Unicode 17 width and grapheme functions where it was written against ratatui and unicode-width. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-tui` (no warnings) and `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli`.
- nanocode-tui measures display width and finds grapheme clusters with its own Unicode 17.0.0 tables, and unicode-width and unicode-segmentation leave nanocode-tui and nc-lite (2026-11-12). `nanocode_tui::unicode` (crates/tui/src/unicode.rs) has `width(&str)` for unicode-width 0.2.2's `UnicodeWidthStr::width`, `char_width(char)` for `UnicodeWidthChar::width`, and `graphemes(&str)` and `grapheme_indices(&str)` for unicode-segmentation 1.13.3's `graphemes(true)` and `grapheme_indices(true)` (double-ended, `Clone`, the same `size_hint`); every caller in crates/tui (composer, diff, effort, format, highlight, keybindings, markdown, picker, queue, transcript) and nc-lite's tui.rs uses them, nc-lite through a new path dependency on nanocode-tui. Width walks the text from its end as unicode-width does, through one enum of what follows the character (`Following`: a line feed, emoji presentation, modifier, ZWJ, keycap, tag-flag and regional indicator sequences, variation selectors 1 to 3, 15 and 16, and the Arabic lam-alef, Hebrew, Buginese, Tifinagh, Lisu, Old Turkic, Khmer coeng and Kirat Rai ligatures, whose leftover selector bits are three flags); an ASCII text is its length less its CR LF pairs and an ASCII run inside other text is measured at once. Clusters are UAX #29 with GB9c conjunct linkers, GB11 and GB12/13: forward with a context restarted at each cluster (regional indicator parity, an emoji ZWJ run, a consonant and linker run), backward by deciding each boundary with scans back over the text, so the composer's `next_back` stays cheap. crates/tui/src/unicode/tables.rs is generated by output/unicode-gen/generate.py from the 17.0.0 UCD files (EastAsianWidth, LineBreak, DerivedGeneralCategory, DerivedCoreProperties with InCB, HangulSyllableType, PropList, UnicodeData, GraphemeBreakProperty, DerivedJoiningGroup, DerivedJoiningType, emoji-data, emoji-variation-sequences) under unicode-width's own width rules: one three-level trie (a 272-byte root, 24 middle blocks of 32, 184 leaves of 128; 24,592 bytes) maps each code point to one of 53 property records (width kind, grapheme category, InCB, and the emoji presentation, narrow text presentation, modifier base, joining-transparent and ligature-transparent flags), and running it again gives the same bytes. Proven with output/unicode-equal, which links unicode-width 0.2.2 and unicode-segmentation 1.13.3 beside a copy of the module: every scalar's char width, one-character width and clusters (1,112,064 each) and grapheme properties (3,336,192); unicode-width's width state machine against ours as a product automaton from the empty suffix, all 132 reachable state pairs times every scalar (146,792,448 transitions) give the same columns, so every string's width is equal, and no running total goes below 0 (Bellman-Ford over the 2,319 transitions), so the checked sum cannot fail; every ASCII string up to 3 characters (2,113,664); every scalar before and after each of 185 representatives (one or two per combination of our record, unicode-width's state and the old category and InCB, plus 140 chosen characters) 411,463,680; representative triples 6,331,625; quadruples of the 140 chosen characters 384,160,000; 40,000,000 seeded random strings biased toward emoji ZWJ sequences, skin tones, selectors after emoji bases, regional indicator runs, tags, keycaps, Hangul jamo and syllables, Indic consonants with linkers and InCB extends, prepends, spacing marks, CR LF, controls, CJK, European text and the ligature scripts, with each cluster's width (24,496,034) and 64-step interleavings of next and next_back (5,000,001); the 7,581 emoji-test, ZWJ and variation sequences; GraphemeBreakTest.txt's 766 cases (all also match the file's breaks); and the 55,683 UTF-8 files under ~/.cargo/registry/src and the repo (928 MB, whole and line by line, 3,776,345 lines, plus 859,392 mutated slices): 0 differences. Not carried over because nothing calls them: `width_cjk`, non-extended clusters, `Graphemes::as_str` and the chunked `GraphemeCursor`. Benchmark (output/unicode-equal `bench`, interleaved, best of 201 rounds on 64 KiB texts, hosted Hand at load 45 to 55), old against new: `width` of a whole ASCII text 1.41 against 75 GB/s, per ASCII line 0.92 against 2.70 GB/s, and European, CJK and emoji text 0.98 to 1.02x (1.44 against 1.43, 1.29 against 1.31, 0.88 against 0.89 GB/s); `graphemes().count()` 5.3x on ASCII (73 against 387 MB/s), 3.2x European, 1.9x CJK, 3.2x emoji; clusters with each one's width per line, as wrapping does, 2.45x, 2.07x, 1.62x, 2.34x; `next_back` per line 1.2 to 1.5x.
