Claude Code 2.1.318 does not avoid this: Bun's `process.title = "claude"` changes only comm, and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` of `claude -p "please optimise my-sql-query now"` still held the prompt on this machine. Once clap has copied the arguments, `arguments::hide` reads `startstack`, `arg_start` and `arg_end` from /proc/self/stat, points each argv entry at a leaked copy and zeroes the area after the program name through /proc/self/mem, with no unsafe code. std's `args_os()` reads argv on every call (reload and restart use it), so it still sees the arguments, while `/proc/self/cmdline` shows only the program. If the layout is not the one exec left (argc or an argv entry disagrees), it changes nothing and says why on stderr. A job's cancellation was already scoped: each Bash command runs in its own process group, and TaskStop kills that group. In output/parity-harness, a background `sleep 301 & sleep 302 & wait` (pgid 65747: the shell and both sleeps) was gone after TaskStop, and no other process was touched. Measured on 2026-11-12. With output/argv-harness, a binary built with the same module and given the prompt "Optimize my-sql-query so it runs faster": without hiding, `pkill -f my-sql-query` from its child ended it with SIGTERM; with hiding, `args_os` was unchanged, cmdline no longer held the string, pkill matched nothing and the binary exited 0. With output/parity-harness built with the module (`HIDE=1`, no wrapper process): the agent survived, and its Bash call reported exit 143, because its own shell was killed (that shell's argv holds the command, as Claude Code's `eval` shell's does); without the module the agent was terminated. Still exposed: a launcher whose own argv carries the prompt (a `timeout` or `bash -c` wrapper) is killed, and `timeout` passes the signal on, which also ended the agent in the harness. nc-lite is unchanged. Commands: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-cli` (no warnings in bin/nanocode; with `-D warnings` it stops on nanocode-subagents' existing `fetch_update` deprecations).
- `arguments::hide` also works when the dynamic loader starts nanocode (`ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 --library-path <dir> nanocode exec -- "..."`), as the Terminal-Bench harness does to run a binary against its own glibc in task images (2026-11-12). Run as a program, glibc's loader (2.39 here) removes its own arguments by moving argv down the stack and lowering argc there (`_dl_start_args_adjust`), so argc no longer equals the arguments in the area and master refused with "the argument area does not hold the arguments exec gave", leaving the prompt in /proc/<pid>/cmdline. hide now accepts an argc smaller than the area, takes the leading arguments as the loader's, checks that each remaining argv entry points at the matching later argument, and zeroes the whole area after the first one; any other disagreement still changes nothing and says why. Checked live on 2026-11-12 in the query-optimize task image (alexgshaw/query-optimize:20251031) with the toolkit's glibc 2.39 loader, a black-holed HTTPS proxy keeping each process waiting for its first request, and the prompt "please optimize my-sql-query zebra": master 168a133dd under the loader printed the warning, its cmdline held the prompt and `pgrep -f my-sql-query` matched it; this build under the loader showed only the loader's path and pgrep matched nothing; started directly, both builds showed only the program. `cargo build --release -p nanocode-cli` built with no warnings. The harness's own `bash -c "... > stdout 2> stderr"` wrapper still holds the prompt (bash forks rather than execs a command with redirections), so the rerun passes the instruction as `exec ... -- "$(cat file)"`.
- The Claude driver keeps a conversation's images in its requests up to the Messages API's per-request image limit, 100 for a model whose context window is 200,000 tokens and 600 otherwise (Anthropic's vision documentation), instead of `DEFAULT_INLINE_IMAGES` (8) (2026-11-12). Claude Code 2.1.318 never removes an image from a conversation before compaction, which replaces each image with `[image]`, and for a many-image error it tells the user to /compact. With eight, the ninth image turned the four oldest into omission text: that moved the request's changed prefix back to the first image and took away images the model had already seen. The audit's financial-document run read invoices 89 and 208 times against Claude Code's 17, even after the cache repair 723bc13d9, which this keeps (the floors still mark the first kept image and the latest image-bearing message). A host that sets an `ImageHistory` keeps its own window. Measured on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness, 12 image reads (24 requests; `./run.sh new default 12` against `./run.sh old8 8 12`, analyze.py comparing each request's messages with the previous request's, cache markers aside): with the new default every request repeats the previous messages byte for byte and the last one carries all 12 images; with `ImageHistory::new(8)` the request after the ninth read rewrites from message 2 and every later request carries 4 omission texts. Across a restart (ckpt.sh: three image turns, then `open_session` in a new process over the same JSONL home and two more), the first request after restoring repeats all 11 earlier messages byte for byte, cache markers included, with the same system and tools. Not measured: server cache reads. Not exercised: compaction. Not handled: the 32 MB request limit, which large PNGs (about 1 to 2 MB each in base64) can reach before 100 images; that request now fails with the provider's error, as Claude Code's does, where eight images never reached it.
- Claude's `Read` gives Code Mode its media as `{content: [...]}`, the content array of the tool result Claude Code builds for an image (2.1.318's Read `mapToolResultToToolResultBlockParam`: `{type: "tool_result", content: [{type: "image", source}]}`), and `image()` takes such a result whole (2026-11-12). In the Terminal-Bench 2.1 audit of the frozen 0.6.7 run (`eed3f234`) the model called `.content[0]` on a Read result, the pattern the exec description teaches for MCP results (`image(result.content[0])`), failed on the bare array and only then found `[0]`. Text reads are still strings. A direct call's structured result was already the serialized content (`take_structured_result`), so events and journals carry nothing new. `image()` unwraps `content` before its array path, so the description's `image(await tools.Read({ file_path }))` still works, and its text now says it takes a tool result whose `content` is an array of image items. The host adapter's image Read returns the same shape. Checked on 2026-11-12 with output/parity-harness (the facade's native Claude agent, code-only, Opus 5.5, against mock.py, a local mock of the streaming Messages API; `./run.sh new default 12 18611`): 12 turns each read a PNG in a cell, alternating `image(r.content[0])` and `image(r)`; every cell printed `object 1 input_image` and every tool result carried its image block. Not changed: a PDF read is still rendered only through Poppler (`pdfinfo`/`pdftoppm`), and a document block cannot cross Code Mode (`[document content is available to direct Claude tools, not Code Mode]`), whereas Claude Code sends a whole PDF as a document without Poppler; the audit's financial-document attempts had neither tool. Commands: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-tools -p nanocode-code-mode -p nanocode-code-mode-engine`, again with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --locked --lib` on the same crates natively (`-D warnings`) and for wasm32 (all pass).
- Integration recheck of the five durability listing changes below on master (2026-11-12, run off the owner's Mac on a 5-core Linux Hand with another build beside it): `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl` native and wasm32 and clippy on nanocode-store-jsonl pass. Harness (output/durability-ledger, release with mimalloc, built for this commit and for 1b57e8631; on Linux its `current_rss` reads /proc/self/statm and the scripts copy with `cp -R`): matrix 3000 on memory, jsonl, sqlite and rows, kill/resume on jsonl, sqlite and rows, kill-twice on the three, both tree checks (30 x 100, and with MAX_AWAKE=0 at 300 ms latency) and cross-version kill/resume in both directions (1b57e8631 to this build and back) on jsonl and sqlite end with every agent completed. The stop check's CLOSE with MAX_AWAKE=0 at 2,000 agents does not settle within 60 s on this machine, on 1b57e8631 as on this build (three runs each), so it is older than these changes and still open. 20,000 agents on jsonl at 2,000 concurrent, interleaved: user CPU 58.2 and 62.3 s at 1b57e8631, 59.2 and 58.9 s with these changes, max RSS 1,100 and 1,068 MB against 1,034 and 1,071 MB, logical bytes an agent 40.8 KB both: unchanged within the noise of the shared machine.
- A listing leaves a journal closed when its subagents were remembered at its length (2026-11-11). Every listing opened each journal that has subagents to read their revisions from its index, so it parsed the index header of every such session however little had changed: 9 MB of JSON for 10,000 subagents. A subagent's summary is remembered with the journal's length, as its root's is, so when every subagent of a journal was remembered against the file as it is now, identity and length, the listing takes them as they are and leaves the journal closed. When the journal has changed it is opened as before, and a subagent found at its remembered revision takes the new length, saved with the root's new summary, so the next listing leaves the journal closed again. Second and later listings, three runs each, user CPU: one journal of 10,000 subagents 0.10/0.10/0.10 s to 0.05/0.05/0.05 s, max RSS 87-88 MB to 48-49 MB, wall 103-343 ms to 38-59 ms; a home of 404 session files with 7,300 subagents in 4 journals 0.06/0.07/0.07 s to 0.04/0.04/0.04 s; no journal opened where 1 and 4 were.
- JSONL replay keeps each line's length as it reads it (2026-11-11). Replay read a block of a journal line by line and then looked for every newline of the block again, a byte at a time, to find where its lines lie: 13% of a listing that replays an older build's journals. It now keeps each line's length as it reads the line, and carries the lengths of the lines it holds over to the next block with their bytes. First listing of a home without remembered summaries, interleaved runs, user CPU: 400 journals of 2,147 MB written by an older build 4.88/4.77/4.56 s to 3.91/3.82/3.79 s; 40 journals of 823 MB written by this build 1.56/1.41/1.28 s to 1.11/1.04/0.96 s. Every open of a journal without an index replays it, so a resume gains the same share.
- A listing reads an archived session from a temporary copy and leaves the archive (2026-11-11). A listing that had to summarize an archived session restored it: the journal was written back beside the others and synced, the archive deleted, and nothing archived it again, so a home listed without its summaries grew to its unarchived size and stayed there. A read of a state the last listing reported as unknown now opens an archived journal from a decompressed temporary copy in the sessions directory (`.listed-<pid>-`, one at a time, removed when the next is opened and when the summaries are remembered, and cleared with the other temporaries if its process died), and the summary is remembered against the archive with its anchor. Any other access, and every write, restores the archive as before. A home of 404 session files with 280 archived, listed without any remembered summaries, is 1,078 MB with its 280 archives afterwards where it was 2,421 MB with none. The CPU is what it was (user 4.67/4.65 s and 4.75/4.73 s, system 3.11/2.93 s and 3.05/2.97 s): the copy is written and read back through the page cache as the restored file was, without the syncs; reading it from memory would need the journal to work without a file and the profile gives the copy's write 4%.
- A summary remembered without an anchor is held by its file's length and its state's last replacement (2026-11-11). Summaries remembered by older builds have no anchor, so on a copy of such a home every one was computed again: each journal replayed, each archive restored. Such a summary is now held when the file has the remembered length and the last line that replaces its state, found by reading the journal backwards from its end (an archive is decompressed in memory), carries the remembered revision; it then gets its anchor. The remembered revision came from a replay, and a file of the same name and length that ends its state at that revision is that file unless two histories of one session meet at the same byte length and revision, or the file was edited in place, which the inode check never saw either. A journal that ends in a torn line, a last replacement that does not parse and a different revision all leave the summary unknown, and it is computed as before. First listing of a copy of a home of 404 session files, 280 archived, 1.0 GB on disk, with an older build's summaries, two interleaved runs: user CPU 3.75/3.76 s to 0.48/0.49 s, system 2.27/2.33 s to 0.13/0.15 s, no journal replayed where 400 replayed 2,147 MB, and the copy stays 1,078 MB with its 280 archives where it grew to 2,421 MB with none. What remains is a decompression of each archive and one read of each journal's last line.
- A remembered summary is valid for a copy of its file (2026-11-11). A remembered summary was valid only for the device and inode its session file had, so a copied, restored or migrated home had none and a first listing read every session again. A summary now also keeps an anchor: the position of the journal's last line and the SHA-256 of the file from there to its end, or for an archive the SHA-256 of the whole file, which the archiver hands over when it writes one. When a file has the remembered length under another identity, the listing reads those bytes, and if they hash to the anchor the summary stands and takes the file's identity, which the listing saves once. A state of a journal that keeps an index (a root with subagents and its subagents) is held the same way by the revision the index gives it. Older builds ignore the field and drop it when they save. First listing of a copy, harness on mimalloc, three interleaved runs, user CPU: a home of 404 session files (2.4 GB written by an older build) and 4 indexed journals with 7,300 subagents, its summaries remembered by this build: 3.96/4.38/4.44 s to 0.15/0.15/0.15 s (400 replays of 2,147 MB to none), max RSS 331-387 MB to 96-97 MB, the same 7,704 sessions listed; the same home with 280 of its files archived and summaries an older build remembered, without an anchor: 4.64/4.78 s to 3.75/3.76 s.
- Integration recheck of the five psh round-3 changes below on master (2026-11-11, load 25-55): workspace `cargo check --locked`, clippy on nanocode-home, nanocode-process, nanocode-psh, nanocode-psh-embedded, nanocode-shell and nanocode-cli, the wasm32 check, the dependency boundaries and psh-wasm (8,396,810 bytes) pass. With the bundled tools and machine mode in the same tree: psh-spec exits 0 (oils 2321, brush 2826, agent 725, utilities 1001 of 1001); git 1,339 commands with 0 failed on the machine's files and the one known /tmp path case over MemFs; archives 88, patch 41, small tools 226, curl and wget 81, 0 failed; system bash against psh over the 727 agent cases 685 identical, with the system's utilities 711; in place against a psh process 0 of 727 differ through run_bash and exec_command. The Linux figures in the entries below are the branch's own (two containers on this machine); they were not rerun here.
- psh's utilities speak one dialect on every system: GNU's output, GNU's and BSD's flags both accepted, and `PSH_UTILS_OFF=names|all` hands a utility back to the system's (2026-11-11). The corpus (dialect.py over 151 of 3,759 local session files, aggregates only) shows agents writing both dialects in the same sessions and reading GNU-shaped output: `wc -l` 11,912 uses of which 46 strip the BSD padding and 2 compare the count as a string; `uniq -c` 4,060; `timeout N` 10,788 (absent on macOS); `sed -i ''` 619 against GNU's `sed -i script` 32; `stat -c` 419 against `stat -f` 188; `readlink -f`/`realpath` 665; `base64 -d` 888 against `-D` 1; `md5sum`/`sha256sum` 145 against `md5`/`shasum` 180; `nproc` 213; `tac` 68; `find -printf` 27; `nl -ba` 590; ls's status tested 6,083 times, as zero or not. A 30-form probe under psh on macOS (dialect-check.sh): all 30 are accepted; 20 give the system's bytes, 7 are GNU forms the macOS tools reject (sed -i script, stat -c, date -d, head -n -N, find -printf, grep -P, tac/nproc/timeout), 3 differ in output (wc's padding, uniq -c's width, ls's status 2 for a missing file). Against system bash on 727 agent cases the dialect is 27 differences on macOS (11 wc padding, 7 ls status, 2 uniq -c width, 2 GNU sed -i, and one each of sed's status for a missing file, cmp's wording, seq -w, nl's blank lines, head -n -N) and none on Linux; with PSH_UTILS_OFF=all it is none on macOS either (711 identical, 13 shell name, 3 notice). No code changes with this entry.
- A script psh runs in the Hand's own process gives exec_command its stdout and stderr in the order it wrote them (2026-11-11). exec_command joins the two streams by the order two readers see them; with a process that is two pipes and a race, and the same script (six lines to each stream in turn) gave 21 different outputs in 40 runs under system bash and 27 under a psh process on macOS. In place there are no pipes: the engine writes both streams from one thread, so both sinks now feed one channel (`embedded::Streams::InOrder`, `ProcessOutput::Stream`), while run_bash keeps them apart. In place: 7 distinct outputs in 40 runs before, 1 in 200 after, on macOS and in a Linux arm64 container; a psh process and system bash are as they were (27 and 21 of 40 on macOS, 7 and 6 of 40 on Linux). 727 agent cases, in place against a psh process, through run_bash and exec_command: 0 differ on both systems.
- psh runs `select`, exports what `declare` assigns under `set -a`, ends its own foreground utility on a trapped INT, accepts `local -g`, and lists an empty value as `NAME=`; coproc is the one construct nanocode-psh still hands to bash (2026-11-11). Taken in the order the session corpus uses them (41 of 3,759 files, text matches: set -a 36, trap on EXIT/INT/TERM 10, select 5, printf -v 4, export -n 0, local -g 0, coproc 0). A trapped INT now ends psh's utility with 130 before the trap runs, because a terminal sends INT to the whole foreground group and the program in the utility's place would have got it: `sleep 3` under `trap … INT` ran its three seconds first. Five scripts (9 set -a and export cases, 15 printf -v and listing cases, 13 select scenarios with four menu layouts, INT to the group with a trap that exits and one that returns) give the bytes and statuses of Homebrew bash 5.2.26 and nix bash 5.3 on macOS and of bash 5.2.37 in a Linux arm64 container. psh-spec: oils 2306 to 2308, brush 2820 to 2825. Not changed: PIPESTATUS 141 for a writer into a closed pipe equals bash's in 24 cases on macOS and differs in 2 on Linux where bash's own answer depends on timing and psh's utilities write 64 KiB at a time; printf -v with subscripts and export -n showed no difference; `$0` of a script found through a relative PATH entry is still the absolute path; coproc is unsupported. Upstream difference: psh-engine exec.rs (run_select, select_menu), signals.rs (Gives::Interrupt), util.rs, builtins/declare.rs, builtins/read.rs, builtins/mod.rs.
- psh's find takes a file's kind from the directory listing and calls lstat only when a test needs more (2026-11-11). `Host::read_dir_kinds` is a new method with a default that knows no kind, so hosts other than the Unix one are unchanged; find uses it when the expression reads only paths and kinds (-name, -path, -regex, -type, -depth, -prune, -quit, -print), links are not followed and -xdev is off. A file that is not a directory, and a test that stands alone, get no future on the heap. CPU, interleaved, same output: on macOS `find src -name '*.rs' | wc -l` over 2,000 files 10.9 to 6.3 ms (Homebrew bash with /usr/bin/find 16.0); in a Linux arm64 container as a process 4.74 / 5.42 / 6.54 to 2.74 / 3.19 / 3.88 ms (p10 / p25 / median of 500), where bash with GNU find takes 1.59 / 1.76 / 2.20 and 1.0 ms of psh's is its start; through the Hand in its own process 1.49 ms against 3.83 for the system's, wall p10 0.97 against 1.79 ms. Eleven groups of find invocations give the same output and statuses before and after. Upstream difference: psh-engine host.rs (KnownEntry, read_dir_kinds), util.rs, psh-os unix/mod.rs, psh-utils find/mod.rs.
- psh's awk reads a field's number, its length and its printed text where they lie in the record, and is faster than mawk on the bench's awk workload on Linux (2026-11-11). The record is one buffer the reader fills, with the shared text of $0 made only when the program reads it as a value; `$N` under + - * / % ^, unary minus and += is a number without a string value; `print $a, $b` and `length($N)` work on the record; a record already read is taken without a future; `s += $1` is four steps instead of seven; % of whole numbers is the integer remainder (Rust's fmod on aarch64 Linux was 17% of the samples of `NR % 2`). CPU median, interleaved, same output: on macOS `awk '{s+=$1} END {print s}'` over 1,000,000 lines 142.6 to 74.3 ms (Homebrew bash with /usr/bin/awk 281.0), `awk '{print $1}'` 171.8 to 83.7 ms (571.5), `awk -F: '{print $1, NF}'` 267.5 to 204.6 ms (782.7); in a Linux arm64 container the first is 175.0 to 84.4 ms as a process against mawk's 115.8, and 78.5 ms in the Hand's process against 116.5. Over twelve more awk programs on Linux psh is ahead of or level with mawk on five (sum 68 against 97 ms, print $1 77 against 104, a two-awk pipeline 134 against 150, eight fields to two 156 against 174, print $1, NF 171 against 173) and still behind on seven (array count 233 against 128, regex pattern 60 against 37, comparison pattern 150 against 115, length 65 against 48, printf 293 against 266, NR arithmetic 89 against 64, concatenation 200 against 153). Running the plain steps in an ordinary loop outside the future was measured and reverted: no gain (sum 93.4 to 90.4 ms, NR arithmetic 102 to 116). Upstream difference: psh-utils awk/compile.rs, awk/interp.rs, awk/io.rs.
- A standalone psh starts the thread that wakes it for a signal only when it first parks, so a script that never waits runs with one thread fewer (2026-11-11). The handler already sets the signal's bit for the engine; the watcher thread exists only to wake a parked shell, and a signal caught before it starts waits in the pipe. Interleaved spawns in a Linux arm64 container (600 runs, CPU p10 / p25 / median): `psh -c true` 1.131 / 1.324 / 1.654 to 1.019 / 1.191 / 1.513 ms and `psh -c 'echo hi'` 1.097 / 1.309 / 1.685 to 0.970 / 1.140 / 1.520 ms, against 0.454 / 0.520 / 0.631 for bash; on macOS (400 runs) 2.852 / 2.993 / 3.230 to 2.809 / 2.920 / 3.113 ms, against 4.741 / 4.993 / 5.368 for Homebrew bash. Ten signal scenarios give the status and output they gave before and that bash 5.2.26 gives. What is left of the Linux gap is the kernel's: psh's user time for `-c true` rounds to 0.00 ms, and it takes 251 page faults where bash takes 103; a non-PIE build of the same psh takes 119 faults and 0.491 ms where the PIE takes 0.635 ms (bash 0.346, 600 runs), but that removes address randomization from the executable and was not committed; the engine's own thread costs a spawn and a join (140 µs in the container, 65 to 80 µs on macOS, 2,000 of each) and stays because Linux gives the main thread 8 MB of stack where the engine reserves 20 MB. Upstream difference: psh-os unix/signals.rs (WATCHER, watch), psh-engine std_host.rs (drive_parking), psh lib.rs.
- Integration recheck of the 47 changes below on master (2026-11-11, load 20-45): durability round 2 (8), psh in WebAssembly and machine mode (7), the bundled tools (15) and the djs VM (17), built together. Workspace `cargo check --locked`; clippy on the durability crates, nanocode-store-sql, nanocode-subagents, nanocode-agent-core, nanocode-shell, nanocode-python, nanocode-psh and the two code-mode crates; the wasm32 check; the dependency boundaries (51 crates); vendored psh and djs checks and `scripts/bgen.sh --check` pass; psh-wasm is 8,378,117 bytes (2,843,459 gzip). Merge notes: the tools branch was rebased onto the machine-mode branch, and the shell's machine-mode gate now turns off every bundled name the machine's answers do not run from the shell's own list (the registry, the host facts, curl and wget), not from psh-utils' registry alone; the workspace lock gains only gix-imara-diff and three dependency lines, written by hand because an unlocked resolve also moved itertools and getrandom under three unrelated packages; the djs VM branch was rebased over the text leaves without textual conflict and the text agent then checked the merged engine (upstream's tests in debug, the corpus reset test, difftest with suspension and GC stress, test262 39,325 of 39,365, 33 cells on one reused instance byte-equal to the image after every reset) before it landed. Harness on the merged tree: `cells` and `preludecheck` (also `EXTRA=1`, 39 lines) identical once the bootstrap's line number in stack traces (800 to 810) is normalized; `cellreplay` 4 ok and the known failure; `sinkreplay` 5 ok; `isocheck` 41 cells on one runtime, 25 repeated outputs identical; `stuck` ends six runaway scripts within 0 to 83 ms of the limit, a 20,000-operator `**` chain as a SyntaxError and a cell under a 64 MB cap as out of memory; `rawcheck` ok; for Claude and Codex matrix 3000 on four stores, kill/resume on three, kill-twice, both tree checks, stop and release complete; cross-version kill/resume both directions on jsonl and sqlite; the old 10,000-agent store reopens. 20,000 agents on jsonl against the previous master, interleaved: Claude user CPU 35.6, 35.7, 36.4 s to 35.0, 35.6, 37.0 s and max RSS 1,509, 1,528, 1,523 MB to 1,141, 1,216, 1,293 MB; Codex 37.7, 37.7 s to 37.9, 38.1 s and 1,745, 1,663 MB to 1,407, 1,416 MB. `jsbench` against a build of the previous master with the same harness, two rounds, CPU per cell and instructions per cell: trivial 42 to 34 us (320K to 265K), worker 97 to 76 and 71 us (801K to 680K), tools 247 to 226 us, compute 16.0, 15.5 to 15.2, 14.8 ms, strings 7.0, 6.5 to 6.6, 6.4 ms, 5,000 cells waiting at once 148, 190 to 75, 69 us and max RSS 1,098, 1,303 MB to 164, 160 MB; a trivial cell under a 95 KB prelude 264 to 41 us. Listing a copied home (the durability worktree's harness, twice each): 42 files of 1.03 GB, user CPU 3.92, 3.86 s to 1.17, 1.11 s, 166 journal opens replaying 3,431 MB to 42 replaying 823 MB, max RSS 471, 435 MB to 323, 317 MB; 1,000 one-turn sessions 0.27, 0.29 s to 0.12 s; `indexcheck.sh` reuses a copied index and refuses a foreign, a pre-compaction and a too-long one with the same listing each time; a killed store copied with its index resumes to 3,000 completed. Shell (the tools worktree, whose shell sources are byte for byte master's): psh-spec exits 0 (oils 2319, brush 2820, agent 725, utilities 1001 of 1001); git 1,339 commands against /usr/bin/git 2.50.1 with 0 failed on the machine's files, 2 over MemFs and 1 over a later-answering filesystem (the harness's /tmp path and a blame that prints the current second); archives 88 checks, patch 41 scenarios, small tools 226 commands, curl and wget 81 commands, 0 failed; system bash against psh over the 727 agent cases 685 identical as before, and in place against a psh process 0 differ.
- A host can cap a cell's heap (2026-11-11, asked for by the nanocode-ts work). A cell's instance had Limits { memory: usize::MAX }, djs's own 4 GiB: on WASM a cell that keeps allocating grew linear memory, which never shrinks, to 755 MiB and 2.48 GiB in their measurements, past a Workers isolate's 128 MB, before djs reported anything. nanocode_code_mode::code_mode::set_cell_memory(bytes) (nanocode_code_mode_engine::set_cell_memory, next to set_interrupt_checks but for native hosts too) sets the cap of the cells started from then on; a cell that reaches it ends with 'Script stopped: the cell ran out of memory.' as it did at 4 GiB. A spare instance made under another cap is not reused. The default stays unlimited: choosing a cap is the host's policy. Close to the cap djs collects more and more often, so a cell that fills its heap slowly spends up to a few seconds before it fails.
- A chain of ** operators counts toward the djs parser's nesting limit (2026-11-11, found on WASM by the nanocode-ts work). parse_binary recurses once per operator of a right-associative ** chain and, unlike every other production, did so without the depth guard: new Function('return ' + '1 ** '.repeat(10000) + '1') overflowed the native stack, which on WASM kills the whole runtime and natively the process's thread. The recursion for ** now enters the parser's depth count (compiler/expr.rs), so a chain deeper than the limit (MAX_DEPTH 550) is 'SyntaxError: stack overflow' like any other nesting. This is a script-visible change only for chains of more than about 550 ** operators, which used to evaluate up to a few thousand. The commit is a fix, not a performance change, hence its prefix.
- new Date(value) in a cell no longer goes through Reflect.construct (2026-11-11, found by the djs-text work). bootstrap.js replaces Date with a journaled wrapper that built every Date as Reflect.construct(OriginalDate, args, new.target): 1.45 us a construction against 0.27 us on bare djs. Only the call without new and the construction without arguments read the host's clock, so the wrapper now constructs the original directly for new Date() and new Date(value) when new.target is the wrapper itself (the result has the same prototype object), and keeps Reflect.construct for subclasses and the other arities.
- A host prelude runs once, when its snapshot is built, if that is the same as running it in every cell (2026-11-11, from the nanocode-ts work's measurement and patch, changed as the integrator asked). runCell ran the prelude in every cell: 245 us and 3.5M instructions of every cell natively with a 95 KB prelude of nanocode-ts's size, 0.9 ms a cell on WASM by their measurement. cell.rs now builds a prelude's snapshot first with __nanocodePreludeAtSetup: bootstrap.js calls the prelude inside prepareCell and then asks djs-embed's setup probe whether anything is queued. That build fails, and the snapshot is built with the prelude in every cell exactly as before, when the prelude calls a host function while it initializes (Date.now, new Date(), Math.random, performance.now, a tool call, __nanocodeBytes.random, text, notify, load, a timer, a tool's description or schema), when it throws (including exit()), or when it leaves a job or an unhandled rejection behind (a cell would have run that job after its first synchronous part). The preludes that need the cell are remembered (weakly, by content) so a later tool catalog does not try again; a prelude that does not compile is reported as before. What a prelude that runs at setup sees is what it saw at the start of a cell, and each cell gets its own copy of what it built, because a cell is a copy of the image. Known difference, accepted: an Error the prelude creates while it initializes carries the setup's frames in its stack instead of 'at runCell'; functions it defines and a cell calls later have the same stacks as before. A cell journal written before this replays: a prelude that made no host call wrote no journal entry. preludecheck is identical, and 22 further cells in the harness (EXTRA=1: a prelude reading Date.now() and Math.random(), throwing, calling a tool, printing, keeping state, rejecting, queueing a microtask, an async function, patching globals and Array.prototype, store, random bytes, stack traces, exit, a timer, tool names, a description) print the same as on master.
- djs-embed's snapshot setup can ask whether it left anything queued (2026-11-11). Setup sources may not call host functions. Builder::setup_probe declares one sync host function that setup answers itself with whether the VM has nothing queued at that moment: no job and no promise rejected without a handler (Vm::quiet, promise::quiet). It exists so that setup code can run an embedder's script once, in place of every call, only when that is the same thing (the next entry). Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/{interp/run/promise.rs,vm/mod.rs}, djs-embed/src/snapshot.rs, CHANGES.md.
- The fields a djs cell gets where it is allocated skip the tracked prefix's compare (2026-11-11). They cannot be below it: an object's class, prototype, slots and flags (alloc_object), a closure's template, a flat string's length and a rope's parts now use write_untracked, as the cell header, the value stack and the collector do; debug builds check each one. This takes the compute cell from +1% to below master and leaves strings at parity (+0.1 to 0.4% instructions against master, the only benchmark cell that is not faster; its time is in the regexp replace builtin's bytecode). Measured and left out: unrolling the frame fill for short frames instead of the platform's memset_pattern16 (1 to 4% of samples): the same instructions and cycles within noise. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/{object.rs,string.rs}.
- Terminating a cell interrupts the native operation it is in (2026-11-11). A terminate could not land while a cell's step was inside one native operation: the actor's task was in it, and a tokio worker with it. Each LiveCell now has an Interrupt that request_terminate raises before it signals the actor; EmbeddedHost::start_cell takes it (one more argument), gives it to the cell's instance at start and after each wake, and an interrupted step ends the cell without an event, so the actor's terminate branch reports the termination as before. Files: crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/{host.rs,lib.rs}, crates/runtime/code-mode/src/code_mode/mod.rs. Not solved: the worker is still held until someone terminates; a watchdog that interrupts a step after a CPU budget (as set_interrupt_checks does on WASM) is now possible but is a policy decision.
- A djs host can stop a step that is inside a long native operation (2026-11-11). djs checks fuel between instructions and a native operation runs to its end: 'x'.repeat(1 << 28).split('') or a join of 50 million elements is one instruction that takes seconds, and the split costs about 530 instructions per character. Arena::set_interrupt takes a flag another thread raises; once raised the arena refuses to grow, the path a host out of memory takes (HeapError::HostOutOfMemory, D1690, which every native operation already handles), and the run ends at once. The flag is read where the zeroed frontier moves (every 16 KiB allocated) and for each string appended past it, so it costs nothing measurable. djs-embed: Interrupt, Instance::set_interrupt, Error::Interrupted (the enum is non_exhaustive); a reset takes the interrupt away so a spare instance never carries another cell's. This is not fuel-slicing: an operation that does not grow the heap while it runs (a 300,000-digit BigInt product, encodeURIComponent of 30 MB, JSON.parse, which builds on the host's side) still runs to its end, and no operation yields its worker; making them resumable means restructuring the string and array builtins (owned by the djs-text work) or JSON.parse.
- Only a cell whose heap beyond the image is smaller than the image is parked (2026-11-11). A parked cell keeps what its heap has beyond the image and frees the heap. The root cell of a swarm holds megabytes of pending promises and gets a result every few milliseconds: parked after each quiet millisecond it copied its whole heap out and back (park::delta::flush's memmove 0.55% of a 20,000-agent swarm's samples). Machine::parks in host.rs now requires heap_used - image_len < image_len; a larger cell stays awake as it did before parking existed, held or not.
- Parking and resuming a cell no longer copy the image (2026-11-11). Parking dropped the instance and resuming copied the image into a new one, 20 us a round trip: a cell that slept 2 ms eight times cost 346 us of CPU where it cost 188 us unparked. Instance::park now returns the parked call and the instance itself, reset by its written pages, which the engine keeps as a spare; Parked::resume_in applies the parked difference to a spare's heap (Vm::take_heap) instead of a copy of the image, and falls back to Parked::resume when no spare is free. The delta's word scan compares integers: comparing 8-byte slices was a memcmp call per word, half of park's time. Files: djs-embed park.rs, snapshot.rs, djs-core vm/mod.rs, engine cell.rs and host.rs. Instance::park's return type changed from the first parking commit (nothing else used it).
- A finished cell's djs instance starts the next cell (2026-11-11). The pool of spare instances tried on 2026-11-10 gave nothing because Instance::reset copied the image; with reset_written it costs the pages the cell wrote. crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/cell.rs: each prepared snapshot keeps spare instances in nanocode_sync Slots, one per core (std::thread::available_parallelism, 1 on WASM); host.rs: a cell that finishes normally has its instance reset by its written pages and kept, and one whose heap was collected (it grew past the first collection threshold, 777 KB here) is dropped, so a spare never holds more than a cell's first allocation (393-786 KB). Spares die with their snapshot, which is held weakly by its tool catalog as before. An idle process therefore holds up to cores x 0.4-0.8 MB per live catalog and prelude.
- A djs instance notes which pages of its image it writes, so resetting or parking it costs what the call wrote (2026-11-11). Starting a cell copied the snapshot's 318 KB image (8.7 us, a quarter of a trivial cell) and parking compared all of it (13.5 us: comparing two 318 KB streams is bound by memory bandwidth and slower than the copy, so a compare-based reset was measured and dropped). crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/arena.rs: Arena::track makes the arena note, a bit per KiB, the pages below a tracked prefix that its write methods touch; they are the one place every write goes through (the debug-build prefix barrier already sat there), except the interpreter's hot loop, which writes the value stack, and a Box's value in run/hot.rs, which now notes its page. What every run writes (the Interp registers, the value stack, the job queue, the host call table) accounted for over 90% of the noted writes, so Vm::move_interp_to_end puts those cells last in a snapshot's image (djs-embed Builder::setup calls it before seal) and the image from the first of them on counts as written: such a write pays one compare like any write above the image. A collection ends the tracking (Heap::without_barrier); the collector's own writes, the stack's general-path writes and a new cell's header use write_untracked, which debug builds check. Vm::restore_image / Instance::reset_written copy the noted pages and the tail back; Instance::reset tries that first; Instance::park compares only those pages. The cost is one compare per arena write: +2.7% instructions on a fresh-instance trivial cell, +1.0% on compute, +0.8% on strings at this commit (6c5253698 brings compute to parity). Measured and left out: noting inline (compute +10%), two always-written ranges checked inline (+3 to 6%), an XOR-fold block compare for the scan (no gain). Correctness is the isolation between cells that reuse an instance: in the development copy 600 difftest corpus scripts (518 run to completion) give the same output on one reused instance as on fresh ones, and after 585 of them the reset left the heap byte-equal to the image (15 had collected and were copied); a build with the debug assertion in Arena::restore turned into a release assertion ran cells, preludecheck, jsbench and every regression script without a mismatch. wasm32 and builds without djs-core's embed feature are unchanged.
- A Code Mode cell that waits is parked (2026-11-11). A cell waiting on a tool call or a timer held its whole heap, 320 KB each: 1.1-1.4 GB for 5,000 cells waiting at once against 560-600 MB on QuickJS. In crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/host.rs a machine's instance is Awake or Parked. A cell is parked at once when it is held, or when it waits on no tool call and its next timer is at least PARK_AFTER away (the wait is known); a cell waiting on a tool call is parked once it has been idle for PARK_AFTER = 1 ms, the resolution of the timer that wakes it, so a tool that answers at once costs nothing. A queued tool result or a due timer resumes it; events, the journal and replay are untouched (parking happens only after replay has finished). The first form of this commit (delay only) left a burst of 5,000 cells at 909-976 MB because the park timers fire late under load; parking known timer waits at once brought it to 112-125 MB. In a 20,000-agent swarm the worker cells' tool calls take more than a millisecond, so they park: max RSS falls by a fifth and the run executes about 2% more instructions with no measurable change in user CPU; PARK_AFTER is the knob if that trade is wrong for a host.
- djs-embed can park an instance as its difference from its snapshot (2026-11-11). A djs heap is a byte image and an instance starts as a copy of its snapshot's; a nanocode cell waiting on its first tool call has changed 101 words of the 318 KB image and allocated 3.3 KB. Instance::park gives the heap back and keeps the runs of bytes that differ (taken from the image form, dead stack slots cleared) together with the call's handles and fuel; Parked::resume copies the image and applies them through the same Vm::from_bytes_trusted an instance starts with (upstream's suspend/restore stress mode exercises that path at every Nth instruction). For a durable host: Parked::to_bytes writes the state with an FNV-1a fingerprint of the image (Snapshot::fingerprint) and Snapshot::parked loads it into a snapshot with the same image, verifying the heap cell by cell (Vm::from_bytes); nothing in nanocode stores it yet and the cell journal path is untouched. The limits and a call's deadline are not in the bytes. New file crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-embed/src/park.rs; lib.rs, snapshot.rs and CHANGES.md list it. The vendored tree has no test directory: the tests (a call parked at every wait and between any two 5,000-fuel slices across collections ends with the same result, host calls and fuel as one never parked, in memory and through bytes; bytes of another snapshot or damaged bytes are refused) are in the development copy, saved as /tmp/swarm-djs-vm/djs-upstream-0e58f62.patch.
- A cell's Math.random seed no longer reads the system's randomness (2026-11-11). Every cell start called getentropy for eight bytes: 5.06% of a trivial cell's CPU through CodeModeRuntime with mimalloc and 0.28% of a 20,000-agent swarm. crates/runtime/code-mode-engine/src/host.rs reads the system once per process and gives each cell the next SplitMix64 output over it (the algorithm's published constants). Math.random is not a source of secrets: crypto.getRandomValues and randomUUID still call fill_random for every request (bytes.rs), and Math.random's values stay journaled, so replay is unchanged. A script that recovers its own xorshift state could in principle derive other cells' seeds; that was judged acceptable for Math.random.
- A djs string leaves the heap by its flat pieces (2026-11-11). Heap::str_to_string decoded every string through char::decode_utf16 one code unit at a time: the cell's source on its way to the compiler (builtins/eval.rs) and every host-call argument that is a rope (djs-embed ValueRef::as_str falls back to it), 3.4% of a 1.7 KB cell that only compiles. It now walks the string's pieces: an ASCII piece is appended as it is, a Latin-1 piece by byte, and only two-byte pieces are decoded, with a high surrogate carried across pieces (lone surrogates still become U+FFFD). Instance::start_export no longer formats its error label on every call. Files: crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/string.rs, djs-embed/src/instance.rs.
- A native djs arena grows to its collection threshold at once, and an instance starts with one arena page beyond its image (2026-11-11). A djs heap is one Vec that grew by an eighth (64 KiB at least): the wasm policy, where memory grows in place at the end of linear memory. A native allocator moves a block that grows, so every growth copied the whole arena: a cell that allocated 12 KB paid a second 320 KB copy (the worker cell's heap is 331 KB against a 327 KB first allocation), and the root cell of a 20,000-agent swarm spent 1.24% of the run's samples in Arena::zero_ahead's reallocation while Promise.allSettled grew (promise_combinator_run -> value_array_regrow). crates/patches/djs/crates/djs-core/src/heap/arena.rs: outside wasm32, growth below the collection threshold goes straight to it (double when there is none); past it the quarter step stays. djs-embed/src/snapshot.rs: a native instance's buffer has IMAGE_ROOM = 64 KiB beyond the image. Measured and left out: the whole first-collection capacity up front (841 KB a cell): worker 75-76 us but trivial 38-40 us against 35-37 and more system time, because the block leaves mimalloc's cheaper size class; growth-to-threshold without the room: worker 87-89 us against 80-83 (the one growth then allocates the 786 KB block). 64, 128 and 192 KiB of room measured the same. wasm32 is unchanged. Commands: output/durability-ledger jsbench qjs 64 2000 <kind> (mimalloc added to the harness's jsbench), LIMIT=300 ./matrix.sh <bin> 20000 2000 jsonl, sampled.sh + inclf.py.
- psh's SHA-1 is twice as fast, because git status is a SHA-1 of every file the index cannot vouch for (2026-11-11). The index says a file is unchanged when its size and times match and it was recorded before the index was written; over a filesystem that does not keep those times, and for files written in the index's own second after a clone, git must hash the content, and real git amortizes that by rewriting the index, which this read-only git does not. psh's sha1_block chose the round function by a division per round over an eighty-word schedule; it is four loops of twenty rounds over sixteen words. Difference from upstream to re-apply: sha1_block in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/sum_hash.rs.
- The bundled tools were measured against the machine's programs and nanocode-ts's TypeScript shell, and the five that lost to one of them were fixed (2026-11-11). output/bench-tools/bench.py runs each command as a process started by bash (children's CPU, an empty loop taken off), in nanocode-shell over MemFs (tools-harness membench) and in nanocode-ts's TypeScript shell over its MemoryFileSystem (tsbench.mjs), interleaved, least of three rounds of ten. gunzip, gzip, xxd, od and tac were slower than a process or than the TypeScript. The CRC-32 of gzip and zip was one table lookup per byte: it is slicing-by-8 with eight tables built at compile time. xxd, hexdump -C and od's one-byte types went through format! for every byte: they index a digit table. tac compared a slice at every byte: it scans for the separator's first byte.
- curl and wget are nanocode-shell utilities over one host capability, `Fetch` (2026-11-11). A `Request` (method, URL, headers, body, how many redirects to follow, a timeout, the most bytes to keep) gives a `Response` (protocol, status, reason, headers, body, the final URL, the redirects taken) or a `Failure` (Resolve, Connect, Timeout, Redirects, Secure, TooLarge, Denied, Other). `Shell::set_fetch` gives it (Config is unchanged, so no struct-literal user breaks); without one both end with `network access is not available in this shell` (curl status 7, wget 4). They live in nanocode-shell, not psh-utils, because they need the capability; it reaches them through a thread-local that `Shell::step` sets for the step it runs, because a psh utility is a function pointer, so psh-engine is unchanged. Their files go through the shell's files: they are in the change report and under its limits. curl covers -s -S -f -L -I -i -o -O -X -H, -d and its kin (@file, --data-raw, --data-binary, --data-urlencode, --json, -G), -u, --oauth2-bearer, -A, -e, -b, -r, -T, -D, -m, --max-redirs, --compressed, -w with the variables agents print, several URLs, and curl's statuses (3, 6, 7, 22, 23, 28, 47, 60, 63); wget -O -P -q -nv -nc --spider -S --header --post-data --method --body-data -U --user/--password (after a 401) --max-redirect, numbered names for files that exist, statuses 4 and 8. No progress meter; forms, cookie jars, recursion and -v are answered as missing. curl is 1.4% of external programs in psh's corpus.
- nanocode-shell's utilities are psh-utils' registry plus its HOST_FACTS, one list built once (2026-11-11). `utilities()` in crates/core/shell/src/shell.rs is a `OnceLock<Vec<UtilEntry>>` (REGISTRY, then HOST_FACTS, then curl and wget from the next commit) that the shell sets as `engine.utilities.entries`. An agent's first commands (uname -a, whoami, id) are answered from the Identity the host configured instead of being commands that are not found. After the rebase onto swarm/psh-vfs, `Shell::build` (agent 6's machine mode) builds its off list from this same `utilities()` list, so in a shell that stands in for a machine every bundled name the machine's Answers do not run, these five and curl and wget included, is added to `off_names`; `off_names` is the switch for all of them (psh-engine checks it by name for any entry).
- dd and install are psh utilities after GNU coreutils (2026-11-11). dd: if= of= bs= ibs= obs= count= skip= seek= conv=notrunc status=none|noxfer, reading a device block by block so that `dd if=/dev/zero count=N` ends, with GNU's records lines and summary. install: -d, -m, -D, -t, -T, -v, -p; owners are left alone. PATH fallbacks. Differences from upstream to re-apply: dd.rs, two registry entries and a mod line, the names in OWN_PARSER.
- tree is a psh utility after tree 2.1 (2026-11-11): -a -d -f -i -F -L -I -P -s -h -p, --dirsfirst, --noreport, --charset. The root counts among the directories and a link to a directory counts as one without being entered; names are in byte order; lines are UTF-8 where the locale is and ASCII with spaces escaped otherwise, as tree prints to a pipe. A PATH fallback. Differences from upstream to re-apply: tree.rs, its registry entry and mod line, its name in OWN_PARSER.
- expr, factor, envsubst, truncate, sponge, yes and uuidgen are psh utilities, and uname, hostname, whoami, id and nproc are a separate list, HOST_FACTS, that only an embedder without a machine takes (2026-11-11). expr is GNU's (operators, `:` and match with POSIX basic regexes, substr, index, length; statuses 0, 1, 2), factor covers 64 bits (Miller-Rabin and Pollard's rho), envsubst is gettext's, truncate GNU's (-s with + - < > / %, -r, -c), sponge moreutils', uuidgen prints a random UUID in lower case as util-linux does. The five that answer from HostInfo were first registry entries too, and psh-spec then had one regression: utils/env/basic/7 relies on uname not being a psh utility. So they are `psh_utils::HOST_FACTS`, outside REGISTRY: the psh program keeps the machine's uname, and nanocode-shell adds the list. What the host does not say (the kernel's release and version) prints as unknown; nproc is the parallelism the process has (one on wasm32). bc and df are left out. Differences from upstream to re-apply: small.rs, seven registry entries, HOST_FACTS, a mod line, the names in OWN_PARSER.
- tac, rev, fold, expand, unexpand, column, join, shuf and split are psh utilities after GNU coreutils 9 and util-linux (2026-11-11). tac (-b -s), rev, fold (-w -s -b), expand and unexpand (-t lists, -i, -a, --first-only; unexpand is GNU's loop, so one space before a tab stop becomes a tab only when more blanks follow), column (-t -s -o and the filled columns), join (-1 -2 -j -t -a -v -e -o and auto), shuf (-n -e -i -r -o -z, seeded from /dev/urandom), split (-l -b -n, l/N, -d -a, --additional-suffix). fmt and csplit are left out. Differences from upstream to re-apply: lines.rs, nine registry entries and a mod line, the names in OWN_PARSER.
- xxd, od, hexdump, strings and base32 are psh utilities (2026-11-11). xxd as vim's (-p -r -i -b -c -g -l -s -u), od as GNU coreutils 9 (-A, -t with sizes and z, -j -N -w -v, the short forms), hexdump (-C, the default words, -x -d -o -b -c, -n -s -v), strings as binutils' (-n, -t), base32 as GNU's (-d -i -w). PATH fallbacks: where the machine has the program, that runs. Differences from upstream to re-apply: dump.rs, five registry entries and a mod line, the names in OWN_PARSER.
- A utility can read the host's HostInfo (2026-11-11). `UtilCtx::host_info()` returns what the Host says of the user and the machine (uid, groups, host name, OSTYPE, HOSTTYPE), which until now reached only the shell's variables; uname, hostname, whoami and id for a host without a machine answer from it. Difference from upstream psh e5f136e to re-apply: one method in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/util.rs.
- patch is a psh utility after GNU patch 2.7 for unified diffs (2026-11-11). -p -R -N -f -t -s -i -o -d -r -F -b -z -E -l, --dry-run, --no-backup-if-mismatch; git headers (new and deleted files, renames). A hunk is looked for where it says it is, then ever further on both sides, then with one and two context lines ignored, as GNU's locate_hunk does; rejects go to FILE.rej, a file patched with an offset or fuzz is kept as FILE.orig, and a question GNU would put to a terminal takes its default (a reversed patch is skipped). Context, normal and ed diffs are answered as missing. The Mac's patch is Apple's, whose defaults and reject files differ, so the scenarios compare the patched files and the status, and GNU's messages were written from memory of GNU patch, not from a differential run: the largest unverified text in this branch. Differences from upstream to re-apply: patch.rs, its registry entry and mod line, its name in OWN_PARSER.
- tar, gzip, gunzip, zcat, zip and unzip are psh utilities on miniz_oxide, in GNU's and Info-ZIP's dialects (2026-11-11). tar after GNU tar (create, extract, list; -f -C -z -v -O -k -m -p -P -h, --exclude, --strip-components, the old `tar czf` style; writes GNU format with L entries and 10240-byte records, reads GNU, ustar and pax, detects gzip by its magic); gzip/gunzip/zcat after GNU gzip (-c -d -k -f -t -l -n -N -q -v -S, levels); zip and unzip after Info-ZIP (zip -r -q -j -x -y -D -X, adding to an archive that exists; unzip -l -o -n -q -p -t -j -d -x -Z1, patterns; stored and deflated members with Unix modes and times). GNU rather than BSD because the sandbox stands for Linux; this Mac has bsdtar, so tar's -v lines and statuses are GNU's from its documentation and were not compared with a GNU tar. bzip2, xz and zstd in tar, encryption and zip64 are answered as missing rather than adding crates: tar is 0.2% of external programs. Archives are held in memory; members are written in name order. Deflate is miniz_oxide's (the dependency git added), so compressed bytes differ from zlib's while each side reads the other's. They are async utilities over UtilCtx, so a filesystem that answers later needs no replay. Differences from upstream to re-apply: the new files codec.rs, gzip.rs, tar.rs, zip.rs; four registry entries and mod lines in lib.rs; the names in tests.rs's OWN_PARSER; wildmatch exported from git/mod.rs.
- git grep and git ls-files -m/-d go on past a file the host has yet to give (2026-11-11). The inline replay runs a utility again once its open questions are answered; these two stopped at the first such file, so a search of n files ran n times. They now ask for the rest and end the run then, as status and diff already did: one more run, however many files. Commands: `python3 output/git-diff/run.py extra.cases --later -k grep` and `python3 output/git-diff/run.py misc.cases --later -k ls-files`.
- git's read commands are a psh utility that reads the repository through the shell's file system; gitoxide was measured and only its diff engine kept (2026-11-11, Georgios: the bundled shell 'must also be faster', and every command it cannot answer starts a machine). In psh's corpus of 295,401 agent commands (research/corpus/tables.md) git is 23.8% of external programs: status is in 26,015 commands, diff 26,007, log 14,543, show 7,743, rev-parse 4,812, branch 2,517, ls-files 1,001, merge-base 464, grep 453, blame 417 (commit 7,481 and add 7,160 are the writes this does not do). Candidate: gitoxide (output/git-probe/gix: gix-odb 0.87.0, gix-pack 0.77.0, gix-index 0.58.0, gix-ref 0.69.1, gix-object 0.66.1, gix-diff 0.70.0, gix-revwalk 0.38.0, gix-hash 0.28.1; 114 packages in its lock) checks and builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown, and a probe that opens the object database, one reference, one commit, the index and diffs two strings is 392,198 bytes of wasm (157,875 gzip, 128,017 brotli; 733,216 native), but its stores read std::fs paths and memory maps, which bypass the host's FileSystem on any target: it cannot read a repository the shell is given. So the reader is written here (crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-utils/src/git, 15 files, about 10,080 lines): loose objects, packs with version 2 indexes (pread where the files are the process's own, one whole read on a host's), alternates, index versions 2 to 4 with its cache tree, loose and packed references, linked worktrees, shallow clones, configuration. Two dependencies: miniz_oxide 0.8.9 (inflate) and gix-imara-diff 0.3.3 (Myers with xdiff's heuristics and its indent heuristic), which makes patches byte-identical to git's on the corpus. Commands: status (short, porcelain v1, long, -b, -u), diff (worktree, --cached, revisions, ranges; patch, --stat, --shortstat, --numstat, --name-only, --name-status, --check, -U, -M, --diff-filter, -R), log and show (built-in formats, format strings, dates, decorations, path limiting with history simplification, ranges, --since, --author, --grep), rev-parse, rev-list, cat-file, ls-files, ls-tree, merge-base, branch, tag, remote, config, symbolic-ref, show-ref, describe, blame, grep, stash list/show, worktree list; renames as diffcore-rename finds them (exact, base name, similarity). It matches git 2.50.1 (/usr/bin/git), including its default abbreviation length, which with a multi-pack index counts the index's objects plus those of the packs outside it and of the packs already touched. What writes, needs the network, or is an option, a combined diff, a merge in progress or a filter attribute this lacks ends with status 127 and `git: WHAT (this simulated shell has no ...)`, the words Pyramid's NEEDS_A_MACHINE looks for. It is a PATH fallback like python3: where the machine has git, that runs. It runs as a blocking body that only reads, so over a filesystem that answers later it is replayed. Differences from upstream psh e5f136e to re-apply: the directory src/git, `mod git;` and one registry entry in lib.rs, `git` in tests.rs's OWN_PARSER, the two dependencies in psh-utils/Cargo.toml, and both lock files (psh's gains adler2, foldhash, gix-imara-diff, miniz_oxide; the workspace's gains gix-imara-diff and psh-utils' dependency lines). Corpus and commands: `python3 output/git-diff/mkrepos.py` builds repositories under /tmp/nc-git (history with merges, renames, binary files, symlinks, tags, a dirty worktree and index, packed and loose, a linked worktree, a bare one, detached, ahead, an empty one, stashes, a clone of the psh repository); `output/git-diff/all.sh [--mem | --later]`, `python3 output/git-diff/run.py real.cases`, `python3 output/git-diff/run.py writes.cases`, `python3 output/git-diff/bench.py 40 3`.
- A blocking utility can read a symlink's target, and a host that answers later is asked again by the replay (2026-11-11). `SyncCtx` had open, stat and read_dir with the inline replay behind them, but nothing for a link's target; git hashes the target of a tracked symlink to say whether it changed, so over a filesystem behind a promise that question had no path. `SyncCtx::read_link` is `std::fs::read_link` on the process's own files and one more kind of question the replay keeps (`Waiting::Link`, `Replay.links`, its arm in `settle`). Difference from upstream psh e5f136e to re-apply: those four additions in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/util/blocking.rs. It is exercised through git: `output/git-diff/all.sh --later` (every answer on the second poll) over repositories with tracked symlinks.
- A one-path psh-regex pattern that closes with the end of the text is tried only at the start that reaches it (2026-11-11). When the last instruction is `$` without `newline` (or the end-of-buffer assertion) the match holds a known number of characters, so in byte mode, or when the last that-many bytes are ASCII, it can only start that far before the end; any other text takes the walk from every start. Three interleaved runs, user CPU ms: in WebAssembly `sed -E 's/([0-9])([0-9])$/\2\1/'` 383/416/391 to 248/246/267 (TypeScript 429/388/352); natively 209/201/228 to 141/123/126. `awk '/9$/'` moves within noise (163/168/161 to 154/151/165). Difference from upstream psh: psh-regex compile.rs (`Prog.tail`), exec.rs (the start of `M::line`).
- A psh-regex pattern without alternation, repetition or back-reference is matched by walking its one path from each start, subexpressions included (2026-11-11). Such a program has at most one match from a start, so the first start that matches is the leftmost-longest match and the positions it passes are its subexpressions: no thread lists, no backtracking pass, no allocation beyond the result. Three interleaved runs, user CPU ms: in WebAssembly `sed -E 's/([0-9])([0-9])$/\2\1/'` 822/842/851 to 383/416/391 and `awk '/9$/'` 206/221/221 to 163/168/161; natively 605/549/607 to 209/201/228 and 164/156/165 to 99/94/118. Difference from upstream psh: psh-regex compile.rs (`Prog.straight`), exec.rs (`M::line`, `M::path`).
- A psh-regex search skips to the bytes every match starts with, and `find` returns the bounds without a captures vector (2026-11-11). The compiler records the ASCII literals a program begins with; an unanchored search is not simulated at all when they are not in the text and restarts where the first one is next. This is what is left of 41463eabc after agent 10's byte search for plain-text patterns replaced its literal case. Against that version, three interleaved runs, user CPU ms: in WebAssembly `awk '/9$/ {c++} END {print c}'` 383/335/377 to 206/221/221 and `sed -n '/9[0-9]*7$/p'` 380/351/345 to 241/243/245; natively 277/248/264 to 164/156/165 and 256/233/263 to 165/154/173. awk sum, sed with a literal, grep -c and grep -rn are unchanged. Difference from upstream psh: psh-regex compile.rs (`Prog.prefix`), exec.rs (`find`, `locate`, `M::span`, the skip in `bounds`), lib.rs (`find_at`).
- A nanocode-shell made with `Shell::with_answers` stands in for a machine: it runs a script only when it has that machine's answer for all of it, and otherwise ends with `Ended::Unanswered(what)` (2026-11-11). `Answers` names the programs and variables whose answers the caller has. Admission is static and happens before anything runs: psh-classify lists every command, including those under xargs, find -exec, wrappers, `bash -c`, substitutions and here-documents fed to a shell, and a walk of the syntax tree checks variable reads against what is definitely assigned. Refused: programs not listed, paths and dynamic names, eval, source, trap, exec, builtin, `bash` without a literal script, the builtins the TypeScript machine mode refused, background jobs, time, coproc, select, `$$`, RANDOM and the clock parameters, `${!x}`, `~user`, unknown variables, and a script that does not parse. At run time a program outside the list is not spawned, bundled utilities outside it are turned off, and reading standard input that was not given is refused. This is stricter than the TypeScript mode, which refused only what a run reached: a script is answered whole or not at all, so nothing it printed before a refusal is lost on the rerun. `Ended` loses `Copy`; the module's ABI is 5 (the shell configuration ends with the answers, a result carries what was unanswered, a spawn says when stdin has no answer). The module grows by 57,838 bytes raw and 19,918 gzip over agent 10's tip.
- A host command's read brings everything that is ready and the end of its input in one answer, and its last write waits for no answer (2026-11-11). A command the JS side runs paid one crossing per pipe chunk, one more to learn the input had ended, and one for the acknowledgement of output it wrote just before exiting. `Stream::read_ready` polls without waiting, a read's `K_DONE` carries `READ_END`, and `psh_proc_write` with request 0 is not answered: a broken pipe on it ends the command with 141. With the glue, 4 interleaved rounds of 7, user CPU ms: 200 execs of `echo abc | rev` 28.39 to 24.31, 200 `rev` calls in one script 21.38 to 17.77. Both are still slower than the TypeScript shell (18.5 and 10.0 against 25.3 and 14.1 in the final run): what remains is the pipeline's subshell and the per-command objects on the JS side.
- An idle psh shell is put back as it was made instead of being rebuilt for the next script (2026-11-11). `psh_engine::Shell::renew` restores the variables, functions, options, working directory and descriptors of its `ShellConfig` from a copy taken at construction (the variables are shared copy-on-write), gives the shell a new job table and restarts `SECONDS` and `RANDOM`; `nanocode_shell::Shell::renew` and the module export `psh_shell_renew` expose it. Making a shell was 48 of the roughly 127 microseconds an `echo hi` exec cost in WebAssembly. Measured together with the glue that uses it (nanocode-ts 27cbf85) and the bridge commit, 4 interleaved rounds of 7, user CPU ms: 500 execs of `echo hi` 40.39 to 22.80 (TypeScript 20.65); in the final state 19.5 against 23.2. Difference from upstream psh: psh-engine lib.rs (`Shell::renew`, the `fresh` field).
- psh's sed reuses its line and substitution buffers and asks the regex for subexpressions only when the replacement names one (2026-11-11). sed allocated a line, a result and a captures vector for every line and every match; it now reads each line into one buffer, builds the result in another, and calls `find_at` unless the replacement uses `\1`..`\9` or `&` needs more than the bounds. `memchr` becomes a direct dependency of psh-utils (one line in each lock file). On agent 10's version (3a9a90bf4, which finds literal patterns by comparing bytes), three interleaved runs, user CPU ms: in WebAssembly `sed 's/1/one/g' big.txt | tail -1` 226.7/215.6/223.4 to 171.1/166.5/164.4, `sed -E 's/([0-9])([0-9])$/\2\1/'` 960/963/968 to 862/883/819, `sed -n '/9[0-9]*7$/p'` 460/452/450 to 393/392/380; natively 152/130/140 to 73/69/68, 652/614/613 to 614/559/549 and 299/279/276 to 268/246/244. Difference from upstream psh: psh-utils sed/exec.rs and Cargo.toml.
- A JSONL index saved beside another copy of its journal is reused when its anchor matches (2026-11-11). A saved index names the device and inode of its journal and `checked_index` refused one whose journal had another identity, so a copied, restored or migrated store replayed every journal that has an index (the harness worked around it with `fixindex.py`). The index also carries the SHA-256 of the last line it covers and that line's position, which the same check already compares with the journal; that is now what decides. An index whose anchor matches the journal it lies beside is reused, takes that journal's identity and is saved again when the journal is opened, so the next open finds it by identity. The identity never proved more than the anchor does about a journal's content, and a wrong index is still caught where it was: record values are verified against their digests when read and a head line against its state id, and either discards the index and replays. Checked with `indexcheck.sh`: a copied index is reused and lists the same 1,501 sessions as a replay without it; the index of another journal, an index saved before a compaction left beside the compacted journal, and an index that covers more than the journal holds are each refused, the journal replayed and the listing the same. First listing of a copied home, three interleaved runs, user CPU: one 489 MB journal of 10,000 subagents whose index covers 405 MB 1.75/1.92/1.84 s to 0.86/1.01/0.95 s (489 MB replayed to 84 MB) with max RSS 314-364 MB to 232-238 MB; 42 files of 1.03 GB, two of them indexed, 1.55/1.70/1.82 s to 1.19/1.37/1.34 s (1,030 MB replayed to 823 MB) with max RSS 376-457 MB to 274-325 MB. With all three listing commits the CLI itself, `nanocode sessions --all --home <copy>`, goes from 4.73/4.69/4.67 s to 1.91/1.73/1.75 s user on that home.
- JsonlStore remembers a summary with what its peek saw (2026-11-11). `remember_summaries` opened each session's journal again to read the revision and length it keeps beside a summary, and by the end of a listing all but the last 32 journals are closed, so remembering replayed almost every session file once more. `list_summaries` now notes the states it reports as unknown, `peek` records the file identity, indexed length and revision at which it answered such a state, and a summary handed back for that revision is remembered with those; a summary for a state that was not listed, or for another revision than the peek saw, takes the old path and opens the journal. What is kept is an observation (this state was at this revision when the file had this identity and length), so it is valid on exactly the terms the cache already uses. First listing of a copied home, three interleaved runs, user CPU: 42 files of 1.03 GB 2.45/2.45/2.58 s to 1.55/1.70/1.82 s (84 journal opens replaying 1,852 MB to 42 replaying 1,030 MB, each file once) and system 0.76/0.66/0.59 s to 0.48/0.54/0.53 s; 1,000 one-turn sessions 0.27/0.19/0.19 s to 0.17/0.11/0.11 s (2,000 opens to 1,000); the single 489 MB journal is unchanged at 1.75/1.92/1.84 s.
- A listing summarizes its unknown sessions one after another (2026-11-11). `SessionStore::list` built the summary of every session the store did not know in one `try_join_all`. A summary is three store calls (peek, hydrate, first prompt), so the store received every peek, then every hydrate, then every first prompt, and `JsonlStore`, which keeps 32 journals open, reopened and replayed each session file once per pass; that is why listing a home whose remembered summaries are missing or no longer valid (a copied, restored or first-seen home: the summaries are keyed by inode) took minutes. The sessions are now summarized in listing order, one at a time, so a file is opened for its sessions and left. First listing of a copied home, harness on mimalloc as the CLI is, three interleaved runs, user CPU: 42 session files of 1.03 GB holding 4,542 sessions 4.26/4.11/4.37 s to 2.45/2.45/2.58 s (166 journal opens replaying 3,431 MB to 84 replaying 1,852 MB); 1,000 one-turn sessions 0.30/0.27/0.27 s to 0.27/0.19/0.19 s (3,000 opens to 2,000). The cost is on one large file: a 489 MB journal of 10,000 subagents is opened once either way and now pays for 30,000 calls made one by one instead of queued together, 1.81/1.76/1.76 s to 1.81/1.85/1.94 s user and 0.25/0.27/0.23 s to 0.44/0.52/0.56 s system; the index commit below more than recovers it.
- An agent record's changed fields are found without parsing it (2026-11-11). A delta wrote an agent record as a patch of its changed top-level fields, and found them by parsing the previous and the new JSON into maps. The record is now serialized through a `serde_json` formatter that notes where each top-level field starts and ends, so the comparison is on byte spans of text already produced. Parses 0.55/0.57% of a 20,000-agent JSONL run to 0.01/0.04%, with 0.14/0.12% for the comparison, and `JournalSnapshot::encode` 3.76/3.63% to 3.50/2.92%. Checked on 300,000 generated record pairs: 281,000 patches equal to the parsed ones, 19,000 written whole by both, none different. A hand-written field scanner was measured first and cost 0.81/0.79% against the 0.75/0.62% it replaced, so it was not kept. Two things differ in what is written, neither in what is read back: the first delta after a restore carries the whole record, since a loaded record has no spans, and patch fields are in declaration order rather than sorted.
- A journal record reaches the store with the key the journal computed (2026-11-11). The child journal hashes each record to decide whether it changed, then handed only the JSON on, and the durable store hashed the same bytes again for the payload key. `JournalFill` and `ChildJournalStore::save` now carry `(key, json)` pairs and `EncodedPayload::keyed` builds the payload from a key its caller already holds; a record is still verified against its key when it is read. The gain is small: `Fenced::save_deferred` 0.33/0.38% to 0.27/0.25% and `content_hash` 2.10/2.32% to 1.89/2.07% at 20,000 JSONL agents, of which the key hashing removed is about 0.17-0.20%; the hashing that remains is the chunk layout.
- A persist clones the session record only for a caller that reads it (2026-11-11). Every persist built a receipt carrying a clone of the `SessionRecord`, and the deferred and batched paths dropped it unread. The persist now returns an internal `Persisted` and the receipt is built in `append` and `commit_standalone`, the two callers that hand it out. `Option<&SessionRecord>::cloned` 0.19/0.32% of a 20,000-agent JSONL run to 0.00/0.00%.
- SqlStore and RowStore pass a commit's Settle to their host (2026-11-11). Twelve of the seventeen commits of a three-tool turn are Ordered (tool results with the next step, and the cell journal), yet the SQL stores ran every one as a fully synchronous transaction because `Sql` had no way to say otherwise. `Sql::write(settle, operation, statements)` is a new defaulted method that calls `transaction`, so a host that does not override it stays durable; `SqlStore` and `RowStore` override `commit`, and a `commit_many` batch is Ordered only when every member is. `SqlxSql` begins an Ordered transaction with `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off`: Postgres returns after the WAL insert and the record is flushed by the WAL writer or by the next synchronous commit, so an Ordered commit can be lost if the database server dies first but is never torn, and admission, tool intents and turn completion stay Durable. Store level, 200 commits, ms per commit durable to ordered, twice: with write-through fsync pg 12.5/14.8 to 3.0/2.4, pgrows 11.6/11.1 to 2.5/1.7, sqlite 22.8/14.7 to 6.1/4.9, rows 12.1/10.8 to 4.3/2.8; with the macOS default fsync, which does not reach the platter, the difference does not resolve (pg 4.2/3.2 to 3.8/4.4, sqlite 2.4/2.4 to 2.1/1.7). Wall per turn on write-through Postgres 320.6/398.8/210.7 ms to 145.1/125.9/127.4 ms. `kill -9` of the process after 200 Ordered commits reads all 200 back on jsonl, sqlite, rows, pg and pgrows; `pg_ctl stop -m immediate` after 200 Ordered commits leaves pg at revision 199 and pgrows at 197 with the head intact and a consistent prefix, and one Durable commit before the stop keeps all 200. SQLite is host-defined: only the measurement harness's adapter implements it (synchronous=NORMAL for that transaction); no shipped SQLite host changes.
- A child's pending turn is answered by its open session, not by a store peek (2026-11-11). The subagent harness asks every turn whether the child has an admitted turn waiting, and each ask read the head back from the store although the session that owns that state was open in the same process. `SharedStore` now keeps a map from state id to the live session driver, and the ask goes to the driver as `Command::PendingTurn`, answered `Unacquired`, `Idle` or `Turn`; the store peek remains for a driver that is unacquired, stopped or not registered, so a restored child is answered as before. Whole-run samples at 20,000 JSONL agents, two per build: `SharedJournal::pending_turn` 1.06/0.95% to 0.28/0.23%, `JsonlStore::peek` 1.11/1.08% to 0.02/0.02%, `Journal::state` 0.42/0.48% to 0.01/0.01%; the map costs 0.51/0.37% (insert 0.08-0.20%, remove 0.21-0.23%), so the net is about 1.9 points of the run. The harness still asks every turn.
- Integration recheck of the python and turn-path changes below on master (2026-11-11, load 30-130): workspace `cargo check --locked`, clippy on nanocode-python, nanocode-shell, nanocode-cli, nanocode, the two Codex crates, nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-agent-core and nanocode-subagents, the wasm32 check, the dependency boundaries (51 crates) and psh-wasm (7,111,641 bytes) pass. One change made while landing: the facade no longer re-exports nanocode-python and the CLI names the crate itself, because a host with its own lock file (output/durability-ledger is one) stopped building when the facade linked RustPython: a fresh resolve takes rustpython-ruff and get-size2 versions RustPython 0.6.0 does not compile with, and the three vendored RustPython patches do not reach a dependent. The psh program's `settings` gives the embedder's utilities to the standalone and the embedded shell alike (the merge with the in-place scripts). Turn path, against the a18548433 build with the same harness: request bodies byte-identical for Claude (150 turns), Codex replay (150) and Codex stored mode (60); Claude events identical (1,140), Codex events differ only in `run.completed` timing (60 of 1,373, same key sets); `cells` and `preludecheck` identical, `cellreplay` 4 ok and the known failure, `sinkreplay` 5 ok; for each backend matrix 3000 on four stores, kill/resume on three, kill-twice, both tree checks, stop and release all complete; cross-version kill/resume both directions on jsonl and sqlite for Claude (against the previous master) and Codex (against a18548433) complete; the old 10,000-agent store reopens. 20,000 agents on jsonl, three interleaved runs: Codex user CPU 40.4, 41.2, 41.1 s to 36.3, 36.0, 36.2 s, system 4.5, 4.6, 4.5 s to 3.6, 3.5, 3.4 s, max RSS 2,340, 2,332, 2,285 MB to 1,714, 1,659, 1,609 MB, logical bytes an agent 83.2 KB to 43.0 KB; Claude 34.8, 35.0, 36.8 s to 34.2, 36.1, 34.3 s (not resolved). `turns memory x 400 3 4000`: Codex 1.23, 1.14, 1.13, 1.21, 1.19 s to 1.23, 1.11, 1.11, 1.21, 1.11 s; Claude 1.55 s both. Python on the merged tree (output/python-bench): 56 of 57 standard-library workloads; the hostile scripts of limits.py end refused or cancelled with the next run printing 42; through nanocode-shell 300 `python3 -c` calls take 51 to 87 ms of CPU and 300 here-document edits 75 to 151 ms, whether the host answers at once or later, against 0.14 to 0.24 s through the psh utility and 7.7 to 9.8 s when psh starts the python3 program; decimal's precision carries from one call to the next within a session (28, then 50), as documented. The first run of this recheck used binaries left by an earlier build, because the harness build had failed behind `| tail`; the script now stops when a build fails and every number here is from the rebuilt binaries.
