- djs: literal runs match in one matcher step, match arrays take the short define, and a `@fast` call no longer fills its argument array (2026-11-11). Three costs the regexp profiles showed once the builtins were leaves (`Machine::run` 28% of an anchored `test`, `create_data_property` 17% of an `exec`, `_platform_memset_pattern16` 2-3% of any `@fast` call loop). `regexp/exec.rs`: a run of plain CHAR instructions (a word of the pattern) executes in one step instead of one dispatch a character; each still costs its unit of fuel and the run stops where the fuel does, so step counts, suspension points and results are as before (upstream's fuel-slicing tests and the corpus under --suspend-every 97 and 1009 pass). `heap/object.rs`: `create_data_property`'s short path (a new key on an extensible object, no descriptor to build and validate) also takes an Array when the key is no array index, which is what a match array's `index`, `input` and `groups` are. `builtins/regexp.rs`: `exec_is_original` answers "no own exec" from the one-own-property check first. `interp/run/fastpath.rs`: `try_fast_call` builds its argument array with `core::array::from_fn` instead of filling six slots with undefined and overwriting them. Each measured by interleaved runs of djs-cli (CPU ns per operation, best of 5, before -> after): anchored regex test 310, 310 -> 291, 290; exec 527, 527 -> 492, 493; exec loop over 62 KB 824, 846 -> 741, 750 us; matchAll 3735, 3977 -> 3574, 3575; replace(regex with groups, fn) 2810, 2988 -> 2763, 2751; Math.floor+round+abs 159, 159, 159 -> 152, 152, 153; isNaN+isFinite 124 -> 116; startsWith 81 -> 79. Through `CodeModeRuntime` (us per benchmark run, QuickJS in brackets): anchored test 2278 -> 1790 (1191-1284); exec 3806 -> 3042 (2223-2599); match 5365 -> 4812 (4012); matchAll 9003 -> 8187 (5423-5557). Final state of the four commits, three interleaved runs: `strings` 26.5-28.2 ms at master, 7.5-8.0 ms now, QuickJS 8.8-9.3 ms; `compute` 17.1-18.0 -> 16.5-17.2 ms; swarm of 20,000 unchanged (user CPU 41.0, 40.4 s at master; 40.6, 40.6 s). Where djs still stands above QuickJS after this (ratio of us per benchmark run): replace(regex with groups, fn) 1.7, regex test of an anchored pattern 1.45, exec 1.26, match 1.2, matchAll 1.5, startsWith/endsWith 1.4, slice/substring 1.8, Math.* 1.5, shift/unshift/splice 1.5, btoa+atob 1.7, charCodeAt loop 2-4, template literal 1.5, trim of a rope 2.7. None of that is the leaves any more: the samples put it in the tier-0 loop's exit and re-entry for a `@fast` call, minor collections (8-16% of every string loop), `%RegExpCreate` for a literal (45-65 ns through `step_once` and `ordinary_define`), `Heap::flatten`'s two Vecs per rope, and the matcher's dispatch (about 6 ns an instruction).
- djs: matchAll, Array.from and Date timestamps skip their bytecode, and atob decodes bytes (2026-11-11). What was left above QuickJS after the two passes above and is the builtins' own. String.prototype.matchAll ran three builtin-language frames before its first match (the `g` flag check through the flags getter, RegExp.prototype[@@matchAll], a RegExpCreate with a flags string): a `@fast` entry makes the iterator directly for a pristine global RegExp whose @@matchAll is the original (now an `@intrinsic`, so the entry can check it), over a copy of the RegExp that shares its program (`regexp::copy`). Array.from of a dense array, or of a string's code points, into a fresh Array copies in one `%ArraySliceDense` instead of a Get and a CreateDataProperty per element in bytecode (only for %Array% itself: another constructor's result keeps the loop, whose failures must throw). `@fast` entries for Date.now, Date.prototype.getTime and toISOString. A match array's captures are collected on the stack (up to 8 groups) instead of a Vec. atob decodes whole groups of four digits straight from a one-byte string's bytes and hands the rest (white space, padding, a partial group) to the general decoder. Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (us per benchmark run, before -> after, QuickJS in brackets): matchAll over 2000 lines 13621 -> 9003 (5423); Array.isArray + Array.from(words) x5000 10867 -> 4688 (4397); `[...str]` + Array.from(str) x2000 9986 -> 5148 (3791); btoa+atob of 62 KB x50 15543 -> 10660 (6010); `d.toISOString()` x20000 on one Date 7822 -> 5333. The `strings` cell over the three commits, three interleaved runs: 26.2-28.4 ms at master, 7.5-8.2 ms, QuickJS 8.3-9.2 ms; `compute` 17.6-18.3 -> 16.3-16.8 ms (QuickJS 25.5-27.8); a 20,000-agent swarm: user CPU 40.2, 39.9, 40.0 s before, 40.1, 39.9, 39.7 s after, RSS 1604-1656 against 1638-1708 MB. Found and not ours to fix here: in a cell `new Date(ms)` costs 1.45 us (20000 x `new Date(t).getTime()` is 29.3 ms a cell) because the bootstrap's JournaledDate forwards with a rest array and Reflect.construct, which also bypasses djs's `@fast` `new Date(v)`; bare djs does `new Date(ms).toISOString()` in 273 ns.
- Math, the number functions, shift/unshift/splice and base64 run as djs leaves (2026-11-11). The same cost the String methods had, in what scripts call per element: `Math.floor(x)` was a builtin-language frame around one libm call (20,000 x floor+round+abs: 8.2 ms against QuickJS's 1.9 ms), isNaN and parseInt likewise, Array.prototype.shift/unshift/splice ran the spec's element loop in bytecode (7.9x QuickJS), and btoa/atob read the string through a per-unit rope iterator, pushed one digit at a time and used the per-unit decoder (8.8x; upstream compiles the whole-group decoder only into its dump module). `builtins/fast.rs` gains `@fast` entries for Math.abs/ceil/floor/round/trunc/sign/sqrt/cbrt/exp/log/log2/log10/sin/cos/pow/atan2, isNaN, isFinite, Number.isNaN, Number.isFinite, parseInt, parseFloat, Number.prototype.toString, Array.isArray, Array.prototype.shift/unshift/splice over dense arrays (through `Heap::array_splice_dense`; splice with as many items as deleted elements needs a writable `length`, which a frozen array caught in testing), btoa and atob. btoa reads a one-byte string in place and writes whole groups (`typed::to_base64`); the whole-group fast path of `from_base64` is on for `feature = "embed"` as well as `dump`. padStart/padEnd and repeat write short one-byte results from the stack, String.fromCharCode keeps its units there, reverse swaps in place, and an int32 argument skips ToIntegerOrInfinity's trunc. One edit outside: `interp/run/intrinsics.rs`, the `%Btoa`/`%Atob` arm calls `dom::btoa/atob(heap, s)`. Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (`cmp2.sh`/`cmp3.sh` as in the entry above, us per benchmark run, djs before -> after, QuickJS in brackets): Math.floor+round+abs x20000 8244 -> 4048 (1899); trunc+sqrt+pow+ceil 10421 -> 4705 (2863); isNaN+isFinite+Number.isNaN 6785 -> 2920 (2427); parseFloat+parseInt 6960 -> 2506 (3359); parseInt+Number() 5928 -> 2886 (3511); String(x)+toString(16) 8702 -> 4913 (3572); shift+unshift+splice x5000 13735 -> 2735 (1644); btoa+atob of 62 KB x50 53358 -> 15543 (6010); repeat 3142 -> 1786 (1146); padStart 4770 -> 3583 (2312); fromCharCode 3105 -> 2575 (1507). What is left of the Math calls is not the leaf: sampling `Math.floor(i / 3) + Math.round(i * 0.7) + Math.abs(i - 100)` gives `run_hot` self 61.5%, `try_fast_call` 10%, `decline_fast` 8%, the `Math` global and `.floor` lookups 14%, and the libm calls 3%: a `@fast` call leaves the tier-0 loop and comes back, about 67 ns a call where QuickJS takes 32 ns. That is the interpreter's (reported to the djs-vm work).
- djs's String and RegExp builtins run as leaves, and a replacer function gets one frame (2026-11-11). Against QuickJS the `strings` cell was 3.3x slower (28 ms against 8.5 ms). Sampling djs-cli on one microbenchmark at a time (`sample` at 1 ms, `selff.py`/`treef.py`) showed neither the regexp engine nor the string code: `Exec::run_hot` was 37-67% of every loop, because each String method without a `@fast` entry, and all of RegExp.prototype[@@replace] with a function, ran as a builtin-language bytecode frame: `'x'.startsWith('y')` 417 ns where the `@fast` `indexOf` is 92 ns, and replace(regex, fn) 1.6 us a match (a match array, a captures array, an args array and a CallWithArray per match, all in bytecode). What changed, all in `crates/patches/djs`: (1) `builtins/fast.rs` has `@fast` entries for startsWith, endsWith, lastIndexOf, codePointAt, localeCompare, concat, toLowerCase/toUpperCase and the locale forms, trim/trimStart/trimEnd, substr, replace and replaceAll with a string pattern and a string template (GetSubstitution as pieces), Array.prototype.reverse and concat over dense arrays. (2) `FastFn::metered`: entries that run the regexp matcher, for RegExp.prototype.test/exec, %RegExpStringIteratorPrototype%.next and String.prototype.match/search/split/replace/replaceAll with a pristine RegExp (and, for replace, a string template). Such an entry takes at most `FAST_STEPS` = 16,384 matcher steps (about 50 us at 3 ns a step), charges them to the run's fuel afterwards as the other run-to-completion leaves do, and declines a longer match with nothing charged, so the builtin runs it and suspends as before. The first version drew from the remaining fuel and declined when it ran out; upstream's `vm::tests::budgets_with_collections_and_suspended_regexps` caught that (the state after a budget depended on how the fuel was sliced), which is why the bound is a constant that depends on the RegExp and the string alone. (3) RegExp.prototype[@@replace] with a function on a pristine RegExp: `%RegExpMatchSpans` (suspendable like `%RegExpSplitRaw`) finds every match, `%EachDense` mode 9 calls the replacer with (matched, position, string) in one reused frame while it returns strings (a non-string result goes back to the builtin for ToString, so the order of user-visible conversions is the spec's), a RegExp with capture groups gets its arguments from `%RegExpReplaceArgs` and CallWithArray, and `%RegExpReplaceJoin` writes the result once. lastIndex, `this`, the arguments and the call order are as the spec's loop has them. (4) The pristine-RegExp check (`builtins/regexp.rs::pristine`, moved out of the interpreter) reads %RegExp.prototype%'s properties from remembered entry slots (a static hint per property, validated by key on every read) instead of fifteen table searches and an `own_keys` Vec: it was 270 ns a call. The metered entries reuse one matcher state per heap (`Heap::regexp_state`, kept up to 4 KiB) instead of a malloc and free a match. toLowerCase/toUpperCase of ASCII and localeCompare of one-byte strings read the string in place. (5) The vendored tree gains what regenerates it: `builtins/*.ts`, `builtins/intrinsics.d.ts`, `crates/djs-bgen` and `scripts/{bgen.sh,gen-intrinsics.py}` (`cd crates/patches/djs && scripts/bgen.sh --check` passes; `python3 scripts/gen-intrinsics.py` rewrites the intrinsic table). Edits outside the text files, kept minimal: `interp/run/fastpath.rs` (try_fast_call passes `&mut self.fuel`), `interp/run/each.rs` (mode 9, about 30 lines), `interp/run/json_regexp.rs` (the new leaves; `regexp_pristine` delegates), `heap/mod.rs` (the scratch field), `heap/object.rs` (`only_own_key`), `bytecode/intrinsics.rs` (regenerated: +7 leaves, +3 `@intrinsic` builtins). Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (output/durability-ledger `jsbench qjs 1 30 strings`, CPU per cell, three interleaved runs, load 200-330): 28.1-29.4 ms -> 8.6-9.3 ms, QuickJS (`/tmp/ledger-bin/qjs/jsbench`) 8.5-9.1 ms; `compute` 18.3-19.4 -> 18.5-18.9 ms. Per benchmark run (`SCRIPT=... jsbench qjs 1 3 x`, the difference of 12 and 2 repetitions in one cell, us; djs before -> after, QuickJS in brackets): replace(/[aeiou]/g, fn) over 2000 lines 35611 -> 7896 (7810); replace(regex, string) 3363 -> 1839 (6214); non-global replace 7353 -> 1164 (1556); replace(string, string) 3531 -> 928 (860); replaceAll(string) 13739 -> 1933 (1811); match(/g) 12391 -> 2164 (2853); search 7534 -> 2170 (2062); regex test 2608 -> 1600 (1820); regex split 3836 -> 2188 (5685); split-reverse-join 4359 -> 2064 (2482); startsWith 9075 -> 1803 (1304); endsWith 6984 -> 1563 (965); toUpperCase 5710 -> 2604 (4413); localeCompare sort of 2000 lines 33274 -> 5960 (31468); slice().reverse().concat() 40992 -> 3668 (6765). A 20,000-agent swarm is unchanged (user CPU 40.0, 40.4 s before; 39.7, 40.3 s after). Measured and left out: the fuel-drawing metered entries (above); a first replace-with-function that appended per match from bytecode (`%RegExpReplaceArgs` + an append leaf): 15.8 -> 5.95 us a replace in djs-cli where mode 9 plus one join gives 3.3 us; the pristine check with plain lookups (4.5% of a replace).
- A JSONL journal line carries its JSON documents after the entry, not inside strings (2026-11-11). A replacement's payload and every inline record are JSON documents, and the journal wrote each as a JSON string inside its line: every byte went through the escaper on the way in, through serde's string skipping on every replay, and through unescaping on every read. Writing them as JSON in place (`"payload":{...}`) was built first and does not pay: the reader finds where an embedded document ends by parsing it, so the writer must first prove it parses (and that it is exactly one document), and that proof cost what the escaping did: `nanocode_store_jsonl::encode` 2.05/1.16/1.16% before, 1.58/1.36/1.18% after with the validation 0.93/0.96/0.67% inside it, and 1.15% to 1.55% with WORKER_CELLS=1; it is not in the tree. What is in: a line whose entry has documents is a JSON array, `[entry,document,document,...]`. In the entry, a payload or record value that is a number is the byte length of its document, taken in order (the payload, then the records); a record's document is its value without the leading `=`. The reader parses the entry with a streaming deserializer and slices the documents by length (`Documents`), so nothing is escaped, validated or skipped, and a value comes back byte for byte. A value goes after the entry when it starts with `{` or `[` and holds no newline; anything else (chunks, manifests, shared-record marks, plain text, an empty payload) stays a string in the entry. A line that starts with `{` is the format every earlier build wrote and is read as before, so the first byte of a line is its format version. The index, the value digests and compaction work on stored bytes and carry either form through unchanged (compaction re-frames a line it copies). A line holds its documents as their writer encoded them, so a generic JSON reader accepts a line exactly when it accepts the documents. An older build cannot read an array line: the 5a73d5320 build stops at open with `unknown variant \`type\`, expected one of \`acquire\`, ...` on a store this build wrote, so a home must not go back to an older build once this one has written to it. Measured, 20,000 agents on JSONL, whole-run samples at 1 ms, two of each build: `encode` 1.50/1.90% to 0.60/0.52%, `Journal::state` 0.99/1.27% to 0.39/0.36%, the JSONL worker thread 8.99/10.52% to 5.43/5.65%. Three interleaved `matrix.sh` runs: user CPU 38.8/38.7/38.5 s to 37.5/37.6/39.0 s, stored 54.4/53.8/54.3 KB an agent to 51.3/50.8/51.4 KB. Replaying a 20,000-agent journal with no index (`rm *.index*; swarm resume`, three runs each): user CPU 2.6/2.5/2.6 s to 1.7/1.7/1.8 s, journal 975 MB to 909 MB. Old stores: a copy of /tmp/ledger/fin10k (10,000 agents, written by an older build) read by `jsonlcheck` gives `states 10001 records 120597 bytes 131472077 sum 259300154316524` with its saved index, with the index rebuilt from the journal, after `compact` (489 MB to 341 MB) and after reopening, the same line an independent reader of the original journal prints (output/durability-ledger `jsonlcheck2.py`, which reads both line forms); `swarm resume` lists its 10,000 agents completed and again after this build has appended to it. New and mixed stores: a 3,000-agent store written by this build, and one killed by the 5a73d5320 build and resumed by this one, each give the same line from `jsonlcheck2.py` and from `jsonlcheck` through saved index, rebuilt index, compaction and reopen, and resume after compaction. `rawcheck` writes 25 payloads and 50 records (objects, arrays, text with leading or trailing space, inner newlines, a string document, numbers, invalid JSON that starts with a brace, two documents in one value, text shaped to inject a field or a record, duplicate keys, lone surrogate escapes, a raw control character, 300 levels of nesting, 140 KB, a manifest, the empty string) and reads every one back byte for byte after writing, reopening, replaying without an index, compacting and reopening again. Left as it is: inline payloads inside a state head are still strings in the head (`serialize_within`, 0.4 to 0.6%); writing them as JSON there has the same validation cost.
- A child's pending turn is not looked for in a head that holds no operation (2026-11-11). Every subagent turn start asks the child journal for a pending durable turn (`Harness::start_turn` -> `Registry::pending_turn`). `SharedJournal::pending_turn` peeked the child's state and reduced the whole head (session record, checkpoint reference, sealed receipts) to find its operations map empty. It now reads just that map (`session::retains_no_operation`) and answers at once when it is `{}`; any other head, or one that does not parse that way, goes through the full reduction as before, so a head in a format this build cannot read is still reported where the session is opened. Whole-run samples of a 20,000-agent JSONL swarm, two of each build: `session::reduce` 0.58/0.57% to 0.12/0.13% plus 0.12/0.10% for the new check; `SharedJournal::pending_turn` 1.06/1.12% to 0.71/0.58%. Not removed: the store peek under it, about 1% on the JSONL worker (a job, a stat, a read of the child's head line and its parse). The question itself cannot be dropped in the harness (lifecycle owner, 2026-11-11): after a kill, a child the root journal still lists as unstarted is built again with its recorded session id, and if the kill landed after that child's first turn was admitted but before the root journal recorded the start, its own state already holds a pending operation; `pending_turn` is what turns that into a recovery with the same request id instead of a second dispatch, and the harness cannot tell a state it created from one it found. The peek can go another way: by the time `start_turn` runs, the child's `DurableSession` is already acquired and reduced in this process, so the answer can come from that session's in-memory state, or from a bit the acquisition returns saying the state was created fresh. That is not built.
- A journaled agent's record is hashed when it settles, not on every save (2026-11-11). `JournalSnapshot::encode` hashed every agent record it serialized with blake3 only to compare the key with the one cached from the last save. The cache already keeps the JSON of a record that is still changing (a turn in flight or a completion pending) so a delta can name its changed fields; `CachedAgent` now holds `Written::Changing(json)` or `Written::Settled(key)`, the comparison uses the JSON for a changing record, and a key is computed only for a record that is not changing, whose JSON the cache does not keep. A changing and a settled record never serialize alike (`turn_in_flight` is always written, `pending_completion` is written when set), so the two kinds compare unequal without a hash. What is written to the journal is unchanged. Whole-run samples at 1 ms of a 20,000-agent JSONL swarm (`./sampled.sh <name> 0.3 60 ...`, which is steadier than a 7 s window because the window lands on different phases under load), two of each build: `subagents::durable::record_key` 1.63/1.63% to 1.01/0.67%, `JournalSnapshot::encode` 4.50/4.22% to 3.94/3.34%. Left in `encode`: serializing the records (0.8%), `changed_fields` parsing both JSONs to diff them (0.5%), the keys of leaves, deltas and settled records (0.8%).
- An owner id is a platform UUIDv7 on every target (2026-11-11). `OwnerId::new` called `uuid::Uuid::now_v7` on native and `nanocode_platform::uuid_v7` on WASM. The platform's id draws eight random bytes with one read of the kernel's entropy and by the profile costs less than half of uuid's, so both targets now take that path, and whatever is done to make the platform's randomness cheaper reaches owner ids (session owners, the cell journal's owner, a JSONL batch id) without another change here. Three 7 s profiles of each build of a 20,000-agent swarm: `OwnerId::new` 0.70/0.48/0.57% to 0.35/0.22/0.18%. Owner ids stay opaque strings in every stored form.
- The JSONL store reads the core count once and keeps its colocation file open (2026-11-11). `Journal::read_records` and the recovery reader called `thread::available_parallelism` on every call, which is a sysctl (0.17% of a 20,000-agent swarm), and `Sessions::colocate` opened, appended to and closed `sessions/.homes` for every child session (open and close 0.51%). The count is read once per process (`cores()`), and `Sessions` keeps the append handle (`colocations`), opened on the first colocation. Three 7 s profiles of each build: `available_parallelism` 0.17% to 0.00%; `Sessions::colocate` 0.88/1.34/2.01% to 1.05/0.65/0.22%, with no open or close left under it; what remains is the stat that looks for an archived journal and the write. The per-commit stat in `Journal::sync` (it detects a journal replaced by a compactor in another process) is left: it is what makes the store safe to share between processes.
- A payload's content key is hashed when something asks for it (2026-11-11). `EncodedPayload::from_json` hashed every payload with blake3 as it was built, and chunked the large ones, whether or not the key was ever read. A payload that stays inline in its state (a continuation under 16 KB, a step's input or output under 1 KB) is written as its JSON and its key is never stored; a Claude child's continuation alone was 0.87% of a 20,000-agent swarm through `owner_write`. The payload is now `Body::Reference(key)` or `Body::Content { json, keyed: Arc<OnceLock<Keyed>> }`: key and chunk layout are computed on the first `key()`, `reference()`, comparison with a keyed payload or staging as a record, and shared by the payload's clones. Sharing is required, not a nicety: with a cell per clone the first build hashed a cached 14 KB tool catalog and the prompt template once per clone and `content_hash` rose to 10.2%. Two payloads neither of which has a key compare by content, which is the same answer; `Serialize`/`Deserialize` are written by hand and produce what the derive did, so stored forms are unchanged. Measured with `sample` at 1 ms over a 7 s window of a 20,000-agent JSONL swarm, three profiles of each build: `content_hash` 4.41/3.13/3.97% to 2.51/2.41/2.80%. User CPU does not resolve it (40.2 and 41.3 s before, 40.3 and 41.4 s after). What still hashes is content that is stored under its key: messages, the subagent journal's records, chunk layouts. Found and left: `child_journal`'s `save_deferred` hashes again every record the subagent journal already keyed (0.25 to 0.35%), because `JournalFill` carries only the JSON; passing the keys needs a change to `nanocode_agent_core::backend::JournalFill` and `ChildJournalStore::save` and makes the store trust keys it did not compute. A NEON single-block compress for blake3 was not attempted: all durability hashing goes through `content_hash` in `core/durability/src/payload.rs` if someone does it.
- A turn waits only for the commits that record an intent (2026-11-11). One session of three cells a turn made 17 commits on JSONL and waited for an fsync after each (16.5 measured, 12.7 ms a turn on a quiet machine). Read off the journal, only five of them record something that must be durable before the turn goes on: the admitted prompt (the caller is told it was accepted), the three tool calls about to run (an effect must not start before its intent is durable), and the completed turn (the caller is told the result). The other twelve are results and bookkeeping: a tool's result committed together with the next model request, which the driver already treats as a rerunnable step (StepRecovery::Rerun, only model steps in both backends), and the cell journal's header, finished mark and removal. `StateCommit` and `OwnedCommit` gain `settle: Settle`: `Durable` resolves when the write is durable, as every commit did; `Ordered` resolves when the write is applied in its state's order, and is durable no later than the next `Durable` commit to that store. `JsonlStore` answers an `Ordered` commit once its line is appended and indexed (the reply path `acquire` already used) and still hands the journal to the sync thread at once, so a result is on disk about a millisecond later as before; a batch is answered early only if every commit in it is `Ordered`. Stores that do not read the field (SqlStore, RowStore, MemoryStore, StagedStore) stay durable. `Driver::commit_writes` persists with `Ordered` when the caller asked for a deferred commit, which it does only for rerunnable steps; `DurableCellJournals` commits an update `Ordered` unless it carries a nested call that has not completed (Queued or Running: what a replay must not send twice), and `forget` is `Ordered`. A crash before an `Ordered` write is synced loses a result, not an intent: the step is still pending, and recovery reports its outcome as unknown exactly as it does for a crash between the tool finishing and its commit today. A failed fsync still stops the store. Measured with output/durability-ledger `turns jsonl <dir> 150 3 4000`, six interleaved pairs at load 130 to 170, counting the store's `durability.jsonl.sync` spans that carry a reply: fsyncs a turn waits for 16.5 to 5.0 (15.5 are still issued, in the background); wall per turn 29.8/50.0/61.9/57.2/53.4/70.1 ms to 23.0/52.4/38.0/40.9/35.7/36.9 ms; with 20 ms of model latency (LATENCY_MS=20, 60 turns) 136/137 ms to 119/127 ms. 20,000 agents: user CPU 39.9 to 40.4 s before, 40.3 to 40.9 s after (unchanged). With a zero-latency mock a waited commit can queue behind a background sync in flight; with a real model's latency it does not. Not done: SqlStore does not honour `Ordered`, and a parallel tool batch still commits each result durably (ResultTiming::Now). Checked: matrix on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows, kill and resume, kill twice, trees with and without hibernation, cancel and close, clean reopens, a store killed by the 5a73d5320 build resumed by this one and the reverse, `cells`, `cellreplay` and `sinkreplay` as at master.
- An agent's statuses, capture flags and a root's counters are no longer in the subagent Registry's process-wide maps (2026-11-11). At master (27e08d189) 4.84% of a 20,000-agent swarm's CPU samples were `Atom` writes, and the largest group was the status queue: every status burst of an agent (Running, then the settle) created an `Arc<StatusQueue>` with an mpsc channel, inserted it into `status_queues` (0.44%), spawned a worker and removed the queue again (`retire_status_queue` 0.36%), 1.72% with the jobs. Reads of the per-agent sets cost as much as their writes, because each walks a 20,000-entry trie keyed by `(String, AgentId)` and allocates the key: `journal_holds_conversation` 0.40%, `recorded_conversation` 0.17%. (1) Each `ChildSession` owns an `Arc<AgentMarks>`: `statuses` (a `StatusLane`: a `nanocode_sync::Inbox<OrderedJob>` and a `running` flag), `captured` (was `captured_once`: the journal already holds this agent's conversation), `completed_tool` (was `completed_tools`) and `capturing` (was `progress_captures`). `enqueue_status` pushes the job and, if the lane was not running, spawns the worker; the worker drains in push order, clears `running`, and re-checks the inbox so a job pushed while it was leaving is not lost. Jobs of one agent therefore still run one at a time in the order they were enqueued, and agents run side by side, as before; `OrderedJob` carries `Status` or `Completion` data instead of an `AgentUpdate` so it is `Clone`, which the inbox needs. Every caller of `enqueue_status` already reads or changes the session inside the registry's mailbox, so it takes the marks from the session there (`hold_unstarted`, `closing_updates`, `release_unstarted`, `harness_turn_started/finished/start_failed`, `fail_unstarted`, the two completion announcers); `forward_events` receives them with its start signal (`oneshot<(u64, Arc<AgentMarks>)>`, so `Registry::insert` now returns the marks and `tools.rs` passes them on); `ResidentEviction` carries them for `evict`. Restore and thaw set `captured` on a session whose stored `conversation` flag is set when the store does not record sessions, which is what the two `captured_once` inserts did. A session that cools is dropped with its marks, so `forget` no longer cleans those sets, and `coolable` asks the session's own marks (`unobserved`) instead of two maps. (2) `pending_checkpoints` and `evicting` were std `HashMap`s keyed by root inside an `Atom`, cloned and swapped by every finished turn; they are an `AtomicUsize` and a small `Rerun` state (idle, running, run again) on the root's `ScopeLocks`. `Rerun` is also what `capturing` is. (3) `settle_notice` reads `completion_routes` before it writes. Measured with output/durability-ledger: `for i in 1 2 3; do for b in m 6; do LIMIT=300 ./matrix.sh /tmp/swarm-lifecycle/bin/swarm-$b 20000 2000 jsonl; done; done` (load 120 to 170): user CPU 39.8, 39.9, 40.0 s -> 38.1, 38.2, 38.4 s. `sampled.sh`, `inclf.py` and a new `atoms.py` (share under any `Atom` write, by map type and caller): all Atom writes 4.84% -> 3.47%; `enqueue_status` 1.72% -> 0.83% (what is left is the jobs: the mailbox call that sends the update, the journal request; the lane itself is the inbox push 0.09%, drain 0.08% and the task spawn 0.13%); `journal_holds_conversation` 0.40% -> 0; `recorded_conversation` 0.17% -> 0; `capture_progress` 0.84% -> 0.33%; `harness_turn_finished` 0.99% -> 0.68%; pending-checkpoint counters 0.24% -> 0.07%. With only the lane (first build): `enqueue_status` 1.72% -> 1.09% and user CPU 38.9, 39.5, 39.1 s -> 38.8, 38.5, 39.0 s. The journal is written as before: `turns memory x 40 3 4000` (682 commits, 4,077,560 logical B) and `turns jsonl <dir> 20 3 4000` (342 commits, 2,007,613 B, store 2,194,310 B) are byte-identical to master. A swarm's journal is not deterministic at master either: `AGENTS=3 MAX_CONCURRENCY=1` twelve times gave twelve different results on master (100 to 104 commits, 75,652 to 77,330 B per agent) and eleven on the new build (100 to 104 commits, 75,890 to 77,440 B); on a quiet machine both builds most often write 35 commits and 94,815 B for one agent and 102 commits and 76,298 B per agent for three. Left as they are, each 0.03 to 0.2% of the swarm: `checkpoints` (0.17%; durable.rs reads the whole map), `completion_routes` (0.15%), `completion_dispatch` and `completion_retries` (0.03% each), `wait_reported` (keyed by the waiting session, not the agent), `result_readers`, `session_handles` (0.12% plus its removal: a child's handle must be registered before its own children can be rehydrated, so it cannot wait for the first spawn). Folding the completion routing into the marks needs the marks carried through `schedule_parent_continuation`, `continue_root`, `dispatch_parent_batch`, `continue_parent`, `route_completions` and `settle_notice`; that is the parent's wake-up path and was not worth the risk for about 0.3%.
- 2026-11-11: **python3 keeps one interpreter per thread, because RustPython 0.6.0 does not free one; and nanocode-python runs on wasm32-unknown-unknown.** A new interpreter per call costs 3.8 ms and memory that never comes back. Measured with output/python-bench's py (`PYBENCH_REPEAT=n /usr/bin/time -l py -c 'import json; print(1)'`): 200 calls on new interpreters left the process at 1,566 MB (7.7 MB a call), and at 635 MB when each interpreter is finalized before it is dropped (3.0 MB a call). A kept interpreter whose imported modules are removed before each run, which would have given every python3 a clean standard library, grows 7.3 MB a run (2,968 MB after 400 runs of `import json, re, argparse`), and 2.3 MB a run with a collection after each (966 MB). One kept interpreter with its modules kept stays at 34.8 MB over 400 runs, and removing only the script's own modules does not grow it (25.6 MB after 400). So the psh utility keeps a `Python` per thread: on the engine's thread where the host has no operating system, and on one thread of its own, fed by a channel, where the files are the process's own and every call has a new worker. A `Python` that is dropped is finalized first. The cost is fidelity. Standard-library modules stay imported, so state a script leaves in them is seen by the next python3 on the same thread: two runs of `print(decimal.getcontext().prec); decimal.getcontext().prec = 50` print 28 and then 50. A script's own modules, sys.argv, sys.path, the environment, the working directory, stdio and __main__ are new for every run. A host that must separate tenants keeps a `Python` per tenant and reuses it rather than dropping it. Through psh (output/python-bench's pshpy, 300 calls in one script, three interleaved rounds, CPU): `python3 -c "import json; print(1)"` 0.16-0.22 s bundled against 7.9-8.8 s with psh starting the python3 program and 8.3-8.7 s with bash starting it; a here-document that reads, replaces and writes a file 0.28-0.36 s against 8.2 s; 36.5 MB peak. Per run in-process: print(1) 5.2 ms new and 0.11 ms kept; open/replace/write 6.3 and 0.39; json from stdin 16.9 and 0.22; an argparse script over a CSV 56.6 and 2.0; workload median 19.3 and 0.41, against 31.6 ms of CPU for a python3 process. CPU-bound code stays slower than CPython: 109 ms against 68 ms for 200,000 loop iterations, a sieve and recursion. wasm32-unknown-unknown (output/python-wasm: a cdylib with an in-memory Files, a platform host and `__getrandom_v03_custom`, run in Node 22 with run.mjs and probe.mjs): 25.2 MB at opt-level 3 (11.3 MB gzip, 8.8 MB brotli), 20.1 MB at opt-level z with LTO (10.6 MB gzip, 8.4 MB brotli; code 7.7 MB, data 11.4 MB). Compile 48-62 ms, instantiate 3.6 ms; the first print(1) is 225-243 ms while V8 compiles, then 21 ms on a new interpreter and 0.4-0.6 ms kept; 16.4 MB of memory after the first run. RustPython's native _datetime aborts the module there (datetime.now(), fromtimestamp()), so on wasm datetime is the pure-Python one; time.timezone, altzone, daylight and tzname are defined; time, random, os.urandom and uuid go through nanocode-platform. 21 of 21 standard-library probes and 40 of 40 edge probes (recursion to the limit and with the limit raised, a 64 MB string, catastrophic regex, exit paths, missing modules) end without a trap. Sleeping is refused on wasm (`Limit::Sleep`): nothing there can wait. Also in this change: a regular file's write reaches the host when Python's write does (an append when it extends the file, a replacement otherwise), so a flushed file is visible before it is closed and files left open are closed when the run ends; opening a directory is IsADirectoryError; time.sleep takes an int; a standard-library module with no frozen stub (resource, mmap, select) is reported as needing a machine; sys.executable is empty. Measured and left out: the pure-Python datetime on every target (+3.1 ms on a new interpreter, 7.8 to 14.8 ms kept on a report with 400 strptime calls, and IsoCalendarDate prints without its module); clean modules per run, for the leak above. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `cargo fmt -p nanocode-python --check`, 56 of 57 workloads, and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-platform -p nanocode-process -p nanocode-sandbox -p nanocode-home` with libc 0.2.189.
- 2026-11-11: **`SyncFiles::on(native)` and `SyncFiles::native()` in psh-engine.** python3 keeps its interpreter on one thread for the life of the process, while a blocking utility on the process's own file system runs on a new worker thread for every call. `native()` gives the OS path function when the files are the process's own, and `on(native)` builds the same view on another thread, so the utility's worker hands its call to the thread that keeps the interpreter. Difference from upstream psh e5f136e: two functions in crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/util/blocking/files.rs, a file this branch added. No measurement of its own. `cargo check --offline -p psh-engine` and the same for wasm32-unknown-unknown pass.
- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-python` (crates/core/python): python3 for the embedded shell is RustPython 0.6.0 in-process over a host `Files` trait; scripts that need packages or a machine end `Needs` before they run** (Georgios: "help us also provide python & other shit bundled by default"). What agents run. psh's research corpus (295,401 commands): python3 is in 10.8% of commands and is 10.9% of the external programs that remain, here-documents are in 13.4% of commands and 81% of them feed an interpreter, flags seen are -c 2,256 times, -m 357, - 233; package installs are 0.5%. Mined here from 187 randomly chosen session logs of 3,758 under ~/.nanocode/sessions and ~/.codex/sessions (1.8 GB read, aggregates only, output/python-bench/mine): 3,598 distinct inline scripts, 3,015 of them `python3 - <<'PY'` and 582 `-c` (beside 1,539 `python file.py`, 171 pytest, 103 `-m`: unittest 42, http.server 13, json.tool 10, venv 8, py_compile 7, pip 4); 10% are one line, 31% 2-5, 47% 6-20, 12% longer; 83% import only the standard library, 14% import nothing, 2.7% import a package or a local module. The workload set is 63 commands (output/python-bench/workloads/gen.py): 40 one-liners, 19 here-documents, 4 script files; 57 need only the standard library, 2 start processes, 3 need numpy, pandas or matplotlib, 1 needs the network; expected output from CPython 3.14.7. Candidates, measured on those (CPU ms on a 10-core Mac with load average 90-320; wall time meant nothing): - RustPython 0.6.0 (MIT, pure Rust, frozen standard library): 56 of 57 once sandboxed as below (51 of 57 in a bare harness, 4 of the 6 being that harness's stdio encoding and 1 its missing -m). print(1) 5.2 ms on a new interpreter (3.8 ms of it the interpreter), 0.11 ms on a kept one; workload median 19.3 ms new, 0.41 ms kept. Adds about 26.5 MB to a stripped native binary (psh with it 39.2 MB, psh 12.7 MB) and a 20.1 MB wasm module (10.6 MB gzip, 8.4 MB brotli at opt-level z with LTO; 11.4 MB of it data, mostly the frozen library). 33-35 MB resident. Builds for wasm32-unknown-unknown with no C toolchain. No snapshot. - pydantic/monty 1.5.0 (MIT, Rust, a deliberate subset): 15 of 57. No sys.stdin, no arguments, no class inheritance, no yield or del, no statistics, textwrap, argparse, struct, io, shutil, tarfile, zlib, glob, uuid, urllib, ast or xml. print(1) 0.03 ms; 0.2 ms median on what it passes; 10.6 MB stripped CLI, 8 MB resident; suspends on every OS call, so an asynchronous host filesystem fits; snapshots built in. - CPython 3.15.2 for wasm32-wasip1 in wasmtime 50.0.1: 51 of 57 (that build has no zlib). 3.6 s and 362 MB to compile once, then 32 ms of CPU for print(1) from a precompiled module and 125 ms median; 32.4 MB module (12.2 MB gzip), 16.8 MB precompiled, 12 MB library, 25 MB resident. wasmtime does not build for wasm32-unknown-unknown; in wasmi 2.0 print(1) is 120-140 ms and `import json, re` 1.1 s; in Node through node:wasi the first run is 186-195 ms and later ones 32-43 ms. - Pyodide 314.0.7 in Node 22 (MPL-2.0, JS hosts only): 56 of 57 and the three package workloads; 1.9-2.0 s of CPU to load, then 0.17-0.23 ms for print(1) and 1.3-1.8 ms for the first `import json, re`; 193-199 MB resident (30 MiB heap), 497 MB with numpy, pandas and matplotlib loaded; 9.6 MB wasm (3.5 MB gzip) plus a 2.5 MB library archive. - MicroPython 412a7e6: 10 of 57; 0.07 ms kept and 15-17 ms to load in Node, 450 KB wasm, needs a C toolchain. Decision: two tiers. The bundled tier is RustPython, because the scripts agents write are standard-library scripts with classes, argparse and file I/O that the subset interpreters refuse. The second tier is full CPython with packages: Pyodide where a JS host has it, a machine's python3 elsewhere (the CLI's PATH, Pyramid's Hand). The rule is decided before the script starts: its top-level imports (ruff's parser), or the `-m` module's package, are imported first unless the script's own directory has them, and any that fail end the run as `Ended::Needs(Vec<Missing { module, why: Package | Machine, error }>)` with nothing run. The psh utility prints `python3: numpy: No module named 'numpy' (this simulated shell has no Python packages, only the standard library)` and exits 127, which Pyramid's NEEDS_A_MACHINE markers match. An import inside a function or a try is not checked first and fails where it runs. The crate. `Python::new()?.run(Run { argv, stdin, cwd, env, limits }, Rc<dyn Files>) -> Ran { ended: Exited(i32) | Needs(..) | Refused(Limit), stdout, stderr, changes }`. `Files` is synchronous, because the interpreter cannot suspend: stat, read(limit), write(Replace | Append | New), list, mkdir(mode), remove(File | Dir), rename, paths as bytes. It is nanocode-shell's FileSystem without Reply, and a host whose answers are all Reply::Now maps one to one. RustPython is built without its host_env feature, so it has no os, no open and no stdio of its own. A posix module and a FileIO written in Python (src/posix.py, src/boot.py, compiled to bytecode at build time by py_compile!) sit on thirteen native functions, so os, io.open, pathlib, shutil, tempfile, tarfile and imports of the script's own modules reach only the trait. Clock and entropy come from nanocode-platform. `Limits { output, file, sleep }` bound what it prints, one file's size and how long it may wait. `UTILITY` is the psh entry (python3 and python, PathFallback). Lock and build. The workspace lock gains 111 packages. libc moves 0.2.186 to 0.2.189 because rustpython-vm 0.6.0 names ENOTCAPABLE while declaring 0.2.186. The rustpython-ruff_* crates are held at 0.16.5 and malachite at 0.12.0, as in RustPython's own lock, because 0.6.0's manifests accept releases it does not compile with (0.16.10 and 0.14.0; a fresh resolve fails). Sixteen existing entries changed only by a version suffix or an activated optional dependency; no other version moved. .cargo/config.toml sets `--cfg getrandom_backend="custom"` for wasm32-unknown-unknown: RustPython's dependencies need getrandom 0.4 there and the workspace builds without wasm-bindgen, so whoever links a wasm module defines `__getrandom_v03_custom`. Commands: `cd output/python-bench && cargo build --release`; `python3 workloads/drive.py ref /opt/homebrew/bin/python3`; `INPROC=9 python3 workloads/drive.py nanocode-python target/release/py`; `WARM=1 INPROC=9 ...`; `python3 workloads/table.py`. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-python`, `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs`. Measured and left out: a full collection at the end of every run to close files held only by reference cycles (5.2 ms on a new interpreter, 0.28 ms kept; files reachable from __main__ are closed by clearing it); parsing the two Python sources at start instead of freezing them (print(1)'s run went 7.65 to 1.26 ms frozen).
- 2026-11-11: **psh-engine has `SyncFiles`, a blocking utility's file system as a value it can keep, with the operations that change files.** A blocking utility body gets `&mut SyncCtx`, whose file system only reads (open, stat, read_dir) and cannot outlive the borrow. python3 needs both: the interpreter it starts calls back into the host from native functions that must be 'static, and scripts write files. `SyncCtx::files()` returns `SyncFiles`, an owned handle on the same two backends (std::fs on the OS paths on a worker thread, Host futures polled once inline, where a host that cannot answer at once gets "the host cannot answer this at once") with stat, read_dir, read (bounded by a caller limit, FileTooLarge beyond), write (by OpenOptions), mkdir, remove_file, remove_dir and rename. Difference from upstream psh e5f136e, to re-apply on update: the new file crates/patches/psh/crates/psh-engine/src/util/blocking/files.rs, the lines `mod files; pub use files::SyncFiles;` in util/blocking.rs, and `SyncFiles` added to the `pub use blocking::{...}` list in util.rs. It is a child module so that it can read SyncCtx's private fields with one line touched in blocking.rs, which the psh-vfs work edits at the same time. No measurement: an interface, no existing path changed. `cd crates/patches/psh && cargo check --offline -p psh-engine`, the same with `--target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo check --offline -p psh -p psh-wasm` pass.

- Subagents do not keep their request body between rounds (2026-11-11). Keeping the last body through a turn holds it while tools run and leaves its buffer with room to grow (up to twice the body after a reallocation). That pays in a long conversation and costs memory in proportion to how many agents are mid-turn. Subagents are the sessions that exist in the tens of thousands, their bodies are small (27 KB in the swarm, where growing in place saved nothing measurable), and one waiting in a cell would hold its body for as long as it waits; so `State::run` takes `WireCache::keep_body()` only for a session whose lineage origin is not `Subagent`. The rule is by role, like parking, not by size. Cumulative result of the seven commits, interleaved runs at load 200 to 290: one session of 400 turns of three cells on the memory store (`/usr/bin/time -l turns-<v> memory x 400 3 4000`), user CPU 2.64/2.65/2.72/2.76/2.80 s on master and 2.31/2.36/2.36/2.45/2.53 s here, 6.6 to 7.0 ms a turn to 5.8 to 6.3 ms, about a quarter of which is still the harness mock; 20,000 agents on JSONL (`LIMIT=300 ./matrix.sh <bin> 20000 2000 jsonl`), 39.3/39.7/40.0 s on master (39.3 to 40.9 s over nine runs) and 36.8/38.3/38.3 s here, resident 1.61 to 1.75 GB against 1.62 to 1.81 GB; a hibernating 30x100 tree (`MAX_AWAKE=0 LATENCY_MS=200 ./treecheck.sh <bin> 30 100 1000 jsonl`) 15.5/16.4 s to 14.6/15.0 s. In the swarm profile frames under the Claude backend go from 44.6% to 41.4% and `State::run` from 32.7% to 29.3%, with the mock steady at 4.4% and 4.3%. Not resolved: 20,000 agents with every request in flight at once (`EXTRA="env LATENCY_MS=1500" ./matrix.sh <bin> 20000 20000 jsonl`) were 6.9 and 8.2 GB resident on master, 8.8 and 9.4 GB with subagents keeping bodies and 7.4 and 8.7 GB without, so the memory this rule saves is argued from what is held, not shown. What is left in the Claude turn at swarm scale, each at or under about 0.6%: the cursor's JSON (0.64%), hashing a cursor or step output that is stored inline (0.62%), serializing the request head and tail into temporaries before copying them into the body (0.6%), identity strings in snapshots, `candidate_id`'s `getentropy` (0.34%), and nested-call metadata in claude_tools.rs (0.6%, another owner's file).
- Cache markers are read where they are typed; the per-message layout cache is removed (2026-11-11). `validate_cache_layout` runs four or five times per request (`cache_floors_with`, `cache_system_tail_with`, `cache_tools_tail_with`, `prepare_cached_wire`). For each client tool with a marker it built a `Value` from the typed `CacheControl` and parsed it back, and for each marked system block it cloned the marker's `Value` to parse it; the typed marker is now read directly and a block's marker is deserialized by reference. The per-message `CacheLayout` cache that came with the request-body change is removed because it did not measure: with it `validate_cache_layout` was 1.30% of the turns profile against 1.09% without (mock at 23.6% and 20.9%); the walk is bound by reaching each message, not by reading its blocks. `AdmittedIds` allocates its map on the first insert and its `Clone` no longer builds a default, so an empty conversation costs no allocation again (the persistent map had added one per snapshot, 0.09% of the swarm). 20,000 agents on JSONL, master to head: `validate_cache_layout` 0.37% to 0.11%, `cache_tools_tail_with` 0.14% to 0.03%; with the system-block clone gone since the request-body change, `cache_system_tail_with` is 0.27% to 0.01%. Measured and left: in a long conversation the four or five walks over the history are still 0.7 to 1.3% of the turns profile. Skipping the walks whose result cannot change the outcome (no image floors, system already marked) would leave two, and would move where an invalid layout is reported from `cache_system_prefix` to `prepare_wire`, which is why it is not done.
- An initial checkpoint and an assistant message are serialized once (2026-11-11). `persist_initial` built a `Value` tree of the child's snapshot for `ClaudeExecutionPolicy::initial_checkpoint`, which serialized and dropped it. The trait has `initial_checkpoint_encoded(Box<RawValue>, model)` beside it, as `advance_encoded` stands beside `advance`: the default decodes for policies that implement only the `Value` form, the durable policy implements the encoded one and maps the `Value` form onto it, and `persist_initial` serializes the snapshot directly. The stored checkpoint has the same fields, in declaration order where a build without `preserve_order` sorted them. A model receipt (`Effect::model_completion`) serialized and hashed the assistant message, and the history then serialized and hashed the same message again for the wire and for its record; `model_completion` now returns the JSON and record it made (`Recorded`) and `run_rounds` builds the history message with them (`HistoryMessage::recorded`). 20,000 agents on JSONL, master to head: `persist_initial` 1.57% to 1.30% (0.91% in the profile taken at this commit; what remains is `DurableSession::prepare`, `OwnerId::new` and the pool adoption in crates/runtime/durability), `HistoryMessage::json` 0.29% to 0.13%, `HistoryMessage::record` 0.65% to 0.47%. - A request clones its tools once, and a kept request shares them (2026-11-11). A `ClaudeToolSpec` owns its description and schema (about 20 KB for `exec`), and each round copied the tool list four times: `run_rounds` cloned the template's tools to pass them beside the template, `request_response` cloned the template (tools included) and dropped one copy, `keep` cloned the whole request and the sent message list for cache refreshes, and `publish_side_request` cloned the template for side questions. `request_response` now takes tools only when they differ from the template's (`Option<Vec<ClaudeToolSpec>>`), `KeptRequest` holds the request and the sent messages by `Arc`, and the side request is republished only when the template or wire profile changed (`FrozenWireProfile` and `SubscriptionIdentity` derive `PartialEq`). One clone per request remains: the request marks its last tool for caching. 20,000 agents on JSONL, master to head: frames under `MessagesRequest` (clone, drop, markers) 1.80% to 1.10%, `publish_side_request` 0.30% to 0.22%. Left: sharing the tool list itself (`Arc<[ClaudeToolSpec]>` in `MessagesRequest`, or an `Arc` per definition) would remove the last clone and its drop (about 0.5%), and changes a public field that tool assembly in other crates writes.
- A turn encodes its cursor once before its first request, and a snapshot no longer copies what grows (2026-11-11). A new operation's cursor was encoded in `State::cursor` and again a few lines later, once the prompt was prepared; `Journal::advance` replaced the first before anything was written, so a third of `encode_cursor` (2.4% of a 20,000-agent swarm) was thrown away. `cursor()` no longer stages it; `stage_cursor` does at the three places where the journal is flushed before the prompt is prepared: a lifecycle hook that handles the event (`flush_for_lifecycle`), compaction at the start of a turn, and manual compaction. What changes: a turn that fails before its prompt is prepared (a hook blocks it, a lifecycle or policy call errors) no longer leaves an unprepared continuation in the journal; it had made no model call, and a retry builds the cursor again as it would for a new operation. Snapshots: `AdmittedIds` is an `imbl::Vector` and a `nanocode_sync::Map` (a clone was a `HashMap` copy per snapshot, several snapshots per round, growing with every tool call the session ever made); the date shown in the environment text is kept beside it instead of found with `rfind` on every snapshot; `Snapshot::provider` is borrowed; `template_record` and `WireCache::system` compare a system prompt by pointer before by value (`TemplatePrompt::system` and `system_fingerprint` take the `Arc`). The stored JSON is unchanged. 20,000 agents on JSONL, master to head: `encode_cursor` 2.37% to 1.67%, `defer_cursor` 3.08% to 2.13%, `template_record` 0.33% to 0.03%. turns, master to head: `AdmittedIds` 0.99% to 0.16%, `State::snapshot` 1.53% to 0.50%, `publish_boundary` (dropping snapshots) 1.09% to 0.25%. Left: a snapshot still clones the model, workspace, conversation id and lineage strings (0.18% plus drops) and `kept_context` (0.19 to 0.32%); what remains of `encode_cursor` is the cursor's own 2.4 KB of JSON (0.64%, most of it identical from one encode to the next within a turn) and the message records.
- A turn's request bodies grow in place, and the conversation digest is hashed incrementally (2026-11-11). `api_body` allocated a new body for every request, copied every message's cached JSON into it, and hashed all message digests again for the durable input; in one session of 400 turns of three cells that was 10.5% of the profile, most of it `memmove` into fresh pages. `WireCache` now keeps the last streamed body with its per-message end offsets, the per-message digests and the two running blake3 states (`Assembled`) while a turn holds `WireCache::keep_body()`; `api_body` takes it back when nobody else holds the bytes, keeps the prefix whose head bytes are identical and whose message digests match, truncates there and appends the rest and the tail. The conversation digests are the same values (blake3 over the same digest sequence), fed from the kept state when the prefix is whole and rebuilt otherwise. The guard is dropped when the turn ends, so an idle session holds no body; requests that are not streamed (cache refreshes) or that carry a message thread do not take part. `cache_system_tail_with` no longer clones the system blocks to find that they already carry a marker. The bytes sent are unchanged: 601 request bodies of a 150-turn session, up to 3.87 MB and across compactions, have the same digest and length as master's (`BODY_LOG=<file> turns-<v> memory x 150 3 4000`, `cmp`). turns on the memory store, `sample` at 1 ms: `api_body` 10.49% to 5.58% with the mock at 20.9% and 23.6% (what remains is one whole copy on a turn's first request, one reallocation when the buffer grows, and the tail); user CPU for 400 turns 2.66 to 2.77 s before, 2.41 to 2.68 s after. A swarm's bodies (27 KB) are too small to show it. This commit also cached each message's cache-marker layout; that did not measure and is removed two commits later. Measured and left: the first request of a turn still copies the body and rehashes the digests, because keeping the state across turns would cost every idle session the body and 3.8 KB of hasher state; a host transport (`HttpTransport`, the WASM path and the harness mock) still gets its own `String` copy of the body (`body.to_string()` in `ClaudeClient::post`, 2.35% of the turns profile), which is `HttpRequest`'s public shape.

Every event a turn emits was a `json!` tree: built, given its `turn_id` by a map insert, serialized from the tree and dropped; `State::publish` with what its callers built was about 3% of a 20,000-agent swarm. `State::emit` and `State::publish` now take any `Serialize`; `agent/event.rs` holds typed payloads for what every turn emits (`input.accepted`, `run.started`, `run.completed`/`run.failed`, `model.call.started`, `model.call.completed`, `assistant.message`, `tool.call` and `tool.result`, top-level and nested), and `InTurn` appends `turn_id` as the payload is written. - 2026-11-11: **`nanocode_tools::plain_schema`: a derived JSON Schema as a person would have written it, beside `schema_for`, which is unchanged.** A host that moves hand-written tool definitions onto derived ones wants the same bytes, so the model's cached prompt survives; schemars says more than a hand-written schema does. `plain_schema(schema)` takes any generator's output as a `Value` (tempoxyz/pyramid-core feeds it schemars 1's draft 2020-12 with subschemas inline; nanocode itself stays on schemars 0.8.22 and `schema_for` does not call it) and returns it without the root's `$schema`, `title`, `description`, `$defs` and `definitions`; with `Option<T>` as `T` (the `null` type, a `null` in an `enum` and a `{"type":"null"}` branch go, and a branch left alone merges into its parent); without an integer's or number's `format`, `additionalProperties: true` or a trivial `default` (null, false, 0, "", [], {}); and with an internally tagged enum as one object: the tag as a string `enum` of the variants' names in declaration order, each property's schema from the first variant that has it, and `required` what every variant requires. The rules are the ones pyramid-core's tool registry was built with (its NOTES.md, Tool registry), moved here so any host's `FunctionTool::typed_with_parameters` can use them. Checked on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-tools` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, no warnings; `output/schema-plain` 3 of 3: a struct with an enum of strings, optional fields, bounds, a serde default and a free object, and an internally tagged enum, each derived with schemars 1.2.3 and compared byte for byte with the hand-written schema, and `schema_for` of a struct equal to its bytes before (`format: uint32`, `minimum: 0.0` and all).
- 2026-11-11: **A blocking body that writes keeps its one run (vendored psh, util/blocking.rs).** The inline replay of b231a2287 runs a utility again when its body asked a host that answers later, which is right only for bodies that read. The python branch adds a body that writes (its bundled Python through `run_blocking`), so `SyncCtx::no_replay()`, called before the first change, marks the run: when the body returns, its open questions are dropped, its output and status are kept, and the late answers stay the `WouldBlock` errors it saw. rg, grep, fd and jq never call it. For hosts that answer later the intended plug for Python stays a `Commands` implementation that copies its subtree in first (what nanocode-ts does for Pyodide). Difference from upstream to re-apply: `util/blocking.rs` (`Replay.changed`, `SyncCtx::no_replay`, the pending end of `run_blocking`).
- 2026-11-11: **psh's wasm profile is opt-level 3 (upstream: "s").** Georgios asked for the shell to be faster than what it replaces; under V8 the module at 3 takes 20 to 34% less CPU in the arithmetic loop, awk, sed and jq, where psh at s lost to nanocode-ts's TypeScript shell, for 1.40 MB more (0.43 MB gzipped). Measured and not taken: opt-level 2 (7,079,407 bytes, no smaller than 3); the psh crates and nanocode-shell at 3 with their dependencies at s (6,732,418 bytes, 2,264,681 gzipped; loop 93.2, awk 370.5, sed 568.6, jq 93.5: about the same speed for 0.34 MB less, kept out because it needs five `[profile.wasm.package.*]` tables that must follow the crate list; a host that counts bytes can take it). At 3 string appending in a loop is slower than at s (67 against 40 ms for 2,000 appends), which is in psh-engine. Difference from upstream to re-apply: `[profile.wasm] opt-level` in crates/patches/psh/Cargo.toml.
- 2026-11-11: **psh-wasm: an answer given during the call is the call's return value, and the module counts its live bytes against the host's budget.** A filesystem that answers synchronously still paid `psh_in`, `psh_complete` and an insert and remove in the module's operation table (a SipHash map) per operation. `K_FS` now returns the length of the answer in the input buffer, a negative errno, or `LATER` (i32::MIN) when `psh_complete` will follow; only a later answer is registered (which also removes a window in which an answer arriving before the future's first poll was dropped). `cap.rs` is a global allocator over `System` that counts live bytes: `psh_memory_limit(bytes)` sets the most the module may hold, an allocation past it fails as any failed allocation does (the module aborts), `psh_memory_exceeded()` tells the JS side why, and the JS side reports the budget and loads a fresh instance. The limit is the module's (shells running at once share it), and it bounds live heap bytes, not the 16 MiB stack or allocator slack. Differences from upstream to re-apply: `cap.rs` (new), `lib.rs` (the `#[global_allocator]` on wasm32), `sys.rs` (`LATER`), `ops.rs` (`next`, `wait`; `take_now` removed), `host.rs` (`fs`).
- 2026-11-11: **Fuel is commands and loop iterations, not a utility's inner loop (vendored psh, sched.rs).** `Shell::spent` counted every safepoint, and utilities take one per chunk or line through `UtilCtx::check`, so `cut -c1-2 big.txt | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3` over 1,000,000 lines spent more than 1,000,000 units and nanocode-ts's `maxCommands` of 1,000,000 ended it with 'too many commands'. `UtilCtx::check` and the blocking thread loop now pass `sched::checkpoint`, which yields at the step's budget exactly as before (so a long utility still gives the embedder its turn and a cancel reaches it) and is not counted. Alternatives weighed: synchronous answers only (excludes SqlFileSystem and every remote store), prefetching the operands' trees before the body (the body decides what it reads; gitignore rules prune), making the argument types `Clone` to rerun the body alone (touches every argument type in psh-utils and fd's `-x` would still run on partial results). Chosen: the inline backend keeps what the body asked in a `Replay` (`stat`, `read_dir`, `open`); an open question gives the body `WouldBlock`; when the body returns with questions open, nothing it printed is written, `run_blocking` never returns, `util::run_with` drops the utility's future, awaits the questions (a file is read to its end, stdin is kept from the first run) and calls the utility again with the same argv. A walk costs about depth + 2 runs, each over answers already there; a host that answers at once never replays. Bodies only read, so a second run changes nothing; what the async front end printed before its body would print twice (none of the four does). Differences from upstream to re-apply: `util/blocking.rs` (`Replay`, `Held`, `Waiting`, `Refused`, the three `SyncCtx` file operations, `FileInner::Held`, `run_blocking`'s stdin and its pending end, `block_on_once` removed) and `util.rs` (`UtilCtx::replay`, the loop in `run_with`).
- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-shell` (crates/core/shell): psh's engine and its in-process utilities over a host-supplied filesystem, for hosts without an operating system** (Georgios: "a vendored bash here in rust that we re-export / use in both nanocode-ts via wasm and/or via nanocode-swift"; Pyramid's hand-free workspace wants it in-process). It is in `core/` because it depends on nothing above it and both a native host and the WebAssembly module embed it. The contract: `FileSystem` is whole-file operations on absolute, normalized byte paths (`stat(path, follow)`, `read(path, limit) -> Bytes`, `write(path, data, Replace | Append | New)`, `list`, `mkdir`, `remove(File | Dir)`, `rename`, and optional `symlink`, `read_link`, `set_mode`, `set_mtime` that default to Unsupported), each answering `Reply::Now(result)` or `Reply::Later(future)`. psh's engine is synchronous and stepped and waits only through wakers, so a step suspends for host I/O by a task's future staying pending: `Shell::step(budget)` answers `Blocked`, the host completes its future and wakes the waker it was given (`Shell::set_waker`), and steps again; `Shell::run(script, budget)` is the same as a `!Send` future for any executor. No async runtime, thread or lock is in the crate (`Rc`, `Cell`, `RefCell`; the shell stays on the thread that made it). `Commands { has(name), run(Call) -> future of the status }` is the host's own commands (a bundled Python, git, the network): a `Call` has argv, env, cwd and three `Stream`s over the shell's pipes and files; psh finds a host command as `/usr/bin/NAME`. `Machine` is the clock, timers and entropy; `Identity` the user, host name and `OSTYPE` facts. `Limits { fuel, output, file, operations, depth }` all come from the host: fuel is commands and loop iterations, output is bytes of stdout and of stderr kept (more is dropped and `Ran::truncated` set), file is the largest file read or written whole, operations is filesystem calls. A run ends `Exited(status)`, `Cancelled` or `Refused(Fuel | Operations | Missing)` (`Config::strict` makes a command that is not found end the run) and reports `Changes`: paths written, removed, made, linked, chmod-ed and moved, with a path created and then moved reported under its last name. Open files live in the crate: a read is one `read` and a `Bytes` cursor; a redirect is one empty `write` at open (Replace, Append or New, so a read-only or missing parent fails where bash fails) and one Append per engine write (utilities buffer 64 KiB); `<>` and in-place writes hold the file and replace it whole. `/dev/null`, `/dev/zero`, `/dev/random` and `/dev/urandom` are the crate's. Pipes to host commands hold 65,536 bytes, Linux's pipe capacity. `MemFs` is the in-memory `FileSystem` (a tree of `Bytes`, symlinks, modes, times). Root manifest: `psh-engine` and `psh-utils` as workspace path dependencies and `[patch.crates-io] grep-printer` (upstream's patched copy with a clock that exists on wasm32); the lock adds psh's dependencies and moves exactly two existing packages, globset 0.4.19 to 0.4.21 and regex-automata 0.4.16 to 0.4.18, which psh-utils requires (deser-json is pinned to psh's 0.10.1; the alloy and tempfile entries cargo re-resolved were put back). Text for crates/README.md's core table: `nanocode-shell` | The psh shell and its in-process utilities over a host `FileSystem`, with host commands, limits and a change report. Measured (output/shell-harness, release, MemFs, user CPU, medians of 9, three interleaved rounds): a filesystem operation costs 30-50 ns more as `Reply::Later` than as `Reply::Now` and 140-170 ns more when it suspends once; whole workloads over output/psh-bench/data: echo 0.04 ms, view 0.13, smallpipe 0.22, find 2.75, rg 11.6, grepr 19.1, sortpipe 17.1, catall 37.6, jq 55.7, cutsort 114, loop 72, awk 250, sed 387 (the last three are psh's own cost). Why: tempoxyz/pyramid-core gives every statement a name and a latency histogram, and since its durable sessions run on `RowStore` through `SqlxSql` (e853b6bda) those statements are nanocode's batches, which the host could not see: `SqlxSql` dropped the operation name. Checked on 2026-11-11 on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-sql`; output/rowcheck `pg` 49 of 49 with a host that counts `ran` calls and prints them per operation.
- RowStore serves a database that several processes share and that holds more states than fit in memory (2026-11-11, for tempoxyz/pyramid-core, whose durable sessions move from a store of its own onto this one; Georgios: "reusing 100% of upstream for durability"). Eight changes, each because that host needs it. (1) The index is per state: a record is stored once in every state that names it, as JSONL stores it once per session file, where one map covered the database and a record any state had written was never written again. A host with 100,000 threads cannot hold every key, a state's dead records cannot be deleted while other states read them out of its pages, and what a root's sessions share already goes through the pool (f2e065514). An unbounded store, the default, still reads the whole index with two statements at its first read; `bounded(keys)` reads a state when something names it and drops the least recently used states past `keys`. A state another process wrote is noticed by its tail's length and page count at `acquire`, by the page count at `put_records`, and by a reload when a read misses or a page is gone; a reload takes effect only if its revision and page count are not behind the index's. (2) `put_records` is implemented: records staged ahead of a commit become a page of their own, written only while the state's page count is the one the index holds, and retried once after a reload. (3) `lent(host)` is the store over a connection a host lends inside its own transaction: it keeps no shared index, since the transaction may roll back, writes a page for a commit that carries records and only moves the head for one that does not, and the shared index learns of the commit as it would of another process's. `nanocode_store_sql::SqlxTransaction` is public for it. (4) `in_schema(name)` places both tables; the statement texts are rendered once per schema and kept. (5) `examine` and `compact` delete what a head no longer reaches, when the dead records weigh at least what stays or a page is not yet packed; `unswept` lists the states whose revision moved since, by `state_rows.swept` (rows format 2); `collect` takes the dead keys from the caller as SqlStore's does. A compaction moves the fence and the page count, so an owner or a staged page from before it is refused and never left naming a deleted record. (6) `packed(codec)`: pages go through a `PageCodec` the host gives (`nanocode_store_sql::Zstd`), and on Postgres `state_pages.body` is `BYTEA` (rows format 3), a packed page being a newline and the codec's bytes; SQLite keeps the page as text, the bytes in base64. A sealed page is now built by the store rather than as `tail || ?` in SQL, guarded by the tail's length. (7) A commit that adds no record leaves the tail column alone, where `tail || ''` rewrote it. (8) The conversion from SqlStore's tables gives every state its own copy of a record several hold. Checked on 2026-11-11 on dev-georgios (output/rowcheck and output/rowbench, their own workspaces; Postgres 18 in Docker and SQLite through a rusqlite `Sql` host in the harness; load 8 to 22). `rowcheck`: 3,000 random steps a seed against a model, two store instances standing for two processes plus reopens, over six states (acquire, commit with fresh records, repeated ones and other states' records, put_records, collect, examine and compact, lent commits that commit or roll back, reads of held and absent keys, list_records, owner and peek after every step, a fresh instance reading every state whole at the end): 24 of 24 seeds on SQLite and 48 of 48 on Postgres (half in a named schema, half bounded to 40 keys, a third packed with zstd), and the conversion of five SqlStore states that share 12 records, each read whole and one continued. `rowbench`, the build before against this one, interleaved, 200 states of 30 commits of 3 fresh records of 600 B plus one record every commit of every state repeats: Postgres WAL 42.6 to 43.0 KB a state before and 41.9 to 42.5 KB after, the tables 6.5 MB before and 6.9 MB after three runs (the repeated record once per state instead of once); SQLite 44.7 MB before and 47.0 MB after, writes 0.55 to 0.57 s both; a new store's first commit on a database of 600 states 0.027 s before and 0.002 s after. 100,000 states of 20 records (`seed-scale.sql`): before, a new store's first commit takes 1.3 s and the process holds 462 to 635 MB; unbounded now, the first read loads the index and it holds 535 MB; `bounded(250000)` commits in 0.01 s and holds 13 MB after 2,000 states were read. The conversion of 2,000 SqlStore states holding 668,002 records of 1.18 GB (`seed-big.sql`): 32 to 41 s, 78,000 pages, 1.44 GB of WAL. pyramid-core on this store (its runtime harness against mocks of the Responses and Messages APIs): the model requests of a six-turn session with cells, a handoff mid model call, a subagent handoff and a crash at each of 50 commit points equal those on its own store but for one crash request whose text depends on a race (it differs between two runs of either build); sessions converted from SqlStore's tables, then swept and repacked, continue with the same requests; its measurements are in its NOTES.md. `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-durability-core -p nanocode-durability -p nanocode-store-sql` natively and the first two for wasm32-unknown-unknown.

Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-mcp` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; output/lanes-check: a pair from `from_random` is valid and verifies, another pair's challenge, an empty side, `plain`, a short or padded or non-base64url challenge, a 42 or 129 character verifier and one with `+` or a space are refused.
- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode_sync::Lanes::bounded`: per-key batches with every bound named and nothing dropped unseen.** nanocode-sync had a `Lanes` whose bounded mode dropped items silently and lost it (9238bf177), then lost the unbounded one for want of a user; tempoxyz/pyramid-core kept its own for the Hand broker's admissions and receipts, and that one moves here with its numbers as arguments. `Lanes::bounded(Bounds { queued, batch, idle, lanes }, refused)` routes each `send(key, item, commit)` to its key's lane: a lane commits what arrived together, at most `batch` at a time and in order, one commit at a time per key, ends after `idle` without an item and is replaced when the key's next item comes (the new lane waits for the old one's last commit); finished lanes are swept once more than `lanes` are known. Both ways an item is turned away are visible: `send` gives the item back when `queued` items already wait for the router, and an item that reaches a lane already holding `batch` goes to `refused`, so the host answers whoever waits on it. `together(batch, commit)` is the commit helper that goes with it: one commit for the batch, and when that fails, one per item, so one bad item fails alone; an item whose own commit returned nothing is `Ok(None)`. Native only, like the other task-owning blocks here (it spawns and uses timers). Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; output/lanes-check on dev-georgios (bounds 64 queued, batches of 8, 200 ms idle): 30 items over 5 keys all commit in key order in batches of at most 8; 200 items sent at once for one key are 8 committed in order, 56 refused by the full lane and 136 handed back by the full queue, none unaccounted; after the idle time the key's next item commits on a new lane; `together` on a failing batch of three answers `Ok(Some)`, the item's own error and `Ok(None)`. pyramid-core's broker runs on it with its bounds unchanged (16,384 queued, 4,096 a batch, 5 s idle, 1,024 lanes).
- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-observability` maps nanocode's spans to the GenAI conventions, holds a request's spans until its root says whether to keep them, and gives a host its events as lines and its counters by name.** Three pieces a server host needs beside `ObservabilityBuilder`, each from tempoxyz/pyramid-core's `telemetry.rs` with its names turned into arguments; none changes what `ObservabilityBuilder::install` does. `GenAi<E>` wraps a span exporter: `model.call` becomes `chat <model>` with `gen_ai.request.model`, the response id, token counts and the provider (taken from the span, else from the backend crate that emitted it), `tool.call` and `tool.execute` become `execute_tool <name>`, the host's own agent span (`Agent { span, name }`) becomes `invoke_agent <name>`, and the content events nanocode emits when message content is captured (`prompt`, `model.input`, `model.output_item`, `reasoning`, `tool.arguments`, `tool.output`, `tool.panic`) are folded into `gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages` and the tool call attributes; every other span and event passes through. `Held<P>` wraps a span processor: spans whose target is one of `Holding::targets` wait until their trace's server root ends, and the trace is exported whole if the root took `slow` or longer, failed, or its trace id is a multiple of `one_in`; otherwise the root's subtree is dropped and whatever else the trace held is exported. A trace whose root does not arrive within `slow` is released, at most `most` spans wait, and without a `Holding` everything passes. `Lines` is a layer that formats an event as `LEVEL target: message field=value` for a host's log function, `Counters` turns the `monotonic_counter.*` fields of `nc_metrics` events into `nanocode_<name>_total` for a host's own metrics, and `Exports` is the filter for what a host exports (spans of the listed targets, content events only when `OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT` is true, request spans only when asked). What they count goes to the host through plain functions (`Exported`, `Ended`), because the crate links no metrics library and the names are the host's. The Prometheus listener stays in pyramid-core: it needs `metrics-exporter-prometheus` and axum, which `nc` would then link for nothing, and Cargo features are not allowed here. The crate gains `nanocode-sync` and `imbl` (the held spans are an `Atom` of a `Map` and vectors). Checked on dev-georgios: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-observability` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (the crate is empty there); /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/telemetry-capture builds pyramid-core's `telemetry::init` and `serve_metrics` before (42fbdbf, its own exporter and processor) and after (on these), emits a turn with model calls of four providers, tool calls, every content kind, slow, failed, fast and rootless request traces, log lines and counter events in three settings (slow request traces with content, all request traces, neither), captures the OTLP trace requests on a local server and scrapes `/metrics`: 61 spans decoded attribute by attribute, the log lines and 445 metric lines, 715 lines in all, identical.
