- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-sandbox` runs a confined program for a host: `run::Runner`.** The crate had the parts (`Bubblewrap`, `confine::Policy`, the allowlisting `Egress`, `Budget`) and tempoxyz/pyramid-core had the code that put them together for its organization tools; that assembly is now here, without the names. A `Runner` is a `Confinement` (`Bubblewrap { bwrap, root, work }`, where what the program reads is mounted under `root` and its scratch directory at `work`, or `Landlock { launcher }`, where it reads the host's paths in place), a scratch directory, a socket directory it creates and removes, the proxy's `Reach`, the `Caps` on what comes back and the `Budget`. `Runner::run(Call, compose)` makes the call's own scratch directory and proxy (a unix socket bound into the mount namespace, or a loopback port the Landlock policy allows), builds the confined command from the call's program and `reads`, and hands `compose` the `Seen` (`Mounted` or `InPlace`: where each read, the scratch directory, the proxy and the host socket appear to the program) so the host adds its arguments and environment; nothing about the program's command line or variable names is decided here. It writes `input` to stdin, keeps stdout up to `Caps::output` and the last `Caps::errors` bytes of stderr, and answers with one `Ran`: `Exited` with both and the hosts the proxy refused or could not reach, `TimedOut` after `within`, `Overflowed`, or `Stopped` by the budget's watch of the admission the caller passed. A call with a `Host` gets a socket on which the program sends length-prefixed header and body frames and reads a header and the reply's parts; parts are charged to the budget, and a refusal is the header `Host::busy` gives. A channel failure is handed to `Host::failed` when it happens rather than logged here, and the scratch directory, the host socket and, under Landlock, the process group are removed however the call ends. Admission stays with the caller because what counts as a computing call is its policy. Unix only, as the crate is. Checked on dev-georgios (Linux 6.8, so Landlock ABI 6 is absent and only the bubblewrap arm ran; the Landlock arm is built and reviewed, not run): `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-sandbox` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`; /home/ubuntu/dev/harnesses/sandbox-run builds pyramid-core's `Sandbox` before (eec0437, its own runner) and after (on this `Runner`) and drives 16 cases through a program standing where bubblewrap does, which reports its argument vector and environment, the scratch directory and proxy socket, its stdin and a host channel session (an echo, a host failure, parts within and beyond the budget, a header that is not JSON): a plugin directory and a single file, credentials that override `PATH`, declared hosts, describe, garbage with a 70 KB stderr, 5 MiB of output, a refusal, exit 3, stdin closed early, a 30 s timeout and an input too large to admit. The 700 lines each side prints (results, log lines, metrics, what is left in the scratch and socket directories) are identical.

- 2026-11-11: **`nanocode-machine`: a lifecycle is declared once, as states with wire names and a table of moves.** `machine!` moves here from tempoxyz/pyramid-core's `kernel-protocol`, which now re-exports it, so any host can use what Pyramid's lifecycles are built on. One declaration (`machine! { pub enum Turn stored in "turns"."status" by "id" sql turn { Queued = "queued", Running = "running", Done = "done" } moves { Queued => [Running, Done], Running => [Done] } }`) gives the enum (serde, `Display` and `TryFrom<&str>` by wire name; an unknown name is `Unknown`), `Machine` (`ALL`, `MOVES`, `may`, `next`, which refuses and logs a move the table lacks, `sources`, `terminal`), and for a stored machine the text a SQL host needs so the column, the enum and the write cannot disagree: the column's `CHECK` (`Machine::check`), the fenced move `UPDATE turns SET status = $2 WHERE id = ANY($1) AND status::text = ANY($3) RETURNING id` (`Machine::fence`, with the caller's own `SET` and `WHERE`; a typed key as `by "id" as "bigint"`, several key columns joined by the unit separator, `key` and `Stored::matches`), and with `sql name` a macro `name!(State)` that is the quoted literal for `concat!` (`export sql` exports it; a `sets` block names lists of states, checked against the wires at compile time). It is its own `core/` crate because it is neither a sync primitive nor tied to a store: it depends on `tracing` alone and builds for wasm32. The grammar and every generated string are what pyramid-core had; the two literal-macro arms became one that takes the macro's scope attribute. Checked: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-machine` natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, `node scripts/check-dependency-boundaries.mjs`, and output/machine-dump on dev-georgios: `gen.py` takes all 84 `machine!` declarations of pyramid-core eec0437 and tempoxyz/pyramid 1e3d8bbfc (43 with a literal macro, 18 exported, 5 with sets), `mk.py` builds them once against pyramid-core's `machine.rs` and once against this crate, and each binary prints every state's wire, JSON, `Display`, sources and terminal, every pair's `next` with its refusal and log line, `STORED`, `check`, `fence`, `matches`, `columns`, `text` and all 145 literals: 4,106 lines, identical but for the log line's target (`kernel_protocol::machine` became `nanocode_machine`).
- 2026-11-10: **djs through the CLI on the live API, and cells that never yield.** Measured, nothing changed. `nc` built from `614de7032` (`cargo build --release --locked -p nanocode-cli -p nanocode-cua-driver` in `output/release-cli-b6e1f6688`) and installed over the build from `bd7dbf986`, which is kept in `output/nc-backup-bd7dbf986`. `nc exec -m claude-haiku-5-5 -t low` in an empty home: one cell spawned 17 subagents and waited for them, all 17 completed, 10.5 s of wall and 0.16 s of user CPU (the same run on QuickJS was 0.36 s); resuming that session listed 17 completed agents, messaged agent 3 and read its new result. With the engine on tokio's workers instead of its own threads, what a runaway cell does matters, so output/durability-ledger `stuck` runs one on a two-worker runtime beside a 10 ms ticker and terminates it after 1.5 s: `while (true) {}`, a loop that allocates strings and the catastrophic regex `/(a+)+$/` on 40 `a`s and a `b` each stop within 1 ms of the terminate and the ticker keeps its pace (135 of 150 ticks), because djs meters fuel inside its regex engine as it does in bytecode; a loop that grows an array stops in 62 ms; `'x'.repeat(1 << 28).split('')` is one builtin call djs does not slice and holds its worker for 3.2 s before the terminate lands, while the other worker keeps ticking. On WASM the same cells end with the CPU-budget message once `set_interrupt_checks` slices are used. The VFS session (`01a1c90e`) is about nanocode-ts: what carries over from this work is that a cell's regex can no longer hold a Durable Object's event loop past its budget, and that a djs heap is a byte image a host could store, which would let a held cell be parked as its difference from the snapshot instead of 320 KB of memory or a journal replay; that is not built.
- The cell journal's tool catalog is encoded once per process, and where a swarm's CPU is after djs (2026-11-10). `0e6c253da` cached each catalog's encoding in `DurableCellJournals`, but every session builds its own sink (`agent-host/src/lib.rs`), so each child's first cell still serialized and hashed the catalog: 1.53% of a 20,000-agent swarm at `4d35b9af3`. The cache is now a static, keyed by the shared metadata's pointer as before; the same profile shows `EncodedPayload::encode::<[Value]>` at 0.00%. Three interleaved runs do not resolve it in user CPU (43.4 to 45.1 s before, 43.9 to 44.6 s after, run to run about ±1 s). Measured and left out: a pool of spare djs instances per snapshot (one slot per core, `Instance::reset` on reuse) so a cell copies the image into a heap that is already mapped and already grown: no change in `jsbench` (49 to 54 µs against 50 to 56 µs for `text('ok')`) or the swarm (42.0 to 42.1 s against 41.5 to 41.8 s), mimalloc already hands those blocks back cheaply, so it is not in the tree. What the swarm's samples are now (`deptable.py`, `selff.py`, `treef.py`, `callersf.py` in output/durability-ledger): our crates 34.6%, the allocator and `memmove` 15.9% (`mi_page_thread_collect_to_local` alone 5.1%: blocks freed on another tokio worker than the one that allocated them), serde_json 12.5%, kernel 9.6% (`madvise` 2.4%, the journal's `F_FULLFSYNC` 1.9%, `getentropy` 1.1%), tokio 5.8%, djs 5.5%, arc_swap 4.8%, blake3 4.3% (content keys; aarch64 has no SIMD single-block compress, so short payloads hash on the portable path). By what the work is for: building a child's tools is 3.4% (`claude_tools::install`: `route_workspaces`, `model_specs`, `for_session`) and dropping the child 4.1% (`drop_glue::<Agent>` 2.3%, `CodeModeExecutors::forget` 1.3%, one shared `Atom` that every session's start and end rewrites), so about a tenth of the CPU is a per-agent fixed cost; JSON string escaping and unescaping is about 5% across the JSONL lines, cursors, events and records; `code_mode_definitions` rebuilds the definition list on every cell start to check the cached metadata (0.9%). One session of 400 turns of three cells on the memory store is 9.5 ms of CPU a turn, half of it the harness's mock reading the growing request; of ours, assembling the request body is 7%, persisting 5%, the cursor 3%; on JSONL the same session waits a further 12.7 ms a turn on `F_FULLFSYNC`.
- A cell's setup is in its snapshot, and a script may declare its own `text`, `load` or `console` (2026-11-10). After the move to djs the interpreter was 10.3% of a 20,000-agent swarm, nearly all of it `runCell` rebuilding, for every cell, what does not depend on the cell: parsing the tool definitions, the `tools` proxy, `ALL_TOOLS`, the console, and fifteen globals. Every cell is a fresh copy of a snapshot, so that work now runs once when the snapshot is built: `cell::snapshot` keys snapshots by the shared `Arc<CellTools>` (by pointer, held weakly, pruned when a catalog dies) and the prelude, the definitions enter as a data global, and `runCell(source)` starts the pump, calls the prelude if there is one, compiles the script and runs it. Descriptions and schemas are no longer copied into every cell: `ALL_TOOLS[i].description` and `toolSchema` fetch them from the host on first use (`__nanocodeCatalog`). The script is compiled without parameters and finds the helpers as globals, which fixes what the first djs commit broke: with the helpers as parameters, `const text = ...`, `let image, load, store` and `class console {}` were redeclarations and failed to compile, where QuickJS's script goal had allowed them (output/durability-ledger `cells` 33 to 36). Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (`jsbench`, load 25 to 56, CPU per cell): `text('ok')` 108 to 119 µs to 53 to 63 µs, p50 0.28 to 0.30 ms to 0.10 to 0.11 ms; two tool calls 171 to 181 to 120 to 122 µs; 16 parallel tool calls 387 to 394 to 336 to 341 µs. 20,000 agents, three interleaved runs: user CPU 44.4 to 45.3 s to 41.2 to 42.5 s. `cells` (43), `preludecheck`, `cellreplay`, `sinkreplay`, the swarm matrix, kill and resume, kill twice, trees with and without hibernation and cancel and close pass as before; clippy is clean for native and `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- Code Mode cells run on djs, on the task that drives them (2026-11-10, Georgios: "Let's vendor djs instead of rquickjs"). QuickJS was 25% of a 20,000-agent swarm's CPU and about 0.4 ms of every cell: a context's intrinsics, the bootstrap's bytecode load, the native functions and a teardown collection, on a pool of worker threads reached over channels. `nanocode-code-mode-engine` now builds one djs snapshot per prelude (the bootstrap evaluated once, host functions declared) and a cell is an `Instance` copied from it: a 300 KB image, no compile and no setup. The engine has one host for native and WASM (`host.rs`; `native.rs`, `wasm.rs`, `build.rs` and the WASI header are gone, and with them the C compiler, bindgen and the wasi-libc sysroot a WASM or iOS build needed). There are no worker threads: `EmbeddedHost::read_event` steps the VM in djs's fuel slices (200,000 fuel, about 1 ms) and yields to tokio between them, so a cell runs on the task that awaits it and a busy loop cannot hold a worker; `start_cell`, `send_tool_result`, `hold` and `release` only queue, and take `&mut self`. Every host function is synchronous and answered in call order, so tool call ids, events and journal entries are in the order QuickJS produced and an existing cell journal replays. One async host call, the pump, carries what the host delivers, one macrotask each: a tool result, a timer, the unhandled rejections (from the vendored `resolve_unhandled`), and a settle mark the script asks for when it finishes so rejections are reported before the terminal. The script is the body of an `AsyncFunction` (djs has no script goal at run time); stack positions are rewritten to the cell's own lines. `Date.now()`, `performance.now()` come from the host, `Math.random` is seeded per cell, and the local time zone is the host's offset at cell start. The bytes API reads `ArrayBuffer`s in place instead of through latin-1 strings. On WASM `set_interrupt_checks` now counts fuel slices in one synchronous run, and `hold` works. What changes for a script, from output/durability-ledger `cells` (33 cells, the outputs otherwise identical to QuickJS's): the engine is always strict, so assigning to an undeclared name is a `ReferenceError`, `with` and legacy octal literals are `SyntaxError`s, and `this` in a plain function call is `undefined`; stack frames read `at anonymous (<input>:1:75)` with djs's columns; `import()` is refused with djs's message; a cell's heap is capped at djs's 4 GiB. The compact `exec` description says the engine is strict. Measured through `CodeModeRuntime` (`jsbench`, load 22 to 25, CPU per cell, before to after): `text('ok')` 378 to 385 µs to 118 to 120 µs, p50 1.6 ms to 0.26 ms; two sequential tool calls 461 to 471 to 169 to 175 µs; 16 parallel tool calls 594 to 615 to 390 to 398 µs; 20,000 objects through JSON 30 to 32 ms to 19 ms; 5,000 cells waiting 50 ms 431 to 205 to 218 µs each, p50 234 to 450 ms to 75 to 109 ms. Worse: split, join and regex replace with a callback 8.3 to 8.6 ms to 27.9 to 28.1 ms, and a waiting cell holds its 320 KB heap, so those 5,000 peak at 1.04 to 1.11 GB against 557 to 606 MB. 20,000 agents on JSONL, three interleaved runs at load 22 to 34: user CPU 50.3 to 51.6 s to 44.5 to 46.1 s, resident 2.09 to 2.11 GB to 1.64 to 1.70 GB; djs is 10.3% of the samples, nearly all of it the bootstrap's per-cell setup in the interpreter, which is the next thing to move into the snapshot. Checked: `cells`, `preludecheck` (the bytes API against known digests, a prelude's globals, a prelude that does not compile), `cellreplay` and `sinkreplay` (the same results as before; `divergent_replay_falls_back_without_resending` fails on both engines), the swarm matrix on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows, kill and resume, kill twice, trees with and without hibernation, cancel, close, reopen; `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --lib --bins`, and `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode-engine -p nanocode-code-mode --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`. rquickjs leaves the workspace manifest but not the lock: `cua-driver-core` (gakonst/cua, under `nanocode-computer`) still depends on it.

- A cell's journal update shares its calls and tool catalog, and a Claude checkpoint is serialized once (2026-11-10, Georgios: "yes on the Value trees, you can change the datatypes"). Profiled at `39276d8d2` (20,000 agents on JSONL, `sample` at 1 ms, output/durability-ledger `inclf.py` and `callersf.py`): `serde_json::Value` trees cost about 5.8% of CPU, as 2.0% building them from typed data, 2.4% serializing them and 1.4% dropping them. Two owners were concentrated. (1) `CellRecord::persist`, 2.8%: every update cloned each journaled call out of its `Arc` (its `input` is a `Value`), and every cell's first update cloned the session's tool catalog into the header, where `DurableCellJournals::save` serialized and hashed it only to find the key it had already pooled. `CellJournalUpdate::calls` is `Vec<Arc<JournaledCall>>` and `CellJournalHeader::tools` is `Arc<[Value]>`, both the same JSON as before; the sink keeps each live catalog's encoding by the pointer of the shared metadata, so it is encoded once per process, not once per cell. (2) `ClaudeBoundary::checkpoint`, 0.85% plus the drop: a child's checkpoint was built as a `Value` tree of its whole snapshot and serialized from the tree. `SessionCheckpoint`'s payload is `CheckpointPayload`, either a tree or encoded JSON; the Claude backend writes policy, version and snapshot straight to JSON, readers call `payload().decode()`, and a checkpoint still deserializes from any serde source because the payload reads as a tree. The stored JSON has the same fields, in declaration order rather than sorted. 20,000 agents, three interleaved runs at load 14 to 19: user CPU 51.0 to 51.5 s before, 49.4 to 51.1 s after. The swarm matrix, kill and resume (which replays the root's cell from its journal), kill twice, trees with and without hibernation, cancel, close and reopen end as before. A denied call returns `Tool blocked by host: <reason>; tool was not executed` and a failed hook `PreToolUse hook failed: <error>; tool was not executed`, as Claude's `hooked_handler` words them, as the call's failed result, journaled like any other, with nothing run. Tool search, whose output carries no text, is never asked. Like `before_compaction`, the hook is the root's: a branch's spawner sets none. Only `Deny` is offered, not Claude's `UpdateInput`, because no host needs it yet. Why: tempoxyz/pyramid's turn machine refuses a top-level call while a message the agent read mid-turn has no reply, so a member's steer is answered before the agent goes on; on Claude it does this with `ClaudeToolHooks`, and Codex had no way to. Checked on 2026-11-10: `cargo clippy --locked --lib -p nanocode-backend-codex` natively and `cargo check` for wasm32-unknown-unknown; an out-of-repo harness (output/tool-gate) against a local mock of each provider, whose first response makes two `exec` calls and the hook denies only the first, then one more call: on Codex (HTTPS Responses) through this hook and on Claude (Messages) through `ClaudeToolHooks`, the hook was asked once per call, the denied call's result was the text above and its cell never ran, the call after it ran, and the turn completed, 6 of 6 checks on each. Not checked against the live APIs.

- The JSONL index keeps a record's key as its 32 bytes (2026-11-10). A state's record map was `HashMap<String, Record>`, and nearly every key is `b3:` or `c:` followed by 64 hex digits: a 24-byte `String` and an 80-byte allocation beside each 56-byte record. `records::RecordMap` keys the map by `RecordKey` (`Blake([u8; 32])`, `Chunk([u8; 32])`, `Text` for anything else, which round-trips unchanged) and takes and gives keys as text, so the index file, the journal and every caller are as they were. - Finished subagents leave memory and are read back when something names them (2026-11-10, Georgios: "Cut the rest too"). The registry keeps a `ChildSession` only for agents that are doing something; a leaf of the journal's agent tree whose 16 agents are all settled is cold: `AgentScope::cold` holds its record key and stub key, the task tree keeps each agent's parent and session id, `Sessions::by_spawn` its spawning call, and nothing else of it is in memory. Cooling (`AgentScope::cool`) runs in the journal writer's own registry call, so it sees the writer's cache: a leaf goes cold when it has a stub, every agent in it is settled in memory too (`ChildSession::settled`: no harness, task, hibernation, watcher, held residency lock or in-memory checkpoint), every record is the one the leaf holds (`JournalCache::written`), nothing is pending for it (messages, status jobs, captures, unsaved or unrecorded checkpoints), no operation pins it, and all its agents' children are cold or in the same leaf, so a warm agent always has warm ancestors. The writer offers a leaf when a fold writes its stub and when a snapshot finds an agent of a stubbed leaf touched but unchanged, and runs once more after either. Warming (`Registry::warm`) pins the leaves of the ids it is given and of every cold ancestor, reads cold ones back under one sequencer per root (`thaw`: leaf, profiles, `restored_session`, the same registrations a restart makes) and returns a guard that unpins on drop; cooling and warming an agent is a restart of that agent and nothing more. `wait`, `rewait`, `interrupt`, `close` (their subtree), message delivery and every other rehydration, `child_session_id`, `host_context`, `set_budget`, `respawned`, a reservation by a cold parent, and lookups by session id warm what they name; `list_agents` warms the page it returns (`directory_page`), `directory` with completed agents and `resent` warm everything, `resent_to` only the recipient; `running`, `stop_all` and `activity` read the agents in memory, which are all that can be active; `close_all`, shutdown and `cancel_all` act on the agents in memory, and a full journal write (`close_all`'s final one, a fresh writer) carries the cold leaves over (`JournalSnapshot::cold`). A restart reads a stub instead of a leaf and its 16 profiles unless a delta touches the leaf or a warm agent descends from it (`durable::load_leaves`). Two things this made visible are fixed with it. A root's completion notice now leaves its mark in the child's journaled `waited` when the root reads it, so a restart or a cooled child does not hand the root the same result again as new from `wait_agent`. And a clean shutdown could journal children as closed: `release_scope` marks them closed in memory, and a deferred journal slot open at that moment was filled with that state; this build opens such slots more often (unpinning wakes the writer) and hit it in 2 of 4 rounds, the build before in 0 of 12. `release_scope` now saves the journal first, a released scope answers every later save as frozen, and a slot open when the writer finishes is filled with the last payload saved (`refill`). Measured with output/durability-ledger, Claude mock, JSONL, load 45 to 100, against the build before (`swarm-a1`): memory of a finished child held by the registry 4.1 KB to 1.15 KB (`heapdone.sh` 10,000: the whole heap 21.6 KB to 18.6 KB an agent; what remains is the JSONL index 5.4 KB, the root cell's journal 2.4 KB and the session and spawn maps); reopening a finished 100,000-agent tree (`reopen.sh`, 6,250 of 6,251 leaves cold) restores the registry in 0.46 to 0.54 s instead of 2.5 to 3.0 s, of which 0.30 to 0.33 s is the 100,000-message log, which is still read whole, 0.07 to 0.09 s the stubs and 0.08 to 0.10 s placing them, and the process holds 0.92 to 0.96 GB instead of 2.05 to 2.09 GB; at 10,000 agents 40 to 55 ms instead of 130 to 150 ms and 170 MB instead of 236 MB. What it does not change: opening that store's 4.8 GB journal and the root session takes 2.1 to 7.6 s under this load, far more than the registry (`durability.jsonl.recover` 4.4 s of one 6.2 s open: the harness exits before the final index save finishes); a tree killed while its root still holds unread completions has no settled leaf and restores as before (a 100,000-agent run killed at 25,000 finished: 0 stubs); listing every agent warms every agent (0.33 s at 10,000, the same as before). CPU of a 20,000-agent run 72.6 s to 74.7 s, mean of four interleaved, including the final listing that thaws all of it. Checked: 2,000 agents on memory, JSONL, SQLite and rows; kill and resume and kill twice of 3,000 on JSONL, SQLite and rows; 30x100 trees on JSONL and SQLite, hibernating on JSONL; cancel and close with and without hibernation; a 100,000-agent run (6,245 leaves cold at the end, all listed completed after a thaw); `coldcheck` on JSONL and SQLite (session id, interrupt, a message, close and a budget on cold agents, then the same tree after reopening); `relcheck.sh`, 18 rounds of three clean reopens on JSONL, SQLite and rows with no agent closed.

The stub (`LeafStub`: the leaf's size and, per agent, its id, parent, session id and the call that spawned it) is what a restart needs to place such an agent in the task tree without reading its record or its profile; nothing reads it yet. Stubs are written when a leaf is folded (`JournalSnapshot::encode`, `AgentTree::set_stub`), cost 160 B an agent, and a writer set to version 8 or lower writes none. A journal also folds its deltas when no agent is active, owed a completion notice or being resumed (`Sessions::quiescent`, kept by `refresh`; `JournalCache::folds`), where before it folded only when the deltas outgrew the leaves, so an idle tree's journal is its leaves alone: after a 2,000-agent run 125 of 126 leaves have stubs and there are no delta pages (`output/durability-ledger/stubs.py`). - 2026-11-10: **A Claude session rebuilt in the same build sends the system prompt and tools it sent before, and appends what changed.** A session's `system` and `tools` were fixed for as long as its state lived, but a reopened, reloaded or rehydrated session rendered them again, and a different tool list (a tool added, removed or described differently) re-keyed the whole conversation. The snapshot now references the request template the session last sent (the content-addressed record the turn cursor already pools) together with the identity of the executable, and a session rebuilt by the same executable for the same model keeps that `system` and `tools` byte for byte. What the current tool list has that the kept one lacks or defines differently goes out as `tool_addition` blocks carrying the definition, and what it no longer has as `tool_removal` blocks, in a `role: "system"` message after the prompt, with the `inline-tools-2026-09-15` beta (Anthropic's mid-conversation tool changes; Claude Code 2.1.304 carries the same header). What has been announced is read back from the history, so a compaction that summarizes the message away makes the next request announce it again, and tool calls are checked against the current handlers. A static system block the kept prompt does not hold is listed in the "A section of your instructions was updated" reminder next to AGENTS.md. A system message a later user message would follow is moved after it on the wire, since the API accepts one only between a user turn and an assistant turn or at the end. A request refused for its tool changes drops the kept template for that state, sends the current tools and retries once. A new executable, another model, a switch between Code Mode and plain tools, or a store that does not page records renders fresh as before, and tool changes left in the history are removed then. Forks take their parent's template. `output/cache-loss` `retool` (JSONL store, a session reopened with one tool described differently and one added; the mock refuses a misplaced system message and a tool block without the beta): before, the first request after reopening read 0 tokens and wrote 17,563; after, `tools` is byte-identical, it reads 17,507 and writes the 3,911-token redefinition of `exec`, later turns append nothing, a cell calls the new tool, the turn after a compaction announces again, and a second reopening with a tool removed appends one more change; `REFUSE_TOOLS=1` falls back to the fresh tools and completes. - 2026-11-10: **Cancelling a tree stops the children that had not started, and no longer waits 30 s on the ones it missed.** `cancel_all` and `interrupt` marked the turns that existed and waited for them to end. A child still queued for a turn slot had no turn, so it started afterwards and ran to completion; a child attached but not yet in its first turn got its interrupt before the turn began and then ran un-interrupted; and both kinds then blocked on the message pause the cancel was holding, so the cancel sat until `AGENT_STOP_TIMEOUT` and the children failed or completed afterwards. Three changes. A queued child that has not started becomes `Interrupted` and keeps its unstarted runtime; its queued start finds it no longer pending and stops, a later message starts it with its task and then delivers the message, and a restart restores it interrupted. The interrupt loops instead of waiting: on every change it marks whatever turn is active, tells each harness once and wakes each sleeping child once, so a turn that begins after the first pass is stopped on the next. And a message's delivery is settled by a task of its own once it is committed, so a sender whose turn is cancelled between the commit and the release no longer leaves a message pending for ever (which kept a hibernating tree from ever settling after a cancel). `output/durability-ledger` `swarm`, 500 agents, 300 ms model latency, cancel issued between 60 and 700 ms: before, any cancel that found queued children took 30.0 s and left them running (`before {"pending": 379, "running": 121} after {"interrupted": 288, "running": 212}`, then 212 completed and 9 failed); after, 27 of 27 runs without hibernation and 25 of 27 with it end in 0.02 to 0.4 s with every agent interrupted, one is the harness's own peer messages restarting children after an early cancel, and one hibernating run still left 14 running for the 30 s (hibernation is opt-in and nothing but this harness turns it on; open). - 2026-11-10: **A Claude session waiting past its cache lifetime refreshes the cache instead of rewriting it.** Traces of 2026-11-04..09 re-wrote 556.6M tokens on the five-minute cache; 474M of them (778 calls) were one turn waiting in a single tool call (a Code Mode cell blocked in a long Bash call 142M, cells polling with Bash and sleep 219M, `TaskOutput` 56M, `hands`/`runners` polls 25M, `wait_agent` 19M), 59M subagents waiting for their next instruction, 23M side conversations; idle roots lost another 34M on the one-hour cache.
