A new session's first turn skips the phase-only continuation before its first model call when its warmup sends no request (`websocket_warmup` off, or HTTPS), because a crash before that call restarts the turn from the same state without it, and a follow-on turn's PrepareTurn continuation is applied in memory through `DurableOwner::advance_deferred` and persisted with the next commit, such as a pre-turn compaction's step admission, or replaced by the Generate continuation before it is written; the deferred advance leaves the continuation cache and known records unmarked, so the next continuation stages its records again. Both backends admit steps through one rule in runtime/durability: `DurableOwner::admit_step(operation, writes, step, kind, input, recovery)` applies the writes and the step's admission in memory for a `StepRecovery::Rerun` step (a model call, which a resume runs again anyway) and commits them, with every deferred write before them, for an `AtMostOnce` step (a tool call, which must be recorded before it runs); `ResultTiming::of_batch(calls)` leaves the result of a call alone in its batch for the next commit (`NextCommit`, `DurableOwner::complete_step_at`) and commits that of a call among others at once (`Now`). Claude's policy (`BeginRequest::recovery`, set by `begin_model` and `begin_tool`) and Codex's (`model_call` reruns, every other kind is at most once) both use it, so a round with one tool call commits once, at the tool's admission: a turn with one cell and one tool makes 3 store transactions on either backend (admission, the tool's admission, completion) and a text turn 2. The price is the same on both: a crash during the model call after a lone tool call loses that call's result, which the resumed turn reports as `Tool execution interrupted by a host crash; outcome unknown`, and a tool never runs twice (checked on Codex with a mock that answers that model call after 1.5 s and a reopen during it, on Claude with `claudecrash`). Until 2026-11-04 Codex committed before each model call that followed a tool result, and Claude deferred only the last batch of a round; through `vsagents` (in-memory SQLite) a Codex turn with one cell and one tool now makes 3 transactions instead of 4 (9.3 rows instead of 10.3, a text turn 6.2), and Claude's commits are unchanged (`overhead`: 3 for one round, 6 for four). A receipt names its output items by `output_records`, the history items' own records, and leaves out `pipeline_stats` and `timing`, so a replayed call reports default telemetry; a completed turn's output names the last history item by `final_record` when it is the assistant message whose output text is the final message; and the continuation stores `stats` without zero or null fields. Older binaries refuse all three.
- SharedStore checks `concurrent_handle` once: with handles each operation runs on its own handle and task and flush waits for every earlier operation; otherwise its actor sends mutations already queued for other states together through commit_many, and a read, flush or second mutation of a grouped state ends the group (20 sessions committing 150 transitions each took 2.87 s instead of 17.5 s). Every driver commit carries the current summary when supports_summaries is true, `catalog::summarize` owns the StateSummary mapping, and summary preparation failures are NotCommitted. SessionStore::load renders a running turn from its continuation through `CheckpointFormat::hydrate_continuation` and names it in `StoredSession.in_progress`, `SessionReader` serves clients that hold only a StateReader, and Codex's `ContinuationCache` releases its `SequenceLog` entries only after `commit_writes` confirms them.
- `JsonlStore` keeps one file per session (2026-11-03), where it kept every session in one shared `sessions.jsonl` (28.6 GB on the user's machine that day). `open_home(home)` and its async and background forms store sessions in `<home>/sessions/`, one `<key>.jsonl` per session key, the key being a state ID up to its first `:`, so a root's `:subagents` journal and `:process-routes` state share its file and its companion acquisition stays one atomic append (`acquire_with_companion` refuses states of two files as not committed); a file name percent-encodes every byte outside `[A-Za-z0-9_-]`, a `.` after the first byte excepted. `open(dir)` and `open_async(dir)` take such a directory and refuse a file. A session file is the journal the shared file was, with the same lines, fencing, seals, compaction and stand-ins: the worker opens one when an operation first names it (at most 32 at once, least recently used closed first, two descriptors each), replays it whole (no index sidecar; a synthetic 700 MB session file opened in 1.0 to 2.2 s at load average 100), and never creates one for a read, which answers empty. `list_states` and `list_summaries` read the directory, newest file first, and list each file's key. Session files take two more line kinds: `import` sets a state's owner, at the next fence, and its revision and payload when the state's current owner equals its `after` (absent for none), and `records` adds records under the current owner, so a moved state keeps the revision its payload embeds. Opening a home moves the sessions of a legacy `<home>/sessions.jsonl` into their own files (`migrate.rs`): it opens the legacy journal with its index sidecar and, per session key, writes each state as an `import` owned by `legacy-import-<uuid>` at fence 1 and `records` lines of about 4 MiB (stand-ins resolved, literal `\u{1}` values escaped, values read in legacy file order and coalesced across gaps under 1 MiB into reads of up to 16 MiB) to a temporary file synced with `sync_journal` and linked into place without replacing an existing file, copies the legacy summaries still current, and records in `sessions/.legacy.json` the legacy file's identity and length and each state's revision moved, after a directory sync, every 32 sessions and at the end. When the legacy journal has grown since (an older binary still appends to it), the next open moves each state whose revision changed: an `import` batch with the records the file lacks goes into a file whose state an import still owns, nothing goes into one a writer of this build acquired since (its file wins), and nothing recreates the file of a moved session that was deleted. Before writing a session it checks that at least `HEADROOM_BYTES` (1 GiB, policy so that other writers on the disk keep working) would remain free, and otherwise saves its progress and fails the open naming the bytes needed. The legacy file stays for older binaries, which keep their sessions there; it is no longer read once nothing appends to it, and `sessions.jsonl` and `sessions.jsonl.index` can be deleted when no older binary runs. A one-turn session file holds the instructions and tool chunks a session in the shared journal shared with others (about 40 KB against 13.7 KB). Checked on 2026-11-03 on an APFS clone of the user's journal (28.6 GB, 773 states): the move took 50 s and 486 MB of RSS (243 s before reads were ordered and batched, 108 s with ordering alone) and wrote 752 files of 8.3 GB; `nc sessions --all` listed the same 253 sessions as the previous binary on the legacy file and `nc sessions <id>` printed the same conversation for all 752 state IDs; a session written by the previous binary, moved and resumed by this one kept its context, a turn the previous binary added to a moved session afterwards was moved on the next open and seen by the following resume, and a turn the previous binary added to a session this build had resumed was left out. Over 1,000 session files a listing took 2.5 s once and then as long as one over two sessions.
- store-jsonl takes no file locks: each session file's O_APPEND journal is the linearization point and keeps owner fencing across processes. A writer replays the tail, validates, appends its entries with one write and one disk sync, then replays everything that landed before them and judges its own entries by the rule every reader applies: an acquire needs the next fence and a replacement the current owner and the next revision. On Apple platforms that sync is `fcntl(F_BARRIERFSYNC)` (`sync_journal`; `sync_all` where the filesystem refuses it), which writes the entries to the drive like `fsync` and orders them before any later write: an acknowledged commit survives a process or OS crash, and a power loss can lose only the latest commits, never reorder them, where `sync_all`'s F_FULLFSYNC also flushed the drive's cache. Every durable commit used to pay that flush: on 2026-10-27 on an M1 Max (APFS) a 2 KB append took 5.15 ms with F_FULLFSYNC, 0.64 ms with F_BARRIERFSYNC and 0.04 ms with `fsync`, and a native brain's turn (6 commits: admission, two model steps, the cell, completion) with an empty Code Mode cell and a scripted model took 33.9 ms and now 4.8 ms (`output/native-brain-bench`, a temporary `brain_bench` example over `ClaudeClient::messages_api` and `JsonlStore`; with `MemoryStore` 2.1 ms). The SQLite store already synced with `fsync` (`synchronous = FULL` without `fullfsync`). Other platforms keep `sync_all`. Superseded entries are skipped by every reader and reported as Fenced or Conflict, or retried for acquisitions, and a fence, revision or owner fence beyond the next one is corruption. Multi-entry batches carry a batch id and count and apply all or nothing, commit_many appends independent unbatched lines, a writer after a torn tail starts with a newline, and readers never truncate. Every process sharing a journal must run this protocol; older binaries lock and truncate, so restart every writer after upgrading.
- The legacy shared journal's offset index (`nanocode-jsonl-index-v3`; session files have none and are replayed whole when first opened) is a disposable sidecar bound to the journal identity, committed offset and final indexed entry digest, and any mismatch rebuilds it once from the journal before appending. It is saved at flush, at orderly close and when the idle worker's saved index trails the journal by more bytes than the index file holds, since long-running windows otherwise left openers replaying up to 2.1 GB. Index copies use a 128 KiB buffer: copying and hashing an 11.8 MB sidecar took 37.9 ms with 8 KiB, 18.9 ms with 128 KiB and 18.8 ms with 1 MiB.
- `JsonlStore::compact` is explicit maintenance on the worker and compacts each session file in turn: it keeps every valid acquisition and revision, each state's current payload and every unique record, blanks older payloads so older binaries still read the result, and never prunes records by guessing reachability. It first appends a seal naming its pid; writers whose entries land after a seal poll from 1 ms, doubling to 100 ms (the 12.6 GB production snapshot took 31.4 s to compact, so the cap adds about 0.3%), and retry on the replacement, a dead sealer is unsealed by the next writer, and processes sharing a journal must share a pid namespace. The first acquire entry carries the `nanocode_journal` lineage, `<journal>.compact-<pid>` and `.index-<pid>` temporaries of exited processes are removed at open, and hard-linked journals are rejected.
- `SqliteStore::open`, `open_home` and their async forms put the file in WAL mode with `synchronous = FULL`, as `SqliteSql` already does, so readers do not wait for the writer and a commit stays durable on power loss; a connection a host passes to `from_connection` keeps its own journal mode.
- JsonlStore and SqliteStore are handles to one worker thread each with a one-command job channel: a dispatched mutation or flush runs to completion when its caller drops the future, only reads whose receiver is gone are skipped, dropping the handle never blocks and close awaits the worker. open and open_home validate synchronously before moving the journal or connection to the worker, while open_async, open_home_async and SQLite's from_connection_async do that on the worker. SQLite runs every IMMEDIATE transaction, including busy-timeout waits on another writer, on its worker: a 1 s external write hold left 2.7-4.9 ms maximum heartbeat gaps instead of 1.09 s.
- Local development keeps incremental compilation enabled, omits debug information and skips the post-link strip, which costs about 0.8 s per binary on macOS. .cargo/config.toml compiles workspace crates through scripts/rustc-parallel-frontend, which enables rustc's parallel front end with `-Zthreads=0`; dependencies compile unchanged, clippy keeps its own wrapper, and `RUSTC_WORKSPACE_WRAPPER=` disables it. Release builds use `lto = "off"`: cross-crate thin LTO cost about eleven times the CPU of an edit-to-install rebuild without measurable TUI runtime gains, and the per-crate ThinLTO that `lto = false` still runs cost 37% of an uncached release build (969 against 1,535 CPU-seconds) for 5-9% faster TUI rendering benchmarks. No profile uses fat LTO: on 2026-10-24 dropping it from the wasm profile halved nanocode-ts relinks (16 s against 34 s) with turn times unchanged within run-to-run variation. Use the profiling profile for full symbols and the ci profile for disposable CI builds without incremental artifacts. Measure fresh-target builds separately from cached and edited rebuilds.
- .cargo/config.toml also routes rustc through scripts/buildcache, which shares compiled crates across target directories through ~/.cache/nanocode/build and needs no other tool. The shell script only dispatches: every call runs a helper that it compiles from scripts/buildcache.rs with the calling rustc into ~/.cache/nanocode/build/bin, in the background on first use while those calls run uncached. Clippy units are cached like other workspace units, keyed additionally by the clippy-driver digest, CARGO_PRIMARY_PACKAGE and CLIPPY_* variables, which clippy-driver reads without recording them as env-deps; their lint diagnostics replay from the cached stderr. A registry unit is keyed by rustc version, its arguments without target-directory paths, the identities of its `--extern` inputs and the CARGO_* environment, and its entry is immutable. A workspace unit is keyed the same way plus the workspace root and wrapper contents; its single entry is replaced on each store and is restored only when its `--extern` identities, package and workspace Cargo.toml and every dep-info source digest still match (a unit, or a C object, whose dep-info names a file modified after its compiler started is not stored, since the compiler may have read it before the change: on 2026-10-28 a commit that landed in a checkout during a build stored nanocode-tool-runtime's old rlib under the new sources' digests, and later builds restored code without the new `Hand::environment`), so a fresh target directory of an unchanged tree in the same checkout restores instead of compiling, while other checkouts miss because cargo's `-C metadata` hashes differ there. An output's identity is memoized next to it: the unit key for registry outputs and the rmeta SHA-256 for workspace outputs, written when rustc reports the artifact and before the notification reaches cargo, so pipelined dependents never hash or race it; restores write the recorded identities before replaying stderr. Every restore is a copy-on-write clone checked against the env-deps rustc recorded, and units whose dep-info reaches outside the registry, the workspace or the content-addressed OUT_DIR copies are not stored. Build-script OUT_DIR and native search paths are swapped for content-addressed copies in which cc-rs object names derived from the absolute OUT_DIR, and the matching archive members, are renamed to the names a relative OUT_DIR would produce, so -sys crates key identically in every target directory. C objects compiled by build scripts are cached in direct mode: keyed by compiler version, cwd, arguments, environment and source digest with OUT_DIR mapped out, checked against the digests of every header in the compiler's `-MD` dependency file, and compiled with `-ffile-prefix-map`; sources or headers that use `__DATE__`, `__TIME__` or `__TIMESTAMP__` are not cached. SHA-256 uses the ARMv8 SHA2 instructions when the CPU has them. A target directory filled from the cache has no incremental state, so the first edit there recompiles the affected crates in full. Use `RUSTC_WRAPPER=` for cold-build measurements; deleting ~/.cache/nanocode/build only makes cargo rebuild the crates that referenced it.
- Use cargo check --locked --lib and cargo check --locked --lib --target wasm32-unknown-unknown for SDK checks. Use explicit -p nanocode-tui or -p nanocode-cli for terminal work; --workspace is an intentional whole-repository check.
- Do not add tests or test-only dependencies. Validate changes with focused native and WASM builds and reproducible runtime measurements.
- Benchmark performance changes with reproducible commands, inputs, and before/after results. Separate cold builds, incremental builds, and runtime performance.
- [Principles for fast Tokio applications](https://dial9-rs.github.io/blog/principles-for-fast-tokio-applications/)
- Write lock-free code: no Mutex, RwLock or Condvar from std, Tokio, futures or parking_lot anywhere in the workspace. Use the nanocode-sync primitives: own mutable state in one task and talk to it over channels, an Actor or a Mailbox, publish shared state as an Atom or ArcSwap value changed copy-on-write with side effects performed after the change commits, use Slot, Signal, atomics and OnceLock for take-once values and flags, Ordered to publish effects in commit order, and Sequencer or Owned only where a protocol requires one caller at a time across awaits.
- nanocode-sync semantics: `Atom::update` clones the value, applies the change and retries the compare-and-swap, so a change may run more than once and must be free of side effects; `try_update` skips the store on None and `modify` on an error. `Signal` fires once for current and future waiters (its sender sits in a `Slot`, so firing and dropping one write no arc-swap value), `Slot` put and take swap atomically and never read in place: `is_empty` reads an occupancy count kept beside the value, because loading the value for the check made a concurrent take or put find it shared and drop it. Its value is a crossbeam-utils `AtomicCell<Option<Box<T>>>`, one pointer-sized atomic swap (lock-free on every target, since the type is pointer-sized), not an `ArcSwapOption`: arc-swap's default strategy makes every store, swap and compare-and-swap pay the outstanding read debts of every thread that ever loaded through arc-swap (`Debt::pay_all`), which a `Slot`, never loaded, gains nothing from. In a `sample` profile of 200 concurrent Claude sessions `pay_all` was 59% of the process's CPU, mostly the event channel's per-event `Slot` swaps; with `AtomicCell` 10,000 one-turn sessions (`claude_pool` binary) used 2.59-2.67 s of user CPU instead of 4.14-4.41 s and first-turn p50 fell from 12.4-15.0 ms to 8.6-9.2 ms, and Codex sessions (`pool`) 6.80-6.85 s instead of 7.60-7.73 s. `Inbox::drain` loads the head first and returns without a swap when it is empty, which every event's drain was. `Ordered` delivers values in ticket order, so every ticket must be published exactly once. `Inbox` pushes by compare-and-swap and drains in push order. `SingleFlight` runs one future per concurrent burst, and a cancelled leader hands the flight to the next caller. `Sequencer` admits one `Turn` at a time in arrival order, and a cancelled `enter` passes an admission it already received on. Its queue keeps the waiters in an `imbl::OrdMap` by ticket, so queuing and passing a turn cost O(log n) with n waiters; it was a `VecDeque` that every `enter` and release copied, which was 67% of the CPU of a 3,000-agent task tree whose registry state had thousands of waiters. Until a caller first has to wait, a sequencer admits and releases with one compare-and-swap on a mode byte (free, held), touching no `Atom`; the first `enter` that finds it held switches it (through a brief `switching` mode, which the holder's release spins past) to the queued mode, records the fast holder in the queue as its holder and waits there, and from then on every turn goes through the queue as before, so arrival order and cancellation behave as they did. 300 rounds of 64 tasks making 50 `enter`/`try_enter` attempts each, some cancelled by a 20 us timeout, held no two turns at once and deadlocked none, and `Owned` counted 64,000 of 64,000 increments (`output/hand-wiring`, `sequencer` binary); 10,000 one-turn Claude sessions used 1.91-1.93 s of user CPU instead of 2.63-2.66 s, first-turn p50 6.7-6.9 ms instead of 8.3-8.9 ms. Every arc-swap store (each `Atom` update, `Inbox` push, queued `Sequencer` turn and `Signal` fire) pays the read debts of every thread that ever loaded through arc-swap, exited threads included: 75 ns with no other threads, 0.4-0.5 us with 8, 1.3-1.5 us with 32, 4.6-6.4 us with 128 and 17-21 us with 512, staying at the high-water mark (`output/arcswap-scan`), so keep frequently written state out of `Atom`s (in an owning task or a `Slot`) and SDK state away from large or growing thread pools. `Owned` moves its value to the admitted caller as `Held` or `Leased` and back before the next turn. `Actor` runs jobs on its own task in call order and cancels a job whose caller drops its future; it needs a Tokio runtime natively or an installed platform host on WASM. `Mailbox<S>` owns a value without a task of its own and runs synchronous jobs on it one at a time in submission order: `send(job)` posts a job and returns, `call(job)` posts one and resolves to its result (a job whose caller dropped the future before it ran is skipped), and whoever posts to an idle mailbox runs the queued jobs on its own thread, its own and those other callers post meanwhile, so a caller never waits for a lock, only for its reply. The value sits in a crossbeam `AtomicCell` beside an unbounded channel of jobs and a count of queued jobs: a job is sent before the count is raised, the poster that raises it from 0 runs jobs, putting the value back before each decrement, until the count returns to 0, so no job is stranded and two runners never hold the value. After 128 jobs (Tokio's cooperative budget per task poll) it hands the rest to a spawned task, so a busy mailbox does not keep one caller from returning; a job that panics is dropped (its `call` panics in the caller) and the value is kept. Jobs must be `Send + 'static`, so they capture owned copies of their arguments. With 64 tasks making 50,000 jobs each, a mailbox ran a job in 248-400 ns against 3.0-8.7 us for `Owned` (output/hand-wiring `mailbox`, 2026-11-03), with none lost or out of order.
- Open question, not reproduced: on 2026-10-26 one run of the admission-gate stress (`output/hand-wiring`, `gate` binary, release build, Apple Silicon, arc-swap 1.9.3) died with SIGSEGV at address 0x6. The faulting thread was cloning an `Atom<GateState>`'s value inside `Atom::update` while five other workers were in arc-swap's hybrid `compare_and_swap`, dropping old values (`Arc::drop_slow`). `Atom::update` is safe code, so the freed value points at arc-swap or something below it, and arc-swap has shipped ARM ordering fixes as recently as 1.9.1. No crash followed in about 115 more runs of that stress, about 70 of the previous gate's, 3 under AddressSanitizer, or 32M operations of a plain-thread arc-swap stress. The crash report, harnesses and next steps (an ASan loop, arc-swap's `rwlock-strategy` for comparison) are in `output/arcswap-crash/NOTES.md` on the machine that saw it. Every `Atom`, `Inbox` and `SingleFlight` is built on arc-swap, so record any recurrence (the .ips, the faulting frame, the arc-swap and rustc versions) here.
- Keep blocking native storage work behind an owning worker and asynchronous message/response channels. Batch complete transactions there, including tail replay, index refresh, serialization and disk sync; native journals take no file locks. Async SDK construction and shutdown must await their completion without running filesystem work or joining worker threads on Tokio workers. Preserve synchronous compatibility entry points and durable acknowledgements.
- Route subagent journal writes through the per-root journal writer. Keep subagent message, residency and journal serialization per root so a slow or fenced store for one root cannot stall another.
- A subagent message the recipient's harness refuses leaves the subagent journal: `deliver_message` journals a message before releasing it to the harness and, when the harness refuses it, journals again after the rollback, so a sender told that its message failed never sees it return. After a journal restore, every message still pending in it goes back to its recipient through the harness admission a live send uses (`HarnessHandle::redeliver`): in message ID order, after the interrupted children's resume notices, with its ID, thread, purpose and priority, so it starts, steers or queues as it would have; a message that cannot be delivered, such as one to a closed child, settles as Failed with a delivery update, and no new message is created.
- A finished root child's completion counts as delivered only when the root turn that carries its notice completes without cancellation. `continue_parent` follows the route: a started turn's result, or for a notice steered into a running turn the root's `run.steered` naming the notice's request ID (Codex names it now, as Claude already did) and that turn's `run.completed` or `run.failed`. A notice the root accepted as an identified steer before a reopen produces no new `run.steered`, because the backend answers its route from the durable receipt and the resumed turn skips steers it already delivered, so a carrying turn that completes without one counts the notice as read when the root's steer receipt for its request ID is `Accepted` (`Agent::steer_receipt`). A completed turn acknowledges the completion; a failed turn, or one that ended before the steer was read, takes the next attempt and retries with the completion backoff, and the attempt suffixes the notice's request ID (`subagent-completion:<child session>:<revision>:<attempt>`; the first keeps `…:<revision>`), so idempotent admission cannot answer a retry with the turn that failed; an execution-policy retry keeps the ID and a stopped agent leaves the completion to the next owner. A cancelled carrying turn parks the completion, and while one is parked every other completion of that root parks too: parked completions are journaled with their attempt (agent records gain `completion_parked` and `completion_attempt`, which older binaries reject), are left out of `SubagentActivity::pending_completions`, so `settle` reports the root quiescent, and start no turn, until the root accepts a prompt that is not a completion notice, into which they are steered. The work a root turn delegated parks too when that turn is cancelled, so cancelled work never starts a root turn on its own: while a root has running children or parked completions, the subagent runtime watches its `input.accepted`, `run.completed` and `run.failed` events, attributes each child to the root turn whose `spawn_agent` call created it, or after a restart to the turn whose request ID or turn ID equals the child's recorded host context (a root without a host context of its own gives its children the spawning turn's operation), and when that turn ends cancelled while the agent is not stopping it journals the child's current instruction revision (agent records gain `cancelled_revision`, which older binaries reject); a completion settled at or below that revision parks, and one that follows a later instruction, such as a message from the next user turn, is delivered as usual. The revision stays recorded after the completion settles, so a restore can tell a child whose mark never reached the journal: when a process exits after the cancel but before that write, the cancelled turn is already terminal and nothing replays it, so restore asks the store (`ChildJournalStore::cancelled_turns`, through `SubagentStore::cancelled_turns`) which recorded host contexts of running root children without a mark name a root operation recorded as cancelled, and gives those children the revision their resumed work settles at, journaled with the resume attempts. Delivery is at least once.
- A notice turn that fails with a definite error (`BackendFailure::retryable` false, such as a 403 without `x-should-retry: true`, a 400 or a replayed failure) parks its completion as a cancelled notice turn does: journaled as parked with its attempt, left out of `SubagentActivity::pending_completions` and `deliver_completions`, and steered into the next prompt the root accepts that is not a completion notice, also after a restart, under the next attempt's request ID. A retryable failure leaves the notice turn pending and retries it under the same request ID after `completion_retry_delay` (2 s doubling to at most 300 s), each retry spending the backend's in-process attempts. Cancellation, stops and execution-policy dispositions are unchanged, and a carrying user turn that fails or ends before reading a steered notice still takes the next attempt. This replaces the retry of a failed notice turn described above, so hosts that refuse notice turns once the spawning turn's authority is gone (`completion_origin`), as Pact does, no longer get one every 2, 4, 8, 16 s indefinitely.
- A finished root child's result that wait_agent or list_agents returns counts as read only when a model request carrying that tool output completes. The output holds a `ToolReceipt` (`ToolOutput::with_receipt`) naming the call whose output carries it, at first the wait call itself; Code Mode holds the receipts of nested calls (`carried_by(None)`) and names the exec or wait call that returns the cell's finished output, the embedded runner at the cell's terminal observation and `RemoteClient` when a terminal reply arrives; `RemoteClient` keeps them by callback origin apart from the callback state, because a runner reports a finished cell (`DetachedComplete`) before the reply that returns its output, and holds them weakly so receipts of settled results are pruned, so a yielded chunk, a cell nobody collects and a failed host reply carry nothing. The subagent runtime claims the completion, so no notice duplicates it and list_agents still returns it; every later output that returns a result a tool output routes joins that result's readers, each result has its own watcher, and a result routed to a notice is left to the notice; follows the root's shared `tool.result`, `model.call.started` and `model.call.completed` events, and acknowledges it when the model call that started after the carrier's `tool.result` completes; a root turn that ends first sends it as a notice, a cancelled one parks it as a cancelled notice turn does, and a wait that returns while the root runs no turn, from a cell that outlived its turn, sends the notice at once. The root watcher tracks whether the root runs a turn from `run.started` and its terminal events. A root without a resolvable agent acknowledges at return.
- A reopened root's parked completions are released by the next prompt it accepts, which the subagent runtime observes through the root watch that restoration arms when it finishes. `TurnInbox::drive` first awaits that restoration and arms the watch with its own agent (`SubagentControl::await_restored`), so an inbox host may drive at once; a host that prompts the `Agent` directly calls `await_restored` before its first prompt after a reopen.
- `TurnInbox::steer` and `move_queued` reach any root turn the agent admitted under a request ID, not only the turn `drive` runs from its log: a subagent completion turn, a Claude background-command notice, and an SDK-pending turn `drive` resumes after a restart. `Agent::turn_controls()` lists the `TurnControl` of every unsettled turn admitted under a request ID, oldest first. `steer(None, …)` offers the steer to each in turn until the backend takes it, `steer(Some(id), …)` only to that request's turn, and `cancel` finds a running turn the same way. A turn whose cancellation the host requested, or that `drive` admits only to cancel, refuses steers, because a Claude turn admitted to cancel takes steers until its run ends and never reads them. Only turns `drive` runs from the log map their Codex turn IDs to the request; a resumed or completion turn's events stay under its own turn ID. A steer into a completion turn leaves the child's completion accounting unchanged, and a steer accepted before a restart is answered from its durable receipt, so the resumed turn reads it once and `drive` withdraws a moved prompt instead of running it. Hosts that let a user steer the work a completion turn continues, such as Pact, name the completion's request ID from `turn_controls()`.
- Restoring a subagent journal reads every agent record in one batch and every profile in a second (`SubagentStore::load_records`, `ChildJournalStore::load_records`, which the durable journal serves with `EncodedPayload::load_many` and, for keys it cannot load that way, one load per key as before); it used to read each agent's record and then its profile, two sequential reads per agent ever journaled, at every reopen, which tempoxyz/pyramid does at the start of every turn. The subagent journal `<root>:subagents` is format 6 (2026-11-04): agent state records are stored inline in leaves of 16 consecutive agent IDs (`LEAF_AGENT_BITS`; 16 records of the 600 to 700 bytes one takes stay under `EncodedPayload`'s 16 KiB inline bound, so a leaf is one record, while leaves of 32 crossed it and were chunked and leaves of 8 wrote 21 to 27% more records for the same bytes), under a tree of 64-entry pages of leaf keys whose top the payload holds, and messages inline in leaves of 64 consecutive log positions under a second such tree, so a reopen reads each level of either tree in one batch where format 5 read its message pages one at a time along their chain; each agent's record references a profile record holding the descriptor, binding task, output schema and host context, written only when it changes. At 5 x 2,000 children on SQLite (two interleaved runs at load average 200 to 232) the journal held 28,154 and 31,270 records instead of 109,924 and 117,222 (83 and 97 MB instead of 71 and 76 MB, since a leaf rewrites its unchanged agents too), the database 158,221 and 161,199 instead of 239,791 and 246,951, and a reopen restored the 10,000 agents in 0.51 and 0.77 s instead of 1.47 and 1.49 s. The journal names every record by the key its store files it under, `EncodedPayload`'s: the BLAKE3 hash of the content below 16 KiB and of its manifest above. Builds from b22a444ae until 2026-10-19 named large records by their content hash, so a Codex child's checkpoint (38 KB, mostly its instructions and tool definitions) or a profile with a long task failed with `missing payload record` after a restart, every delegation tool of that root failed with it and the session never became quiescent. The child journal store resolves a key it cannot find by listing the journal's records once per journal (`StateStore::list_records`), assembling every manifest root and matching the BLAKE3 hash of its content (`EncodedPayload::manifests_by_content`), and `matches_key` accepts that content key, so journals those builds wrote load again; records written after a restore use manifest keys, and a child's old checkpoint key is replaced by its next checkpoint. A restored child that cannot resume, such as one whose checkpoint is still unreadable, settles as Failed with an error naming the cause and its in-flight calls, as a failed turn does, so the rest of the tree resumes and the root gets a completion turn for its direct children; a journal that cannot be restored at all keeps failing every delegation tool of its root with the restoration error, writes nothing over it, and counts as quiescent for `settle`, because nothing from it can run. Versions 1 to 5 still load and older binaries reject 6. Every ChildSession change goes through `Sessions::get_mut` or `insert`, which assign a fresh journal generation; a save encodes every leaf that holds a changed agent from the live sessions, since the writer keeps no agent's JSON (only its generation, checkpoint and profile keys, and the JSON of the messages in the last, unfilled message leaf), and an unchanged agent in such a leaf reuses its profile key and checkpoint reference instead of encoding its checkpoint again; the writer updates its cache only after the store acknowledges a save.
- A root's task tree runs 10,000+ subagents on the SQLite and Postgres stores. output/hand-wiring's `swarm` drives an `AgentRuntime` over `SqlStore` (`SqliteSql` or `PostgresSql`) with an in-process Messages mock: `SWARM flat N` spawns N root children from one cell, `SWARM tree K x M` spawns K coordinators that each spawn M workers, `SWARM waited N` spawns N and waits on each with `wait_agent`; every worker messages its predecessor and submits, and the run then reopens the store and restores the tree. On master (2026-11-02, load average 23 to 50) 1,000 root children settled on SQLite in 10.3 s and 22.8 s of CPU, the root's 1,138 notice turns sending 384 MB of requests, a 1,010-agent tree took 11.5 s on SQLite and 56.3 s on Postgres (418 MB of database, mostly dead tuples of the rewritten journal head), and a 3,030-agent tree never settled: children evicted before their first turn began stayed `Running` with no harness. Now 1,000 root children take 4.0 s and 7.9 s of CPU with 8 root requests (1.4 MB); the 1,010-agent tree 2.8 s on SQLite and 11.0 s on Postgres (67 MB); 3,030 agents 21 s and 42 s; 10,100 (100 coordinators of 100) 104 s on SQLite and 153 s on Postgres, restored in 2.9 s and 1.3 s; 10,000 root children 117 s on SQLite with 15 root requests, restored in 3.7 s. Peak RSS (5.3 to 5.9 GB at 10,000) is set by the cells and harnesses running at once. What changed: (1) `TaskTree` indexes agents by session and children by parent; `agent_for_session`, which nearly every registry call made, scanned every agent, and postorders were quadratic. (2) Eviction never takes a `Pending` child, whose first turn has not started (evicting it stopped the turn as it began: 164 of 3,000 children stuck in one run), and picks among resident agents only, where it compared every pair. (3) Each agent has a residency `Sequencer`: a delivery holds its recipient's, and while rehydrating them its evicted ancestors' (child first), eviction takes it with `try_enter`, and the scope's message lock was held only while a message was prepared, enqueued and committed (since replaced by one registry job, below); the scope-wide residency and message locks were held across the journal save and the recipient's admission, so a tree's messages went one at a time. (4) The registry's per-agent `Atom` maps, `CodeModeExecutors`' per-session maps, `RunnerAgents`' agent lists and the runtime's children are `imbl` persistent maps (the runtime prunes dead children when the list's length is a power of two); every update copied the whole map, 35% of the CPU at 3,000 agents. (5) Journal format 5 keeps agent record keys in a tree of 64-entry pages (leaves by agent ID / 64, each level above by page index / 64, the payload holding the top level, at most 64 pages, and its height), and the writer encodes only agents marked changed since its last successful save (`Sessions::get_mut` and checkpoint inserts mark them; a writer's first save encodes every agent) and messages appended since (a removal or an out-of-order commit re-encodes the list), where every save wrote one key per agent (900 KB at 10,000); restore reads each page level, every message record and every agent record in one batch each. (6) A child's available events are tracked under one state acquisition, a progress capture reads its target and settles it in one each, and session-to-root lookups read a lock-free mirror: about 100 acquisitions of the registry state per agent each waited 10 ms at 3,000 agents. (7) `wait_agent` wakes on the listed agents' own `watch` (sent when a session changes and someone listens), not on every registry change. (8) Root children's completions go through one task per root: those that arrive while it routes are routed together, per host context, as one notice joining their prompts under `subagent-completion:<first child session>:<revision>:batch-<b3 key of the members>`, each acknowledged, retried or parked as it would be alone; a lone completion keeps its request ID and prompt, and delivery stays at least once. A root turn's steers and steer receipts live in its durable head, so one steer per notice made every notice rewrite all of them. (9) `list_agents` takes `after_agent_id` and `limit` and answers `next_after_agent_id` while more agents remain. (10) `spawn_agent` reads the parent's settings before the root's spawn admission and runs the spawn on its own task, aborted when the call is dropped, as it already did on WASM, so a cell's `Promise.all` of spawns uses every worker; a new child reads its parent's `SessionRecord` (`SessionStore::record`) for its lineage instead of loading the parent's whole session. (11) A Code Mode cell waited for a QuickJS worker thread when the OS refused one instead of failing: macOS allows 8,192 threads per process, and 1,913 of 10,100 workers whose cells all ran at once failed with `Script failed`; cells now run on a pool of worker threads (below). Half the database is the journal's child checkpoints, which progress captures write several times per turn although a durable child's own session holds the same state (300 MB of 620 MB of records at 10,100 agents).
- Native Code Mode cells run on a process-wide pool of QuickJS worker threads instead of one thread per host (`code-mode-engine/src/native.rs`): `available_parallelism()` workers, each multiplexing many QuickJS runtimes (still one runtime per cell host, so isolation is unchanged) as an event loop over host messages and an ordered set of timer deadlines. `EmbeddedHost::spawn` picks a worker that is not running JavaScript and has a spare runtime (or the least loaded one). A host holds a runtime only while it has a cell running or yielded (since 2026-11-04): a cell's start takes one of its worker's spares, or a new runtime, and the cell's end returns it after the collection that frees the cell's context, so a host between cells holds none. A worker keeps as many runtimes, running and spare, as it ran at once in the last second (`SPARE_WINDOW`, counting the current one), at least one, and trims its spares at each window; only a spare returned to an empty list gets a fresh context, the rest wait bare and prepare one when a cell takes them, because under a swarm's bursts most spares were trimmed again unused, each freeing the context it had been given (at 5 x 2,000 children on SQLite, load average 169 to 193, `JS_FreeRuntime` fell from 6.8% to 3.5% of the process's samples and user CPU from 34.2 and 34.4 s to 32.2 and 33.2 s, while output/hand-wiring's `cell` kept a first cell's p50 at 0.31 to 0.44 ms against 0.29 to 0.34 ms). Until then a host kept its runtime from its open to its close and returned it with a fresh context; before that it kept the peak of live hosts in the window: a swarm's children hold their hosts while their cells wait, so a worker saw thousands live and prepared a fresh context for every host that closed, needed or not; late in a 5 x 25,000 swarm, when children finished and nothing opened new hosts, 90% of the process's samples were in `Prepared::new` under a host's close (at 5 x 10,000 the CPU and settle time did not change: 195.8 and 202.3 s of user CPU before, 197.6 and 197.4 after). Natively a session no longer keeps an idle host in its `CodeModeRuntime` slot; WASM keeps per-session reuse, since its hosts prepare contexts later. The trade-off: a cell running synchronous JavaScript for a long time delays the other cells on its worker, which a thread per host did not; new hosts avoid a busy worker. On 2026-11-02 (output/hand-wiring's `engine` binary, CPU per cell) 5,000 cells each awaiting a 50 ms timer took 0.49-0.53 ms instead of 1.23-1.31 ms, 1.4-1.7 GB instead of 2.2 GB and a p50 of 0.16-0.25 s instead of 0.92-0.95 s, trivial and 16-tool cells cost what they did (0.38-0.40 ms and 0.61-0.66 ms), and the 10,000-agent swarm ran 170-430 threads instead of 3,100 to 8,192 (the macOS limit, which `EmbeddedHost::spawn_available` waited on). output/hand-wiring's `cells` printed the same output for its 33 cells.
- A 10,000-agent swarm on SQLite starts in half the time and settles in less than half (output/hand-wiring `swarm sqlite <path> 'SWARM flat 10000'` with `AGENTS=10000`, which prints when every `spawn_agent` returned and when every child sent its first model request; load average 8 to 15, 2026-11-02): every child added in 3.8-4.0 s instead of 8.1 s, every child started in 6.8-7.1 s instead of 14.0 s, settled in 22 s instead of 53 s, 75 s of CPU instead of 110 s; RSS 9.5-10.3 GB instead of 8.8 GB (the larger SQLite page cache and the cell spares). A 3,030-agent tree settles in 5.8 s instead of 8.5 s on SQLite. What changed: (1) the QuickJS pool above. (2) Eviction keeps an index of resident and idle children in `Sessions` (refreshed from the sessions `get_mut` and `insert` touched since the last check) and checks only idle candidates in last-use order, testing whether a candidate holds a resident descendant through its own subtree; `take_resident_eviction` scanned every session, computed every resident's ancestors and sorted all candidates under the registry state, 318 µs per call and 9.5 s of the 10.4 s the state was held at 10,000 agents, which serialized every other registry call behind it. (3) `admit_spawn` enters the root's spawn admission only while its journal restoration has not finished; afterwards spawns waited in its queue one registry acquisition at a time (2.3 s each at 10,000). (4) The subagent tools' definitions are memoized process-wide (`memoized`, keyed by tool, the spawn policy and whether the root is continued), where every child parsed and cloned their JSON schemas each time a definition was read, about 175 KB of live schema JSON per running child. (5) A child whose session lives in the same store as its root (`SubagentStore::records_sessions` false: the persistent recipe resumes it from its own state and drops the journal's copy) stops writing progress captures once the journal holds a checkpoint with its conversation, which restore needs to skip the assignment prompt; every tool boundary wrote one (9 per child), 13% of the CPU and 105 MB of the database at 10,000. (6) `SharedStore` groups every commit queued, not the first 64 (its command channel is unbounded: each caller awaits its reply, which bounds what is queued), carries a second commit of a state already in the group to the next group instead of ending it, and sends reads and acquisitions that arrive meanwhile on the pipeline instead of ending the group: groups grew from 21 to about 1,000 commits. (7) `SqliteSql` runs WAL checkpoints on a connection of its own (`wal_autocheckpoint = 0` and a `PRAGMA wal_checkpoint(PASSIVE)` after each transaction), where automatic checkpoints ran inside commits and took 31% of the writer thread, and sets a 256 MiB page cache and a 4 GiB memory map: with the 2 MiB default cache, inserts keyed by record hashes read pages back on almost every statement (`unixRead` 22% of the writer); together they took the store's commit latency from 1.8 s to 0.2 s at 10,000.
- `PostgresSql::pool(clients)` runs the store over several tokio-postgres connections, each taken whole by one transaction (`Owned`, tried round robin), and every `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `WITH` statement is prepared once per connection (`prepare_typed` with text parameters) instead of sent as an unnamed statement that Postgres parsed and planned on every execution; a batch holding any other statement, such as migrations' DDL, still runs unprepared. `SharedStore`'s grouped driver runs a group on the store's pipeline handle and keeps dispatching reads and acquisitions meanwhile, one group at a time, where it awaited each group and every read queued behind it; a flush still waits for everything before it. Groups stay one at a time on Postgres too: concurrent groups serialized on the shared records every child names (the instructions template), each `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` locking the row for its whole transaction, and settled slower. A store-backed child (`records_sessions` false) records a journal checkpoint only until one with its conversation is recorded: status settles and evictions skipped it after progress captures already had, where each wrote a 4 KB copy of a checkpoint its own session holds (two per child), 137 MB of 752 MB at 10,000 children. On 2026-11-02 (load average 15 to 25) the 3,030-agent tree settled in 9.5-11 s on Postgres instead of 16-18 s and in 4.8-5.5 s on SQLite; 10,000 root children on Postgres stay bound by the one writer (Postgres spent 60% of its backend time in `heap_hot_search_buffer`, walking versions of the rows a long transaction rewrote) and took 67-190 s.
- Claude defers a model step's admission (`begin_model`, kinds `model` and `model_call`) to the next commit instead of committing it before the request: the SDK policy's `commit_writes` sends model admissions through `DurableOwner::commit_writes_deferred`, which applies the writes and the step's begin to the driver's state within the current revision and persists them with the next commit of any kind, such as the following tool step's admission or the turn's settlement, as `advance_deferred` and `complete_step_deferred` already did. A crash during the model call therefore finds no record of it and sends it again, as a crash before its admission always did; tool admissions still commit before the tool runs. A child's turn made 5 commits and now makes 3: at 10,000 root children the store took 50,000 commits instead of 80,000 and the 3,030-agent tree 15,100 instead of 24,200 (2026-11-02), settling in 4.3 s on SQLite and 9.3 s on Postgres.
- `SharedStore` runs a store's reads and acquisitions next to its grouped commits when the store offers `StateStore::pipeline_handle()` (default none): each peek, owner, record read, listing and acquisition then runs on its own handle, commits and replacements still group through `commit_many` on the actor, and a flush waits for every pipelined operation. Each read used to wait for the one before it to come back through the actor, about a millisecond per hop on a loaded runtime, four per subagent. `SqlStore` offers a handle when its host answers `Sql::concurrent(self: Arc<Self>)` (default none; `SqliteSql` and `PostgresSql` answer themselves, `SqlxSql` and `SqlxTransaction` do not), and its handles share the migrated flag. `PostgresSql` sends a transaction's statements together with `query_typed` and text parameters, one round trip for the whole transaction, where `query` prepared, executed and closed each statement in turn (three round trips per statement); the server still runs them in order, so a statement may use a table an earlier one created.
- The subagent journal writes behind: `SharedJournal`'s writer (`child_journal.rs`) acknowledges a save once it is queued on the `SharedStore` instead of once it commits, coalesces saves into the newest write the store has not yet taken (`SharedStore::replace_latest` sends a `ReplaceLatest` whose `LatestWrite` slot keeps the latest payload and the union of the records staged since; the store takes it when it forms a group, and a later save then queues a new write expecting the revision after it), serves records it queued but has not committed from an overlay (`load_record`, `load_records`), and settles writes in order: a failed write keeps its records for the next save, which first waits for every write in flight, re-reads ownership when the failure was not `NotCommitted` or `Fenced`, and returns the first failure. So a waiter told that its journal write succeeded may lose it in a crash, but nothing ordered after it survives without it: `SharedStore`'s grouped driver now takes writes strictly in arrival order (a write after one for a state already in the group, or while a group is in flight, waits for the next group, with every write behind it), so a commit queued after the acknowledgement, such as the parent's `spawn_agent` result, lands in the same transaction or a later one; this holds when the root's session and its journal share one `SharedStore`, as `AgentRuntime`'s store does. `SqlStore::commit_many` stores each record of a group once: on SQLite one unconditional insert per distinct key, then each commit's holds and head as before; on Postgres three statements for the whole group, an upsert of the distinct records sorted by key (locking each once for the transaction), the holds of every commit whose owner and revision match, and the heads (`json_to_recordset`), without the replacement's hold check, which the holds statement makes true under the owner and record locks it took. Each commit used to insert the records it named, so the instructions and tool records every child shares were rewritten by every commit of a group: on Postgres each `DO UPDATE` added a version of the same row to one long transaction, and the per-commit hold check planned as a nested loop over the state's holds, which for the journal (200,000 holds at 10,000 children) took 27 to 67 s per group. Records of a refused commit in a group may stay stored with no state holding them. `PostgresSql` sets `plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan` on each connection before it prepares statements: generic plans chosen while the tables were empty kept that nested loop after they grew. On 2026-11-03 (load average 22 to 28, output/hand-wiring `swarm`, `SWARM flat 10000`, one run each) 10,000 root children settled in 35 s on Postgres instead of 142 s and in 18.1 s on SQLite instead of 23.9 s, a journal persist waited 0.15 s instead of 15.8 s (Postgres) and 0.14 s instead of 1.09 s (SQLite), and a commit 1.7 s instead of 8.8 s on Postgres; the 3,030-agent tree settled in 4.9 s on SQLite and 8.3 s on Postgres, 2,000 waited children in 3.5 s and 7.0 s, and every run restored its tree. The database grows (655 MB instead of 555 MB on SQLite): each save still encodes its own agent pages and records, so the coalesced writes store page versions that the payload they commit no longer names (on Postgres 183 MB of the 433 MB of records were agent pages, nearly all of them superseded).
- A live agent holds about half the memory it did. Tool definitions share their text: `nanocode_types_core::ToolDefinition`'s `description` fields are `Arc<str>` (constructors take `impl Into<Arc<str>>`, so `&str`, `String` and `Box<str>` still work) and `JsonSchema::shared()` hands out its `Arc<Value>`, and the Claude client's `ToolDefinition` holds `description: Arc<str>` and `input_schema: Arc<Value>` (serialized as before), so `claude_tools::install`, request templates, side-question templates and cursor templates clone pointers where each copied every schema and description (the `exec` description and a description with an output schema appended are built per install and reused while a tool of that name keeps the same text). The encoded request template a cursor records (`TemplatePrompt`, 24 KB of system prompt and tools) is shared process-wide while the next agent's system and tools are equal. `wait_spec` and the `hands` tool definition are built once per process. The per-agent channels box their messages (the durable session's `CommandRequest`, the subagent harness's commands and deliveries), since a Tokio channel allocates a block of 32 slots of its message when it is created: the durable session's was 16 KB. The registry's per-agent status queue runs a drainer only while it has jobs (a counter of queued jobs, the receiver handed between drainers through a `Slot`) instead of a task per agent for the agent's lifetime. On 2026-11-03 (output/hand-wiring `swarm` with `LATENCY_MS=8000 AGENTS=3000`, `SWARM flat 3000` on SQLite, `heap -s` one second after every child sent its first model request, so every agent waits on the model with no cell running) the process held 701-703 MB of malloc'd memory instead of 1,351-1,367 MB, 234 KB per agent instead of 452, and 925-1,035 MB of RSS instead of 1,393-1,487; peak RSS fell from 7.3-9.3 GB to 4.3 GB at 10,000 root children, from 3.1 GB to 2.2 GB for the 3,030-agent tree on SQLite and from 3.1 GB to 1.8 GB on Postgres (load average 60 to 110, so their times are not comparable). The system prompt is shared too: `MessagesRequest::system` is `Option<Arc<Value>>` (mutated copy-on-write; `apply_cache_ttl` copies only when a block lacks its TTL), the default Claude Code blocks are built once per process, an agent builds its system value once and takes the process's previous one when equal, and the request body a native `post` sends is the prepared wire's bytes (`Bytes::from_owner` over its `Arc<str>`) instead of a copy of them. The same snapshot then held 583-585 MB instead of 693-700 MB, 195 KB per agent. What a waiting agent still holds (malloc stacks of the same run): its request body (about 20 KB, mostly the system prompt and tools every agent sends alike) and the futures of its durable driver, harness and turn (about 45 KB).
- The subagent registry's state is a `Mailbox<RegistryState>` instead of an `Owned` lock: every registry operation is a job posted to it (`call` when the caller needs the result, `send` for updates nobody waits on, such as tracking a child's tool calls and settling its progress capture), so concurrent agents never queue for the state, and the job that wins runs the others back to back on its thread. Operations that took the lock twice with work between, such as preparing, enqueuing and committing a message or publishing a message's state and marking it terminal, are one job each, and updates sent while the lock was held are sent from the job. The scope's message lock is gone: a delivery (and a redelivery, a side question's harness lookup and a resident eviction) runs in one job that waits only while a close pauses the scope's messages (`Registry::when_messages_flow`, `MessagePause`, a count in the scope that interrupt, close, close-all and cancel-all raise for their duration under a `closing` sequencer and lower when the pause drops, waking waiters through the registry's revision), so deliveries still wait for a close as they waited for its lock, and no longer for each other. At 10,000 root children on SQLite the registry lock was taken 435,904 times with waits of 194 ms on average and 3.3 s at most (load average 73, 2026-11-03); the mailbox answered 412,143 calls in 40.7 ms on average and 778 ms at most (load average 88 to 104), and the run settled in 44 s instead of 71 s. Each agent still makes about 41 registry calls, and under load a runner that the OS deschedules holds up the jobs behind it. A progress capture also encodes the child's journal checkpoint on its own task instead of through `spawn_blocking`: with 10,000 children the captures kept Tokio's blocking pool busy, and 37.6% of the process's samples were in `parking_lot`'s `lock_slow` on the pool's shared mutex (taking work, spawning it and the idle threads' condvar); without it none were, the process ran 25 threads, and the run settled in 49.7 s at load average 67.
- At five roots of 25,000 subagents the write path is what limits a swarm, and these keep it moving. (1) `SharedStore`'s grouped driver forms a group only when none is in flight and takes it from the front of its queue, stopping at the first second write of a state (strict FIFO) or at a barrier (a flush, or a read on a store without a pipeline handle); reads go to the pipeline as they arrive unless a barrier is queued. It used to move every queued request into a new queue on each wakeup, so with 125,000 children its thread spent 92% of its samples in `memmove` and children waited minutes for their first commit. (2) The subagent journal is written deferred: `ChildJournalStore::save_deferred` (default `None`, `SharedJournal` implements it, `SubagentStore::save_deferred` forwards it) queues a `Command::ReplaceDeferred` whose content is a future, and the journal writer acknowledges every persist request while such a write is queued and untaken; when the store forms the group that holds it, the future asks the writer (through the `JournalFill` sender) for the payload and records, which it encodes from the registry state at that moment and the store then stages, so one encode covers every change since the previous group and the journal stores one version of each agent page per group instead of one per save. A close's final journal waits for the open slot to be filled first. After a fill the writer waits for the next registry change or request before it reserves another write: as first committed (24ef1d91f) it reserved one at once, and since a background write is always wanted, the store's next group asked for another fill with nothing changed, so under `nc exec --ephemeral` (an in-memory store) a root with three children encoded its journal about 40,000 times a second from its first spawn until exit, used 1m42s of CPU in a 90 s run and wrote 12.4 GB of OTLP traces while dropping spans past the export queue; the same run now encodes it 44 times (the build before 24ef1d91f, 95). At 5 x 2,000 children (2026-11-03) journal encodes fell from 70,000-78,000 to 133-217, the database from 627 MB to 400 MB (SQLite) and 662 MB to 393 MB (Postgres), and group time from 48 s to 33 s and 79 s to 36 s. (3) A child whose session lives in the journal's store (`records_sessions` false) no longer captures its whole checkpoint into the journal at its first tool boundary to tell restore that it has a conversation: its agent record gains `conversation: true` (journaled in `AgentRecord`, which older binaries reject), restore skips the assignment prompt for it, and every later capture, status settle and eviction already skipped such children; the capture serialized the child's snapshot and was a third of the process's CPU at 125,000 children. (4) `SqlStore::commit_many` shares one plan across dialects (distinct records once, then each commit's holds and head, commits sorted by state): Postgres runs it as three set-based statements, the records one now `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE false`, which locks an existing record against collection without writing a new version of it (every group used to rewrite every shared record), and none of them sorts (the records arrive sorted by key and the heads by state; the sort spilled to disk past `work_mem`); SQLite, which pays little per statement and parses JSON per access, runs one prepared insert per distinct record and a hold and head statement per commit (the set-based form over `json_each` took 70% longer). (5) `SqliteSql` sets `temp_store = MEMORY`, a 64-statement cache, and serves select-only transactions from read-only connections (one per CPU, on their own threads, WAL readers) while one connection writes. Each multi-row insert in a transaction kept a statement journal in a temporary file: the hold insert took 228 us and the head upsert 73 us, and take 27 us and 12 us in memory, so a 5 x 2,000 run's group time fell from 34 s to 8 s. (6) A finished child turn checks its root's resident limit through one loop per root (`Registry::evicting`): a turn that ends while the loop runs makes it run once more instead of starting a check of its own, and the eviction scan rules a candidate out by its pending messages and harness before it walks the candidate's subtree, which it now walks only for a candidate with children. Every finished turn used to start its own check, each scanning the idle children and allocating each one's subtree, and late in a 5 x 10,000 run the registry's mailbox spent 92% of its samples in that scan. At 5 x 10,000 on SQLite (2026-11-03, two interleaved runs each at load average 20 to 33) the swarm settled in 133 s and 116 s instead of 145 s and 139 s. (7) Acquisitions are grouped writes: `StateStore::acquire_many(Vec<(state, owner)>)` (default one `acquire` each; `CachedStore` forwards it) acquires states together, and `SqlStore` does it in one transaction on both dialects, a set-based owner upsert returning each fence and one read of the heads, falling back to one acquisition at a time for a single state or repeated states. `SharedStore`'s grouped driver treats an `acquire` or `acquire_with` as a write of its state, so the acquisitions at the front of its queue join the group with the commits beside them: the group acquires them in one `acquire_many`, runs each update against its acquired state and commits the replacements in the group's `commit_many`, where a replacement that fails reports the same error as before (`state update failed after acquiring its owner`). Each acquisition used to be a barrier that ran alone, as two transactions (the acquisition and the initial checkpoint), while every other write waited behind it: at 5 x 10,000 on SQLite (2026-11-03) an `acquire_with` took 10.9 s on average and now 0.7 to 0.9 s, in 6 acquisition groups, every child sent its first model request after 12.7 to 17.6 s instead of 25.9 s, and at 5 x 2,000 the swarm settled in 7.2 s and 9.0 s instead of 13.0 s and 11.1 s, with 4.5 to 5.6 s of system CPU instead of 8.9 to 9.2; on Postgres 5 x 2,000 settled in 17.2 s and 20.1 s against 17.8 s and 19.3 s, as its time goes to the commit groups. (8) The journal stages an agent's profile record only when its key differs from the one the journal last wrote for that agent, and an agent record only when its key differs from the agent's last one (`CachedAgent::profile`): every change to an agent re-encoded its record and staged its unchanged profile again, which the store then inserted with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and held again. At 5 x 10,000 on SQLite (2026-11-03) the writer ran 1.48 million record inserts instead of 2.17 million; at 5 x 5,000, 117,569 of the 500,000 records staged had been profiles already stored. (9) While a group commits, the next one forms: `SharedStore`'s grouped driver keeps taking queued writes into the forming group and starts each one's deferred content (a journal fill) at once (`Grouped::prefetch`), so a group no longer waits for its fills after the one before it finished. A store whose host takes several transactions at once runs that many groups in flight (`StateStore::group_writers`, default 1, `SqlStore` asks `Sql::writers`, default 1, which `PostgresSql` answers with its connection count; `CachedStore` forwards it), each with states no other group in flight holds: the forming group stops before a write of a state in flight while a writer is free, and otherwise waits for that state's group before it starts. SQLite and every other store keep one group at a time. `output/hand-wiring`'s `sqlbench` (125,000 states, 7 rounds of 10,000-commit groups, 4 new records and 1 shared record per commit, 2026-11-03) committed 7,000 commits/s to Postgres with one writer and 13,400 with 8, and 5 x 10,000 on Postgres settled in 126 s instead of 146 s. Postgres reads a group's records with `json_to_recordset` over `{key, value}` objects instead of indexing `[key, value]` arrays, which took a 40,000-record group's scan from 250 ms to 188 ms, and record keys are encoded without copying each one into an owned `String` first. (10) `SqliteSql` creates databases with 16 KiB pages (`PRAGMA page_size`, which applies only to a database that has no content yet) and bounds its WAL by the database: after a commit, when the `-wal` file is larger than the database file, the writer stops the background checkpointer's PASSIVE checkpoints and runs `wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE)` itself after each commit until one completes. The background checkpointer never let the WAL restart while the writer kept committing, so `sqlbench` (125,000 states x 7 commits) left a 14.4 GB WAL beside a 4.1 GB database; a TRUNCATE on the checkpointer's own connection blocked the writer past its 5 s busy timeout (`database is locked`), and SQLite's own `wal_autocheckpoint` in the writer (1,000 or 16,384 pages) took 205-208 us a commit. With 4 KiB pages commits took 114.7 us, with 8, 16 and 32 KiB pages and a 2 GiB cache 63.0, 57.6 and 68.0 us, and with 16 KiB pages, the default 256 MiB cache and the bounded WAL 90.5 us (74.6 us unbounded), the WAL staying under 1.8 GB. Random 67-byte content keys put each new record in a random leaf of the key index, so a group's commit writes every leaf it touched to the WAL; larger pages need fewer leaves and levels for the same keys. (11) Natively, `SharedStore`'s driver and its groups and pipelined reads run on one process-wide thread with a current-thread Tokio runtime of its own (`nanocode-durability-store`, started by the first store), not on the host's runtime, so the store pipeline is never queued behind agent tasks; `SharedStore::new` therefore no longer needs a Tokio runtime natively. At 5 x 25,000 on SQLite (2026-11-03, load average 23 to 31 from other processes) a 37,629-commit group's `commit_many` took 46.6 s while the SQLite writer ran no job longer than 8.7 s, its reply waiting for a busy worker to poll it; on the dedicated thread a 21,946-commit group took 3.9 s for 3.6 s of SQL, and the whole run settled in 452 s with 581 s of user and 737 s of system CPU, against 2,166 s, 1,144 s and 1,455 s on 24ef1d91f (every change in (6) to (11) included). (12) With several writers a launched group takes a `writers`th of the forming group (rounded up) and leaves the rest for the next free writer, where it used to take all of it: once a backlog had formed, one Postgres backend inserted a group of 100,000 commits for a minute while the other connections idled. At 5 x 10,000 on Postgres (2026-11-03, two interleaved runs each, load average 22 to 41) the swarm settled in 73.2 s and 71.9 s instead of 126.5 s and 101.0 s, with 76 and 66 s of system CPU instead of 161 and 100; one writer (SQLite) takes the whole forming group as before. (13) `PostgresSql::connect(config, connections)` opens a pool whose connection tasks run on a process-wide thread with a current-thread Tokio runtime of its own (`nanocode-postgres`, no TLS); `pool(clients)` still takes clients whose connections the host drives. Hosts that drive them on the runtime their agents run on starve them under load: at 5 x 25,000, with the connections spawned on the swarm's runtime, `pg_stat_activity` showed a group's transaction waiting on `ClientWrite` for 2 min 9 s, Postgres unable to send rows nobody read, while every other group waited on the rows it held. 5 x 25,000 then settled in 568 s on Postgres with (12) and this; at 5 x 10,000 the two measured within noise (83.7 s and 79.3 s on the agents' runtime, 66.6 s and 98.0 s with the second run at load average 55). (14) `SubagentControl::set_queued_spawns(true)` makes a spawn beyond `set_max_concurrency` wait for a turn slot instead of failing with `sub-agent concurrency limit of N has been reached`, so a root can hand a million spawns to `Promise.allSettled` and the runtime runs `limit` of them at once. Turn slots are a FIFO (`Capacity::acquire`, a `Mailbox` owning the waiters, `Acquire` a future that releases a slot granted after it was dropped): a running child's message turn waits in a queue served before the spawn queue (`Waiter::Resident` before `Waiter::Spawn`), because a child that has queued messages cannot be evicted, and behind a hundred thousand queued spawns every finished child that got a peer message stayed resident (at 1 x 5,000 with a limit of 1,000, 3,441 of 4,224 resident children were idle with queued messages). Harnesses wait on that queue rather than on a `watch` every release woke. `spawn_agent` takes its slot before it starts the task that builds the child, whose future was 13.8 KB while it waited; a waiting spawn now costs about 8.6 KB. Finished children also free what they held: a child's `AgentHandle` leaves `Registry::session_handles` when its harness closes (rehydration restores ancestors, which register theirs again), whose builder recipes kept about 5 KB of each finished child; `RunnerAgents` drops entries of dead agents when its map reaches a power of two, which ends their notice tasks (4.2 KB a child); and children with the same output schema share one compiled validator (1.4 KB each). At 1 x 10,000 with a limit of 1,000 (2026-11-04, `output/hand-wiring/heaptree-end.sh`, MallocStackLogging), the live heap when every child had finished, the SQLite cache aside, fell from about 59 KB a child to 12.5 KB; 5 x 2,000 on SQLite peaked at 1,380 MB of RSS with a limit of 1,000 and 4,702 MB without one, settling in 8.0 s and 9.0 s. (15) `ToolsBuilder::nested_call_limit(n)` (native, `CodeModeRuntime::set_nested_call_limit`; unbounded by default) bounds the nested calls a Code Mode cell has in flight: past it the cell's calls wait in the cell in call order, each input kept as its JSON text, and start as earlier ones finish (a journaled cell records them as queued), so a root that hands `Promise.allSettled` 100,000 `spawn_agent` calls holds 100,000 pending promises instead of 100,000 dispatched spawns. The cell's `tools.*` facade (`code-tools.mjs`) now returns the invoker's promise instead of wrapping it in an async function and marks it observed with one shared no-op handler, so each call holds two fewer promises and its result settles two microtask turns earlier. At 1 x 50,000 with 40,000 calls pending (2026-11-04, MallocStackLogging) the root cell's allocations fell from 273.8 MB to 155.9 MB (6.8 KB to 3.9 KB a pending call), and 1 x 50,000 with a limit of 500 peaked at 2,372 MB of RSS against 2,566 MB without one. (16) A finished child holds about half what it did. When a child's harness closes the registry calls the hook `Registry::set_session_released` installs, which the runtime points at `HostServices::unregister`, so `CodeModeExecutors`, `RunnerAgents` and the code-mode host map forget the child's session (children registered through `track_children` were never unregistered; about 1.5 KB each); a per-agent status queue retires once it drains (its count moves from one job to `RETIRED_QUEUE`, and a later status starts a new queue, so per-agent order holds) instead of keeping its channel for good (1.3 KB); the child journal adds to `Fenced::committed` only the keys its non-deferred saves staged, since the deferred path stages every record anyway (1.4 KB); children with the same output schema share one `Arc<Value>` beside the shared validator; a session's change `watch` is created when a waiter subscribes and dropped once none is left; `completion_dispatch` drops an agent's sequencer once nothing else holds it (`Sequencer::is_unshared`); and the registry boxes each `ChildSession` (920 bytes, 690 with `StoredRuntime::Checkpoint` boxed too), so the session map's spare buckets cost a pointer each. At 2 x 25,000 with a limit of 2,000 (2026-11-04, `heaptree3.sh`, MallocStackLogging) the live heap when every child had finished, the SQLite cache aside, fell from 636 MB to 306 MB (12.7 KB to 6.1 KB a child); without logging the run peaked at 3,316 MB of RSS instead of 4,002 MB with the same CPU (171.6+33.7 s against 168.7+33.2 s), and 5 x 2,000 at 1,184 to 1,198 MB instead of 1,313 to 1,344. (17) `SqliteSql::open_with`, `open_async_with` and `from_connection_with` take `SqliteOptions { cache_bytes }`, the writer connection's page cache (256 MiB by default, as before); SQLite allocates cache pages only as it fills them, so a small database costs nothing more under a large setting. Every record's random 67-byte key lands in a random leaf of the key index, and once that index outgrows the cache each insert reads its leaf back: with 256 MiB, `sqlbench` (125,000 states x 7 rounds of 10,000 commits, 4.4 GB, 2026-11-04, two runs at load average 14 to 31) committed at 133.7 and 107.0 us a commit and its writer spent half its busy samples in `pread`; with 2 GiB at 79.6 and 68.9 us, with 4 GiB at 76.8 us, and with a 1 TiB `mmap_size` (`SQLITE_MAX_MMAP_SIZE` raised at build, since SQLite caps mmap at 2 GiB) at 109.7 us. 10 x 100,000 (one million subagents, `QUEUED`, a limit of 5,000, `NESTED_LIMIT=500`, `SQLITE_CACHE_MB=4096`; 2026-11-04) completed every agent in 2,801 s with 4,560+3,701 s of CPU and 9.5 GB of peak RSS, wrote a 32 GB database, and a reopen restored all 1,000,000 agents in 295 s; the same run with the 256 MiB cache was at 274,000 agents after 430 s where this one took 300 s (that one shared the disk with `sqlbench` from 270 s on). Late in the run the writer is bound by the WAL instead: each commit's 4 or so new keys dirty that many 16 KiB leaves, so the WAL grew at 250 MB/s and `pwrite` took 45% of the writer's busy samples. (18) `Sql::readers` (default 1; `SqliteSql` answers its read-only connections, one per CPU, and `PostgresSql` its connections) lets `SqlStore::read_records` split a batch over that many transactions run at once, since records never change and need no common snapshot; a reopened root reads its 100,000 agent records and then their profiles each as one batch, which one reader used to serve alone. At 10 x 10,000 on SQLite with a 4 GiB cache (2026-11-04) a reopen restored the 100,000 agents in 4.61 s instead of 8.94 s. Smaller pages do not help the WAL-bound writer of (17): `sqlbench` (250,000 states x 6 rounds of 2,000-commit groups, 7.5 GB, 4 GiB cache) committed at 124.2 us a commit with 16 KiB pages, 133.6 with 8 KiB and 153.5 with 4 KiB. (19) The registry answers its per-completion and per-root-turn questions from indexes instead of scanning a root's sessions: `Sessions` keeps the parked completions, the active direct children, the direct children marked `in_spawning_turn` and the direct children by host context, the first three refreshed from the ids `get_mut` and `insert` mark stale (as residency already was) and the last at `insert`, since a child's host context never changes. `park_completion` asked whether any session's completion was parked for every completion it routed, `needs_root_watch` on every root run event, and `unpark_completions` and `root_turn_ended` on every root turn, each a walk of all 100,000 sessions of a root inside the registry's one mailbox; with 100,000 children a root, `park_completion`'s closure took 6.9% of the process's busy samples on Postgres at 450,000 agents. (20) A Postgres group commit locks the records it references `FOR KEY SHARE` (`GROUP_LOCK_RECORDS_PG`, in key order) and inserts the missing ones with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, where it used to take each existing record's row lock with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE ... WHERE false`. A key-share lock still holds off a collection's delete until the group commits, but key-share locks do not conflict with each other, while the update lock serialized every concurrent group that referenced one shared record (a child's shared prompt chunks, or any identical message, such as a reply of `ok`): at 450,000 agents two to four of the eight backends waited on `Lock: transactionid` in the records insert. With (19), 10 x 10,000 on Postgres (2026-11-04) settled in 77.2 s instead of 86.6 s at 5.7 GB of peak RSS instead of 6.6, and 5 x 2,000 in 8.3 s instead of 14.1; SQLite measured the same within noise (77.5 s against 79.3 s).
