(21) `SharedStore`'s grouped driver no longer stops forming a group at a queued write whose state another group is committing: it converts that write (prefetching its deferred content while groups are in flight, as before), holds it beside the forming group until its state's group completes, and keeps taking later writes of other states, skipping any further write of a state that is forming, held or skipped, so each state's writes stay in order and none passes a barrier. Before, the first such write at the head of the queue (usually a root's journal, which every group carries) stopped the forming group, and a group holding one could not launch while any writer was free, so with eight Postgres writers most backends sat `ClientRead` while commits waited: at 10 x 100,000 a commit waited 1,019 ms on average for groups that took 224 ms. At 10 x 10,000 (2026-11-04) a commit waited 248 ms instead of 473 ms on Postgres, which settled in 75.3 s instead of 82.4 s, and 194 to 200 ms instead of 278 to 304 ms on SQLite, which settled in 82.4 and 83.8 s against 85.8 s (its one writer was already the limit). Ten roots of 100,000 subagents on Postgres with (19) and (20) and before this (2026-11-04, eight connections, a limit of 5,000) completed every agent in 1,749 s with 3,658+1,656 s of CPU and 6.8 GB of peak RSS, settled in 1,933 s, wrote 31 GB, and a reopen restored all 1,000,000 agents in 118 s. (22) Ten roots of 100,000 subagents on SQLite with (16) to (21) (2026-11-04, a 4 GiB cache, sharing the machine with a WASM build, two deploys and a workerd fault run for its last half) completed in 2,801 s as with (17) alone, at 8.8 GB of peak RSS, while a commit waited 856 ms instead of 1,147 ms and a reopen restored the 1,000,000 agents in 102 s instead of 295 s. At 10 x 10,000 on Postgres a concurrency limit of 10,000 or 20,000 finished no sooner than 5,000 (84.4 s and 85.8 s against 81.2 s) while a commit's wait grew with it (555 and 784 ms against 272 ms): the swarm's process used 6.2 of the 10 cores and Postgres 1.2 to 1.7, so past 5,000 running children the CPU, not the store's latency, bounds it. (23) `PostgresSql` runs a statement list that only reads (every statement a `SELECT`) on the connection without `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`: at Postgres's default READ COMMITTED each statement takes its own snapshot inside a transaction too, so the two round trips bought nothing, and a peek or record read held one of the eight connections a group commit also needs for three round trips instead of one. And `SqlStore::read_records` splits a batch over the readers only into parts of at least `READ_PART_KEYS` (1,024) keys, so a reopened root's 100,000 agents still read over every connection while a child's few-key load stays one statement on one connection: (18) split every batch of two keys or more over all eight, so each such load held eight connections. At 10 x 10,000 on Postgres (2026-11-04, two interleaved runs each at load average 45 to 59 from other processes) the swarm settled in 78.2 s and 96.0 s instead of 101.2 s and 107.7 s, with 22.6 to 23.9 s of system CPU instead of 35.0 to 35.9, and a reopen restored the 100,000 agents in 3.0 to 3.2 s instead of 6.4 to 8.2 s. Separate read connections did worse: with eight more for reads alone, a commit waited 13 to 50 ms but a peek 0.57 to 1.36 s, the faster children drove each root through 1,316 to 7,447 turns instead of about 320, each resending a history of up to 4 MB, and the swarm settled in 70 to 165 s. Ten roots of 100,000 subagents on Postgres with (21) and this (2026-11-04, the machine at load average 45 to 78 from other builds for most of the run) completed every agent in 2,244 s and settled in 2,653 s, at 7.5 GB of peak RSS, and a reopen restored the 1,000,000 agents in 116 s; under that load a commit waited 602 ms on average but up to 56 s, and one child's harness ran 22 minutes.
- Spawned and restored Claude children share their parent's system context (the environment section and project instructions, `share_system_context`, which forks already used) when they run in the parent's workspace and the parent's environment section still names today's date, instead of each walking the workspace for git and instruction files: at 5 x 2,000 children building them was 4.1% of the process's samples (`ProjectHome::discover` and the `stat`s of `environment_section`). A child spawned the day after its parent started computes its own, so its date is current, and a child sees the instruction files its parent read, as a fork does. The Code Mode catalog a cell offers (`shared_nested_tool_metadata`, every nested tool's name, description and schemas as JSON) is shared process-wide by registries with the same definitions, through a list of weak references, where each registry built its own (3.9% of the samples). At 5 x 2,000 children on SQLite (2026-11-04, two interleaved runs at load average 150 to 202) the swarm used 28.4 and 29.2 s of user CPU instead of 29.7 and 30.2 s, 3.1 and 3.5 s of system CPU instead of 6.2 and 4.6 s, and peaked at 4,386 and 4,246 MB instead of 4,695 and 5,244 MB. A cell's encoded catalog (`CellTools`, the definitions, descriptions and schemas JSON that each `CodeModeRuntime` kept for its last catalog) is shared the same way by runtimes whose catalogs are equal, found first by the shared metadata's pointer: at 3,000 children running at once each session held its own (36.7 MB, 12 KB a child, the largest Rust allocation site after SQLite's cache), and at 5 x 2,000 children the swarm used 25.3 and 26.4 s of user CPU instead of 27.3 and 27.2 s.
- `nanocode::process::Redactor` (crate `nanocode_process_contracts`) replaces secret values in text (`text`), in every string of a JSON value (`json`, object keys untouched) and in stored JSON text (`json_text`, redacted as text when it does not parse), longest form first, skipping values shorter than its minimum. `Redactor::new(min)` also matches each value JSON-escaped (`json_escape`), as JSON text or a string literal in Code Mode code holds one with quotes, backslashes or control characters; `Redactor::raw(min)` matches it only as it is. Each value reads as the placeholder `add(value, placeholder)` gives (which says whether it added a new form), `[NAME]` for `named` pairs or `[REDACTED]` for `values`; `forms()` lists them for hosts that also replace them themselves, such as with SQL. `redact_and_limit` runs on `Redactor::raw(MIN_REDACTED_SECRET_BYTES)` unchanged; tempoxyz/pyramid redacts organization tool results, secrets saved from a message and typed text in turn traces with it instead of three copies of its own.
- [Fast Rust Builds](https://matklad.github.io/2021/09/04/fast-rust-builds.html)
- Keep logs, traces, and benchmark artifacts in ignored output/. Never commit credentials or personal test data.
- Answer performance and telemetry questions from the recorded OTLP data with `node scripts/otel.mjs`: `tails`, `outliers`, `trace <id>`, `sessions`, `report` and raw `sql` over an incremental SQLite cache in output/telemetry.
- The local OTLP trace file is written by `file::TraceProcessor`: span end reserves a queue slot with a compare-and-swap and sends over an unbounded channel without I/O or blocking, and the worker writes each frontier it snapshots as one grouped OTLP JSON line. At most `OTEL_BSP_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE` ended spans wait, 2048 by default as in the OpenTelemetry specification and opentelemetry_sdk 0.32.1, and an unparsable value fails installation; beyond that span end drops and counts spans and the next force_flush or shutdown reports the total, because an unbounded queue reached 12 GB RSS in 2 s at 1M spans/s against 190-310 MB bounded. force_flush and shutdown are synchronous, so call them outside Tokio worker threads.
- tracing-opentelemetry ends a span at its last exit, so keep a span entered for the whole operation it measures and record `duration_ns` when the measured work excludes queueing. `--telemetry` and NANOCODE_TELEMETRY select off, agent (the default) or all, and `nanocode hand` defaults to off (`ObservabilityOutputArgs::builder` takes the command's default): a hand's agent telemetry recorded every nested tool call's arguments and output into `<home>/log/otel/<process>/traces.jsonl`, which nothing on a visitor's machine prunes (about 3.8 KB per small brain callback and a 1 MiB argument in full; one benchmark hand wrote 57 MB in a minute and this machine held 3.7 GB in 906 process directories on 2026-10-28), and its writer thread cost the hand a fifth of its CPU: in nanocode-ts's `bench/hands.ts` hand CPU per turn fell from 163-166 to 112-131 ms for 500 sequential callbacks and from 101-107 to 81-86 ms for 500 parallel ones, with turn times unchanged within noise. The brain's telemetry covers the hand's calls; pass `--telemetry agent` to record them on the hand too; spans with `target: TUI_TARGET` are exported only with all, and `nc_metrics` events feed only the metrics layer. Agent-path spans (model.call, tool.call, tool.execute, code_mode.cell, code_mode.cell_actor and code_mode.wait) carry `session.id` themselves because parents are exported only when they end, and `typed::restore_integers` turns u64 fields, which tracing-opentelemetry records as Debug strings, back into integers.
- otel.mjs ingests complete new lines of every `<home>/log/otel/*/traces.jsonl` and metrics.jsonl by byte offset into output/telemetry/telemetry.sqlite; table changes bump SCHEMA_VERSION and views are recreated on every open. `spans.dur_ms` is the larger of the span length and `duration_ns`, `session_id` comes from the span, its nearest exported ancestor (`session_from = 'parent'`) or the only session among its trace's agent spans (`'trace'`), `ui = 1` marks terminal spans, other attributes are JSON in `attrs`, and tool arguments and outputs are `events` rows. Resources carry process.pid, process.executable.path and nanocode.executable.modified for `builds` and `--by build`. `breakdown` assigns each moment of a turn to model calls, tools, store writes or other, `outliers` counts slow overlapping spans in other processes to expose machine-wide stalls, and `prune --older-than` deletes fully ingested raw directories that no live process writes.
- Prefer simple code and small changes. Preserve unrelated work. Use subagents only when explicitly requested.
- `nanocode::ModelInfo` is a model as a catalog lists it, from its `ModelCapabilities`: harness, ID, display name, accepted efforts (lowest first), default effort, fast mode, service tiers and reasoning modes, with `runs(thinking, fast)`; `ModelInfo::of(&selection)` reads native capabilities and `model_catalog(transport)` lists every built-in harness's models. Context windows stay with each backend. tempoxyz/pyramid's modes keep their own model allowlist and read efforts, defaults and fast mode from it instead of deriving them. Native hosts that call a provider directly with an API key build its client with `ClaudeClient::messages_api(base_url, api_key, connect_timeout, idle_timeout)` (the Messages endpoint under `base_url`) and `OpenAiBuilder::http_timeouts(connect_timeout, idle_timeout)`, which install the rustls provider and build the reqwest client with those connect and read timeouts.
- A host that runs the CLI with a Codex endpoint of its own (`ModelClients::openai_endpoint`) names the models that endpoint serves with `ModelClients::models(models)`: `-m`, `/model`, the model picker and `nanocode models` then offer exactly those as the Codex models, in the host's order, beside the built-in Claude models, and refuse a catalog Codex model the host did not list (`ModelClients::parse_model`; `host::parse_model` and hosts that list no models are unchanged). An ID outside the catalog is a `Model::Custom`, so it gets the custom-model prompt naming it, low default thinking and the provider's reported cost instead of a GPT model's. gakonst/nanocode-machines lists what a paid endpoint's `/v1/models` returns, where it used to send one `CUSTOM_MODEL` by rewriting each request's `model` while the CLI showed and prompted as Luna. `NANOCODE_OPENAI_BASE_URL` (`custom_endpoint.rs`) does the same without a host of its own: unless the host supplies its own Codex client, Codex sends to `<base>/responses` over HTTPS with `NANOCODE_OPENAI_API_KEY`, else `OPENAI_API_KEY`, as its bearer token (none without either), and after parsing its arguments the CLI reads the OpenAI model list at `NANOCODE_MODELS_URL` (default `<base>/models`; a host with its own client may set only that), failing when the list fails or is empty. Each listed ID is a `Model::Custom` (`nanocode::CustomModel`), even one the catalog knows, so an endpoint's model never gets a built-in model's service tiers or thinking limits. With models listed, a session started without `-m` (or with only `--harness codex`) runs the first of them at its own default thinking, where it ran Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh. Reasoning summary and content stream events without `summary_index` or `content_index` read as index 0, as LiteLLM's Responses stream leaves them out, where every such turn failed with "Responses API event did not match its declared type" (#1115; its author checked a LiteLLM endpoint of 43 models: `nanocode models` listed only them, `-m gpt-6.1-sol` was refused with their list, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GLM-5.3 Flash and Kimi K3 completed turns naming themselves).
- Model a value's lifecycle as one enum whose variants carry only what that phase has, not as booleans and `Option`s that must agree with each other, so a state no transition reaches cannot be built: Codex's `Response` stream (`Progress`: `Running`, `Succeeded`, `Failed`, where three flags and an `Option` result allowed a finished run without a result), the zsh drain's `Reading`, the lazy durable executions' `Deferred` (the existing flag, journal claim, attempt and Claude's initial settings, which only a deferred acquisition has) and `Acquired` (whether the acquisition reopened state, known only once it ran), a cell journal's `Saving` (`Unsaved`, `Saved` with what was persisted and the next update's sequence, `Stopped`, held through `Owned` instead of a `Sequencer` beside four atomics), the ChatGPT connection's `Handshake`, a cell's `CellLife`, and a zsh server command's `Busy` (`Stage`: `Forking` holding the caller's reply and release channel, `Running`, `Unreported` once it exited without its EXIT trap's status and the server's wait was asked, `Waited`; and `Owed`, the exit sender and the FIFO keepers that always went together, where an optional reply, an optional PID and two booleans could disagree), and an adopted agent's `Lifecycle` (`Live`, `Stale` once a failure needs a reopen, `Closed` for good after `disconnect` or `shutdown`), where `stopped` and `closed` flags let a heal that finished after a close mark the closed agent live again; a closed agent now reports `is_stopped`. A subagent's `ChildSession` keeps its completion as `Completion` (`None`, `Pending { revision, attempt }`, `Parked { revision, attempt }`, where a parked flag without a pending revision was possible and checked for everywhere), its harness as `Residency` (`Detached`, `Resident(harness)`, `Evicted`, which an `evicted` flag beside an optional harness encoded) and its runtime when not resident as `StoredRuntime` (`None`, `Checkpoint`, `Journaled`, which an optional checkpoint beside a `journaled_runtime` flag encoded); the journal record keeps its three completion fields, so stored journals are unchanged. A child's in-flight tool call keeps its state as `CallState` (`Restored` with the two flags its journal record carries, or `Live` with its parent call and a `CallProgress` of `Started`, `Recorded`, `Yielded`, `Settled` or `Committable`) instead of `result_recorded`, `yielded`, `live`, `settled` and `committable` booleans; it serializes through `JournaledCall`, the record's former shape, field for field. A Claude agent's `State` keeps one `AgentLife` (running, stopped by a failure or `disconnect`, closing after `shutdown`) moved by `stop` (only from running) and `close`, where `stopped` and `closing` flags were stored one after the other. On 2026-11-01 a nanocode-ts brain in Node (`output/subagents-check.ts`: two children with `max_resident_subagents` 1, a follow-up message to the first after it completed, then a reopen) behaved the same on the release build-f964a9d module and on this build. On 2026-11-03 the same went for: the Codex HTTPS stream (`ResponsesHttpStream` is `Chat` or `Sse`, and an `SseStream` holds one `SseBody`, `Reqwest`, `Layered` or `Host`, until the body ends, where four `Option`s of which one was set and an `ended` flag said it), a Chat Completions stream's `ChatPhase` (`Reading(body)`, `Drained`, `Done`, for an optional body, `ended` and `finished`), a freeform call's `InputScan` (`Seeking`, `Reading(at)`, `Closed`, for a cursor and `closed`), the Codex WebSocket and the time it connected as one `Option<(ResponsesSocket, Instant)>`, the Codex driver's `Intake` (`Open`, `Closed`, `Detached`, for `commands_open` and `detached`; `close` keeps `Detached`), a Codex tool call's `ToolStep` (`Run { recover }` or `Recorded { output, persist }`, for `interrupted`, `recover` and an optional recovered output) and the turn loop's `first_batch`, which `can_drain_steers` only ever negated; the Claude Messages SSE reader's pending data as `Option<FrameData>` (for a line range and a joined string) and its stream as `unfold` over `Option<SseState>` (for `done`); the MCP SSE parser's `Start` (`Bom(matched)`, `Body`, for `started` and `bom_matched`) and its event as `Option<Event>` (for `has_fields`); an attachment connection's `Drain` (`Attached`, `Requested`, `Acknowledged`, for `detaching` and `draining`), its ping as `Option<(nonce, sent at)>` (for two `Option`s and an `expect`) and a retained call's `Progress` (`Running(task)`, `Pending`, `Settled(receipt)`, for an optional task and an optional receipt, and the receipt is `Utf8Bytes`, so a resend shares it instead of copying it); a durable session driver's `Ownership` (`Unacquired(Seed)`, with `Existing`, `Described(record)` or `New(record)`, or `Owned(token)`, for `owner`, `pending_record` and `create`) and `SharedStore`'s group scan `Admits` (`Writes`, `Reads`, `Nothing`, for `ordered` and `barrier`); a spawned process's `Reaping` (`Waiting(task)`, `Reaped(status)`, for two `Option`s of which one was set, an unreachable error and an `expect`) and a zsh server owner's `Life` (`Serving`, `Retiring`, `Stopped`, for `retiring` and `alive`); and the TUI `RenderScheduler`'s pending `Option<Frame { deadline, streaming }>` (for a deadline and a `streaming` flag that only a deadline can have). Then a Claude background Bash job's `AtomicPhase` (`Foreground`, `Background`, `Delivered`, advanced with `fetch_max`, for `backgrounded` and `delivered` atomics that could disagree) and a subagent harness's `Contract` (`Pending { assignment }`, `Delivered`, for `contract_delivered` and `rehydrated_assignment`). Then a subagent child's turn, `Option<ActiveTurn { revision, stage }>` with `TurnStage` `Working`, `Steering` or `Submitted(output)` (for `active`, `active_instruction_revision`, `steering` and `submitted_output`, which a turn's end cleared together; the journal record keeps `accepted_output` and `accepted_revision`, and the settled revision of a finished turn is its own revision, without the fallback that could not be reached); a subagent scope's `ScopeLife` (`Open`, `Closing`, `Frozen`, for `closing` and `journal_frozen`, set only together by `close_all`); `SubagentActivity::restoration`, a public `Restoration` (`Restored`, `Restoring`, `Failed(error)`) where `restoring` and `restore_failure` were two fields (serialized as `restoration`; no host on this machine read either); the Claude agent's `ThinkingMode` (`Automatic`, `Adaptive`, `Disabled`), one `AtomicThinkingMode` where `set_thinking` stored `adaptive_thinking` and `thinking_disabled` one after the other (the checkpoint records keep their two fields); and the zstd decoder's `DecoderState::Frame { frame, stage }` (for a state and an optional current frame that had to agree; whether input arrived is read from the bytes received). Also a Codex run's `UsageCost` (`Unreported`, or `Reported { rate_estimated, estimated }`, for `reported`, `rate_estimated` and `estimated_cost`; a turn's usage is built with its `CostStatus`, so the hidden `TurnUsageCounts` and `TurnUsage::from_counts` went), a Responses attempt's `Replay` (`Incremental(previous_response_id)` or `Full`, for `full_replay` and a `previous_response_id` it masked), the Codex builder's `PromptCacheKey` (`Prefix`, `PerSession`, `Explicit(key)`, for an optional key and `per_session`), a tool-host admission's `Grant` (`Fast`, `Shared { token, origin, epoch }`, `Exclusive { token }`, for `fast`, `exclusive` and the fields only a gated admission has; output/hand-wiring's `gate2` ran 1,800 rounds of 48 tasks, 384,647 exclusive and 161,425 cancelled, with no violation), the zsh dispatcher's `Probed { probe, direct }` (the direct-spawn snapshot lives with the probe it was taken under, and a probe of another fingerprint drops it), and the egress proxy's response `Framing` (`Chunked`, `Length`, `UntilClose`, for `chunked` and `length`). output/hand-wiring's `swarm` (200 flat, 5 x 20 tree, 100 waited, each restored), `pool` and `claude_pool` (300 sessions each), `execcheck` and `directcheck` (no differences between the server and direct paths) ran on a copy of master with these changes. Checked on 2026-11-03 by a throwaway decoder harness over the `zstd` CLI's frames (levels 1 and 19, no checksum, `--long=27`, two frames, a skippable frame) fed 1, 7, 4,096, 65,536 and 1 MiB bytes at a time, all decoded exactly, with truncation, a bad checksum, `single_frame` over two frames and a mid-frame reset failing as before. Left as they are: `*_explicit` flags beside a configured value (whether a host chose it, a product rather than exclusive states), Claude's `automatic_cache` and `cache_one_hour` (the TTL applies to every cache marker, automatic or not), the flags of Claude's durable `Conversation` and `Cursor` (independent facts in stored checkpoints), and single-flag drop guards, which are already two-state. Nothing a peer, store or model sees changed: the eight SDK crates build natively and for WASM and pass clippy, as does nanocode-tui, and output/hand-wiring's `pool` (Codex over HTTPS) and `claude_pool` ran 200 sessions each against `responses-mock.mjs` with 200 deltas a reply, `claude_pool` also with each event's data split over several `data:` lines ending in CRLF, and `execcheck` gave the same exit codes and output for five commands through the zsh server.
- Avoid magic constants, arbitrary caps, and speculative defensive checks. Limits must come from a real protocol constraint, measured resource requirement, or explicit caller policy; document their source. Surface invalid states instead of hiding them with silent truncation, clamping, or fallback values.
- Work in the main checkout on master and push each completed change directly to master. Never create worktrees or feature branches. Commit only your own changes and leave other dirty or untracked files alone; if a push is rejected, rebase onto origin/master, resolve conflicts and push again.
- Hosts that drive a root agent themselves (`without_subagent_continuation`) wait for its subagents with `SubagentControl::running(root)`, the pending, running or closing ones, and `RunningSubagents::next_completion(timeout)`, which is woken by the registry's change notifications rather than polling and returns the first to complete, fail or be interrupted with its `completion_continuation_prompt` (`None` once all are closed, or on timeout); `SubagentControl::stop_all(root, timeout)` interrupts them as `cancel_all` does and says whether they stopped in time (`None` when none is pending, running or closing: the root started none, or every one already ended, so a call still running is the root's own and the host need not treat the turn as interrupted). `RunSteered` carries the `message_id` a host steered with (`steer_with_id`), as both backends already emitted, so a host knows which messages a pass read instead of counting `run.steered` events. `nanocode_types_core::events::AssistantText` folds streamed assistant deltas and final messages into each message's text so far, keyed by item ID or `model-<model_call_index>`, and `AssistantTextUpdate::delta` is the text a streamed delta added (`None` for a complete message), so a host that persists or forwards incremental text appends it instead of copying the whole message on every delta, which tempoxyz/pyramid's PR 219 did, quadratic in the message's length. `UsageRecord` (`UsageRecord::new(model, &TurnUsage)`, `From<&RunTerminal>`, `TurnResult::usage_record`) is one turn's or run's tokens and cost under its model. tempoxyz/pyramid's engine used to poll `agents()` every 500 ms, count steers, key and append deltas, and map both usages itself.
- Image eviction boundaries take precedence over optional Claude prefix markers (2026-11-10). A custom system prompt on the subscription wire used all four protocol cache breakpoints for tool, system, identity and automatic tail, so the production prefix-first allocator left no image boundary; its zero-spare guard could not even reclaim a system slot. The production request now marks image floors first and then adds optional system/tool boundaries only within the final wire budget, including the subscription identity. The existing prefix API retains its reserve-one policy; the floors-first API can use all remaining slots. Invalid over-budget layouts are errors rather than saturating to zero. The previous image floor excludes the latest image-bearing message rather than the last two history messages, so an image-free text tail cannot erase the boundary needed when eviction advances. output/cache-budget-v1 compares authentic pinned full upstream tools/system blocks and production HistoryMessage, image eviction and prepare_cached_wire: 168 baseline and 168 candidate requests over default/custom systems, API/subscription wire, top-level/tool-result images, image-free tails, 11-image bursts and no-image controls. All 147 candidate image-bearing requests carry every requested floor and all 168 requests stay within four markers; custom subscription baseline has no floors in 84 requests. At the thirteenth ordinary image read the prior unchanged message prefix is explicitly cached through message 129 (custom tool) or 124 (top-level), instead of no message-prefix boundary; with an image-free tail it is message 105. These are offline wire observations, not measured server cache hits. Commands: CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/home/ubuntu/nanocode-eval/repo/output/cache-prefix-repro-v1/target cargo run --offline --locked --manifest-path output/cache-budget-v1/{baseline,candidate}-harness/Cargo.toml -- output/cache-budget-v1/{baseline,candidate}; python3 output/cache-budget-v1/analyze.py; cargo check --locked --offline --lib -p nanocode-backend-claude -p nanocode-backend-claude-client, again with --target wasm32-unknown-unknown (passed); git diff --check (passed). No live inference in this repair validation.
- On Linux every TLS verifier shares one parsed copy of the system trust roots (2026-11-10). reqwest 0.13 builds a `rustls-platform-verifier` `Verifier` for each client, and the vendored verifier called `rustls_native_certs::load_native_certs()` in each, which reads `/etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt` and every file in `/etc/ssl/certs` and parses them all: one `nc exec` opened 2,420 files under `/etc/ssl/certs` (ten loads of 241 entries) and read the bundle 20 times, and PEM base64 decoding was the largest user-space cost in a profile of it. `verification::others::system::roots` keeps the parsed `RootCertStore` in an `ArcSwapOption` keyed on `SSL_CERT_FILE` and `SSL_CERT_DIR` and reloads it after 300 s, the age `nanocode_tls` already uses; the crate exports it as `system_roots`, and the sandbox's egress `Tls::new` takes its roots from it instead of loading them again, so a process loads them once. Interleaved on an AMD EPYC 4245P (Ubuntu 24.04, bench/cli on the cli-bench branch: `suite.mjs --parts=firstframe,oneshot --rounds=30` under `tools/netguard.sh`, release builds of 5aa3971ee with and without the change, 2026-11-10): a one-shot `nc exec --ephemeral` took 8.96 ms instead of 18.9 (CPU 9.9 ms instead of 22.0, spawn to request 6.7 ms instead of 16.9), and the terminal interface drew its first frame in 4.99 ms instead of 7.96 (CPU 12.2 ms instead of 23.7); `--version` did not change.
- `nc exec` flushes stdout whenever it has written every event already delivered, instead of at most once per display frame (2026-11-10). `stream_turn` still takes every queued event with `Turn::try_next` before one flush, so under load deltas share a write; at low rates each delta goes out as it arrives. The 60 Hz pacing (entry above) made each token wait 8 to 10 ms on average and 16 to 18 ms at p99 between the fixture writing it and stdout showing it, where fx, pi and Claude Code show it in 0.01 to 0.03 ms. Interleaved on an AMD EPYC 4245P (bench/cli `sweep.mjs --mode=cli --rates=100,1000,10000 --samples=10` under `tools/netguard.sh`, release builds, 2026-11-10): per-token lag p50 0.015, 0.010 and 0.008 ms at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 tok/s instead of 10.0, 8.0 and 8.3 (p99 0.04, 0.012 and 0.010 instead of 18, 16 and 16.5), whole-run CPU 268 ms instead of 251 at 10,000 tok/s (5.4 µs per token instead of 5.0), with the trust-root change also in the new build.
- The terminal interface paces streamed text at 120 Hz (`app::DISPLAY_FRAME` 8.333 ms) instead of 60 Hz (2026-11-10). At 60 Hz a token waited half a frame on average before it reached the screen, so nc trailed Codex and pi on on-screen lag at 1,000 tok/s while leading on CPU. Interleaved on an AMD EPYC 4245P (bench/cli `sweep.mjs --mode=tui --rates=100,1000,10000 --samples=10`, 120x40 PTY replayed through pyte, under `tools/netguard.sh`, release builds of 0fbd0054a with each pace, 2026-11-10): on-screen lag p50 0.12, 4.1 and 3.1 ms at 100, 1,000 and 10,000 tok/s instead of 7.1, 7.4 and 8.1 (p99 0.25, 8.3 and 8.5 instead of 16), against Codex 5.5 and pi 7.7 at 1,000 and fx 22 at 10,000; whole-session CPU 71, 119 and 592 ms instead of 57, 103 and 561 (fx 48, 217 and 2,452), and terminal bytes per token 58.6 instead of 32.8 at 10,000 tok/s.
- Code Mode's `image()` takes an array of image items, and the exec description says how to show an image file (2026-11-10, Georgios on the nanocode.xyz demos, where a Python chart saved as a PNG never reached the chat: "it should be able to plot direct things from python ... with the image tool in code mode no?"). Claude's `Read` returns an image file as an array of `{ image_url, detail }` items and `image()` refused arrays, so Haiku 5.5 base64-encoded the PNG through `Bash` instead, whose nested output stops at `NESTED_STREAM_BYTES` (128 KiB): the data URL ended early and the image became `image content omitted because it could not be processed`. `image(array)` now appends each item, after checking them all, and refuses an empty array. When the cell's tools include `Read` or `view_image`, the description adds a Nanocode extension line: `image(await tools.Read({ file_path }))` (or `tools.view_image({ path })`) shows an image file, and a shell's base64 is cut off. Checked on 2026-11-10 with nanocode-ts's module built on this tree (its `output/image-check.ts`, a scripted model and the nanocode-ts shell): `image(await tools.Read(...))` of an 1800×1200 PNG reached the next Claude request as an image block, `image(await tools.view_image(...))` reached Codex as `input_image`, each request's exec description carried its harness's line, and the `Bash` base64 path still came back 131,072 characters long with `truncated: true` and the placeholder. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-code-mode`, also for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, passed.
- A `Tools` set with `ToolExposure::DirectOnly` now reaches the model as plain function tools, without Code Mode's `exec` and `wait` (2026-11-11). The Codex and Claude backends set `CodeModeOnly` on every tool set they built, which overwrote a caller's exposure, and `model_specs` always put `exec` and `wait` first. The backends now keep the exposure the caller chose (the default is still `CodeModeOnly`), and `DirectOnly` drops `exec` and `wait`. `crates/nanocode/examples/nc_lite.rs` is nanocode cut down to what fx ships, for the CLI benchmark: one harness (Codex), any model through the AI Gateway, plain function tools, a JSONL session store, `exec`, `--continue` and `sessions`, and no TUI, MCP, computer use or runners. Measured against bench/cli's fixture on one machine, five interleaved runs each (2026-11-11): its first request is 36.9 KB instead of 45.3 KB (12 function tools, 15.0 KB, instead of a 20 KB `exec` and `wait`, against fx's 30 KB request with 16 tools), the request at step 50 of a shell turn is 55.0 KB instead of 67.0, and wall time for 10 and 50 steps did not change beyond noise (median 148 against 159 ms, and 672 against 686). The release `nanocode` CLI still advertises only `exec` and `wait`. `cargo check --locked --lib` of nanocode-tool-host, nanocode-backend-codex and nanocode-backend-claude passed for native and `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- A JSONL home keeps each record at least one filesystem block long once, in `records/<blake3>`, and a session file holds a reference to it (2026-11-11). Every session wrote its own copy of the system prompt and tool catalog, the same 33 KB for nc-lite and 53 KB for nanocode in each session, while a resumed session rebuilds its prompt from the running binary's configuration anyway (a nc-lite session resumed with `open_session` before this change sent Codex's 18 KB prompt rather than the one it was created with). fx stores neither; this keeps exact replay and pays for them once per home. `shared.rs` writes a new record to a temporary file, syncs it and renames it without replacing (an existing name is the same content), then syncs the directory, so the reference is never durable before the record. A value below the block size stays inline, and one that starts with the marker (U+0002) is escaped by doubling it; reading checks the content against its name. When a session written before this change commits a record it already holds, the journal compares the decoded values, so old sessions resume (checked: a session written by 9f373a4b9 resumed twice by the new build). Measured on the bench fixture (2026-11-11): a one-turn nc-lite session is 8.9 KB instead of 42.7 KB of file (13.6 KB instead of 52 KB by `du -k`), and a nanocode one is 14.0 KB instead of 68.1 KB, with 37 KB and 53 KB of shared records once per home; 50 saved nc-lite sessions took 18 ms each. What remains per session is nanocode's own state: the environment context stored in both the head record and the history, the permissions text, usage, and the payload written again on every commit. An older build cannot read a record moved to `records/`. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, also for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, passed.
- nc-lite is its own crate, `bin/nc-lite`, built from the SDK with what fx ships and no more (2026-11-11): one harness (Codex), any model through the AI Gateway, plain function tools, a JSONL home, `exec`, `--continue`, `sessions`, and an inline terminal interface. Its system prompt is fx's (`prompt.md`, adapted under Apache-2.0 as `NOTICE` says: the name, and the lines about skills, context-update blocks and fx's own docs, which nc-lite lacks, are removed), set on the runtime builder so a resumed session gets it too. Its first request is 23.9 KB instead of 36.9 KB with Codex's prompt, against fx's 26 to 30 KB; 15 KB of it is the tool catalog. The interface (`tui.rs`, `markdown.rs`) draws its header before building the runtime, streams each delta as it arrives and restyles a line as Markdown once it is complete, and reads keys on an owning thread that forwards them to one select loop. On the Hand against the fixture, preliminary: first frame 8 to 19 ms against fx's 10 to 13, idle CPU 0.63 ms/s against 6.86, key echo p50 0.21 ms against 1.1, RSS after the first frame 15 MB against 8.8, and the screen 4.7 to 5.3 ms behind the server's last token at 50,000 tokens/s. Its dist binary is 26.9 MB against fx's 12.8.
- A session a CLI is done with is archived: compacted, then stored as `<id>.jsonl.zst`, one format byte and a zstd frame (level 1) against a dictionary built into the binary (`session.dict`, 41.6 KB: compacted nanocode and nc-lite sessions), and the summaries cache is `.summaries.json.zst` (2026-11-11). After shared records (above), a one-turn session was still 7 to 9 KB, mostly template text (permissions, environment context, field names), revisions the journal no longer needs, and hex hashes; the dictionary carries the template, compaction drops the revisions, and zstd packs the rest. `JsonlStore::archiver` returns a handle whose `archive()` compacts and archives every session this process wrote; nc-lite and nanocode call it after `Runtime::shutdown`, after listing once so the summaries cache holds the session, and the cache entry follows the file (compaction's rename, then the archive), so listing never opens an archive. Opening an archived session restores `<id>.jsonl` first (decompress to a temporary file, rename without replacing, remove the archive), so the journal's format and its multi-process rules are unchanged while a session is in use; a session restored only to be read is archived again. Archiving checks that the file did not change while it was read, but a second process writing the same session at that moment can fail with a missing file instead of a fence (eight concurrent `--continue` runs on one session: six fenced, as before, and two missing-file errors); concurrent writers to one session were already refused. `session.dict` belongs to format 1 and must not change; a new dictionary needs a new format byte. Measured on the bench fixture (2026-11-11): 100 one-turn nc-lite sessions take 837 bytes each in `sessions/` (archives and summaries) plus 19.8 KB of shared records per home, against 8.9 KB before this change and 42.7 KB before shared records; nanocode's take 661 bytes plus 52.8 KB (68 KB at the start of the day); a 10-step tool turn is 1.6 KB; fx keeps 2.6 KB per one-turn session. Each archive still occupies a filesystem block, so `du -k` counts 4 KB a session. A save took 35 ms instead of 18 on a loaded Hand with slow fsync (compaction, two summary writes and the archive add four fsyncs). Old homes (plain sessions, `.summaries.json`) open and migrate. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-store-jsonl`, also for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, passed.
- nc-lite links only the crates it runs (2026-11-11). `bin/nc-lite` depends on `nanocode-agent`, `nanocode-agent-host`, `nanocode-backend-codex`, `nanocode-durability`, `nanocode-store-jsonl` and `nanocode-tool-runtime` instead of the `nanocode` facade, and composes `nanocode_agent::Runtime<nanocode_agent_host::Defaults<CodexHarness, CodexHarness>>` itself. The facade's `Defaults` names `ClaudeHarness`, which links the Claude driver, client and tools (1.7 MiB of the dist build's 21.2 MiB of text by `cargo bloat --crates`), and its default `cua` feature links `nanocode-computer` with zbus, AT-SPI and x11rb; nc-lite uses neither. This adds no Cargo feature (AGENTS.md allows only `local-cells`) and changes no library crate. Codex fills the second slot: `default_backends` adds nothing once `.openai()` registered the codex backend, and the format registry replaces a format of the same family, so it is registered once. Measured on the Hand (5 cores, Linux 6.18) with the cli-bench harness (`suite.mjs --parts=startup,firstframe,oneshot,disk --rounds=10`, medians), dist profile, before and after: binary 27,267,368 to 22,209,736 bytes; RSS one second after the first frame 8.00 to 5.97 MB (PSS 7.76 to 5.87, USS 7.68 to 5.80); one-shot peak RSS 18.25 to 16.47 MB. The bench fixture saw the same three requests for a two-step shell task from both builds, byte for byte apart from random chunk IDs and wall times (23,646, 24,844 and 26,042 bytes), and `exec`, the terminal, `sessions` and `--continue` on a JSONL home work. Making QuickJS optional on native was not done: `code_mode::{CellJournals, CellGuard, CodeModeCell, NestedToolCall}` are used under `cfg(not(target_family = "wasm"))` in tool-host, agent-host and the Codex driver, so it needs a feature in each of them; QuickJS is never run by nc-lite, so its pages are not resident, and its share of the dist text is about 1 MiB (code_mode 755 KiB, the engine 125 KiB, rquickjs about 170 KiB).
- nc-lite ships from `--profile lite`: dist with `opt-level = "z"` and identical code folding, still position-independent (2026-11-11). Resident memory of a CLI this size is almost all executable file pages: after a one-shot `exec` of the dist build 12.7 of 19 MB were its `.text` and 1.3 MB were heap. Linux 6.18 maps file pages a 64 KiB folio at a time or more (one byte read per MiB of a cached file adds 64 to 72 KiB of RSS, with `MADV_RANDOM` too), so RSS follows how many folios the code that runs is spread over, and the dist build touched 85% of its text in one `exec`. Each step, same harness and medians (binary bytes; first-frame RSS; one-shot peak RSS): `opt-level = "s"` 15,139,768, 6.49 MB, 14.09 MB; `"z"` 13,887,016, 7.55 MB, 13.22 MB (less inlining spreads the start-up path over more folios, so the first frame costs more while everything else shrinks); `-no-pie` 13,178,344, 6.84 MB, 12.47 MB, which drops 32,257 relative relocations (778 KB of `.rela.dyn` read at every start, and the `.data.rel.ro` pages they dirtied) at the cost of a fixed load address, as fx (static, non-PIE) has; `-Wl,--icf=all` 12,978,952, 7.00 MB, 12.65 MB (200 KB; RSS within noise). One-shot wall time stayed at 128 to 137 ms against 140 ms for the dist build. `bin/nc-lite/build.rs` passes `--icf=all` only for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, whose default linker is rust-lld; other linkers do not take it. fx is 12,814,000 bytes, 8.41 MB after its first frame and 7.36 MB at the end of a one-shot. Shipped without `-no-pie`, which waits on a decision about a fixed load address: rebuilt on master 5a73d5320 with the archive and its dictionary, the lite build is 14,306,136 bytes, 8.31 MB after the first frame (fx 8.57) and 13.88 MB at the end of a one-shot (fx 7.36), medians of 10. Command: `cargo build --locked --profile lite -p nc-lite`.
- nc-lite's hot code can be linked first (2026-11-11). `scripts/nc-lite-symbol-order.py BASE_URL PROMPT` builds `--profile lite` with a link map (`NC_LITE_LINK_MAP`, which leaves the binary byte for byte the same), runs one terminal turn and one `exec` of PROMPT against BASE_URL under valgrind's lackey, maps every superblock it ran to its symbol, and links `target/lite/nc-lite` again with those symbols first (`NC_LITE_SYMBOL_ORDER`, lld's `--symbol-ordering-file`); each build starts from `cargo clean -p nc-lite` because cargo did not relink when only the order file changed. A list is only valid for the build it came from: symbol names carry crate hashes that change with versions, features, the profile (`strip` too) and the compiler, which is why it is generated per build and not committed. Against the bench fixture (`Reply BENCH[run=order]`, 5,718 symbols, about 1.7 MB): first-frame RSS 7.00 to 3.58 MB (PSS 3.51, USS 3.49), one-shot peak 12.65 to 10.11 MB, same size. What still lands outside are folios of code that runs natively but not under valgrind (AVX2 `memchr`, thread wake-ups, timers), each 64 to 384 KiB here; a list from callgrind on a `strip = false` build reached 2.35 MB and 7.3 MB, so a fuller trace is worth more. Needs valgrind and Python 3.
- Measured for nc-lite, not adopted (2026-11-11): mimalloc as its global allocator (as `nc` has) costs 0.8 MB of RSS at the first frame and in a one-shot and 110 KB of binary, since nc-lite's heap is about 1.3 MB; `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=1` and `glibc.malloc.tcache_count=0` save under 0.2 MB; `-z keep-text-section-prefix` moves 140 KB of cold functions and saves 0.06 MB; `MADV_RANDOM` on the text mapping saves nothing, because the kernel maps whole folios.
- `Owned` records where its value was taken and who waits for it, and `nanocode_sync::slow_waits(longer_than)` lists the locks with a wait older than that, each with the first waiter's call site, how many wait and the holder's call site (2026-11-11). On 2026-11-11 a tempoxyz/pyramid turn's Claude run ended (`run.completed`) and its result never reached the host: every thread of the process was idle in gdb, the turn ignored cancellation and its time limit for hours, and nothing said which `.await` it was in; a turn's steering and conversation live behind `Owned`, so a holder that never releases looks exactly like this. `acquire`, `acquire_owned`, `try_acquire` and `try_acquire_owned` are `#[track_caller]`, so `acquire` and `acquire_owned` return `impl Future` instead of being `async fn` (callers that await them are unchanged). Taking the value stores the caller's `Location` in an `AtomicCell` and releasing clears it; a wait that has to queue counts itself on the lock and, as the first waiter, stores its `Location` and start; each `Owned` registers a `Weak` of its record once, in an `Atom` of an `imbl::Vector` pruned of dead entries when its length is a power of two, so waits touch no shared state. The holder's age is not kept: it would put a clock read on every uncontended acquire. If the last waiter leaves while a new one arrives, the record can lose the new waiter's site until the next first waiter. Measured with output/owned-bench (release, 4 tokio workers, six interleaved runs, medians): uncontended `acquire` 45.2 to 53.3 ns, four tasks contending with a yield while holding 1.16 to 1.23 µs per acquire; a first version that kept every wait in a global map took 75 ns and 1.74 µs. `cargo check --locked --workspace --lib` and `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sync` and `-p nanocode-backend-claude` for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` passed.
- A host that holds back the state format also holds back what the Claude backend writes inside it (2026-11-11). `SessionStore::with_state_format` and `SubagentRuntime::set_journal_version` let a host keep writing what its previous build reads while both share one store during a rollout, but the Claude snapshot gained `context` (the kept system context, written after any model request), which a build from before it refuses because `Snapshot` denies unknown fields, and server compaction stores `Compaction` blocks that such a build cannot read. `SharedStore::holds_back_formats` and `DurableSession::holds_back_formats` say whether the store writes an older format than `JournalState::NEWEST_FORMAT`; `ClaudeExecutionPolicy::holds_back_formats` passes it to the agent, which then writes no `context` (so no `instructions` or `template` pages, and no `ToolAddition` or `ToolRemoval` blocks, which only follow a restored context) and summarizes in a prompt instead of by server compaction. A host that writes the newest format sees no change. Checked on 2026-11-11 with a temporary example (`durable_session` over `SqlStore` on Postgres 18) built at this commit and at f4522379, against a mock Messages endpoint: with `with_state_format(8)` the new build ran two turns, the f4522379 build continued the session, and the new build continued after it; without the cap the f4522379 build refused the session with "unknown field `context`". Server compaction was not exercised. `cargo check --locked --workspace --lib`, `cargo clippy --locked --lib` for nanocode-backend-claude, nanocode-durability and nanocode-durability-core, and `cargo check --locked --lib` of nanocode-backend-claude and nanocode-durability for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` passed.
- CLI release builds are laid out by BOLT on Linux: `scripts/build-cli.sh PACKAGE BIN [TARGET]` (`PROFILE`, default dist) builds the binary non-PIE (`-Crelocation-model=static`), with `--emit-relocs` and, for `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` whose linker is rust-lld, `--icf=all`; instruments it with `llvm-bolt -instrument`; runs `scripts/train-cli.py` on the instrumented binary; and relinks it with `-reorder-blocks=ext-tsp -reorder-functions=cdsort -split-functions -split-all-cold -split-eh -icf=all` before stripping it into `target/cli/<target>/<bin>` (2026-11-12). The training script needs only Python 3: it serves the Responses stream from a local server (tools read from the request's `tools` or its `additional_tools` item, an `exec_command` function call or Code Mode `exec` cell per step, then a markdown reply), runs `--version`, `--help`, an ephemeral `exec`, a saved three-step `exec`, `--continue` and `sessions`, then two terminal sessions in a pty (type, submit, wait for the reply, edit keys, quit), and works for both `nanocode` and `nc-lite`. `release-cli.sh` builds the macOS and Linux `nanocode` through it; the Linux container installs `bolt-21` from apt.llvm.org. Other targets build as before, since BOLT reads only ELF. Resident memory of these CLIs is mostly their own code pages (an nc-lite one-shot held 7.3 MB of `.text` and 0.4 MB of heap), and Linux maps them a folio at a time, so what matters is how many folios the code that runs is spread over: BOLT packs everything the training ran into 1.35 MB of `.text` (2.9 MB for nanocode) and moves cold blocks out of hot functions. It replaces nc-lite's `build.rs` and `scripts/nc-lite-symbol-order.py`. Measured on the Hand (5 cores, Linux 6.18) with the cli-bench harness against its fixture, medians of 10 to 15, nc-lite `--profile lite` at 3c16e6c8e: binary 14,806,216 bytes (PIE) / 14,055,456 (non-PIE) / 19,515,824 (BOLT), gzip -9 6.57 / 6.42 / 8.81 MB; RSS after the first frame 8.21 / 6.64 (non-PIE with a function order, below) / 3.44 MB; one-shot peak 13.56 / 12.97 / 7.73 MB; one-shot CPU 10.2 / 7.8 / 8.8 ms; fx 0.0.16 is 12,814,000 bytes (5.65 MB gzip), 8.84 MB after its first frame and 7.73 MB at the end of a one-shot. nanocode dist at the same commit, non-PIE without and with BOLT: 70,450,456 and 82,935,784 bytes (31.9 and 37.2 MB gzip), 24.75 and 15.82 MB after the first frame (18.3 and 15.5 ms to it), one-shot peak 30.73 and 18.18 MB. BOLT costs file size because ring's assembly cannot be moved, so `-use-old-text` (which needs every function rewritten) refuses and the original `.text` and `.eh_frame` stay beside the new copies. Measured and not adopted: PGO (`-Cprofile-use` with `-z keep-text-section-prefix`) reached 5.54 MB and 11.80 MB but grew the binary to 18.65 MB because hot call sites are inlined (4.75 MB of `.text.hot`); an lld `--symbol-ordering-file` from `llvm-profdata order` (temporal instrumentation) kept the size but reached only 6.64 and 12.97 MB, since 4,628 of its 11,870 symbols were inlined or renamed by fat LTO in the final build; `-Cforce-unwind-tables=no` left `.eh_frame` at 1.70 MB. Command: `PROFILE=lite LLVM_BOLT=/usr/lib/llvm-23/bin/llvm-bolt scripts/build-cli.sh nc-lite nc-lite`.
- A CLI that is done with its sessions summarizes only the ones it wrote, and the summaries cache is a journal (2026-11-12). `JsonlArchiver::written()` returns the state IDs of the journals this process touched (each file's own session and the states colocated in it, which is what listing reports), and `SessionStore::summarize(ids)` computes and remembers just those summaries; nanocode and nc-lite call them before `archive()` instead of `SessionStore::list()`, which read, checked and rewrote the summaries of every session in the home on every save. `.summaries` replaces `.summaries.json.zst`: a 4-byte length and one zstd frame of every entry (the same dictionary and format byte as archives), then one JSON line per change, `{"remember":{id: summary}}` or `{"moved":{from, to, length, anchor}}`. A writer appends its line after reading only the length and the last byte, without loading the cache; once the lines would outgrow the frame, or the tail is torn, it loads the cache, applies the change and rewrites the file through a renamed temporary, so the file stays under twice its compacted size. Readers apply the lines in order and, holding the same file, read only what was appended since. It is still a cache checked against each file's identity and length, so a line lost to a concurrent rewrite only costs a later recomputation. Old homes load `.summaries.json.zst` or `.summaries.json` and the first write converts them. Measured on the Hand with nc-lite (release profile with line tables, bench fixture): a save into a home of 1,000 sessions ran 13.2M instructions instead of 197M (callgrind; 57% had been rewriting and recompressing the cache, 32% the shutdown listing), creating the 1,000 sessions took 17.9 s instead of 46.0 s, and the cache took 111 KB instead of 100 KB; with the cli-bench harness at 300 sessions (`suite.mjs --parts=store --sessions=300`), CPU per saved session 8.25 ms instead of 16.22, listing 6.65 ms of CPU instead of 11.00, continuing the latest 15.4 ms instead of 29.7, and 1,602 bytes per session instead of 1,557. Saving, `--continue`, a three-step tool turn, `sessions` and a home with the old cache (1,002 sessions listed after conversion) were checked with nc-lite, and saving, a tool turn, `--continue` and `sessions` with nanocode. `cargo clippy -D warnings` on the changed crates, and `cargo check --lib` for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, passed.
- nc-lite reads an event's `text` and `tool` through a borrowed struct, as nanocode's `stream.rs` does, instead of parsing every payload into a `serde_json::Value` (2026-11-12). That parse was 22% of a headless run's instructions at 10,000 tokens/s (callgrind, 20,000 tokens). Median CPU of five headless runs streaming 50,000 tokens at 10,000 tokens/s (`sweep.mjs --mode=cli --rates=10000 --samples=5`, release profile, the Hand): 582 ms instead of 699, fx 300 to 317 ms on the same machine. Measured and not adopted: building an event payload with `turn_id` by serializing the payload and splicing the field in, instead of `#[serde(flatten)]`, took 317 ns instead of 218 because `RawValue::from_string` validates the result again; the plain payload alone takes 144 ns.
- Clippy 1.99's `chunks_exact_to_as_chunks` and the deprecation of `fetch_update` (renamed `try_update`) failed `cargo clippy -D warnings` in nanocode-python, nanocode-observability and nanocode-subagents; they use `as_chunks` and `try_update`, with the same behavior (2026-11-12).
- A Hand can say what machine it is (2026-11-12). `HandHostInfo` (code-mode `remote`, re-exported from `nanocode` beside `HandEnvironment`) carries OS name and version, kernel, architecture, hardware and CPU model, core count, total and available memory, running programs (name, pid, command line), listening ports (protocol, address, port, process) and Tailscale (running, its own name and addresses, peers with name, addresses, online and OS). Every field is optional and the record rides in the catalog as an optional `host`, so a brain from before it decodes the catalog as before (its `Catalog` ignores fields it does not know) and a catalog from before it decodes with `host: None`. A fresher record comes from `CodeModeHost::host_info`, which sends the new `RemoteOperation::HostInfo` as a call; a hand from before it cannot decode that operation (unknown variant), so the brain sends it only to a hand whose catalog carried a record, as it relies on `tool_selection` and `caches_local_tools` only when the catalog says so, and no frame type was added. The hand collects the record through `ExecutorOptions::host_info`, a `HostInfoSource` closure called for each catalog and each `HostInfo` request; `Hand::host_info(record)` and `Hand::host_info_source(closure)` set it, and a hand with neither reports nothing, as before. `local_host_info()` fills what std reaches on every platform (OS, kernel from uname, architecture, cores). `HandDescription` keeps the catalog's record under `host` without serializing it, so what the hands tool shows the model is unchanged. Lists are a `HandList { items, omitted }`, and `Hand` applies `HostInfoLimits` (caller policy through `Hand::host_info_limits`; by default 500 entries per list and 4,096 bytes per command line, cut at a character boundary) and counts what it cut in `omitted` and `command_line_omitted_bytes` instead of dropping it silently: with 2,000 programs whose command lines are 10 KB, 2,000 listeners and 2,000 peers, the record encodes to 20.5 MB unlimited and the catalog to 2.2 MB limited, against the 64 MiB default frame policy. Checked with a harness in `output/hooks-check` (catalog round trip; a `HandCore` publishing its source's record and answering a `HostInfo` request with a fresher one without reconnecting, and refusing it without a source; the brain asking only a hand that published a record; the limits) and `output/hooks-old` built at 21eec9a9, which decodes the new catalog and cannot decode a `HostInfo` request, while the new build decodes its catalog. Skipping `host` when decoding, or not cutting lists, failed five checks. `cargo check --locked --workspace`, `cargo check --locked --lib` of nanocode-code-mode, nanocode-tool-runtime, nanocode-backend-claude-tools, nanocode-backend-claude and nanocode natively and for `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and `cargo clippy --lib -D warnings` on them passed. Files: `crates/runtime/code-mode/src/remote/{mod,frame,hand}.rs`, `crates/runtime/code-mode/src/embedded/mod.rs`, `crates/integrations/tool-runtime/src/remote/{hand,native,mod}.rs`, `crates/nanocode/src/lib.rs`.
- An embedder can confine a Hand's Claude file tools to its directory (2026-11-12). `ClaudeWorkspaceFiles::machine` roots Read, Edit and Write at the filesystem root and nothing checked a resolved path against the root, so they reach the whole machine; `ClaudeWorkspaceFiles::confined(directory)` roots them at the directory and refuses any path whose canonical form is outside it: absolute paths, `..` escapes and symlinks to outside files or directories, for reading, editing and writing an existing file. Writing a new file checks before creating directories: the nearest existing ancestor of its parent must resolve inside the directory and every component still to be created must be a plain name, so a new file under a symlinked outside directory, through a dangling symlink to outside, or through `..` under a directory that does not exist yet is refused and creates nothing; the created parent is canonicalized and checked again. `HandFiles { Machine, Confined }` picks one in `hand_tools_with` (Claude backend) and `nanocode::hand::{tools_with, connect_with, listen_with}`; `hand_tools`, `tools`, `connect` and `listen` keep `HandFiles::Machine`, so nothing changes unless an embedder asks. Bash and the Codex workspace tools still run commands on the machine, so this confines the file tools, not the Hand. Checked with `output/hooks-check` (`confined` binary, against a temporary tree): inside relative and absolute paths, `..` that stays inside and a symlink that stays inside work for Read, Edit and Write, including new nested directories; `/etc/hosts`, `../x`, a symlink to an outside file and a path under a symlinked outside directory are refused for Read, Edit and Write, as are new files under a symlinked or not-yet-existing parent, and nothing outside changed or appeared; `machine` still reads `/etc/hosts`, `../x` and symlinks and writes under a symlinked directory. With the checks disabled, 17 checks failed (outside files read, edited and written). The same builds and clippy as the entry above passed. Files: `crates/backends/claude/tools/src/tools/workspace_files.rs`, `crates/backends/claude/src/{defaults,lib}.rs`, `crates/nanocode/src/lib.rs`.
- nanocode-tui has `CellKind::Said`, a message from someone shown as chat apps show one, and `Transcript::scroll_to`, and its terminal layer gains the rest of what pyramid-tui used of ratatui and crossterm (2026-11-12, Georgios: "bump Pyramid TUI to utilize them"). pyramid-tui pinned the gakonst/nanocode fork at 2db2cbe5a for `Said`; that commit is cherry-picked here (it applied cleanly over the terminal-layer change), so pyramid-tui depends on nanocodexyz/nanocode. A `Said` has an optional header (none continues the message above as one group), its words as Markdown where a line break stays one (`markdown::render_chat`), an optional bar colour and an optional band on the code background; `scroll_to(index)` scrolls so that cell starts at the top. Added under ratatui's and crossterm's names, as the terminal-layer entry promised callers only change imports: `KeyModifiers::{intersects, difference, set}`, `KeyEventState::empty`, `KeyEvent::{new_with_kind, new_with_kind_and_state}`, `Buffer::{area, set_line}`, `Block::{bordered, style}` (the style fills the area under the borders, as ratatui's did) and `Paragraph::wrap` with `Wrap { trim }`, which wraps each line with the transcript's own `markdown::wrap_spans_with_whitespace` (word-preferring, whitespace kept unless `trim`) rather than porting ratatui's WordWrapper, so a wrapped paragraph breaks where the transcript would. `KeyEvent`'s equality and hash now normalize a shifted ASCII letter as crossterm's did (`a` with SHIFT equals `A` with SHIFT): the derived ones made pyramid-tui's kitty-protocol test and shifted key bindings miss. Kitty's keyboard-flag reply and DECSCUSR cursor shapes stay out: pyramid-tui keeps its own. Checks: `cargo clippy --locked -p nanocode-tui` (no warnings), `cargo check --locked -p nanocode-cli -p nc-lite`, and pyramid-tui's `cargo clippy --all-targets` (no warnings of its own) and `cargo test` (497 passed, 1 ignored) against it.
- A program started on one of the shell's pipes gets the pipe itself when the pipe already holds bytes, as a child of bash does (2026-11-12). `printf '1\n2\n' | while read X; do dd if=/etc/hostname bs=1 count=2 2>/dev/null > "r_$X"; done` wrote `r_1` and ended, where bash writes `r_1` and `r_2`. A pipe between two vprocs is a buffer of the engine; an external started on its read end got an OS pipe only while that buffer was empty (D1068), and otherwise a pump copied whatever the buffer held into a pipe of the program's own, so a program that reads nothing (`dd if=FILE`, `true`, anything given a file) still took every line the loop had not read yet. The same happened to a here-document or here-string that feeds a loop (a preloaded buffer), to `{ read a; program; read b; }`, and, when a program writes the lines, to what `read` had read ahead of its line from the OS pipe and given back to the engine's buffer. `PipeReader::os_end` now makes the pipe an OS pipe whenever a program is started on its read end: what the buffer holds becomes a backlog that goes into the OS pipe in order, as far as it has room, whenever a vproc reads or writes the pipe and while the program runs (`pipe::Feed`, polled by the wait for the program as its pumps are, so a pipe or here-document larger than the OS pipe arrives whole and in order); vproc writes join the backlog while one is left, an external writer gets a pump meanwhile, and the engine lets go of the OS write end once the backlog is gone and no writer is left. `read` takes an OS pipe a byte at a time, as bash takes any pipe, also when the pipe became one while the read waited, so nothing it gives back sits in front of what the next program reads. What a program does read is gone for the loop, as in bash: `printf '1\n2\n3\n' | while read x; do head -n 1; echo got $x; done` prints `2`, `got 1`, `got 3` in both. The cost is bash's: 200,000 lines from a program into `while read X; do :; done` take 0.75 s instead of 0.14 s (bash 5.2: 1.35 s); lines from a utility of psh, which stay in the engine's buffer, take what they took. Not matched: bash keeps a here-document larger than a pipe in a temporary file, in which a program such as `head` seeks back to the end of what it used; psh gives a pipe, from which it takes a block. Tests: three in psh-engine's `tests.rs` on a test host with OS pipes (`TestHost::set_os_pipes`; its pipe holds 4096 bytes, so the backlog is exercised), each also with every host operation pending once; without the change all three fail. Upstream delta: psh-engine pipe.rs, exec.rs, builtins/read.rs, testhost.rs, tests.rs.
- A program started while the shell's stdout or stderr is a file the host cannot give it gets a pipe, and the engine moves the bytes (2026-11-12). A script the hand runs in its own process (nanocode-psh-embedded) has the caller's sinks as stdout and stderr; it starts no program by itself, but a utility that hands an option it does not implement to the program on `PATH` does (`grep -P 'foo(?=1)'` for a look-ahead, `ls` and `stat` for a few options), and the start failed with "not a file of this host". `Host::inherits` says whether a file can be passed as a descriptor (the Unix host: its own files); for one that cannot, `spawn_program` asks for a pipe and the wait pumps it into the file, as it does for a pipe of the engine with bytes in front. Test: psh-engine `a_program_writes_through_a_file_the_host_cannot_give_it` (`TestHost::set_gives_stdio`).
- A utility whose body runs on a thread or through the host reads a process substitution among its arguments (2026-11-12). `grep -c x <(cmd)`, `grep -f <(cmd) file` and `jq . <(cmd)` failed with "/dev/fd/63: No such file or directory": the substitution is a pipe of the engine under one of the shell's descriptors, which `UtilCtx::open` resolves but a blocking body, which opens files itself, cannot. `run_blocking` now reads the engine's pipes that the arguments name as `/dev/fd/N` (alone or after an option's `=`) to their end before the body starts, once per utility run, and `SyncCtx::open` and `stat` answer for them. The whole stream is in memory before the utility sees its first byte; `rg`, which opens its files through the walker, still fails on one (the real `rg` reads it). Tests: psh-utils `tests.rs` (`grep` and `jq` on substitutions).
- `sed -i` starts every file's output afresh, `n` and `N` without a next line end the file and not sed, and a last line without a newline gets one only before more output (2026-11-12). `printf a1 > m1; printf 'b1\n' > m2; sed -i -E 's/1/2/g' m1 m2` left `\nb2\n` in `m2`: the newline that `m1`'s last line lacks is owed to whatever the same output gets next (GNU's rule, kept in `Out::missing`), and the flag survived the change of output from one edited file to the next. `Run::set_sink` clears it. Three more differences from GNU sed 4.9 found by comparing outputs over files with and without a final newline in every position, with and without `-i`, `-s` and `-n`: (1) `n` and `N` on the last line of an input ended sed, so with `-i` or `-s` the files after one with an odd number of lines were not edited (`sed -i 'N;s/\n/+/' a b` left `b` as it was); they now end the cycle as GNU does (printing unless `-n`), which ends that input only. (2) The reader marked a file's unterminated last line as terminated whenever more input followed, so `sed -n '/a/p' a b` and a `w` file got a newline GNU does not write; the line now stays unterminated and the newline is supplied lazily, per output, and `q` supplies it as GNU's does (`sed 1q` on `a1` prints `a1\n`). (3) `addr1,~N` from a line that is a multiple of N matched that line only; GNU goes to the next multiple (`seq 12 | sed -n '4,~4p'`: 4 to 8). Left as it is: on the unterminated last line of a file that is not the last, GNU's `N` ends the cycle instead of joining the next file's first line, and `s//x/` whose empty regex was not yet used at run time is an error in GNU where psh takes the last regex of the script. Tests: four in psh-utils `sed/tests.rs`. Upstream delta: psh-utils sed/exec.rs, sed/tests.rs.
- On a machine a utility that does part of what its program does never answers in the program's place (2026-11-12). In an image without git or python3, `which git` said "git: shell builtin", `git --version` "git version 2.50.1", `git clone URL` and `git ls-remote URL` "network access is not available in this shell (this simulated shell has no git that reaches other repositories)" with status 127 (0 behind `| head`), and `python3 -c 'import urllib.request'` "No module named 'email' (this simulated shell has no processes, sockets or native extensions for Python)"; a model reading that concluded it could fetch nothing and stopped, where bash says "command not found" and the model installs the program. It began when psh became the only shell of the agent's commands (c311bbedb; before it a hand ran the machine's shell): git (ad2cd4318, db71cd78d) and the bundled python3 (fa1d67ef0) were `PathFallback` utilities, which run when `PATH` has no such program. `Mode::SandboxOnly` is new: such a utility runs only where no programs exist (`UtilPolicy::sandbox`: the WebAssembly hosts and nanocode-shell, unchanged) or when `PSH_UTILS_FORCE` names it; on a machine the name is the program `PATH` has or is not found, with status 127, and `type`, `command -v`, `hash` and `which` say so, since all of them ask `util::lookup`. It is the mode of every utility that says of itself that it lacks something its program has: git, python3 and python (no network, processes, sockets or native extensions), tar (plain and gzip archives only), zip and unzip (no encryption, no zip64) and patch (unified diffs only). The `PathFallback` utilities that are the whole of a small program stay as they are and still fill in where the program is missing (gzip, xxd, od, hexdump, strings, base32, tac, rev, fold, expand, unexpand, column, join, shuf, split, expr, factor, envsubst, truncate, sponge, yes, uuidgen, tree, dd, install); node, npm, pip, curl and wget were never utilities of psh (curl and wget are nanocode-shell's, for hosts without a machine). The utilities that shadow a program on purpose (`Mode::Always`: sed, grep, awk, find, xargs, jq and the rest) are unchanged. A stand-in's own refusal already ended with 127, never 0. `psh --utils` shows the mode as X. Tests: psh-engine `a_sandbox_only_utility_never_stands_in_on_a_machine`, psh-utils `a_stand_in_is_not_found_on_a_machine`. Upstream delta: psh-engine util.rs, psh-utils lib.rs and tests_misc.rs, psh utils.rs and lib.rs; nanocode-python psh.rs.
- Four differences between psh's utilities and the GNU ones, found by running the same commands under both, are gone (2026-11-12). output/psh-differential (`harness.mjs`, `corpus.txt`) runs each case of a corpus twice in directories prepared the same way, under psh through a hand's Bash tool (or exec_command, or `psh-shell -c` directly) and under bash 5.2 with GNU coreutils, sed 4.9, grep, findutils, gawk 5.2 and jq, and compares stdout, the exit status and the files left behind (names, kinds, modes, contents); stderr is compared apart. The 108 cases are the loop, sed and missing-program reproductions with their neighbours, the reference solutions of two tasks of an eval suite that the first two defects broke, and commands agents write with grep, find, xargs, tr, cut, sort, uniq, awk, head, tail, wc, cat, tee, cp, mv, rm, ln, ls, stat, du, test, diff, cmp, base64, the checksums, od, date, seq, printf, jq, the shell's own expansions and builtins, and tar, gzip and zip. The hand released at 5f8b457de agreed with bash in 46 of them; with the entries above and this one 106 agree through the Bash tool with and without `--own-processes` and directly, and the two left are the here-document that bash keeps in a file and `find -exec` of a missing program (psh's find ends with 1, GNU's with 0). Through exec_command, whose output is both streams as they arrive, 99 agree as sets of lines; the rest differ in the wording of stderr (`env`, `timeout` and `xargs` say "command not found" for a missing program where GNU's say "No such file or directory", `sed`'s usage text is shorter, no "Killed" line for a job a signal ended). What changed here: (1) `diff <(a) <(b)` failed with "/dev/fd/63: No such file or directory", because diff asked the host for the file's time before reading it; a descriptor of the shell has none and gets the current time. (2) `xargs` ran nothing for input without items, BSD's rule, kept on purpose (D1170); GNU's runs the command once unless `-r` or `-I`, which `echo | xargs echo x` and a pipeline that expects `xargs grep`'s status rely on, and psh's does the same on Linux now (elsewhere as before). (3) awk is gawk for the programs it runs, and a program it cannot compile (`asort`, `asorti`, `isarray`, `typeof`, `patsplit`, arrays of arrays, `@include`) or that names what only gawk acts on (`IGNORECASE`, `BEGINFILE`, `ENDFILE`, `FPAT`, `FIELDWIDTHS`, `PROCINFO`, `SYMTAB`, `FUNCTAB`, `BINMODE`, `ERRNO`, `ARGIND`, `TEXTDOMAIN`, `LINT`, also `-i inplace`) now goes to the program of that name on `PATH` when there is one, which runs it or says what is wrong with it; without one psh's error stands. On a machine whose awk is mawk such a program fails in mawk, as it does under bash. Tests: psh-utils `tests.rs` (xargs), `tests_misc.rs` (diff), `awk/tests.rs` (a fake gawk on the test host's PATH). Upstream delta: psh-utils diff.rs, xargs.rs, awk/mod.rs and their tests.
- Code objects read from marshalled or frozen bytecode keep no per-instruction location table; the interpreter decodes their line table the first time a frame asks (2026-11-13). `CodeObject::locations` held two `SourceLocation`s (16 bytes on wasm32) per code unit, rebuilt by `linetable_to_locations` when marshal deserialized a code object, while `linetable` holds the same positions in CPython's compact form. A baked nanocode-ts `python.wasm` reaches 3,730 code objects and 435,398 code units from its ~50 preimported modules, about 7 MB of locations, a third of its 23.6 MB data section. Marshal now leaves `locations` empty and `marshal::LineTableLocations` iterates the line table with the same results as before (`linetable_to_locations` collects it). `PyCode::location(idx)` answers from `locations` when the compiler filled it, as it does for a script's own code, and otherwise from a table it decodes once per code object and keeps, so a frame that raises often pays once; `CodeObject::all_locations` serves `mark_lines`. Tracebacks, `f_lineno`, line tracing and generator close use it. Measured: nanocode-ts python.wasm at -O2 and baked with the same warm set, 35,153,284 to 27,988,686 bytes (data section 23,645,231 to 16,480,705). Natively (`examples` binary over nanocode-python, `Python::new` then five scripts, 10 interleaved runs on dev-georgios at load ~45, min/median ms): new 9.4/12.8 to 9.0/9.7, `print(1)` 3.9/7.5 to 5.1/8.2, json/re/os/collections/pathlib 39.9/46.5 to 37.6/43.8, importing decimal, inspect, typing, dataclasses, argparse, ast, difflib and traceback 69.6/77.9 to 70.9/76.8, 20,000 `json.loads("x")` errors 211.3/221.9 to 207.3/216.2, 2,000 `traceback.format_exc()` 916.7/1,005.3 to 887.0/1,010.4, and RSS after the run 49.8 to 39.0 MB. Without the kept table, decoding at every traceback entry made the 20,000 errors 233 to 280 ms. Checked: `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-python -p rustpython-codegen` and `-p nanocode-python --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`, and clippy on rustpython-compiler-core, rustpython-vm and nanocode-python, add no warnings.
- `Metered`'s count is one function, not inlined into every allocation (2026-11-13). nanocode-ts's python.wasm installs `Metered<System>` so `Limits::memory` holds on wasm (`held()` answers only under it), and with `count` inlined into each `__rust_alloc` site the code section grew 11,481,245 to 12,595,861 bytes; with `#[inline(never)]` it is 11,545,099 (+64 KB). A dict of 300,000 strings took 309-336 ms against 335-412 ms in three interleaved Node runs on a loaded machine, within its noise.
- The ChatGPT extension's `attach` gets `networkPolicy: {constraints: []}` (2026-11-13). ChatGPT for Chrome 1.26.1102.11740 passes `params.networkPolicy` to its network policy manager, which reads `timeoutMs` from it before anything else, so an `attach` without it failed at once with `attach: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'timeoutMs')` and no browser step ran through the extension (seen on a Pyramid Hand, every `open`). An empty constraint list normalizes to `defaultAction: "allow"` with no rules, which the manager returns on before installing any rule, so a tab is attached as before. Read from the extension's `background.js` as the Chrome Web Store served it on 2026-11-13; not run against a signed-in extension. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-chatgpt-extension` passed.
- `nanocode-sys`'s descriptor passing builds against musl (2026-11-13). `msghdr::msg_controllen` and `cmsghdr::cmsg_len` are `usize` in glibc's libc bindings and `u32` (`socklen_t`) in musl's, so assigning a `usize` failed to compile for `*-unknown-linux-musl` and broke the pyramid-hand release build (aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, E0308 at `unix/mod.rs` 264, 271, 294, 305). Each now converts with `try_into` to the field's type, and the received length goes through `usize::try_from`. `cargo check --locked --lib -p nanocode-sys`, natively and with `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`, passed.
